title: Alerting and on-call
text: Page a human only when users are hurting and a person must act now, and build an on-call rota your team can keep up for years.
body: Ravi is on call for a payments team. His phone rings 23 times on Monday night. "CPU > 80% on db-replica-3." "Disk 85% on worker-7." "Queue length > 1,000." Each alert clears by itself a few minutes later. By 2 a.m. Ravi mutes his phone. He has learned that these alerts never mean anything. At 4:10 a.m., a bad config change makes 12% of card payments fail. There is no alert on failed payments, only on machines. The one CPU alert that fires looks like every other one. The team finds out at 9 a.m. from support tickets. Ravi did nothing wrong. The alerts trained him to ignore them. (This story is made up, but the pattern is common.) Google's SRE book names three kinds of monitoring output . Choose one on purpose for each signal: Page (an alert): wakes a person up. A human must act now, because the problem is happening or about to happen . Ticket: goes to a queue. A human must act, but no harm is done if they act within a few days . Log: nobody needs to look. It is kept for when you debug or investigate later . Google's SRE book says your monitoring answers two questions: "what's broken, and why?" The "what" is the symptom: payments fail, pages are slow. The "why" is the cause: a full disk, a hot CPU, a bad config. Page on symptoms. Use causes to help you debug , for example on dashboards. The Prometheus docs give the same advice: alert on high latency and errors "as high up in the stack as possible" . The book also says, "Every page should be actionable." If a page only needs a fixed, robotic response, it should not be a page . Automate that response instead. The key idea. A person can react with urgency only a few times a day before they get tired . Every useless page spends that attention. Too many useless pages cause alert fatigue, and then real pages get missed. 1. Ask four questions before you add a page The SRE book gives a checklist. Here it is in short : Does it catch something urgent, actionable and visible to users, that nothing else catches? Will I ever ignore it because I know it is harmless? Can I actually do something about it? Is someone else already paged for the same problem? If any answer is wrong, make it a ticket, a dashboard, or delete it. 2. Page on SLO burn rate You already know SLOs and burn rate from Observability and SLOs. A burn-rate alert is the best symptom alert, because it measures user pain directly. A good alert has high precision (few false pages) and high recall (few missed problems). It should also fire fast and stop fast after the fix . One window cannot do all four. So the SRE Workbook uses a multiwindow, multi-burn-rate design. Each rule fires only when a long and a short window both pass the same burn rate . For a 99.9% SLO over 30 days, it recommends : Long window Short window Burn rate Budget spent Action 1 hour 5 minutes 14.4 2% Page 6 hours 30 minutes 6 5% Page 3 days 6 hours 1 10% Ticket Check the first row yourself. One hour is 1/720 of 30 days. At burn rate 14.4, one hour spends 14.4 ÷ 720 = 2% of the budget. In error terms, 14.4 × 0.1% = 1.44% of requests failing. The short window is 1/12 of the long one . It makes the alert stop about 5 minutes after the errors stop, not an hour later . Step through a fast, a slow and a tiny burn. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. The cost is many numbers to manage . Our advice: put them in shared recording rules, not in every team's copy. With very low traffic, one failure is a large share of requests. The Workbook suggests four fixes: synthetic traffic, combining small services for alerting, changing the product so one failure matters less, or a lower SLO or longer window . 3. Group, route and silence One broken network link can fire hundreds of alerts at once. Prometheus Alertmanager can group them by labels such as cluster and alertname, so you get one page, not hundreds . It also has inhibition: if a "cluster not reachable" alert fires, it can mute every other alert for that cluster. Silences mute alerts for a set time, for example during planned work . The routing tree sends each alert to a receiver, such as PagerDuty for pages or email for less urgent alerts . By default, Alertmanager waits 30 seconds to gather a new group, 5 minutes before it sends updates to that group, and 4 hours before it repeats a notification . Use a severity label to route. PagerDuty's own scheme has High (act now, any hour), Medium (act within 24 hours, work hours only), Low, and Notification, which never pages anyone . 4. Make each alert useful at 3 a.m. PagerDuty says alerts with generic titles cause confusion. Each alert should say what is wrong and why it matters. It should also list the steps or link to a runbook . Prometheus adds: link to a console that shows which part is at fault . Test every new alert. PagerDuty says, "An untested alert is equivalent to not having an alert at all" . Also check that the alert resolves by itself when the metric is normal again . 5. Design the rota Google caps on-call at 25% of an SRE's time, and operations work in total at 50% . Say two people are always on call, a primary and a secondary, in week-long shifts. Then one site needs at least eight engineers, so each one is on call one week in four. With two sites, Google suggests at least six per site . Two sites far apart can run follow-the-sun. Each team covers its own day, so nobody works night shifts, which harm health . Set a load limit. Google aims for at most 2 incidents per 12-hour shift. A real incident, with its cleanup and postmortem, takes about 6 hours . The book's example targets for overload are fewer than 2 paging events per shift and fewer than 5 tickets a day. Noisy alerts should be tuned toward one alert per incident . Typical response times at Google are 5 minutes for user-facing services and 30 minutes for less urgent ones . PagerDuty recommends a 5-minute timeout before a page goes to the backup. It says you sometimes cannot answer in time, and that is why there is a backup . At handoff, tell the next person about issues that are still open . Pay for it. Google gives time off or cash for on-call hours, capped at a share of salary . Rota design Night pages? People needed Main risk One site, primary only Yes Fewer. No backup when the primary misses a page. Burnout. One site, primary and secondary Yes At least 8 for 25% on-call . Night shifts still hurt sleep and health. Two sites, follow-the-sun No, if the sites cover the clock. At least 6 per site . Handoffs between sites lose context. Everyone on call, no rota Yes Whole team. Nobody owns the page, so everyone waits for someone else. On-call too rare (big team, few pages) Few. Many. People forget the system. Google calls this underload . Count two numbers every week: pages per 12-hour on-call period, and pages per real incident. A week-long rota has 14 such periods. Compare them with Google's numbers: fewer than 2 pages per shift, and close to 1 alert per incident . Hold a short review after each shift. For each page ask: was it real, did it need a human, was the runbook right? Then fix, downgrade or delete the alert. Delete alerts and dashboards nobody uses. Google says rarely used alerting is "up for removal" . Turn repeat noise into work. PagerDuty says an alert that keeps firing for a preventable non-issue, like a disk filling up, should become a fix task . Many teams call this toil. Runbooks and reducing toil covers it. Monitor your monitoring. Prometheus suggests alerts on Alertmanager itself and an outside blackbox check . At GitLab in 2017, backup failures were sent only by email. The emails were rejected because of an email setting (DMARC), so nobody knew the backups were failing . Give the person who was up all night the morning off. "Here is our Alertmanager config and the last 30 days of alerts as CSV. Group the alerts by name. For each, show how often it fired, how often someone acted, and whether it is a symptom or a cause. Suggest which to delete or downgrade to a ticket." "Write Prometheus alert rules for a 99.9% checkout SLO. Use the SRE Workbook's three multiwindow rules. Page at 14.4 over 1 h and 5 m, and at 6 over 6 h and 30 m. Open a ticket at 1 over 3 d and 6 h. Add a runbook_url and summary annotation to each." What to ask the agent The burn-rate thresholds match your SLO. For 99.9%, a burn rate of 14.4 is an error rate of 1.44%. For 99.5%, the same burn rate is 7.2%. Both windows in each rule use the same burn rate. Every page has a runbook link that really opens, and the runbook names real commands and dashboards. group_by labels make sense. Grouping by too little merges unrelated problems; grouping by too much sends hundreds of pages. The agent did not add new cause alerts (CPU, disk) as pages. What to check yourself Before this: Observability and SLOs explains SLIs, error budgets and burn rate. Next: Incident response covers what to do after the page. Runbooks and reducing toil covers how to write runbooks and remove repeat work. Related: Debugging production goes from a symptom to a cause. Safe deploys shows how to watch alerts during a rollout.

title: API gateways and edge concerns
text: An API gateway does the shared work for every request at the edge. Learn what belongs there, what does not, and how to stop it taking everything down.
body: This is a real incident, retold from Google's official report. Google and Google Cloud APIs are served through an API management layer. For each incoming API request, it checks that the request is authorized and within policy and quota. The core program that does these checks is called Service Control. It is a regional service, and it sits in the request path of each API call that comes in. On June 12, 2025, a policy change with blank fields was copied to every region within seconds. A new quota check in Service Control read the blank fields and crashed, again and again, in every region. API requests got 503 errors around the world. So one shared check, in front of everything, took down many Google Cloud products at once. Engineers found the cause within 10 minutes and finished turning the check off within 40 minutes. One of the larger regions, us-central1, took up to about 2 hours 40 minutes to recover fully. Among Google's fixes: make Service Control fail open, so a failing check does not block API requests. And copy global data changes in stages, with time to catch problems. The code-level story (no error handling, no feature flag) is in Error handling and defensive design. The lesson for you: the layer that every request passes through is also the layer that can stop every request. See the incident. An API gateway is one front door for many services. Clients call one address. The gateway does the shared work, then sends each request to the right service. Without it, every service must do its own TLS, token checks, rate limits and logging. With it, you do those once, in one place. Microsoft calls this "offloading" shared jobs to the gateway. The key idea. Put shared, generic work in the gateway: checks that are the same for every service. Keep business rules in the services. The gateway must be as boring and as reliable as possible, because everything depends on it. What a gateway does A request passes through the gateway's steps in order. A cheap check that fails stops the request before any expensive work. TLS termination. The gateway decrypts the request. Microsoft's guidance is to then open a new TLS connection to the backend, not plain HTTP. Authentication. Check the token or API key. See Authentication and authorization. Rate limiting. Reject clients that send too much. For example, as of October 2026, AWS API Gateway's default limit is 10,000 requests a second per account and Region. A token bucket allows bursts of up to 5,000 requests. Some newer Regions have lower defaults. See Rate limiting. Request validation. AWS API Gateway can check that required parameters exist and that the body matches a JSON schema. A bad request gets a 400 error at once, so your backend never sees it. Routing. Send /orders to the orders service and /search to search, by URL, header, IP or port. Transformation. Rewrite headers, redirect an old URL to a new one, or add a correlation ID for logs. Observability. Log and measure every request in the same way, even for services that are not well instrumented. Step through one request. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Gateway, load balancer or service mesh? These three overlap, and one product can play several roles. Ask what each one knows. A load balancer spreads requests across copies of one service. It knows about servers and their health. See Load balancing. An API gateway sits at the edge, in front of many services. It knows about APIs: keys, users, plans, routes and versions. A service mesh handles calls between your own services. It uses proxies, often one next to each service. It adds things like mutual TLS, traffic control and metrics without app code changes. Istio is one mesh, and it is built on the Envoy proxy. See Service mesh and sidecars. Backend for frontend A mobile app and a desktop website often need different data. One shared backend that serves both gets pulled in two directions. The backend-for-frontend (BFF) pattern gives each interface its own small backend. Sam Newman says a BFF is usually owned by the same team as the user interface. His guide is "one experience, one BFF". Expect some duplicated code across BFFs; Microsoft lists that as a likely cost. Microsoft's worked example puts one gateway in front for shared checks, with a BFF for each client behind it. See GraphQL and backend-for-frontend. Keep business logic out Microsoft's advice is short: never offload business logic to the gateway. If the gateway holds rules for one service, each change to that service can force a gateway redeploy. If the gateway team releases more slowly, it becomes a bottleneck for every other team. A good test: would this logic be the same for every service? Token checks, yes. "Refunds over ₹10,000 need a manager", no. A single point of failure, and a bottleneck Every request passes through the gateway, so it can become a single point of failure and a bottleneck. Microsoft says to plan for that, and to load test it. Run several instances, size them for peak bursts, not the average, and drain them when you restart. Three more traps from the same guide. Bypass. If clients can call a backend directly, they skip auth and limits. Let backends accept traffic only from the gateway. Forged identity. Do not treat an unverified forwarded header as proof of who the caller is. The gateway must also prove its own identity to the backend. Extra latency. Each hop and each check adds time. Measure it. Decide in advance what each check does when it fails. Google plans to make Service Control fail open. Our advice: a broken rate limiter can fail open, but a broken token check must fail closed. Versioning at the edge The gateway can send /v1 and /v2 to different versions of a service. It can also shift traffic to a new version step by step. If the new version is bad, you roll back with a config change, and clients do not notice. See API versioning. Timeouts and retries at the edge The gateway gives up on slow services. Envoy's route timeout defaults to 15 seconds. It covers the wait for the complete response from the service. On AWS API Gateway, as of October 2026, a REST API's integration timeout is 50 milliseconds to 29 seconds by default. Regional and private APIs can ask for more. Our advice: set the gateway's timeout a little longer than the service's own timeouts. Otherwise the service keeps working after the client is gone. A gateway can also retry. In Envoy, all retries fit inside the overall request timeout. To avoid retry storms, Envoy's docs prefer retry budgets. A retry budget limits the share of active requests that can be retried. Only retry requests that are safe to run twice. See Idempotency, retries and timeouts. Option What you get What it costs Use it when No gateway No extra hop. Nothing shared to fail. Every service repeats TLS, auth, limits and logs. One or two services. One shared gateway Shared checks in one place, one public address. A single point of failure and a team that can become a queue. Many services, one kind of client. Gateway plus BFFs Each client gets an API shaped for it. More services to run. Some duplicated code. Mobile and web need different data. Gateway plus service mesh The same controls for traffic between services. A proxy next to every service, and more to learn. Many services calling each other. Our simple rule: keep the gateway thin and generic. Add BFFs or a mesh only when you feel the pain they fix. For every new gateway rule, ask: "Is this the same for every service?" If not, it goes in the service. Know what happens when each gateway check fails. Write "fail open" or "fail closed" next to it. Treat gateway config like code. Review it, test it and roll it out in stages, as Google now plans to do with global data. Line up timeouts from the outside in: client, then gateway, then service, then database. Each inner one is shorter. Watch gateway latency and error rate per route. A slow gateway makes every service look slow. Make sure backends cannot be called around the gateway. "Read our gateway config. List every route with its upstream, timeout, retry policy and auth rule. Flag any route that retries a POST without an idempotency key." "Here is a gateway plugin we wrote. Point out any business logic in it that should move into a service, and explain why." "Write a test plan for our gateway: kill one instance under load, make the token service slow, and send a request with a forged user header. Say what users should see in each case." What to ask the agent The agent did not invent config keys. Check them against the docs for your gateway. Retries are only on idempotent calls, and they sit inside the overall timeout. Auth checks fail closed. Only checks like rate limits fail open, and that choice is written down. The gateway's timeout is longer than the service's own timeouts. Any new header that carries identity is set by the gateway and cannot come from the client. What to check yourself Read the Netflix Zuul case about moving a gateway to async I/O. Related lessons: REST API design, Backoff and jitter and Circuit breakers and bulkheads.

title: API versioning and deprecation
text: What really breaks a client, how to change an API without breaking it, and how to retire an old version on purpose.
body: Stripe's API moves money for many businesses. Once a business connects its code, it expects that code to keep working for years. A Stripe engineer compared the API to a power grid or water supply: after you hook it up, it should run without interruption. In a 2017 post, Stripe gave an example of a change that would break that promise. A bank account had a true/false field called verified. Suppose Stripe replaced it with a text field called status. Every client that read verified would break, "because it depends on a field that no longer exists." Stripe still needed to make changes like that. By 2017 it had made "almost a hundred backwards-incompatible upgrades" in six years. It also said it had kept compatibility with every version since the company started in 2011. How do you change an API a hundred times and still not break code written years ago? That is what this lesson is about. Stripe's answer used dated versions and a translation layer. You will see both, plus the cheaper habit that should come first. A breaking change is any change that makes a working client fail or behave wrongly. REST API design covered the obvious ones: removing, renaming or retyping a field. The surprising ones are changes in behaviour. Hyrum Wright put it this way: with enough users, "all observable behaviors of your system will be depended on by somebody." That is Hyrum's law. Your docs do not decide what is breaking. Your users' code does. So you have three tools, in this order: Additive change first. Add new fields and endpoints next to the old ones. Nothing breaks. Versions when you must break something. Old clients keep the old contract. Deprecation and sunset to retire an old version on purpose, with dates and data. The key idea. A version is a promise you have to keep running. Add instead of change, version only when you must, and switch an old version off only when your logs show nobody is left. The surprising breaking changes Google's AIP-180 names three kinds of compatibility. Old code must still compile, still talk to the server, and still get "what most reasonable developers would expect." The third kind hides most surprises. New enum values. You add refunded to a status field. AIP-180 warns that user code may not handle new values gracefully. GitHub's GraphQL docs call this a "dangerous" change: queries still work, but clients may behave differently. An old switch with no default case may crash or do nothing. Tighter validation. AIP-180 gives an example: if name formats become stricter, a request that used to succeed now fails. Changed defaults. A client that never sent a page size silently gets a different result. AIP-180 says changing a default value is breaking and must not be done. New required inputs. New required fields must not be added to existing requests. New error codes. Microsoft's guidelines say not to add new top-level error codes without a new version. Rules differ between companies. GitHub's REST docs list adding an enum value as additive, and removing one as breaking. Microsoft says a new enum value can be handled with an extensible enum, and removing a value breaks customer code. Our advice: tell clients in your docs to expect new values and to handle unknown ones. Additive change first Most changes do not need a version. Stripe says it is safe to add a new endpoint, or a new field that was never there before. To "rename" a field, add the new one and keep sending the old one. This is expand and contract at the API level. Additive change only works if clients ignore fields they do not know. Say this in your docs, and test it in your own SDKs. Versioning schemes When you must break something, you need a way for each client to ask for the old contract. URL path, like /v2/orders. Easy to see and to route in an API gateway. But each new major version forces every client to move. Query parameter. Azure requires api-version on every call, as a date like 2021-06-04. It returns 400 if the value is missing or unknown. It also says not to put a version in the path. Header with a date. GitHub's REST API reads X-GitHub-Api-Version. Without it, you get 2022-11-28. Old versions are supported for 24 months after a newer one ships. Dated version pinned to the account. In its 2017 design, Stripe pinned an account to the newest version on its first request. A client could override it per call with the Stripe-Version header. Since 2024-09-30.acacia, monthly versions have no breaking changes. Breaking changes come in two major releases a year. No versions (GraphQL). A GraphQL server returns only the fields a query asks for, so adding fields breaks nobody. That is why GraphQL APIs are usually versionless. You mark old fields with the built-in @deprecated(reason: ...) directive. GitHub announces GraphQL breaking changes at least three months ahead, and makes them only at the start of a quarter. The translation layer Many versions can mean many copies of the code. Stripe avoided that. Each breaking change lives in one small version change module: docs, a transformation, and the resource types it touches. The core code builds every response in the newest shape. Then the layer walks back through the modules, newest first, until it reaches the client's version. Step through it. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. A tiny version of the idea: // Newest first. Each module knows how to undo its own change. const changes = [ { version: "2025-03-01", undo: (c: any) => { c.email = c.emails[0] ?? null; delete c.emails; } }, { version: "2024-06-01", undo: (c: any) => { c.verified = c.status === "verified"; delete c.status; } }, ]; export function render(body: any, clientVersion: string) { for (const ch of changes) { if (ch.version > clientVersion) ch.undo(body); // ISO dates sort as strings } return body; }Changes that do more than reshape a response are harder. Stripe marks such a module has_side_effects. Its transformation then does nothing, and other code checks whether the change is active for this request. Stripe tries to avoid them. Every version is "more code to understand and maintain." Do not forget webhooks. Stripe renders webhook events in the endpoint's version, or the account default. To upgrade, you create a second endpoint on the new version and move over. Deprecation and sunset Two response headers tell clients what is coming. Deprecation: @1767225599 Sunset: Thu, 31 Dec 2026 23:59:59 GMT Link: <https://api.example.com/docs/v1-retirement>; rel="deprecation"Deprecation comes from RFC 9745. Its value is a Unix timestamp after @. A past date means "already deprecated", a future date means "will be". A rel="deprecation" link points to human docs. Sunset comes from RFC 8594. It says when the resource will likely stop responding. It is a hint, not a promise. The Sunset date must not be earlier than the Deprecation date. When the day comes, answer with a clear error. GitHub returns 410 Gone for a version it no longer supports. Measure, then communicate Headers only help if someone reads them. So log the version and the client id on every request. Then you can answer: "Who still calls v1, how often, and on which endpoints?" Stripe shows each customer the versions its own integration uses. Our advice: email the owners of the remaining clients by name, not only a mailing list. Before the final date, consider short planned failures in quiet hours. A client that ignored every email will notice those. Scheme Easy to see and route? Cost for clients Cost for you Use it when URL path (/v2/) Yes High. Each major version is a big move. Medium. Two code paths. Rare, large redesigns. Query or header with a date Partly. You must read the parameter or header. Low. Small steps. Medium. One version per release. Public APIs that change often. Pinned account plus translation layer No It is hidden in account settings. Lowest. Old code keeps working. High. Every module must be maintained. Long-lived integrations, like payments. Versionless (GraphQL) No version to route. Low, until a field is removed. Low, if you only add. Clients pick their own fields. Simple rule: try an additive change first. Version only when you must break something. In every API review, ask: "Could any client see a different result after this change?" That includes defaults, validation, error codes and enum values. Treat new enum values as a change to announce. Tell clients up front to handle unknown values. Before you deprecate, ask: "Who calls this today?" Answer with request logs grouped by client and version, not guesses. Put a date on every deprecation. Send Deprecation and Sunset headers, with a link to a migration guide. Write the support window into your public docs, the way GitHub states 24 months. Keep old-version rules in one layer. If version checks spread into business code, stop and refactor. Add a contract test for each supported version, so nobody breaks an old shape by accident. "Compare this OpenAPI file with the one on main. List every change an existing client could notice, including new enum values, changed defaults, stricter validation and new error codes. Mark each one breaking, dangerous or safe." "Write middleware that reads an API version header, logs it with the client id, and adds Deprecation and Sunset headers for versions older than 2025-01-01." "Turn this breaking change into a version change module with a function that converts the new response shape back to the old one. Add a test for both versions." What to ask the agent The agent did not call a new enum value or a changed default "non-breaking" just because the schema shape stayed the same. Deprecation uses the @ timestamp format, and Sunset uses an HTTP date. Version strings are full ISO dates like 2024-06-01 (not 2024-6-1), so comparing them as strings sorts them correctly. Every translation step has a test with a real old response as the expected output. Webhook payloads follow the same version rules as API responses. What to check yourself REST API design: the basic breaking changes and why old mobile apps matter. Schema migrations: expand and contract, one layer down in the database. API gateway: routing /v1 and /v2 at the edge. Webhooks and async APIs: events your API pushes, which need versions too. Schema evolution and encoding: how JSON, Protobuf and Avro let old and new code read each other's data. Coming later: contract and integration tests.

title: Making architecture trade-offs
text: There is no best architecture, only choices with different costs. Learn how seniors compare options, match the effort to the risk, and write down what they gave up.
body: This story is made up, but many teams will know it. A team of four builds a new booking service. In the kickoff, someone says, "Let's do it properly." They choose six microservices, a self-hosted Kafka cluster and a new database nobody on the team has used. Each tool is good. Each one wins a blog post comparison. The product launches with 300 bookings a day. One Postgres database could hold that many easily. But now the team runs nine separate systems. On-call pages come at night for problems nobody understands. A small feature touches four services and takes three weeks. A year later, the team spends a full quarter moving back to one service and one database. Nobody wrote down why they chose the first design, so nobody could say when it stopped making sense. The team did not pick bad tools. They picked tools for a problem they did not have, and they never wrote down what those tools would cost them. There is no best architecture. Every choice makes some things easier and other things harder. A senior's job is to see both sides, choose on purpose, and say out loud what you give up. The AWS Well-Architected Framework names six areas: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization and sustainability. It says you trade between them based on your business context. For example, you might accept lower reliability in a development environment to save cost. For a critical system, you might pay more for reliability. AWS adds that security and operational excellence are usually not traded away. The key idea. A good decision is not one with no downsides. It is one where you chose the downsides on purpose, matched the effort to the risk, and wrote it down so others can follow, or change it later. Not every decision deserves the same effort. Jeff Bezos split decisions into two kinds. Some are one-way doors: hard or impossible to undo, so you decide slowly and carefully. Most are two-way doors: if you are wrong, you can go back. Those should be made quickly, by a person or a small group with good judgement. He warns that big organisations tend to use the slow process for everything. The result is slowness, too much fear of risk and too little experimenting. Step 1: Requirements and constraints first Start with the problem, not the tool. Write down the numbers that matter: load, data size, latency target and budget. Then write the constraints. Who will run this at 3 a.m.? What does the team already know? What must it connect to? Do not skip this step and compare tools in general. Step 2: Ask how hard it is to undo Martin Fowler offers one way to think of architecture: the things people see as hard to change. He writes that one of an architect's most important tasks is to find ways to remove irreversibility from a design. His example: on one of his projects, a database administrator built a way to change the schema and move the data easily. After that, Fowler says, the schema was no longer architectural. So for each option, ask: if this is wrong in a year, what does leaving cost? A library behind your own interface is cheap to replace. A public API, a data format stored in millions of rows, or a database choice usually is not. Bezos also gives a rule for speed: most decisions should be made with about 70% of the information you wish you had. If you wait for 90%, in most cases you are probably being slow. Either way, you need to be good at quickly noticing and fixing bad decisions. Step 3: Count the cost of running it Dan McKinley's essay "Choose Boring Technology" gives a simple model. Each company gets about three "innovation tokens". Choosing a new or unusual technology spends one. His example is writing your website in NodeJS. Boring does not mean bad. His examples of boring tools include MySQL, Postgres, Python and cron. Their strength is that their failure modes are well understood. He also points to the hidden cost of each new tool: operations. You have to monitor it, test it and learn it. The long-term cost of keeping a system working almost always far exceeds the trouble of building it. His practical test: first ask how you would solve the problem with no new technology at all. Step 4: Compare options in a small table Step through how a team turns options into a written decision. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. A decision table is useful because it forces you to agree on what matters before you argue about tools. But do not trust the total blindly. If one option scores 0 on something you must have, such as security, it is out, whatever its total. Treat the scores as a way to start a conversation, not to end it. Step 5: Build or buy Fowler splits software into two kinds. "Utility" software, like payroll, must work reliably, but it does not set you apart. "Strategic" software is part of why customers choose you. For utility functions, the obvious choice is to buy a package. For strategic functions, you do not want the same software as your competitors. He adds that only a few projects are truly strategic. He suggests the split may be more like 95 to 5. The lesson build vs buy vs open source goes deeper. Step 6: Decide, write it down, and plan to look again When people still disagree, Bezos suggests the phrase "disagree and commit". In his words, you ask: "I know we disagree on this but will you gamble with me on it?" He says bosses should do this too. Then write the decision down. For a big change, write a design doc. For one decision, write an ADR. Michael Nygard's format has a title, context, decision, status and consequences. Consequences should list all the effects, not only the good ones. Good ADRs make it clear when to revisit. Nygard says the time to change an old decision becomes clear from changes in the project's context. Help that happen. Write a revisit trigger, such as "if load passes 1,000 jobs a second". When you reverse a decision, keep the old ADR and mark it as superseded, which means replaced by a newer decision. Approach Good for Risk Use it when Decide fast, small group Speed and learning. You may need to undo it. Two-way doors: easy and cheap to reverse. Slow, careful review Fewer costly mistakes. Slowness if used for everything. One-way doors: data formats, public APIs, core databases. Boring, well-known tech Known failure modes. Easy to hire for and run. May need more effort for a special need. Most of your system, most of the time. New, exciting tech A real edge for one hard problem. Unknown failures. Spends an innovation token. The problem is core to your business and old tools truly cannot solve it. Buy a product Fast start. Someone else runs it. Licence cost, lock-in, less control. Utility functions that do not set you apart. Build your own Full control over a key feature. You own every bug and every on-call page. Strategic functions that customers choose you for. Before you compare tools, write the problem, the numbers and the constraints in five lines. Always show at least two real options. One of them should be "use what we already have". Ask: "Is this a one-way or a two-way door?" Match the review effort to the answer. Name the cost of running each option: who is on call, what to monitor, what the team must learn. Say what you give up, in writing. "We accept X to get Y." Write a revisit trigger with a number or a date, not "if things change". When you lose an argument, disagree and commit. Then help the decision work. When you join a team, read the ADRs before you suggest a rewrite. The reason may still be valid. "Here are our requirements, team size and current stack. Give me three real options for this job queue, including 'use what we already have'. For each, list the cost of running it, the hardest thing to undo, and the main failure mode." "Act as a skeptical staff engineer. Argue against my preferred option. What will hurt in a year?" "Turn this decision into an ADR with title, context, decision, status and consequences. Include the negative consequences and a revisit trigger." "Is this decision a one-way door or a two-way door? List what would make it hard to reverse." What to ask the agent The requirements and numbers are yours. The agent does not know your real load or budget. The options are real. Agents tend to suggest popular tools, even when you do not need them. Every claim about a tool's limits or price comes from its official docs, not the agent's memory. The team's skills and on-call load are in the decision. The agent cannot see who will be paged at night. The decision is yours. You can defend it in review without the agent. What to check yourself Next, read design docs and RFCs, architecture decision records and build vs buy vs open source.

title: Authentication and authorization
text: Prove who the user is, then check what they may do, on every request and for every object.
body: First American is a large US title insurance company. In 2013 it launched EaglePro, an app that sent document images to customers through unique links. From 2014, the app had a defect. A user could take the URL of their own document and change some digits in it. The server then showed other people's documents. The user should not have had access to those images. The company's own security team found this in a manual test. Their report was finished on 11 January 2019. It said that replacing a number in the URL with another sequential number gave access to other documents. A clerical error gave the flaw a lower severity, so its deadline became 90 days instead of 45. That deadline was 8 May 2019, and the flaw was still not fixed after it. On 24 May 2019, a cybersecurity journalist told the company about it. The flaw exposed over 800 million title and escrow document images, going back to 2003. Some held social security numbers and financial information. The executives who answered the press did not know about the January report. In 2021, the SEC charged the company with failing to keep proper disclosure controls. It agreed to pay a $487,616 penalty, without admitting or denying the findings. The bug was one missing check: "Does this document belong to the person asking?" The same mistake is number one on the OWASP API Security Top 10 today. Two questions protect every request. Authentication: who are you? The user proves it with a password, a second factor or a login at another provider. Authorization: what may you do? The server checks if this user may do this action on this object. Authentication happens once at login, and then a session or token carries the answer on each request. Authorization must happen on every request, for the exact object asked for. OWASP says to check permissions on every request, on the server, and to deny by default. The key idea. Logging in proves who you are. It never proves you may touch this order. Check ownership or permission on the server, every time, for every object. Step through one login and one request for an order. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Passwords done right Never store a password as it is. Hash it. A hash is one-way, so even you cannot get the password back. Encryption is two-way, so anyone with the key can. OWASP says to encrypt passwords only in rare edge cases. Use a slow password hashing function, not a fast one like plain SHA-256. OWASP's first choice is Argon2id with at least 19 MiB of memory, 2 iterations and a parallelism of 1. If Argon2id is not available, use scrypt. Use bcrypt only for older systems where neither is available, with a work factor of at least 10. Most bcrypt libraries read at most 72 bytes of a password. Each password gets its own random salt, so two users with the same password get different hashes. Good libraries handle the salt for you. At the login form, OWASP says to: Treat passwords shorter than 8 characters as weak when multi-factor authentication (MFA) is on, and shorter than 15 when it is off. Allow at least 64 characters, so people can use passphrases. Block common and already breached passwords. Show one generic error, like "Invalid user ID or password", so attackers cannot learn which accounts exist. Then add MFA. OWASP calls it "by far the best defense against the majority of password-related attacks". It cites a Microsoft analysis that MFA would have stopped 99.9% of account compromises. Sessions and cookies After login, the server must remember the user. The classic way is a session. The server stores the session and sends the browser a random session ID in a cookie. The browser sends the cookie back with each request on its own. Set three cookie attributes: HttpOnly: JavaScript cannot read the cookie. This limits the damage of cross-site scripting (XSS). Secure: the browser sends it only over HTTPS. SameSite: controls whether the cookie goes with requests from other sites. OWASP says to set Strict (preferred) or Lax on session cookies. The session ID needs at least 64 bits of entropy, so nobody can guess it. Give the user a new session ID after login. On logout, delete the session on the server, not only the cookie. Tokens and JWTs A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact, URL-safe string that carries claims, such as a user ID. It can be signed, as a JWS, or encrypted, as a JWE. This lesson is about signed JWTs. Signed is not secret. The payload is only base64url encoded, so anyone with the token can read every claim. Never put private data in it. The signature only proves that nobody changed it. Give each JWT an exp claim. The exp claim is optional in the standard, but once it is set, the token must not be accepted on or after that time. Your parser must reject tokens with "alg":"none", which have no signature. The big catch is revocation. The server checks a JWT by its signature, with no lookup. So a stolen token works until it expires. Fixes: keep lifetimes short, and if you must revoke early, keep a denylist keyed on the token's jti and issuer. Once you add that lookup, you have a session store again. OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect OAuth 2.0 is about delegation. It lets an app get limited access to an API for a user, without the user's password. Example: a printing app wants to read your photos from a cloud drive. It has four roles: the user (resource owner), the app (client), the authorization server that issues tokens, and the API (resource server). OpenID Connect (OIDC) is about login. It is an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0. It adds an ID token, a signed JWT with claims about how the user logged in. The app must check that iss is the expected provider, that aud holds its own client ID, and that exp has not passed. The app must also check the signature. One exception: if the app got the ID token straight from the token endpoint over TLS, the spec allows it to trust TLS instead. The normal flow today is the authorization code flow with PKCE: The app makes a random secret, the code verifier. It sends its SHA-256 hash, the code challenge, with the S256 method. The user logs in at the authorization server. The server redirects back to the app with a short-lived code. The app swaps the code for tokens and sends the original verifier. The server hashes the verifier and compares it with the challenge. PKCE stops an attacker who steals the code on its way back, because they do not have the verifier. RFC 9700 says public clients, such as mobile and browser apps, must use PKCE. It also says the implicit grant should not be used, and the password grant must not be used. Check every object, with the least privilege Broken object level authorization (BOLA) happens when an API takes an object ID from the client and does not check that the caller may use that object. OWASP calls it "extremely common". The fix is the check in the diagram, in every function that reads a record using an ID from the client. Random IDs make guessing harder, and authorization tests stop regressions. Random IDs alone are not enough. Give each user, service and token only the access it needs. OWASP asks for least privilege. RFC 9700 says OAuth access tokens should get the minimum privileges for the use case. Roles, like "admin" and "viewer", are a good start. Larger products need richer rules. Google's Zanzibar, for example, serves hundreds of services from one shared permission model. See Authorization models: RBAC, ABAC and ReBAC. Option Revoke at once? Server lookup per request? Main risk Use it when Session ID in a cookie Yes Delete the session on the server. Yes One read from the session store. Cross-site requests. Set SameSite. A web app with its own backend. A good default. Long-lived signed JWT No It works until exp. No Only a signature check. Stolen tokens stay valid. Rarely. Prefer the next row. Short-lived JWT plus a refresh token Mostly. The access token dies soon, and you revoke the refresh token. Only when refreshing. More moving parts. Public clients must rotate or bind refresh tokens. Mobile apps and APIs used by many services. Login with OIDC (Google, Okta and others) Depends on the provider and your session. Only at login. Skipping ID token checks. Users already have an account elsewhere, or a company wants single sign-on. Simple rule: for your own web app, use a server session in an HttpOnly, Secure cookie. Use tokens when you truly need them, and keep them short-lived. In every review of an endpoint that takes an ID, ask: "Where do we check that this user may access this object?" Put the authorization check in one place, like a policy function or middleware. Do not copy it into each handler. Write a test for each endpoint where user A asks for user B's object. It must fail with 403 or 404. Never write your own password hashing or JWT code. Use a well-known library, and read its defaults. Ask: "If this token leaks, how long does it work, and how do we kill it?" Give services and tokens the smallest scopes that work. Review admin roles every quarter. "List every API endpoint in this repo that takes an object ID. For each one, show where it checks that the current user may access that object, or say that it does not." "Write tests where user A tries to read, update and delete user B's orders. Every test must expect 403 or 404." "Review this login code against the OWASP Password Storage and Session Management cheat sheets. List each gap with the line number." What to ask the agent Passwords use Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt from a known library. Never MD5, SHA-256 alone or encryption. Every query by ID also filters by the current user or tenant, or calls a permission check first. JWT code checks the signature, exp, iss and aud, and rejects "alg":"none". Session cookies have HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite. A new session ID is created at login. OAuth code uses the authorization code flow with PKCE, not the implicit flow. No secrets, tokens or passwords appear in logs, URLs or test fixtures. AI agents often copy a handler and forget the ownership check. Read each new handler for that line. What to check yourself TLS: why all of this needs HTTPS first. Coming next on this line: OWASP Top 10 and secure coding, Secrets and key management and Enterprise SSO and SCIM.

title: Authorization models: RBAC, ABAC and ReBAC
text: Roles, attributes and relationships. Pick a permission model that still works when your product grows.
body: npm is a package registry for JavaScript code. On 2 November 2021, GitHub, which runs npm, got a report through its bug bounty program. The report showed that an attacker could publish new versions of any npm package from an account without proper authorization. GitHub patched it within six hours. The cause was not a missing check. The check existed. The npm registry ran on several microservices. The authorization service checked the user's rights for the package named in the request URL. But the service that wrote to the registry did not read the URL. It chose the package from the contents of the uploaded file. So a request could be authorized for one package and then applied to a different one. GitHub fixed it by making both services use the same package for the check and for the publish. Its telemetry went back only to September 2020. The bug was older than that. For that window, GitHub said "with high confidence" that it was not exploited maliciously. The lesson for this page: an authorization check is only as good as its model and its placement. You must check the right object, in the right place, with rules that match how the product shares things. The Authentication and authorization lesson showed one check: "Does this order belong to this user?" Real products need more. People share folders, become members of teams, and become admins of a whole company account. There are three common ways to model this. RBAC (role-based access control). Permissions belong to roles. Users get roles. "Editors may edit docs." ABAC (attribute-based access control). A policy reads facts about the user, the object, the action and the environment. "Users in finance may read invoices during work hours." ReBAC (relationship-based access control). Access comes from links between users and objects. "You may view this doc because you are in a group that can view its folder." Most real systems mix them. Roles for staff tools, relationships for sharing, and a few attribute rules on top. The key idea. Choose the model that matches how your product shares things. Then put the check in one place, on the server, for the exact object the action will touch. RBAC: users, roles, permissions In RBAC, each user gets one or more roles. Each role gets one or more privileges. David Ferraiolo and Rick Kuhn formalized it in 1992. The NIST model became the standard ANSI/INCITS 359-2004. RBAC is easy to audit. You can list who has the "admin" role. Its weak spot is per-object rules. A role applies to every object. To share one doc with one person, you need a narrow new role. Many small, one-off roles pile up. This is often called "role explosion". NIST SP 800-162 describes it for rules that depend on context. OWASP adds a practical problem. With many roles, code fills up with checks like hasAnyRole("SUPERUSER", "ADMIN", "ACCT_MANAGER"). It is easy to miss one. ABAC: rules over attributes NIST SP 800-162 defines ABAC as allowing or denying each request based on attributes of the subject and the object, environment conditions, and a set of policies. An attribute is a name-value pair, like department=finance or time=21:00. NIST splits the work into parts. The policy enforcement point sits in your app and blocks or allows. The policy decision point evaluates the rules and returns the answer. ABAC is flexible, but it has a real cost. "Who can see this file?" becomes a hard question. NIST says it may mean simulating the request for every known subject. Auditors often ask exactly that question. ReBAC and Zanzibar Google built one authorization system, Zanzibar, for hundreds of services, including Drive, Calendar and YouTube. It stores permissions as relation tuples: object#relation@user. For example, doc:readme#owner@10 means user 10 owns doc:readme. A user in a tuple can also be a set, such as "members of group:eng". So groups can contain groups. A schema adds rules. One rule says "all owners are editors, and all editors are viewers". Another says viewers of the parent folder are viewers of the doc. A check asks: "Does user U have relation R to object O?" Step through one check. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Zanzibar also had to solve the "new enemy" problem. The paper gives two examples. Alice removes Bob from a folder's ACL. Then Charlie moves new documents into it. Bob must not see them. He may, if the check ignores the order of the two ACL changes. Alice removes Bob from a document's ACL. Then Charlie adds new content. Bob must not see it. He may, if the check uses a stale ACL from before his removal. The fix is a consistency token called a zookie. When content is about to be saved, the client sends a content-change check. If it is allowed, the response holds a zookie, and the client stores it with that content version. Later checks send the zookie. The check snapshot must then be "at least as fresh" as it. This is still fast. Zanzibar answers more than 95% of checks within 10 milliseconds. It caches results and merges duplicate requests. See Caching and cache stampedes for the same ideas. One rule, two models Take a docs app. Docs have an owner, editors and viewers. Docs live in shared folders. Org admins may edit every doc in their org. In RBAC, the rule looks like this: // Any "editor" may edit any doc in the org. function canEdit(user: User, doc: Doc): boolean { return user.orgId === doc.orgId && (user.roles.includes("editor") || user.roles.includes("org_admin")); }This is simple, but it cannot say "Asha may edit this one doc". In ReBAC, the same rules live in a schema. Here it is in OpenFGA's language: model schema 1.1 type user type org relations define admin: [user] type group relations define member: [user, group#member] type folder relations define parent: [folder] define editor: [user, group#member] or editor from parent define viewer: [user, group#member] or editor or viewer from parent type doc relations define org: [org] define parent: [folder] define owner: [user] define editor: [user, group#member] or owner or editor from parent or admin from org define viewer: [user, group#member] or editor or viewer from parentEach doc also needs a tuple that links it to its org, like doc:plan#org@org:acme. Without it, the admin rule never matches. Sharing a doc is now one tuple, like doc:plan#editor@user:asha. No new role. The app asks one question: // fgaClient is an OpenFgaClient from @openfga/sdk const { allowed } = await fgaClient.check({ user: "user:asha", relation: "editor", object: "doc:plan", }); if (!allowed) throw new ForbiddenError();Where to enforce Check on the server, on every request. OWASP says to deny by default and never trust checks on the client. The check must be for the exact object. Missing it is broken object level authorization (BOLA). OWASP calls it "extremely common in API-based applications". The npm bug adds one more rule. The check and the action must use the same object ID, from the same source. Load the object once, check it, then act on that loaded object. A gateway can check tokens. Object checks need your data, so they belong in the service. See API gateways and edge concerns. Put the check behind one interface, so the domain code does not care which engine answers. See Clean and hexagonal architecture. Policy engines and permission services A policy engine keeps rules apart from app code. Your code sends a question with JSON input and gets a decision back. OPA is a general-purpose engine. Policies are written in a language called Rego. Cedar uses permit and forbid policies. If no policy matches, the answer is deny. One matching forbid beats any permit. OpenFGA and SpiceDB are not policy engines in this sense. They are open source permission services inspired by Zanzibar. They store the relationships and answer checks. Keep policies in Git, reviewed like code. Pick a tool for your model, not for its marketing page. Checking versus listing "May Asha open doc:plan?" is one check. "Show me every doc Asha can see" is a different problem. Checking each doc one by one is too slow. OpenFGA's ListObjects API answers it, but its docs aim it at small collections. It has a time limit and a maximum number of results. Zanzibar offers an Expand API, which returns the tree of users and groups behind a relation. Google's clients use it to build search indexes that respect access. Tenants, tests and audits In a multi-tenant app, every query and every object ID must carry the tenant. Never let a tuple or a role from tenant A match an object in tenant B. See Multi-tenancy and noisy neighbours. Write unit and integration tests for authorization logic. Log decisions, but not too much and not too little. Model Easy to answer "who has access?" Per-object sharing Main cost Use it when RBAC Yes List the role's members. No Needs a role per object. Role explosion. Staff tools and admin panels with a few fixed jobs. ABAC No May need a simulation per subject. Yes, through attributes like owner. Hard to audit and to debug. Rules depend on time, place, data labels or training. ReBAC (Zanzibar style) Yes Expand or list the relation. Yes One tuple per share. A new store to run and keep in sync. Sharing, folders, teams and nested groups. Policy engine on top Depends on the model inside. Depends. Another service in the request path. Many services must apply the same rules. Simple rule: start with a few roles. Add relationships when users start sharing things. Add attributes only for rules that truly depend on context. Before you add a role, ask: "Is this really a relationship, like owner or member?" In code review, ask: "Is the object we check the same object we change?" Keep one authorize(user, action, object) entry point. Ban role checks scattered in handlers. Write a permission matrix test: for each role or relationship, try each action, and expect allow or deny. Prepare for the auditor's question, "Who can see customer X's data?", before they ask. Plan for removal. When someone leaves a team, how fast does access end everywhere? Load-test the check path. It runs on every request. "Find every place in this repo that checks a role or permission. Group them by resource, and show any handler that reads or writes an object without a check." "For each endpoint that takes an object ID, show where the ID used for the authorization check comes from, and where the ID used for the write comes from. Flag any that differ." "Write an OpenFGA model for this app: users, groups, folders with parents, docs, and org admins. Then write tests for owner, shared folder, removed member and other-tenant cases." What to ask the agent The check runs on the server and denies by default. The check and the action use the same loaded object, not two copies of the request. Every query and tuple includes the tenant. Removing a user from a group removes their access in a test. Listing pages filter by permission, not only by a hidden button. The AI did not invent APIs. Compare its calls with the engine's docs. What to check yourself OWASP Top 10 and secure coding: broken access control in the wider list. Scaling reads: when the check service gets most of your traffic. Enterprise SSO and SCIM: how users and groups get fed into these models from a customer's identity provider.

title: Backoff, jitter and retry budgets
text: Retries rescue one request but can sink a whole system. Here is how to retry without making an outage worse.
body: On 12 June 2025, many Google Cloud APIs returned 503 errors around the world. A bad policy record made Service Control, the system that checks API requests, crash again and again. Google's engineers found the cause within 10 minutes. Within 40 minutes, they had rolled out a switch that turned the failing code path off. That should have been the end. But in large regions like us-central1, the restarting Service Control tasks all hit the Spanner table they depend on. Google calls this a "herd effect". The report says Service Control "did not have the appropriate randomized exponential backoff implemented to avoid this." Engineers throttled task creation to protect that database. Full recovery in us-central1 took up to about 2 hours 40 minutes. So the bug caused the outage, but the missing backoff stretched the recovery. One of Google's fixes: "audit and ensure our systems employ randomized exponential backoff." You learned in Idempotency and retries that retries need a key, a limit and backoff with jitter. This lesson is about the system as a whole. One retry helps one request. Millions of retries can keep a failing service down. Brooker calls retries "selfish": "when a client retries, it spends more of the server's time to get a higher chance of success". That is fine when failures are rare. It is dangerous when the server fails because it is overloaded. The key idea. Spread retries out in time (backoff with jitter), keep them in one layer, and give them a budget. When the budget runs out, fail fast instead of retrying. Retries multiply across layers You saw in the last lesson that retries multiply when several layers retry. Here are the numbers when each layer makes 1 try plus 3 retries. Step through it with Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Google's SRE book gives the same example: 3 layers that each make 4 attempts send 64 attempts to the database for one user action. Brooker's example has five layers with 3 tries each: 3^5 = 243 times the database load. This is retry amplification. The fix is to retry at one point in the stack. That is Amazon's best practice for low-cost operations. Google adds a rule: only the layer just above the one that failed retries. If its retries fail, it returns an "overloaded; don't retry" error, so callers higher up do not retry again. Amazon does not say which layer. Google picks the layer just above the failure. The diagram lets the app retry. Either way, only one layer retries. Exponential backoff, with a cap Exponential backoff doubles the wait after each failure. Without a limit, the wait grows without end, so implementations set a maximum wait. The AWS SDKs, for example, cap each backoff at 20 seconds. Backoff alone is not enough. In Brooker's 2015 simulation, clients that failed together backed off together. They still arrived in clusters, so contention "hasn't been reduced much". The three jitter rules Jitter adds randomness to each wait. Here are the three rules from the simulator code behind the 2015 post, rewritten as small functions. The base and cap are the AWS SDK values for transient errors. n is the retry number, starting at 0. import random BASE, CAP = 0.05, 20.0 # seconds def expo(n): return min(CAP, BASE * 2 ** n) def full_jitter(n): return random.uniform(0, expo(n)) def equal_jitter(n): v = expo(n) return v / 2 + random.uniform(0, v / 2) def decorrelated_jitter(prev_sleep): # start with prev_sleep = BASE return min(CAP, random.uniform(BASE, prev_sleep * 3))Full jitter picks the whole wait at random, from 0 up to the capped backoff. Equal jitter keeps half the backoff and randomizes the other half. No wait is ever very short. Decorrelated jitter grows from the last random wait, not from the retry number. In the simulation, with 100 clients competing for the same resource, jitter cut the number of calls by more than half compared with plain backoff. Full jitter did the least work. Decorrelated jitter finished slightly sooner but made more calls. Equal jitter was the weakest of the three. In their updated retry behavior, the AWS SDKs use full jitter: random(0, 1) × min(20,000 ms, base_delay × 2^retry). Jitter helps outside retries too. Amazon considers adding jitter to "all timers, periodic jobs, and other delayed work". Restarting tasks, like Google's, need it as well. Retry budgets Backoff spreads retries out. It does not limit their total. When a backend is down for everyone, every request fails, and every request retries. You need a retry budget. Google uses two limits. Each request gets at most three attempts. Each client also retries only while retries stay below 10% of its requests. Without the client budget, load can grow to just under 3 times. With it, load grows about 1.1 times. The SRE book also gives a per-process example: 60 retries a minute, then fail instead of retrying. A token bucket is a common way to build this. Real libraries do it: AWS SDKs, standard mode: a retry quota of 500 tokens. A retry after a transient error costs 14 tokens. A success with no retry gives 1 back. When the retry quota is empty, the SDK returns the error at once. These numbers are for AWS's updated retry behavior. You opt in with AWS_NEW_RETRIES_2026=true until it becomes the default. AWS SDKs, adaptive mode: adds a client-side rate limiter. It can delay even the first request when the service throttles. gRPC: for each server, each failed call with a retryable code takes 1 token, and each success adds back tokenRatio. Retries stop while the count is at or below half of maxTokens. Which errors to retry Retry only errors that may pass. Do not retry permanent errors or malformed requests, because they will never succeed. gRPC goes further: in general, retry only codes that show the server did not handle the request. Listen to the server. A 503 with Retry-After says how long the service expects to be unavailable. The value is seconds, like Retry-After: 120, or a date. gRPC servers can send the grpc-retry-pushback-ms metadata key: a delay in milliseconds, or a negative value for "don't retry". Deadlines Retries must fit inside the caller's time limit. Pass the time left down the chain. If a server has a 30-second deadline and spends 7 seconds, it gives the next server 23 seconds. Do not start a retry that cannot finish in time. Option Protects the backend? Cost Use it when Retry at once, no backoff No Retries pile onto a sick service. Nothing to build. Never, for remote calls. Exponential backoff, no jitter Partly. Clients still retry in clusters. A little code. Rarely. Add jitter. Backoff with full jitter Yes Retries spread out evenly. Some calls wait longer than needed. Your default for remote calls. Decorrelated jitter Yes Similar to full jitter. Slightly more calls in the 2015 simulation. You want slightly faster completion. Retry budget (token bucket) Yes Total retries stay small. Some requests fail that one retry could save. Many clients call a shared service. Retries at every layer No Retries multiply. Hidden until an outage. Never. Pick one layer. Simple rule: retry in one layer, with capped backoff and full jitter, under a retry budget. Draw the call chain in design reviews. Ask: "Which layer retries? How many attempts in total, top to bottom?" Read your library's defaults. HTTP clients, SDKs, service meshes and queues often retry on their own. Ask what happens when the backend is down for everyone, not just for one request. A budget should cap the total. Tell callers how to behave when you are overloaded: a 503 with Retry-After to say when to come back, or a "don't retry" error so upper layers do not retry. Add jitter to cron jobs, cache TTLs, reconnect loops and restarts, not just to request retries. Watch the retry rate on a dashboard. A rising retry rate is an early warning of overload. Pair retries with circuit breakers, which stop calls to a failing service for a while. See circuit breakers, bulkheads and fallbacks. "Find every place in this repo that retries a network call: our code, HTTP client settings, SDK configs and service mesh rules. List the layer, max attempts and backoff for each." "Wrap this client in a retry policy: at most 3 attempts, full jitter with a 50 ms base and a 20 s cap, and a token-bucket retry budget. Only retry 503, 504 and connection errors. Respect Retry-After." "Write a test where the backend fails every call for 60 seconds. Assert that retries stay under 10% of requests." What to ask the agent The wait is random from 0 to the capped backoff. It is not a fixed wait plus a tiny random part. The cap is applied before the random pick, not after. Only one layer retries. Other layers pass the error up. Client errors like 400 and 403 are not retried. A 429 is retried only after a wait: the Retry-After value if there is one, or your backoff if not. Retries stop when the deadline has passed or the budget is empty. Calls that change data are idempotent before they are retried. What to check yourself Related lessons: Idempotency and retries, Tail latency and queueing, Rate limiting, Caching and cache stampedes and Error handling. Read the Google Cloud incident for the rest of the story.

title: Backpressure and flow control
text: When the consumer is slower than the producer, you must buffer, drop or slow the sender. Learn to slow the sender, so your queues stay small.
body: On 25 March 2026, voice and video on Discord were badly degraded from 12:13 to 15:30 PDT. Most users could not start or join calls. They saw "Awaiting Endpoint". It began with a routine config change. Kubernetes stopped pods before their sessions could hand off cleanly. About 17% of sessions across Discord stopped without warning. Those users all tried to reconnect. Discord has a start-session rate limit that "provides backpressure when we have a flood of requests". But that limit had not been re-tuned after a recent migration. Too many session starts got through, and gateway nodes in one zone began to run out of memory. The voice service had a second problem. Its Elixir processes read one message at a time from a mailbox, "a queue of incoming messages". Each new outbound connection went through a single supervisor process. To start a process, that supervisor scanned its mailbox for one message. With about 100,000 messages waiting, each start took about 1 ms longer. So the longer the queue got, the slower it drained. In total, the mailboxes on 15 voice syncers grew to nearly 1 million messages and kept rising. The connection that sends health reports to etcd also went through those supervisors. After the 60-second TTL, instances dropped out of service discovery. Early restarts helped only briefly, because the queues filled again. Recovery came after the team set lower spawn limits and doubled the instances. A producer sends work. A consumer does it. Sometimes the producer is faster for a while. What then? You have three choices, and only three: Buffer. Store the extra work and do it later. Drop. Throw some work away, on purpose. Slow the producer. Make the sender wait until the consumer is ready. The third one is backpressure. The slow part pushes back on the fast part. A buffer only buys time. If the producer stays faster on average, the buffer fills, and then you are back to choosing between dropping and slowing. Load shedding is choice 2: drop work early and cheaply. Backpressure is choice 3. You often need both. You can slow your own services, but you cannot slow a user who is tapping a button. The key idea. A queue does not add capacity. It only moves the wait. Give every queue a limit, and decide what happens when it is full: the sender waits, or the sender gets an error. Unbounded queues hide the problem Many queues have no limit by default. In Python, asyncio.Queue() has maxsize=0, and that means "the queue size is infinite". Java's Executors.newFixedThreadPool uses "a shared unbounded queue". The Java docs say what this means. An unbounded queue smooths out short bursts. But it allows "unbounded work queue growth" when tasks keep arriving faster than they finish. As the Tail latency and queueing lesson showed, a long queue also means a long wait for every item in it. Node.js measured the cost. It compressed a file of about 9 GB with streams, once with backpressure and once without. With backpressure, the process used about 87.81 MB of memory. Without it, about 1.52 GB. A bounded queue has a fixed size. Java's docs say it "helps prevent resource exhaustion". The hard part is the next question: what happens when it is full? Wait or reject When a bounded queue is full, the producer either waits or gets an error. Pick one on purpose. In asyncio, await queue.put(item) waits for a free slot. put_nowait(item) raises QueueFull at once. Here is both, in a small sketch: import asyncio queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=100) # at most 100 jobs wait (Python 3.10+) async def producer(jobs): for job in jobs: await queue.put(job) # waits while the queue is full async def worker(): while True: job = await queue.get() try: await handle(job) finally: queue.task_done() def enqueue_from_request(job): # a handler that must not wait try: queue.put_nowait(job) return 202 except asyncio.QueueFull: return 503 # caller should back off and retry laterWaiting is real backpressure: the producer slows to the consumer's speed. Use it inside your own system, such as a batch job. Rejecting turns the decision into load shedding. Use it at the edge, where callers are users or other teams. Return 503 with Retry-After, as in the load shedding lesson. Java gives you both choices too. The default policy, AbortPolicy, throws RejectedExecutionException. CallerRunsPolicy runs the task on the thread that submitted it. The docs call this "a simple feedback control mechanism" that slows down new submissions. Pull and credits instead of push In a push system, the sender decides the rate. Kafka's docs say a push consumer "tends to be overwhelmed" when it is slower than the producer. So Kafka consumers pull. A slow consumer "simply falls behind and catches up when it can". A more general form is credit-based flow control. The receiver says how much it can take. The sender sends no more than that. Reactive Streams. The subscriber calls request(n) to ask for n more items. The publisher must never send more items in total than were requested. The goal is that the receiver "is not forced to buffer arbitrary amounts of data". HTTP/2. Each stream and each connection has a flow-control window. The receiver opens it with WINDOW_UPDATE frames. The RFC calls it "a credit-based scheme". Both windows start at 65,535 octets, and only DATA frames count. TCP. Every segment carries a window: how many more bytes the receiver will accept. If the window drops to zero, the sender stops and sends small probes, with growing gaps, until it opens. This is flow control: one receiver protecting itself from one sender. It is different from congestion control, which protects the network. The TCP/IP lesson covers both. How backpressure travels, and where it stops Backpressure works best when it travels back, hop by hop, to whoever started the work. Step through it. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. The chain is only as good as its weakest link. Three things break it: An unbounded buffer anywhere. The signal stops there. That part just grows. In Discord's outage, the mailboxes kept growing until the team lowered rate limits upstream. An async boundary that answers early. "202 Accepted" ends the caller's wait before the work is done. From then on, only the queue's limit protects you. Reactive Streams exists to carry the signal across exactly these boundaries. Fire-and-forget calls. A call nobody waits for can never slow anybody down. A durable log is a special case. A Kafka producer does not slow down when a consumer falls behind. The log on disk is the buffer, and the cost shows up as consumer lag. Inside the consumer, you can still apply backpressure. max.poll.records limits how many records one poll returns. pause() stops fetching from chosen partitions until you call resume(). But keep calling poll(). If you wait longer than max.poll.interval.ms, the consumer leaves its group. At the very front, users will not slow down. So the last hop of backpressure becomes a choice: make them wait a little, or reject with a clear error. Option Memory safe? What the producer sees Use it when Unbounded buffer No It grows until something crashes. Nothing. Every send succeeds. Never on purpose. Find these and add limits. Bounded queue, producer waits Yes Slower sends. Inside your own system: pipelines, batch jobs, workers. Bounded queue, reject when full Yes Fast errors, such as 503. At the edge, where callers can retry later. Drop oldest or newest item Yes Nothing. Data is lost quietly. Only the latest value matters, like metrics or presence. Pull or credit-based flow Yes The receiver sets the pace. Streams, brokers, protocols you control on both sides. Durable log (Kafka) Yes, on disk, until retention. Nothing. Lag grows instead. Consumers may fall behind and catch up later. Simple rule: every queue gets a limit. Inside your system, let the producer wait. At the edge, reject fast. Draw the path of one request and mark every buffer: thread pools, channels, mailboxes, connection pools, broker queues. Ask: "What is its limit, and what happens when it is full?" Search for default constructors that hide unbounded queues, such as newFixedThreadPool or asyncio.Queue(). Give each a size from Little's law and your latency target. Size a queue from time, not memory. If you can wait 2 seconds and do 100 jobs a second, 200 is the limit. Alert on queue length and the age of the oldest item. Also track time spent blocked in put(). After a migration or a resize, retune every limit that provides backpressure. Discord's limit had not been re-tuned after a migration. Never let health checks or heartbeats wait behind normal work. Give them their own path. When you add an async API that returns 202, write down who protects the queue behind it. "List every queue, channel, thread pool and buffer in this service. For each, give its size limit, or say 'unbounded', and what happens when it is full." "Replace this unbounded asyncio.Queue with a bounded one. Producers inside the batch job should wait. The HTTP handler should return 503 with Retry-After when the queue is full." "Write a load test where the consumer is 50% slower than the producer for 10 minutes. Record queue length, memory and p99 latency every second." What to ask the agent No queue uses a default that means "no limit". Read the docs of each constructor the agent used. The handler that must stay fast uses a non-waiting call, like put_nowait or offer, not a blocking put. A blocking put never runs on an event loop thread or while holding a lock. The load test runs long enough for the queue to fill. Memory flattens out instead of climbing. Rejected work is counted in a metric, so you can see shedding happen. What to check yourself Before this: Queues vs logs and Tail latency and queueing. Next to it: Load shedding and Rate limiting. For flow control in protocols, see TCP/IP and HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC.

title: Batching and pipelining
text: Many small calls waste time on fixed costs. Learn how batching and pipelining share those costs, and how much waiting time you pay for it.
body: This story is made up, but the shape is common. A team runs a nightly job that copies 2,000,000 product prices into Redis. The job runs in one zone and Redis runs in another. The code is a simple loop: send one SET, wait for the reply, send the next. Each round trip between the zones takes about 0.5 ms. The job takes 2,000,000 × 0.5 ms = 1,000 seconds, about 17 minutes. Redis is almost idle. The job spends nearly all its time waiting for the network. An engineer switches to pipelining. She sends all 2,000,000 commands first, then reads the replies.
