The job is fast now, but Redis memory jumps, because Redis must hold every reply until the client reads it. The final fix sends 10,000 commands at a time, reads those replies, and repeats. Many operations have a fixed cost that does not depend on how much data they carry. The fixed part of a network round trip, a system call, a disk flush or a packet header is the same for 1 item or for 100. Batching means grouping many items into one operation, so they share that fixed cost. Pipelining means sending the next request before the reply to the last one arrives, so the round trips overlap. Both raise throughput: more items per second. Both have a price. With batching, an item may wait for more items to arrive and fill its batch. With pipelining, both sides buffer more data, and one slow item can hold up the rest. The key idea. Batching and pipelining spread a fixed cost over many items. You gain throughput and pay with waiting time and memory. Always put a limit on both the size of a batch and how long an item may wait. The arithmetic of batching Say each call to a service costs 1 ms of fixed overhead, plus 0.01 ms per item. You have 1,000 items. One at a time: 1,000 × (1 + 0.01) = 1,010 ms. That is about 990 items a second. Batches of 100: 10 × (1 + 100 × 0.01) = 10 × 2 = 20 ms. That is 50,000 items a second. The work per item did not change. You paid the fixed cost 10 times, not 1,000 times. Now look at the wait. Items arrive at 2,000 a second. A batch of 100 takes 100 / 2,000 = 0.05 s to fill. So the first item in each batch waits about 50 ms before anything is sent. In tail latency and queueing, you saw that a busy server builds long queues. Batching adds waiting time to each item. But it also raises capacity, so the server is less busy and its queue is shorter. Here, sending one at a time handles only about 990 items a second. At 2,000 arriving a second, its queue would grow without end. Two knobs: size and time Every batcher needs two limits. A size limit sends the batch when it is full. A time limit sends it when the oldest item has waited long enough. Kafka's producer shows both. It groups records for the same partition into batches. batch.size sets the batch size in bytes, with a default of 16384. linger.ms is how long the producer waits for more records. It sends when the batch is full or the linger time ends, "whichever happens first". The default for linger.ms changed from 0 to 5 in Kafka 4.0. The docs say "the efficiency gains from larger batches typically result in similar or lower producer latency despite the increased linger." But the docs also warn that a value of 50 "would add up to 50ms of latency to records sent in the absence of load". In the example above, a 5 ms time limit at 2,000 items a second gives batches of about 2,000 × 0.005 = 10 items. Each batch costs 1 + 10 × 0.01 = 1.1 ms, or 0.11 ms per item. That is about 9 times better than one at a time. At normal load, an item lingers at most about 5 ms. Kafka warns that broker backpressure can make the real wait longer. Group commit in databases A durable commit must reach the disk with fsync. That flush is a large fixed cost. If several transactions commit at the same moment, one flush can cover all of them. This is group commit. With made-up numbers: one flush takes 2 ms. One commit per flush allows at most 1,000 / 2 = 500 commits a second. If 8 commits share each flush, the same disk allows up to 4,000. PostgreSQL already groups sessions that need to flush while the previous flush runs. The setting commit_delay (in microseconds, 0 by default) adds a short sleep before the flush, so more commit records can be added to it. It skips the sleep if fewer than commit_siblings other sessions are in active transactions. The docs suggest starting at half the flush time that pg_test_fsync reports for one 8 kB write. They also warn that a value that is too high can add so much latency that throughput falls. Nagle's algorithm and TCP_NODELAY TCP batches too. In 1984, John Nagle described a problem with keyboard traffic. Each typed character went out alone, as a 41-byte packet: 1 byte of data and 40 bytes of headers. His fix, now called Nagle's algorithm: while earlier data on the connection is still unacknowledged, hold new data. Send it together when the acknowledgement comes. Today's version holds data only until it can fill a full-sized packet. TCP should still implement this rule, and must let an application turn it off per connection. The trouble is the receiver. It may hold back its acknowledgement for a short time, so it sends fewer of them. This is a delayed acknowledgement. The delay must be less than 0.5 seconds. RFC 9293 says the two features together "can result in poor application performance" for request-response traffic. RFC 9293 gives no example, so here is a common one. Your client sends a request in two small writes: header, then body. The header goes out at once. Nagle holds the body until the header is acknowledged. The server's TCP delays its acknowledgement. The server app cannot reply yet, because it still waits for the body. Nothing moves until the delayed-acknowledgement timer fires. The usual fix is the TCP_NODELAY socket option, which turns Nagle off for one connection. A better habit is to build the whole request in memory and send it in one write. That is batching in your own code. Pipelining Pipelining cuts the cost of round trips. CPUs use the same idea inside: an instruction pipeline starts the next instruction before the last one is done. If the round-trip time is 250 ms, a client that waits for each reply can do at most 4 requests a second, even if the server can handle 100,000. With pipelining, the client sends many commands, then reads all the replies. You pay the round trip once for the group. Step through it. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. It also cuts system calls. Without pipelining, Redis does a read() and a write() per command. With it, one read() takes in many commands and one write() sends many replies. Redis reports up to 10 times the throughput this way. Pipelining cannot help when the next command needs the last reply. A read, compute, write sequence must wait. Redis suggests a server-side script for that case. HTTP/1.1 pipelining and why it faded HTTP/1.1 allows pipelining too. But the server must send responses "in the same order that the requests were received". So a slow first response blocks every response behind it. This is head-of-line blocking. Browsers do not turn HTTP pipelining on by default. MDN gives three reasons: buggy proxies, it is hard to implement correctly, and head-of-line blocking. HTTP/2 replaced it with multiplexing. Each request gets its own stream, so a stalled response does not block the others. But TCP head-of-line blocking remains: a lost packet still delays every stream on the connection. HTTP/3 fixes that; see HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC. Adaptive batching A fixed time limit makes every item wait, even when the system is idle. Martin Thompson describes a better way, which he calls smart batching. One thread sends data as soon as any is available. Items that arrive while a send is in progress form the next batch, up to the buffer size. A lone item goes out alone, with no timer. In his example, writing one buffer to the network and getting it acknowledged takes 100 µs. Then 10 messages arrive at once. If each thread writes its own message, the writes queue up, and the last one finishes after 1,000 µs. With smart batching, no message takes more than 200 µs. Batches grow only when load grows. So at low load you get low latency, and at high load you get big batches. Bound the queue, though. Thompson warns that an unbounded queue "could grow out of control". Option Throughput Latency Use it when One at a time No Pays the full fixed cost per item. Lowest at low load. Traffic is light, or each step needs the last result. Batch with size and time limits Yes Big gains under load. Adds up to the time limit per item. Producers, log shippers, bulk writes. Adaptive (smart) batching Yes Batches grow with load. Low at low load, no timer. You own the sender loop and the downstream is serial. Pipelining Yes Pays the round trip once per group. Low, but one slow reply can block in-order replies. Many independent commands on one connection. Group commit Yes One flush for many commits. Adds a short wait, if you set a delay. Many concurrent writers, flush-bound disk. Find the fixed cost first. Ask: "What do we pay per call, whatever its size?" Usually it is round trips, system calls, flushes or headers. Never batch without a time limit. Check the worst wait an item can have against your latency target. Measure at low load too. A time limit that helps at peak adds pure delay at 3 a.m. Decide what happens when one item in a batch fails. Return a result per item, and retry only the failed items. Plan for a bad item (sometimes called a poison message). One bad record should not block the whole batch forever. Move it to a dead letter queue. For request-response protocols over TCP, send each request in one write, or set TCP_NODELAY. "This loop calls Redis once per item. Rewrite it to pipeline in chunks of 10,000 commands, and keep a result for each item." "Our Kafka producer sends 200 records a second at night and 20,000 at peak. Estimate the batch size and added latency for linger.ms = 5 and 50. Show the arithmetic." What to ask the agent Every batch has both a size limit and a time limit, and the numbers came from your traffic, not a guess. A failure of one item does not lose or silently retry the other items in the batch. The new code does not depend on the reply to a command that is still in the same pipeline. What to check yourself Tail latency and queueing Latency numbers and back-of-envelope maths Mechanical sympathy: CPU caches and memory OS essentials for backend engineers HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC

title: Behavioural interviews and STAR stories
text: Build a bank of true stories, tell each one in about two to three minutes with STAR, and make the "I", the trade-offs and the result easy to hear.
body: This story is made up, but each mistake in it is common. Kiran is a backend engineer with three years of experience. He passed the coding rounds of a big-tech loop. Then he met the behavioural interviewer. "Tell me about a time you failed," she said. Kiran answered, "I sometimes care too much about code quality, so I work late." She waited. He had nothing else. "Tell me about a conflict with a teammate." Kiran talked for eight minutes. Most of it was about the system. He said "we" twenty times. When she asked, "What did you do yourself?", he could not say. For the third question, he told the same story again. He never gave a result. He never said what he learned. The feedback said "not enough signal". Kiran had done good work in his job. He just had not prepared to show it. A behavioural question asks what you really did in the past. "Tell me about a time…" is the usual opening. The interviewer is not looking for a right answer. They want evidence of how you behave. Google's re:Work guide explains the logic. Behavioural questions "are good at revealing patterns of behavior". Hypothetical questions show how you might handle something new. At Google, these questions are part of a structured interview. Every candidate gets planned questions and is scored on the same scale. Google's hiring page says it uses "the same rubrics for everyone" for a role. Google's guide says academic research has backed this for about 20 years. In Google's own data, structured interviews predicted job performance better than unstructured ones. Google says it stopped asking brainteasers because they did not predict job success. Amazon says it avoids them for the same reason. The key idea. The interviewer can only score what you say clearly. Prepare true stories in advance, tell each one with a clear structure, and make your own actions, choices and results easy to hear. The big-tech loop lesson covered where this round fits. Here we go inside one answer. Step through it with Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. The time split is our advice, not a company rule. STAR, as the companies write it Amazon's guide lists the four parts of the STAR method: Situation, Task, Action and Result. It says to focus on "your individual contributions" and to use "I" instead of "we". It wants numbers in the result if you have them. Google writes the same idea with one small change. Its A is "Activity": the steps you took and your role. The meaning is the same. Amazon also says STAR is "not the only way" to tell a story. The Tech Interview Handbook suggests an extra R, for Reflection: what you learned. It says this can "show seniority". Build a story bank Do not prepare one answer per question. Prepare stories, then map each story to the themes it can answer. This is a story bank. Our advice is 8–10 stories, as in the loop lesson's plan. Cover these common themes: Conflict: you disagreed with someone and worked it out. Failure: a real mistake, with its cost. Ambiguity: an unclear problem you turned into a plan. Influence: you changed a decision you did not own. Ownership: you fixed something that was not strictly your job. Mentoring: you helped someone else grow. A hard technical call: you chose between two options with real costs. One project can feed several themes. The Tech Interview Handbook suggests starting from 3–5 big projects with high impact, high complexity and high involvement by you. Google calls this "a broad library of examples". Amazon asks for range too: risks, successes, failures and growth. Write each story as five bullet points, not a script. Amazon says it does not expect "rehearsed scripts". Leadership principles: Amazon as the public example Amazon publishes the behaviours it hires for. As of November 2026, its page lists 16 Leadership Principles. Its interview page says "All candidates are evaluated through the lens of these principles". Some principles map directly to themes. "Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit" asks leaders to "respectfully challenge decisions when they disagree". That is your conflict story. "Ownership" says leaders "never say 'that's not my job.'" The Tech Interview Handbook says most top tech companies judge candidates against their own values. Read your target company's list before you pick which stories to tell. How stories change with level Google's guide advises judging leadership "with different expectations based on the level of the role". The handbook says people skills matter more as an engineer becomes more senior. In our experience, four things change: Scope. A mid-level story is often about one feature. A senior story is about a system, a team or several teams. "I" and "we". Say "we" for the team's result. Say "I" for your part. At senior level, "I" often means "I aligned three teams", not "I wrote the code". Numbers. "Latency went from 900 ms to 200 ms" beats "it got faster". Trade-offs. Name the option you did not take, and why. Seniors are judged on choices, not only on effort. One story, weak and strong This example is made up. The question is "Tell me about a hard technical call." Weak version: "We had a refund bug. It was a big problem. We worked hard and fixed it. The launch went well." There is no "I", no choice, and no number. The interviewer has nothing to score. Strong version: S: "I was on the payments team. We planned to launch a new refund API in two weeks." T: "I owned the retry logic for the API." A: "In a load test, I found 3 duplicate refunds in 2,000 runs. The cause was a client retry after a timeout. I saw two options: launch on time and clean up by hand, or delay one week to add idempotency keys. I wrote a one-page note with the cost of each. I asked to delay and launch to 5% of users first." R: "The product manager agreed. We had zero duplicate refunds in the first month. I learned to raise this kind of risk at design review, not after it." Said out loud, this takes under a minute. In a real interview, add more detail to the Action, for about two to three minutes in all. Each line answers a probe before it is asked. Follow-up probes Expect follow-ups. Google says so on its tips page. Its re:Work guide shows a behavioural question with three planned follow-ups. Amazon suggests you pause and ask if the interviewer wants more context. Common probes are "Why that option?", "What would you do differently?" and "What did your manager think?" Answer them directly. If you do not remember, say so. Common mistakes No result. The story stops at the action. Blaming others. Others may have made mistakes, but your story is about what you did. A false failure. "I work too hard" is a boast. Amazon says what matters is "what you learned and how you grew". Too long. Google advises "concise narratives". Our advice is about two to three minutes per story. Made-up stories. Never invent one. Follow-ups test the details, and invented details break. Amazon asks for "real examples from your past". Approach Works under follow-up? Cost Use it when Improvise on the day No Stories run long and lose the result. None up front. Never for a loop you care about. Memorise word-for-word scripts Partly. You sound rehearsed and stall on new probes. Many hours. Never. Learn bullets instead. Story bank of 8–10 bullet-point stories Yes A few evenings of recall and writing. Almost always. Map stories to the company's principles Yes Reading the company's list and choosing well. When the company publishes one, as Amazon does. Simple rule: prepare true stories, not answers. Map them to themes, and practise telling each in about two to three minutes. Keep a work log. Each Friday, write one line on a decision, a number or a conflict. Your next story bank writes itself. After an incident, note your own part and the result. The incident review gives you the facts. Save the doc links. A design doc shows the options you weighed. When you interview others, ask for one specific time, then probe: "What did you do?" and "What happened next?" Score against the rubric, not your first impression. The re:Work guide warns about confirmation bias in interviews. When you mentor someone who is job hunting, help them find their stories. See mentoring and sponsorship. AI is a good practice partner. It must never write a story you did not live. "Act as a behavioural interviewer for a senior backend role. Ask me one question. After my answer, ask two follow-up questions that test my own part. Then tell me which STAR part was weakest." "Here is my story as five bullets. Mark every 'we' where my own action is unclear. Tell me where a number is missing. Do not add any facts." "Here are my eight stories. Make a table of which themes each one covers: conflict, failure, ambiguity, influence, ownership, mentoring, technical call. Show the gaps." What to ask the agent Every fact in the story is true. Remove anything the agent added. You can answer three follow-ups on each story without notes. Each story takes two to three minutes when you say it out loud with a timer. The failure story has a real cost and a real change. Claims about how a company hires match its current careers page. What to check yourself Before this: big-tech interview loops and what senior really means. For better stories at work: reviewing human and AI code and idempotency, retries and timeouts. Next: negotiation.

title: Billing, metering and usage-based pricing
text: Count every unit of usage once, put it in the right billing period, and turn it into an invoice you can prove.
body: This story is made up, but each part of it happens. A small company sells an SMS API and charges per message sent. In March, a network problem slowed the link to the billing service. The API servers retried their usage reports. The retry code built each report again, with a new random id each time. The billing service saw many "new" events. It added them all. Forty customers got invoices for about twice the messages they sent. A large customer noticed first, because their own logs showed half the number. The team could not show the real count. The monthly job had stored only running totals, not the events behind them. It took two weeks to rebuild the numbers from server logs. The company refunded everyone. Then it had to answer a harder question: were earlier months wrong too? With usage-based pricing, the bill depends on what the customer did: API calls, messages, gigabytes or tokens. So billing is now a counting problem. If you count wrong, you charge wrong. Counting looks easy. But events get repeated and arrive late. Months start at midnight, but whose midnight? Prices have tiers, and customers change plans mid-month. You need four things: Count each piece of usage exactly once. Put it in the right billing period. Turn the count into money with exact arithmetic. Keep the raw events, so you can prove every number later. The key idea. An invoice is a calculation over raw usage events. Keep the events, give each one a stable id, and you can always recompute and explain the bill. The pipeline Most metering systems have the same steps: Emit. Your service writes a usage event: id, customer, meter name, value and timestamp. Log. The event goes to a durable, append-only log, such as a Kafka topic or an events table. See queues and logs. Dedupe. Copies of the same event are dropped. Aggregate. Combine events per customer, meter and billing period. Rate. The price plan turns the quantity into money. Invoice. At period end, create the invoice, then make it final. Collect. You charge the card or wait for a transfer. Stripe meter events carry an event name, a customer id, a value and an optional timestamp. Stripe aggregates them asynchronously, so totals can lag behind the latest events. Dedupe: exactly-once in effect Networks lose messages, so senders retry. That gives you at-least-once delivery: the same event can arrive twice. The fix is the same as for any idempotent write: a stable id per event. Stripe enforces a unique identifier per meter event within a rolling period of at least 24 hours. OpenMeter handles events that share the same id and source only once. Lago uses a transaction_id. The id must be created once, when the usage happens. It must not be created when you send. Use a UUID or ULID stored with the event. Watch the whole dedupe key, not just the id. On Lago's ClickHouse event store, the timestamp is part of the key. A retry with the same transaction_id but a different timestamp is billed again. So resend the original payload, byte for byte. Stripe only promises its check for at least 24 hours. So run your own dedupe too, on your log, across the whole billing period. Late events and closing a period An event belongs to the period of its event time, not its arrival time. Lago assigns a late event to the right past period by its timestamp. If that period's invoice is already final, the event does not change it. A grace period is the time after a period ends in which late events still count. Stripe's default is 1 hour, and you can set up to 72 hours. It applies to the end-of-cycle invoice, not to threshold invoices. Stripe accepts event timestamps up to 35 days in the past. But an accepted event can still miss its invoice. Usage reported after the grace period is not added to the finalized invoice or to the next one. So decide in advance what happens to very late events. Common choices: bill them as a separate line on the next invoice, or write them off below a set amount. Either way, keep them and count them in reconciliation. Timezones and period boundaries Store every timestamp in UTC. Then define each period boundary as an exact instant. A customer in India expects "November" to start at 00:00 IST on 1 November. That is 18:30 UTC on 31 October. If your job uses UTC days, five and a half hours of usage land in the wrong month, at both ends of the month. Tools often mean a UTC day by "a day". Stripe's pre-aggregated ingestion keeps only the latest event per UTC hour or day. Choose the billing timezone per customer, store it, and test the hours around midnight. Aggregation types A meter says how to combine events. Lago lists count, count unique, sum, max, latest and weighted sum. Stripe meters offer sum, count and last. Type Bills for Example Sum The total of a value Tokens, gigabytes sent Count The number of events API calls Max The peak value Most parallel jobs at once Latest The last reported value Storage used at period end Count unique Distinct values of a property Active users this month Rating, rounding and minor units Price tiers are common. In graduated pricing, each tier's units get that tier's price. Take this plan: the first 10,000 calls are free, the next 90,000 cost ₹0.10 each, and calls above 100,000 cost ₹0.05. For 250,000 calls: 90,000 × 10 paise = 900,000 paise 150,000 × 5 paise = 750,000 paise Total: 1,650,000 paise, which is ₹16,500 Never use floats for money. Unit prices can be smaller than one paise, so store them as exact decimals: a decimal type, or an integer count of a tiny unit. Store line totals and invoice amounts as integers in minor units. Lago allows charges with up to 15 decimal places. It rounds to the currency's smallest unit, such as cents or paise, on the invoice. Multiply exactly, then round once, on the line total. Suppose one request costs 0.555 paise. If you round each event up to 1 paise, you charge about 80% too much. Plan changes and proration A plan change in mid-period splits the fixed fee by time. This is proration. Stripe's example: a move from a £10 plan to a £20 plan halfway through gives a £5 credit and a £10 charge, so the customer owes £5 more. Stripe prorates to the second by default. Usage-based charges are not prorated. Instead, split the usage at the moment of the change. Rate each part with the plan that was active then. Test this path well. Stripe warns that after a mid-cycle price change, usage reported in the grace period does not reach any invoice. Credits and prepaid balances Many customers prepay. Lago calls this a wallet of credits, for example 1 credit = $5. It takes credits off the invoice after tax and after any credit notes. Treat a wallet like an account in your ledger: every top-up and every use is its own entry. Showing usage, and proving it Customers want to see their usage before the invoice. Lago's current-usage endpoint shows the open period and warns that amounts can still change. Label the number "estimated" until the period closes. Once a period is closed, Lago treats its usage as final. A later price change does not touch past invoices. Do the same. Corrections are new entries, never edits. Stripe lets you cancel a meter event only within 24 hours of sending it. It does not change a finalized invoice. Finally, reconcile. Every day, sum the raw events per customer, meter and period. Compare that with your running totals and with the invoice lines. Any gap is a break with an owner. Option Accuracy Cost Use it when Send every raw event to the billing provider Yes The provider sees everything. High. Rate limits apply (Stripe: 1,000 calls a second). Low volume, simple pricing. Pre-aggregate, then send totals Yes, if your own dedupe is correct. Lower. You run the counting. High volume. Keep raw events anyway. Short grace period (1 hour) Lower. More late events miss the invoice. Invoices go out on time. Your senders are fast and reliable. Long grace period (up to 3 days) Higher. Fewer late events missed. Invoices and cash arrive later. Senders batch usage or run on devices. Keep only running totals No You cannot recompute or prove a bill. Cheapest storage. Never for billing. Simple rule: stable ids at the source, raw events kept, one place that rounds, and a daily check that raw events equal invoice lines. In design review, ask: "Where is the event id created?" If the answer is "in the sender, on each send", that is a double-billing bug. Ask: "Can we rebuild last month's invoice from raw events alone?" If not, keep the events before you launch. Write the billing timezone and grace period into the plan data, not into a cron job. Put a test on every tier boundary: 9,999, 10,000, 10,001 and so on. Alert when the daily recon finds a gap, and when late events after close go above a set share. Give each tenant an "estimated" usage page before the first invoice. It catches bugs early. "Write a usage event producer. Create the event id once, when usage is recorded, and resend the same bytes on every retry. Test that three retries carry one id." "Write SQL that sums raw usage events per customer, meter and billing period, using each customer's billing timezone. Compare it with invoice line quantities and list every mismatch." "Write a function that rates graduated price tiers. Store unit prices as exact decimals, multiply exactly, and round once to an integer number of paise per line. Add tests at every tier boundary and for a unit price below one paise." What to ask the agent No floats anywhere in rating. Unit prices are exact decimals; line totals and invoices are integers in minor units. Rounding happens once per line, not per event. Period boundaries come from the customer's timezone. Test 23:59 and 00:01 in that zone. The event id is not generated inside the retry loop. A late event after close is kept and flagged. It is not silently dropped. Corrections add new rows. No UPDATE on raw events or final invoices. What to check yourself Stream processing: windows, watermarks and late events in depth.

title: B-tree vs LSM-tree
text: Every database pays for keeping data sorted on disk. A B-tree pays when you write. An LSM-tree pays later, in the background and on reads.
body: In 2017, Discord stored its chat messages in a Cassandra cluster of 12 nodes. By early 2022, the same cluster had 177 nodes and trillions of messages. The on-call team was paged often, and latency was hard to predict. Writes were cheap. In Cassandra, a write is added to a commit log and to a table in memory. Reads cost more, because they may have to look in memory and in several files on disk. Those files must be merged in the background. This is called compaction. Discord's nodes often fell behind on it. Then reads got more expensive. When a node tried to compact, Discord saw latency that cascaded to other parts of the system. So the team did what they called a "gossip dance". They stopped sending traffic to one node, let it compact, brought it back, and repeated this until the backlog was empty. This is not a Cassandra bug. It is the price of the design that makes its writes cheap. In this lesson you will see where each storage engine pays, so you can choose the costs you can accept. A database keeps data sorted by key, so it can find a row without reading everything. There are two main ways to keep it sorted on disk. A B-tree keeps one sorted tree made of fixed-size pages. It changes those pages in place. To insert a key, it finds the right page and writes that page again. Postgres creates B-tree indexes by default, and MySQL's InnoDB stores its indexes as B-trees. An LSM-tree never changes a file after writing it. It collects new writes in memory, writes them out as a new sorted file, and later merges files in the background. Cassandra works this way, and so do RocksDB and LevelDB. The key idea. A B-tree does the sorting work when you write, in place. An LSM-tree puts that work off and does it later in big batches. Batched work is cheaper per write, but you still pay for it: in background disk work and in slower reads. The LSM-tree paper says it is most useful when you add entries to an index more often than you look them up. The real answer for your data comes from your own load test. Step through one write in an LSM-tree, then one insert in a B-tree. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. B-tree: pages and page splits Disks are read in blocks, so a B-tree is built from pages. In InnoDB a page is 16 KB by default. In Postgres, leaf pages hold keys that point to the table rows. In InnoDB, the primary key index stores the rows themselves. Pages above the leaves hold keys that guide you down to the right leaf. In Postgres, usually over 99% of all pages are leaf pages. A lookup starts at the root and goes down one page per level. Trees stay shallow. Here is a rough example. Say each page is 4 KB and points to 500 pages below it. Then four levels of branching reach 500 × 500 × 500 × 500 = 62.5 billion pages. At 4 KB each, that is about 256 TB. So a handful of page reads can find any key. When a new key does not fit in its leaf page, the page splits. Some keys move to a new page, and the parent page gets a pointer to it. If the parent is full too, it splits as well. When the root splits, the tree gets one level taller. The order of your keys matters. InnoDB tries to leave 1/16 of each page free. If you insert keys in order, pages end up about 15/16 full. If you insert them in random order, pages are between 1/2 and 15/16 full. Random keys, like random UUIDs, cause a second problem. Each insert lands on a different page. When the index is too big for memory, each insert may need a page read and a page write on disk. The LSM-tree paper shows the same effect for an index whose keys arrive in random order. Its example is an index by account ID on a fast-growing History table. A B-tree there can double the disk input and output (I/O) of each transaction. The write-ahead log Changing pages in place is risky. A crash in the middle can leave a page half written. So the database first writes a record of the change to the write-ahead log (WAL) and flushes it to disk. Only after that may the data pages change. After a crash, the database replays the log to redo the missing changes. The log is written in order, so flushing it costs much less than flushing data pages. One flush can even commit many small transactions at once. LSM engines keep a log too. Cassandra calls it the commit log. LSM-tree: memtable, SSTables, compaction A write is added to the commit log on disk. Then it goes into the memtable, a sorted table in memory. When the memtable reaches a size limit, it is flushed to disk as an SSTable. This is a sorted file that is never written again. Over time you get many SSTables. Compaction merges several of them into a new one. Then the old SSTables can be removed. While it merges, compaction drops values that were overwritten. LevelDB's docs say this plainly. A delete is also a write. Cassandra writes a marker called a tombstone. By default, compaction can remove it after 10 days. A read checks the memtable first, then the SSTables. With many SSTables, that can mean many files. A Bloom filter avoids most of this work. Each SSTable has a small filter that answers "this key may be here" or "this key is surely not here". It is sometimes wrong when it says "may be here". It is never wrong when it says "not here". The filter uses memory. In RocksDB, about 10 bits per key gives about 1% false positives. Two ways to compact Size-tiered. Wait until there are several SSTables of a similar size, then merge them. Cassandra starts when it has 4 by default. This rewrites data less often than leveled compaction. But versions of one row can spread over many files, so reads get slower. During a big compaction, the old and new files must fit on disk at the same time. Leveled. Keep files in levels, and make each level about 10 times bigger than the one above. Inside one level, files do not overlap. So a read needs to look at only one SSTable per level. Leveled compaction needs less spare disk, about 10%. But it uses much more disk I/O and CPU when there are many writes. Three kinds of amplification Engineers compare storage engines with three numbers: Write amplification: how many bytes go to disk for each byte your app writes. Read amplification: how many places one read must look. Space amplification: how much disk is used, compared with the size of the live data. You cannot make all three small at once. The RocksDB docs say it plainly. Leveled compaction keeps space low, but costs more reads and writes. Tiered compaction keeps writes low, but costs more reads and space. For leveled compaction, write amplification is often larger than 10. B-trees have write amplification too. In Postgres, each change goes to the WAL first, and later to the data page. So each change reaches disk at least twice. Also, the first change to a page after a checkpoint writes the whole page to the WAL, even if only a few bytes changed. This is on by default. Engine Writes Reads Disk space Watch out for B-tree (Postgres, InnoDB) WAL plus a page write in place. Slows down when the index no longer fits in memory. Fast and steady: one walk from root to leaf. Pages are partly empty, more so with random keys. Random keys, page splits, big indexes. LSM, size-tiered Cheapest. Data is rewritten less often. Slower. One key can be spread over many SSTables. Needs free disk for old and new files during a compaction. Compaction backlog. Slow reads after a burst of writes. LSM, leveled More rewriting. Often over 10x in RocksDB. Better. One SSTable per level. Low. About 10% spare in Cassandra. Heavy compaction I/O and CPU under many writes. Simple rule: start with a B-tree database like Postgres or MySQL. Choose an LSM store when writes clearly dominate, for example events, logs, metrics or chat messages, and plan for compaction from day one. Before you pick a store, write down the read/write ratio, and whether reads are by one key or by a range. That decides more than any benchmark blog. On an LSM store, put pending compactions and SSTables per read on a dashboard. Alert when they keep growing. A backlog that keeps growing is a problem, even before anything fails. Keep enough free disk for compaction to write new files before it deletes the old ones. Put this in the capacity plan. Pick the compaction strategy for the data. The Cassandra docs suggest leveled for read-heavy tables or tables with many updates and deletes. They suggest time window for time-series data with a TTL, and UCS (Unified Compaction Strategy) for new workloads. For B-tree tables with heavy inserts, prefer keys that grow over time, like time-ordered IDs. Random keys spread writes over many pages. Treat deletes on an LSM store as writes. A mass delete creates many tombstones, and they stay until compaction removes them. Load test long enough. A B-tree slows down most when the index outgrows memory. A compaction backlog shows only after hours of writes. "Here is our table schema, our 10 most common queries and our write rate. Tell me whether a B-tree database or an LSM store fits better, and why. For each, say what it costs us in disk space and background work." "Write a load test that inserts 50 million rows into Postgres twice: once with a random UUID primary key and once with a time-ordered key. Report the insert rate over time and the final index size." "Our Cassandra table has slow reads. Here is the schema and the compaction settings. Explain how many SSTables one read may touch, and suggest a compaction strategy with reasons and risks." What to ask the agent Any number the agent gives, like "LSM is 10x faster", comes from a source or from a test you ran. The load test runs long enough for the index to outgrow memory and for compaction to start. The test machine has the same disk type and memory size as production. Free disk for compaction is in the capacity plan, not left to chance. A change of compaction strategy is tried on one node or on a copy first. Bloom filter memory is counted when you size the machines. What to check yourself Next: Secondary, composite and special indexes. It builds on the B-tree pages you saw here. For an LSM database in production, see Cassandra in depth.

title: Caching and cache stampedes
text: A cache makes reads fast and cheap, until one popular key expires and every request rushes to the database at once.
body: This story is made up, but it is common. A shopping app runs a flash sale at 8 pm. The product page for one phone gets 5,000 requests a second. The page data sits in Redis with a TTL of 60 seconds. The database is sized for the normal load: a few hundred queries a second. This works while the cache answers almost every read. At 8:01 pm the key expires. In the next 200 ms, about a thousand requests find nothing in the cache. Each one runs the same heavy query against the database. The database slows down, so the queries take longer. More requests miss while they wait, and they also go to the database. The product page times out, and the sale page shows errors for ten minutes. Nothing was wrong with the code or the cache. One popular key expired at the worst moment. A cache is a fast copy of data that is slow or costly to get. You read the copy instead of asking the database every time. A cache hit is fast. A cache miss means you must go to the source. Every cache has to answer three questions: How does data get in? The app fills it, or the cache fills itself. When does data leave? It expires (TTL), it is deleted on a write (invalidation), or it is pushed out when memory is full (eviction). What happens on a miss? If a key is popular, a miss is not one query. It can be thousands. The key idea. A cache does not just make reads faster. It hides load. When a hot key expires, all that hidden load hits the database at once. Design for that moment. That moment is called a cache stampede. A popular item expires, and many requests miss and rebuild the same item at the same time. The Facebook memcache paper calls a similar problem a thundering herd: writes keep deleting a hot key, so many reads go to the database. Ways to fill a cache Cache-aside. The app checks the cache. On a miss, the app reads the database and writes the value into the cache. Facebook uses its memcache this way. On a write, it updates the database and then deletes the cache key. It deletes instead of updating because deletes are idempotent. Read-through. The app only talks to the cache. On a miss, the cache itself loads from the database. Write-through. Each write goes to the cache and the database together. The cache stays fresh, but every write is slower. Write-behind. Writes go to the cache first and reach the database later, in batches. Writes are fast, but you can lose data if the cache dies first. AWS calls a cache that the app code manages a "side cache", like cache-aside. Read-through and write-through are "inline caches". With an inline cache, the app needs no cache code. But if the cache fails, the app cannot work around it. TTL, invalidation and eviction A TTL sets how long a value lives. Pick it from two facts: how old the data may be, and how often the source changes. Then measure cache hits and misses, and adjust. Invalidation removes a key when the data changes. It keeps data fresh, but you must find every place that writes the data. Eviction removes keys when memory is full. In Redis you set a maxmemory limit and a policy. allkeys-lru removes the least recently used keys. Redis calls it a good default when some keys are read far more often than others. The stampede, step by step Step through what happens when a hot key expires. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Now try it yourself. Turn request coalescing on and off, and change the traffic. Four ways to stop a stampede 1. Request coalescing (single-flight). Only one load runs per key. Others wait for it and share the answer. Go's singleflight package does exactly this inside one server. AWS uses coalescing so only one request is pending for an uncached item. 2. Locks or leases in the cache. Coalescing inside one server still leaves one query per server. With 200 servers, that is 200 queries. A shared lock in the cache fixes this. Facebook's memcache gives out a "lease" token on a miss. By default, it gives at most one token per key every 10 seconds. Other clients are told to wait a moment and try again. In Facebook's case, the herd came from writes that kept deleting a hot key. Over one week, for keys prone to thundering herds, peak database load fell from 17,000 to 1,300 queries a second. 3. Refresh early, with randomness. Refresh a hot key a little before it expires, so it never goes missing. If every server refreshes at the same moment, you get a smaller stampede. So each request decides at random, and the chance rises as expiry gets closer. Also add jitter to TTLs, so keys loaded together do not all expire together. 4. Serve stale while you refresh. Keep the old value a little longer and return it while a refresh runs in the background. Serving stale data does not by itself limit the refresh to one request. Add coalescing or a lock, so only one request fetches the new value. HTTP has a header for serving stale data: stale-while-revalidate. With max-age=600, stale-while-revalidate=30, a response is fresh for 600 seconds. A cache may then serve it stale for 30 more seconds while it checks for a new copy. AWS describes a similar idea: refresh after a "soft" TTL, and keep using the old value until a "hard" TTL if the source fails. Fix Stops the stampede? Cost Use it when Request coalescing in each server Partly. One query per server, not one in total. Small code change. Always, as a first step. Lock or lease in the shared cache Yes One query in total. Waiting clients add latency. Lost locks need a timeout. Many servers and very hot keys. Early refresh with jitter Yes, for keys that are read often. Some extra loads before they are needed. Hot keys you can predict. Stale-while-revalidate Yes, with coalescing. Users get the old value fast. Users may see data a few seconds old. Data where a little staleness is fine, like product pages. Longer TTL only No It only makes stampedes rarer. More stale data. Data that rarely changes. Simple rule: add coalescing everywhere. For your top keys, add stale-while-revalidate or a lease too. Ask in design reviews: "What happens to the database if the cache is empty?" If the answer is "it crashes", you depend on the cache. Plan for a cold start. Know your hot keys. Track the top keys by reads. A sale, a viral post or a homepage banner creates new ones. Decide how stale each kind of data may be. Write it down: "prices: 5 seconds, product text: 10 minutes". Watch hit rate, evictions and database load on the same dashboard. A falling hit rate is an early warning. Never flush the whole cache in production without a plan. It turns every key into a miss at once. Cache "not found" and error results too, with a short TTL. Otherwise a missing item sends every request to the database. AWS suggests a separate TTL for error results. "Wrap this getProduct function with cache-aside in Redis. Use request coalescing so only one database call runs per key at a time." "Add a soft TTL and a hard TTL. After the soft TTL, return the cached value and refresh it in the background. Add 10% random jitter to both." "Write a load test where 1,000 requests ask for the same key just after it expires. Assert that the database gets at most 1 query." What to ask the agent The coalescing key is the cache key, not something that differs per user. A failed or slow load does not leave other callers waiting forever. There is a timeout. A lock in Redis has an expiry, so a crashed server does not hold it forever. On a write, the code deletes or updates the cache after the database commit. Error results are not cached for as long as good results. What to check yourself Related lessons: Distributed caches, CDN and HTTP caching and Redis in depth.

title: CAP, PACELC and consistency models
text: When the network splits, every copy of your data must choose between answering and being right. The rest of the time, it chooses between fast and right.
body: A shoe brand runs a flash sale in two regions, Mumbai and Singapore. There are 500 pairs. The stock count lives in a database that copies data between the regions. Both regions accept orders. Ten minutes into the sale, the link between the regions breaks for four minutes. Both sides keep selling. Each side thinks it has the full count. When the link comes back, the team finds 620 orders for 500 pairs. Support spends a week on refunds and apologies. In the same company, the payments team uses a different database. During the same four minutes, it refused every write in Singapore. Those users saw "Payment failed, try again". Both teams wrote the same thing in the incident channel: "the database broke". It did not. Each database did exactly what it was built to do. Nobody had written down which choice the business wanted. This story is made up, but each part of it happens in real systems. You keep copies of your data on several machines, called replicas. Sometimes the network between them fails, but the machines keep running. This is a network partition. During a partition, a replica that gets a request has only two options: Answer now. It may return old data, or accept a write that conflicts with the other side. The system stays available. Wait or refuse. It does not answer until it can check with the other side. The data stays consistent. That is the CAP theorem. Gilbert and Lynch proved it in 2002. No system can promise both consistency and availability when messages between nodes can be lost. People often say CAP means "pick 2 of 3". Eric Brewer presented the idea in a keynote talk in 2000. In 2012 he wrote that "2 of 3" is misleading. You cannot simply pick "no partitions", because networks can fail. But partitions are rare. When there is no partition, a system can be both consistent and available. The key idea. CAP is a rule for one bad moment: the network is split. In that moment, each cut-off replica chooses between answering and being right. The rest of the time, the real choice is between fast and right. Step through the shoe sale with one item left. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. What C and A mean in CAP The words in CAP are narrow. Consistency means linearizability: the system must act as if there is one copy and each operation happens at one instant. It is not the C in ACID. Availability means every request that reaches a working node gets an answer that is not an error. Not "most requests", and not "some node answers". With these strict meanings, many real databases are neither CP nor AP. Kleppmann gives an example: one leader with async followers. A client cut off from the leader cannot write, so it is not available. Reads from a lagging follower can be stale, so it is not linearizable either. So do not label a whole database. Ask what each operation does during a partition. PACELC: the trade you make every day Abadi pointed out a second trade-off that matters more day to day. He called the full picture PACELC: If there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency. Else, in normal running, choose Latency or Consistency. Why is there a trade when the network is fine? As soon as you copy data, a consistent read or write must coordinate with other replicas or a leader. That takes time. Over long distances, you cannot avoid this wait. Abadi gives an example from a study of Cassandra. Reads that check several replicas were compared with reads from any one replica. The latency difference could be a factor of four or more. Who chooses what Abadi classified well-known systems by their original default settings: PA/EL: Dynamo, Cassandra and Riak. They give up consistency during a partition, and for lower latency in normal running. PC/EC: VoltDB/H-Store, Megastore, BigTable and HBase. They pay in availability and latency to stay consistent. PC/EL: Yahoo's PNUTS. Fast and less consistent normally, but it refuses updates to data whose master node is cut off by a partition. PA/EC: MongoDB, as it worked in 2012. Many of these systems let you change the trade. In Cassandra-style stores, you can ask more replicas to answer each read and write. You get more consistency, though still not linearizability, and pay with latency. GitHub saw the cost of a short partition in 2018. A 43-second network cut caused a failover. Both data centres then had writes the other did not have. During recovery, they chose "to prioritize data integrity over site usability and time to recovery". The site was degraded for 24 hours and 11 minutes. The consistency ladder "Consistent" and "eventually consistent" are not the only options. There is a ladder of consistency models in between. Each step down promises less, and is easier to keep available and fast. Linearizable. Once a write is done, every later read, by anyone, sees it. The system acts like one copy. Use it for a lock, a unique username, or the last item in stock. It cannot stay available during a partition. Sequential. Everyone sees all operations in the same order, and each client's own order is kept. But that order does not have to match real time. Like linearizability, it cannot stay available during a partition. Causal. If one operation may have caused another, everyone sees them in that order. A reply never appears before the comment it answers. Unrelated operations may appear in different orders to different people. Read-your-writes. After you save something, your own later reads show it. Other users may see it later. Eventual. If writes stop for a while, all replicas end up the same. The basic promise says nothing about when, or what you see before that. Causal consistency and read-your-writes can stay available during a partition, if each client keeps talking to the same server. That makes them useful for feeds, comments and profiles. Model During a partition Normal latency Good for Linearizable No Cut-off nodes must wait or refuse. Highest. Operations must coordinate with other replicas or a leader. Locks, unique names, stock counts, money moves. Sequential No Same as linearizable. High. Cases where all must agree on one order, and a short delay is fine. Causal Yes, if each client stays on one server. Low to medium. Comments and replies, chat, feeds. Read-your-writes Yes, if each client stays on one server. Low. Profiles and settings a user just changed. Eventual Yes Lowest. Like counts, view counts, caches, search indexes. Simple rule: decide per operation, not per database. Ask what a wrong answer costs and what an error costs, then pick the weakest model the business can live with. For each write path, ask: "If the network splits right now, should this fail or should it accept and fix later?" Write the answer in the design doc. Treat "CP" and "AP" in vendor docs as a hint, not a fact. Read which operations wait, which refuse, and what the default settings are. Measure the latency cost. A consistent read in another region costs a round trip on every request, partition or not. If you choose AP, design the repair before launch: how to detect conflicts, which side wins, and who tells the customer. Brewer calls this partition recovery. Use stronger models only where they are worth the cost. A stock count may need linearizable writes. The product description next to it does not. Test with a real partition. Cut the network between replicas in a test environment, and watch what your app does. "Here is our order service. List every database write. For each, tell me what happens if the replicas in two regions cannot talk for 5 minutes, with our current settings." "We use Cassandra with replication factor 3. Explain which read and write consistency levels give us read-your-writes for one user, and what each choice costs in latency." "Write a test that starts two replicas, cuts the network between them, writes on both sides, heals the network, and checks that our conflict rule keeps both orders." What to ask the agent The agent's claims about a database's behaviour match that database's own docs and version. CAP labels on blogs are often wrong. The settings it suggests are the ones your code really sends. Many clients have their own default consistency level. The partition test cuts the network between replicas. Killing a node is a different failure. The conflict rule never silently drops a paid order or a payment. Every operation that needs linearizable behaviour is listed, and a person agreed to its latency cost. What to check yourself Before this: Replication explains replication lag and read-your-writes in detail. Next: Quorums and leaderless replication, and Multi-region systems and data locality for what these choices cost across regions.

title: Career ladders and level expectations
text: Your company writes down what each level means. Learn to read that document, find your gap, and show the next level with real evidence.
body: This story is made up, but it happens in many companies. Priya is a mid-level backend engineer at a product company in Bengaluru. She closes more tickets than anyone on her team. Her code reviews are fast and careful. In March she expects to become a senior engineer. Her manager tells her the promotion was not approved. Priya is shocked. "I delivered more than anyone," she says. Her manager opens the company's career ladder. Priya has never read it. The senior level asks for three things she has not done. Own a project with an unclear goal. Lead work with other teams. Help newer engineers grow. Priya did excellent mid-level work, faster than anyone. But she never showed the next level. Her manager also made a mistake. He never showed her the ladder, and he never gave her work that could show those skills. Neither of them had read it closely until the day of the "no". A career ladder is a document that says what each job level expects. It has three parts: the levels, the dimensions, and the expectations for each level in each dimension. The prereq lesson, what senior really means, explained scope, ambiguity and ownership. This lesson is about the document itself: how to read it and use it. Levels. Many ladders go from junior to mid-level, senior, staff and principal. Names differ a lot. Dropbox uses IC1 to IC7 for engineers, and M3 to M7 for managers. CircleCI's 2018 matrix went from E1, for an Associate Engineer, up to E6, for a Principal Engineer. Rent the Runway's public ladder used names like Engineer II and Senior Engineer I. At GitLab, the manager track is a separate path, not a promotion. GitLab says staff-level and engineering manager roles "are equivalent in terms of base compensation and prestige." So at GitLab, moving to management is a change of job, not a step up. Many companies work the same way. Check your own ladder. Dimensions. Each ladder groups skills differently. In this lesson we use five common areas: Technical skill: design, code quality, debugging. Delivery and impact: shipping work that matters. Scope and ambiguity: how big and how unclear your problems are. Influence and communication: how far your ideas reach. People: mentoring and helping others grow. Dropbox's five core responsibilities are Results, Direction, Talent, Culture and Craft. Rent the Runway's ladder had the columns Technical Skill, Get Stuff Done, Impact, and Communication & Leadership. Each company's ladder is its own. Always read yours, not another company's. The key idea. A ladder describes the next level. You get promoted by showing evidence for it, not by doing your current level faster. Scope grows as you go up: task, then feature, then project, then many teams, then the org. Dropbox's ladder shows this in its own words. IC2 works "on defined projects to achieve team-level goals". IC3 owns "projects in service of quarterly goals on the team". IC4 owns "semi-annual/annual goals for my team", and its reach is "beginning to extend outside my team". IC5, the staff level, delivers "multi-year, multi-team product or platform goals". The weight of each dimension also changes. Rent the Runway's notes say technical skill and getting things done are "the primary drivers of promotions at lower levels". At higher levels, the weight "gradually shifts" to impact, and to communication and leadership. Priya's story fits this pattern. Step through how to read your own ladder. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Here are the steps in words: Get the ladder. Ask your manager for the current version. Read your level and the next one. Map your evidence. For each dimension, write real examples with links: design docs, pull requests, incident notes. Find the gap. Look for empty rows. One thin row matters more than three strong ones. Agree on it. Show the map to your manager in a one-on-one. Ask: "Do you see the same gap?" Get the work. Ask for a project that can show the gap. Then do it and record the results. Ladders are guides, not checklists. Dropbox says its framework "is not a promotion checklist". CircleCI calls its matrix "a guideline" and expects "smaller deviations". Rent the Runway notes that not everyone grows in every column "in lockstep". The promotion process At many companies, your manager writes or sponsors a promotion case. Will Larson suggests you also write your own promotion packet, early, as a guide. His template for staff promotions asks about your projects and their impact, people you mentored, your glue work, and your known gaps. In the end, it goes to "an internal promotion committee or process". Many companies also hold calibration meetings. Larson describes them as "rounds of reviewing performance designations and reviews". Promotions are "typically also considered" there. In calibration, people from other teams compare cases, so your evidence must be clear to strangers. Doing the job before the title GitLab separates coaching from promotion. Coaching shows what you need to do. The promotion process "documents what an engineer has already done". So you usually show the next level before you get it. This has real limits. You may do bigger work for months at your old pay. Some steps also need an open role. At GitLab, moving from senior to staff or manager needs "a position of need". Larson found that about a third of the staff engineers he surveyed changed companies to get the title. Roughly half of the women he spoke with had to change companies to get the staff title. So the system is not always fair. Agree on clear goals and a timeline with your manager. Way to use the ladder Gets you promoted? Cost Watch out for Ignore it and work hard No Speed at your level rarely shows the next level. Low effort now, a surprise later. You find the gap on the day of the "no". Treat it as a checklist Sometimes. You chase lines, not impact. Ticked boxes with no real result do not convince a committee. Map evidence and agree on the gap Yes This is the clearest path. Regular talks with your manager, and some writing. A manager change can reset the agreement. Keep it written down. Switch companies for a title Sometimes. A new team and new trust to build. The title may not mean the same level at the new company. Titles do not travel. Level names do not move cleanly between companies. Rent the Runway's ladder uses names like "Senior Engineer I". Dropbox uses codes like "IC3 Software Engineer". So compare scope and pay, not the word on the title. On Levels.fyi you can search self-reported pay by company, job title and career level. For pay talks, see negotiation and compensation. Glue work. Tanya Reilly uses "glue work" for things like unblocking teammates, reviewing design docs and onboarding new people. She calls it technical leadership. But she warns that "doing glue work too early can be career limiting". In her story, the engineer did so much glue work that she did not get better at coding. If you do glue work, make it visible and connect it to a ladder dimension. Read the next level of your ladder this week. Write one line of evidence per dimension. Keep a "brag document": a running list of your work, with links and results. Julia Evans suggests this, and says many people update it "every 2 weeks". In your next one-on-one, ask: "Which dimension is my weakest for the next level?" Ask for work that tests that dimension. For influence, offer to write a design doc for a cross-team change. For the people dimension, mentor one newer engineer. See mentoring and sponsorship. Show impact in business terms, not only in tickets. Working with PMs helps here. When you lead others, help them read their ladders too. Count their glue work in their reviews. When you change jobs, compare scope and pay, not titles. Interviewers check level too: see big-tech interview loops and behavioural interviews. An AI assistant is useful for organising your evidence. It cannot judge your level. Only your company's ladder and the people in calibration can do that. "Here is my company's ladder for the next level, and my list of work from the last six months. Map each piece of work to one dimension. List the dimensions with no evidence." "Rewrite these three project notes as short evidence lines. Each line should say what I did, what changed, and a number if I gave one. Do not add facts." "Here is the gap my manager and I agreed on. Suggest three kinds of work that would show it." What to ask the agent Every line of evidence is true, and you can link to proof. The agent did not add numbers or results you never gave it. It used your company's ladder words, not general career advice. Your manager agrees with the gap. The agent's view does not count in calibration. You did not paste private company data into a tool your company does not allow. What to check yourself Before this: what senior really means. Related: negotiation and compensation and mentoring and sponsorship.

title: Cassandra in depth
text: Cassandra makes writes cheap and pays later, in compaction, tombstones and repair. Learn where each cost lands, so deleted data stays deleted and reads stay fast.
body: Uber runs Cassandra as an internal service. In 2023 it had tens of thousands of nodes and tens of millions of queries per second. Clusters ranged from 6 to 450 nodes. Teams that used it reported a strange problem: "data inconsistency due to data resurrection". Data they had deleted came back. Uber's write-up names the usual causes: "Frequent data deletions and downed nodes". The fix was repair, the background job that makes replicas agree. Uber's repairs were slow. Its p99 repair time was "tens of days". With Cassandra's default grace period of 10 days, a repair that takes tens of days cannot keep up. Uber's post does not say which grace period it used. So Uber made repair part of Cassandra itself, like compaction. It works through the ring node by node and needs no outside control plane. The p99 repair time fell to "just under a single-digit number of days". Some use cases that relied heavily on lightweight transactions saw higher error rates "every other week". The cause was in node replacement. The new node kept looking up the old node's hostname. When that lookup failed, its view of pending ring changes no longer matched the other nodes. None of this is a bug in your queries. It is how Cassandra stores and deletes data. This lesson shows the parts you must run yourself. You already know two halves of Cassandra. Quorums and leaderless replication covers consistency levels, hints, read repair and Merkle-tree repair. B-tree vs LSM-tree covers the memtable, SSTables and compaction. Data modelling for NoSQL covers partition keys and time buckets. This lesson joins them. Cassandra never changes a file on disk. So a delete cannot remove data. It writes a marker instead, a tombstone. Every replica must see that marker before any replica throws it away. The key idea. In Cassandra, a delete is a write that must reach every replica before its grace period ends. Compaction cleans up, and repair makes sure there is nothing left to bring back. You must run both well. The write path A write first goes to a commit log on disk, added at the end. Then it goes into the memtable in memory. By default the commit log uses "periodic" sync. The write is acknowledged at once, and the log is synced every 10 seconds. A crash can lose up to that period, or more if a sync is late. When the memtable is full, Cassandra flushes it to a new SSTable. That file is never written again. So one partition is usually spread over several SSTables. The read path A read must merge the memtable and every SSTable that may hold the partition. Each SSTable has a Bloom filter. It says "surely not here" or "maybe here", so most files are skipped. For a file that may have it, a partition index points to the data's place in the file. The read keeps the newest value for each cell, by timestamp. A tombstone hides every older value. So a read for live rows must still step over tombstones. The default false-positive chance is 0.01 for most tables and 0.1 for leveled ones. Going from 0.1 to 0.01 roughly triples the filter's memory. Tombstones and the grace period Step through one delete. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. The grace period is the table setting gc_grace_seconds. Its default is 864000 seconds, which is 10 days. After that, compaction may drop the tombstone. It needs every older SSTable for that partition in the same compaction. An expired TTL also becomes a tombstone. By default, Cassandra does not run repair for you. Since 5.0.8 it has a built-in scheduler, Auto Repair, but you must turn it on. With the default grace period, the docs say to repair every node at least once every 7 days. If you lower gc_grace_seconds, repair must run more often. You can also set only_purge_repaired_tombstones, so only repaired tombstones are dropped. Too many tombstones A scan keeps the tombstones it sees in memory. That can hurt performance and even exhaust the heap. So cassandra.yaml sets two limits. By default, tombstone_warn_threshold is 1,000 and tombstone_failure_threshold is 100,000. A read that scans more than 1,000 tombstones logs a warning. More than 100,000 and the read fails. The classic way to reach them is a queue in a table. Workers read the oldest rows in a partition and delete them. Every read for "the next job" now walks past all recent deletes. The yaml file links to a DataStax post about this anti-pattern. Use a real queue or log instead. See queues vs logs. Large partitions A partition lives on one set of replicas. A huge one cannot be spread across the cluster. Cassandra 5.0 has guardrails, partition_size_warn_threshold and partition_size_fail_threshold. They are off by default. The fix is in the key, for example a time bucket. The NoSQL modelling lesson shows how. Compaction strategies Strategy Best for Watch out for Size-tiered (STCS) The default, a fallback. Data that is not strict time series, or when LCS costs too much I/O. Reads touch more SSTables. Leveled (LCS) Read-heavy tables, or many updates and deletes. Not for immutable time series. Time window (TWCS) TTL'ed, mostly immutable time series. Out-of-order writes and USING TIMESTAMP mix old and new data. Unified (UCS) Recommended for new workloads. New in 5.0. TWCS merges each closed window into one SSTable, then leaves it alone. When everything in it expires, Cassandra can drop the whole file. Aim for about 20 to 30 windows. With a 90-day TTL, 3-day windows fit. UCS has one scaling setting. Tiered values act like STCS, leveled values like LCS. Its default, T4, is STCS with a threshold of 4. Lightweight transactions and counters INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS and UPDATE ... IF use Paxos. The docs warn of "a non-negligible performance cost". The legacy Paxos (v1), still the default, needs about 4 round trips for a write. Paxos v2 needs about 2. Cassandra 4.1 added v2. INSERT INTO usernames (name, user_id) VALUES ('asha', 42) IF NOT EXISTS; -- check [applied] in the resultCounters are a special column type. Apart from its primary key, a table with a counter can hold only counters. You cannot set a value or give it a TTL. Counter updates are not idempotent. After a timeout, a retry "may or may not lead to an over count". The token ring Each node owns tokens on a hash ring. With virtual nodes, a node owns many small ranges. Cassandra 4.0 cut the default num_tokens from 256 to 16. A smarter token allocator now spreads data well with few tokens. Many tokens tie many nodes together and raise the risk of an outage. ScyllaDB calls itself "a drop-in replacement for Apache Cassandra 3.11", with some 4.0 features. Check its table for the features you use. Choice Good for Cost Lower gc_grace_seconds Yes Fewer tombstones to scan. Repair must finish inside the shorter window. Otherwise zombies. TTL instead of deletes, with TWCS Yes Whole files expire. Breaks with out-of-order writes. Lightweight transactions Yes Check-and-set in one partition. More round trips than a plain write. Counters Yes Fast increments. Retries can over count. Commit log in batch mode Yes A write is acknowledged only after the log is synced to disk. Each write waits for that sync. Simple rule: if a table has deletes, schedule repair inside gc_grace_seconds before you go live. If a table works like a queue, move it out of Cassandra. For each table, write down how rows die: delete, TTL, or never. Pick the compaction strategy from that answer. Alert when repair has not finished on every node within the grace period. Missing it is silent until data comes back. Watch tombstone warnings in the logs. Each one names a query that scans too much. Before a design review, ask, "Does any read step over many deleted rows?" Queues, inboxes and "latest status" tables are the usual suspects. Use lightweight transactions only where a race costs money or trust, such as unique usernames. Measure their latency. Keep the same num_tokens on every node in a data centre. A new node with a different value owns a different share of data. "Here is our Cassandra schema and every query. For each table, tell me how rows are removed, the compaction strategy you would pick, and why. Flag any table that behaves like a queue." "Write a test on a 3-node cluster. Stop one node, delete a row, set gc_grace_seconds to 60, compact the others, start the node and run repair. Show whether the row comes back." "Find every counter update and IF condition in this code. For each, say what happens on a timeout and a retry." What to ask the agent Repair is scheduled, finishes, and alerts on failure, at least once per gc_grace_seconds. The agent's compaction advice matches your Cassandra version. UCS needs 5.0. No code retries a counter update blindly. Version-specific defaults the agent quotes, like num_tokens or paxos_variant, match your cassandra.yaml. A test that "proves" deletes work also includes a node that was down during the delete. What to check yourself Before this: Quorums and leaderless replication, B-tree vs LSM-tree and Data modelling for NoSQL. Related: Sharding and consistent hashing and Consensus and Raft, for what Paxos-style agreement costs.

title: CDNs and HTTP caching
text: A CDN answers from a copy near the user. Your HTTP headers decide what it may copy, for how long, and for whom.
body: Early on 25 December 2015 (Pacific time), the Steam Store was under a denial-of-service attack. Traffic to the store rose by 2,000% over the average during the Steam Sale. To reduce the load on its store servers, Valve deployed caching rules managed by a web caching partner. During a second wave of the attack, a second caching setting was deployed. In Valve's words, it "incorrectly cached web traffic for authenticated users". So pages built for logged-in users were cached and returned to other users. Between 11:50 and 13:20 PST, store page requests for about 34,000 users may have been shown to someone else. Those pages could contain a billing address, the last four digits of a Steam Guard phone number, purchase history, the last two digits of a card number, or an email address. Full card numbers and passwords were not exposed. Valve shut down the store and deployed a new caching setting. The store stayed down until all caching settings were checked and cached data was purged from the edge servers. Valve called it a configuration error. The cache did what its settings said, and the settings were wrong. This lesson is about writing those settings well. A CDN (content delivery network) keeps copies of your content in data centers that are closer to users than your own servers. This makes pages faster and takes load off your servers. The data centers near users are called edge locations. Your own server, which has the real content, is the origin server. An edge location is a shared cache: it stores responses and reuses them for more than one user. A browser cache is a private cache: it serves one user only. The CDN must answer two questions for each response: May I store this, and for how long? Your Cache-Control header answers this. Which later requests may get this copy? The cache key answers this. The key idea. A CDN is only as safe as your headers and your cache key. If two different users can produce the same cache key, they can see each other's pages. Step through two users and one deploy. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Cache-Control: the rules you send You set the rules with the Cache-Control response header. The main directives, from RFC 9111 section 5.2: max-age=N: the response is fresh for N seconds. s-maxage=N: the same, but only for shared caches like a CDN. It overrides max-age there. public: a shared cache may store this, even for a request with an Authorization header. private: a shared cache must not store this. A browser may. no-cache: you may store it, but you must check with the origin before each reuse. no-store: do not store any part of the request or the response. The names no-cache and no-store confuse many people. MDN says it plainly: no-cache does not mean "don't cache". If you mean "don't store", use no-store. MDN also says to add private to pages made for one user, especially after login. Without it, a shared cache may reuse the page for many users and leak personal data. That is what happened to Steam. CDNs add their own defaults on top. Cloudflare does not cache HTML or JSON by default. It also skips responses with private, no-store, no-cache or max-age=0, or with a Set-Cookie header. Fastly does not cache private responses, and reads s-maxage before max-age. Check your own CDN's docs. They differ. ETag and 304: checking without downloading When a cached copy becomes stale, the cache does not have to download it again. The origin can send an ETag, a short ID for this version of the content. Later, the client sends that ID back in an If-None-Match header. If the content has not changed, the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body. The client keeps using its copy. You save bandwidth, but you still pay one round trip to the origin. The cache key, and Vary The cache key decides which requests share one stored copy. In the standard, it is at least the request method and the URL. Fastly uses the URL, including the query string, plus the Host header. Cloudflare's default key also uses the full URL, plus a few headers such as Origin. Notice what is not in the key: the cookie or the logged-in user. Two users who ask for /account get the same key. So a shared cache must never store a personal page. Sometimes one URL can return different versions, chosen by the request headers. The Vary header names those request headers. Caches then store a separate copy for each value. A cache may reuse a copy without checking the origin only if those request headers match. Every extra part of the key splits your traffic into more copies. Cloudflare warns that custom cache keys can reduce your cache hit rate. The cache hit ratio is the share of requests the edge answers from its own copy. A high ratio means a cheap, fast origin. A low ratio means the CDN mostly forwards traffic. Changing content: purge or a new name When content changes, you have two choices. A cache purge. You tell the CDN to drop copies.
