Cloudflare can purge one URL, a prefix, a tag, a hostname or everything. It recommends purging single URLs. Fastly has URL, surrogate key and purge-all options. A soft purge marks a copy stale, so it can still be served while a new one is fetched. A hard purge removes it, so the next request goes to the origin. Purge-all is always hard. A new file name. Put a version or a hash in the file name, like app.c3d4.js. Never change a file at the same name. This is called cache busting. Each file can then use a long max-age plus immutable, and the HTML can use no-cache. The HTML is checked on each load, and it points to the new names. Stale content and failures Two more directives help when a copy goes stale. With stale-while-revalidate, a cache may serve the stale copy for a short time. Meanwhile it fetches a fresh one in the background. With stale-if-error, it may serve the stale copy when the origin returns a 500, 502, 503 or 504 error. Both come from a separate standard, RFC 5861, not from RFC 9111. The lesson on caching and cache stampedes shows why this matters for hot keys. At a CDN, many users may miss on the same URL at once. Fastly's request collapsing sends only one of them to the origin, and the rest share the answer. Origin shield A CDN has many edge locations. Each one that misses goes to your origin. A shield adds one more layer. Edges ask a chosen shield location, and only the shield asks the origin. Cloudflare's Tiered Cache works the same way, with lower tiers and upper tiers. This reduces origin requests. The cost: traffic between Fastly locations counts toward your bill. Also, a request that reaches the origin counts as two misses, so your reported hit ratio can look lower than you expect. Choice Fresh content? Origin load Use it when Long max-age + hashed file names Yes A new name is fetched at once. Very low. JS, CSS, images and fonts from your build. Short max-age (seconds to minutes) Mostly. Users may see data that old. Medium. Public pages that change often, like a product list. no-cache + ETag Yes Every reuse is checked. One small request per reuse. HTML pages that point to hashed files. Purge on change Yes, after the purge. A burst of misses after each purge. Content you cannot rename, like an article URL. private or no-store Yes High. The CDN answers none of these requests. Anything personal: accounts, carts, tokens. Simple rule: hash your static files and cache them for a long time. Mark every logged-in response private. Cache public HTML only for a short time. Set Cache-Control on every response, on purpose. Do not leave the choice to CDN defaults. For each new endpoint, ask: "Is this response the same for every user?" If not, it is private or no-store. When you add CDN rules, test them with two different logged-in users. Check that user B never sees user A's data. Review CDN config changes like code. The Steam leak came from a cache setting deployed in a hurry. Fastly's 2021 outage came from a valid customer config change that hit a hidden bug. About 85% of its network returned errors. Track the cache hit ratio and origin requests per second. A sudden drop often means a new query string or header split the cache key. Avoid purge-all in busy hours. At Fastly, purge-all is a hard purge, so every object must be fetched from the origin again. Know your plan B. If the CDN fails, can your origin carry the full traffic? "List every HTTP endpoint in this service and the Cache-Control header it sends. Mark any response that depends on the logged-in user but is not private or no-store." "Change our build so JS and CSS files get a content hash in the name. Serve them with max-age=31536000, immutable, and serve index.html with no-cache." "Write a test that logs in as two users, requests /account through the CDN, and fails if the second user sees the first user's email." What to ask the agent No response with personal data can be stored in a shared cache. Look for Set-Cookie and Authorization paths. The agent did not add Vary: Cookie or user IDs to the cache key "to be safe". That splits the cache into one copy per user. Hashed file names change when the content changes, and only then. The CDN config change is reviewed, and you know how to roll it back. What to check yourself Related lessons: Caching and cache stampedes, HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, Scaling reads and Safe deploys and config changes.

title: Chaos engineering and game days
text: Break your system on purpose, a little at a time and with a stop button, so you find its weak spots before a real outage does.
body: Slack has an internal tool called Confabulator. Engineers use it to change configuration, including during incidents. In one bad incident, it did not work, and the team had to deploy the change by hand. The tool had an emergency mode. When Slack itself was down, emergency mode skipped the check that needed Slack. On paper, that was the fallback. So the team rebuilt the failure on purpose, in a planned exercise. They cut Confabulator off from Slack and tried a change that did nothing. The error came back. The cause was small. Both modes posted a notice of each change to a Slack channel. That post had no timeout. With Slack down, the post hung. The whole request then hit its own time limit before the change was made. So even emergency mode could never finish a change while Slack was down. Slack then improved its deploy tools and checked the timeout and retry settings of its critical systems. A real incident showed the symptom. A planned exercise reproduced it safely and found the cause. Chaos engineering is "the discipline of experimenting on a system in order to build confidence in the system's capability to withstand turbulent conditions in production." In plain words: you cause a small, real failure on purpose. Tools call this fault injection. You watch whether users still get what they need. If they do, your confidence grows. If they do not, you found a weak spot while you were ready for it. A game day is the team version. You plan a failure, everyone who would respond takes part, and you review what happened afterwards. The key idea. Every timeout, failover and fallback is a guess until it has run. A chaos experiment runs it on purpose: small, watched, with a stop button, at a time you pick. Where it came from Netflix built Chaos Monkey for its move to the AWS cloud. It "randomly disables our production instances", to check that Netflix survives that common failure. Netflix ran it during business days, "with engineers standing by". Today the tool still randomly ends virtual machines and containers. Its idea: if engineers see failures often, they build services that survive them. In April 2011, AWS had a large outage in US-East. Netflix kept running, with more errors and latency than usual. But leaving the bad zone took manual work by many teams. Chaos Monkey killed single services, but Netflix did not simulate a whole zone going down. Engineers started to talk about a "Chaos Gorilla" for that. By July 2011, Netflix described a whole Simian Army, some of it still only planned. Latency Monkey adds delays between services. Chaos Gorilla would simulate the loss of a whole availability zone. The principles The site principlesofchaos.org describes an experiment in four steps: Define the steady state: a measurable output that shows normal behaviour. Guess that this steady state will continue in a control group and in an experimental group. Add real-world events, such as servers that crash or network links that are cut. Try to prove the guess wrong, by looking for a difference between the two groups. It then gives five advanced principles: Build a hypothesis around steady state behaviour. Measure the system's outputs, such as throughput or errors, not its internal attributes. Vary real-world events. Pick events by impact or by how often they happen. Include non-failures, like a traffic spike. Run experiments in production. Real traffic is "the only way to reliably capture the request path". Automate experiments to run continuously. Manual runs do not last. Minimise blast radius. Some short-term harm is allowed, but the chaos engineer must keep it small and contained. An experiment is not a test A test checks a behaviour you already know, and it passes or fails. An experiment asks a question about the whole system under real conditions. The principles say chaos "verifies that the system does work, rather than trying to validate how it works." AWS asks you to do both. Keep your normal resilience tests, and add chaos experiments to find what you did not know. Once an experiment passes, AWS suggests keeping it as an automated regression test in your pipeline. Run one experiment safely Step through an example experiment on a checkout service. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Measure normal first. AWS gives an example: a payments system that handles 300 transactions a second, with 99% success and a 500 ms round trip. Use the metrics from Observability, SLOs and error budgets. Write the hypothesis. AWS's template: "If {specific fault} occurs, the {workload name} workload will {describe mitigating controls} to maintain {business or technical metric impact}." Start outside production. AWS recommends trying each fault in a non-production environment first. There you also check that your stop conditions fire. Slack runs every exercise in dev first. Then it decides whether to go on to production. It seriously considers stopping if automatic repair did not work, did not work perfectly or was slow. Most of all, it considers stopping if customers would see more than a short, minor rise in latency. Keep the blast radius small. In production, use a control group and an experiment group, as in a canary release. A feature flag can pick the 1%. Set a stop condition. In AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS), a stop condition is a CloudWatch alarm. If it fires, FIS stops the experiment, and you cannot resume it. Pick the time and the people. AWS suggests off-peak hours for your first production runs. Netflix ran Chaos Monkey on business days, with engineers standing by. Pick a quiet time of day when the team is at work and watching. Slack picks a well-announced time, with the experts in one room or video call. Tell support and operations teams, and give them a way to report trouble. Restore, record, repeat. Bring the system back to a known-good state. Save dashboards and notes with the time and conditions. Here is an FIS stop condition, linked to an alarm you created: { "stopConditions": [ { "source": "aws:cloudwatch:alarm", "value": "arn:aws:cloudwatch:eu-west-1:123456789012:alarm:checkout-p99-high" } ] }What to inject, and with what Start with the failures your design claims to survive. AWS lists: lost instances, a database failover, CPU and memory stress, added latency, dropped packets and DNS failures. To test a fallback, block a third-party provider for seconds or hours. Slack's Confabulator exercise shows that a config tool can be a weak spot too. Gremlin groups its faults into three kinds. Resource faults use up CPU, memory or disk. State faults shut down hosts, kill processes or move the clock ("Time Travel"). Network faults add latency, drop packets or block traffic. Tools at a high level: Chaos Monkey ends instances at random. It needs Spinnaker. AWS FIS is a managed service with stop conditions built in. Chaos Mesh and Litmus are open-source tools. FIS can run their faults too, for example on a Kubernetes pod. Gremlin is commercial. Any tool should track the experiment's state, log what it does and undo it. AWS discourages home-made scripts that cannot do these. Gremlin's agent undoes its faults if it loses its connection. But a shutdown or a killed process cannot be rolled back. Game days A game day tests people and processes, not only machines. AWS says to involve the same teams who would handle a real event. Business decision makers should take part too. Google's yearly test is called DiRT. It breaks live systems, and it also keeps key people and leaders from helping. The incident response lesson mentioned it; here is what it found. In one test, exactly one person found the emergency phone bridge. In the next drill, more than 100 people found it, but the bridge held only 40 callers. Give the game day clear roles. Slack has one or two hosts who write a detailed plan, with exact commands and a hypothesis. Google's DiRT has a technical team, a coordination team and a command center ready to undo a test. Run the scenario, and then watch. Slack's advice is to hold back and let the system heal itself. Use the incident process you would use for real. End with a blameless review. Slack asks: How long did it take to detect and to resolve? Did any users notice? Did any humans have to step in? Was any documentation wrong? Were any dashboards out of date? What you learn Wrong runbooks. Tom Limoncelli wrote a fictionalized account of a DiRT drill. A restore command needed new parameters, and the restore area had become too small. Fix runbooks on the spot. Missing alerts. AWS says experiments should check that alerts fire and teams get notified. See Alerting and on-call. Fallbacks that fail. Like Confabulator's emergency mode. Test the timeouts, breakers and fallbacks from Circuit breakers and bulkheads this way. Hidden dependencies. In one DiRT test, teams moved services to their own workstations. The test had also cut off their office, so those moves failed. Login systems failed in unexpected ways too. Retries that amplify. Watch the load on the failing service during the test. See Backoff, jitter and retry budgets. When not to do it You cannot see the effect. Slack lists its logs, metrics and alerts before each exercise. Without them, you cannot tell when to stop. Add traces and dashboards first. You cannot undo it. AWS asks for a rollback plan for every experiment. Have a way back, as in disaster recovery. You already know it will break. "If you know that the workload will fail, do not run the experiment." At Google, services can "prefail" a test and skip it. Fix the weak spot first. Option Finds real problems? Risk to users Use it when Tabletop walk-through Partly. It finds gaps in docs and plans. No Nothing breaks. Before any real fault, and for a new team. Staging experiment Partly. Staging may not match production. No First run of every new fault. Production, 1% of traffic Yes Real traffic, real config. Small, if stop conditions work. Staging passed and you can see and undo. Automated, continuous Yes, and it catches new regressions. Small, every day. The experiment passes reliably. Company-wide game day Yes, including people and processes. Can be large. Google says DiRT has caused outages. Smaller tests already pass. Ask of every fallback: "When did this last run?" If nobody knows, plan an experiment. Write the hypothesis and the stop condition before the fault. Get one other engineer to review it. Start with one instance in staging. Then 1% in production, at a quiet time when people are at work and watching. Pick faults from your past postmortems. AWS suggests the same. Turn every finding into a tracked action item with an owner, then rerun the experiment. After a pass, add the experiment to the pipeline so it keeps passing. "Here is our service's dependency list and the timeouts in our config. For each dependency, suggest one chaos experiment: the fault, the steady-state metric, the hypothesis and a stop condition." "Write an AWS FIS experiment template that adds 3 seconds of latency to 1% of tasks in the checkout ECS service for 10 minutes. Use the CloudWatch alarm checkout-p99-high as the stop condition." "Draft a game day plan for losing our primary database: roles, timeline, the exact commands, what we watch, when we abort, and the debrief questions." What to ask the agent Targets. Check the selected resources. A wrong tag or filter can hit all instances, not 1%. The stop condition. Make the alarm fire in staging before you trust it. The undo. Know how to stop the fault by hand, and whether it can be undone at all. Action names. Check every fault name against the tool's docs. An agent can invent ones that do not exist. People. Tell support and on-call before you start, not after. What to check yourself Related lessons: Incident response and postmortems, Circuit breakers and bulkheads, Load shedding and graceful degradation, Disaster recovery and backups and Runbooks and reducing toil.

title: Checkout and the order state machine
text: Give every order a clear list of states and allowed moves, so checkout stays correct when payments time out, webhooks arrive late and stock runs out.
body: This is a made-up story, but each failure in it is common. Ravi's team runs a shoe shop. On a sale day, the payment provider was slow. The checkout service called "authorize payment" with a 3-second timeout. Many calls timed out. The code treated a timeout as a decline. It marked those orders "failed" and released the stock. The app showed "Payment failed, please try again". Many buyers tapped Pay again. But many first payments had worked. The provider just answered late. Its webhooks arrived a minute later, saying the payments succeeded. The webhook handler set those orders to "paid", even though they were "failed" and their stock was gone. So some buyers paid twice for one pair of shoes. Some "paid" orders had no stock, so the warehouse could not ship them. Support spent two weeks on refunds. The root cause was simple. Any code could write any value to orders.status. Nobody had written down which moves were allowed, and "we do not know yet" was not a state at all. An order is a state machine. At any moment it is in exactly one state. Only a short list of moves can change that state. A common set of states looks like this: pending_payment: the order exists, the stock is held, and the money is not yet secured. authorized: the provider holds the money on the card. confirmed: you have committed the stock and accepted the order. shipped, then delivered. failed, cancelled and refunded: end states. Nothing moves out of them. Write the allowed moves in one table, in one place in the code. Every change goes through one function that checks the table. A webhook, an admin tool and a cron job all use that same function. The key idea. Make illegal moves impossible, not just unlikely. One transition table, one function that changes state, and one history row for every change. Step through one order, including the two cases that break most shops. The checkout sequence Hold the stock with a TTL. Reserve the items for a short time, for example 30 minutes, as in the flash-sale lesson. If you use Stripe Checkout, a session can expire between 30 minutes and 24 hours after you create it. The default is 24 hours. Stripe sends checkout.session.expired so you can return the held items. Make the two times match. Set expires_at no later than the end of your stock hold, or call Stripe's expire endpoint when the hold ends. Otherwise a buyer can pay for stock you already released. Create the order in pending_payment, in the same database transaction as the hold. Authorize the payment. On Stripe, after the card is approved with manual capture, the payment's status is requires_capture. If the card is declined, the payment goes back to requires_payment_method, so the buyer can try again. The order stays in pending_payment while they do. Confirm. Commit the stock and move the order to confirmed. Capture when you ship, or at once for digital goods. An online card hold is usually valid for 7 days. Some are shorter. For example, a Visa payment that you start without the customer is held for about 5 days. The charge's capture_before field shows the exact expiry. If the hold expires, the funds are released and the payment's status becomes canceled. Do not hold a database transaction open while you call the provider. Airbnb's library splits each request into three parts. It saves the request, makes the network call, then saves the result. The two database parts never make network calls, and the network call never touches the database. Airbnb learned that network calls inside those database parts can quickly use up the connection pool. The transition guard Here is a small guard in TypeScript. The WHERE state = $2 part makes it safe when two workers race. type State = "pending_payment" | "authorized" | "confirmed" | "shipped" | "delivered" | "failed" | "cancelled" | "refunded"; const ALLOWED: Record<State, State[]> = { pending_payment: ["authorized", "failed"], authorized: ["confirmed", "cancelled"], confirmed: ["shipped", "cancelled"], shipped: ["delivered"], delivered: ["refunded"], failed: [], cancelled: [], refunded: [], }; interface Tx { // your database client update(sql: string, args: unknown[]): Promise<number>; insert(table: string, row: object): Promise<void>; } async function move(tx: Tx, orderId: string, from: State, to: State, why: string) { if (!ALLOWED[from].includes(to)) throw new Error(`illegal ${from} -> ${to}`); const n = await tx.update( "UPDATE orders SET state = $3 WHERE id = $1 AND state = $2", [orderId, from, to]); if (n === 0) throw new Error("state changed, reload and decide again"); await tx.insert("order_events", { orderId, from, to, why }); await tx.insert("outbox", { type: `order.${to}`, orderId }); }If the row count is 0, another worker moved the order first. This is a compare-and-swap; see Transactions and isolation levels. The same transaction writes a row to order_events and a row to the transactional outbox. The history row gives you an audit trail: who changed what, when, and why. The outbox row lets a relay publish order.confirmed to email and the warehouse without a dual write. Sagas, outbox and CDC explains the relay. One checkout, one key per attempt The app creates one idempotency key when the checkout page opens. It sends that key with every "Place order" retry. The server saves the key with a unique index, so a repeat returns the same order. Pass a key to the provider too. Stripe saves the status code and body of the first request for a key and returns them on retries, including 500 errors. It may remove keys after they are at least 24 hours old. It also returns an error if a retry sends different parameters. Use one provider key per payment attempt, for example order-8812-attempt-1. Send the same key on every retry of that attempt. If the card is declined and the buyer tries again, that is a new attempt with a new key. Airbnb also builds keys from the entity. Its example payment-1234-refund makes sure payment 1234 is refunded only once. Unknown is a real result A timeout does not mean "declined". Airbnb's library sorts errors into retryable and non-retryable. Network and server errors (5XX) are retryable. Invalid requests (4XX) are not. On a retry, it can first ask the downstream service for the transaction's status. So keep the order in pending_payment, and ask the provider about this order. Never start a new attempt with a new key while the old one is still unknown. Keep timeouts short, too. Shopify suggests starting with a 1-second connect timeout and a 5-second read timeout, then tuning from your own data. Webhooks: late, repeated and out of order Stripe does not promise to send events in the order they happened. It also says not to use an event's created time to order events. Track event IDs to find duplicates, and fetch the latest object from the API when you need it. So the webhook handler should not set a state directly. It reads the payment's current status and asks the guard for a move. A late success for a cancelled order is refused. If the payment is only authorized (requires_capture), cancel it, which costs nothing. If it has already succeeded, refund it, because a succeeded payment can't be cancelled. Log both cases. Stripe also says your fulfilment code may be called many times, even at the same moment, for one Checkout Session. The WHERE state = $2 check handles that. Snapshot prices, then handle partial work When you create the order, copy the unit price, discount, tax, currency and shipping fee onto each order line. Store money as integers in minor units. Later price changes must not change old orders, receipts or refunds. Money and double-entry ledgers shows how to record the amounts. Partial shipments need care. On Stripe, most payments allow only one capture, and a partial capture releases the rest. So capture once, then refund items that never ship. Stripe allows several refunds on one charge, but never more than the original amount in total. Keep shipments and refunds as their own rows that point to order lines, instead of adding more order states. Option Good Bad Use it when Free-form status column Yes Fast to start. Any code can write any value. Bugs show up as money problems. Never for real money. Transition table plus one move() function Yes Illegal moves fail loudly, and all writers follow one rule. You must update the table when the business adds a step. The default. Workflow engine (Temporal, AWS Step Functions) Yes Retries, timers and history come built in. A new system to run and learn. Long flows with many timers and services. Capture at checkout Yes One step, no hold expiry. Refunds for items you can't ship. Digital goods, and stock that ships the same day. Authorize now, capture on ship Yes You can cancel at no cost before capture. The hold can expire if shipping is late. Physical goods that ship within a few days. Draw the order states on one page before you write code. Mark every end state, and every state that needs a timer. Ask: "If this call times out, what state is the order in? Who finds out the real answer, and when?" Keep one move() function. Search the code for any other write to the state column, and remove it. Run a job every few minutes for orders stuck in pending_payment past their TTL. It asks the provider, then moves each order or releases the stock. Alert on refused transitions. Each one is a race or a bug that someone should look at. Reconcile your orders with the provider's records. Shopify checks single records, such as charges and refunds. It also checks totals, such as the balance it has not yet paid out to a merchant. "List every place in this repo that writes to orders.state. For each one, show the old state it expects and the new state it sets." "Draw our order state machine as a Mermaid diagram from the code. Mark any state with no way out, and any move the business rules don't allow." "Write tests for checkout where the payment call times out, the webhook arrives twice, and the webhook arrives after the order was cancelled." What to ask the agent The idempotency key is created once per checkout, not once per request. A common bug is calling uuid() inside the retry loop. No network call runs inside a database transaction. The webhook handler verifies the signature and fetches the current payment before it moves the order. Prices and tax on order lines are copied values, not joins to the product table. Hold windows and session limits match your provider's docs, not the model's memory. What to check yourself Payment lifecycle: every state of the payment itself, from authorization to payout. Idempotency, retries and timeouts: keys, backoff and safe retries in depth.

title: Choosing a database
text: Pick a database from how you read and write your data, not from what is popular. Then count what it costs to run.
body: Discord built the first version of its app in early 2015. Every chat message lived in one MongoDB replica set. This was on purpose, and the team planned a path to move later. Around November 2015, they had 100 million stored messages. Then the data and the index no longer fit in RAM. Latency became unpredictable. Before they picked a new database, they studied how the app really used messages. Reads were very random, and reads and writes were about 50/50. They also wrote down what they needed: linear scaling, automatic failover, low maintenance, predictable speed, a proven product, and open source. Cassandra was the only database that met all of these needs. It also came with a trade-off. It gives up strong consistency to stay available. Discord wanted that, and accepted eventual consistency. In 2017 the cluster had 12 Cassandra nodes. By early 2022 it had 177. Hot partitions, compaction backlogs and garbage collection pauses caused latency spikes. In May 2022, Discord moved to 72 nodes of ScyllaDB, a Cassandra-compatible database. The p99 latency to read old messages fell from 40–125 ms to 15 ms. So a choice is not "right forever". It fits a set of access patterns at one size. In this lesson you will learn to ask the questions Discord asked, before your data outgrows your database. There is no best database. There are databases that fit some ways of reading and writing data, and fit others badly. So start from your access patterns: which questions the app asks, how often, and how fast the answer must be. Then add your requirements: transactions, consistency, size, and who will run it at 3 a.m. The key idea. First list how you will read and write the data. Then pick the simplest database that serves those patterns, and that your team can run. Popularity is not a requirement. DB-Engines sorts hundreds of systems by data model. Its main groups include relational, key-value, document, wide column, search engines, time series, graph and vector. Some systems belong to more than one group. The AWS decision guide uses a similar list. It adds in-memory as a group and has no search engine group. Step through the questions. Each "yes" points to a family. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. The main families, as their own docs describe them Relational (Postgres, MySQL). Tables, joins, constraints and ACID transactions. Postgres also stores JSON and supports every SQL isolation level. Key-value (DynamoDB, Redis). Get and put by key. AWS suggests it for session stores and shopping carts. DynamoDB is fully managed and also has ACID transactions across tables. Redis keeps data in memory. Document (MongoDB). JSON-like documents with nested fields, in collections without a fixed schema. Wide-column (Cassandra). Tables split into partitions across many nodes, with eventual consistency. Search engine (Elasticsearch). Built on Apache Lucene, it stores JSON documents in indices for search and analytics. Time-series (TimescaleDB, InfluxDB). TimescaleDB splits Postgres tables into chunks by time. InfluxDB is built for event and time-series data, like server and sensor monitoring. Graph (Neo4j). Nodes and relationships. The links are stored with the data, so queries follow them without joins. Vector (pgvector). Finds the nearest vectors, for example similar texts. pgvector does this inside Postgres, next to your other data. What each one is bad at Each family pays for its strength somewhere. Cassandra chose not to support transactions across partitions, distributed joins or foreign keys. Fast queries must give the partition key. So you design one table per query, and changing the questions later is hard. MongoDB has multi-document transactions. Its docs warn that a distributed transaction costs more than a single-document write, and that it does not replace a good schema. Redis keeps data in memory (Redis in depth goes further). If you turn on its append-only file, the default policy syncs to disk once per second. A crash can then lose about 1 second of writes. With snapshots only, you can lose minutes. That may be fine for a cache, but usually not for money. Elasticsearch makes a new document searchable within about 1 second, not at once. So keep the real data in your main database, and copy it into the search index. Transactions and consistency Ask: must several records change together, or not at all? Money, stock and bookings usually need this. Relational databases are built for it: Postgres has been ACID-compliant since 2001. If you pick a store with weaker transactions, your app code must handle the gaps. The transactions lesson and the CAP lesson explain what you give up. Scale Write numbers, not adjectives. How many rows in two years? How many reads and writes per second at peak? Kailash Nadh, the CTO of the Indian trading platform Zerodha, makes this point. A Postgres node with a replica, good partitions and indexes can hold hundreds of billions of records and terabytes of data. He argues that you often do not need a distributed database. This lesson agrees: most apps fit one Postgres for a long time. When they do not, replication and sharding come next. Running cost and team skills Someone must back it up, upgrade it, watch it and fix it at night. If you host it yourself, your team does the maintenance, monitoring and patching. A managed service takes most of that work. It usually costs more per hour, so compare that with the engineer time it saves. Skills matter too. AWS suggests that a team already running Postgres should first try pgvector before a new vector store. Dan McKinley says a new technology brings more "unknown unknowns". He suggests a young company gets only a few "innovation tokens", maybe three, to spend on new tools. Polyglot persistence Using several stores in one system is called polyglot persistence. AWS gives a shop example: a document store for the catalogue, DynamoDB for fast browsing, and Aurora for orders and stock. Martin Fowler wrote about it in 2011. He warns that it costs complexity. Each new store is a new interface to learn and to tune. You also have to keep the copies in sync. The table sums up the sources above. The "Bad at" column is partly this lesson's own advice, so test it against your own case. Family Good at Bad at Typical use Relational Joins, constraints, ACID transactions, new queries later. Writes beyond one big node need sharding. Users, orders, payments. Most apps. Key-value Very fast get and put by key at huge scale. Queries not by key need extra indexes. No joins. Sessions, carts, cache. Document Nested records that match your code. Data with many links between records. Multi-document transactions cost more. Catalogues, profiles. Wide-column Heavy writes spread over many nodes. Joins, cross-partition transactions, new query shapes. Messages, events at very large scale. Search engine Ranked full-text search, typos, filters. Being the main copy of the data. New data is not searchable at once. Product and log search. Time-series Cheap writes and time-range queries. Data that is not mostly timestamped points. Metrics, sensors, prices. Graph Following many hops of links. Simple lookups any database can do. One more system to run. Fraud rings, recommendations. Vector "Find similar" by embedding. Being the only store. You still need the source data. Semantic search, RAG. Write the access patterns first: the top 10 queries, read/write ratio, peak rate, and data size in two years. Mark which data needs transactions. Money and stock usually do. Start with the database the team already runs well. Ask "what can't it do?" and prove it with a test. Prefer a feature of the current database (JSON column, pgvector, TimescaleDB) before a new system. For each new store, name the owner, the backup plan, the on-call runbook and the monthly cost. Choose managed unless you have a clear reason and the people to self-host. Plan how data gets into a second store, for example with change data capture, and how you rebuild it. Write the decision down in a short record with the patterns, options, and the reason. Checklist before you pick: Access patterns listed? Transactions needed where? Size and rate in two years, as numbers? Can the current database do it? Who runs it, and is it managed? How do you leave it later? "Here are our 10 most common queries, our read/write ratio and our data size. For each database family, say which queries it serves well and which it serves badly. Do not recommend a product until the end." "We run Postgres. We need vector search for 2 million documents. Compare pgvector with a separate vector store, including backups, sync and on-call work." "List the operational tasks our team takes on if we self-host Cassandra instead of using a managed service. Link each task to the official docs." What to ask the agent The agent's family descriptions match the official docs, not a blog post or its memory. Every claim like "scales to millions" names a source or comes from your own load test. The comparison includes running cost: backups, upgrades, monitoring and on-call. The answer says how data stays in sync between stores. The agent did not pick the newest tool just because it is new. What to check yourself Next: Data modelling for NoSQL shows how to design tables around access patterns. For how storage engines pay for writes, see B-tree vs LSM-tree. For search, see Search and inverted indexes.

title: CI/CD and trunk-based development
text: Merge small changes every day, let a machine build and test each one, and ship the same tested build to production.
body: On 1 August 2012, Knight Capital's trading system sent millions of orders it should not have sent. In about 45 minutes it got over 4 million executions (filled trades) in 154 stocks. Knight lost over $460 million. The cause was a deploy. Starting on 27 July, Knight put new code on its eight order-routing servers, a few at a time. A technician did not copy the new code to one of the eight. No second technician reviewed the deploy, and no written procedure asked for one. The new code reused an old flag. On seven servers the flag turned on the new feature. On the eighth, it woke up old code called Power Peg, unused since 2003. A 2005 change had broken how that code counted filled shares. So it never knew an order was filled, and kept sending more. It got worse. While trying to fix it, the team removed the new code from the seven good servers. Now those servers ran the old code too. The SEC report is about missing controls, not about CI tools. But the pattern is common. A manual, step-by-step deploy means each server can end up different. In our view, an automated pipeline that ships one build to every server, and checks the version, makes this mistake much harder. Three ideas work together. Continuous integration (CI). Everyone merges small changes into one shared branch, often. Fowler suggests every developer commits to the mainline every day. Each merge is built and tested by a machine. If the build breaks, you fix it right away. Continuous delivery. Your software can be released to production at any time. Deploying any version is one button press. Continuous deployment. One step further. Every change that passes the pipeline goes to production with no human step. With continuous delivery you are able to deploy often, but you may choose not to. Trunk-based development is a branching model and "a key enabler of Continuous Integration". Developers work on one branch, called trunk or main, and avoid long-lived branches. The key idea. Small changes, merged often, each one built and tested by a machine. Small changes are easy to review, easy to test and easy to undo. Step through one commit, from trunk to users. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Why big merges hurt When a branch lives for weeks, everyone else keeps changing trunk too. At the end, you face a long merge with many conflicts. Fowler calls the worst case "integration hell": every integration bug you fix shows two more. Short-lived feature branches avoid this. A branch should live a couple of days at most, with one developer, or two when pairing. You open a pull request, CI runs, a teammate reviews, you merge and delete the branch. For work that takes weeks, merge it in small parts behind a feature flag that is off. Users see nothing until you turn it on. Deploying code and releasing a feature become two separate decisions. The pipeline A deployment pipeline starts on every change. The first stage, the commit stage, should take only a few minutes. Each passing stage starts the next one. A common shape is: Build. Compile the code and resolve dependencies. Test. Run unit tests, then slower integration tests. Package. Make one build artifact, such as a container image. Deploy. Send that artifact to staging, then to production in stages. Build once, then promote. "Only build packages once" is one of the core pipeline practices. You want to be sure the thing you deploy is the thing you tested. Deploy it the same way to every environment. Knight's servers ran different code. With one artifact, promoted everywhere, that is much less likely. Keep main green A red build on trunk blocks everyone. If the commit stage fails, fix it at once, and nobody adds new work on top. Often the fastest fix is to revert your change, then fix it calmly on a branch. GitHub can enforce part of this. With required status checks, nobody can merge into a protected branch until the checks pass. Keep feedback fast Google's CI chapter says the cost of a bug grows almost exponentially the later you catch it. So CI aims for fast feedback. Google runs only fast, reliable tests before submit. Slower tests run after submit. Fowler says a ten-minute build is reasonable. Flaky tests hurt CI badly. They erode trust in the build, similar to a broken test. They also make it harder to find which change to roll back. See Testing strategy for how to keep a suite fast and trusted. Measure delivery: the DORA metrics DORA studies software delivery. Its guide now names five metrics, in two groups. Throughput: Change lead time: time from a commit in version control to that change running in production. Deployment frequency: how many deploys you do in a period, or the time between them. Failed deployment recovery time: how long it takes to recover from a deploy that fails and needs immediate action. Instability: Change fail rate: the share of deploys that need immediate action after they go out. Deployment rework rate: the share of deploys that are unplanned and happen because of an incident in production. Note that recovery time counts as throughput here, not instability. DORA says speed and stability are not trade-offs. For most teams the metrics are correlated. Protect the pipeline itself Your pipeline can run code from strangers, so it is also an attack path. GitHub advises pinning third-party actions to a full-length commit SHA. A tag can be moved or deleted by someone who gets access to that repository. Our advice: pin your dependencies with a lockfile, scan them for known flaws, and sign what you build. SLSA is a checklist of controls that help stop tampering with builds and packages. See Dependency and supply-chain security and the OWASP lesson. Option Merge pain Needs strong automated tests? Fits Trunk-based, short branches Yes, low. Small daily merges. Yes CI is the safety net. Most teams that deploy a web service often. Long-lived feature branches (GitFlow style) No, high. Weeks of drift, then a big merge. Less, but bugs show up late. Software with several versions in use at once, like installed apps. Continuous delivery Not about merging. Yes Every build must be releasable. Teams that want a human to choose the release time. Continuous deployment Not about merging. Yes, plus good monitoring and fast rollback. Teams with trusted tests, staged rollouts and feature flags. The author of GitFlow wrote in 2020 that web apps are usually delivered continuously. For them he suggests a simpler flow. GitFlow still fits when you must support several versions in use at once. Simple rule: start with trunk-based development and continuous delivery. Move to continuous deployment once your tests and rollback are trusted. Keep pull requests small. If a PR is open for more than two days, ask how to split it. Ask "can we ship this unfinished, behind a flag?" before anyone creates a long-lived branch. Treat a red main branch as an urgent problem for the whole team. Revert first, debug second. Watch the CI time. When it grows past about ten minutes, move slow tests out of the merge check or run them in parallel. Quarantine flaky tests with an owner and a date. Never make "just re-run it" the normal fix. Check that production runs the exact artifact that passed tests. Ask: "Can anyone deploy a build that did not go through the pipeline?" Track change lead time and change fail rate together. Use them to find slow or risky steps, not to rank people. Remove dead code and old flags. Knight's old code stayed callable for years. AI coding agents now open pull requests on their own. On GitHub, Copilot's cloud agent can push to only one branch. By default, CI does not run on its pull request until a person with write access approves the workflow run. The person who asked the agent cannot approve its pull request. In our view, CI becomes the main safety net for agent code. It runs on every change and does not get tired. "Here is our CI workflow. Find steps that are slow or run in series but could run in parallel. Estimate the time saved for each." "List every third-party action and dependency in this repo that is not pinned to an exact version or commit SHA. Propose the pinned versions." "This feature is too big for one PR. Split the plan into PRs of under 200 lines. Each must keep main green, with new behaviour behind a flag that is off." What to ask the agent The agent's tests test real behaviour. A test with no real assertion is always green. The pull request does not change the CI workflow, skip tests or loosen checks without a clear reason. New dependencies are real, well-known packages at pinned versions. The agent did not "fix" a red build by deleting or disabling a failing test. A human reviewed the diff before merging, even when every check is green. What to check yourself Related lessons: Safe deploys, Testing strategy, Feature flags, DORA metrics and Working with coding agents.

title: Client prediction and lag compensation
text: The server owns the truth, but players cannot wait for it. Learn how games predict your moves, fix them quietly, and rewind time to judge shots fairly.
body: This story is made up, but each part of it happens in real games. A small studio ships an online shooter. Each player's game decides what happened and tells the server: "I moved here. I hit player 7." The server passes the news on. It feels fast. In the first week, cheaters arrive. A changed client reports a headshot on every enemy. The server believes it. Honest players quit. The team moves the truth to the server. Now your game sends only "I pressed forward" and waits to hear where you are. Cheating gets much harder. But now every step starts a fraction of a second after you press the key. The game feels slow. The team needs both: a server that cannot be fooled, and a game that reacts at once. This lesson shows how real games get both. The server is the authority. Gabriel Gambetta's rule is short: "don't trust the player." A hacked client may claim 10000% health. The server still knows the real value, so the player still dies. VALORANT is built the same way. Riot writes that its server "must never trust a client's view of the world". But the network is slow. Light alone would need about 13 ms to cross the 4,000 km from San Francisco to New York. Real internet paths are slower. Gambetta says delays of 100, 200 or even 500 ms are not unusual. A half-second delay makes a game unplayable. The time for a message to go to the server and come back is called the round-trip time, or ping. So games use three tricks, one for each kind of thing on your screen: Your own character: predict. Move at once, as a guess. Fix the guess when the server answers. Other players: interpolate. Show them a little in the past, between two real updates. Shots: lag compensation. The server rewinds time to what the shooter saw, then checks the hit. The key idea. The server decides what is true. The client decides what you see right now. Prediction, interpolation and lag compensation are ways to hide the gap between the two, and each one has a price. Tick rate: how often the server updates The server runs the game in small, fixed steps called ticks. In each tick it reads player inputs, moves everything and checks the rules. In Valve's Source engine, the default tick is 15 ms, about 66 ticks per second. A higher tick rate is more exact, but it needs more CPU and bandwidth. VALORANT runs movement at exactly 128 steps per second, on both client and server. The server does not send every tick to every player. It sends snapshots of the world at a set rate. In Source, a client receives about 20 snapshots per second by default. Client-side prediction Without prediction, you press forward and see nothing until the server answers. Valve's example: with 150 ms of latency, you see your own move 150 ms late. With prediction, your game runs the same movement code as the server, at once. You move now. The server still has the final word. This works well only if the game is deterministic enough: the same state plus the same inputs should give the same result. Server reconciliation Prediction has a trap. The server's answer is always old by the time it arrives. If you copy it, you jump backwards. Step through the fix below. It follows Gambetta's example: 250 ms of lag, and two presses of the right arrow. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. The fix needs two small things. Numbered inputs. Each input gets a sequence number: #1, #2, #3. Acknowledgement. Each server update says, "this is your state after input #N." The client throws away inputs up to #N. It resets to the server's state and replays the inputs the server has not seen yet. Riot uses numbered, fixed-size moves in the same way. When a client says "I simulated move #408", the server knows exactly which move it means. Sometimes the guess is truly wrong. Maybe another player blocked your path. Then the client must move you to the server's position. Source can spread this fix over a short time, so the view does not jump. In VALORANT, only the player with the bad network sees the fix. The other nine players keep smooth movement. Entity interpolation for other players You can predict yourself because you know your own key presses. You cannot know another player's. Gambetta describes dead reckoning: assume the player keeps the same speed and direction. It works for cars or ships. It fails for players, who run, stop and turn very quickly. So games show other players in the past. They draw smooth movement between the last two real updates. Source does this with a 100 ms delay by default. With 20 snapshots per second, one lost snapshot still leaves two real ones to draw between. The result: you see yourself in the present, and everyone else about 100 ms ago. Lag compensation: the server rewinds time Now you aim at an enemy and fire. You aimed at where they were on your screen, which is in the past. By the time your shot reaches the server, they have moved. Without help, you would have to aim ahead of moving targets. Lag compensation fixes this on the server. Source keeps one second of recent player positions. When your shot arrives, the server estimates when you fired : fire time = server time − packet latency − your interpolation delayIt moves the other players back to that moment, checks the hit, and puts them back. Why not let the client say "I hit him"? Valve's answer: a server cannot trust clients with such decisions. Even a clean client's packets could be changed on the way by a "cheat proxy". The price: shot behind a wall Rewinding time favours the shooter. You can reach cover on your screen and still die, because the server checked the shot at an earlier moment, when you were still in the open. Valve says this "can't be solved in general". Gambetta calls it "somewhat unfair", but "the most agreeable solution for everyone involved". So games limit the rewind. Riot writes that without limits, a player with 500 ms latency could kill you half a second after you reached cover. Peeker's advantage The same delays help the attacker. When you step around a corner, you see the defender at once, thanks to prediction. The defender sees you only after your move goes to the server and on to them, plus buffering. Riot added up these delays. With its model's assumptions, the peeker had about 141 ms longer to react. Lower network latency, with a target of 35 ms ping, and 128-tick servers cut about 40 ms of that. With those changes, a client running at 144 frames per second (FPS) brings it down to about 71 ms. Small numbers matter. In Riot's blind tests, skilled players noticed changes of about 10 ms. A glimpse of rollback netcode Some fast games are peer-to-peer, with no central server. Each player's machine runs the full game. The old way was to wait for the other player's inputs, which feels slow. Rollback netcode predicts the other player's inputs and keeps going. When the real inputs arrive and differ, it re-runs the game from the point where they differed. Like prediction, this needs a fully deterministic game. See lockstep and rollback netcode. Technique What you gain What you pay Use it for Wait for the server Yes Always correct and simple. No Every action is late by the round-trip time. Slow games, like turn-based games. Client-side prediction Yes Your own moves feel instant. Shared, deterministic code. Small fixes when guesses are wrong. Your own character's movement and actions. Dead reckoning Others look current. No Big jumps when a player turns suddenly. Things that move in a steady way, like cars or ships. Entity interpolation Yes Smooth, and uses only real positions. Others are shown about 100 ms in the past. Other players in fast games. Lag compensation Yes Shots hit where you aimed. Targets sometimes die behind cover. Needs a rewind limit. Hit checks in shooters. Rollback netcode Yes No input delay for local inputs. Must save, load and re-run game states fast. Needs full determinism. Fast peer-to-peer games, which GGPO was built for. Ask first: "Who is the authority for this piece of state?" Health, money, hits and inventory belong to the server. Write a latency budget. List network, buffering, tick and frame time in milliseconds, like Riot's peeker's advantage sum. Test with fake lag and packet loss (network data that never arrives) from day one. Prediction bugs hide on a fast office network. Keep movement code shared and deterministic, with a fixed time step. Log every correction. A rise in corrections after a release means client and server code have drifted apart. Set a maximum rewind time for lag compensation, and write down who it is unfair to. Notice the pattern outside games. An app that shows a "like" before the server confirms it is predicting, and needs a plan for when the server says no. "Here is our movement code for client and server. List every place where the two could give different results for the same input, such as floats, random numbers, frame time or order of updates." "Write a test that runs 1,000 random inputs through the client predictor and the server, with 150 ms of fake latency, and checks that the final positions match after server reconciliation." "Explain our lag compensation code step by step. What is the maximum rewind time, and where is it set?" What to ask the agent The agent did not move any authority from the server to the client "to make it faster". Inputs carry sequence numbers, and acknowledged inputs are dropped. Otherwise the replay list grows forever. The tests use real lag, jitter and packet loss, not only a perfect local network. Any number in a latency budget comes from your own measurements or a cited source. The rewind limit is a deliberate choice that you can explain to players. What to check yourself Start with tick rate, snapshots and bandwidth. Next, read authoritative servers and anti-cheat and lockstep and rollback netcode.

title: Time, clocks and ordering
text: Server clocks drift, jump and disagree. Learn which clock to use for what, why timestamps can lose data, and how logical clocks put events in order.
body: At midnight UTC on 1 January 2017, a leap second was added to the world's clocks. At that moment, some DNS lookups through Cloudflare began to fail. Their DNS software, RRDNS, is written in Go. For CNAME records, it asked upstream DNS servers. It measured how long they took to answer, with code like time.Now().Sub(start). Around the leap second, time.Now() could return a time earlier than start. So the measured time was negative. The negative numbers flowed into the code that picks which server to ask next. That code called rand.Int63n, which panics if its argument is negative. Lookups for customers who use CNAME records failed. At the peak, about 0.2% of DNS queries to Cloudflare were affected. The post names the root cause as one belief: time cannot go backwards. The code assumed the difference between two times would be, at worst, zero. At that time, the post notes, Go did not offer a monotonic time source. The fix was live worldwide by 06:45 UTC. Every server has its own clock, and no two agree exactly. NTP keeps them close, but not equal. Over the public internet, NTP can usually keep clocks within tens of milliseconds. Uneven routes and busy networks can sometimes cause errors of 100 ms or more. So you often cannot tell which of two events came first by comparing their clock times. Leslie Lamport made this point in 1978. In a distributed system, he wrote, it is sometimes impossible to say which of two events occurred first. The key idea. Use a clock to measure how long something takes, on one machine, with the monotonic clock. To decide what came first across machines, use counters, messages or one server that assigns the order. Do not trust wall-clock timestamps for that. Two clocks on every machine Your operating system gives you two clocks. Linux calls the first one CLOCK_REALTIME. It is the wall clock, which shows the real date and time. It can jump if someone sets it, and NTP also adjusts its speed. The second is CLOCK_MONOTONIC. Nobody can set it. It counts from some point in the past, and that point has no meaning of its own. Go's documentation puts the rule simply: "the wall clock is for telling time and the monotonic clock is for measuring time." In its example, an operation measured with time.Now() and Sub gives a positive time of about 20 ms. This holds even if the wall clock changes during the operation. Skew, NTP and leap seconds Clock skew is the gap between two clocks. NTP shrinks it, but cannot remove it. Wall-clock time also has kinks. Leap seconds and jumps in system time can make timestamps go backwards. A leap second is one extra second added to UTC. A clock that steps back for it can break code like Cloudflare's. Google spreads the extra second over the hours around the leap instead. This is called a leap smear. Google recommends a 24-hour linear smear, from noon to noon UTC. During the smear, each second is about 11.6 μs longer than normal. Our advice: use the same time source for every server in a fleet. Our own arithmetic shows why: halfway through a 24-hour smear, a smeared clock is about half a second away from one that is not smeared. Why "last write wins" can lose data Many stores settle conflicts with last write wins. Cassandra does this, with a separate timestamp on every column. The timestamp comes from the client's clock, or from the clock of the node that coordinates the write. Cassandra says its correctness depends on these clocks, and tells you to run NTP. Dynamo also describes last write wins: the version with the largest physical timestamp is kept. Now add skew. If one server's clock is a little behind, a newer write can get an older timestamp. It then loses to the write it should replace. Nothing fails, and no error is logged. The data is just gone. Step through it. Ordering without clocks: Lamport clocks Lamport defined order by what could affect what, not by time. Event a happens-before event b if one of three rules holds. Both are in one process and a comes first. Or a sends a message and b receives it. Or a happens-before c, and c happens-before b. If neither event happens-before the other, they are concurrent. A Lamport clock gives each event a number with two rules. Each process adds one to its counter between any two of its events. Each message carries the sender's counter. The receiver then moves its own counter past that value. These rules give the Clock Condition: if a happens-before b, then a's number is smaller than b's. To get one total order, sort by the number, and break ties by a fixed order of the processes, such as their IDs. Know the limit. The reverse is not true. A smaller number does not prove that a happened first, because the two events may be concurrent. In the diagram, the counter fixed the order only because Server B read the price before it changed it. Vector clocks, in one paragraph A vector clock is a list of (node, counter) pairs, one list per version of the data. Dynamo uses them to see whether two versions have a causal order or sit on parallel branches. If they are on parallel branches, Dynamo keeps both and the client must merge them. So vector clocks can find conflicts that a Lamport clock hides. The cost is size: the list can grow with the number of nodes. Hybrid logical clocks A hybrid logical clock (HLC) mixes the two ideas. Like a Lamport clock, it follows the happens-before order. It also keeps its value close to the NTP clock, so the timestamp still means roughly "when". An HLC fits in the 64-bit NTP timestamp format. It only reads the physical clock and never sets it. It keeps working, and still tracks causality, even when NTP has small problems. TrueTime and commit wait Google's Spanner takes a different path: it makes clock error visible. Its TrueTime API does not return one time. TT.now() returns an interval, [earliest, latest]. The true time is always inside it. TrueTime uses GPS and atomic clocks as time sources. This keeps the uncertainty small, generally under 10 ms. In Google's production, the error bound moved between about 1 and 7 ms in each poll interval. Its average was 4 ms most of the time. For each write, Spanner picks a commit timestamp no smaller than TT.now().latest. Then comes commit wait. Clients cannot see the new data until TT.after(s) is true, that is, until the timestamp has surely passed. This gives external consistency. If transaction T1 commits before T2 starts, T1 gets the smaller timestamp. The price is waiting: in the paper's tests, commit wait was about 5 ms. The HLC paper notes that TrueTime needs special hardware, which is not possible for many systems, such as those on leased cloud machines. Option Orders events across servers? Cost Use it when Wall-clock timestamps No Skew can make a newer write lose. Free and simple. Showing dates to people. Rough order is fine. Monotonic clock No It means nothing outside one machine. Free. Timeouts, retries, durations and rate limits. One server assigns sequence numbers Yes, for everything that goes through it. Every write goes through one place. Most apps. Let the database or leader give the order. Lamport clock Yes, it respects happens-before. It cannot spot concurrent events. One counter on every message. You need one total order that respects cause and effect. Vector clock Yes, and it can find conflicting versions. Size grows with the number of nodes. Many nodes take writes, and the app can merge conflicts. Hybrid logical clock Yes, and stays close to real time. A little more logic than a plain counter. Databases that need timestamps that are both causal and near real time. TrueTime Yes, with external consistency. Special hardware, and a short wait on every commit. You run on a platform that offers it. Search the code for durations computed from wall-clock time. In Go, keep the value from time.Now() and use Sub, so the monotonic reading is used. In other languages, find the monotonic clock in the official docs. Never trust client clocks for order. A phone's clock is set by its user. Store the client time as information only. Let one place assign order when you can: a database sequence or a leader. See unique ID generation. In a design review, ask: "If two of our servers' clocks are one second apart, what breaks?" If the answer is "the newest write might be lost", you have last write wins on wall-clock time. Do not build locks or leases on clocks from different machines. See leader election and leases. Watch clock offset on every host, and alert when NTP stops syncing. "Find every place in this repo that subtracts two wall-clock readings to get a duration or timeout. Show the file and line, and suggest the monotonic clock call for this language. Link the official docs for it." "This table uses last write wins with an updated_at set by each app server. List the cases where a newer update could be lost, and suggest a fix with a version number or a database sequence." What to ask the agent Every suggested clock call is the monotonic one, checked in the language's official documentation. The agent did not "fix" ordering by adding more NTP servers. Smaller skew still allows lost writes. Any version check is done in the database, in one atomic step, not read first and compared later in app code. Code that runs during a leap second, or a clock jump, still works. Ask for a test that moves the wall clock backwards. What to check yourself Before this: why distributed systems are hard. Next: quorums and leaderless replication, CRDTs and coordination avoidance, and distributed transactions.

title: Reviewing code written by humans and AI
text: Review for correctness, design and shared understanding, and check harder when an AI wrote the code.
body: This story is made up, but each part of it has happened to real teams. Ravi asked his coding agent to add signature checks to the payment webhook. Ten minutes later he had a 600-line pull request. The code looked clean. There were twelve new tests, and all of them passed. His teammate Lina was busy. She skimmed the main file, saw green checks, and wrote "LGTM" ("looks good to me"). She did not open package.json. One new line there added a package called webhook-signature-verify. The agent had invented that name. No such package existed when the model learned to code. But someone had since published a package with that exact name. It had an install script. When CI installed it, the script read the environment variables and sent the payment API key to a server outside the company. The twelve tests did not catch it. Each one mocked the new package: it replaced the package with a fake version. So the real code never ran. One catch block also swallowed every error and returned true. So a webhook with a broken signature would have been accepted too. The team rotated the key, removed the package and added a dependency check to CI. The code had passed review. The review had not really happened. Code review means someone other than the author reads the code before it is merged. Google's guide says it uses review "to maintain the quality of our code and products". Review has three jobs: Correctness. Does the code do what it should? Does it break on edge cases, such as empty or very large inputs? Design. Does the change fit the system? Will the next person understand it? Google calls design the most important thing to cover. Shared understanding. After review, at least two people know how this code works. That helps the team on a bad night months later. Review is not for spacing, import order or quote style. A linter and a formatter can check those every time, for free. (This is our advice. Google's guide also says reviewers should not block a change only because of their personal style. ) The goal is not perfect code. Google's main rule is to approve a change once it clearly improves the overall health of the code. Its guide says there is "no such thing as 'perfect' code—there is only better code". The key idea. Review is where a team decides "we understand this, and we will own it". With AI, the code arrives faster, so that decision needs more care, not less. A good review has layers. Each one catches different problems. Step through them with Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. As the author Your job is to make the review easy. Keep it small. Small changes are reviewed faster and more carefully, and they cause fewer bugs. Google suggests about 100 lines is usually fine and 1,000 lines is usually too large. A 200-line change in one file may be fine. Spread across 50 files, it is usually too large. Write a clear description. The first line says what the change does, as a short order: "Delete the FizzBuzz RPC and replace it with the new system." The body says why, and what the known weak points are. "Fix bug" is not a description. Add tests in the same change. Review it yourself first. Read your own diff before you ask anyone else. GitHub's docs say this catches mistakes early. Tell the reviewer where to look first. As the reviewer Start with risk. Do not read files in alphabetical order. First find the parts where a mistake costs the most: data deletes and migrations, money, login and permissions, secrets, and code that runs in parallel. Concurrency bugs are hard to find by running the code, so you must reason about them while you read. (The risk list is our advice.) Read every line you are asked to review. Google's guide says you can sometimes skim generated code and data files. But do not skim a human-written function and assume it is fine. If you cannot understand it, ask the author to make it clearer. Read the tests. Ask one question: "Will the tests actually fail when the code is broken?" Tests do not test themselves, so a person must check them. Ask questions. "What happens if this list is empty?" works better than "This is wrong." Write kind, specific comments. Comment on the code, not the person. Explain why. Label each comment, so the author knows what is required: Nit: small, fine to skip. Optional: a good idea, but not required. FYI: something for the future. When you see good work, say so. Be fast. Google says one business day is the maximum time to respond. You can approve with comments when you trust the author to fix small points. What changes when AI wrote the code The rules above stay the same. What changes is the kind of mistake. More code, faster. An agent can write 600 lines in minutes. Your reading speed did not change. Ask for smaller changes. Plausible but wrong. The code has good names and comments, so it looks reviewed. Read it anyway. Google's "do not skim" rule names human-written code. Our advice is to apply it to AI-written code too. Invented APIs and packages. A study of 16 models and 576,000 code samples found that, on average, at least 5.2% of the packages that commercial models suggested were invented. For open-source models it was 21.7%. An attacker can publish a real package under an invented name. The paper calls this a form of package confusion attack. Many people now call it "slopsquatting", a name credited to Seth Larson of the Python Software Foundation. The same invented names often come back: 43% of them appeared again in all 10 repeats of the same prompt. So an attacker can predict them. Missing edge cases. Empty lists, time zones, retries, a second request at the same moment. Tests that test nothing. Tests that mock the code under test, or check only that "no error was thrown". Over-broad changes. "While I was there, I also cleaned up..." Every extra file is extra risk. Instructions hidden in the input. An agent may read a README, an issue or a web page with hidden instructions in it. This is indirect prompt injection. It can steer the code the agent writes. So you are still responsible for reviewing everything the agent proposes. A checklist for AI-written diffs This list is our advice. Use it on top of a normal review. Does every new package exist, with the exact name, in the official registry? Is it the one you meant, and is it maintained? Does every API, method and config option exist in the version you use? Are there files in the diff that the task did not need? Does any catch or except hide an error, or return a default value? Would each test fail if the code were wrong? Is the code under test mocked? Are edge cases covered: empty input, nulls, limits, time zones, a repeat call? Are there secrets, tokens or personal data in the code, tests or logs? Can the author explain every line without asking the agent? AI as a reviewer AI review is a good second pass. Anthropic's Code Review service runs several agents over a pull request, checks their findings, and leaves comments on the exact lines. It never approves or blocks a pull request, so the decision stays with your team. Its docs also warn that a review with no findings does not mean the code is free of errors or secure. You can also run /code-review before you open the pull request. It reviews the changes on your branch. By default it runs in a separate subagent with its own context. Review style Catches deep bugs? Cost Use it when Skim and "LGTM" No It approves what it never read. Almost none, until something breaks. Never for real code. Full human review of every line Yes, if the change is small. Slow on big diffs. Reviewers get tired. Risky code: money, data, security. Risk-first human review with automated checks Yes Time goes where mistakes cost most. Needs good CI and a linter set up once. Most changes. Add an AI second pass Yes, as an extra layer. Can be noisy or miss things. Tokens or a paid service, and more comments to read. Larger diffs, and all AI-written code. AI review only, no human No Nobody owns the decision. Cheapest. Never as the final check. Simple rule: the less you wrote yourself, the more carefully you read. Before you ask for review, read your own diff on the review page, line by line, as if a stranger wrote it. Put "How to review this" in the description: "Start with ledger.ts. The rest is renames." Split agent output into small pull requests before anyone reviews it. A 1,500-line AI diff is a request to skim. Ask: "What is the worst thing this change can do in production?" Review that part first. For every new dependency, open its page in the registry yourself. Check the owner, age and downloads. Search the diff for catch, except, TODO, mock and skip before you read the rest. Mark every optional comment with Nit: and approve. Do not block a good change because of your personal taste. "Before I open a pull request, list every new dependency you added, with a link to its registry page. Flag any you are not sure exists." "Review this diff as a strict senior reviewer. Focus on data loss, security and error handling. Ignore style. For each issue, give the line and a test that would show the bug." "For each test you wrote, tell me what bug it would catch. If a test would still pass with the function body deleted, say so." What to ask the agent Each new package exists, has the exact name you expect, and comes from the official registry. Tests call the real code and would fail if it were wrong. No error is swallowed and turned into a quiet success. The diff touches only what the task needed. No input the agent read (an issue, a README, a web page) could have carried hidden instructions. You, not the AI reviewer, made the final decision, and you can explain every line. What to check yourself Before this: Working with coding agents. Next: Security risks of AI-written code and Testing strategy.

title: Working with coding agents
text: Explore, plan, build and verify, and treat the agent's context like a budget you can run out of.
body: This story is made up, but it may have happened to you. Arjun has a flaky checkout test. His agent session is already long: a CSS fix, a question about logs, a big stack trace. He types: "fix the flaky checkout test". The agent reads forty files. It finds a timing problem and adds a two-second sleep to the test. On the way, it "cleans up" a helper in the payment code. It reports: "Fixed. The test should pass now." Arjun did not ask it to run the test 50 times. He did not read the diff closely. The next day, a reviewer finds the changed payment helper. The test is still flaky. It just fails less often. He tries again: /clear, plan mode, and the exact command that shows the failure. The agent finds a missing await, writes a plan, fixes it, and runs the test 50 times. All pass. The diff is four lines. The agent was the same both times. Only the way he worked with it changed. A coding agent is not a smarter autocomplete. It works in a loop. Claude Code describes three phases: gather context, take action, and verify results. It searches and reads files, edits code, runs commands, reads the output, and decides the next step. It repeats this until it thinks the job is done. Two facts shape everything about working with it. First, context is a budget. The context window holds your whole conversation: every message, every file the agent reads, and every command output. It fills up fast. As it fills, the model can forget earlier instructions and make more mistakes. This is not only a Claude problem. An Anthropic engineering post calls context "a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns". Second, the agent stops when the work looks done. Without a check it can run, "looks done" is its only signal. Then you become the checker for every mistake. The key idea. Spend context on what matters, and give the agent a way to prove its work. Most good habits with agents come from these two rules. Step through one task and watch the context fill up. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Explore, plan, implement, commit The Claude Code guide recommends four phases. Explore. Press Shift+Tab until plan mode is on. In plan mode the agent reads files and answers questions, but does not change them. Plan. Ask for a plan: which files change, and why. Press Ctrl+G to open the plan in your editor and change it. This is the cheapest moment to catch a wrong idea. Implement. Approve the plan or leave plan mode, and let it code against the plan. Ask it to write tests and run them. Commit. Ask for a clear commit message and a pull request. Plan mode has a cost, so skip it for small work. The guide's test: if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan. Give it a check it can run A check is anything with a clear pass or fail: a test suite, a build, a linter, a script, a screenshot to compare. Put the check in the prompt. Then ask for evidence, not claims: the command it ran and the output. Manage the budget Run /clear between unrelated tasks. Run /context to see what uses space. When the context gets full, Claude Code compacts it: it clears old tool output and then summarizes. Early instructions may be lost. You can run /compact with a focus, like /compact focus on the API changes. Correct early. Esc stops the agent. Esc twice, or /rewind, goes back to an earlier point. If you have corrected it twice on the same issue, run /clear and write a better first prompt. Project memory: CLAUDE.md Each session starts with a fresh context. CLAUDE.md is a file the agent reads at the start of every session. Put in it what the agent cannot guess from the code: build and test commands, unusual style rules, branch rules and known traps. Leave out what it can read from the code. /init creates a first version for you. Keep it short. The docs suggest under 200 lines. For each line, ask: "Would removing this cause mistakes?" If not, cut it. A long file makes the agent ignore your real rules. Remember that CLAUDE.md is context, not enforced configuration. Check it into git, so your team improves it together like code. Four extensions, one paragraph each Subagents run in their own context window with their own allowed tools, and send back a short summary.
