Use them for research that reads many files, or for a review in a fresh context. The reviewer sees only the diff and your criteria, not the reasoning that produced it. Skills are Markdown files (SKILL.md) with knowledge or a repeatable workflow, each in its own folder under .claude/skills/. The agent sees only their descriptions at the start. The full text loads when a skill is used, or when you run it with /skill-name. Hooks are scripts that run at fixed points, for example after every file edit. CLAUDE.md instructions are advice. Hooks are deterministic and always run. Use a hook to run the linter after each edit, or to block writes to a folder. If a rule must hold every time, make it a hook. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that connects AI tools to outside systems, such as files, databases and other tools. An MCP server can read your data and take actions for you. So treat it like any other dependency: install only servers you trust, and give them the least access you can. Plugins package skills, hooks, subagents and MCP servers so a team can share one setup. When not to use an agent The change is faster to type than to explain. You are learning something new. Doing it yourself first builds the skill. See "With AI" below. The action touches live systems. Checkpoints undo edits made with the agent's file-edit tools. They do not undo shell commands. Use git as well. They also cannot undo changes to remote systems, such as databases, APIs or deployments. Run those live steps yourself, on purpose. You cannot check the result. The guide says it plainly: if you can't verify it, don't ship it. What the evidence says The evidence is mixed, so read it carefully. In a 2025 randomized study by METR, 16 experienced developers did real tasks in large open-source projects they knew well. With early-2025 AI tools, tasks took about 19% longer. Yet the developers believed AI had made them about 20% faster. METR now says these results are out of date. Its 2026 update says developers are probably faster with newer tools, but the data is too weak to say by how much. Google's DORA 2025 report found that AI acts as "an amplifier". It makes a team's existing strengths and weaknesses bigger. This is survey data, so it shows what people report, not a measured cause. The lesson: do not trust how fast it feels. Measure it. Way of working Quality Cost Use it when Write it yourself Yes You understand every line. Slower for large or boring changes. Small fixes, new topics you are learning, risky code. One vague prompt, no check No It may solve the wrong problem. Feels fast. Review and rework come later. Quick experiments you will throw away. Explore → plan → implement → commit Yes, if the check is good. A few minutes of planning and setup. Most real tasks across several files. Add subagents for research and review Yes Your main context stays clean. More tokens in total, and more output to read. Large codebases, or work you want checked with fresh eyes. Simple rule: the less you watch the agent, the stronger its checks must be. Before you prompt, ask yourself: "How will the agent know it is done?" Write that check into the prompt. Start every new task with /clear. One session, one task. Use plan mode for anything that touches more than one or two files. Read the plan as you would read a design doc. Keep CLAUDE.md short and in git. When the agent makes the same mistake twice, add one line. When a line stops mattering, delete it. Turn "must always" rules into hooks, and leave advice in CLAUDE.md. Review agent code like code from a new teammate: read every line, run the tests yourself, and check for changes outside the task. Ask for a fresh-context review before you open the pull request. The bundled /code-review skill reviews your diff in a fresh subagent. This whole lesson is about AI, so this section covers one risk: using an agent in a way that stops you from learning. Anthropic ran a randomized study with 52 mostly junior engineers. They learned a new Python library, with or without AI help. On a quiz afterwards, the AI group scored 50% and the group without AI scored 67%. The biggest gap was on debugging questions. The AI group was only about two minutes faster, and that difference was not statistically significant. How people used AI mattered. Those who asked conceptual questions, or asked for explanations of the code, scored 65% or more. Those who handed over the work, or let AI do the debugging, scored under 40%. The authors say the sample was small, the quiz came right after the task, and their pattern analysis does not prove cause. So when the goal is to learn, use the agent as a teacher, not as a typist. "Don't write the code. Explain how this library handles errors, then give me a small exercise to try myself." "Here is my solution. Before you show yours, list the bugs and edge cases I missed, and explain why each one matters." "Explain this diff line by line. Then ask me three questions to check that I understood it." What to ask the agent You can explain every line the agent wrote, without asking it again. You could debug this code alone at 2 a.m. during an incident. The tests check real behaviour, and the agent did not weaken a test to make it pass. The diff contains only what the task needed. No quiet changes elsewhere. What to check yourself Next on this line: Project memory: CLAUDE.md and rules files and Extending agents: skills, hooks and MCP. To keep your skills sharp: Skill atrophy and deliberate practice.

title: Locking and MVCC in practice
text: Pick the right tool when two requests change the same row, and learn how your database keeps reads fast while rows change.
body: On 2 March 2014, a small Bitcoin exchange called Flexcoin lost every coin in its hot wallet. The attacker took 896 BTC. The next day, Flexcoin closed for good. The attacker did not break in. They created a normal account and deposited some coins. Then they used Flexcoin's feature for transfers between users. They sent thousands of transfer requests at the same moment. Coins moved out of the sending account "until the sending account was overdrawn, before balances were updated". They repeated this across several accounts to grow the amount, then withdrew it. Flexcoin did not publish its code. Our reading of the notice: each request checked the balance, then wrote a new balance a moment later. Many requests passed the check before the first writes landed. You have seen this bug before as the lost update. This lesson is about the tools that stop it, and what each one costs. The transactions lesson showed that a transaction alone is not a lock. Here you choose how to protect the rows you change. There are three main tools. One atomic statement. The database checks and changes the row in a single UPDATE. No read in your app code, so no gap. Pessimistic locking. You lock the row first, then read and change it. Others who want to change it wait. Optimistic locking. You read with no lock. When you write, you check that nobody changed the row in between. If someone did, you retry. All three protect writers from each other. None of them should slow down plain reads. That is the job of MVCC, the way the database keeps old row versions so readers do not wait. The key idea. First try to make the change one statement. If you must read first, lock when conflicts are common and the lock is short. Check a version when conflicts are rare or a person is thinking. Pessimistic: lock the rows you will change For a transfer, lock both accounts in one statement, in ID order: BEGIN; SELECT id, balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN (17, 42) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE; -- app checks: balance of 17 >= 50 UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = 17; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 50 WHERE id = 42; COMMIT;FOR UPDATE stops other transactions from updating, deleting or locking these rows until you commit. Plain SELECTs are not blocked. In Read Committed (the default), a second Flexcoin-style request would wait here, then read the new balance. There are softer and faster versions: FOR SHARE blocks updates and deletes, but other FOR SHARE readers can lock the row too. Use it when the row must not change while you work, but you will not change it yourself. NOWAIT returns an error at once if a row is already locked. Use it to tell a user "someone else is editing this" instead of making them wait. SKIP LOCKED skips rows that are locked. Postgres added it in 9.5. MySQL 8.4 has NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED too. SKIP LOCKED is built for job queues: SELECT id, payload FROM jobs WHERE status = 'ready' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;Each worker gets a different job, and nobody waits. Both manuals warn that skipping rows gives an inconsistent view. So use it for queue-like tables, not for general work. Optimistic: check a version when you write Add a version column. Read it with the row. When you save, require that it has not changed: UPDATE tickets SET body = $1, version = version + 1 WHERE id = 7 AND version = 3;Step through two agents saving the same ticket. Postgres answers UPDATE 1 or UPDATE 0. A count of 0 is not an error. So your code must read the count. On 0, reload the row and retry, or show the user a conflict. What if the other writer has not committed yet? In Read Committed, your UPDATE waits for it. Then Postgres checks your WHERE again on the new row. The version no longer matches, so you get 0 rows. The big win is time. The read and the write can be minutes apart, in two HTTP requests. No lock is held in between. Martin Fowler's catalog calls this pattern Optimistic Offline Lock. It "assumes that the chance of conflict is low". The atomic statement, again For counters and balances you often need no version at all: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = 17 AND balance >= 50;In Read Committed, 0 rows means "not enough money" (or no such account). A waiting update checks its WHERE again on the new row. In Repeatable Read, you get error 40001 instead. The check and the change are one step. That is the shape Flexcoin's transfers needed. The flash sales lesson uses the same idea for stock. MVCC: why readers do not wait The Postgres docs say it plainly: "reading never blocks writing and writing never blocks reading". The trick is that a write keeps the old version of the row for readers who still need it. In Postgres, each UPDATE makes a new row version. Each version has hidden columns. xmin is the ID of the transaction that created it. xmax is the ID of the transaction that deleted or replaced it. It is 0 for an undeleted row. A visible row can still show a number, usually because the deleting transaction has not committed or was rolled back. Try SELECT xmin, xmax, * FROM accounts; on a test database. The old version stays on disk. It must not be removed "while it is still potentially visible to other transactions". VACUUM later frees that space for reuse. Autovacuum runs it for you. Plain VACUUM does not usually give space back to the operating system. After a big spike of updates, a table can bloat until you need VACUUM FULL. That takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, so the table is unusable while it runs. Here is the trap. A row version stays while it is "still potentially visible to other transactions". So, we infer, one transaction left open for hours can stop VACUUM from removing dead versions. This applies to a transaction that holds a snapshot or has written something. Table bloat grows. Find such transactions in pg_stat_activity, where the docs check backend_xid and backend_xmin. In MySQL InnoDB, the row is changed in place. The old content goes to an undo log. Each row has a hidden transaction ID and a pointer to its undo record. Readers rebuild older versions from there. A background purge removes old undo records. It can only discard them when no open snapshot needs them. The manual asks you to commit regularly, "including transactions that issue only consistent reads". Same lesson, different engine. Deadlocks: two locks, opposite order Transfer A locks account 17, then wants 42. Transfer B locks 42, then wants 17. Each waits for the other forever. Postgres waits deadlock_timeout (default 1 second) before it checks for this. Then it aborts one transaction. Which one "is difficult to predict and should not be relied upon". The error code is 40P01. InnoDB also detects deadlocks by default and rolls back a victim. The fix has two parts. Lock rows in a consistent order, like the ORDER BY id above. Then retry the whole transaction on a deadlock, because the InnoDB manual says you must handle retries "even if your application logic is correct". Advisory locks, and beyond one database Sometimes you want to lock an idea, not a row. For example: "only one nightly billing job runs". Postgres advisory locks take a number you choose. The database does not enforce their meaning; your code must ask for them. BEGIN; SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(4242); -- true or false, no wait -- if true: do the work COMMIT; -- releases the lockThe xact versions take the lock without waiting or with a wait, as you choose. They are released at the end of the transaction. Session-level ones stay until you unlock them or the session ends, even after a rollback. Our advice: with a connection pool, prefer the transaction-level versions. For a long job, take a session-level lock on one connection that you keep for the whole job, and unlock it at the end. Or use a lock row with an expiry. Locks across several databases or services are a different problem. They need a distributed lock with expiry and a fencing token. Don't reach for one if a single database can do the job. Option Best when Waits? Watch out for Atomic UPDATE ... WHERE The rule fits in one statement: counters, balances, stock. Briefly, only on the same row. Read the row count. 0 means the rule said no. Optimistic (version column) Conflicts are rare, or a person edits between read and write. Briefly, at write time, only if another write to the row is in progress. Every caller must check the count and retry. Many retries under heavy contention. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE Conflicts are common and the logic needs a read first. Yes Hold time. Never call a slow API or wait for a user inside it. Lock order. FOR UPDATE NOWAIT A user should hear "busy" now, not wait. No It fails fast. You must handle the error. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED Many workers pull from a queue table. No Inconsistent view. Queues only. Advisory lock You lock a task, not a row. Your choice. Not enforced. Session locks can leak through a pool. In code review, find every read-then-write on a shared row. Ask: "Can this be one UPDATE ... WHERE?" Often it can. Check that every optimistic or atomic update reads the row count. An ignored UPDATE 0 is a silent bug. Keep lock hold time to milliseconds. No HTTP calls, no queue publishes, no user input between FOR UPDATE and COMMIT. Sort IDs before you lock several rows. Write the rule in a comment so the next person keeps it. Put the retry in one helper. Catch deadlocks (40P01) and serialization failures (40001), back off, and retry the whole transaction. Make it safe to repeat, as in idempotency and retries. Add an index for the WHERE of every locking query. InnoDB's deadlock advice includes this. Alert on old open transactions. A query on pg_stat_activity ordered by xact_start finds them. Remember that schema changes queue behind long transactions too. See schema migrations. "List every place in this repo that reads a row and later updates it in the same request. For each, say if it can become one UPDATE ... WHERE, needs FOR UPDATE, or needs a version check." "Add optimistic locking to the tickets table: a version column, a migration, and an update that returns a conflict error when 0 rows change. Include a test with two concurrent saves." "Write a Postgres query that lists transactions open longer than 5 minutes, with their state and query text." What to ask the agent The code checks rows affected after every guarded UPDATE. Agents often drop this. Locks are taken in a fixed order, and nothing slow runs while they are held. The retry repeats the whole transaction, with a limit and backoff, not only the failed statement. SKIP LOCKED is used only on queue tables, never on balances or stock. The test uses real parallel connections to a real database. A mock cannot show a race. The agent did not add a lock in app memory. It breaks as soon as two servers run. What to check yourself Before this: Transactions and isolation levels. The same ideas in app code: Locks, atomics and deadlocks. Next: Inventory and flash sales, where one hot row meets thousands of buyers. Related: Money and double-entry ledgers and Secondary and composite indexes, which shows how VACUUM affects index-only scans. For vacuum, wraparound and HOT updates in depth: PostgreSQL in depth.

title: Locks, atomics and deadlocks
text: Two threads that touch the same data can quietly break it. Locks and atomics stop that, and lock order stops the deadlocks that locks can cause.
body: This is a made-up example, but the bug in it is real. A team runs a small API that counts video views. Each request starts a thread, and each thread runs views = views + 1 on a shared counter in memory. In tests, 1,000 requests give 1,000 views. In production, traffic is high and the server has many CPU cores. The dashboard shows fewer views than the access logs. The gap is small, so nobody notices for weeks. There is no error and no stack trace. The bug is easy to reproduce. The OSTEP textbook runs two threads that each add 1 to a shared counter 10 million times. The answer should be 20,000,000. Sometimes the book gets the right answer. But one run gave 19,345,221, and the next gave 19,221,041. Wrong totals that change from run to run are the mark of a race condition. In this lesson you will see why it happens, and the tools that fix it. views = views + 1 looks like one step. OSTEP shows that on x86 it becomes three instructions: load the value into a register, add 1, and store it back. If the scheduler switches threads between those steps, two threads can load the same old value. Both store the same new value. One add is lost. OSTEP calls this a race condition: the result depends on the timing of the threads. The code that touches shared data is a critical section. It must not run in more than one thread at a time. The key idea. Shared data that changes needs one of three things: a lock, so only one thread is inside at a time; an atomic operation, so the change cannot be split; or no sharing at all. Step through the lost update, then the two fixes. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Mutexes and locks A mutex (mutual exclusion lock) has two states, locked and unlocked. In Python, acquire() on a locked lock blocks until another thread calls release(). Go's sync.Mutex works the same way. Put the critical section between lock and unlock: mu.Lock() views = views + 1 mu.Unlock()Keep the critical section short. Never do a network call or slow disk read while you hold a lock. Every other thread that needs it waits. Atomics and compare-and-swap For one number, a lock is often more than you need. Java's AtomicLong and AtomicInteger have atomic increment methods. Go has atomic.AddInt64. The base tool under many of these is compare-and-swap (CAS). Go's docs describe it as one atomic step: if the value still equals old, set it to new and return true; otherwise return false. Java calls it compareAndSet. With CAS you read the value, compute the new one, and try to swap. If another thread changed it first, the swap fails and you try again. OSTEP shows how locks themselves are built from instructions like this. Go warns that its atomic functions "require great care to be used correctly". Outside low-level code, it suggests channels or the sync package instead. Read-write locks Many readers can safely read at the same time. Only writers need to be alone. A read-write lock allows many readers or one writer. Java's docs say the gain is fully seen only on a multi-processor, and only when data is read often and changed rarely. If reads are very short, the extra cost of the lock can eat the gain. Go also warns against taking a read lock again while you hold one. A waiting writer blocks new readers. Deadlock Locks bring a new risk. Thread 1 holds lock A and waits for lock B. Thread 2 holds B and waits for A. Neither can move. This is a deadlock. OSTEP lists four conditions, which it credits to a 1971 paper by Coffman, Elphick and Shoshani. All four must hold for a deadlock: Mutual exclusion. A thread has a resource, such as a lock, to itself. Hold and wait. A thread holds some locks while it waits for more. No preemption. Nobody can take a lock away from its holder. Circular wait. There is a cycle of threads, each waiting for a lock the next one holds. Break any one condition and deadlock cannot happen. Lock ordering breaks circular wait. Decide a global order, for example "always lock A before B". OSTEP calls this probably the most practical way to prevent deadlock. Try, then back off. OSTEP shows a thread that cannot get its second lock. It releases the first lock and starts again. The book discusses this under no preemption. In Python, acquire(timeout=2) returns False if it cannot get the lock in 2 seconds. Livelock and starvation Livelock: threads keep trying and backing off, but none makes progress. OSTEP suggests a random delay before each retry. Starvation: one thread never gets the lock, because others always win. Simple spin locks are not fair and can cause it. The same ideas in a database A database has the same problems, one level up. Two requests that read a row, add 1 in app code, and write it back can lose an update. The transactions lesson shows the fixes: one atomic UPDATE, or a row lock with SELECT … FOR UPDATE. Row locks can deadlock too. The Postgres docs show two transactions that update the same two accounts in opposite order. Postgres detects the deadlock and aborts one of them. Which one is hard to predict. The fix is the same as in memory. Postgres says the best defence is to take locks on many objects in a consistent order. You can also set lock_timeout, so a statement stops instead of waiting too long for a lock. More in locking and MVCC in practice. Across machines A mutex works only inside one process. When many servers share one job, you need a distributed lock. Kleppmann says it should expire after a time, so a crashed client cannot hold it forever. A lock with a timeout is called a lease. Leases have a trap. Martin Kleppmann describes a client that pauses for garbage collection. Its lease expires, another client takes the lock, and then the first client wakes up and writes anyway. His fix is a fencing token: a number that grows each time the lock is given out. The storage rejects any write with an older token than one it has already seen. He also asks: is the lock for efficiency or for correctness? If two nodes doing the same work only costs a little, a simple lock on one Redis node is enough. Redis in depth covers Redlock and the debate about it. See leader election and leases and Raft. Prefer higher-level tools Go's sync docs say higher-level synchronization is better done with channels. Java gives you thread pools and blocking queues for producer-consumer designs. The best lock is the one you do not need. Give each piece of data one owner, for example one worker reading from a queue. Pass immutable values between threads. Actors, covered in threads, async and actors, follow the same idea. Tool Good for Cost Watch out for Mutex Any critical section, many variables at once. Threads wait. Slow if held long. Deadlock, forgotten unlock. Atomic / CAS One counter or one reference. Retries under heavy contention. Two atomics together are not atomic. Read-write lock Many reads, rare writes. More complex than a mutex. Little gain on one core. Busy readers can delay a writer for a long time. Database row lock Shared rows across many app servers. Waiting transactions, deadlock aborts. Lock order, lock_timeout, retries. Lease (distributed lock) One worker per job across machines. A lock service to run. Expiry during a pause. Needs fencing for correctness. Queue or single owner No shared changing data at all. Extra hop, ordering design. A slow consumer becomes the bottleneck. When you see shared state that changes, ask "who else writes this?" first. This one question finds many race bugs. Prefer no sharing, then atomics for one value, then a mutex. Use a read-write lock only after a profile shows it helps. Write the lock order down in a comment or in the design doc, and keep it the same in every code path. Never call the network or wait on I/O while you hold a lock. Run your tests with a race detector where the language has one. In SQL, update rows in a fixed order, for example by ID, and retry on deadlock errors. For a distributed lock, ask whether it is for efficiency or for correctness. For correctness, use fencing tokens, or better, a database constraint. When a bug "only happens under load" and the numbers are a little off, suspect a race condition. "Here is our Go service. List every variable that more than one goroutine can write. For each, say how it is protected today, and suggest the simplest safe fix." "This Java class uses two locks. Draw the order in which each method takes them, and tell me if any pair of methods can deadlock." "Write a test that runs this counter code with 8 threads and 1 million increments each, and fails if the total is wrong." What to ask the agent The agent's fix protects every read and write of the shared data, not just one of them. A "thread-safe" claim is tested with many threads and many runs, not one run. No lock is held across a network call or a callback. Two separate atomic operations were not treated as one atomic step. Code that uses a distributed lock for correctness also has fencing or a database check. What to check yourself Next: Lock-free programming and memory models goes deeper into CAS loops and memory visibility. OSTEP's chapter on common concurrency bugs is free and short.

title: Connection pooling and database limits
text: Learn why databases run out of connections, how to size and guard a pool, and what breaks when you put PgBouncer in front of Postgres.
body: On 30 October 2026, some requests to github.com hung for up to about 10 seconds. Then they failed with a server error. At the worst point, about 43% of pull request merge attempts failed. About 3.5% of API calls failed too. GitHub's report blames a connection pool, not the database itself. A pool used by many github.com services had reached its limit. For several minutes, no connections were available. The pool was already near its limit. Then some update requests began to hold their connections far longer than expected. Each one started writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds. During that lookup, the connection was "reserved but unused". New requests waited for a free connection. When the connection timeout expired, they failed. GitHub changed the order. The slow lookup now runs before the write starts, so it holds no connection. GitHub is also looking at limits on how long a pooled connection can be held. A database connection is expensive to open and expensive to keep. So apps open a few, keep them, and lend them out. That set of reusable connections is a connection pool. A pool is a tiny resource with a queue in front of it. A request borrows a connection, uses it and gives it back. If all connections are out, the next request waits. If it waits too long, it fails. So a pool works only if two things are true. The pool is the right size. And every borrower gives the connection back quickly. The key idea. The database can serve only a few connections well. Keep pools small, count them across every app instance, and hold a connection only while you are actually talking to the database. Why connections are scarce The Postgres lesson showed the process-per-user model. For every new connection, the postmaster starts a new backend process. Before the first query, that backend must also check the client's credentials. AWS describes this as "the memory and CPU overhead" of opening a connection. The default max_connections is typically 100. Postgres sizes some resources, including shared memory, from it. Three slots are reserved for superusers by default. Your app gets the rest. Why not just raise it to 5,000? Memory is not the main problem. Andres Freund measured idle connections at below 2 MiB each with a good setup. The real cost is that every open connection makes the others slower. In tests he published in 2020, a single active connection ran less than half as fast with 5,000 mostly idle connections open. Few connections, kept busy, beat many idle ones. Sizing an app-side pool A pool like HikariCP for Java has four settings that matter most: Maximum size (maximumPoolSize). Idle plus in-use connections. Default 10. Minimum idle (minimumIdle). The authors recommend leaving it unset, so the pool stays a fixed size. Acquire timeout (connectionTimeout). How long a caller waits for a connection before an error. Default 30 seconds. Max lifetime (maxLifetime). Retire a connection after this age. Set it "several seconds shorter" than any limit imposed by the database or network. How big? Smaller than you think. HikariCP's "About Pool Sizing" page describes an Oracle demo. Cutting the pool from 2,048 connections to 96 cut response times from about 100 ms to about 2 ms. A database server has a few CPU cores. Beyond some point, more connections only add switching and waiting. The page gives a formula from the PostgreSQL project as a starting point: connections = ((core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count)core_count excludes hyper-threads. effective_spindle_count is zero if your active data is fully cached. It grows toward the number of disks as more reads miss the cache. The page says there has been no analysis yet of how well it works with SSDs. So treat it as a first guess. Load test around it and keep the size that gives the best latency. There is also a floor. If one request needs several connections at once, a small pool can deadlock. The minimum is threads × (connections per thread − 1) + 1. Our advice: better still, design each request to need only one connection. To check the app side, use Little's law from the tail latency lesson. Connections in use = requests per second × seconds each request holds one. At 500 requests a second and 10 ms per hold, about 5 are in use. GitHub's lookups took several seconds. At 3 seconds you would need 1,500. The multiplication problem Every app instance has its own pool. So the database sees the sum. Take 30 pods with a pool of 20 each. That is 600 connections against a limit near 100. Autoscaling and rolling deploys make it worse, because old and new pods run at the same time. Our advice: treat serverless functions as the extreme case. Each running copy may open its own connection, and many copies can start at once. Write the sum down. pods at peak × pool size + admin tools + cron jobs must stay below the database limit. When it cannot, put a shared pooler in the middle. External poolers: PgBouncer and RDS Proxy PgBouncer can accept many client connections and share a few server connections among them. It has three pooling modes: Session pooling. A client keeps one server connection until it disconnects. Every Postgres feature works. It is the default. Transaction pooling. A client gets a server connection only for one transaction. This is where the big savings are. Statement pooling. Transaction pooling that forbids multi-statement transactions. Transaction pooling breaks anything that lives in the session, because your next transaction may run on another connection. PgBouncer's docs list these as unsupported: SET and RESET. LISTEN. Session-level advisory locks. SQL PREPARE and DEALLOCATE, and WITH HOLD cursors. Temporary tables that live past one transaction, and LOAD. Two common workarounds: SET LOCAL, which lasts only for the transaction, and pg_advisory_xact_lock, which is released at commit. RDS Proxy, for example, does not pin on transaction-level advisory locks. Prepared statements used to be the big pain. PgBouncer 1.21.0 added support for protocol-level named prepared statements in October 2023. Since 1.24.0, it is on by default, with max_prepared_statements at 200. SQL-level PREPARE still does not work. Also note that PgBouncer is single-threaded and uses one CPU core per instance. On AWS, RDS Proxy is a managed pooler. It queues or throttles connections it cannot serve at once. Past your limits, it rejects them. When a Postgres session uses SET, LISTEN, SQL PREPARE, session advisory locks, temporary tables or even nextval, among others, the proxy "pins" that client to one database connection. Pinned connections cannot be shared, so watch the pinning metric. Exhaustion and leaks Here is a simplified model of what happened at GitHub. The pool size and timings are made up: Pool exhaustion looks strange from the outside. The app is slow and returns errors. But the database CPU is low and its queries are fast. The time is spent waiting for a connection, not running a query. The acquire timeout is your safety valve. A 30-second default means callers hang for 30 seconds first. Set it below your request deadline, so a full pool fails fast. Then load shedding and backpressure can do their jobs. A connection leak is a borrow without a return. Each leak shrinks the pool by one, until nothing is left. The psycopg docs warn that forgetting putconn() "will deplete the pool". # Leaks: if execute() raises, the connection never goes back. conn = pool.getconn() conn.execute(sql) pool.putconn(conn) # Safe: the block always returns it. with pool.connection() as conn: conn.execute(sql)To find leaks, turn on HikariCP's leakDetectionThreshold. It logs a message when a connection has been out of the pool longer than that. It is off by default. On the server, look in pg_stat_activity for sessions in the state idle in transaction. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout to end them. Option Gain Cost Use when No pool Simple. A new backend process per request. Scripts and one-off jobs. App-side pool No extra hop. Every feature works. Total = pods × size. A fixed, small number of instances. PgBouncer, session mode Every feature works. Saves little. One client still holds one connection. Many short-lived client connections. PgBouncer, transaction mode Many clients share a few connections. No session state, LISTEN or session locks. Many pods or serverless functions. RDS Proxy Managed. Queues, then rejects. Pinning stops sharing. You run on RDS and want no pooler to operate. Raise max_connections One config line. More shared memory, and slower active connections. Small steps only, after measuring. Simple rule: small app pools, a sum you have written down, and a transaction-mode pooler once instances multiply. Keep a table of every client of the database: service, peak instances, pool size. Check the sum against max_connections before each scale-up. Ask in review: "Does this code hold a connection while it waits for something else?" HTTP calls, queue publishes and file uploads go before or after the transaction. Set the acquire timeout below the request deadline. Alert on time waiting for a connection, not only query time. Graph pool metrics: active, idle, waiting and time to acquire. Turn on leak detection in staging and production, set to a few times your longest normal transaction. Before moving to transaction pooling, search the code for SET , LISTEN, pg_advisory_lock, PREPARE and temporary tables. Keep maxLifetime below any timeout in PgBouncer, proxies or load balancers. "List every place in this service that borrows a database connection. For each, say what else happens while it is held: HTTP calls, sleeps, retries or queue sends." "We have 24 pods, a HikariCP pool of 30 and Postgres with 4 cores and max_connections 200. Work out the total connections at peak and during a rolling deploy, and propose pool sizes." "We plan to put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of this app. Search the code for session state that will break: SET, LISTEN, advisory locks, SQL PREPARE, WITH HOLD cursors and temporary tables." What to ask the agent Every getconn or manual borrow has a matching return in a finally block or a with block. The proposed pool size came from a load test, not just from the formula. The agent counted all instances during a deploy, not only at normal load. Lock code uses pg_advisory_xact_lock, not session-level advisory locks, if you use transaction pooling. Your PgBouncer version is 1.21 or later before you rely on prepared statements, and max_prepared_statements is not 0. What to check yourself Before this: Postgres and Tail latency and queueing. Next to it: Backpressure, Load shedding and Circuit breakers and bulkheads.

title: Coordination services: ZooKeeper and etcd
text: ZooKeeper and etcd keep a small amount of critical data that every node must agree on. Learn what they give you, where they break, and what not to put in them.
body: On 28 October 2021, Roblox engineers saw that Vault was slow and one Consul server had high CPU load. Players were still fine. Roblox runs over 18,000 servers. Consul gave them service discovery, health checks, session locking and a key-value store. Nomad and Vault both depended on it. So when Consul was sick, services could not find each other. No new containers could start, and no secrets could be read. Roblox wrote: "the system failed because Consul was a single point of failure, and Consul was not healthy." Writes to Consul's key-value store usually took under 300 ms at the median. Now they took 2 seconds. The team replaced hardware. Later they shut down the whole cluster and restored a snapshot from before the outage. Neither fixed it. Latency stayed at about 2 seconds, or came back to it once load returned. There were two causes. A new Consul streaming feature caused contention under very high read and write load. And a usage pattern that arose during the incident hit a slow path in BoltDB, the store under Consul's Raft log. One log store was 4.2 GB but held only 489 MB of real data. The outage lasted 73 hours. Monitoring also depended on Consul, so the team was partly blind while they debugged. Afterwards they split some critical services into their own Consul clusters. They also began moving data out of the key-value store. Some services had used it "as a convenient place to store data". You met consensus in Consensus and Raft. Few teams run Raft themselves. They use a coordination service such as ZooKeeper, etcd or Consul, which runs consensus for you and offers a small, strongly consistent store. ZooKeeper lists what this store is for: configuration, naming, synchronization and group membership. In practice, that means: Config that every node must see the same way. Membership: which workers are alive right now. Service discovery: where each service runs. Locks and leader election. Leader election and leases covers leases, fencing tokens and ephemeral nodes in depth. This lesson does not repeat them. It is not a database. ZooKeeper "was not designed to be a general database or large object store". Its data is usually measured in kilobytes. It works best when reads outnumber writes by about 10 to 1. The key idea. A coordination service holds the few facts your whole fleet must agree on. Keep that data small and slow-changing. Every extra use you add is one more thing that breaks when it breaks. ZooKeeper: a tree of znodes ZooKeeper stores data in a tree of paths, like a file system. Each node in the tree is a znode. A znode holds data and can have children. Reads and writes of a znode's data are atomic. Two flags make it useful for coordination. An ephemeral znode lives only as long as the session that created it. A sequential znode gets a 10-digit counter added to its name, such as lock-0000000001. Locks and elections combine both. A session is the client's link to the cluster. If the cluster hears nothing from the client within the session timeout, it expires the session and deletes its ephemeral znodes. All writes go to one leader. The servers agree on them with an atomic broadcast protocol. The admin guide calls it ZAB. A write is committed once a quorum of servers acknowledges it. Each change gets a zxid, a number that shows its place in the total order. Writes are linearizable. Reads are not. Any server answers a read from its local copy, without asking a quorum. So client A can write a value, tell client B, and B can still read the old one. The guide says B should call sync() first. Even sync() is not a strict guarantee, because it is not a quorum operation. Standard watches fire once A client can set a watch when it reads. A standard watch is a one-time trigger. After it fires, you must set a new one. Between the event and your next read, the znode can change again. So you cannot reliably see every change. ZooKeeper 3.6 added persistent watches that stay after they fire. Step through how this differs from etcd. etcd: flat keys and revisions etcd has no tree. Keys sit in one flat, sorted key space. You read ranges of keys, so a prefix like /services/ works like a folder. etcd keeps old versions of every key, which is MVCC. A store revision counts every change to the whole key space. Each key records the revision that created it, the revision that last changed it, and a version count. The revision only goes up. Revisions make watches stronger. You can watch a key or range from any revision still in history. Events arrive ordered by revision, and none are dropped inside the history window. A broken watch can resume just after the last revision you saw, if that revision is still in history. A lease has a TTL and is kept alive by keepalives. When it expires, every key attached to it is deleted. This plays the role of ZooKeeper's ephemeral znodes. A Txn is an atomic if/then/else. If every compare is true, the success operations run; otherwise the failure ones do. This is compare-and-swap across keys. Here is "create the key only if nobody has": key := "/jobs/nightly/owner" resp, err := cli.Txn(ctx). If(clientv3.Compare(clientv3.CreateRevision(key), "=", 0)). Then(clientv3.OpPut(key, "worker-7", clientv3.WithLease(leaseID))). Commit() // resp.Succeeded is false if another worker created it first.Reads are linearizable by default. You can ask for a serializable read instead. One member answers it from its local copy, which is faster but may be stale. Limits and failure modes Small values only. etcd rejects any request over 1.5 MiB by default. ZooKeeper checks that a znode holds less than 1 MB. The size quota. etcd's default storage limit is 2 GiB, and 8 GiB is the suggested maximum. Past the quota, the cluster raises an alarm and accepts only reads and deletes. History grows. Old revisions stay until you compact them. Compaction leaves gaps inside the database file, so deleting data does not shrink it on disk. Defragmentation gives the space back, but it blocks reads and writes on that member while it runs. Roblox's BoltDB log store shows how far a file can drift from its data: 4.2 GB on disk for 489 MB of data. Slow disks. A majority must write every request to disk. If those writes take too long, heartbeats can time out and start an election. ZooKeeper also syncs each write to its log on disk before it answers, and wants a dedicated log device. The herd effect. If many clients watch the same znode, one change wakes all of them, but only one can act. The recipes avoid this by having each client watch only the node just before its own. etcd's gRPC proxy merges many watchers of one key into a single watcher on the server. Why Kafka left ZooKeeper Kafka used to keep its cluster metadata in ZooKeeper. KIP-500 listed the costs. Operators had to run a second system with its own config and tools. After an election, a new controller had to load all state from ZooKeeper, which took a long time. KIP-500 also wanted Kafka to support more partitions. The fix stores metadata as a log inside Kafka. Kafka calls this KRaft mode. Kafka 4.0, from March 2025, is the first major release that runs entirely without ZooKeeper. Option Strong consistency? Extra system to run? Use it when Row lock in your database (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) Yes, inside one database. No The data you protect lives in that database. Postgres advisory lock Yes, but the app must use it correctly. No Many processes share one Postgres and need a named lock. ZooKeeper Writes yes; reads can be stale. Yes You already run it, or a tool you use needs it. etcd Yes by default; serializable reads are optional. Yes You need watches that can resume from a past revision. Your own Raft inside the product Yes No, but you own the code. The metadata is core to your product, like KRaft. Simple rule: if the thing you protect lives in one database, lock it there. Reach for a coordination service when many systems must agree and there is no single database between them. Ask of every key: "Is this coordination data, or just data?" If it is large, changes often, or only one service reads it, move it to a database. Count who depends on the cluster. Split critical users into their own clusters before an outage forces you to, as Roblox did afterwards. Keep monitoring off the cluster it watches. Alert on etcd database size against the quota, and on leader changes. Set up auto-compaction and plan defragmentation one member at a time. Put the members on fast SSDs that other processes do not share. In ZooKeeper, re-read after each watch event, and design for missed middle states. In etcd, use a linearizable read when a decision depends on the latest value. In ZooKeeper, call sync() first, and remember it narrows the gap but does not close it. "List every key our services write to etcd. For each, give the size, writes per minute and readers. Flag anything that looks like application data, not coordination data." "Here is our ZooKeeper watch code. Check that it sets a new watch after each event and reads the current value, and show what happens if the node changes twice quickly." "We use an etcd lock to stop two workers handling the same order. The orders live in Postgres. Rewrite it with a row lock and explain what we lose and gain." What to ask the agent The agent did not store blobs, logs or per-request data in the coordination service. Watch code handles a compacted revision by reading the current state, not by crashing. Lock code that needs fresh data does not use serializable reads. The agent did not add a coordination service where a database row lock would do. What to check yourself Before this: Consensus and Raft, leader election and leases and failure detection and membership. Related: DNS and service discovery, CAP and consistency models and locks, atomics and deadlocks. For row locks and advisory locks, see PostgreSQL in depth. Kafka internals shows the KRaft controllers that replaced ZooKeeper there. See the Roblox incident page.

title: CQRS and read models
text: Split the model you write with from the models you read from, keep each read model rebuildable, and design the screen for the moments when it lags.
body: On 1 April 2026, GitHub code search failed every query from 14:40 to 17:00 UTC. That is the report's timeline. Its header lists the incident from 15:02. It started with a routine upgrade to the messaging system behind search. An automated change was applied too aggressively. Internal services lost coordination, search indexing stopped, and results began to go stale. During recovery, an unintended deployment cleared internal routing state. That turned stale search into no search at all. At 17:00 search came back, but in a degraded state. Results did not show any repository change made after about 07:00 UTC. Search only showed current data again at 23:45. The fix is the interesting part. The team reset the search index to a point before the problem, and indexed again from there. No repository data was lost. The report explains why: the search index is a secondary index derived from the Git repositories, and those were not affected. The index was a read model. It could be wrong for hours, and then be rebuilt from the source of truth. Most code uses one model for everything. The same Order class and table handle "ship this order" and "show my last 20 orders". CQRS, Command Query Responsibility Segregation, splits that. You use one model to change data and a different model to read it. Fowler first heard the idea from Greg Young. A command asks for a business task, like "Book hotel room". It is not a raw field update like "set status to Reserved". The write model checks the rules and saves the change. A query never changes data. It returns data shaped for one screen. The two models may share one database, or use separate ones. With separate stores, you can pick a different technology for each, such as a relational write store and a document read store. CQRS does not need event sourcing. The read side can be fed by events, by change data capture, or by a plain database view. Event sourcing usually needs read models, because replaying a stream for every query is too slow. The key idea. The write model is the truth. Every read model is a disposable copy, shaped for one kind of read. Make each copy easy to rebuild, and design the screen for the time when it is behind. Feeding the read side When the stores are separate, the write side must tell the read side what changed. A common way is to publish events. You usually cannot put the database and the broker in one transaction, so use an outbox and make the read-side consumer idempotent. The sagas, outbox and CDC lesson covers that pipe. The code that turns those events into a read model is a projection. Microsoft calls such a view "completely disposable", because it can be rebuilt from the source data. One write model can feed several read stores, each with its own projection: A SQL table shaped like the screen, for example order_view with status and total, so the list page needs no joins. A search index for text and filters. See search systems. A cache of the pages people read most, such as recent orders. Each one lags by a different amount, and each needs its own rebuild plan. Position, order and duplicates A projection reads events in order and remembers how far it got. In KurrentDB you subscribe from a stored position. To resume after a restart, you must save the position of the last event you handled. That saved position is a checkpoint. Marten's projection daemon stores its progress too. When a shard stops, it flushes its progress row, so the next start "picks up exactly where this one left off". Delivery is still at least once. Marten says so directly. A crash after you apply an event, but before you save the checkpoint, replays that event. So the handler must be idempotent. Order matters within one aggregate. "Shipped" before "Paid" would leave the wrong status. Route all events of one order to one handler at a time. With Kafka, you key messages by order ID, as in queues vs logs. Order across different orders rarely matters. Store the last applied version on each read-model row. Then a duplicate or an old event is easy to spot. Step through it. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Here is a handler for an event-sourced order. Each event carries its stream version and its global position. // CREATE TABLE order_view (order_id text PRIMARY KEY, status text, version int NOT NULL); // CREATE TABLE checkpoints (name text PRIMARY KEY, position bigint NOT NULL); // One runner reads the log in order. Seed: INSERT INTO checkpoints VALUES ('order_view', 0); // version is 1 for a stream's first event (add 1 to a KurrentDB revision, which starts at 0). type Stored = { streamId: string; version: number; position: bigint; type: "OrderPlaced" | "OrderPaid" | "OrderShipped" }; const statusAfter = { OrderPlaced: "placed", OrderPaid: "paid", OrderShipped: "shipped" }; async function project(db: Db, e: Stored): Promise<void> { await db.transaction(async (tx) => { const rows = await tx.query( "SELECT version FROM order_view WHERE order_id = $1 FOR UPDATE", [e.streamId]); const have = rows[0]?.version ?? 0; if (e.version <= have) return; // already applied: skip if (e.version > have + 1) // an earlier event is missing throw new Error(`gap in ${e.streamId}: have ${have}, got ${e.version}`); await tx.query( `INSERT INTO order_view (order_id, status, version) VALUES ($1, $2, $3) ON CONFLICT (order_id) DO UPDATE SET status = $2, version = $3`, [e.streamId, statusAfter[e.type], e.version]); await tx.query( "UPDATE checkpoints SET position = $1 WHERE name = 'order_view'", [e.position]); }); }The row update and the checkpoint commit together, so they never disagree. A gap throws and stops the projection on that event. It will not heal by itself, so you get an alert instead of a wrong status. With several partitions and workers, keep one checkpoint row per partition. With CDC instead of events, use a version column or the source log position in the same way. Rebuilding a projection You will rebuild. A bug corrupts rows, or a screen needs a new field. Run the projection from the first event into a new table, such as order_view_v2. Tools help with the replay: Marten's daemon has RebuildProjectionAsync. Building next to the old table and swapping is your job. Keep readers on the old view while the new one builds. Microsoft's advice is to build and validate the new view, then swap to it. GitHub's recovery was the same idea at scale: go back to a known good point and index forward. Time a full rebuild before you need one. If it takes two days, you need snapshots or a faster path. Microsoft notes that building views from many events can cost a lot of time and compute. When the read model lags After a user's command, the read model is behind for a moment. Microsoft calls this out: the read side may not show the newest changes at once. The user clicks "Ship" and the list still says "Paid". The general fixes are in read-your-writes. For CQRS, use these: Return the new state from the command. The write side knows it. The UI shows it at once, without asking the read side. Return a version token. The command replies "order 42 is at version 5". The next query passes it. The read side answers only once it has applied version 5. Wait with a timeout. Marten's QueryForNonStaleData waits until a projection reaches the latest events. By default it throws a TimeoutException if they cannot catch up in time. A mode to return stale data instead also exists. In a UI, wait a second or two, then show "updating…". Also watch lag in production. Microsoft warns that a lost or late refresh signal makes a view serve stale results with no error. Alert when its age passes your limit. Option Reads fast for every screen? Main cost Use it when One model, one store (CRUD) No Complex screens need joins. Low. Most services. Fowler says many systems fit CRUD. CRUD plus a reporting database Yes, for reports. One copy job to run. A few heavy queries. Fowler points to this when the domain does not suit CQRS. CQRS, one store Partly. Separate read code and views. More code, no lag. Read and write logic differ, but one database copes. CQRS, separate read stores Yes Each store fits its reads. Lag, rebuilds, idempotent handlers, more systems. Reads outnumber writes , or reads need search, caches or other shapes. Fowler's warning is blunt: "for most systems CQRS adds risky complexity". Use it only on specific parts of a system. Microsoft adds that it may not suit simple domains, or apps where CRUD screens are enough. Apply it per bounded context, not to a whole system. Ask first: "Which screen is slow or awkward, and why?" Often an index or a reporting replica fixes it without CQRS. For every read model, write down its owner, its source, its usual lag and how to rebuild it. Time the rebuild. Put a version on every read-model row and on every command reply. It costs one column and makes duplicates and stale reads easy to spot. Never let a command handler write the read model in a second call. That is a dual write. Let the projection do it. Alert on projection lag in seconds, and on handlers stuck on one event. Design each screen for lag. Decide what the user sees during the first second after they act. When a read model is wrong, rebuild it next to the old one and swap. Do not patch rows by hand. "Here is our OrderShipped projection handler. Write a test that delivers the same event twice and an older event after a newer one. Assert the row ends at the right status and version." "List every read model fed from the orders service. For each, show its source, how its checkpoint is stored, and the command to rebuild it from scratch." "Change the ship-order endpoint to return the new status and stream version. Then change the order page to show that status until a query returns the same version or higher, with a 2-second timeout." What to ask the agent The row update and the checkpoint save are in one transaction. The handler compares versions. A plain upsert with no version check lets an old event overwrite a new one. Events for one aggregate cannot be handled by two workers at the same time. The rebuild path writes to a new table and swaps. It does not truncate the live one. The rebuild does not send emails or call other services. Those belong to other handlers. No code in the command path writes to a read store directly. What to check yourself Before this: event-driven architecture and event sourcing. Related: sagas, outbox and CDC, scaling reads, search systems, database replication, exactly-once and effectively-once and domain-driven design.

title: Data models and query languages
text: Relational, document and graph models, and how the shape you pick makes some queries easy and others painful.
body: This story is made up, but it is a common one. A small team builds an events app on MongoDB. Each event is one document. Inside it is an array of attendees: user id, name and photo URL. The event page loads with one read. It is fast and the code is simple. Six months later, three requests arrive in the same sprint. First, a user changes her name. Her old name still shows on 40 past events. Someone has to write a script that finds and updates every copy. Second, a big conference sells 30,000 tickets. Its document keeps growing. Every read of the event page now loads all 30,000 attendees. Third, product wants a page: "events your friends are going to". Users and events now link both ways, and the app has no easy way to ask that question. The team writes code that loads friends, then events, then filters in memory. Nothing was wrong with MongoDB. The data had changed shape. It started as a tree, one event with its attendees. It became a web of users, events and friendships. The model had not changed with it. A data model is the shape you give your data: tables, documents or a graph. A query language is how you ask the data questions. Each model makes some questions cheap and others expensive. The relational model stores rows in tables. Tables point to each other with ids. You combine them with a join when you read. The document model stores a whole record, with its nested parts, as one JSON-like document. MongoDB is a common example. The graph model stores nodes and the links between them. Neo4j is a common example, and Cypher is its query language. The key idea. Look at the relationships in your data. If records mostly contain their parts, a document fits. If many records point to many others, tables or a graph fit better. The model decides which queries are easy. To pick a product, read Choosing a database. This lesson is about the shape of the data, which comes first. Step through the diagram. It shows one rename in two models. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Normalise or embed Normalisation means each fact is stored in one place. Other rows point to it by id. A rename is one write. The cost moves to reads: you join tables to show a page. Embedding puts related data inside the parent document. MongoDB's guide says to embed when one thing "contains" another and when you read them together. It says to use references when the child list can grow without limit, or when the child can exist on its own. Copying data to avoid joins is called denormalisation. MongoDB says duplicates can speed up reads. It also warns that if a copied field is updated often, a reference may be the better choice. Many-to-many links One user goes to many events. One event has many users. This is a many-to-many relationship. In SQL you store it as a third table. The PostgreSQL docs show order_items, which links products and orders. It has two foreign keys, one to each table. A foreign key means a value must match a row in the other table. The database rejects a ticket for a user that does not exist. You can also choose what happens on delete. CASCADE removes the linked rows too. In MongoDB you store ids and join with $lookup, a left outer join. Its docs warn that it can be slow on large collections without an index on the joined field. Schema-on-write and schema-on-read In Postgres, a table has a fixed schema. The database checks every write against it. This is schema-on-write. A MongoDB collection does not require all documents to have the same fields. The structure still exists, but your reading code decides what it means. This is schema-on-read. You can add a field without a migration. But your code must handle old documents that lack it. The line is not sharp. MongoDB has schema validation: rules for field types and ranges. By default, it rejects writes that break them. Postgres has jsonb columns for flexible parts. Its docs still advise a "somewhat fixed structure" for JSON documents. Declarative and imperative queries An imperative query is a loop you write: fetch users, then for each one fetch events. You choose the order and the method. A declarative query says what result you want. SQL and Cypher both work this way. The database's planner compares possible plans and join orders, and picks the cheapest. When the data changes, it can pick a new plan with no change to your code. Usually the new plan is better, but not always. A planner can suddenly switch to a slower plan as the data shifts. So watch the plans of your most important queries. Graphs and many hops Cypher draws the pattern you want. (a:User)-[:FRIEND]->(b:User) reads like a picture of two nodes and an arrow. A quantified relationship like -[:FRIEND]->{1,3} matches paths of one to three hops. SQL can do this too, with WITH RECURSIVE. The query repeats a step until it finds no new rows. The PostgreSQL docs warn that it can loop forever if the links contain a cycle. They show how to track the path, or use the CYCLE clause, to stop it. So deep, variable hops are possible in SQL, but they are easier to write in a graph language. The cells sum up the sources. Some cells are this lesson's own advice, so test them on your own data. Option Rename or update shared data Read one record with its parts Many-to-many and many hops Schema Relational, normalised Yes One write. No Needs joins. Yes Join tables; WITH RECURSIVE for hops. On write, checked by the database. Document, embedded No Every copy must change. Yes One read, one atomic write. No$lookup or code; slow without an index. On read by default; validation is optional. Document, with references Yes One write. No Needs $lookup or several reads. Partly. You search by ids in a way that is close to relational. Same as above. Graph Yes One node. Partly. Fine for small shapes. Yes Hops are part of the language. Usually flexible. Postgres with a jsonb column Yes, for the table parts. Yes, for the JSON parts. Yes, for the table parts. Mixed. Keep JSON documents small. Simple rule: embed what is read together and owned by one parent. Put anything shared by many parents in its own table or collection. Start from the access patterns you listed in Choosing a database. For each one, ask: "Which data is read together?" For each relationship, write "one-to-one", "one-to-many" or "many-to-many". Many-to-many is the warning sign for heavy embedding. Ask: "Can this list grow without a limit?" If yes, do not embed it. MongoDB says the same. When you copy data for speed, write down who updates each copy, and how you find copies that disagree. Use a jsonb column for truly varied fields, like product attributes per category. Keep ids, money and status as real columns. Add schema validation to a document collection once its shape settles. Add a graph database only when hop queries are a core feature. Try WITH RECURSIVE first. Read the query plan. A declarative query is fast only if the planner finds a good plan, which usually needs the right index. "Here are our entities and the screens that read them. Draw a relational schema and a MongoDB document schema for them. For each query, say how many reads or joins it needs in each design." "List every place this MongoDB schema copies the same data. For each copy, show the code that must change when the source changes." "Rewrite this loop that fetches users, then their orders, as one SQL query. Then run EXPLAIN and tell me which indexes it uses." What to ask the agent The agent marked each relationship correctly. Many-to-many is easy to miss. Embedded arrays have a clear upper limit, such as "at most 50 addresses". Foreign key columns you join or delete on have an index. Postgres does not create it for you. The agent did not put money, ids or status inside a JSON blob without a reason. A recursive query has a stop rule, so a cycle cannot loop forever. Each copied field has a named owner and an update path. What to check yourself Choosing a database: pick a product from your access patterns, once you know your data's shape. Data modelling for NoSQL: design tables around queries in DynamoDB- and Cassandra-style stores. Product catalog modelling: attributes that differ by category, a common use for jsonb. Schema migrations: how to change a schema-on-write table without downtime. For a longer comparison of the three models, read chapter 2 of Designing Data-Intensive Applications (1st edition).

title: Domain-driven design
text: Learn how to keep code and business words in step, split a big model into bounded contexts, and draw aggregates around real rules, and when all of this is too much.
body: This story is made up, but each part is common. An online shop sells kitchenware. One products table serves the catalogue team, the billing team and the warehouse team. It has 64 columns and a flag called active. The catalogue team wanted to reshoot photos of a popular steel bottle. So a developer set active = false to hide its page for a week. That was the meaning of "active" in catalogue code. The warehouse restock job also read active. To the warehouse team, it meant "keep ordering this from the supplier". So the job stopped buying bottles. The page came back a week later. Stock was nearly zero. Over the next weekend, 300 orders waited on bottles the shop did not have. Support spent days on apology emails. Nobody wrote a bug. Each team used the word correctly, in its own sense. The code had one word for two different ideas. In the hexagonal architecture lesson, you put business rules in a core with no framework or database code. That tells you where the rules live. Domain-driven design (DDD) tells you how to shape them. Fowler describes DDD as building software around a domain model with "a rich understanding of the processes and rules of a domain". The name comes from Eric Evans's 2003 book. Fowler says it fits complex domains with "a lot of often-messy logic". Evans sums DDD up in three points. Focus on the core domain. Explore models together with business experts. And "speak a ubiquitous language within an explicitly bounded context." DDD works at two levels. Evans says it "addresses both tactical and strategic design". Strategic design splits a large system into bounded contexts and maps how they relate. Tactical design gives you building blocks inside one context: entities, value objects, aggregates and domain events. The key idea. One word should mean one thing inside one part of the system. Draw a boundary around each part, give it its own model, and translate where the parts meet. Inside each part, group objects around the business rules that must always hold. A shared language Business experts and developers often use different words for the same things. Evans warns that the words of daily talk are often disconnected from the words in the code. So the team agrees on one ubiquitous language. It is used in talk, in documents, and "in the code". Evans adds that "a change in the language is a change to the model". If the experts start saying "reserve stock", rename holdItems() to reserveStock(). Experts should object to awkward terms, and developers should watch for unclear ones. Bounded contexts One language for the whole company does not work. Fowler saw the word "meter" mean subtly different things to different groups at a power company. He says the same confusion comes up again and again with "Customer" and "Product". Fowler quotes Evans's book: "total unification of the domain model for a large system will not be feasible or cost-effective". A bounded context is a boundary, "typically a subsystem, or the work of a particular team", inside which one model applies. Different contexts can model the same idea in completely different ways. Microsoft's example: one person is a User in one service, a Buyer in another, a Payer in a third and a Customer in a fourth. Step through the shop from the story. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Context maps A context map names each bounded context and its points of contact, with "explicit translation for any communication". Evans lists common relationships. Three you will meet often: Shared kernel. Two teams share a small part of the model and its code. Keep it small. Neither team changes it without talking to the other. Customer/supplier. One team depends on another. The downstream team's needs are part of the upstream team's planning. Anti-corruption layer. You depend on a system whose model does not fit yours, such as a legacy app. You build a layer that translates its model into your own words. Entities and value objects An entity has an identity that lasts while its data changes. An order is still the same order after its address changes. Evans says "the model must define what it means to be the same thing." A value object has no identity. You care only about its values, as with an amount of money. Treat it as immutable. To change one, you replace it with a new one. Watch the words. Fowler notes that "entity" is often used to mean a database table, which is not the DDD sense. Aggregates: consistency boundaries An aggregate is "a cluster of domain objects that can be treated as a single unit", such as an order and its line items. One entity is the aggregate root. Outside code holds references only to the root, and the root enforces the rules. Apply rules synchronously inside the boundary and asynchronously across boundaries. Vaughn Vernon shows why size matters. A Scrum tool modelled Product as one big aggregate holding all backlog items, releases and sprints. Bill added a backlog item, and the Product version went up. Joe then scheduled a release. His save failed, because his copy was based on the old version. No real rule linked the two changes. Vernon calls these "false invariants". His four rules: Model true invariants in consistency boundaries. An invariant is a rule that must always be true. Only objects tied by such a rule belong in one aggregate. Design small aggregates. On one project, about 70% of aggregates were just a root entity with some value properties. Reference other aggregates by identity, not by object. Use eventual consistency outside the boundary. He also says to change only one aggregate per transaction in most cases. These are guidelines, not laws. He lists reasons to break them, such as batch screens or having no messaging system. How do you pick? Vernon passes on a test from Evans. Is it the job of the user doing this action to make the data consistent? Then try to make it transactional, while still following the other aggregate rules. If it is another user's job, or the system's, let it be eventual. Domain events A domain event records "something happened that domain experts care about". It is usually immutable and often carries a timestamp and the IDs of the entities involved. Vernon uses events to update other aggregates, each in its own transaction, with retries if one fails. A worked example The Ordering context has an Order aggregate. Money is a value object. Customers and products are referenced only by ID. // ordering/money.ts: a value object export class Money { private constructor(readonly paise: number) {} static inr(paise: number): Money { if (!Number.isInteger(paise) || paise < 0) throw new Error("bad amount"); return new Money(paise); } add(o: Money) { return Money.inr(this.paise + o.paise); } times(n: number) { return Money.inr(this.paise * n); } equals(o: Money) { return this.paise === o.paise; } // equal values, equal objects } // ordering/order.ts: Order is the aggregate root type Line = { productId: string; qty: number; unitPrice: Money }; export type OrderPlaced = { type: "OrderPlaced"; orderId: string; customerId: string; totalPaise: number; at: string }; export class Order { private lines: Line[] = []; private status: "draft" | "placed" = "draft"; readonly events: OrderPlaced[] = []; constructor(readonly id: string, readonly customerId: string) {} addLine(productId: string, qty: number, unitPrice: Money) { if (this.status !== "draft") throw new Error("order already placed"); if (!Number.isInteger(qty) || qty < 1 || qty > 10) throw new Error("qty must be 1 to 10"); this.lines.push({ productId, qty, unitPrice }); } total(): Money { return this.lines.reduce((sum, l) => sum.add(l.unitPrice.times(l.qty)), Money.inr(0)); } place(now: Date) { if (this.status !== "draft" || this.lines.length === 0) throw new Error("cannot place"); this.status = "placed"; this.events.push({ type: "OrderPlaced", orderId: this.id, customerId: this.customerId, totalPaise: this.total().paise, at: now.toISOString() }); } }The use case saves one aggregate and its event in one transaction. The outbox from the sagas lesson then publishes the event. await db.transaction(async (tx) => { const order = await orders.get(tx, orderId); order.place(new Date()); await orders.save(tx, order); // one aggregate per transaction await outbox.add(tx, order.events); // the event commits with it });Billing calls a customer an "account". Its translation layer turns Ordering's words into its own. Teams often call any translator like this an anti-corruption layer, though Evans keeps that name for the defensive kind. // billing/from-ordering.ts: Billing's own copy of the message shape type OrderPlacedMessage = { orderId: string; customerId: string; totalPaise: number }; export async function onOrderPlaced(e: OrderPlacedMessage) { if (await invoices.existsFor(e.orderId)) return; // fast path for repeats const accountId = await accounts.idForCustomer(e.customerId); // their word → ours // invoices.order_ref is UNIQUE; the insert uses ON CONFLICT (order_ref) DO NOTHING await invoices.openOnce({ accountId, orderRef: e.orderId, amountPaise: e.totalPaise }); }The outbox may deliver the same event twice, even at the same moment. The unique order_ref column is what stops a second invoice. The early return only saves work. Line items, prices and quantity limits live in one place. Billing never imports Order. The money and ledgers lesson explains why amounts are whole paise. From contexts to services Bounded contexts are a good first guide to service boundaries. Microsoft notes that one bounded context may hold several services, "but not vice versa". You chose well if typical operations rarely need data from several models. A common trap is one service per table: Product, Customer, Order. Most features then need all three. Microsoft says that if two services must collaborate a lot, "they should probably be the same microservice". Splitting along contexts, not tables, is the idea the monolith and microservices lesson builds on. When DDD is too much Microsoft says to use DDD only for "complex microservices with significant business rules". A CRUD service can stay simple. It also notes that people find the patterns hard to learn. The important part is aligning code with the business and its words. Fowler notes the book has "a reputation for being a hard book to read", but says it repays the effort. A common mistake is the opposite of skipping DDD: using every tactical pattern in a simple app, and skipping the talks with experts. Evans himself says to spend the best effort on the core domain. For generic parts, he suggests off-the-shelf solutions. Option Same word, same meaning? Cost Use it when One shared model for everything No Each team bends the shared words. Low at first. Changes get risky as teams grow. A small app with one team and few rules. Bounded contexts in a modular monolith Yes, inside each module. Translation code where modules meet. The default for a growing product with several teams. Bounded contexts as separate services Yes, inside each service. Network calls, eventual consistency, more to run. Teams need to deploy on their own, and the boundaries are proven. Full tactical DDD (aggregates, events) Yes More classes and more design time. The core domain, where rules are complex and change often. Plain CRUD Not a concern. Lowest. Admin screens and generic parts with few rules. When a meeting gets confused, ask: "Which team's meaning of this word are we using?" Write the answer down. Keep a short glossary per context in the repo. Rename code when the business words change. Before you add a field to a shared table, ask which contexts read it, and whether they read it the same way. When you design an aggregate, list its true invariants first. If you cannot name one rule that links two objects, keep them apart. If a use case changes two aggregates in one transaction, ask whose job the consistency is. Most of the time, an event will do. Draw the context map before you draw the service map. Skip the tactical patterns for CRUD screens. Spend the effort where the business makes its money. "List every place in this codebase that reads or writes the products.active column. For each one, say in one line what the code assumes 'active' means." "Here are three of our team glossaries. Find words that appear in more than one, and show where the meanings differ." "This Order class is saved with its customer and every product in one transaction. List the business rules it enforces. For each rule, say which objects it really needs. Suggest smaller aggregates that reference others by ID." What to ask the agent The agent's rules came from the code or from experts, not from its guesses about your business. Each proposed aggregate protects at least one real invariant. It is not just a group of related tables. Cross-aggregate updates use events, with retries and idempotent handlers. The translation layer turns their words into yours. Your model does not import the other context's types. Simple CRUD parts did not get new layers they do not need. What to check yourself Before this: clean and hexagonal architecture. Next: monolith, modular monolith or microservices. Related: checkout and the order state machine, sagas, outbox and CDC, billing, metering and usage pricing and SOLID, coupling and cohesion.

title: Debugging production
