text: When production breaks, first stop the harm, then find the cause with data, one hypothesis at a time.
body: On 18 November 2025 at 11:05 UTC, Cloudflare changed the access rights on one of its databases. From 11:20, its network began to fail to deliver core traffic. Many websites behind Cloudflare showed error pages. An automated test caught the problem at 11:31. At 11:35 the team opened an incident call. The team first thought it was a huge DDoS attack. Two things pointed that way. Cloudflare had recently fought a wave of very large attacks. And its status page, which runs outside Cloudflare, went down at the same time. That was a coincidence, but it made some people think an attacker was hitting both. The errors were strange, too. The network failed, recovered, then failed again. The real cause was a file of bot features that was rebuilt every five minutes. The database cluster was being updated step by step, so each run could make a good file or a bad one. The bad file came from the database change. A query started to return duplicate rows, so the file doubled in size. The proxy had a limit of 200 features and normally used about 60. The bigger file went over the limit, and the proxy failed. At 14:24 the team stopped making new files, and a test with an older file worked. By 14:30 core traffic was mostly flowing again. Every service was back at 17:06. Note what misled them: a coincidence, and a symptom that came and went. In production, real users are hurting while you debug. So you have two goals, in this order: Stop the harm. This is called mitigation. Find the cause. Then fix it so it does not come back. Google's SRE book says that in a big outage, you may want to start hunting for the root cause at once. Its advice: "Ignore that instinct!" Instead, make the system work as well as it can for now. After that, use a loop. Look at the data. Make one guess, called a hypothesis. Test it. If the test says no, make the next guess. The book calls this the hypothetico-deductive method. The key idea. Mitigate first, debug second. Then let data, not the loudest opinion, choose between hypotheses, and test them one at a time. Step through one incident from the alert to the postmortem. 1. Stop the bleeding The fastest safe action is usually one of these: Roll back the last deploy or config change. In one Google emergency, an engineer pushed another config change to roll back the first one, and services began to recover. Turn off a feature flag for the new code path. Shed load or move traffic. The SRE book gives examples: send traffic away from a broken cluster, or turn off subsystems to reduce load. Fast action can still save evidence, such as logs. Take a minute to save logs, a heap dump, or one bad host out of traffic. If you feel overwhelmed, pull in more people. 2. Ask "what changed?" A system tends to keep running until something acts on it, such as a config change or a new kind of load. So start with recent changes. Check four kinds: Deploys: code, images, OS updates. Config: settings, feature flags, firewall rules, generated data files. Traffic: a spike, a new customer, a bot, a new client version. Dependencies: databases, caches, cloud services, other teams' APIs. In the Cloudflare story, the change was in a database, not in the proxy that failed. So look beyond your own service. 3. Read the right signals The observability lesson covers metrics, logs and traces. Two short checklists tell you where to look first. The RED method is for services. For each one, check rate (requests per second), errors (how many fail) and duration (how long they take). The USE method is for resources like CPU, memory, disks and network. For every resource, check utilization, saturation and errors. Saturation means extra work the resource cannot handle yet, often waiting in a queue. Tom Wilkie, who created RED, says RED cares about how happy your users are, and USE about how happy your machines are. Start with RED to find the service that hurts, then use USE on its machines. 4. Test one hypothesis at a time Write each hypothesis down, for example: "The new connection pool is too small." Say what data would prove it wrong. Test the most likely idea first, and think about risk to the system: "when you hear hoofbeats, think of horses not zebras." Take notes on each idea, each test and each result. Do not ignore a clear "no": negative results are useful too. 5. Narrow it down Split the problem in two, again and again. The SRE book calls this divide and conquer, or bisection. You can split by: Time: what happened in the minute before the first error? Region or zone: is one region bad and the others fine? Version: do errors come only from hosts on the new build? Tenant: is it one customer, one card type, one app version? Each good split roughly halves the search. 6. Follow one request Metrics tell you that something is wrong. A trace and its logs show what happened to one request. When service A calls service B, A sends a trace ID and a span ID with the call, in the W3C traceparent header. OpenTelemetry can add these IDs to your log records. The trace ID then works as a correlation ID: search for it and see that request's logs in every service. Safe experiments in production Sometimes you must test in production. Change one thing, on one host or a canary, and know how to undo it. Such tests can also change the results of the next test. Common traps The SRE book lists traps that send teams the wrong way. Wrong symptoms: looking at metrics that do not matter, or misreading what a metric means. Old causes: "it happened once, so it must be happening again." Coincidences: two things that move together by chance. Add two more. Confirmation bias means you see only the data that fits your first idea. Chasing the loudest symptom means you fix the error that fills the logs, not the one that came first. The worst trap is many people changing things at once. Google tells of an engineer whose change, made without telling anyone, made an outage worse. Its rule: only the operations team changes the system during an incident. Incident roles Google uses clear roles. The incident commander holds the overall picture and gives out the work. Operations makes the changes. Communication sends regular updates to people outside the call. Planning handles longer jobs, like filing bugs and handing over to the next shift. PagerDuty adds: "the Incident Commander is NOT a resolver." The commander leads; experts fix. The blameless postmortem A postmortem is a written record of an incident: its impact, the actions taken, the root causes and the follow-up steps. A blameless postmortem looks for the contributing causes "without indicting any individual or team." As Google puts it, you cannot fix people, but you can fix systems and processes. Blame makes engineers stay silent, and silence makes incidents longer. So ask "what" and "how", not "who" or "why". Cloudflare's follow-up list is a good example: check its own generated config files like user input, and add more global kill switches. Option Speed Risk Use it when Roll back Yes Minutes, if automated. Low, unless data or schema changed too. A change lines up with the start of the errors. Roll forward (ship a fix) No Write, review, deploy. Medium. A rushed fix can add a bug. Rollback is impossible, like after a one-way migration. Turn off a feature flag Yes Seconds. Low, if the "off" path was tested. The new code is behind a flag. Shed load or move traffic Yes Minutes. Medium. Some users fail on purpose. Overload, or one region is broken. Wait and investigate No Users keep failing. High for users. Impact is small and stable, and quick actions could make it worse. Simple rule: if a change lines up with the start of the errors, undo it first and ask questions later. Ask in the first five minutes: "Are users hurting? What changed in the last hour? How fast can we undo it?" Make rollback and flag-off a single, tested command. Practise it on a quiet day. Keep one timeline in the incident channel: each change, hypothesis and test, with the time. Say hypotheses as "I think X, because Y. If I am right, we will see Z." When a theory fits too well, look for data that would break it. Write the postmortem within a few days. Name systems and gaps, not people. Give every action item an owner and a date. "Here are 2,000 log lines from the checkout service between 14:00 and 14:20. Group the errors by type. For each group, give the count, the first time it appeared and three example trace IDs." "Here is our deploy log and config history for the last 24 hours. List every change that happened in the 30 minutes before 14:05." "Draft a blameless postmortem from this incident channel export. Use 'the on-call engineer', not names. Mark every claim you could not find in the export." What to ask the agent Every cause the AI gives is only a hypothesis. It can sound sure and still be wrong. Ask for the exact log lines, then open them yourself. The counts and times match your dashboards. Summaries can drop or merge errors. The AI saw the whole time window, not just the part that fit in its context. No secrets or personal data went into the prompt. You still do the reasoning. In Anthropic's January 2026 trial, 52 mostly junior engineers learned a new Python library, Trio. One group had an AI assistant. The AI group scored 50% on the quiz and the hand-coding group 67%. The biggest gap was on debugging questions. People who asked for explanations and conceptual answers learned more. The study was small and tested learning only shortly after the task. What to check yourself Related lessons: Safe deploys and config changes, Incident response and postmortems and Skill atrophy and deliberate practice.

title: Complexity and deep modules
text: Learn why code gets hard to change, and how to hide each hard decision behind a simple interface so one change stays in one place.
body: This story is made up, but it is common. Meera works on the payments team of a grocery app. Every night, a job writes the day's invoices to a CSV file. A second job reads that file and pays the shops. The writer builds each line with join(","). The payout job splits each line with split(",") and reads the amount from column 2. A finance report does the same split in a third place. Nobody planned it this way. Each engineer copied what worked. Then the tax rules changed. Meera added a tax column after the id, in the writer. Her tests passed. The pull request was small and looked safe. That night, the payout job read the tax as the amount. Hundreds of shops got paid only their tax. The report showed the wrong totals too. Finance found it the next morning. The bug was not in Meera's change. It was in the design. The file format was a decision that three classes shared, and nothing in the code said so. John Ousterhout teaches software design at Stanford. He uses the word complexity for anything in the structure of a system that makes it hard to work on. He adds that the reader of the code judges it, not the writer. He names three symptoms. Change amplification. A simple change needs edits in many places. Meera's tax column needed three. Cognitive load. You must hold a lot of information in your head to make a change. Unknown unknowns. You need to know something before a change, but it is not clear where to find it. You may not even know you need it. Ousterhout calls the worst case a crucial fact hidden in far-away code you have never heard of. He names two causes. Dependencies: if one piece of code changes, another must change too. Obscurity: it is not clear how the code works or why. No single choice makes a system complex. Thousands of small dependencies and obscurities add up. The cure is old. In 1972, David Parnas proposed a way to split a system into modules. Make a list of the "difficult design decisions or design decisions which are likely to change." Then design each module "to hide such a decision from the others." This is information hiding. The key idea. Give each hard decision one owner. Hide it behind a small, simple interface that does a lot of work. Then a change to that decision stays inside one module. Ousterhout calls this a deep module: a small interface with a lot of function behind it. A shallow module has a complex interface, or does little, or both. Step through the same format change in two designs. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Deep: Unix file I/O Ousterhout's example of a deep interface is Unix file I/O. You need only a few calls: int fd = open("invoices.csv", O_RDONLY); char buf[4096]; ssize_t n = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf); // bytes read; 0 at end, -1 on error close(fd);Look at what you do not see. Before Unix, systems often had separate calls for sequential and random access, and different calls for each kind of device. Unix uses the same calls for both kinds of access. The kernel keeps your position in the file. Each read moves that position forward by the bytes it returned. The kernel also hides its buffer cache and device differences. Devices use the same basic calls as files: open, read, write, lseek (called seek in early Unix) and close. One extra call, ioctl, handles device-specific work. Shallow: a wrapper that hides nothing Now compare a wrapper like this one, written in TypeScript: class RawFile { constructor(private fd: number) {} readBytes(buf: Buffer, off: number, len: number, pos: number) { return fs.readSync(this.fd, buf, off, len, pos); } }Every argument goes straight through. You still track the position yourself. You must learn one more name and get nothing back. Ousterhout says a class is shallow when calling it is not much easier than writing its code. He lists pass-through methods like readBytes as a red flag. Each layer should offer a different idea from the layers above and below it. Information leakage Information leakage is the opposite of information hiding. Implementation details are exposed, and other classes depend on them. Meera's CSV format leaked into three classes. Ousterhout calls this kind "back-door leakage": it is not visible in the interface. A common cause is splitting code by the order things happen: one class reads, the next one parses, the next one saves. Parnas saw the same problem in 1972. His first design made each processing step a module. If the way lines were stored changed, every module had to change. In his second design, "knowledge of the exact way that the lines are stored is entirely hidden from all but module 1." The fix for the payments team is one module that owns the format: interface InvoiceFile { write(path: string, invoices: Invoice[]): void; read(path: string): Invoice[]; }The column order, quoting and escaping now live in one place. The payout job gets Invoice objects and never sees a comma. Pull complexity down When some complexity cannot be removed, put it inside the module, not on its callers. Ousterhout's words: "Let a few module developers suffer, rather than thousands of users." He also writes that a simple API matters more than a simple implementation. One form of this is to handle a problem rather than pass it up. Each configuration setting you expose is a question for the user. Ousterhout asks: if you do not know the right value, how will a user or administrator find it? Another form is to define errors out of existence. Shape the API so the error case has a normal meaning. For example, "delete this key" can simply succeed when the key is already gone. Fewer callers then need special handling. He warns that it is easy to take this idea too far. It is for cases that are not really errors. Real bugs should still fail loudly, as the error handling lesson explains. General-purpose beats special-purpose Ousterhout advises making classes "somewhat generic". Build only what you need today, but shape the interface so it could serve other uses. His text editor example compares two APIs. The special-purpose one has methods such as insertChar, backspace, delete and deleteSelection. The general one has two methods: insert(position, text) and delete(start, end). Both serve the editor's keys. He says the general approach gives a simpler and deeper interface. Size is not the goal Ousterhout calls small classes taken to the extreme classitis. Each class adds as little as it can. He says classes of 200 to 2,000 lines are fine, and depth matters more than size. This is where the honest debate starts. Robert Martin's Clean Code asks for very small functions. Between September 2024 and February 2025, he and Ousterhout discussed it and published the result as a written debate. They agreed that modular design is good and that you can split code too far. Martin argued that small, well-named methods show how an algorithm works, even at the cost of some entanglement. He said that if he must err, he would rather err on the side of splitting, since you can always inline later. Ousterhout worried that tiny methods become shallow and entangled: you must read one to understand another. Martin summed it up: they both value splitting code, and both avoid entanglement, but "we disagree on the relative weighting of those two values." So "deep" is a judgment, not a metric. Parnas also noted a cost. If each function in his second design were a separate procedure call, it could be much less efficient. He suggested having the assembler insert the code inline instead. Design choice Easy to change? Cost Use it when Deep module with a small interface Yes Hidden decisions change in one place. More thought up front. Some calls may be slower. The decision is hard or likely to change. Many small, shallow classes No Each change crosses many interfaces. More names to learn, more jumping between files. Rarely. Merge them when they always change together. Special-purpose API Yes, for today's case only. Grows a new method for each new need. Rarely. Ousterhout advises making classes somewhat generic instead. Somewhat general API Yes New uses fit the same methods. A little more design time. Several callers, or a clear family of uses. Expose every setting Yes, for experts. Every caller must learn and choose values. The right value truly depends on the caller. Simple rule: before you add a class or a method, ask what it hides. If the answer is "nothing", do not add it. For each module, write one sentence: "This module hides ___." If you cannot fill the blank, the module is probably shallow. In code review, look for the same knowledge in two places: a format, a table layout, a magic string, an order of steps. Ask: "If this changes, how many files change?" See reviewing code. Count the files in a recent small change. If adding one field touched eight files, that is change amplification. Add it to your tech debt list with the count. When a class just forwards calls to another class with the same arguments, merge them or give the upper one a real job. When a caller must "remember to" do something, move that step inside the module. Apply the same thinking to REST APIs: a small set of resources that hide your database layout. "List every place in this repo that reads or writes the invoice CSV format. For each one, show the line that depends on the column order." "Find classes whose public methods only call one other method with the same arguments. List them, and say what each one adds, if anything." "Propose one module that hides this file format. Show its interface first, with at most three methods. Then list every caller that must change." What to ask the agent The agent's list of places is complete. Search for the format yourself, including SQL, scripts and tests. The new interface really is smaller. An agent can add a wrapper layer that just renames things. The agent did not split one clear function into many tiny ones to look "clean". Read the result top to bottom. Errors that were removed by design are cases with a natural meaning, not bugs that now pass silently. Behaviour is the same. Run the old tests before and after the change. What to check yourself Next: error handling and defensive design. SOLID, coupling and cohesion builds on this one, and so will a later lesson on functional programming ideas. Related: managing technical debt, reviewing code written by humans and AI and REST API design.

title: Deep dives and explaining trade-offs
text: Pick the riskiest part of a design, size it with numbers, compare a few options on your requirements, and say your trade-off in one clear sentence.
body: Ravi had three years of backend experience. He was in a system design interview for a senior role. The task was "design a photo-sharing app". After 20 minutes, his high-level design was fine. Then he tried to cover everything. Feed: "Kafka and Redis." Storage: "Cassandra, because it scales." Search: "Elasticsearch." He spent about two minutes on each box. None of them had a number. With 8 minutes left, the interviewer asked a question. "A famous user's post gets tens of millions of likes in its first hour. What happens to your like count?" Ravi said Cassandra handles it. The interviewer asked how many writes one row could take. Ravi did not know, so he said again that the database scales. The feedback said: "Good breadth, no depth. Could not explain why he chose anything. Defended answers instead of reasoning about them." He got an offer, but at the mid level. This story is made up, but each mistake in it is common. This lesson shows how those 8 minutes could have gone. A deep dive is the part where you take one hard piece of your design and work it out properly. Hello Interview gives it about 10 minutes of a design interview. You use them to meet the non-functional requirements, handle edge cases and fix bottlenecks. Depth is not knowing many tools. It is sizing one real problem, comparing a few fixes, and picking one for a reason others can check. That reason is the trade-off. Every fix gives you something and costs you something. Malte Ubl, describing design docs at Google, calls the doc "the place to write down the trade-offs you made". The same habit works when you speak. The key idea. Pick one risky part. State the problem with a number. Give two or three options. Compare them on the requirements you agreed. Pick one, say what it costs, and say what would change your mind. Step through one deep dive on the like counter from the story. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Choose where to go deep You cannot go deep everywhere, so choose the part most likely to break the design. Good places are: The hardest non-functional requirement, such as a write rate or a latency target. Hello Interview's examples, for a Twitter-like app, are scaling to over 100 million daily users and fast feed loads. A bottleneck you noticed and parked during the high-level design. Where the interviewer steers. Xu advises working with the interviewer to choose and rank the parts to go deep on. Skip parts that are interesting but prove little. Xu's example: going into Facebook's EdgeRank feed ranking in detail "is not ideal". Say your choice out loud and check it. "The like counter on viral posts worries me most. Shall I go deep there?" Step 1. State the problem with numbers A problem without a number is an opinion. Make a quick back-of-envelope estimate, and label guesses as guesses. See latency numbers and estimation. Suppose the counter lives in DynamoDB. Most likes on a viral post come in the first few minutes, so guess a peak of 20,000 likes per second. Each like adds 1 to one row. Now find the limit. A DynamoDB partition is designed for at most 1,000 write units per second. One write unit is one write of up to 1 KB per second. DynamoDB stores each item in one partition, chosen by a hash of its key. So one counter row can never get more than one partition's limit. It is about 20 times too slow. It is a hot key. The limit depends on the store. Firestore's docs give no fixed limit for one document. They say it depends on the workload, and advise load testing. Their counter sample assumes about one increment per second for each shard. Name the store you assume, then use its number. Step 2. Give two or three options One option is not a choice. Six options is a list, not a decision. Two or three is enough. A. One counter row. Simple and exact. It fails at our peak. B. Sharded counter. Keep 50 rows for the post, such as post42#1 to post42#50. Each like updates a random one. AWS calls this write sharding with a random suffix. To read the total, you read all the shards and add them up. C. Batch in the app. Each app server counts likes in memory and writes the sum once a second. That means few writes. But a crash loses the likes the server has counted and not yet written, about a second's worth. If the app has already shown those likes as saved, they vanish. Step 3. Compare on the requirements Do not compare options in general. Compare them on the requirements you wrote at the start. See requirements and non-functional needs. Suppose you agreed on three: Handle 20,000 likes per second on one post. The count on the page may lag up to 5 seconds. A like the user saw succeed must never vanish. A fails the first. C fails the third. B meets all three, but it moves the cost to reads. Firestore's docs say read cost grows in step with the number of shards. Too many shards make reads slow and expensive. So add one small piece. A job sums the shards each second and stores the total. Pages read that one value. Firestore's docs describe this kind of roll-up, at the cost of a total that lags behind. Requirement 2 allows that lag. Step 4. Pick, with a trade-off sentence Use one sentence shape every time: "X gives us A at the cost of B. Given requirement R, that is the right call." For the counter: "50 shards cut each key to about 400 writes per second, well under the 1,000 limit, at the cost of reading 50 rows for a total. The count may lag 5 seconds, so we read a cached total, and that cost is fine." The numbers are simple: 20,000 ÷ 50 = 400 writes per second for each shard key. That leaves room even if two shard keys land on the same partition. The sentence names the gain, the cost and the deciding requirement. A listener can check, or challenge, each part. Step 5. Say what you would watch, and what would change your mind End with how you would know it is going wrong. For the counter, watch throttled writes and how stale the total gets. Then name what would flip the decision. If counts had to be exact, like votes in an election, a cached total would not be enough. If only a few posts ever go viral, you could shard only those keys and keep one row for the rest. Xu's advice fits here: never say your design is perfect, because "there is always something to improve upon". When the interviewer pushes back A question is usually a hint, not an attack. Improving the design based on the interviewer's probes is part of the deep dive. Hello Interview warns against talking over the interviewer, and says to leave room for questions. So update, do not defend. "Good point. In that case B breaks here, and I would change this part." Changing your mind for a stated reason is a strong signal. Repeating "it scales" is a weak one. Common failure modes Defending instead of updating is one. Here are three more. Listing technologies. "Kafka and Redis" is not a design. Say what each one does, and for which requirement. Going deep everywhere. Two minutes on each of six parts shows no depth at all. No numbers. Without a rate and a limit, nobody can check your choice. How depth is judged at each level Hello Interview describes what interviewers expect at each level. Mid-level: "the expectation for depth is limited". You lead the early parts, and the interviewer may lead more later. Senior: go deep in "around 2 places", using your real experience. You spot limits in your own design and discuss alternatives. Staff: depth "in multiple areas". You foresee problems and lead almost the whole interview. Hello Interview also says senior candidates should find the weak spots themselves and lead the discussion. A later lesson, level calibration, covers levels in more detail. Way to spend the deep-dive time Shows depth? Cost Use it when Go deep on 1–2 risky parts Yes Other parts stay at high level. Almost always. Cover every part briefly No Sounds like a list of tools. Never as the main plan. Go deep on a part you know well but that is low risk Partly. Proves skill, but not that the design works. Only if the interviewer asks for it. Propose a part, then check with the interviewer Yes A few seconds. Every time. Simple rule: one risky part, with numbers, two or three options, one trade-off sentence, and one thing you would watch. A design review is a slow deep dive. The same shape works there. Ask "what is the riskiest part of this design, and how deep did we go on it?" Ask for the number behind each worry: the rate, the limit and the room left. Write the trade-off sentence in the "alternatives considered" section of the design doc. Ubl says this section shows "why the selected solution is the best given the project goals". Turn "what I would watch" into a dashboard or an alert before launch. When a reviewer pushes back, repeat their point in your words. Then ask if it changes a requirement or only the design. Keep one review meeting to one or two deep dives. Park the rest as open questions. "Here is my high-level design and my requirements. Which one part is most likely to break first, and why? Give me the number that shows it." "Give me exactly three options for this part. Compare them only on these three requirements, in a table. Do not add new requirements." "Act as an interviewer. Probe my sharded counter design with one hard question at a time, and tell me if I defend instead of updating." What to ask the agent Every limit the agent quotes matches the docs of the store you chose. Agents often mix up stores and units. The comparison uses your requirements, not general pros and cons. You can say the trade-off sentence without notes: gain, cost, deciding requirement. You know what would change your mind. If you cannot say it, you have not finished the deep dive. What to check yourself Before this: the system design interview method and making architecture trade-offs. Also useful: requirements and non-functional needs, design docs and RFCs and latency numbers and estimation. Next: level calibration.

title: Design docs and RFCs
text: A short written plan, shared before you build, finds problems while they are still cheap. Learn when to write one, what goes in it and how to get it agreed.
body: This story is made up, but it is common. A shop has a warehouse system from 2015. It reads each order ID and expects a number with exactly 10 digits. In a kickoff meeting, an engineer named Ravi says, "Do not change the order ID format. The warehouse parses it." Everyone nods. Nobody writes it down. Four months later, Ravi has moved to another team. A new engineer, Mei, gets a task: make order IDs safe to create on many servers at once. She chooses UUIDs, a common and good choice. The code review looks fine. Tests pass, because the warehouse is not part of the test setup. On a Friday evening, the change goes live. The warehouse system rejects every new order. For six hours, paid orders pile up and nothing ships. The team rolls back, then spends two days moving the stuck orders by hand. Mei did nothing wrong. The constraint lived only in the heads of the people at that meeting. One line in a design doc, "Constraint: the warehouse parses order IDs as 10-digit numbers", would have stopped this. So would a short decision record next to the code. A design doc is a short written plan for a piece of work. You write it before you build. It says what problem you solve, what you will not solve, the options, and why you chose one. Malte Ubl, who wrote about design docs at Google, lists what they are for. They find design problems early, while changes are still cheap. They build agreement across the organisation. And they become a memory of why decisions were made. The key idea. A design doc is not paperwork. It is how you think clearly, get others to find your mistakes early, and leave a record for the people who come after you. An RFC (request for comments) is the same idea with a more formal process. Many companies use the names in different ways. HashiCorp, for example, uses an RFC to propose a solution, after a separate document has defined the problem. When to write one. Will Larson suggests a design doc for any work that takes more than a month of engineering time. He also suggests one for work that other projects will build on, or that strongly affects users. When not to. If the right solution is clear, a doc adds little value. If you are still prototyping and changing things fast, writing and reviewing a doc may slow you down. Our advice: fixing a bug or adding a field needs a clear ticket, not a design doc. Step through the life of one design doc. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. A good structure Most good design docs have the same parts. Here is a short template you can copy: # Order IDs that are safe across servers Author: Mei · Status: In review · Reviewers: Ravi, Ana ## Context Why now, and what exists today. Two paragraphs. ## Goals and non-goals Goals: unique IDs from any server; keep the 10-digit number format. Non-goals: changing IDs of old orders. ## The design How it works. One diagram. Key APIs and data. ## Alternatives considered A: UUIDs. B: database sequence. C: Snowflake-style IDs. Why we chose B, and what we give up. ## Constraints, risks and rollout Warehouse parses IDs as 10-digit numbers. Rollout: 1% of orders, then 100%. Rollback: flag off. ## Open questions Who owns the ID service on-call?A few sections deserve special care: Non-goals. Ubl explains that a non-goal is something that could reasonably be a goal, but you chose to leave out. "The system should not crash" is not a non-goal. Non-goals stop scope from growing in review. Alternatives considered. Ubl calls this one of the most important sections. It shows why your choice is better than the others. Cross-cutting concerns. Security, privacy and observability. Ubl says each team should agree on which of these its docs must cover. Constraints. Write down the facts you cannot change, like the warehouse format. These are what new people do not know. Keep it short. Ubl says 10 to 20 pages works for large projects. A small change can use a "mini design doc" of 1 to 3 pages. HashiCorp's guide says the background takes a paragraph or two, and the proposal takes one. How reviews work First, share the draft with a few people who know the area. Larson's advice is to gather input together but write alone. A doc written by a group is usually harder to fix. Do not wait for perfect. A good doc in front of people now beats a better one next month. Then share more widely. Most review happens as written comments in the doc. Ubl describes this light path, and a heavier one: a formal review meeting with senior engineers. At HashiCorp, anyone can comment, but you need explicit approval only from the right team leads. Gergely Orosz reports that at Uber, the process started as an email to every engineer. Later it moved to mailing lists per area, such as backend, mobile and web. Some processes are more formal. Oxide keeps each RFD (its name for an RFC) in a git repo and discusses it in a pull request. Each one moves through states such as discussion, published and committed. The Rust project ends each RFC with a final comment period of ten calendar days, so people have a last chance to object. ADRs: the lightweight cousin A design doc covers a whole project. An ADR (architecture decision record) covers one decision. Michael Nygard proposed them in a 2011 blog post. Each ADR has a title, context, decision, status and consequences. It is one or two pages, and it lives in the code repo. Nygard's reason is simple. Without the "why", a new person can only blindly accept an old decision, or blindly reverse it. Both can hurt the project. When you reverse a decision, you do not delete the old ADR. You mark it as superseded (replaced by a newer decision) and link to the new one. The set of ADRs in a project becomes its decision log. Common mistakes Solution first. The doc opens with "We will use Kafka" before it explains the problem. Readers cannot judge a fix for a problem they do not understand. No real alternatives. Only one option, or two fake ones that nobody would pick. Too long. Thirty pages of detail that nobody reads. Put the decision and the trade-offs at the top. No non-goals. Every reviewer adds a feature, and the project doubles in size. Hidden constraints. The one fact that matters, like the warehouse format, stays in someone's head. Write in simple English Many of your readers do not speak English as a first language. They read on a phone, between meetings. Use short sentences. Use one word for one thing. Put the conclusion first. HashiCorp designs its RFC template so readers can stop at any time. Someone with a small stake can read only the background and the proposal. Option Who it helps Cost to write Use it when Just a ticket Your team, this week. Minutes. The fix is clear and easy to undo. ADR Future engineers who ask "why?" 30 to 60 minutes. One decision that is hard to reverse or easy to break by accident. Design doc Your team and the teams around you. Days. More than a month of work, many teams, or the right answer is unclear. Formal RFC process The whole company or community. Days to weeks, plus review time. Changes that affect many teams or public users, like a new API or language feature. Simple rule: match the weight of the document to the cost of being wrong. Ubl warns that heavy reviews can turn into overhead. Before a big task, ask: "If we get this wrong, how much does it cost to undo?" If the answer is weeks, write a doc. Write the problem and the non-goals first. Share those two parts before you design anything. Show at least two real alternatives, with what each one costs. Name the decision owner and a decision date in the doc header. Reviews without a deadline never end. Ask reviewers for specific help: "Ana, please check the database part." Close every comment: accept it, or explain why not. Unanswered comments look like open problems. After the decision, write an ADR and link it from the code. Link the design doc too. When you review someone else's doc, ask: "What constraint would a new person not know?" "Here are my notes and the current code. Draft a design doc with these sections: context, goals and non-goals, design, alternatives, risks, rollout, open questions. Mark anything you guessed with [GUESS]." "Act as a strict senior reviewer. List the five weakest points of this design doc. Look for missing non-goals, hidden constraints, missing failure cases and a missing rollback plan." "Rewrite this section in simple English for non-native readers. Keep every fact. Use sentences under 20 words." "Turn this decision into an ADR with title, context, decision, status and consequences, in under one page." What to ask the agent Every fact about your system is true. The agent may invent APIs, limits or numbers. The alternatives are real options your team could choose, not weak options added only to be rejected. The constraints come from people and systems, not only from the code. The agent cannot know what was said in a meeting. The decision and the trade-offs are yours. You must be able to defend them in review without the agent. The doc is short. Agents tend to write too much. Cut it. What to check yourself Next, read Architecture decision records and Clear technical writing.

title: Design patterns that still matter
text: Learn the few design patterns you will meet every week, how modern languages made them smaller, and how to spot a pattern that makes code worse.
body: This story is made up, but both halves are common. Ana works on a food delivery app. The delivery fee lives in one function, deliveryFee(order). It started with one if for each of three cities. Two years later it had nine cities, a rain surcharge and a late-night rule. The function was 300 lines long. A change for Pune once broke the fee in Delhi, because both cases used the same variable. A new teammate had just read about design patterns. He rewrote the code with a FeeStrategy interface, a FeeStrategyFactory, an AbstractFeeRule base class and a FeeRegistry singleton. That was 11 new files. The Delhi bug was gone. But now the tests failed only when they ran in a certain order. One test put a fake rule into the shared FeeRegistry. The next test still saw it. They needed one simple pattern. They got four, and one added hidden global state. A design pattern is a named answer to a problem that keeps coming back in a certain situation. The idea comes from building design. Venners describes Alexander's architecture work as having "inspired the software patterns movement". In 1977, Christopher Alexander and his co-authors published A Pattern Language. It has more than 250 patterns for towns and buildings. Each has a problem, a discussion and a solution. In 1994, Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides published Design Patterns. People call them the "Gang of Four" (GoF). The publisher describes it as "a catalog of simple and succinct solutions to commonly occurring design problems", with 23 patterns. A pattern gives you two things. The first is a shared name. Gamma says patterns "provide you with a vocabulary to describe and discuss a particular design." The second is a set of trade-offs, not "a pat solution" (a ready-made answer). Many patterns have become smaller since 1994. In 1996, Peter Norvig found that "16 of 23 patterns are either invisible or simpler" in Lisp or Dylan. He compared them with C++, for at least some uses of each pattern. He called a pattern invisible when it is "so much a part of language that you don't notice". One reason is first-class functions, which simplify four of them, including Strategy and Template Method. TypeScript, Java and Python all have first-class functions today. The key idea. Start from the problem, not the pattern. Name the pain first: a growing if, a vendor API that does not fit, a step you must add around every call. Then use the smallest form of the pattern that removes it. Often that is a function, not a class. In the SOLID lesson, you learned to hide details behind small interfaces that the caller owns. Patterns are common shapes for doing that. Step through Ana's fee code. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Strategy: swap an algorithm Problem: one decision has many variants, and a branch grows with each one. Norvig's slides give the GoF intent: "Define a family of interchangeable algorithms". In classic Java, the Strategy pattern means an interface and one class per variant. With first-class functions, Norvig writes, "the strategy is a variable whose value is a function". type FeeRule = (o: Order) => number; const rules: Record<string, FeeRule> = { blr: () => 30, pune: (o) => 20 + 5 * o.km, }; function deliveryFee(o: Order): number { const rule = rules[o.city]; if (!rule) throw new Error(`no fee rule for ${o.city}`); return rule(o); }Java has had this since lambdas arrived. Interfaces in java.util.function, such as Function<T,R>, are targets for lambda expressions. Gamma calls Strategy his "prototypical example for the flexibility of composition over inheritance". Observer: tell others that something changed Problem: when one object changes, several others must react. The first object should not need to know them all. The intent on Norvig's slide: "When an object changes, notify all interested". The Observer pattern is now built into most platforms. In the browser, EventTarget gives you addEventListener, removeEventListener and dispatchEvent. const orders = new EventTarget(); orders.addEventListener("placed", (e) => sendReceipt((e as CustomEvent).detail)); orders.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("placed", { detail: order }));Node's event emitters and reactive streams use the same idea. Pub/sub applies it across services. Remove listeners you no longer need. Forgotten ones keep objects in memory. Decorator: add a step around a call Problem: you want timing, logging, retries or an auth check around many calls, without editing each one. The Decorator pattern wraps a function or object and keeps the same interface. const withTiming = (rule: FeeRule): FeeRule => (o) => { const start = performance.now(); try { return rule(o); } finally { metrics.record("fee_ms", performance.now() - start); } }; rules.pune = withTiming(rules.pune);Norvig's slides show Lisp "around methods" used the same way, for example to add tracing. Web frameworks give you a related tool, but it is a chain, not a wrapper. In Express, a middleware function gets the request, the response and next. If it does not end the request, it "must call next()". Each middleware runs in turn, so it adds a step before your handler without editing it. Adapter: fit an API you do not own Problem: a vendor client has the wrong shape for your code. The Adapter pattern uses a small class that implements your interface by calling theirs. In the SOLID lesson, EmailApiNotifier was an adapter. It turned orderPlaced(order) into the vendor's call. Keep all vendor types inside the adapter. Then a vendor change touches one file. Factory and Builder: create objects in one place Factory problem: callers should not choose the concrete class. In a dynamic language, a class is a value, so the class itself can be the factory. Today a factory is often one function in your wiring code: function makeGateway(cfg: Config): PaymentGateway { return cfg.env === "test" ? new FakeGateway() : new StripeGateway(cfg.key); }Builder problem: an object has many optional fields. A constructor with eight arguments is easy to call in the wrong order. Java's HTTP client uses a builder. HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder() .uri(URI.create("https://api.example.com/orders")) .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)) .header("Accept", "application/json") .GET() .build();In TypeScript, an options object with named fields usually does the same job. Iterator: walk a collection Problem: go through the items without knowing how they are stored. This pattern is now part of most languages. In JavaScript, an object with a [Symbol.iterator]() method works with for...of, spread and destructuring. Norvig noted that closures remove the need for iterator classes when you pass a function to each item, as forEach does. When you need to step through items yourself, write a generator function, not an Iterator class. Template Method or composition Problem: many jobs share the same steps, and only one step differs. Template Method puts the steps in a base class. Subclasses fill in the step that differs. Fowler notes that here "the super-class defines the flow of control". This ties each subclass to its parent. Gamma says inheritance is "brittle, because the subclass can easily make assumptions about the context". The GoF book's introduction gives the principle "Favor object composition over class inheritance." In 2005, Gamma said: "I still think it's true even after ten years." So pass the step that differs as a value: async function runImport(lines: AsyncIterable<string>, parse: (line: string) => Row) { for await (const line of lines) await save(parse(line)); }When a pattern makes code worse Too many patterns. Gamma warns: "Trying to use all the patterns is a bad thing, because you will end up with synthetic designs." He advises: "Do not start immediately throwing patterns into a design". He likes to use them "after the fact, refactoring to patterns". Ana's teammate wrote 11 files to do the job of a map of functions. Singleton as global state. Hevery puts it plainly: "Singletons are nothing more than global state." Objects can then reach things their APIs do not declare. In his example, tests broke when the order of setup calls changed. If you need one instance, create it once in main and pass it in. That is dependency injection. Speculative abstraction. A factory for one class, or a strategy with one variant, is often built for a future that may never come. Fowler names four costs of building for a future need: the cost of build, delay, carry and repair. He says the same argument applies to abstractions built for future flexibility. An anti-pattern is the result. Andrew Koenig, quoted by Fowler, calls it "something that looks superficially like a solution but isn't one." Option Easy to read? Cost Use it when Plain if or switch Yes, while it is short. Grows; cases start to share variables. Two or three stable cases. Map of functions (Strategy) Yes One lookup, and names for each rule. One decision with many variants that change often. Interface plus a class per variant Mostly. More files and names. Each variant has its own state or several methods. Base class with steps to fill (Template Method) No You read two classes to follow one flow. Subclasses depend on the parent's details. A framework you do not own asks for it. Singleton Yes, at first. Hidden global state, tests that depend on order. Rarely. Create one instance and pass it in. Before you name a pattern in a design review, state the problem in one sentence. If you cannot, you do not need the pattern yet. Use pattern names to save words in reviews: "This is an adapter. Keep the vendor's types inside it." Wait until a branch really grows before you extract a Strategy. Prefer the language feature first: a function, an event emitter, a generator. Search for getInstance() and static mutable fields. Put them on your tech debt list, and pass the instance in when you next touch that code. In a decorator, keep the error behaviour the same. Rethrow, do not swallow. See error handling. If a factory or interface still has one implementation and no test fake after months, delete it. "Find switch or if/else chains in this module that choose between variants of one decision. For each, say how often it changed in the last year, using git log." "Find classes that use getInstance() or static mutable state. List the callers that depend on them without a constructor parameter." "Refactor this switch into a map of functions. Do not add new classes, factories or interfaces. Keep the behaviour and the tests the same." What to ask the agent The agent did not add an interface, a factory and a base class where one function would do. Unknown keys in a strategy map fail with a clear error, not undefined. Decorators keep the same return value and the same errors as the wrapped call. The tests pass alone and in a random order. What to check yourself Before this: SOLID, coupling and cohesion. Related: complexity and deep modules. Next: testing strategy. Low-level and object-oriented design builds on this one.

title: Disaster recovery and backups
text: Pick an RPO and an RTO, keep backups that a bad script cannot reach, and time real restores until you know you can get your data back.
body: On 5 April 2022, a cleanup script at Atlassian deleted 883 sites. They belonged to 775 customers. You met this outage in incident response, from the communication side. Here is the restore side. Atlassian was not careless about backups. It kept them for 30 days. It could restore any data store to a chosen point in time. It also kept immutable backups and tested its restores. The data did come back. For most customers, Atlassian restored to five minutes before the deletion. For 57 customers restored early, some databases first went back further, and Atlassian recovered the missing data later. It says no customer lost more than five minutes of data. Time was the problem. The first customers got their sites back on 8 April. The last sites came back on 18 April. Some customers waited up to 14 days. Why so slow? Atlassian regularly restored one customer or a small set of customers, and it could restore all customers into a new environment. It had no tested way to restore hundreds of sites into the live, shared environment. Each data store held data for many customers. So the team had to pull each deleted site out of the backups, piece by piece. With its first method, Atlassian estimated three weeks to restore everyone. In its own words: "we missed our RTO but met our RPO". Disaster recovery (DR) is your plan to get data and service back after something big goes wrong. That can be a lost data centre, a bad script, or ransomware. Two numbers set the goal. The RPO (recovery point objective) is how much data, measured in time, you accept to lose. The RTO (recovery time objective) is how long you accept to be down. Atlassian describes them with two questions. How fresh is the data after you restore it? How quickly can you give it back to the customer? Smaller numbers cost more. AWS calls the choice a trade-off between RTO and RPO on one side, and cost and complexity on the other. It also warns against a strategy that is stricter than you need. You saw in the replication lesson that a follower copies every change from the leader. That includes a wrong DELETE, so a replica is not a backup. AWS says continuous replication "will not protect you against data corruption or destruction" unless you also have point-in-time recovery. The key idea. A backup counts only after you have restored it and timed the restore, at the size and shape of the disaster you fear. Until then, it is a hope. Kinds of backup A full backup copies everything. It is simple to restore, but big and slow. An incremental backup holds only what changed since the previous backup. Since version 17, Postgres can take one with pg_basebackup --incremental. To restore it, you need it and every earlier backup it depends on. Postgres does not track that chain for you, so you must not delete a backup that a later one needs. A differential backup holds everything that changed since the last full backup. To restore, you load the full backup, then only the newest differential. Differentials grow every day, so Microsoft suggests a new full backup at set times, for example weekly. There is a second split. A logical backup, like pg_dump, writes rows as SQL. A physical backup copies the database's own files, or a disk snapshot of them. Postgres says logical dumps "do not contain enough information to be used by WAL replay". So they cannot give you point-in-time recovery. Point-in-time recovery Point-in-time recovery (PITR) needs two things: a base backup of the data files, and an archive of every write-ahead log (WAL) file since then. To recover, you load the base backup and replay the WAL. You can stop the replay at any moment after the base backup ended. Step through a recovery from a bad DELETE. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. You choose the stop point by time, by a named restore point, or by a transaction ID. You need an unbroken chain of WAL files back to the base backup. One missing file breaks it. Postgres advises you to set up and test WAL archiving before you take your first base backup. A physical PITR restores the whole database cluster, not one table or one customer. Atlassian hit a similar problem at a much larger scale: its data stores were shared by many customers. Restoring one customer from a shared store means a restore to a side server, then a careful copy back. Where the copies live The 3-2-1 rule says: keep 3 copies of important data (1 primary and 2 backups), on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite. A 2012 US-CERT paper states it and credits it to the second edition (2009) of The DAM Book, a book for photographers by Peter Krogh. In the cloud, "offsite" should also mean "outside your blast radius". AWS says copying backups to another account helps against insider threats or a stolen account. Attackers know where backups are. CISA says "many ransomware variants attempt to find and subsequently delete or encrypt accessible backups". It asks you to keep offline, encrypted backups. An immutable backup cannot be changed or deleted until its retention time ends. CISA notes that some cloud vendors offer this, but says to use it "with caution". It may not meet some compliance rules, and a wrong setting can be costly. Seatbelts against your own mistakes Deletion protection. Amazon RDS will not delete a database while deletion protection is on. It is on by default for databases created in the console. If you delete without keeping automated backups, RDS deletes those backups in the same region. A delayed replica. In Postgres, recovery_min_apply_delay = '1h' makes a standby apply each commit only an hour after the primary made it. That gives you time to stop it before a bad change arrives. Longer delays fill its disk with waiting WAL files. Soft delete. Mark data as deleted and remove it only later. After the outage, Atlassian committed to soft deletes, keeping deleted data until a retention period ends. Test the restore, and time it GitLab learned this in 2017. An engineer wiped the primary database while fixing replication, and the replica's data had already been wiped. The team restored from a disk snapshot made six hours earlier, which sat on a staging server. Copying it took around 18 hours, because the disks were throttled to about 60 Mbps. GitLab also wrote that nobody owned the backups, so "nobody was responsible for testing this procedure". AWS says your backup strategy "must include testing your backups", and suggests restoring on a schedule. CISA also asks you to test backups "in a disaster recovery scenario". A good restore test is a job, not a promise. Every week it restores the newest backup to a fresh server. It checks row counts and a few known records. It records how long the restore took, and it pages someone when any step fails. A game day goes further. The team acts out a whole disaster, with people, runbooks and the clock running. After the outage, Atlassian committed to regular DR exercises that restore every product for a large set of sites at once. AWS lists four strategies in order of rising cost and complexity, and falling RPO and RTO. The middle two, pilot light and warm standby, keep a second site partly ready. The ranges below are AWS's own. Strategy RPO and RTO (AWS) What runs at the second site Use it when Backup and restore RPO in hours, RTO in 24 hours or less. PITR can bring RPO as low as 5 minutes in some cases. Only backups. You rebuild servers and restore data after the disaster. Most internal tools and young products. It is cheap and simple. Pilot light RPO in minutes, RTO in tens of minutes. Data is replicated and always on. App servers are off until you need them. Downtime of an hour hurts, but a second full stack is too costly. Warm standby RPO in seconds, RTO in minutes. A smaller but working copy of the whole system. You scale it up. Customer-facing systems where minutes matter. Multi-site active/active RPO near zero, RTO potentially zero. Full production in every site, all taking traffic. You already need several regions for users or law. Simple rule: every strategy still needs point-in-time backups. Even with active/active, a data disaster's recovery point "will always be at some point before the disaster was discovered". Ask the business for the RPO and RTO of each system, and write them down. Ask, "Which restore have we timed this quarter, and how long did it take?" If nobody knows, the RTO is a guess. List the disasters you plan for: a lost zone, a bad migration, a deleted customer, ransomware. Check that each one has a tested restore of the right shape. Keep at least one backup copy in a separate account, with different credentials, that production scripts cannot delete. Before a risky migration or bulk delete, take a fresh backup and know the restore time. See schema migrations. Alert when a backup job fails or the newest backup is too old. "Here is our Postgres setup. Write a weekly job that restores the newest base backup and WAL to a fresh server, runs these five checks, records the restore time, and fails loudly if any step fails." "Read our Terraform. List every database, bucket and backup vault. For each, tell me if deletion protection, versioning or object lock is on, and who can delete it." What to ask the agent The restore test runs against a real, recent backup, not a tiny test database. Restore time grows with data size. The checks look at data, not only at "the server started". The backup credentials are different from the production credentials the agent saw. Code that can reach both is a single point of failure. Retention is long enough to reach back past the time a bug could go unnoticed. What to check yourself Before this: Database replication, to see how followers copy every change. Next: Multi-region systems and data locality, for running in more than one region every day, not only after a disaster. Related lessons: Incident response and postmortems, Safe deploys and config changes and Requirements and non-functional needs. Case study: the GitLab incident.

title: Distributed caches
text: One cache server is not enough. Learn how to spread keys over many, what each lost node costs you, and how to keep the copies honest.
body: On 22 February 2022, just after 6 a.m. Pacific time, Slack users started to have trouble connecting. Responders found very high load on one part of the database. Slack kept hot data in Memcached, in front of its sharded database. Mcrouter sent each key to a cache node by consistent hashing. A control plane called Mcrib replaced any missing cache node with an empty spare. A node that came back after some time away was flushed. That morning, a routine upgrade restarted the Consul agents on 25% of the servers. Each time a cache node's agent restarted, the node left service discovery. Mcrib swapped in an empty spare, and the cache hit rate dropped. One query made this much worse. When a client started, it loaded the members of every group direct message the user was in. That data was sharded by user, so "even one channel missing from cache" meant a query on every shard. Database load grew "superlinearly" as misses grew. Most of those queries timed out, so the cache could not fill again. Pausing the upgrade early on did not help. Slack had to limit how many clients could start. It also changed the query to read only the missing data. Mcrib worked as designed. It was so fast at replacing nodes that the cache emptied faster than it could refill. A distributed cache is many cache servers that act like one big cache. You need one when a single server cannot hold the data your app reads, cannot serve the request rate, or would hurt too much if it died. This lesson builds on caching and stampedes and sharding. Here you add four new questions: Where does each key live, and what happens when nodes come and go? What gets thrown out when memory is full? What about one key that is far too busy? How do you keep the cache in step with the database? The key idea. Your database is sized for the misses, not for the full traffic. The hit rate is a capacity number. Anything that empties part of the cache (a lost node, a deploy, a new region) sends a sudden wave of load to your database. Why one node is not enough In 2013, Facebook ran hundreds of Memcached servers in each cluster, to take load off its databases. One popular page fetched 521 different cached items on average. So one request can touch many cache servers. Once you have many nodes, every app server needs a rule that maps a key to a node. Three ways to spread keys A library in each client. The app hashes the key itself, usually with consistent hashing. There is no extra hop. But every client, in every language, must use the same hash and the same server list. A proxy. The app talks to a router, and the router picks the node. Mcrouter is "a memcached protocol router". Its README says it handles "almost 5 billion requests per second at peak". Its HashRoute picks a node from the key hash, with Ch3 as the default hash. Twemproxy does the same job for Memcached and Redis. It keeps the number of connections to cache servers low. Its default ketama mode is consistent hashing. Redis Cluster. The servers own the map. Each key goes to one of 16,384 hash slots, and each primary owns some slots. Clients cache the slot map. If a client asks the wrong node, it gets a MOVED reply with the right one. There are no proxies. For details, see Redis in depth. Adding or losing a node When Redis Cluster moves a slot, it moves the keys to the new node with MIGRATE. The data stays warm. A plain Memcached pool keeps no copies. A new node on the ring takes over about 1/(N + 1) of the keys, and those keys simply miss. A dead or replaced node loses all its keys. With 10 nodes, and keys and traffic spread evenly, losing one costs you about a tenth of your hits. That is what happened to Slack, one node at a time. Facebook chose not to rehash a dead server's keys over the others. One key can be 20% of a server's requests, so the server that takes it over may fall over too. Instead, failed requests go to a small spare pool called Gutter, about 1% of the servers. Its entries expire quickly. This cut client-visible failures by 99%. Eviction and sizing When memory is full, the cache must evict something. The main policies in Redis are: LRU (allkeys-lru) drops the key used least recently. It is the suggested default when some keys are read far more than others. LFU (allkeys-lfu) drops the key used least often. Its counters decay, by default every minute, so old favourites can leave. TTL-based (volatile-ttl) drops keys with the shortest time left to live. Redis does not track exact LRU. It samples a few keys at random and drops the ones unused the longest. maxmemory-samples sets how many. Size the cache from your working set: the data you read in a day or a week, not all the data you have. Facebook's paper shows the daily and weekly working sets of two families of keys. Then check the result. Hit rate is keyspace_hits / (keyspace_hits + keyspace_misses). If it is low and evicted_keys is high, the right keys are being thrown out too often. Hot keys One hot key can get more traffic than its node can serve, however many nodes you add. First, find it. Count requests per key in the client or proxy, on a sample of traffic. Then pick a fix: A near cache. Keep the hottest keys in each app server's memory. Redis can help: with tracking on, the server remembers which keys a client read. It sends an invalidation message when one of them changes. If that message can beat a read's reply, store a "caching-in-progress" placeholder first. Flush the local cache if that connection drops. Put a maximum TTL on every local key. Copies of the key. Facebook copies some keys to several servers in a pool. In its example, each request needs all 100 keys. Splitting them over two servers still sends every request to both. Copying them halves the load on each. Every write must then delete every copy. Split the key. For a hot counter, split it into many keys, as in the sharding lesson. Keeping the cache in step with the database Facebook updates the database, then deletes the key from the cache. It deletes, not updates, because a delete is idempotent. Deleting still leaves a race. Step through it. Facebook calls this a "stale set". Its fix is a lease: a 64-bit token the cache gives a client on a miss. The client must show the token to set the value. A delete cancels the token, so a late set with an old value is rejected. Across regions. To reach other clusters, Facebook does not rely on web servers to send deletes. A daemon called mcsqueal reads the SQL each database commits and sends the deletes to the caches. Because deletes live in the database log, lost ones can be replayed. Mcsqueal also runs on the replica databases in other regions. Each one sends a delete only when the change reaches its own database. So a reader there is less likely to put old data back in the cache. Cold start and warm-up A new or rebuilt cache cluster has a very poor hit rate. Facebook lets a cold cluster read misses from a warm cluster, not the database. That brings it back to full capacity "in a few hours instead of a few days". To avoid a race, deletes in the cold cluster block new adds for two seconds. Mcrouter offers this as WarmUpRoute. Gets try the cold node first and fall back to the warm one. If you have no warm copy, let traffic in slowly, as Slack did. Option Extra hop? When a node changes Watch out for Hashing in each client No Keys on the moved arc miss. Every client must agree on the hash and the server list. Proxy (mcrouter, twemproxy) Yes Keys on the moved arc miss, unless you add warm-up or copies. The proxy is one more thing to run and scale. Redis Cluster No Clients may get a redirect. Keys move with their slot. Multi-key commands need all keys in one slot. Near cache No network at all. Not affected. Stale local copies if invalidations are lost. Copies of hot keys Depends on the router. Other copies keep serving. Every write must delete every copy. Simple rule: start with a proxy or a cluster client and LRU. Add near caches and copies only for the keys you have measured as hot. Ask: "If we lose one cache node, or a whole cluster, how much extra load hits the database?" Then test it. Make misses cheap. A large part of Slack's problem was a miss that queried every shard. Limit how fast nodes are replaced or flushed. Fast churn empties the cache faster than misses refill it. Chart hit rate, evictions and the top keys per node, next to database load. Write down which data may be stale and for how long. That decides between delete, leases and near caches. Plan warm-up before a migration, a new region or a full restart. "Here is our cache-aside code. Find every place that sets a cache value after a database read. Show me the race with a concurrent write, and add a version check." "Write a script that replays 1 hour of our key access log against an LRU cache of 4, 8 and 16 GB. Print the hit rate for each size." "Add a near cache for these 20 keys with a 5-second maximum TTL, Redis client tracking, and a flush when the tracking connection drops." What to ask the agent Writes delete the cache key after the database commit. Every local copy has a maximum TTL and a memory limit. The replay test uses real, skewed traffic. Uniform fake keys hide hot keys. There is a limit on how many clients can start at once, for the day the cache is empty. What to check yourself Before this: Caching and cache stampedes and Sharding and consistent hashing. Next: Redis in depth, CDN and HTTP caching and Load shedding.

title: Distributed tracing in practice
text: A trace shows where one request spent its time across many services. Learn to pass the trace ID along and read the waterfall.
body: In 2020, Logz.io received reports that its product was slow. It happened mostly between 2 PM and 7 PM, when European and American customers were online together. Their own staff saw the same slowness . Logs showed slow endpoints in that window. They also showed a growing number of calls to an internal service that serves user session tokens from the database. Metrics showed big database commits and replication lag at the same times . Both said that something was wrong. Neither said where. The team then filtered traces to show only requests slower than 5 seconds. At peak times, almost every endpoint was slow when it fired a search request . The obvious suspect was Elasticsearch, the search database. The trace said no. Matched with its logs, it showed that the Elasticsearch query took only 15 ms . With Elasticsearch ruled out, the team found the cause in the session token service: too many requests reached it . The fix was a two-line change to the session token cache's eviction policy. Calls to that service dropped by more than 80%, and latency fell on all affected endpoints . The trace ruled out Elasticsearch, so the team could look elsewhere. A trace is the story of one request as it moves through your services. It is made of spans. Each span is one piece of work with a name, a start time and an end time . Spans form a tree. The first span is the root span and has no parent. Every other span stores its parent span ID. All spans in the tree share one trace ID . Google described this tree of spans in its Dapper paper in 2010 . OpenTelemetry uses the same model today . A span can carry more detail : Attributes: key-value pairs, like cart.items = 5 or http.route = /checkout. Events: a named moment with a timestamp inside the span, like "retry started". Status: Unset (the default, meaning no error), Error, or Ok when the developer marks success on purpose. Links: a pointer to another span, often in a different trace, that is causally related to this one. Your tool draws the spans as a waterfall: one bar per span, placed on a time line. Child bars sit under their parents. The key idea. Metrics and logs tell you that a request is slow. A trace shows which span used the time. Read the critical path first: it is the only place where saving time makes the request faster. Passing the trace ID along For one trace to cover many services, each call must carry the trace ID and the caller's span ID. This is context propagation . Instrumentation libraries usually do it for you. OpenTelemetry's default uses the W3C Trace Context headers . The main header is traceparent : traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01 │ │ │ └ trace-flags │ │ └ parent-id (16 hex) │ └ trace-id (32 hex) └ versionversion is 00 today. The value ff is invalid . trace-id is 16 bytes as 32 lowercase hex characters. All zeros is invalid . parent-id is 8 bytes as 16 lowercase hex characters: the caller's span ID . trace-flags is 8 bits. Only the lowest bit is defined: 01 means the caller may have recorded this trace ("sampled") . When a service receives a valid traceparent, it keeps the trace ID. Before it calls the next service, it sets a new parent-id: the ID of its own current span. This is the normal case . If the header is invalid, the service starts a new trace . A second header, tracestate, carries vendor-specific data . Step through one checkout request. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Across a queue A message may wait in a queue for minutes. One consumer may also process many messages in one batch. So OpenTelemetry's messaging rules say the producer should attach a creation context to each message, for example in the message headers . The consumer then adds a span link to it by default, not a parent. A span can have only one parent, but it can link to every message in a batch . For one message at a time, using the producer as parent is allowed . See Queues vs logs for how messages move. from opentelemetry import trace from opentelemetry.propagate import inject, extract tracer = trace.get_tracer("orders") with tracer.start_as_current_span("publish order", kind=trace.SpanKind.PRODUCER): headers = {} inject(headers) # adds traceparent of this span queue.publish(body, headers=headers) # consumer ctx = trace.get_current_span(extract(msg.headers)).get_span_context() with tracer.start_as_current_span("process order", kind=trace.SpanKind.CONSUMER, links=[trace.Link(ctx)]): handle(msg)Where the spans come from OpenTelemetry has two ways to instrument code . Zero-code instrumentation records spans from the libraries you already use, such as web frameworks and database clients. Code-based instrumentation uses the API to add spans for your own business logic. You can use both at once . The API is what libraries depend on. It has no effect until the application also adds the SDK . The SDK is the part that records and exports spans. OpenTelemetry recommends sending spans to an OpenTelemetry Collector running next to the service . It can retry, batch, filter sensitive data and send to one or more backends . Reading the waterfall Open a slow trace from your tail latency graph and look for four shapes: The critical path. Follow the chain of spans that ends last. Only shortening these spans shortens the request. Calls in a row that do not depend on each other. They could run in parallel. N+1 calls. The same short span repeats many times, once per item. Replace them with one batched call. Gaps. Time where no span is recorded. It is often queue wait, a busy thread pool, or code without spans. To estimate if a span's time is reasonable, compare it with latency numbers. You rarely keep every trace. There are two ways to choose: head sampling decides when the request starts, and tail sampling decides after the trace ends . Choice Keeps rare slow and error traces? Cost Use it when Keep every trace Yes Very high at scale. Low traffic: tens of traces per second or fewer . Head-based sampling (for example 5%) Not reliably. It decides at the start . Low. Easy to set up. You need a cheap first step. Dapper kept about 1 trace in 1,024 and still had enough data for busy services . Tail-based sampling Yes It can keep every error and every slow trace . High. Needs stateful collectors that hold spans until the trace ends . You must catch rare failures, and you can run the extra servers. Head first, then tail Only among the traces the head sampler kept. Medium. Very high volume: head sampling protects the pipeline, tail sampling picks the useful traces . The sampled flag in traceparent carries the caller's decision to the next service, so all services keep or drop the same trace . Put the trace ID in every log line. Then a slow trace leads you straight to that request's logs. OpenTelemetry SDKs can add it for you . The debugging lesson shows how to use it during an incident. Turn on exemplars on latency histograms. An exemplar stores the trace ID of one real request with the metric point . In tools that support it, you click a spike on the p99 graph and land on a slow trace. Put high-cardinality data, like user ID or order ID, on span attributes. Never put it in metric labels. Each new combination of label values creates a new time series, so storage and cost grow . Check every hop for broken propagation. A proxy or API gateway that drops unknown headers cuts the trace in two. Test it: send a request and confirm one trace ID in all services. Watch thread pools and async code. Dapper kept the trace context in thread-local storage. It had to copy that context into every callback sent to a thread pool . Most OpenTelemetry SDKs, or the language's own context tools, can carry the context into a task. Check yours. Expect clock skew. Spans from different hosts use different clocks . A child that seems to start before its parent is usually a clock problem, not a bug. Do not trust incoming trace headers from the internet. An attacker could set sampled on every request and run up your tracing bill . Start a new trace at your edge. During an incident, compare a slow trace with a fast one for the same endpoint. The span that differs is your best lead. "Add OpenTelemetry to this Python service. Use zero-code instrumentation for Flask, requests and psycopg. Add one manual span around price_cart with the item count as an attribute. Export to a local Collector over OTLP." "Here is a trace as JSON. List the spans on the critical path, any repeated spans that look like N+1 calls, and any gaps longer than 10 ms between a parent and its first child." "This worker reads from a queue. Show how to inject trace context into the message headers on publish and add a span link on consume." What to ask the agent The traceparent header really reaches the next service. Agents often forget proxies, queues and thread pools. The trace ID is in your logs, in the same format your tracing tool shows. No user ID, email or order ID ends up as a metric label. Span attributes contain no passwords, tokens or personal data. The sampling setup matches your goal. Head sampling alone will not keep every error trace.
