The service ignores or restarts trace context from untrusted callers. What to check yourself Before this lesson: Observability and SLOs covers metrics, logs and error budgets. Next, use traces to find slow requests in Tail latency and queueing.

title: Distributed transactions and two-phase commit
text: Two-phase commit makes several databases commit as one. Learn how it works, why it can freeze when the coordinator dies, and what to use across services instead.
body: In April 2009, an administrator posted to the PostgreSQL admin mailing list. She had inherited a test server running PostgreSQL 8.2.9. It had 315 databases. The server refused to work. Every connection got "database is not accepting commands to avoid wraparound data loss". She followed the hint and ran VACUUM in single-user mode. The server still would not start normally. She started a new thread when she could not drop a database. Tom Lane, a core Postgres developer, asked one question: "Maybe you've got some prepared transactions laying about?" She checked. There were three. The oldest had been waiting since July 2008. She did not know what had created them. She ran ROLLBACK PREPARED on each one. VACUUM worked again, and she was "back in business". Most of their code was Java on JBoss. Another list member suggested a likely cause: XA two-phase commit code that assumed a rollback on disconnect. Nobody confirmed it. The same day, Tom Lane told the developers' list that this was "another instance" of the problem. He proposed turning the feature off by default. That evening, he committed the change. The commit message said the project had seen this "several times now". A transaction in one database is all or nothing. You saw this in transactions and isolation levels. Now one action changes two databases. You want both changes, or neither. This is the atomic commit problem. You cannot just commit one, then the other. If the second fails, the first is already committed. Two-phase commit (2PC) solves this with a coordinator. In phase one, it asks every database, "Can you commit?" In phase two, it tells all of them the same answer. The catch is in the middle. A database that says "yes" gives up its right to decide. It must wait for the coordinator, however long that takes. The key idea. 2PC makes many machines agree, but one machine holds the decision. If that machine dies at the wrong moment, the others wait with their locks held. Modern databases avoid most of this by replicating the decision with consensus. The two phases XA, a standard that many databases support, calls the coordinator a transaction manager. Each database is a resource manager. Prepare. The coordinator asks each database to prepare. Each one writes its changes to stable storage and votes yes or no. Commit or abort. If every vote is yes, the coordinator tells all of them to commit. If any vote is no, it tells all of them to roll back. Every machine writes its state to disk before it sends a message. After a crash, it reads that state and carries on. The coordinator's log entry is the real moment of commit. Once it says COMMIT, the transaction is committed, even if no database has heard yet. Why it blocks Step through one order that changes two databases. If a database does not answer phase one, the coordinator simply aborts. The bad case comes later. If the coordinator fails right after every database has voted yes, the databases cannot know whether it committed or aborted. The protocol blocks until the coordinator is repaired. A transaction in this state is an in-doubt transaction. It keeps every row lock it holds. Other transactions that need those rows wait too. The cost is also visible when nothing fails. With the coordinator on the same node as one database, a commit takes three message delays. Add disk writes for each prepare and for the decision. Postgres: PREPARE TRANSACTION Postgres gives you the database side of 2PC: -- needs max_prepared_transactions > 0 BEGIN; UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 'tee-m'; PREPARE TRANSACTION 'order-42'; -- later, from any session: COMMIT PREPARED 'order-42'; -- or ROLLBACK PREPAREDAfter PREPARE, the transaction no longer belongs to your session. Its state is on disk, and it can almost always still commit after a crash. Any session can finish it. The docs say this command is not meant for applications. It is for an external transaction manager. They also warn that leaving a transaction prepared for a long time is unwise. It keeps its locks, it stops VACUUM from reclaiming space, and in extreme cases it can force a shutdown to prevent transaction ID wraparound. That is what happened to the test server above. The fix since 2009: max_prepared_transactions defaults to 0, which turns the feature off. Keep it at 0 unless a transaction manager tracks every prepared transaction. You can list open ones in the pg_prepared_xacts view. Making 2PC fault-tolerant The weak point is one coordinator on one machine. So replicate it, the way Raft replicates a log. Gray and Lamport's Paxos Commit goes a step further. It runs Paxos on each database's vote, uses 2F+1 coordinators, and makes progress while F+1 of them work. Classic 2PC is the case F = 0. Spanner. Google's Spanner splits data into Paxos groups. A transaction inside one group does not need 2PC. If it spans several groups, their leaders run 2PC, and one group acts as coordinator. Each prepare record and the commit record go through Paxos. So the coordinator's state is replicated. The paper says "Running two-phase commit over Paxos mitigates the availability problems." CockroachDB. CockroachDB also runs 2PC on top of consensus. A transaction's record is replicated the same way as its writes. Each write is a write intent: "a replicated lock and a replicated provisional value". The coordinator heartbeats the transaction record. If the heartbeats stop, the record is moved to ABORTED, so others stop waiting. A STAGING transaction is the exception, as below. Its older protocol needed two consensus rounds in a row: the writes, then the commit record. Parallel commits writes a STAGING record and the writes at the same time. Once every listed write has reached consensus, the transaction counts as committed. Cockroach Labs says this commits cross-range transactions in half the time. If the coordinator dies, another transaction checks the listed writes. If all are there, the transaction is committed. If any is missing, it first stops that write from ever landing, then marks the transaction aborted. What it still costs Consensus removes the single point of failure. It does not remove the waiting. In Spanner's tests, a commit with 1 participant took 17 ms on average. With 50 it took 42.7 ms, and with 200 it took 150.5 ms. The paper calls up to 50 participants reasonable. Participants release their locks only after the commit is applied. So locks are held longer as participants grow. Option Atomic across all parts? Blocks if the coordinator dies? Use it when One database transaction Yes No coordinator. The data fits in one database. Prefer this. Classic 2PC or XA Yes Yes Locks stay until it returns. Rarely. A tested transaction manager owns recovery. 2PC over consensus (Spanner, CockroachDB) Yes Not when one machine dies. It waits only if most replicas of a group are down. You already run such a database. It handles 2PC for you. Saga, outbox and idempotent steps No Each step commits alone and compensations undo. No global locks. Several services, each with its own database. Simple rule: inside one distributed database, let the database run 2PC. Across services, use a saga. When a design says "update both in one transaction", ask: "Is this one database, or two?" If it is two, the answer is 2PC or a saga, never two plain commits. Across services, use a saga with an outbox. Make every step idempotent, as in idempotency, retries and timeouts. Inside one Spanner or CockroachDB cluster, trust its transactions. Keep them short and touch few ranges. Check max_prepared_transactions on every Postgres server. If nothing uses it, set it to 0. If you do use XA, alert on prepared transactions older than a few minutes. In Postgres, query pg_prepared_xacts. Write a runbook for in-doubt transactions. Say who decides commit or rollback, and how to check the coordinator's log first. "Here is our checkout code. List every place where one request writes to two databases or to a database and a broker. For each, say whether a crash between the writes leaves them out of step." "Write a monitoring query for Postgres that alerts when any row in pg_prepared_xacts is older than 5 minutes. Include the gid, owner and database." "Explain what our XA transaction manager does on restart with in-doubt transactions. Point me to its recovery log settings." What to ask the agent The agent did not "fix" a cross-service write by adding PREPARE TRANSACTION in app code. The Postgres docs say not to. Any ROLLBACK PREPARED in a runbook first checks the coordinator's decision. Rolling back a transaction that the coordinator committed breaks atomicity. Timeouts do not abort a transaction that already voted yes. That is the coordinator's job. Claims about Spanner or CockroachDB match their own docs, not a blog summary. What to check yourself Before this: transactions and isolation levels and consensus and Raft. Related: time, clocks and ordering, for Spanner's commit wait, and leader election and leases. Next: sagas, outbox and CDC, and exactly-once delivery.

title: DNS and service discovery
text: Every request starts with a name. Learn how DNS turns it into an address, why changes take time to spread, and how services find each other inside your system.
body: Late on 19 October 2025, AWS services in its Northern Virginia region, us-east-1, started to fail. The cause was one DNS name: dynamodb.us-east-1.amazonaws.com, the public address of DynamoDB in that region. DynamoDB keeps hundreds of thousands of DNS records for its load balancers. Automation keeps them up to date. One part, the DNS Planner, writes new plans. Three copies of another part, the DNS Enactor, apply the plans in Route 53, AWS's DNS service. That night, one Enactor hit unusually long delays. Another Enactor applied a newer plan, then started to delete old plans. At that moment, the slow Enactor wrote its much older plan over the new one. It had checked that its plan was newer, but only at the start, and that check was now out of date. The cleanup then deleted the old plan, which was now live. All IP addresses for the endpoint disappeared. From 11:48 PM PDT, every system that used the public endpoint got DNS failures. That included AWS's own services. The servers behind the name were fine. Nobody could find them. Engineers found the cause at 12:38 AM and restored the DNS records at 2:25 AM. Even then, clients came back only as their cached DNS records expired, between 2:25 and 2:40 AM. Other services, like EC2 launches, took many more hours. Computers talk to IP addresses, like 192.0.2.44. People and code use names, like www.example.com. DNS connects the two. DNS is not one server. It is a tree of names, spread over many name servers. Each name server is responsible for its own part of the tree, called a zone. Resolvers walk the tree for you and cache what they learn. Inside your own system, services have the same problem. Servers start, stop and move, so their addresses change. Service discovery is how one service finds the current addresses of another. The key idea. DNS is a cache spread over the whole internet. Every answer has a TTL, and a change reaches users only after the old answers expire. Plan every DNS change, and every failover, around that delay. A lookup, step by step Your app does not walk the tree itself. It asks a recursive resolver, often run by your internet provider or your company network. The resolver does the work and answers your app. RFC 1034 calls this a recursive query. The resolver itself asks each name server iteratively: each server either answers or points to a server closer to the answer. At the top of the tree are the root name servers. IANA lists 13 named root server authorities, run by 12 operators. Below them are the servers for top-level domains like .com. Below those is the authoritative name server for your zone, which holds your records. Step through a lookup from a cold cache. The second lookup is fast because of caching. In the Route 53 guide's example, the resolver keeps the .com referral to a domain's name servers, typically for two days. Record types you will meet A: an IPv4 address, 32 bits. AAAA: an IPv6 address. CNAME: an alias. It says "this name is another name for that name". If a name has a CNAME, it should have no other records. MX: the mail servers for a domain. TXT: free text. NS: the authoritative name servers for a zone. SRV: where a service runs: a host name and a port, with a priority and a weight. Clients must try the lowest priority number first. Among equal priorities, a bigger weight gets more traffic. TTL: why changes take time Every record has a TTL in seconds. It is the time limit for keeping the record in a cache. A TTL of zero means "use it for this lookup only, do not cache it". The TTL is a trade-off. The Route 53 guide explains it. A long TTL, such as two days, means fewer queries, lower latency and a smaller bill. But a change, like a new IP address, takes longer to reach users. So, before you change a record that is in use, lower its TTL first, for example to 300 seconds. Raise it again after you confirm the change works. Our advice: lower it at least one old TTL before the change. Caches that read the record yesterday may still hold the long TTL. Negative caching: "does not exist" is cached too Resolvers also cache negative answers. NXDOMAIN means the name does not exist. NODATA means the name exists, but has no record of the type you asked for. The time limit for a negative answer is the smaller of two values in the zone's SOA record. RFC 2308 also says resolvers should cap it, and that a cap of one to three hours works well. This causes a classic bug. A deploy script looks up a new name before the record exists. The resolver now remembers "no such name". You create the record, and lookups still fail until that negative answer expires. DNS load balancing and failover A DNS name can return several addresses. Route 53 can attach a health check to each record and answer only with healthy ones. Two details matter. Route 53 runs health checks on a schedule, not when a query arrives. And a record without a health check is always treated as healthy. DNS failover has a hard limit: the TTL. A new answer helps only clients that ask again. Everyone else keeps the cached address until its TTL ends. AWS saw this in the outage above: clients reconnected only as their cached records expired. DNS also knows nothing about load. It cannot see that one server is busy and another is idle. For that, put a load balancer behind the name. See load balancing. Service discovery inside your system Kubernetes explains the problem well. Pods come and go, and each Pod has its own IP address. A client should not need to track which Pods exist right now. There are three common answers. Plain DNS. Put internal names in DNS, with short TTLs. It is simple, and every language can use it. You still get the TTL delay, and DNS alone does not check health. A service registry. Each instance registers itself in a registry like Consul. Health checks keep the list current. In Consul's DNS interface, you ask for <service>.service.consul. Instances that fail their health check are left out of the answer. SRV answers also return the port. Kubernetes Services. A Service gets a DNS name like my-svc.my-namespace.svc.cluster.local. For a normal Service, it resolves to one cluster IP, which does not change when Pods change. Kubernetes updates the Service's list of Pods whenever the set of Pods changes. A headless Service has no cluster IP. Its name returns the IP of every Pod, and the client must choose. A registry is a dependency of everything. In October 2021, Roblox was down for 73 hours. Roblox services used Consul to find each other, and when Consul was unhealthy, servers struggled to connect. Their telemetry also depended on Consul, so they lacked the data to see what was wrong. Option Speed of change Health aware? Main risk Public DNS, long TTL Slow. Old answers can live for the whole TTL. No A bad record stays in caches for a long time. Public DNS, short TTL Fast. No, unless you add health checks. More queries and a higher DNS bill. DNS with health checks (Route 53) Limited by the TTL. Yes Records without a health check always count as healthy. Service registry (Consul) Fast, if clients do not cache for long. Yes Every service depends on it. Kubernetes Service (cluster IP) Fast. The IP stays the same. Partly. Kubernetes keeps the Pod list current. Only works inside the cluster. Headless Service Fast. Partly, like a normal Service. The client must pick a Pod and handle changes. Simple rule: put a load balancer or a Kubernetes Service behind a stable name, and let DNS change rarely. Use DNS for "where is the front door", not for "which server is free right now". Before a migration, write down the current TTL of every record you will change. Lower each TTL at least one old TTL before the move. Never look up a name before you create it. Create the record first, then test it, so no negative answer gets cached. Treat DNS automation like code that can break everything. Ask: "What stops this tool from writing an empty or stale record?" The AWS outage came from exactly that gap. Keep the tools you use in an outage independent of the systems they watch. Roblox later removed the circular dependency between its telemetry and Consul. Add a health check to every record in a failover group. A record without one counts as healthy. When a service "cannot connect", check name resolution first: run dig against your resolver, and read the TTL in the answer. "Here is our DNS zone file. List every record with its TTL. For a move of api.example.com to a new load balancer, write a step-by-step plan with the time each step must wait." "Search this repo for places where a service address is hard-coded, or where DNS answers are cached forever. Show the file and line, and how to make each one respect the TTL." What to ask the agent Every TTL and wait time in the plan matches the real zone, not a guess. Run dig and compare. The plan does not depend on deleting and re-creating a record. That can cause negative caching. Any claim about caching in your language or HTTP client is backed by its official documentation. For Kubernetes, the agent used the right namespace. A short name only finds Services in the Pod's own namespace. What to check yourself Before this: TCP/IP and the network stack. Next: load balancing, which sits behind most DNS names, and CDN and HTTP caching, another cache with time limits.

title: DynamoDB in depth
text: Know what DynamoDB does with each request, and you can predict what it costs, when it throttles, and which guarantees you really get.
body: On Sunday, 20 September 2015, DynamoDB in AWS's US-East Region began returning errors at 2:19 a.m. Pacific time. Inside DynamoDB, each table is split into partitions spread across storage servers. A server's list of partitions is its "membership". An internal metadata service keeps these lists. Servers check their list from time to time. If one cannot get it in time, it retries and stops taking requests. Customers had rapidly adopted global secondary indexes (GSIs). Each GSI has its own partitions, so membership lists grew. A table with many partitions could see its share of these lists double or triple. AWS later wrote: "We did not have detailed enough monitoring for this dimension (membership size)". Then a short network blip made many servers ask for their lists at once. The metadata service slowed past the time limit. Servers that got no answer took themselves out of service and retried, which added more load. Even healthy servers started to fail their next renewals. By 2:37 a.m., errors were far above anything seen in three years. They settled at about 55% of requests. At 5:06 a.m., AWS paused requests to the metadata service. That cut the retries and took load off the service, so AWS could add capacity. By 7:10 a.m., errors were low enough for most customers to work normally. SQS, EC2 Auto Scaling, CloudWatch and the AWS Console were hit too. A GSI looks like a small feature. Inside, it meant more partitions, more metadata and more work. That is why it helps to know what DynamoDB does with your table. DynamoDB is a key-value and document database that AWS runs for you. You never see a server. You see tables, keys, indexes and a bill. Under that, three simple rules decide almost everything: Every request costs capacity units, based on item size and read type. Every table is a set of partitions. Each partition has hard limits per second. Every partition is a small replica group with one leader, spread across zones. How to choose keys is covered in Data modelling for NoSQL. This lesson is about what happens after that: cost, limits and guarantees. The key idea. In DynamoDB, a cheap design is a correct design. Count the units each request uses, keep each partition under its limits, and read the fine print on every guarantee: indexes, transactions, TTL and global tables each have one. The path of one request DynamoDB is made of many services. The core ones are request routers, the metadata service and storage nodes. A router authenticates each request, looks up where its key lives, and sends it on. Each partition has replicas in different Availability Zones. They form a replication group that uses Multi-Paxos to elect a leader. Only the leader serves writes and strongly consistent reads. Step through one write. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. A write is acknowledged once a quorum, two of the three replicas, has saved its log record. Any replica can serve an eventually consistent read, so that read may miss the newest write. Reads are eventually consistent by default. Capacity units: the math A read capacity unit is one strongly consistent read per second of an item up to 4 KB. An eventually consistent read costs half. A write capacity unit is one write per second of an item up to 1 KB. Sizes always round up. A 3,500-byte read counts as 4 KB. A 500-byte write counts as 1 KB. A transactional read or write costs double. An UpdateItem pays for the larger of the old and new item, even if you change one attribute. Worked example: 500 strongly consistent reads per second of 6 KB items. 6 KB rounds to 8 KB, so each read costs 2 units: 1,000 units in total. Make them eventually consistent, and it drops to 500. A Query adds up the sizes of all items it returns, then rounds once. So a few small items in one Query cost far less than many separate GetItems. On-demand or provisioned On-demand is the default and the recommended mode. You pay per request. A new on-demand table can take 4,000 writes and 12,000 reads per second. It instantly handles up to double its previous peak. Grow past double within 30 minutes, and you can be throttled. Provisioned mode charges per hour for the capacity you set, used or not. Auto scaling moves it toward a target utilization. AWS recommends 70%. It acts only after two minutes over target, and alarms can add a few more minutes. So it follows ramps, not sudden spikes. Hot partitions: burst, adaptive capacity, split One partition takes at most 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second. DynamoDB saves up to 300 seconds of unused capacity for short bursts. Adaptive capacity instantly gives more of the table's capacity to a busy partition. It can also move hot items apart, even to one item per partition. DynamoDB also splits a partition for consumption, at a point chosen from the keys it sees. Splits usually take minutes. A split does not help one hot item or keys accessed in sequence. For those, see Scaling writes and hot keys. GSI and LSI A GSI has its own partitions and, on a provisioned table, its own read and write capacity. It is updated asynchronously, so it supports only eventually consistent reads. A table write succeeds only if every affected GSI has enough write capacity. Otherwise the table write is throttled. That is back-pressure from the index onto your table. A local secondary index (LSI) keeps the table's partition key with a different sort key. You can only create it with the table, and you get up to five. It allows strongly consistent reads. The catch: with any LSI, one partition key value can hold at most 10 GB, table and index items together. Past that, writes that grow it can fail with ItemCollectionSizeLimitExceededException. Adaptive capacity will not split such an item collection either. Conditional writes and optimistic locking One UpdateItem is atomic. The risk is read, change, write back: someone else can write in between. The fix is optimistic locking: keep a version attribute, and write only if it has not changed. That check is a conditional write: the condition is tested on the current item, and a false condition stops the write. // ddb is a DynamoDBDocumentClient (@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb) try { await ddb.send(new UpdateCommand({ TableName: "Users", Key: { PK: "USER#42", SK: "PROFILE" }, UpdateExpression: "SET #n = :name, #v = :next", ConditionExpression: "#v = :seen", ExpressionAttributeNames: { "#n": "name", "#v": "version" }, ExpressionAttributeValues: { ":name": "Asha", ":seen": 7, ":next": 8 }, })); } catch (e) { if (e.name !== "ConditionalCheckFailedException") throw e; // Someone wrote first. Read the item again, redo the change, retry. }A failed condition still uses write capacity. Set ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure to ALL_OLD to get the current item with the error, at no read cost. Transactions TransactWriteItems changes up to 100 items, all or nothing. Each item costs two writes, and a cancelled transaction still pays them. Two transactions on the same item can cancel each other, so keep them small. For safe retries, pass a client token. It is valid for 10 minutes. TTL and Streams With TTL, you store an expiry time in epoch seconds. DynamoDB deletes the item "typically within a few days" after it expires, at no write cost. Until then, reads still return it. Filter expired items out yourself. DynamoDB Streams records every item change. Each record appears once, in order for each item. Records live for only 24 hours. A consumer that falls a day behind loses changes. See Sagas, outbox and CDC for how to use a change feed. Global tables A global table keeps replicas in several Regions. The default mode, MREC, copies changes "typically within a second or less". If two Regions change one item at once, the latest timestamp wins. AWS calls this "last writer wins". Condition checks only see the local Region's copy, so version checks do not stop conflicts across Regions. The newer MRSC mode copies each write to at least one other Region before it returns. It always spans exactly three Regions: three replicas, or two replicas and a witness. A clashing write fails with ReplicatedWriteConflictException, and you retry. Writes are slower, and MRSC does not support TTL, LSIs or transactions. Multi-region covers when each model fits. Pages and filters A Query returns at most 1 MB per page. If the response has LastEvaluatedKey, pass it as ExclusiveStartKey in the next call. You are done only when it is missing. A filter runs after the read, so it does not lower the cost. The 1 MB limit applies before the filter, so a page can come back empty and still not be the last. If you throw most items away, fix the key or add an index. Choice Good for Cost Watch out for On-demand Yes New or spiky traffic. Pay per request. Throttles if traffic more than doubles within 30 minutes. Provisioned with auto scaling Yes Steady, forecastable traffic. Pay per hour, used or not. Reacts in minutes, not seconds. GSI A new access pattern, added any time. Its own writes and storage. Stale reads, and throttling of table writes. LSI Another sort order with strong reads. Shares the table's capacity. Must exist at table creation. 10 GB per partition key. Global table, MREC Fast local writes in many Regions. Replicated writes in each Region. Last writer wins can drop a write. Global table, MRSC No lost writes when a Region fails. Slower writes and strong reads. Exactly three Regions. No TTL or transactions. Simple rule: start with on-demand and no LSI. Add a GSI per proven access pattern. Move to provisioned only when traffic is steady and the bill matters. Write the unit cost next to each access pattern: item size, read type, calls per second. Ask: "What is the peak per partition key, not per table?" 1,000 write units a second (1,000 writes of up to 1 KB) is the ceiling. Before you add a GSI, check its write capacity can match the table's. AWS says it should be equal or greater. Avoid an LSI unless you need strong reads on another sort key. Ask if any partition key can grow past 10 GB. Add a version attribute to every item that users edit, and use a condition on every write. Treat TTL as cleanup, not as a timer. Filter expired items in reads. Alarm on stream consumer lag well below 24 hours. Before a global table, list the items two Regions might change at once. "Here are our access patterns with item sizes and peak rates. For each one, compute read or write capacity units per second, showing the rounding. Then name the partition key value with the highest load." "Rewrite this read-modify-write code to use a version attribute and a ConditionExpression. Handle ConditionalCheckFailedException by reading again and retrying at most 3 times." "Find every Query and Scan in this service that uses a FilterExpression. For each, estimate how many items it reads versus returns, and propose a key or index that avoids the filter." What to ask the agent Sizes are rounded up per the rules: 4 KB for reads, 1 KB for writes, and doubled for transactions. Pagination loops until LastEvaluatedKey is missing, not until a page is empty. Code reading a GSI does not expect read-your-writes. No condition check is trusted across Regions in an MREC global table. Retries on throttling use backoff, as in Backoff, jitter and retry budgets. What to check yourself Before this: Data modelling for NoSQL and Scaling writes and hot keys. Related: Secondary and composite indexes, Locking and MVCC in practice, and Cassandra in depth. Another DynamoDB outage, from DNS automation: AWS, October 2025.

title: Error handling and defensive design
text: Sort errors into the ones you expect and the bugs, handle each kind on purpose, and never hide one.
body: On 12 June 2025, many Google Cloud APIs started to return errors around the world. The cause was one part of Service Control, the system that checks quota and policy for incoming API requests. On 29 May, Google had added a new quota check to Service Control. It rolled out region by region, but the code path that failed never ran. It needed a certain policy change to trigger it. The report says this change had no proper error handling, and it was not protected by a feature flag. On 12 June, a policy change was copied to every region within seconds. The policy data had blank fields that nobody intended. The new code read a blank field and hit a null pointer. The report says that "without the appropriate error handling, the null pointer caused the binary to crash." The binaries restarted, read the same data and crashed again: a crash loop. In big regions, the restarting tasks all hit the database table they depend on at once. Service Control did not have randomized exponential backoff to prevent this. Full recovery in us-central1 took up to about 2 hours 40 minutes. Google's fixes include better error handling and testing for invalid data. They also say parts of Service Control should "fail open" when they break. Errors come in two kinds, and you should handle them differently. Expected errors happen in normal life. A user types a wrong date. A file is missing. Another service is busy for a moment. Your code should plan for these and handle them. Bugs are broken assumptions. A value that "can never be empty" is empty. An index is past the end of a list. Retrying will not fix a bug. A person has to fix the code. Rust's official book uses the same split. It calls them recoverable and unrecoverable errors. It says unrecoverable errors "are always symptoms of bugs." The key idea. Decide on purpose what happens for every error. Handle the expected ones close to where you can do something useful. Make bugs loud, so a person sees them and fixes them. Never hide either kind. Never swallow errors. An empty catch block, or a "log and return null" with no plan, hides the problem. The program carries on in a bad state, and the real failure shows up later, far away, where it is much harder to debug. Step through a request where one downstream call fails. Watch how each layer decides what to do. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Validate input at the boundary Check data where it enters your system, before any business logic uses it. Check the shape (type and format) and the meaning, for example "the end date is after the start date". Define what you accept and reject everything else. Do this on the server, even if the browser already checks the same field. OWASP also says to validate data from internal APIs, partner feeds, queues and stored records when it crosses a trust boundary. The Google Cloud policy data came from inside Google, and it still had blank fields. Errors are part of your API Give each error a type or code that tells the caller what it can do next. Three questions cover most cases: Can I retry? For example, "service busy" or a timeout. Must I change the request? For example, "invalid email" or "amount too large". Is this a bug on your side? Then the caller can only report it. For HTTP APIs, RFC 9457 gives a standard JSON shape for this, called problem details. It has fields such as type, title, status and detail. The REST API lesson covers status codes. Exceptions or result values Some languages throw exceptions. Others, like Rust and Go, return an error as a normal value. Rust's book gives a simple rule that works in any language. When failure is expected, return an error value, so the caller must decide what to do. Its examples are a parser given bad data and an HTTP call that hits a rate limit. When a contract is broken, stopping is reasonable, because it shows a bug in the caller. The style matters less than one habit: every error must be visible in the code that calls the function. Fail fast or degrade gracefully Fail fast means you stop at the first sign of trouble with a clear error. Do this for bugs, bad config at startup, and requests that are too large. Google's SRE book advises that under overload you should "fail early and cheaply." Graceful degradation means you still serve the user, with less. A product page can show without recommendations. The SRE book says degraded mode "shouldn't trigger very often", and that you should test it. The choice depends on the feature. A missing recommendation is fine. A missing fraud check on a payment is not. Retries, timeouts, circuit breakers and fallbacks Retries. Retry only transient errors, the ones that may pass in a moment. Do not retry client errors or malformed requests, because the same request will fail again. Calls that change data need idempotency first. The idempotency and retries lesson covers keys, backoff and retry limits. Timeouts. Put a timeout on every remote call. Amazon's advice is to set a timeout on any remote call, and in general on calls between processes on the same machine too. Better still, pass a deadline down the call chain, so lower services stop work the user has already given up on. Circuit breakers. A circuit breaker stops calls to a service that keeps failing, for a short time. This protects the failing service and saves your threads. Amazon notes a cost: breakers add modal behavior that is hard to test, and they can slow recovery. Fallbacks. A fallback is a second way to get the answer, used only when the first way fails. Amazon usually avoids them. Fallback code is hard to test and may rarely run in production, so it can hide bugs. In an Amazon outage around 2001, web servers fell back to a database when their caches failed. They all hit the database at once, and the whole website went down. Amazon prefers to make the main path more reliable, or to run both paths all the time, which turns the fallback into failover. If a fallback is essential, Amazon exercises it as often as possible in production. Messages for users, logs for engineers Users and engineers need different things. The user needs a short, calm message and a next step: "We could not load delivery dates. Please try again." Engineers need the details: error type, which call failed, how many attempts, and a request ID. Never send stack traces, SQL errors or server versions to users. They help attackers learn your system. Return a generic response and log the details on the server. Also keep secrets, tokens and personal data out of error messages and logs. The observability lesson covers what to log. Approach Good for the user? Risk Use it when Fail fast No They see an error now. Low. The problem is clear and close to its cause. Bugs, bad config at startup, invalid input. Retry Yes, if the error was brief. Retries add load to a struggling service. Transient errors on idempotent calls, with a limit. Degrade gracefully Yes They get most of the page. The degraded path may be untested. Optional parts, like recommendations or reviews. Fallback to another source Yes, if the fallback works. Rarely run code can fail or overload a shared system. Only when you run and test it often. Swallow the error No Wrong results later. High. Nobody knows something broke. Never. Simple rule: for each call that can fail, write down which errors are expected and what happens for each. Everything else is a bug, and a bug should fail loudly. In code review, ask about every catch: "What does the caller see, and what do we log?" An empty catch is a finding. Ask "What happens if this field is empty?" for data from files, configs and other teams, not only from users. Check that every remote call has a timeout, and that retries happen in one layer only. Mark each dependency as critical or optional. Optional ones get a degraded mode. Critical ones fail with a clear error. Make sure a degraded mode shows up on a dashboard, so it does not stay on for weeks unseen. Keep one error format across all your APIs, with a code and a request ID in every response. "List every place in this module where an error is caught and ignored, logged without being returned, or turned into null. For each one, say what the caller will see." "For each remote call in this service, list the timeout, the retry policy and what happens on failure. Mark calls with no timeout." "Write tests that send empty, missing and oversized fields to this parser. Each test must expect a clear validation error, not a crash." What to ask the agent The agent did not add broad catch blocks that hide errors to make tests pass. Retries are only on transient errors and only on idempotent calls. Error responses do not contain stack traces, SQL, tokens or personal data. New fallback code has a test that makes the main path fail. Validation is on the server, at the boundary, not only in the client. What to check yourself Related lessons: Idempotency and retries, Safe deploys, Debugging production and Secure coding.

title: Estimation and planning under uncertainty
text: Give estimates as honest ranges, shrink them by removing unknowns, and keep your plan true when the facts change.
body: This story is made up, but it happens often. Meera's team runs checkout for an online pharmacy. In a planning meeting, the PM asks how long it will take to add a second payment provider. Meera has done one before. "About two weeks," she says. By the evening, "two weeks" is on the roadmap as a launch date. Marketing books a campaign for the day after. In week 2 Meera finds the problems. The new provider handles refunds in a different way. Its test system is down for days at a time. The finance team needs a new daily report. None of this was in her head when she said "two weeks". She tells the PM in week 5. The campaign is cancelled. The feature ships in week 7. Seven weeks was a normal result for this kind of work. The real failure was a quick guess that became a promise, and the late warning. Steve McConnell separates three things that people mix up: An estimate is "a prediction of how long a project will take or how much it will cost". A target is "a statement of a desirable business objective", such as a trade fair date. A commitment is "a promise to deliver defined functionality at a specific level of quality by a certain date". When managers ask for an estimate, they often want a commitment, or a plan to meet a target. McConnell says estimation should be unbiased. Planning, in contrast, is biased on purpose toward a goal. Mix them, and the target quietly replaces the estimate. McConnell also says a single-point estimate is "usually a target masquerading as an estimate". Outcomes have a long tail on the late side. There is a limit to how well a project can go, but no limit to how badly. Why are early guesses so optimistic? Bent Flyvbjerg sums up the research. In 1979, Kahneman and Tversky found human judgment to be generally optimistic. So people underestimate the costs, time and risks of their plans. Flyvbjerg cites a 2003 paper by Lovallo and Kahneman that calls this behavior the planning fallacy. They say it comes from the "inside view": you think about the details of your own plan, not about how similar work turned out. The key idea. An estimate is a range with a level of confidence. You make it smaller by removing unknowns, not by thinking harder. Keep it separate from the target, and decide the commitment only when the range is small enough. The working with PMs lesson shows the Cone of Uncertainty and why you give ranges. Here you learn how to make the range, and how to shrink it. Step through one estimate as the team removes unknowns. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. 1. Start from the outside view Before you list tasks, ask: how long did similar work take us before? This is reference class forecasting. Flyvbjerg gives three steps. Pick a class of similar past projects. Find how their results were spread. Place your project in that spread. His best-known story is about Kahneman himself. Kahneman's team was writing a school curriculum, and its members guessed 18 to 30 months. Then a curriculum expert on the team was asked about similar teams. About 40% of them never finished. The rest took seven to ten years. The team went on anyway and finished eight years later. For you, the reference class is your ticket history. Look up the last five similar features and what they really took. 2. Break the work down Then use the inside view to check the outside one. Split the work into pieces of a few days. Write the unknowns next to each piece: "Does the vendor support partial refunds?" Shape Up separates imagined tasks, which you list before you start, from discovered tasks, which you find while doing the real work. So your list will grow. Leave room for that. 3. Remove unknowns with spikes You cannot make an estimate more accurate just by spending another week on it. McConnell says the only way to reduce the variability in an estimate is to reduce the variability in the project itself. The cone narrows only as you make decisions that remove variability. The cone also shows the best case. In a project that does not remove unknowns, the range can stay wide to the end. A spike solution is a very simple program that explores one hard question and ignores everything else. Expect to throw it away. Its goal is to reduce risk or make an estimate more reliable. For a hard problem, XP suggests putting a pair of developers on it for a week or two. Shape Up gives the same order: push the scariest, most unknown work "uphill" first. 4. Give a range and a confidence Say it like this: "5 to 9 weeks. I am about 80% sure we finish within 9." Flyvbjerg shows how the safety margin depends on the risk you accept. For UK road projects, a 50% chance of going over budget needed a 15% uplift. A 20% chance needed 32%. The lower the risk you accept, the bigger the buffer. Make the buffer visible, one line in the plan. He also warns that a large reserve can be spent just because it exists. 5. Fit the plan to the target McConnell says the main purpose of estimation is not to predict the outcome. It is to check if the targets are realistic enough to control the project to meet them. If the first target and the first estimate are within about 20% of each other, the project manager can usually adjust features, schedule or team size to meet it. With a much bigger gap, talk with your PM about changing the target or the scope. Shape Up's answer is to fix the time and let scope vary. Decide with your PM which parts are must-haves before work starts. 6. Track and re-estimate Every week, compare done work with the plan, and update the range. Say what changed and why. McConnell counts using measured team speed from early iterations to project the end date as estimation, and calls it "a really effective form of estimation". 7. When you will miss the date Tell people the day you know. Bring options: cut scope, move the date, or both. Agree on the cut list early, so this talk is short. Cutting scope keeps quality; cutting tests does not. A debated view: #NoEstimates Woody Zuill started the #NoEstimates hashtag. He said estimates are not always needed. He did not claim they are bad in all cases. Teams in this style deliver small working pieces often and decide based on what they deliver. McConnell disagrees. He lists many business uses of estimates, such as budgets, staffing and release-date commitments to the market. He says estimation is a skill every true software professional needs to develop. He also agrees that in some contexts, estimates add little value. A fair middle: slice work small, and still be able to give a range when the business asks. Approach Accuracy early on Effort Use it when Single number from a gut feeling No Often a hidden target. Seconds. Never for a date that others will plan around. Task breakdown only (inside view) Often too optimistic. Hours. You also check it against past data. Past data (outside view) Yes, if the past work is truly similar. An hour with your ticket history. You have done similar work before. Spike first, then estimate Yes It removes the biggest unknown. A few days. One unknown drives most of the range. Fixed time, variable scope The date holds; the scope moves. Needs clear priorities. A hard date, such as a sale or a law. No estimates, small slices No long-range date. Low. The business can work without a date. Simple rule: start from past data, remove the biggest unknown first, and commit only when the range is small enough for the decision at hand. When asked "how long?", ask back: "Is there a target date? What decision does this estimate support?" Never give a number in a meeting. Say: "I will send a range tomorrow." Keep a simple sheet of past features: first estimate, real time, and what surprised you. Write the top three unknowns into the estimate, each with a plan to remove it. Run spikes before you commit. Time-box them, and throw the code away. Give a range with a confidence, and a date when the range will shrink. Re-estimate every week, and share the new range even when it is worse. When a slip appears, tell the PM the same day with options. See technical debt management for how debt silently widens your ranges. "Here is a feature description. Break it into tasks of 1 to 3 days. For each task, list the unknowns and the question a spike should answer." "Here are our last 10 features with first estimates and real durations. Show me the ratio of real to estimated time, and the spread. What range would a similar new feature get?" "Write a short update for my PM: our range moved from 5–9 weeks to 7–9 weeks. Say why, what we will cut if needed, and when we will know more." What to ask the agent The task list includes the boring work: tests, rollout, monitoring, docs and the review cycle. Agents often skip it. The past data really is similar work. A wrong reference class gives a confident, wrong range. The agent's numbers come from your data, not from typical figures it invented. An agent can make coding faster, but the unknowns stay. Vendor answers, reviews and approvals take the same time. The update states the bad news plainly in the first line. What to check yourself Before this: working with PMs and the business. Next: leading a multi-team project. Related: technical debt management.

title: Event-driven architecture and event sourcing
text: Events can tell other services what changed, carry the data with them, or become your database. Know which one you are building, and what each costs.
body: In 2019, engineer Chris Kiehl wrote up a year of running an event-sourced system in production. He had made the design call, and his team built it from scratch in Java. The pitch had been simple. Every change is an event in a log. Any service can subscribe and react. You get an audit log and time travel for free. The real system was different. In his view, letting services read each other's raw events was both "extremely coupled" and "excruciatingly opaque". It became hard to tell which services produced or consumed which events. About a month in, a change in focus made some stored events "no longer relevant, at all". The team had to either translate old events on read or rewrite the log. Either way, he writes, they could no longer reproduce exactly how the system looked before the change. He also warns about the next stage. Once the data grows, reads must move to projections. Those lag behind writes, so new items can return 404 and deleted items can stay visible for a while. His advice at the end: ask what core problem event sourcing solves for you. If you cannot answer clearly, a history table or a plain queue may be enough. "Event-driven" means at least three different things. Martin Fowler separates them. Kiehl's own closing question points at this mix-up: "Is what you actually want just a plain old queue?" Event notification. A service sends an event to say "something changed". It does not expect a reply. The receiver calls back if it needs details. Event-carried state transfer. The event carries the changed data. Receivers keep their own copy, so they never need to call the sender. Event sourcing. Every change to your own data is stored as an event. The event store is the main source of truth. Current state is whatever you get by replaying the events. The first two are about how services talk. The third is about how one service stores its data. You can use the first two without the third. The key idea. Events between services are messages. Event sourcing makes events your database. The first is common and useful. The second is a big, hard-to-undo decision for the parts of a system that need full history. Events between services Event notification gives low coupling. The sender does not know who listens. Microsoft adds that you can add new consumers without changing the producer. The cost is that the flow is hidden. Fowler warns that "it can be hard to see such a flow as it's not explicit in any program text". Debugging is harder too, because there is no shared call stack. Put a correlation ID in every event so you can link the steps into one trace. Event-carried state transfer gives more resilience. Receivers keep working when the sender is down, and they need no remote call. The cost is many copies of the data. Those copies are eventually consistent. For a while after an event, different services see different states. The sagas, outbox and CDC lesson shows how to publish these events safely. Event sourcing: the stream is the truth In event sourcing, each aggregate (an account, an order) has its own stream. A stream is the ordered list of every event for that one object. You never update or delete an event. To undo a change, you append a new event that reverses it. This is the same rule as a double-entry ledger, applied to any kind of data. To load an aggregate, you start from an empty state and apply every event in order. Fowler calls the full version a "complete rebuild". You can also stop at a past time to see the state as it was then. Step through one account stream. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Appending with an expected version Two requests can load the same stream at the same moment and both pass your rules. Event stores stop this with optimistic concurrency control. They reject an append if the stream changed since it was read. The loser reloads, checks again, and retries. Purpose-built stores support this directly. In KurrentDB you pass the revision you read as the expected stream state. If the stream is not in that state, the append throws an error. In Postgres you can get the same result with a primary key on (stream_id, version). // CREATE TABLE events (stream_id text, version int, type text, data jsonb, // PRIMARY KEY (stream_id, version)); type Event = | { type: "Opened" } | { type: "Deposited"; paise: number } | { type: "Withdrawn"; paise: number }; type Account = { open: boolean; balance: number; version: number }; function apply(s: Account, e: Event): Account { switch (e.type) { case "Opened": return { ...s, open: true }; case "Deposited": return { ...s, balance: s.balance + e.paise }; case "Withdrawn": return { ...s, balance: s.balance - e.paise }; } } async function load(db: Db, id: string): Promise<Account> { const rows = await db.query( "SELECT version, data FROM events WHERE stream_id = $1 ORDER BY version", [id]); let s: Account = { open: false, balance: 0, version: 0 }; for (const r of rows) s = { ...apply(s, r.data), version: r.version }; return s; } async function append(db: Db, id: string, expected: number, events: Event[]) { try { await db.transaction(async (tx) => { for (const [i, e] of events.entries()) await tx.query("INSERT INTO events VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4)", [id, expected + 1 + i, e.type, e]); }); } catch (err: any) { if (err.code === "23505") throw new ConflictError(id, expected); // someone wrote first throw err; } } async function withdraw(db: Db, id: string, paise: number) { const acc = await load(db, id); if (!acc.open) throw new Error("account not open"); if (acc.balance < paise) throw new Error("insufficient funds"); await append(db, id, acc.version, [{ type: "Withdrawn", paise }]); }If another writer already saved the next version, the insert breaks the primary key. Postgres reports that as error code 23505, unique_violation. The caller catches ConflictError, loads again, and retries. Always pass the version you loaded. This check only proves that the next version is free. Snapshots Long streams are slow to replay. A snapshot is a saved copy of the state at one version, taken every N events. To load, you read the latest snapshot and replay only the events after it. Snapshots are only a speed-up. The stream stays the truth, and you can rebuild any snapshot from it. Replay and the outside world Replaying must not repeat side effects. If a replay calls the payment provider or sends emails again, real people are affected. Fowler suggests a gateway in front of each outside system that knows when it is in replay mode and skips the call. Versioning old events Events live forever, but your code changes. Microsoft lists four strategies, which you can use alone or together. Tolerant deserialization. Ignore unknown fields and default missing ones. This handles fields you add. Event versioning. A version number in each event, so the reader picks the right logic. Upcasting. Functions convert old event shapes to the current one when they are read. Stored events stay unchanged. In-place migration. Rewrite stored events to the new shape. Use this only as a last resort, because it breaks the audit trail. The general rules for changing data formats are in schema evolution and encoding. Kiehl's story shows the limit. Upcasting keeps your code working, but a change in what an event means can still blur the past. Deleting personal data Laws like the "right to be forgotten" clash with a store that never deletes. Microsoft's first advice is to keep personal data outside the event store and refer to it by ID. If you cannot, use crypto-shredding. You encrypt each person's data with their own key. To forget them, you delete the key. It adds encryption work on every read and write, and needs careful key management. Verraes notes that it only helps if consumers such as projections also keep the data encrypted. It does not cover values that consumers computed from the data. Verraes also asks whether this counts as deletion under GDPR. An update to his post quotes a reader whose lawyer said it does not. That reader prefers keeping personal data in a separate store you can delete from. Read models Replaying a stream on every query is slow, so you build read models (projections) that are updated from the events. They lag behind writes. The next lesson, CQRS and read models, covers them. Option Full history? Main cost Use it when CRUD + history table Partial. You log what you choose. Low. Most services, including admin screens and settings. Event notification No Hidden flows, and callbacks to the sender. Other services need to react, but can fetch details. Event-carried state transfer No Many copies of data, eventually consistent. Receivers must keep working when the sender is down. Event sourcing Yes Every change, in order. Versioning, snapshots, replay safety, projections, and new skills for the team. Ledgers, orders and other areas where history and audit are core business needs. Microsoft's summary: for most systems, and most parts of a system, plain data storage is enough. Its poor fits include simple CRUD, short-lived prototypes, systems that need real-time consistent views, mostly static data, and teams new to event-driven design. Apply event sourcing to the few parts that need it, not to the whole system. When someone says "event-driven", ask: "Notification, state transfer, or event sourcing?" Then argue about one thing at a time. Before you event-source anything, write down the core problem it solves. If the answer is "audit", ask whether a history table is enough. Name events for business intent, like SeatsReserved, not "remaining seats changed to 42". Do not let other services read your raw stored events. Publish separate integration events as your public contract. Microsoft notes that stored events are often too low-level for this. Always append with an expected version. Test what happens when two writers race. Plan event versioning and personal data on day one. Both are painful to add later. Put a correlation ID in every event, and check that your tracing follows it. "Here is our event-sourced Account aggregate. Write a test where two writers load version 3 and both append. Assert that exactly one succeeds and the other gets a conflict error." "List every event type in this codebase. For each one, say whether it is a notification, carries state, or is a stored domain event. Mark any stored event that another service reads directly." "We renamed amount to amount_paise in the Deposited event. Write an upcaster for old events, and a test that replays a stream with both versions." What to ask the agent The append really checks the expected version. An agent may write a plain insert with no unique key, which quietly allows lost updates. Replays and projection rebuilds do not call outside systems or send messages. No migration edits stored events in place. Old shapes are handled by upcasters. Personal data is either outside the store or encrypted with a per-person key. Event handlers are idempotent, since delivery is usually at-least-once. What to check yourself Before this: queues vs logs. Related: sagas, outbox and CDC, domain-driven design for aggregates and domain events, schema evolution and encoding, and money and double-entry ledgers. Next: CQRS and read models.

title: Exactly-once and effectively-once
text: No network can deliver a message exactly once. You can still make its effect happen once, if the check lives where the effect is saved.
body: In May 2023, the payments company Ezypay processed some customers' regular payments twice. A few were debited four times. Only Australian bank direct debits were affected. Ezypay's batch billing services must run as a single instance. Before each batch, the service takes a lock, so no other copy can work on the same batch. A scheduled deploy started a new instance next to the old one. The lock code hit a particular exception and handled it wrongly. For a short time, two instances ran. One batch failed, because both instances tried to write its file at once. The team fixed that one. But an earlier batch had already written a complete file, with duplicated debits in it. Its usual check before going to the bank was missed. A later reconciliation found the problem. Ezypay reversed every duplicate within 24 hours. Its action items include locks that survive every failure and alerts for duplicate payments. Notice where the protection was. A lock tried to make sure the work started once. The one check at the end, a reconciliation of the file, was skipped that day. Nothing in the data itself stopped a second debit for the same customer and period. You already know the three delivery promises from queues vs logs. This lesson is about why the third one, exactly-once delivery, cannot be built from messages alone. The reason is old. In the two generals problem, two sides talk over a link that can lose messages. Neither can ever be certain the other got the last message, however many acknowledgements they send. So a sender that hears nothing has two choices. It can stop, and risk losing the message: at-most-once. Or it can retry, and risk doing the work twice: at-least-once. What you can build is effectively-once processing. You accept at-least-once delivery. Then you make the effect idempotent, or you deduplicate it. The work may run twice, but the effect is the same as if it ran once. Kleppmann's notes call this exactly-once semantics. The key idea. Delivery is at-least-once. Processing becomes effectively-once when the place that saves the effect also rejects the repeat. Step through a lost ack. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. The ack lost after the work Look at frame 3. The consumer did the work and committed. Then the ack was lost, or the consumer crashed before it sent it. The broker now sees nothing. That looks the same as "the consumer died before it started". No timeout can tell the two apart. If the broker wants no message lost, it must redeliver. A Kafka producer that hits a network error has the same problem: it cannot tell if the write succeeded. A dedupe table in the same transaction The fix is a table of message IDs you have handled. Insert the ID in the same transaction as the effect. Here it is in PostgreSQL: CREATE TABLE processed_messages ( consumer text NOT NULL, message_id text NOT NULL, processed_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), PRIMARY KEY (consumer, message_id) ); BEGIN; INSERT INTO processed_messages (consumer, message_id) VALUES ('billing', 'm42') ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING message_id; -- 0 rows back: a copy already ran. ROLLBACK, then ack. -- 1 row back: do the work in this same transaction. INSERT INTO charges (order_id, amount_paise) VALUES (7, 149900); COMMIT; -- Only now ack the message or commit the offset.ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING skips a row that would break the primary key, with no error. RETURNING gives back only rows that were really inserted. So your code knows at once if this is a repeat. If two copies arrive at the same moment, the second insert waits for the first transaction, then gets 0 rows. Order matters. The dedupe row and the charge commit together, or neither does. The ack comes last. A crash at any point leaves you either "not done, will retry" or "done, will skip". Two common mistakes break this. One is checking a separate store, like Redis, before the work. A crash between the work and the "seen" write lets the next copy run again. The other is writing "seen" first, in its own transaction. A crash after it means the work is skipped forever. Kleppmann's notes add that dedupe records must be in stable storage, so they survive a crash. The effect may live in another company's system, like a card network. Then you cannot share a transaction with it. Pass the message ID as an idempotency key, so their side does the dedupe. How long to keep the IDs The table grows forever unless you delete old rows. Most teams add a TTL, such as "delete IDs older than 30 days". That TTL is a risk. Any copy that arrives after its ID is gone will run again. Copies can come late: a Kafka consumer rewound to an old offset, a replayed dead-letter queue, a partner who resends last month's file. Set the TTL longer than the longest replay you allow. Write that number down. Short windows exist elsewhere too. SQS FIFO queues drop a retried send only within a 5-minute deduplication interval. That stops producer retries, not a consumer that runs a message twice. What Kafka's exactly-once covers Kafka gives you two tools. The idempotent producer stops duplicates from producer retries. The broker gives each producer an ID and drops repeats by sequence number. It is on by default (enable.idempotence=true). But it turns itself off if you set a conflicting option, such as acks=1, unless you set it to true yourself. But without a transactional ID, this holds only within one producer session. Transactions let one producer write to many partitions as one unit. For a read-process-write job, the producer also sends the consumer's offsets inside the transaction. The input then counts as consumed only if the transaction commits. You set transactional.id on the producer. When a restarted instance starts with the same ID, Kafka fences off the old one, so a "zombie" cannot finish its transaction. Readers must opt in. Set isolation.level=read_committed and turn off auto-commit. The default, read_uncommitted, returns every message, even from aborted transactions. Now the limit. All of this covers Kafka in, Kafka out. If your code also sends an email or calls a payment API, a retried transaction calls it again. Kafka's docs say exactly-once delivery to other systems "generally requires cooperation with such systems". Flink: checkpoints plus two-phase commit You met Flink's checkpoints in stream processing. They make Flink's own state exactly-once. Since Flink 1.4.0, TwoPhaseCommitSinkFunction stretches this to some outside systems. Flink 1.20 deprecates that class in favour of the Sink V2 API. The two-phase idea stays the same. When a checkpoint starts, the sink pre-commits its open transaction. When the checkpoint completes, Flink tells the sink to commit. On a failure, the job goes back to the last good checkpoint. The sink must support real transactions, as Kafka does. After a restore, Flink may commit the same transaction again, so the commit must be idempotent. The end-to-end argument Why can't the broker just do the dedupe for you? Saltzer, Reed and Clark answered this in 1981. The journal version of their paper is from 1984. Their end-to-end argument says some functions can be done "completely and correctly" only with the help of the application at the end points. Lower layers can offer a partial version as a speed-up. Duplicate suppression is one of their examples. Even if the network removes its own duplicates, the application makes new ones in its own retries. The network sees those as different messages. Only the application can spot them. They make the same point about acks. A delivery ack says the message arrived. What you want to know is whether the target "did it". Ezypay relied on a lock at the start of the job. By the end-to-end argument, the check that matters belongs where the debit is saved. Option Duplicate effects? Lost messages? Cost Use it when At-most-once No Yes Cheapest. Metrics or logs, where losing a few is fine. At-least-once, no dedupe Yes, unless the write is idempotent. No Cheap. The write is idempotent by nature, like "set status to shipped". At-least-once + dedupe table in the same transaction No No One table, a TTL, and the effect must be in that database. Most consumers that write to a database. Idempotency key to an outside API No, if the API keeps keys long enough. No You depend on the other side's rules. Payments, emails and other calls you cannot put in your transaction. Kafka transactions No, for Kafka outputs. No Readers see output only after the commit, and must use read_committed. Kafka in, Kafka out, for example Kafka Streams. Flink two-phase commit sink No, for that sink. No Output is visible only after each checkpoint. The sink supports transactions, and you need Flink's state. Simple rule: assume at-least-once everywhere. Put the dedupe where the effect is saved, and nowhere else is enough. When someone says "exactly-once", ask: "Exactly-once of what, between which two points?" Delivery, Kafka writes and a card charge are different answers. Give every message a stable ID at the source. A new ID on each retry makes dedupe impossible. Read the transaction boundary in code review. The dedupe insert and the effect must be in one BEGIN … COMMIT, and the ack must come after it. Write the dedupe TTL next to the longest replay you allow. Then check that the TTL is longer. For batch jobs, add a unique key on the business fact, such as one debit per customer per period. A lock is a helper, not the guarantee. Keep reconciliation as the last line. Ezypay's later reconciliation is what caught its duplicates. Alert on dedupe hits. A sudden rise means a retry storm, a replay, or two instances running. "Here is our Kafka consumer that writes to Postgres. Add a processed_messages table, and insert the message ID in the same transaction as the write, with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. Commit the offset only after the transaction commits." "List every side effect in this consumer that is outside our database: emails, HTTP calls, other queues. For each one, say how a redelivered message would repeat it, and propose an idempotency key." "Write a test that kills the consumer after the database commit but before the offset commit. Restart it and assert there is exactly one charge row." What to ask the agent The dedupe insert and the effect share one transaction. A "check, then do" in two steps lets two copies through. The message ID comes from the producer, not from the consumer's clock or a random value made on receipt. The agent did not claim Kafka transactions cover an HTTP call. They don't. Consumers of transactional topics set read_committed. The default reads aborted data. The cleanup job for old IDs uses a TTL longer than your Kafka retention or replay window. What to check yourself Before this: Queues vs logs and Idempotency, retries and timeouts. Related: Sagas, the outbox pattern and CDC for the inbox on the consumer side, Stream processing for checkpoints, and Webhooks and async APIs for dedupe across companies. Why distributed systems are hard covers lost replies in general. Distributed transactions and two-phase commit shows the other way to get all-or-nothing across systems. Kafka internals covers acks, replicas and consumer offsets in detail.

title: Failure detection and membership
text: A cluster must decide when a node is dead, but it can never be sure. Learn how heartbeats, phi accrual and SWIM gossip make that guess, and what goes wrong after it.
body: In September 2012, GitHub ran its main MySQL database on a 3-node cluster. A tool called Percona Replication Manager, running on Pacemaker, ran health checks on the primary. If the checks failed, it moved the "active" role to another server. On Monday, a database migration put more load on the primary than the team had seen before. The primary was busy, not broken. But the load made its health checks fail. So the cluster did what it was told. It moved the active role and the primary database to another server. The new server had a cold cache, so it "performed rather poorly". Under real traffic, its health checks failed too. The active role moved back to the first server. A GitHub engineer turned on Pacemaker's maintenance mode, which turns off all health checks and automatic failover. The site recovered slowly as the cache filled. After the incident, GitHub changed its setup so that only a person from operations starts a failover of the primary database. The health check could not tell "busy" from "dead". Each wrong decision made the next server weaker. A cluster needs to know which nodes are alive. It uses that list to route requests, place data and pick leaders. But you saw in Why distributed systems are hard that silence has many causes. A node can be dead, paused, overloaded, or behind a bad link. The SWIM paper puts it plainly: a process that loses messages looks the same as one that has failed. So a failure detector can only guess. Every design picks a point between two mistakes: Too fast: you mark healthy nodes dead. This is a false positive. Too slow: a dead node keeps getting traffic for a long time. The key idea. A failure detector does not find dead nodes. It finds nodes that are late. Choose how late counts as dead, and design what happens next so that a wrong guess is cheap. Heartbeats and a fixed timeout The simplest design: each node sends a heartbeat every second. If you hear nothing for, say, 5 seconds, you call the node dead. Raft uses this idea for leaders. A follower that hears no heartbeat for one election timeout starts an election. You can read more in Consensus and Raft. A load balancer health check is the same idea, but it asks instead of waiting. Load balancing covers those settings. A fixed timeout has a problem. A good value on a quiet network is too short on a busy one. The phi paper calls this the trade-off between conservative and aggressive detection. Phi accrual: a score, not a yes or no Hayashibara and others proposed the phi accrual failure detector in 2004. It does not answer "trust" or "suspect". It gives a suspicion level on a continuous scale. The level keeps rising while no heartbeat arrives. The phi detector keeps a window of recent gaps between heartbeats. From these, it learns what "normal" looks like. Then it asks: how unlikely is it that the next heartbeat is still on its way? import math, statistics def phi(now, last_beat, gaps): mean = statistics.mean(gaps) std = max(statistics.stdev(gaps), 0.1) # avoid a zero spread late = now - last_beat # chance a heartbeat still arrives after this long p_later = 0.5 * math.erfc((late - mean) / (std * math.sqrt(2))) return -math.log10(max(p_later, 1e-300))This is the formula Akka documents, using a normal curve. Each step of 1 in phi means about ten times fewer mistakes. With a threshold of 1, about 10% of suspicions turn out wrong. With 2 it is about 1%, and with 3 about 0.1%. Say heartbeats come every 1 second. With a spread of 0.1 seconds (the smallest the code allows), 1.6 seconds of silence gives phi of about 9. With a spread of 0.3 seconds, the same silence gives phi of only about 1.6. With a threshold of 8, the first node is suspected and the second is not. The detector adapts to the network you really have. Akka and Cassandra both use a default threshold of 8. Akka suggests 12 on cloud networks such as Amazon EC2. A low threshold gives many wrong suspicions but finds crashes fast. A high one makes fewer mistakes but is slower. SWIM: membership by gossip Heartbeats raise a second problem: who talks to whom? If every node sends heartbeats to every other node, the network load grows with the square of the group size. SWIM splits the job into two parts: failure detection and spreading the news. Step through one probe round. In each protocol period, a node pings one random member. If no ack comes in time, it sends a ping-req to k other members. They ping the target and relay any ack. This avoids blaming a node for congestion on one path. If nobody gets an ack, the target is marked "suspect", not dead. A suspected node can refute this by sending an Alive message with a higher incarnation number. If the suspicion times out first, a Confirm message removes the node. The news does not need its own messages. It rides on the pings and acks that are already flowing. The paper calls this infection-style dissemination. The expected detection time and the load on each member do not grow with the size of the group. SWIM is a gossip protocol: news spreads from node to node, with no central server. Lifeguard: when the accuser is the slow one The SWIM paper itself notes a weak spot. A slow process, for example one that drops packets from full buffers, can declare several healthy processes faulty. HashiCorp hit this in memberlist, the library inside Serf, Consul and Nomad. CPU exhaustion, network delay or loss made members wrongly declare others faulty. Their fix, Lifeguard, assumes the local failure detector may be the problem. It has three parts: Self-awareness. A node keeps a score of signs that it is unhealthy itself. While the score is high, it is slower to accuse others. Dogpile. The suspicion timeout starts long and gets shorter as more members confirm the suspicion. A lone, slow accuser gets no support, so the target has time to refute. Buddy system. A suspected node is told directly in the probe it receives, so it can refute at once. HashiCorp reports more than 50 times fewer false positives under CPU exhaustion. With the new memberlist defaults, failures were found 20% faster with 20 times fewer false positives. After detection Detection is only half of the story. The action you take next often does more damage. Rebalancing. Data and traffic move off the "dead" node. HashiCorp notes that false accusations move traffic away from healthy members and cause needless data rebalancing. Flapping. The node comes back, then is removed again. GitHub's role moved away and then back on one day. Cascading failure. Moving work to the rest of the cluster adds load. In 2011, AWS EBS nodes that lost contact assumed their peers had failed. They all searched for space for new copies at once. This "re-mirroring storm" left about 13% of volumes in one zone stuck. Removing a slow node is not free. The work it held lands on the nodes that are left. Option Detects a crash fast? Few false positives? Use it when Fixed timeout, short Yes No Pauses and slow links trip it. Cheap actions, such as skipping a server for a few seconds. Fixed timeout, long No Yes Expensive actions, such as moving data. Phi accrual Yes, on a steady network. Yes It adapts to jitter. Peer-to-peer databases and actor systems such as Cassandra and Akka. SWIM gossip with Lifeguard Yes Time does not grow with cluster size. Yes Indirect probes and suspicion help. Large clusters that need a shared member list, such as Consul. A human decides No Yes Rare, risky moves, such as failing over a primary database. Ask: "What does this cluster do when it marks a node dead, and what does a wrong guess cost?" Size the timeout to the cost of the action. Use different thresholds for different actions.
