The phi paper's example: stop sending new work at a low level, and remove the worker only at a high one. Know your longest normal pause: garbage collection, a big compaction, a slow disk. Your timeout must be longer. Rate-limit removals. If many nodes "die" at once, suspect the network or the detector first. When you see false positives, find the cause before you raise the threshold. Akka lists long GC pauses, overload and tight CPU limits. Plan the rebalance. Check that the remaining nodes can take the extra load. Make removal and rejoin cheap and gradual, so flapping does not move all the data each time. "Read our cluster config. List every failure detection setting: heartbeat interval, timeouts, phi threshold, suspicion multiplier. For each, explain what action it triggers." "Our Cassandra nodes are marked down during GC pauses. Show me how to confirm this from the logs, and compare raising the phi threshold with fixing the pauses." "Write a test that pauses one node for 10 seconds in our 5-node cluster. Show what moves, how long it takes, and what happens when the node returns." What to ask the agent The agent did not raise every timeout without saying what gets slower. Longer detection means a dead node gets traffic for longer. The proposed timeout is longer than your real worst pauses, taken from metrics, not guesses. Automatic actions after detection have a limit, such as "remove at most one node per 10 minutes". Any code that counts members handles a node that is "suspect", not only "alive" or "dead". What to check yourself Next: leader election and leases, which use failure detection to pick one leader. Related: Consensus and Raft, Sharding and consistent hashing, and Circuit breakers and bulkheads. See the GitHub incident page.

title: Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read
text: Learn the two ways a post reaches millions of feeds, what each one costs, and how big apps mix them for accounts with millions of followers.
body: Around 2012, Twitter had about 150 million active users. The Twitter numbers in this lesson come from a detailed 2013 summary of a talk by Raffi Krikorian. Your home timeline was a ready-made list in a large Redis cluster. When someone tweeted, Twitter copied the tweet's ID into the list of every follower. For most accounts this worked well. A tweet to 1 million followers took a couple of seconds to reach them all. The goal was under 5 seconds. Then a few accounts had tens of millions of followers. A tweet from Lady Gaga could take up to 5 minutes to reach her 31 million followers. Queues for these large fan-outs backed up all the time. The delay caused strange bugs. A fan who got her tweet early could reply at once. Other fans saw the reply before the tweet it answered. This is likely because the reply had a small audience, so it was delivered fast. Twitter's plan was to stop pushing tweets from the biggest accounts. Instead, it would merge their tweets into your timeline when you read it. Raffi Krikorian described Twitter's timelines in a talk at QCon San Francisco in late 2012. A feed shows posts from many people you follow. You can do the gathering work at one of two times. Fan-out on write (push). When someone posts, copy the post's ID into a list for each follower. Opening your feed is then one cheap read of your own list. Fan-out on read (pull). Store each post once, with its author. When you open your feed, fetch recent posts from everyone you follow and merge them. Writing is cheap. Every read does the work. Neither one wins every time. Push hurts when one author has millions of followers. This is the celebrity problem. Pull hurts when one reader follows thousands of accounts, and readers open the app all day. The key idea. Push pays per follower, at write time. Pull pays per followed account, at read time. Most big feeds push for normal accounts and pull for the few huge ones. Step through one normal post and one post from a huge account. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Do the cost maths first Write cost with push is posts per second × average followers. Read cost with pull is feed opens per second × accounts followed. Compare the two before you choose. Example with made-up numbers: an app gets 1,000 posts a second, and the average author has 200 followers. Push makes 200,000 list writes a second. Each write is tiny, and reads become one lookup. Now one author has 30 million followers. One post from her is 30 million writes. That is 150 seconds of the whole app's normal push work, for one post. Real apps read much more than they write. Around 2012, Twitter served about 300,000 timeline reads a second, but only about 6,000 write requests a second. With that ratio, doing the work once at write time is usually the better deal. Store timelines as capped lists of IDs Keep only IDs in the list, not the full post. Twitter stored the tweet ID, the author's ID and 4 bytes of flags, such as "this is a retweet". Each home timeline was capped at 800 entries, and each timeline entry was kept on 3 machines in the Redis cluster. When a reader opens the app, the server loads full posts for the IDs it shows. Short IDs keep the list small, and an edited post changes in one place only. Mastodon, the open-source social server, works the same way today. Its home feeds live in Redis. Each feed keeps at most 800 items, and a trim step removes anything older. Skip inactive users Most people do not open the app every day. Pushing posts into their lists wastes memory and work. Twitter kept only active users in Redis, meaning people who had logged in within 30 days. Others got no entries. When they came back, Twitter rebuilt their timeline. It looked up who they follow, read those posts from disk and put the list back in Redis. Mastodon pushes posts only to local followers who signed in within the last 7 days by default. Feeds are kept for the same 7 days. When such a user signs in again, Mastodon queues a job that rebuilds the feed from the accounts they follow. A code comment states the trade-off. A shorter window saves work when many people sign up but rarely visit. A longer window means less catch-up work when people come back. The cost is a slow first load for a returning user. Show a "loading your feed" state, not an empty screen. Fan out through a queue Never fan out inside the request that saves the post. Save the post, put one job on a queue, and answer the user. Workers do the copying later. Mastodon's fan-out code reads followers in batches. It then queues one small job per follower, and each job adds the post to that follower's feed. Its queues run in priority order. Posts from other servers go to a lower-priority queue, "so that local users still see their posts when the server is under load". Notifications use the same path. At Twitter, delivery reached in-memory timelines, push notifications and emails. Your workers rarely send to each phone one by one. They call a push service. Firebase Cloud Messaging can send one message to every device subscribed to a topic. Its docs say topic messages are built for throughput, not low latency. They also limit each project to 1,000 fan-outs running at once. For urgent alerts to a few people, Firebase advises sending to device tokens instead. For delivery guarantees and retries, see Queues vs logs. Fill in old posts when someone follows Push only adds new posts. If you follow Asha today, her older posts are not in your list. You must merge them in once. Mastodon's feed code has a merge step for this. It copies up to 200 recent posts from the new account into your feed. It does this only for users who signed in recently. If your feed already has 200 or more items, it skips posts older than the oldest one in it. Then it trims the feed back to 800. A reverse step removes an account's posts from your feed after an unfollow. Merge and rank at read time The hybrid reads two things. It reads your pushed list, and it reads the latest posts of the few huge accounts you follow. Then it merges them by time, or by a score. Ranking pushes many apps further toward pull. In 2015, Facebook described its News Feed backend this way. "Leaf" servers kept recent actions in memory. An aggregator sent each query to the leaves, then ranked what came back. In other words, Facebook built the feed when you asked for it. LinkedIn chose pull in 2016. Its tests found that pre-built feeds needed 62 times more data. Pre-built feeds are also stored in ranked order. So testing a new ranking model means re-sorting every stored feed. By 2023, X's published code built the For You and Following tabs at read time. The Following tab fetched posts from the Earlybird search index. The For You tab gathered candidates from several sources, then scored them with a model using about 6,000 features. Option Write cost Read cost Best for Fan-out on write High. One write per active follower. Very high for huge accounts. Low. One list read, then load the posts. Read-heavy apps where most accounts have a modest audience. Fan-out on read Low. One write per post. High. One lookup per followed account, then a merge. Ranked feeds, users who follow few accounts, and early products. Hybrid Push for normal accounts, nothing extra for huge ones. One list read plus a few pulls. Big social apps with a few accounts that have millions of followers. Push to active users only Lower. Inactive users cost nothing. Slow first load when a user returns. Apps where many users visit rarely. Simple rule: start with pull while you are small. Add push when reads hurt. Add the hybrid when one account's post takes minutes to deliver. Multiply first. Ask: "Posts per second × average followers, and feed opens per second × accounts followed. Which is bigger?" Ask for the follower count at p99 and the maximum, not the average. The largest account decides your worst case. Pick a clear threshold for "huge account", and store it as a setting. Watch how many accounts cross it. Watch fan-out lag: the time from "post saved" to "last follower's list updated". Alert on it. Keep timelines rebuildable. The database is the truth, and the cache list is a copy you can throw away. Decide what happens on block, delete and unfollow. Each one must remove posts from lists that are already built. "We have 2 million users. The average user follows 150 accounts and opens the app 8 times a day. Users make 500,000 posts a day, and the largest account has 4 million followers. Estimate writes per second for fan-out on write and reads per second for fan-out on read. Show the maths." "Write a fan-out worker in Node with BullMQ and Redis. It reads followers in batches of 1,000, skips users not seen in 14 days, adds the post ID with ZADD (score = post ID), and trims each feed to 800 with ZREMRANGEBYRANK. Make a retried job safe." "Add read-time merge for accounts with more than 1 million followers. Merge their latest posts into the cached list by post ID, and remove duplicates." What to ask the agent The worker does not load all followers into memory at once. Agents often write getAllFollowers() and loop. A retried job does not add the same post twice. Check for duplicates or use a sorted set keyed by post ID. The list is trimmed after every insert, so memory stays bounded. Deletes, blocks and unfollows remove posts from lists that are already built. The merge sorts by a stable key, such as a time-ordered post ID, so pages do not repeat posts. What to check yourself Scaling reads: caches, replicas and read models, the tools under any timeline. Presence and real-time fan-out: the same push-or-pull choice for live status and chat. Caching and cache stampedes: what happens when many timelines rebuild at once. Sharding and consistent hashing: how timelines are spread over many Redis servers.

title: Feature flags and entitlements
text: Use flags to release safely and to run experiments, keep paid-plan rules apart, and remove every flag you no longer need.
body: On 1 August 2012, Knight Capital, a large US trading firm, sent millions of unwanted orders in about 45 minutes. It lost more than $460 million. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) later described what happened. Knight was adding new code to SMARS, its order router, for a new New York Stock Exchange program. The new code was meant to replace old code for a feature called "Power Peg". Knight had stopped using Power Peg in 2003, but the code was still there and could still be called. The new code also reused a flag that used to turn on Power Peg. The plan was simple: delete Power Peg, so that the flag would now turn on the new code. From 27 July, Knight deployed the new code to its servers in stages. A technician did not copy it to one of the eight servers. No second technician reviewed the deploy, and no written procedure required a review. On 1 August, orders arrived with the reused flag set. Seven servers ran the new code correctly. The eighth server ran Power Peg. Power Peg's counter of filled shares had been moved in 2005, and the old code was never tested again. So it sent new orders again and again without checking how many shares were already filled. For 212 incoming orders, the system sent millions of orders. That gave 4 million executions in 154 stocks in about 45 minutes. A feature flag is an if statement whose answer comes from config, not from code. You can change the answer while the program runs, for some users or for all, without a new deploy. Flags let you separate two things: deploying code and releasing a feature. You deploy the code switched off. Later, you turn it on for 1% of users, then more. Pete Hodgson names four kinds of flags, and they live for very different lengths of time. Release flags hide new or unfinished code. They should usually not stay "much longer than a week or two." Experiment flags split users for an A/B test. They must stay stable long enough to give a clear result. Ops flags let operators switch off a feature, for example under heavy load. Most are short-lived, but some stay as long-lived kill switches. Permissioning flags turn features on for some users, such as paying customers. They can live for years. The key idea. Every flag is a branch you must test and a switch that can break production. Give each one an owner, a reason and an end date, and delete it when its job is done. Step through one flag check for one user. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Context, rules and variants Your code asks a question like "is new-checkout on for this request?". It passes an evaluation context: data about the request, such as the user ID. You can add your own fields, such as the plan. The flag's rules look at that context. OpenFeature calls this targeting: rules, user overrides or a percentage split. The answer is a variant, such as on, off or blue. Keep the check in one place. Hodgson suggests a toggle router that makes the decision, so the rest of your code does not know how the decision is made. Percentage rollouts and stable buckets A 10% rollout must not flip a user between on and off on each request. So tools hash a user field instead of using a random number. Unleash uses MurmurHash on the user ID and a group ID to get a number from 0 to 100. By default the group ID is the flag name, so each flag splits users in its own way. Users whose number is at or below the rollout percentage get the feature. The same input always gives the same number. So raising 10% to 20% keeps the first 10% and adds more users. If there is no user ID or session ID, Unleash falls back to a random number, and the result is not stable. Server or client evaluation On a server, one process checks flags for many users, each with their own context. In a browser or phone app there is one user. The app usually fetches all its flag results at once and caches them. When the context changes, for example after login, the cached results are stale and must be fetched again. Two habits follow from this. First, never trust a flag result that a client sends you for anything that matters, like access to a paid feature. Check it again on the server. Second, decide one flag per request, early, and pass the result down. Otherwise one request can see the flag as on in one service and off in another. When the flag system fails Your flag service can be slow or down. OpenFeature says a flag check must never throw an error, and must return the default value you supplied when something goes wrong. So choose defaults with care. For a new feature, the safe default is usually off. Entitlements are not release flags An entitlement is what a customer's plan allows: "Pro can export to PDF", "Free gets 3 projects". It looks like a permissioning flag. Hodgson even uses paid features as an example of one, and says to manage each kind of flag differently. We go one step further: treat entitlements as their own system. This is our advice, not Hodgson's, for three reasons. Entitlements come from billing data, not from engineers. They last as long as the plan, so the "delete old flags" rule does not apply. And a wrong value can give away paid features or block a paying customer. Read the plan from your billing or account data, behind one function like canUse(account, "pdf-export"). You can still put a release flag around a new paid feature while you build it. The multi-tenancy lesson covers per-customer limits. Flags are config changes, and they cost you Turning a flag on for everyone changes production in seconds. Treat flag changes like config: review them, roll them out in steps and watch the metrics. The safe deploys lesson covers this. After its June 2025 outage, Google said changes to critical binaries must be behind flags that are off by default. Each flag doubles the paths through one piece of code. Hodgson says you do not need to test every combination, because most flags do not interact. Test the setup you expect in production. Many teams also test with all flags on. Old flags are flag debt. Hodgson describes teams that treat flags as inventory with a cost. Some add a removal task when they create a release flag. Some add "time bombs": tests that fail when a flag is past its end date. The tech debt lesson shows how to track this kind of work. A standard API: OpenFeature OpenFeature is "an open specification that provides a vendor-agnostic, community-driven API for feature flagging". A provider is the "translation layer" between this API and your flag tool. Your code calls one API, so you can change tools without rewriting every flag check. Where the flag lives Change without deploy? Risk Use it when Constant in code No A deploy is needed. Low. Easy to find and delete. A small team hides unfinished work on trunk. Config file or env variable No A restart or redeploy is needed. A typo can reach every server at once. Rare changes, like ops limits. Flag service with SDK Yes Seconds. A bad change is global in seconds. The service can fail. Gradual rollouts, kill switches and experiments. Entitlement system Yes Driven by billing data. Wrong data gives away paid features or blocks customers. What each plan allows. Simple rule: a release flag is temporary, so plan its removal on the day you create it. A rule that lasts as long as a plan is not a release flag. Give each flag a clear name, an owner, a kind (release, experiment, ops or permissioning) and an end date. Never reuse a flag name. Create a new flag, and delete the old flag and its old code. Ask in review: "What does this do when the flag service is down?" The default must be safe. Roll out by percentage with a stable user ID, and watch errors at each step before going wider. When a release flag reaches 100%, open the cleanup pull request within a few weeks. Delete the flag and the old code path. Keep a list of flags with their age. Bring old ones to the team's planning meeting. Keep plan rules in an entitlement check, and check them on the server. "Find every feature flag in this repository. For each one, list the name, where it is checked, its default value, and whether one branch is now dead code." "Remove the flag new-checkout, which is now on for 100% of users. Keep the 'on' path, delete the 'off' path and its tests, and remove the flag from config." "Write tests for this function with the flag on and with it off. Also add one test with all flags on." What to ask the agent The agent kept the correct branch when it removed a flag, and removed no other flag. The default value used when the flag service is down is safe. No paid feature depends only on a flag value sent from the client. Rollouts use a stable user ID, not a random number per request. The removed flag is also gone from the flag tool's config, so nobody can turn it on again by mistake. What to check yourself Related lessons: Safe deploys, CI/CD and trunk-based development and Testing strategy.

title: Clean and hexagonal architecture
text: Learn how to keep business rules apart from the web framework and the database, why tests get faster, and when the extra layers are not worth it.
body: This story is made up, but each part is common. Ravi works on the orders service of an online pharmacy. The POST /orders handler is 250 lines long. It reads the JSON body, checks the prescription rules, applies discounts and writes SQL to save the order. The rules for prescription drugs changed. Ravi only needed to change one check. But the check sat between an Express req object and a database transaction. To test it, he had to start a server and a real Postgres in Docker. The test suite took 14 minutes. People stopped running it before they pushed. Two weeks later, a discount bug reached production. Nobody had run the test that would have caught it. Then the company wanted orders from a nightly CSV import too. The rules lived inside the HTTP handler, so the import team copied them. Now the same rules existed in two places, and they slowly drifted apart. The business rules were tangled with HTTP and SQL. That made them slow to test and hard to reuse. In the SOLID lesson, you learned dependency inversion: business code owns a small interface, and details implement it. This lesson applies that idea to a whole application. In 2005, Alistair Cockburn described Ports and Adapters, also called the hexagonal architecture. His goal: an app should be "driven by users, programs, automated test or batch scripts" equally. It should also be "developed and tested in isolation from its eventual run-time devices and databases." The app sits in the middle. It talks to the outside only through ports. Cockburn says a port "identifies a purposeful conversation". An adapter translates between a port and one real technology. There will "typically be multiple adapters for any one port". Cockburn credits the Adapter pattern from the Design Patterns book with helping him understand the hexagon. The design patterns lesson covers that pattern. Here it is used at the edge of the app. The six sides mean nothing. Cockburn writes that "the number six" is not important. The shape just leaves room to draw more ports. The key idea. Put the business rules in a core that imports no framework and no database driver. The core owns its interfaces. Everything outside depends on the core, never the other way round. Step through one order. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Two sides: driving and driven Cockburn splits the outside world in two. A primary actor "drives the application", such as a user or a test. A secondary actor is one "that the application drives", such as a database. He says you can also call them driving adapters and driven adapters. Ports come in the same two kinds. The core: a use case and a port A use case is one thing a user can do, such as "place an order". PlaceOrder.run is the driving port: the API the core offers to the outside. Some teams also write it as an interface. The core also defines the driven port it needs, in its own words. // core/orders.ts: no imports from express or pg export type Order = { id: string; userId: string; totalCents: number }; export interface OrderRepository { // a driven port save(order: Order): Promise<void>; countToday(userId: string): Promise<number>; } export class PlaceOrder { // a use case constructor(private repo: OrderRepository) {} async run(userId: string, totalCents: number): Promise<Order> { if (await this.repo.countToday(userId) >= 5) throw new Error("daily limit"); const order = { id: crypto.randomUUID(), userId, totalCents }; await this.repo.save(order); return order; } }Driven adapters: Postgres and in-memory // adapters/pg-orders.ts import { Pool } from "pg"; import type { Order, OrderRepository } from "../core/orders"; // points inward export class PgOrderRepository implements OrderRepository { constructor(private db: Pool) {} async save(o: Order) { await this.db.query("INSERT INTO orders (id, user_id, total_cents) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)", [o.id, o.userId, o.totalCents]); } async countToday(userId: string) { const r = await this.db.query("SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1 AND created_at >= current_date", [userId]); return Number(r.rows[0].count); } } // test/in-memory-orders.ts export class InMemoryOrderRepository implements OrderRepository { orders: Order[] = []; async save(o: Order) { this.orders.push(o); } // in a test, every saved order counts as "today" async countToday(userId: string) { return this.orders.filter(o => o.userId === userId).length; } }A driving adapter: HTTP // adapters/http.ts import type { Express } from "express"; import type { PlaceOrder } from "../core/orders"; // points inward export function orderRoutes(app: Express, placeOrder: PlaceOrder) { app.post("/orders", async (req, res) => { try { const order = await placeOrder.run(req.body.userId, req.body.totalCents); res.status(201).json(order); } catch (e) { if ((e as Error).message === "daily limit") res.status(409).json({ error: "daily limit" }); else res.status(500).json({ error: "internal" }); } }); } // main.ts: the only file that knows every piece orderRoutes(app, new PlaceOrder(new PgOrderRepository(pool)));The adapter turns HTTP into a call, and a core error into a status code. The CSV import from the story becomes a second driving adapter. It calls the same run method. The rules now live in one place. Onion and Clean: the same idea In 2008, Jeffrey Palermo described the Onion Architecture. The domain model is the centre, and "all coupling is toward the center." Repository interfaces live in the core. Their implementations live at the edge. "The database is not the center. It is external." In 2012, Robert C. Martin wrote "The Clean Architecture". He listed hexagonal and onion among the designs it brings together. He drew four circles: Entities, Use Cases, Interface Adapters, and Frameworks and Drivers. He adds that there is no rule you must have only four. His dependency rule: "source code dependencies can only point inwards." When the inner code must call outward, you use the dependency inversion principle. Data that crosses a boundary takes "the form that is most convenient for the inner circle." So the three names share one idea. Business rules sit in the middle. Frameworks and databases are details at the edge. Dependencies point inward. How it helps testing The unit test drives the use case with the in-memory adapter: test("blocks the sixth order of the day", async () => { const repo = new InMemoryOrderRepository(); const place = new PlaceOrder(repo); for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) await place.run("u1", 100); await expect(place.run("u1", 100)).rejects.toThrow("daily limit"); });No server, no Docker, no network. Cockburn suggests a mock, in-memory database as the natural test stand-in for a database. Most rule tests can now be fast unit tests, at the bottom of the test pyramid. The fake does not run your SQL. Vocke uses an in-memory database in his example, but warns it is "risky business". The tests then run against a different database than production. So keep a few integration tests that run PgOrderRepository against a real PostgreSQL. The costs and critiques More files to open. One feature now needs a use case, a port, two adapters and the wiring. For simple features, that is a lot of reading. Mapping between layers. Martin wants data to cross in the inner circle's form. So you often copy fields from a request object to a core type, and from a core type to a database row. Each copy is code to write and test. Too much for simple CRUD. CRUD means create, read, update and delete: screens that only save and load rows, with few rules. Palermo says his design "is not appropriate for small websites". He aims it at long-lived business apps and at apps with complex behaviour. If a screen just saves a form to a table, the core has nothing to protect. Interfaces with one implementation. The SOLID and design patterns lessons warned about these. Here, a driven port is usually worth it, because the test adapter is a real second implementation. A port for every class in the core is not. Add ports only at the edges: the database, the clock, other services, the message queue. Too many rules and layers. Jimmy Bogard says layered, onion and clean designs are "really only appropriate in a minority of the typical requests in a system". He says he tends to see them as "mock-heavy, with rigid rules around dependency management". He adds that one feature often means "touching many different 'layers'". A middle path You do not need the full design everywhere. Start with a clean core only for the part with real rules, such as pricing or order limits. Leave simple CRUD screens simple. Inside a modular monolith, each module can make this choice for itself. Vertical slices: another option Bogard's team once started a long project with an onion architecture. Within a couple of months, problems showed, and they moved away from it, towards CQRS. His vertical slice architecture groups code by request, not by layer. His rule: "Minimize coupling between slices, and maximize coupling in a slice." Each slice "can decide for itself how to best fulfill the request". A simple slice can use SQL directly. A complex one can have a rich core. It has a cost too. Bogard says it assumes "your team understands code smells and refactoring". Without that, logic can grow messy inside each slice. Option Fast tests? Cost Use it when Handler calls the database directly No Rules need a server and a database to test. Low at first. Rules get copied as new entry points appear. Simple CRUD with few rules. Hexagonal, Onion or Clean core Yes Rules run against in-memory adapters. More files, ports and mapping code. Complex rules that live for years and have several entry points. Clean core for one complex module only Yes, where it matters. Two styles in one codebase. A good default for many teams. Protect the hard part. Vertical slices Yes, if each slice keeps its logic testable. Needs steady refactoring; some code repeats across slices. Many independent features and a team comfortable with refactoring. Ask: "Can I test this rule without a server or a database?" If not, the rule is tangled with a detail. Check the imports. Code in the core should not import the web framework, the ORM or the SQL driver. Tools such as dependency-cruiser or eslint-plugin-boundaries (TypeScript) and ArchUnit (Java) can check this in CI. Name ports in business words: OrderRepository.countToday, not executeQuery. Add a port only at a real edge, and name its second adapter, often the test one. Keep one integration test per driven adapter against the real tool. Before you add layers to a CRUD screen, count its business rules. If there are none, keep it simple. When an entry point is added (a queue consumer, a CLI, a cron job), make it a new driving adapter. Do not copy the rules. "List every file under src/core that imports express, pg, an ORM or an HTTP client. For each import, say what the core uses it for." "Find business rules that appear in more than one HTTP handler or job. Show the duplicated lines side by side." "Extract the order limit rule from this handler into a PlaceOrder use case with an OrderRepository port. Add an in-memory adapter and one unit test. Do not change the HTTP behaviour." What to ask the agent The core has no imports from framework or database packages. The port uses business words, not table or column names. The agent did not add an interface for every class inside the core. The in-memory adapter behaves like the real one for the cases you test. A real-database integration test still exists. The HTTP status codes and JSON shape did not change. What to check yourself Before this: SOLID, coupling and cohesion. Related: complexity and deep modules, design patterns that still matter, testing strategy and monolith, modular monolith or microservices. Domain-driven design builds on this one.

title: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
text: Learn what really changed from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, so you can pick settings for clients, load balancers and timeouts with care.
body: A shopping app loads its home screen with about forty small API calls. The API runs on HTTP/1.1. On slow networks, the screen takes many seconds to fill, because requests wait in line for free connections. The team turns on HTTP/2 at the load balancer. Now all forty calls share one connection. On office Wi-Fi, the home screen is much faster, and everyone is happy. Then support tickets arrive from users on trains. Sometimes the whole screen freezes for a second or two, and then everything appears at once. The team checks the servers, and they answered fast. The cause was one lost packet. HTTP/2 sends every request over one TCP connection. TCP hands data to the app only in order. So one lost packet stalls every request on that connection, even requests the loss did not touch . The fix was to also offer HTTP/3 for clients that can use it. This story is made up. But the behaviour is real and written in the standards. HTTP has two parts: Semantics: what a message means. Methods like GET and POST, status codes like 404, and headers. RFC 9110 says all three major HTTP versions rely on the same semantics . Wire format: how those messages travel. This is the part each version changes. So your handler code does not change when the version changes. What changes is speed, how many connections you hold, and what happens when packets are lost. HTTP/1.1 sends text messages over TCP. It cannot mix requests on one connection, so clients open several connections to work in parallel . HTTP/2 uses binary frames instead of text, over one TCP connection. Many requests run at the same time, each in its own stream . HTTP/3 keeps the idea of streams, but runs on QUIC, over UDP. A lost packet blocks only the streams it carried . The key idea. Each new HTTP version keeps the same meaning and fixes the waiting of the version before. HTTP/2 removes waiting between requests. HTTP/3 removes waiting caused by TCP itself. Step through three requests, A, B and C, with one lost packet. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. HTTP/1.1: one request at a time HTTP/1.1 connections are persistent by default. One connection can serve many requests, one after another . This is keep-alive, and it saves a new TCP handshake for each request. Pipelining lets a client send several requests without waiting. But the server must send the responses in the same order . So one slow response still blocks the rest . In practice, clients open several connections to one server instead . RFC 9112 asks clients to limit how many they open, because each one uses server resources. It gives no fixed maximum . Many connections also make congestion control work less well, because TCP does not share it across connections . HTTP/2: many streams, one TCP connection HTTP/2 cuts each message into binary frames . Each request and response pair gets its own stream, and frames from many streams mix on one connection . This is called multiplexing. RFC 9113 says clients should not open more than one HTTP/2 connection to a given host and port . Each side tells the other how many streams it may open at once. RFC 9113 recommends at least 100, so that parallel work is not limited . HPACK. Requests to one server repeat the same headers again and again, which wastes bandwidth . Before HPACK, SPDY compressed headers with DEFLATE. The CRIME attack showed that this could leak secrets . HPACK instead keeps tables of headers that both sides already know. A header can then be sent as a small index . Server push. HTTP/2 added an optional way for a server to send responses the client did not ask for yet . It did not work out well. RFC 9113 itself says push is hard to use well, because the server must guess what the client will ask for . Only 1.25% of HTTP/2 sites used it. Studies had mixed results, with no clear overall gain and often worse performance . Chrome announced that it would turn push off by default in version 106. The post suggests 103 Early Hints and preload instead . What HTTP/2 did not fix. TCP still sees one ordered stream of bytes. RFC 9113 says plainly that TCP head-of-line blocking is not addressed . A lost packet stalls every stream, even streams the loss did not touch . See TCP/IP and the network stack for why TCP works this way. HTTP/3: streams that do not block each other HTTP/3 maps each request and response to its own QUIC stream. If one stream is blocked or loses a packet, other streams still make progress . QUIC does not keep any order between bytes on different streams . Two other changes matter: Faster setup. QUIC includes TLS 1.3. RFC 9114 says this gives security like TLS over TCP, with faster connection setup . See TLS and secure connections for the handshake. Connection migration. A QUIC connection has connection IDs, not only an address and port. These IDs let a connection survive a change of address . Only the client can start a migration, and only after the handshake is confirmed . HPACK assumes data arrives in order, which QUIC does not promise across streams. So HTTP/3 uses a new format, QPACK . How a client picks a version ALPN. In the TLS handshake, the client sends a list of protocols it supports. The server picks one. This adds no extra round trips . HTTP/2 over TLS uses the name h2 , and HTTP/3 uses h3 . Alt-Svc. The URL is still https://, so the client needs a sign that the server also speaks HTTP/3. The server can send one in a response header, like Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400 . The ma value is how many seconds the client may remember this. Without it, the default is 24 hours . The URL and origin do not change . Alt-Svc is only a hint. The client may try QUIC after it sees one . If UDP is blocked, RFC 9114 tells clients to use HTTP over TCP instead . So keep TCP serving too. What changes for backend engineers Load balancers often split the versions. An AWS Application Load Balancer can accept HTTP/2 from browsers. By default it still sends requests to your servers over HTTP/1.1 . You can choose HTTP/2 or gRPC per target group, only behind an HTTPS listener. With HTTP/2 chosen, requests that arrive as HTTP/1.1 fail . One connection means less spread. An HTTP/2 client should open only one connection per host and port . Behind a layer 4 balancer, all its requests then reach one server. See Load balancing. Closing gracefully. HTTP/2 has a GOAWAY frame. Its last stream ID tells the client which requests the server may have acted on . The rest were not processed, so they can be retried on a new connection . In HTTP/1.1, a side that wants to time out should close the connection gracefully . Retries. Idempotent requests can be retried automatically after a connection fails . Others should not be, unless the client knows the first try was not applied . See Idempotency, retries and timeouts. Option Requests per connection A lost packet blocks Good fit HTTP/1.1 One at a time. Clients open several. Only that connection. Simple service calls, old clients, debugging by hand. HTTP/2 Many streams on one TCP connection. All streams on the connection. Browsers and APIs with many small requests, gRPC. HTTP/3 Many streams on one QUIC connection. Only streams with data in that packet. Users on phones and lossy networks. Server push Extra responses the client did not ask for. Not relevant. Avoid. Chrome turned it off by default. Use 103 Early Hints or preload. Simple rule: for users on the internet, serve HTTP/2, and add HTTP/3 at the edge if your CDN or load balancer supports it. Inside your data center, the version matters less than reusing connections. When someone says "HTTP/2 will make it faster", ask: "Faster for which clients, on which network?" Measure before and after. Know which version each hop speaks: client to CDN, CDN to load balancer, load balancer to server. They often differ. Check stream limits on both sides. A low stream limit on one HTTP/2 connection makes extra requests wait in a queue. During deploys, make sure servers send GOAWAY and drain, so clients move to a new connection without errors. Retry only idempotent requests after a connection drops. Use an idempotency key for payments. When you turn on HTTP/3, also watch QUIC errors and UDP traffic. Keep TCP working as the fallback. "Here is our nginx config. Which HTTP versions does it serve to clients, and which does it use to our upstream servers? Show the exact lines." "Our Go service calls another service over HTTP/2. Explain how the client reuses connections, and what happens to in-flight requests when the server sends GOAWAY." "Write a load test that compares HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 with 2% packet loss. Explain what I should expect and why." What to ask the agent Every setting the agent names exists in your server or library version. Check the docs. The agent does not suggest HTTP/2 server push. Chrome turned it off by default . Claims like "HTTP/3 is always faster" are tested on your own traffic, with loss and without. Retries are added only for idempotent requests. The agent knows that the load balancer may speak a different version to your servers than to clients. What to check yourself TCP/IP and the network stack: handshakes, packet loss and head-of-line blocking. TLS and secure connections: how ALPN fits into the handshake. WebSockets, SSE and long polling: long-lived connections on top of HTTP. CDNs and HTTP caching: where HTTP/3 is often turned on first.

title: Idempotency, retries and timeouts
text: Why one retry can charge a customer twice, and the small key that stops it.
body: Priya is on a train with weak mobile data. She taps Pay ₹1,499 in a shopping app. The request reaches the payment server, and the server charges her card. The answer back to her phone is lost. After 10 seconds the app hits its timeout. It keeps the spinner on and sends the same request again: an automatic retry. The server sees a new request and charges the card again. Priya now has two charges of ₹1,499. Support spends a day finding and refunding the double charges. A retry is safe only if doing something twice has the same effect as doing it once. That property has a name: idempotent. Reading a balance is idempotent. "Set the order status to shipped" is idempotent. "Charge ₹1,499" is not: each call takes more money. The key idea. A timeout tells you that you did not get an answer. It does not tell you that the work did not happen. So we make the charge idempotent. The app creates one unique idempotency key for the payment and sends it with every attempt. The server remembers each key and its result. If the same key comes again, the server sends back the saved result instead of charging again. Step through what happens when the answer is lost. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Two details matter in real systems. If a second request with the same key arrives while the first is still running, the server must not start a second charge. Stripe's v1 API does not run it or save a result for it, and the app can retry later. And if the same key arrives with a different amount, the server should reject it: that is a bug in the app. Approach Safe to retry? Cost Use it when Never retry Yes Nothing runs twice. Users see more failed payments. A person can easily check and try again. Retry, no key No It can charge twice. Cheap to build. The call is already idempotent, like a read or "set status to shipped". Retry with an idempotency key Yes Repeats get the saved result. You store keys, handle "still running", and delete old keys. Payments, orders, anything that creates something. Key + backoff with jitter Yes And retries are spread out. One user may wait a little longer. Many clients may retry at the same moment, for example after an outage. Simple rule: add a key to every call that creates or moves something. When you retry, add backoff with jitter, so retries do not hit a struggling service at the same moment. Also limit the number of retries. In design reviews, ask: "What happens if this call runs twice?" Ask it for every call that creates something or moves money. Put a timeout on every network call. A call without one can wait forever and hold a thread or a connection. Retry in one layer only. If the app, the gateway and the service each try 3 times, one tap can become 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 calls. Wait longer between tries with exponential backoff and jitter, so clients don't all retry in the same second. Keep keys long enough to cover every retry. Stripe's v1 API, for example, keeps them for at least 24 hours. "Add an Idempotency-Key header to the create-payment call. Create the key once per payment, before the retry loop." "Write a test where the first response is lost and the client retries with the same key. Assert that the card is charged exactly once." What to ask the agent The key is made outside the retry loop, not inside it. The server saves the key and the payment in the same database transaction. A second request with the same key, while the first still runs, does not charge again. Retries happen in one layer, with a limit and backoff. Keys belong to one customer, so nobody can read another person's result. What to check yourself Coming next on this line: Backoff, jitter and retry budgets. For messages from a queue, see Exactly-once and effectively-once.

title: Incident response and postmortems
text: Run an incident with one leader, one channel and regular updates, then write a blameless postmortem whose fixes really get done.
body: On 5 April 2022 at 07:38 UTC, a script at Atlassian started to delete customer sites. It was meant to remove one old app. By mistake, it was given the IDs of whole sites. It deleted 883 sites, which belonged to 775 customers. The first customer support ticket came at 07:46 UTC. Atlassian started its major incident process at 08:17 and raised the incident to Critical at 08:24. The first status page update went out at 09:03. So far, the response was fast. Then it got hard. For some customers, the outage lasted up to 14 days. Leaders met every three hours, and a global team worked 24/7. More than 450 support engineers checked restored sites in shifts. The talking part went badly. The script had also deleted customer contact details, so Atlassian could not reach many of the customers who were hurt. Its first broad public message, a tweet, came on 7 April at 00:56 UTC. That was about 41 hours after the script started. In its review, Atlassian wrote that it "should have implemented broader communications much earlier". It also said it should have admitted sooner that it was not sure when sites would be back. Its fixes included 24/7 backups for each communications role. Fixing the system is only half of an incident. The other half is people. An incident is a problem too big for one person working alone. The debugging lesson covers how to find and stop the cause. This lesson covers how the team works together, and how it learns afterwards. Google's SRE workbook names three goals, the "three Cs". Coordinate the work. Communicate with responders, the company and the outside world. Control the response. The key idea. An incident needs one leader, one place to talk and a steady rhythm of updates. Afterwards, it needs a postmortem that blames no one, and fixes that really get done. 1. Declare early Google's advice is: "Declare incidents early and often." In its experience, managed incidents are resolved faster. The SRE book gives three tests. If any one is true, it is an incident: You need a second team to help fix it. Customers can see the problem. It is still not solved after an hour of focused work. 2. Pick a severity level A severity level tells everyone how bad it is and how to respond. PagerDuty uses five levels. SEV-1 and SEV-2 are major incidents. SEV-5 is a cosmetic bug that becomes a ticket. Atlassian pages people for severity 1 and 2. Severity 3 goes to the team during work hours. When you are not sure, PagerDuty says to treat it as the higher level. Do not argue about the level during the incident; review it in the postmortem. 3. Give out roles, with one leader Google's model has four roles: command, operations, communication and planning. PagerDuty adds a scribe, who writes the timeline as it happens. The debugging lesson lists what each role does. Two rules matter most: The incident commander (IC) does not fix things. PagerDuty says the IC is "NOT a resolver". The IC is "the single source of truth" and gives out the work. Only operations changes the system. In Google's model, nobody else touches production during the incident. Atlassian says it is "very important to be clear who's in charge". 4. One channel, one timeline Atlassian opens one chat channel per incident, named after its ticket, for example HOT-1234. People write their observations, changes and decisions there as they happen. Atlassian says: "It's okay if it looks like people are talking to themselves!" Google calls a living incident document the IC's "most important responsibility". It can be messy, but it must be useful. This record becomes your postmortem timeline. 5. Update on a clock, even with no news At PagerDuty, the internal liaison sends a short update to the executive team "roughly every 30mins". That rhythm is for internal leaders. PagerDuty gives no fixed rhythm for customer updates. Our advice: pick a rhythm for each audience, put it in every update, and keep it even when nothing has changed. Atlassian's internal template is simple: One or two sentences on the current state and impact. "Current Status": 2–4 bullet points. "Next Steps": 2–4 bullet points. When and where the next update will come. When you do not know something, say so. Atlassian says it is "far better to say 'the root cause is currently unknown'" than to leave it out. Without a shared source of truth, people jump to their own conclusions. For customers, one or two sentences are usually enough. They want to know if it is fixed, and if not, when. At PagerDuty, a public post is the IC's choice, with the rule: "If in doubt, post it out." A sample: "Checkout fails for about 20% of users since 14:05. We rolled back the 14:00 deploy; errors are falling. Cause unknown. Next update 14:50 in #inc-2231." 6. Hand over, and rest Google's SRE book says stress hormones can "impair cognitive functions". Atlassian asks incident managers to watch how long people have been awake and to plan who takes over. In a case in Google's workbook, PagerDuty rotated its responders and its IC every four hours. That gave people rest and brought new ideas. Make handovers explicit. The outgoing IC says, "You're now the incident commander, okay?" and waits for a firm yes before leaving. 7. End it clearly Atlassian says an incident is resolved "when the current or imminent business impact has ended". At PagerDuty, the IC announces the end and moves other talk to Slack. Atlassian's final update gives the impact and duration. Customers hear that service is back and a postmortem will follow. 8. Write a blameless postmortem Google writes a postmortem for user-visible downtime above a threshold, any data loss, a rollback or other fix by the on-call engineer, a long resolution time, or a monitoring failure. At PagerDuty, the postmortem owner schedules the meeting within 3 calendar days for a Sev-1 and 5 business days for a Sev-2. Google's good example includes the impact, causes, timeline, "where we got lucky", and action items. Blameless means you look for the causes without blaming any person or team. Ask what went wrong, not who caused it. Contributing factors. PagerDuty says: "There is no single root cause of major failure in complex systems." A person's action should never be called a root cause. Atlassian still looks for root causes, using the "Five Whys". It separates the proximate cause, which led directly to the incident, from the root cause. The root cause is the best place to change so that the whole class of incident stops. Action items. Each one needs an owner, a tracking number, a priority and an end state you can check. PagerDuty asks you to start each one with a verb and keep it narrow. Atlassian's "priority actions" must be done in 4 or 8 weeks, and managers approve each postmortem. Google quotes: "a postmortem without subsequent action is indistinguishable from no postmortem." Share it. Google says "an unreviewed postmortem might as well never have existed". It shares good ones widely, for example as a "postmortem of the month". 9. Keep on-call healthy Google's SRE book sets limits. Allow at most two incidents per 12-hour shift, because one incident takes about 6 hours of work. A rotation on one site needs at least eight engineers, or six per site on two sites. "All paging alerts should also be actionable." The alerting lesson goes deeper. 10. Practise before it is real Google's DiRT tests create "a controlled emergency". PagerDuty's "Failure Friday" injects failures to learn how systems break. In a Wheel of Misfortune, engineers act out an old postmortem, each playing a role. The chaos engineering lesson covers such a game day. Choice Benefit Cost Use it when Declare early Yes Help and roles arrive fast. Some false alarms. Any of the three tests is true, or you are unsure. One IC, few hands on the system Yes Every change is known and agreed. The IC can become a bottleneck in a huge incident. Almost always. Split into sub-teams if it grows. Everyone jumps in Many ideas at once. No Changes clash, and nobody knows what changed. Never as the default. Experts join when the IC asks. Contributing factors A fuller picture. More actions to track. Large or repeated incidents. One root cause (Five Whys) Simple and focused. Can miss other factors. Small, clear incidents. Say "I am declaring an incident" out loud. Then ask: "Who is IC? Who talks to customers? Who writes notes?" If you are the IC, do not open a terminal. Ask each expert, "What do you see? What do you need?" Put the next update time in every update, and keep it, even if the update is "no change". In long incidents, ask who needs to sleep. Hand over with a written summary and a clear "you are IC now". In the postmortem, replace "Ravi ran the wrong command" with "the tool allowed a bulk delete with no check". Each quarter, count pages per shift and remove alerts that needed no action. "Here is the export of #inc-2231. Build a UTC timeline of each observation, decision, change and update. Mark any line where the time is unclear." "Draft our next internal update: state and impact, current status, next steps, next update time. Use only facts from the channel. Write 'unknown' where we do not know." "Draft a blameless postmortem from this timeline. Use roles, not names. List contributing factors, and propose action items that each start with a verb. Leave owners and dates empty." What to ask the agent Every time and fact. Compare the timeline with your logs. A summary can merge or drop events. Customer updates. Check numbers, scope and promises before they go out. Blame. Remove any wording that points at a person, even softly, such as "failed to notice". Decisions stay with people. The IC picks the severity and fixes; the team picks owners and dates. What to check yourself Related lessons: Debugging production, Alerting and on-call, Observability, SLOs and error budgets, Chaos engineering and game days and Clear technical writing.

title: Big-tech interview loops
text: Know the stages of a big-tech loop, what each round checks, how the decision and your level are made, and how to spend six to eight weeks getting ready.
body: Arjun had three years of backend experience. He applied for a senior role at a large tech company. He spent six weeks on coding problems, about 200 of them. He did not practise anything else. The phone screen went well. In the loop, the first coding round started with a vague problem. Arjun did not ask a single question. He typed in silence for 25 minutes. When the interviewer asked about his approach, he said, "Let me finish first." The design round went worse. He drew boxes for 40 minutes, but never asked how many users the system had. In the behavioural round, his stories were short and vague. "We fixed the outage. It went fine." Two weeks later the recruiter called. There was no offer at senior level. There was an offer one level lower. Arjun was surprised, because he had solved every coding problem. He had never asked which level he was being considered for, or how the rounds were weighted. This story is made up, but each mistake in it is common. This lesson shows how the loop works, so your prep matches it. A big-tech interview loop is a set of separate interviews. Each interviewer checks a different skill. Then a group reads all the notes and makes one decision. Amazon's careers site describes it plainly. You meet "individually with current employees" and each one assesses "different aspects of your skills and experience". The decision has two parts: hire or not, and at which level. Many candidates prepare only for the first part. The second part decides your title and your pay. The key idea. Each round is a separate test with its own notes. Find out the rounds and the level before you prepare. Then spend your time where the weight is, and make your thinking visible in every round. Step through one candidate's path. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. The usual stages The names change between companies, but the shape is similar. Recruiter call. As of 2026, Google's page says you usually have "one or two shorter conversations" with a recruiter before deeper interviews. This is the best moment to ask about the level and the rounds. Technical screen. In 2022, Meta described a 45-minute screen with two coding problems. Amazon's SDE II page instead describes an online assessment: 90 minutes for two technical questions, then 20 minutes of system design scenarios. The loop. As of 2026, Amazon's SDE II page says the loop has "four 55-minute interviews". Google describes "a panel of interviews", over video or in person. Decision and offer. Amazon's SDE II page says the outcome comes within 5 business days. Google says the whole process often takes "roughly 6-8 weeks" once interviews start. What each round looks for Coding. Interviewers watch how you solve, not only what you produce. Meta's advice was to "Think out loud." Amazon asks for "syntactically correct code—no pseudo code". It also wants you to check edge cases and bad input. System design. Amazon says to expect "at least one question" on design. It adds that you should ask questions to complete and check your design. The method is in the system design interview method. Going deep is in design deep dives. Behavioural. You tell real stories from past work. As of 2026, Amazon's SDE II page says each interviewer typically asks two or three such questions, tied to its Leadership Principles. Google suggests the STAR method to structure your examples. A later lesson, behavioural interviews, covers this in depth. Domain knowledge. Some loops add a round on your specialty. Hello Interview's Google L5 guide describes a "Role Related Knowledge" round. It replaces one coding round for candidates on a domain track, such as Android or ML. How the decision is made Each interviewer writes feedback against a fixed rubric. Google says every candidate is assessed with "the same rubrics for everyone" for that role. Feedback is written alone, and early. As of 2026, GitLab's public handbook says interviewers cannot see each other's scorecards, "to help remove bias". Hiring managers can see them all. It asks for scorecards within 24 hours. Then the notes meet. In a 2019 article, Amazon described its bar raisers. A bar raiser is a trained interviewer who acts as an objective third party and guides the debrief. The bar raiser and the hiring manager make the final decision. A bar raiser quoted in the article says the program "avoids having one person make the hiring decision". Hello Interview's guide says Google uses a hiring committee that reviews all feedback before team matching. How the level is set The level comes from the same notes. As of 2026, GitLab's handbook says its engineering scorecards have a "Level" field. An interviewer can score you at two levels, such as Senior and Intermediate. So you can pass at one level and miss the next. Hello Interview says, for Google's senior level, the committee and the behavioural interview "carry the most weight" for the level. Weak leadership signals can mean being "down leveled". How prep differs for senior roles For a senior role, coding must still be solid. Hello Interview reports that, at least at Google, the behavioural round weighs most for a senior level, and design matters a lot too. In design, you lead the discussion and choose where to go deep. In behaviour, your stories should show scope: a project you drove, a conflict you resolved, a decision you owned. See what senior really means. A realistic 6–8 week plan This is our suggested plan, not advice from any company. Google's "6-8 weeks" above is how long its hiring process takes, not how long to prepare. This plan assumes about 1–2 hours on weekdays and more at weekends. Adjust the weights to your loop. Week 1. Ask the recruiter for the round list, the level and the format. Do three timed problems to find your weak spots. Weeks 1–5. Coding, most days. Practise common patterns. Solve in a plain editor, without running the code, and speak while you type. Weeks 2–6. System design, two or three sessions a week. Do one full problem per session, starting with requirements. Weeks 2–6. Behavioural. Write 8–10 stories. Each needs a number and a clear "I", not "we". Weeks 5–7. Mock interviews with a peer, at least one per round type. Ask for blunt notes. Final week. Light review only. Check the video setup, the time zone and the schedule. For a senior role, our own suggestion is to move about a third of the coding time to design and stories. Common mistakes Silent coding. The interviewer cannot write down thinking they did not hear. No clarifying questions. Google says many questions "leave room for clarification" on purpose. Not asking about the level. You cannot aim at a bar you do not know. Waiting for the interviewer to find your bugs. In 2022, Meta advised finding and fixing them yourself. Using AI tools in the interview. As of 2026, Google says they "are not permitted" during interviews. The honest limits Every company's loop is different, and loops change. The pages here are snapshots, and Meta's is from 2022. Confirm the format with your recruiter. Outcomes are also noisy. One interviewer's bad day can change a result. Google itself says not getting a role "can often be a matter of timing". One rejection is data, not a verdict. Prep strategy Fits the loop? Cost Use it when Mostly coding problems Partly. Design and behaviour rounds go unprepared. Early-career roles where coding is most of the loop. Weighted by the round list Yes You must ask the recruiter first. Almost always. Many mock interviews Yes Needs a partner and time. The last 2–3 weeks. A practice loop at a company you care less about Yes Takes extra weeks, and the format may differ. If you have not interviewed in years. Simple rule: ask for the rounds and the level, prepare by weight, and talk through your thinking every time. Seniors also sit on the other side of the table. The same ideas apply there. When you interview, write your notes before you read anyone else's. Then the debrief hears what you saw. Write evidence, not feelings. "Found the off-by-one bug herself" is useful. "Seemed smart" is not. Score against the rubric for the level, not against the last candidate. In a debrief, say which level your evidence supports, and why. When you coach a teammate who is job hunting, ask first: "Which level, and which rounds?" When you move jobs yourself, use the same 6–8 week plan. Plan the negotiation before the offer arrives. "Act as an interviewer for a senior backend role. Give me one coding problem with a vague input. Do not answer my questions unless I ask them. At the end, list what I failed to clarify." "Here are my five behavioural stories. For each one, tell me if it shows my own actions, a number, and a result. Point out every place where I say 'we' instead of 'I'." "Make a 7-week prep plan for a loop with two coding rounds, one system design round and one behavioural round, at senior level. I have 90 minutes on weekdays." What to ask the agent Any claim the agent makes about a company's current loop. Check it against the company's own careers page, or ask your recruiter. That mock feedback names specific moments, not general praise. That the plan gives design and stories enough weight for the level you want. That your stories are true. A made-up story falls apart under follow-up questions. What to check yourself Before this: what senior really means. For the design round: the system design interview method, design deep dives and requirements and non-functional needs. Next: behavioural interviews and STAR stories and negotiation and compensation.

title: Inventory, overselling and flash sales
text: Sell the last item exactly once, even when thousands of people tap "Buy" in the same second, and tell them the truth while they wait.
body: A shop in Bengaluru runs a midnight sale: 500 pairs of a limited sneaker at ₹4,999. Marketing has been posting about it for two weeks. At 00:00, about 40,000 people tap "Buy" within the first minute. The checkout code reads the stock, checks that it is above zero, and then writes the new number. The sale page says "sold out" after 90 seconds. Everyone celebrates. The next morning, the warehouse counts 523 paid orders for 500 pairs. Twenty-three customers get a refund and an apology email. Several post screenshots online. There was a second problem. During the first minute, checkout pages took 20 seconds to load. The stock row was the bottleneck. Every purchase had to wait its turn for that one row. Overselling happens when two requests check the stock at the same time. Both see "1 left". Both decide to sell. Both write. This is a race between a read and a write. It is the same bug as the lost update in transactions and isolation levels. The fix is simple: do not check in your app code. Ask the database to check and change the number in one step. If the number is already zero, the database changes nothing, and you show "sold out". A flash sale adds a second problem: everyone wants the same row. The row lock that keeps you correct also makes buyers wait one at a time. So you also need ways to spread the work, and to let fewer people in at once. The key idea. Correct stock is a single number that only the database may change, in one atomic step. Speed comes from splitting that number, and from controlling who reaches checkout. It never comes from skipping the check. Step through two buyers racing for the last item, and the one-line fix. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Fix 1: an atomic conditional decrement Write the check into the UPDATE itself: UPDATE items SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 7 AND stock > 0 RETURNING stock;In Postgres, under the default Read Committed level, a second UPDATE on the same row waits for the first one to commit. Then Postgres checks the WHERE clause again on the new version of the row. So when stock reaches 0, the next UPDATE matches no row. Postgres reports this as UPDATE 0. That is not an error. Your code must read the count, or the RETURNING result, and treat 0 rows as "sold out". To sell three items, use stock >= 3. Fix 2: lock the row first Sometimes you must read before you decide, for example to check a per-customer limit. Then use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. It locks the row until your transaction ends. Other transactions that try to update or lock it wait. Keep these transactions short. Never call a payment API while you hold the lock. If you lock more than one row, always lock them in the same order, such as by ID. Postgres advises this to avoid deadlocks. Fix 3: reservations with expiry You can hold stock when the buyer starts checkout, not only at payment time. Shopify's inventory model has states for held stock. It splits the units on hand into states such as available, committed and reserved. A reservation is a row like "1 unit for cart 88, until 00:10". Your conditional UPDATE moves one unit from available to reserved. Payment turns the reservation into a sale. A small job, or a check at read time, releases reservations that expire. Without expiry, people who leave without paying keep stock held forever. Pick the expiry from real data, like how long most people take to pay. A short expiry frees stock fast. Too short, and buyers lose the item while typing a card number. The hot row In a flash sale, every buyer updates the same row. A transaction holds the row lock until it commits. So, as Alibaba's PolarDB docs explain, updates to one hot row run one at a time. The docs say sharding the database or tables gives limited gains here. Alibaba calls this the "inventory hotspot" problem. A researcher from its database team says it solved the problem in time for Double Eleven in 2013. You cannot remove this waiting, but you can make each turn shorter. Do only the stock UPDATE inside the transaction. Do the rest of the order, like the address and the email, outside it. Splitting stock into buckets This section is our advice, not a method from the sources above. Split one stock number into several rows. For example, store 500 sneakers as 10 bucket rows of 50. Each request picks a bucket at random and runs the conditional UPDATE on it. Now 10 purchases can run at the same time, not one. When a bucket is empty, try another. Near the end, a buyer may see "sold out" while one other bucket still has a pair. You can handle this with a final pass over all buckets, or a small job that moves leftover units. In Postgres, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED skips rows that others hold. The docs say it gives an inconsistent view, but it suits queue-like tables. That makes it useful to pick any free bucket. Queues and virtual waiting rooms Even a fast database has a limit. So control how many people reach checkout. Shopify learned this in its flash sales. Checkout writes were taking down parts of the platform. It added a throttle, a limit on how many buyers get through, in its load balancers. Buyers over the limit saw a cached queue page that checked again from time to time. The first version picked people at random. Some customers waited up to 40 minutes for a sale that lasted 40 minutes. The fix stored each buyer's first attempt time in a signed cookie, so earlier buyers would not lose out to later ones. You can also buy this as a product. Cloudflare's Waiting Room admits visitors based on two limits: total active users and new users per minute. Others wait in a first-in-first-out queue and see an estimated wait time. Rate-limit checkout, not browsing. See rate limiting. Caching availability vs truth The product page might get 100 times more views than purchases. Do not hit the stock row for each view. Cache "in stock" or "few left" for a few seconds, as in caching and cache stampedes. But the cache is only a hint. The conditional UPDATE at checkout is the truth. A stale cache may show "in stock" for a few seconds after the last sale. That is fine, as long as checkout says "sold out" clearly. Being honest with users Tell people where they stand. Show their place in the queue or an estimated wait. When stock runs out, tell everyone in the queue at once, so they stop waiting. When a buyer reaches checkout, say how long their item is held. If you ever do oversell, refund fast and say sorry plainly. Option Prevents overselling? Speed on one hot item Use when Read, check in app, write No Fast, but wrong. Never for stock. Atomic conditional UPDATE Yes Limited by one row lock. The default for most shops. SELECT FOR UPDATE, then write Yes Slower. The lock is held longer. You need other checks before the write. Reservations with expiry Yes, if made with a conditional UPDATE. Same as the UPDATE. Checkout takes minutes, such as card payments. Stock split into buckets Yes Much better. Flash sales of one product. Waiting room in front Indirectly. It limits load. Protects everything behind it. Planned big sales and ticket drops. Cached availability No It is only a hint. Very fast reads. Product and list pages. Simple rule: make the conditional UPDATE the only way stock goes down. Add buckets and a waiting room when one product gets a planned rush. Search the code for "read stock, then write stock". Replace each case with a conditional UPDATE, and check the rows-changed count. Ask product: "How long do we hold an item in checkout? What do we tell a buyer when it expires?" Before a big sale, load-test checkout for the one hot product, not a spread of products. See load shedding. Add a check that runs every few minutes: units sold plus units available must equal the starting stock. Alert if they differ. Plan for the user, not just the database: a queue page, a clear "sold out" for everyone, and a refund plan. Keep the stock transaction tiny. No payment calls, emails or HTTP calls while a row lock is held. "Find every place in this repo where we read stock and then update it in separate statements. Rewrite each one as a single conditional UPDATE, and handle 0 rows as sold out." "Write a test that starts 50 parallel purchases against a product with stock 10, using a real Postgres database. Assert that exactly 10 succeed and stock ends at 0." "Design a stock-bucket scheme for one product with 500 units in 10 rows. Show how a buyer picks a bucket, and what happens when the chosen bucket is empty." What to ask the agent The test really runs purchases in parallel, against a real database. A loop that buys one at a time proves nothing. The code checks the rows-changed count. An UPDATE that changes 0 rows does not raise an error. No network call happens inside the stock transaction. Expired reservations go back to available stock, and this has its own test. The agent did not "fix" the race with an app-level lock or a mutex. That breaks as soon as you run two servers. What to check yourself Before this: transactions and isolation levels and locking and MVCC in practice. Next: checkout and the order state machine, and sagas, outbox and CDC for releasing stock when payment fails.

title: Kafka internals
text: Kafka is a set of logs on disk, copied between brokers. Learn which settings decide what is safe, what is ordered, and what pauses.
body: In September 2013, Kyle Kingsbury tested a pre-release of Kafka 0.8 with his tool, Jepsen. His question was simple: when Kafka says a write is safe, is it? Kafka keeps each partition on several servers, called brokers. One copy is the leader. The leader tracks which followers are up to date: the in-sync replicas, or ISR. A write counted as committed once every member of the ISR had it. He cut the leader off from its followers. They timed out and dropped out of the ISR, so the leader was alone in it. It kept acking writes that existed only on its own disk. The producer was waiting for every in-sync copy, and it still got "ok". Then the leader lost its claim, and Kafka elected a follower that was far behind. When the old leader came back, its writes conflicted with the new leader's log and were thrown away. Of 987 acked writes, 520 were lost. He suggested that Kafka should "block and sound an alarm" instead of silently dropping data. Kafka later changed its default. Since version 0.11.0.0, it waits for an in-sync replica rather than elect one that is behind. But two settings still decide whether your writes are safe. Most teams never look at them. You know from queues vs logs that a Kafka topic is split into partitions. Each partition is a log: messages are only added at the end, and each gets an offset. This lesson shows what is inside. A partition is a set of files on a broker's disk. It is copied to other brokers. A producer picks the partition for each message. A consumer group splits the partitions among its members, and each member saves its offset. The key idea. Kafka gives every guarantee per partition: the order, the leader, the copies and the consumer's offset. Once you see that, most Kafka behaviour makes sense. Segments on disk A partition is not one big file. It is a series of log segments. Each segment file is named after the offset of its first message, like 00000000000000000000.log. New messages go to the newest segment. When it reaches a size limit, Kafka starts a new one. That limit is segment.bytes, 1 GiB by default. Kafka also rolls a segment after segment.ms, 7 days by default. To read from an offset, Kafka first finds the segment that holds it, then the position inside the file. Next to each segment, an index maps offsets to file positions. Kafka adds an entry about every 4 KiB of data (index.interval.bytes). A second index, the time index, gets entries on the same schedule when the timestamp has moved forward. It lets Kafka find messages by time. Kafka writes to the file system and leans on the OS page cache. It writes to the log without necessarily flushing each write to disk. Its safety comes from copies on other brokers, not from one disk. Retention and log compaction With the default cleanup.policy=delete, Kafka keeps data for retention.ms, 7 days by default. A size limit, retention.bytes, is off by default. Kafka deletes old data one whole segment at a time. So data can live a bit longer than the limit, until its segment is old enough. With cleanup.policy=compact, Kafka keeps at least the last value for each key. Older values for the same key are removed in the background by the log cleaner. Offsets never change. This suits a topic of "current state per key", such as customer addresses. To delete a key, you send a tombstone: a message with that key and a null value. Kafka keeps the tombstone for delete.retention.ms, one day by default. A consumer that falls further behind than that can miss the delete. Producers: partitioner, batching and acks A producer sends each message straight to the leader of its partition. If the message has a key, the default partitioner hashes the key to pick the partition. With no key, it sticks to one partition until at least batch.size bytes have gone there, then moves on. The producer groups messages for the same partition into batches. batch.size caps a batch at 16,384 bytes by default. linger.ms lets the producer wait a little for more messages. Kafka 4.0 changed its default from 0 to 5 ms. Bigger batches mean fewer requests and more throughput, for a few milliseconds of extra delay. The acks setting decides when the producer hears "ok". acks=0: the producer does not wait at all. Retries do nothing. acks=1: the leader writes to its own log and answers. If it dies before followers copy the message, the message is lost. acks=all: the leader waits for every in-sync replica. This is the default.
