The idempotent producer needs acks=all, and stops retries from writing duplicates. Replication: the ISR and the high watermark Each partition has one leader and zero or more followers. Followers fetch from the leader, much like a consumer. A follower stays in the ISR while it keeps its session with the controller and keeps up. If it lags longer than replica.lag.time.max.ms, the leader removes it. A message is committed when all in-sync replicas have it. Consumers see only committed messages. The high watermark marks the end of that committed part of the log. Kafka promises that a committed message is not lost "as long as there is at least one in sync replica alive". Now the trap from Jepsen. "All in-sync replicas" can mean just the leader. acks=all then means one copy. The fix is min.insync.replicas. With acks=all, a write fails with NotEnoughReplicas when the ISR is smaller than this number. Its default is 1. The docs suggest 3 replicas with min.insync.replicas=2. Step through a partition losing replicas. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. If every in-sync replica dies, Kafka must choose. It can wait for one to come back, or elect any replica that returns first, even one that is behind. The second choice keeps the partition up but may lose committed messages. That is unclean leader election. unclean.leader.election.enable is false by default. Even then, a lone last replica that crashes uncleanly can lose committed data. KIP-966 adds Eligible Leader Replicas to close this gap. They are on by default in new clusters since Kafka 4.1, but not in 4.0. Consumer groups, offsets and rebalances Each consumer group has a group coordinator on one broker. When a consumer commits offsets, the coordinator writes them to __consumer_offsets, a compacted topic that keeps the latest commit per partition. By default, the consumer commits offsets every 5 seconds in the background. When a member joins, leaves or stops answering, the group rebalances: partitions move between members. A member that is silent for session.timeout.ms (45 seconds by default) is removed in the classic protocol. With KIP-848, the broker sets this timeout. A member is also removed if it does not call poll() within max.poll.interval.ms (5 minutes). In the old "eager" protocol, every member gives up all its partitions, then waits for a new assignment. Nobody reads during that pause. Cooperative rebalancing, from Kafka 2.4, revokes only the partitions that change owner. Everyone else keeps reading. For the classic protocol, choose CooperativeStickyAssignor. The newer protocol from KIP-848 is generally available since Kafka 4.0. It is "fully incremental" and the broker computes the assignment. On the client it is still off by default: set group.protocol=consumer. The docs expect it to become the client default in Kafka 5.0. Consumer lag is how far a group is behind the end of each partition. kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe shows the current offset, the log end offset and the lag for each partition. Watch it. Lag that keeps growing is your backpressure signal. Ordering, and the partition count Kafka keeps order only inside a partition. Same key, same partition, same order. Across partitions there is no order. That is why the partition count is hard to change for keyed data. Roughly, the default partitioner picks hash(key) % number_of_partitions. When you add partitions, messages for a key "may be routed to different partitions". Kafka does not move the old data. For a while, one key's events sit in two partitions, and a consumer can read them out of order. Kafka also cannot reduce the number of partitions. So pick the count for your peak load, with room to grow. KRaft controllers Kafka now keeps cluster metadata in its own log, run by controllers. This is KRaft mode, covered in ZooKeeper, etcd and coordination. A server can be a broker, a controller, or both. Most clusters run 3 or 5 controllers. A majority must stay alive, so 3 survive one failure and 5 survive two. Don't run combined mode in critical production. Option Lose acked writes? Cost Use it when acks=0 Yes You never know if it arrived. Fastest. Metrics where a gap is fine. acks=1 Yes, if the leader dies before followers copy it. One round trip to the leader. Logs you can lose a little of. acks=all, min.insync.replicas=1 Yes, when the ISR shrinks to the leader. Waits for the ISR. Rarely. This is the default pair, so check it. acks=all, 3 replicas, min.insync.replicas=2 No, while one in-sync copy survives. Writes fail when 2 of 3 brokers are down. Orders, payments, anything you must keep. Unclean leader election on Yes The partition comes back sooner. Almost never. Cooperative or KIP-848 rebalancing n/a Needs a client upgrade or config change. Large groups, frequent deploys. Simple rule: for data you must not lose, use 3 replicas, acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2. Leave unclean election off. Read the topic config before you trust a topic. Ask: "What is min.insync.replicas, and what happens if two brokers die?" Pick the key and the partition count on day one. Write both in the topic's README, with where order holds. Alert on consumer lag per partition, not just per group. One hot partition can hide in an average. Find out why a group rebalances. Slow handlers that miss max.poll.interval.ms cause rebalances that cause more lag. Move consumers to cooperative or KIP-848 rebalancing before scaling a group up. For compacted topics, set delete.retention.ms longer than your slowest consumer can fall behind. "List every Kafka topic in this repo's config with its replication factor, min.insync.replicas, cleanup.policy and retention.ms. Flag any topic where acks=all gives only one copy." "Our consumer group rebalances every few minutes. Read this consumer code and config, and find what could make a member miss max.poll.interval.ms." "We want to grow this keyed topic from 12 to 24 partitions. Write a plan that keeps per-key order, for example a new topic and a cut-over." What to ask the agent The agent did not claim acks=all alone means "on 3 brokers". It means "on every replica in the ISR right now". Any partition change for a keyed topic has a plan for old and new messages of the same key. Offsets are committed after the work, not by a timer in the middle of it. Config changes name the Kafka version. Defaults like linger.ms changed in 4.0. Nobody turned on unclean leader election to "fix" an offline partition without saying what data it loses. What to check yourself Before this: Queues vs logs and database replication. Related: exactly-once and effectively-once for the idempotent producer and transactions, schema evolution and encoding for message formats, stream processing, and sharding and consistent hashing for why changing a partition count moves keys.

title: Latency numbers and back-of-envelope maths
text: Know the speed of memory, disk and network, and size a system in five minutes with simple maths.
body: A food delivery app is about to launch in a new, large city. Arjun owns the order service. His manager asks: "How many servers do we need?" Arjun does the maths. He expects about 40 million requests a day. He divides by 86,400 seconds and gets about 460 requests per second. A load test shows that one server handles about 500. He runs two servers, to be safe. On the first Friday, at 8 pm, everyone orders dinner at once. Traffic reaches about five times the daily average: over 2,000 requests per second. Both servers hit 100% CPU. Requests wait in queues, and responses take 8 seconds instead of 200 ms. The app retries slow calls, which adds even more load. Orders fail for 40 minutes on the busiest night of the week. Arjun's maths was correct. His question was wrong. He sized the system for the average second of the day, but users do not arrive evenly. (This story is made up, but the pattern is common.) Before you build, you should know roughly how big and how fast a system must be. You do not need exact numbers. You need the right order of magnitude: is it 10, 1,000 or 100,000 requests per second? Each answer leads to a very different design. A back-of-envelope estimate gets you there in a few minutes. It uses two tools: The latency ladder. How long common operations take, from a CPU cache read to a call across the ocean. Simple traffic maths. Users → requests per second (QPS) → servers, storage and bandwidth. The key idea. Round hard and write down your assumptions. Then size for the peak, not the average. A system that is fine on an average day can still crash in its busiest hour. The latency ladder These are rough numbers from the well-known table by Jeff Dean and Peter Norvig, as kept up to date by Colin Scott . They are the values his page shows for recent years. Most are estimates, and your hardware will differ. Learn the steps between them, not the exact digits. To make them feel real, pretend that 1 nanosecond (ns) is 1 second: Read from the CPU's L1 cache: about 1 ns (older tables say 0.5 ns) → 1 second. Read from main memory (RAM): about 100 ns → under 2 minutes. Random read from an SSD: about 16 µs (16,000 ns) → about 4.5 hours. Round trip inside one data centre: about 0.5 ms (500,000 ns) → almost 6 days. Round trip from California to the Netherlands: about 150 ms → almost 5 years. Three lessons come from this ladder: Memory is fast, but disk is slow . So a cache in RAM can save you a lot of time. A network call costs far more than local work. Avoid calls in a loop. A call across an ocean costs about 300 calls inside the data centre. A page that makes five such calls, one after another, waits about 750 ms for the network alone. Numbers to keep in your head Powers of two are close to powers of ten. 2^10 is about a thousand (KB), 2^20 about a million (MB), 2^30 about a billion (GB) and 2^40 about a trillion (TB) . A day has 86,400 seconds. Round it to 100,000 (10^5). Now "per day" to "per second" is just "divide by 100,000". The answer is about 14% too low, which is fine for an estimate. Network speeds are in bits, but file sizes are in bytes. One byte is 8 bits, so 100 MB per second needs about 800 Mbit/s. A worked estimate Step through Arjun's estimate, done the right way. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. The steps are always the same: Requests per day. Daily active users × requests per user. Here: 2 million × 20 = 40 million. Average QPS. Divide by 100,000. Here: about 400 QPS. Peak QPS. Multiply by a peak factor. Alex Xu's book example uses 2 . Use your own traffic graphs if you have them. A food app at dinner time can be much more uneven. So this example assumes 5, which is a guess, not a measured number. Servers. Divide peak QPS by what one server handles in a load test. Then add spare servers, so you survive losing one. Storage. Items per day × size × days you keep them. Here: 500,000 orders × 2 KB ≈ 1 GB a day, or about 365 GB a year. One database can hold that. Bandwidth. Peak QPS × response size. Here: 2,000 × 20 KB = 40 MB/s, or about 320 Mbit/s. Peak and average, for latency too Averages hide problems in latency as well as traffic. Google's SRE book gives an example: a service with an average latency of 100 ms can still have 1% of requests take 5 seconds . So estimate and measure percentiles like p99, not only the average. Approach Safe at the peak? Cost Use it when Size for the daily average No The busy hour can be many times higher. Cheapest on paper. Never for user-facing systems. Fine for batch jobs that can run slower. Size for the peak, plus spare Yes You survive the busiest hour and one lost server. You pay for idle servers at night. Most new services, and any launch you cannot afford to fail. Autoscale from the average Partly. New servers take minutes to start, and sudden spikes arrive faster. Lower cost when traffic is calm. Traffic rises slowly and you keep a minimum number of servers running. Load test with real traffic shapes Yes You test the real peak, not a guess. Takes days to build and run well. Big launches, sales events and systems that move money. Simple rule: a quick estimate tells you which design to choose. A load test tells you if the design really works. When someone proposes a design, ask: "How many requests per second at the peak, and how much data per year?" If nobody knows, do the five-minute estimate together. Write the assumptions in the design doc: users, requests per user, peak factor, sizes . Others can then correct one number instead of arguing about the result. Find the peak in real data. Look at the busiest minute of the busiest day, not a daily average. Watch for special days, like a sale, a holiday or a big match. Remember that the peak can arrive overnight. On 4 January 2021, Slack went from its quietest time of the year to one of its busiest days. Its cloud network hubs (AWS Transit Gateways) did not scale fast enough . Count network calls per request. Each call inside the data centre costs about 0.5 ms. Each call across an ocean, such as California to the Netherlands, costs about 150 ms . Plan for servers to run well below 100% CPU at the peak. Many systems slow down before they reach 100% . Agree on a target with your team. "Here are my assumptions: 2 million daily users, 20 requests each, a peak of 5 times the average, 2 KB per order, 20 KB per response. Estimate peak QPS, storage per year and peak bandwidth. Show every step with units." "List every network call this endpoint makes for one request. Mark which ones run one after another and which run in parallel." What to ask the agent Every number has a unit: per second or per day, bits or bytes, KB or MB. The estimate uses a peak, not only the average, and the peak factor comes from real data or is clearly labelled as a guess. The answer is the right order of magnitude. Check one step by hand: divide by 100,000, then multiply by the peak factor. Latency numbers are treated as rough. AI tools often repeat the old table as if it were exact. The server count includes spare capacity, so losing one server does not take you down. What to check yourself Next on this line: Tail latency and queueing explains why servers slow down sharply as they get busy.

title: Leader election and leases
text: Many systems need exactly one node in charge. Learn how leases pick that node, why an old leader can still act, and how fencing tokens stop it.
body: On 2 November 2020, a network switch in one Cloudflare data centre partly failed. It stayed up enough that other systems did not route around it. But it dropped some of the packets it should have passed on. Cloudflare's control plane used etcd, a store built on Raft, to coordinate its database clusters. One etcd node sat behind the bad switch. It could reach one peer, but not the etcd leader. That node kept starting elections and voting for itself. The other follower kept voting for the existing leader. The votes tied again and again. Cloudflare writes that Raft leader elections block all writes until they finish, so etcd became read-only. Now two database clusters could not record in etcd that they had a healthy primary. So the cluster manager promoted a synchronous replica to be the new primary. The promotion lost no data. But a bug in the manager forced a rebuild of every replica. One cluster handled authentication for the API and the dashboard. Its new primary had to carry all the reads alone, and it was overloaded. The switch recovered by itself after about six minutes. The incident lasted 6 hours and 33 minutes. API success fell as low as 75%, and the dashboard was up to 80 times slower. Cloudflare's conclusion: "we may not want to invoke the promotion process so quickly." Many systems want exactly one node to do a job. A database primary is the only node that takes writes. A scheduler must start each cron job once. In a highly available Kubernetes setup, only one kube-controller-manager and one kube-scheduler are active. The other copies stand by. Picking that one node is leader election. Keeping it safe takes two more tools. A lease is leadership with an end time. The leader must renew it often. If it stops renewing, for example because it crashed, the lease runs out and another node takes over. Nobody has to prove the old leader is dead. They only have to wait. But you learned in failure detection that silence is ambiguous. The old leader may be paused, not dead. When it wakes up, it still believes it is the leader. Now two leaders act at once. This is split-brain. So the last check must sit where the damage happens: in the storage. Every new leader gets a bigger number, called a fencing token. The storage rejects a write that carries a smaller number than one it has already seen. Raft calls a similar number a term. The key idea. A lease tells the old leader when to stop. A fencing token protects your data when it does not stop in time. Getting a lease Do not write this yourself on a plain database row and your own timer. Use a coordination service that already runs consensus, or a tested lock library. How these services work inside is the topic of the later lesson on ZooKeeper, etcd and coordination. Here is what you use from the outside. etcd. A session holds a lease with a time to live. The default is 60 seconds. Campaign blocks until you become the leader. Session.Done closes when the lease ends, so you know to stop. ZooKeeper. Each candidate creates an ephemeral node with the sequential flag under one path. The one with the smallest number leads. Each other candidate watches only the node just below its own. So one failure wakes one client, not all of them. Consul. You create a session, then try to acquire a key with it. The answer is true if you are now the leader. Consul warns that this lock "has no enforcement mechanism". Any client can still write the key. Kubernetes. Control plane parts hold a Lease object to stay the single active copy. The client-go leaderelection package gives your own controllers the same thing. DynamoDB. The DynamoDB lock client stores each lock as an item. The owner sends heartbeats that change a record version number. A waiting client takes over only if that number did not change for a full lease period. The record version number is a random UUID, so it is not a fencing token. Notice one thing in the DynamoDB design. The waiting client does not trust a timestamp from another machine. It times the wait on its own clock. client-go does the same: it acts only on timestamps it captured itself. The timing rules kube-controller-manager uses three timing settings. Setting Default Meaning Lease duration 15 s How long other candidates wait after the last renewal they saw. Renew deadline 10 s How long the leader keeps trying to renew before it stops leading. Retry period 2 s The wait between tries to get or renew the lease. The renew deadline must be less than the lease duration. That gap is your safety margin. The leader gives up after 10 seconds without a renewal. The others wait 15 seconds before they take over. So a running leader stops about 5 seconds before anyone else starts. This works only if clocks run at about the same speed. client-go says it tolerates any clock skew, but not any skew rate. Its example: to survive a node whose clock runs twice as fast, set the lease to 60 seconds and the renew deadline to 30. Each node measures how long it waited. It never compares its clock reading with another machine's. The lease duration also sets your failover time. Kubernetes calls it "effectively the maximum duration that a leader can be stopped before it is replaced". Why the old leader thinks it is still leader The margin protects a leader that is running. It does nothing for a leader that is not running at all. Kleppmann describes a client that pauses while it holds a lock. Its lease expires, another client gets the lock, and then the first one wakes up and writes. Stop-the-world GC pauses "have sometimes been known to last for several minutes". A clock jump can do it too. If the lock service's clock jumps forward, it ends the lease while the holder still thinks it has time. Leases need clocks that run at about the same rate and do not jump. A network partition looks the same from outside: the old leader is healthy, but its renewals never arrive. In each case, the old leader's belief is out of date. It checked "am I still the leader?" and then acted. A pause, a clock jump or a lost message came between the check and the act. No check inside the leader can close that gap. Step through it. Fencing: the storage enforces the term Google's Chubby lock service, described in a 2006 paper, handles this with a sequencer. It holds the lock name, the lock mode and a lock generation number. The leader sends it with each request. The server checks it and rejects the request if it is no longer valid. The paper's simplest version is even smaller: pass one extra integer, the lock acquisition count, with each write. The file server adds one if-statement that rejects a count lower than the current one. Kleppmann calls this number a fencing token. With ZooKeeper, you can use the zxid or the znode version. With etcd, Election.Rev gives the creation revision of the leader key. etcd revisions only grow over the life of a cluster, so a newer leader gets a bigger one. In your own database, the check is a conditional write: -- Leader with token 34 writes. A paused leader 33 can no longer win. UPDATE job_state SET last_run = now(), token = 34 WHERE job_id = 'nightly-report' AND token <= 34; -- 0 rows changed? A newer leader exists. Stop at once.This is the same idea as a Raft term in Consensus and Raft. Locks, atomics and deadlocks covers the same fix for a single lock, and Redis in depth covers the Redlock debate. Libraries say plainly that they do not do this for you. client-go "does not guarantee that only one client is acting as a leader (a.k.a. fencing)". If a system cannot check tokens, Chubby offers a weaker fallback, the lock-delay. When a holder fails, nobody may take its lock for a while, at most one minute. Chubby calls it "imperfect". Failover timing A short lease means fast failover. It also means more false failovers, because a GC pause or a slow network looks like a crash. A long lease means fewer mistakes, but a real crash leaves you without a leader for longer. client-go puts it this way: tolerance to clock skew rate "varies inversely to master availability". Also ask what the lease is really measuring. At Cloudflare, the databases were fine. The coordination service was sick, and the promotion logic read that as a dead primary. GitHub saw failover go wrong twice too: in 2012 a busy primary was taken for a dead one, and in 2018 a 43-second network cut led to writes on both coasts. Option Fast failover? Safe if the old leader wakes up? Use it when Short lease (a few seconds) Yes No Pauses cause false failovers, and two leaders can overlap. Duplicate work is cheap, like a cache warmer. Long lease (a minute or more) No Better, but a long pause can still outlast it. Leader work is slow and rare, like a nightly batch. Lease plus fencing token Yes Yes The storage rejects old leaders. Leader writes must be correct: money, orders, primary databases. Chubby-style lock-delay No Adds the delay to every failover. Partly. Chubby calls it imperfect. The storage cannot check tokens. Human-approved failover No Minutes, not seconds. Yes, if the person fences the old primary first. Rare, risky moves of a primary database. Ask: "If two nodes believe they lead for one minute, what breaks?" If the answer is "nothing much", a lease is enough. If it is "money moves twice", you need fencing. Find where the token is checked. It must be in the storage or the downstream service, not in the leader's own code. Make leader code stop when it loses the lease. In etcd, watch Session.Done. In client-go, stop all work in the callback for lost leadership. Measure lease time with a monotonic clock, not the wall clock. Check that the renew deadline is clearly shorter than the lease duration, and that both are longer than your worst real GC pause. Ask what triggers a failover. A sick coordination service should not, by itself, promote a new database primary. Check that the new leader can take the full load before it is promoted. At Cloudflare, it had no local replicas left to help. Alert on leader changes. Many changes per hour mean the lease is too short or something is pausing. "Our report job runs on 3 pods and uses client-go leader election. Show the lease settings and explain what happens if the leader has a 30-second GC pause. Which writes could happen twice?" "Add a fencing token to this job. Take it from the etcd election revision, send it with every write, and make the database reject writes with a smaller token. Write a test for a paused old leader." "List every automatic failover in our system. For each, say what signal triggers it and whether a sick coordination service alone could trigger it." What to ask the agent The token check is a conditional write in the storage, not an "am I leader?" call just before the write. The token always grows. A host name, random ID or timestamp from the leader's clock is not a fencing token. The leader stops all work on lost leadership. It does not finish the current batch first. Timeouts come from your measured worst pauses, not from guesses. The agent did not shorten the lease for faster failover without saying how many false failovers that adds. What to check yourself Before this: failure detection and membership. Related: Consensus and Raft, Database replication, Time, clocks and ordering, Locks, atomics and deadlocks and Redis in depth. Next: ZooKeeper, etcd and coordination. See the Cloudflare incident page.

title: Low-level and object-oriented design
text: Learn a repeatable method for designing the classes of a small system, carried through one parking lot, from the first question to the race at two gates.
body: This story is made up, but the pattern is common. Ravi had a 45-minute low-level design round. The prompt was one line: "Design a parking lot." He started drawing at once. Vehicle got subclasses Car, Bike and Truck. A ParkingLotManager class grew 20 methods: find a spot, print tickets, take payment, send SMS. He added a factory, a singleton and two strategies, to show he knew patterns. At minute 30 the interviewer asked, "Two cars arrive at two gates at the same moment. Can both get spot 14?" Ravi looked at his code. Both gates read the spot as free, then both took it. He had no answer. Then came the second question: "We want different prices for trucks." The price logic sat in four methods of the manager. He had to edit all four. The feedback said: "Knows the patterns. Did not clarify scope. Design breaks under change and under concurrent use." Ravi had written more code than the strong candidates. It was the wrong code. A low-level design (LLD) round gives you a small, self-contained problem. You design its classes, their methods and how they work together. Hello Interview puts it this way: these rounds "test your ability to structure code for a self-contained problem". The round is also called object-oriented design. In a system design round, you draw services, databases and caches for scale. In an LLD round, you design the inside of one program. Hello Interview's summary: "System design is the map. Low level design is the blueprint for a building on the map." Interviewers judge five things: how you analyse the problem, your class design, code quality, how easily the design takes a follow-up change, and how you explain it. Code quality includes choosing composition or inheritance, managing state and the direction of dependencies. Where the round sits in a full loop is in the interview loops lesson. The key idea. Put each rule in the object that owns the data it needs. Add an interface or a pattern only where you can name a change that is coming. Then ask what happens when two callers touch the same object at once. You already have the tools. SOLID, coupling and cohesion told you to group what changes together. Design patterns that still matter told you to start from the problem, not the pattern. This lesson is the method that uses both, under time pressure. Step through the parking lot design as it grows. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Hello Interview's framework has five steps, about 35 minutes in total. Here is a version you can repeat. 1. Clarify requirements and scope The prompt is vague on purpose. Your job is to "turn it into a spec you can actually design around". Spend the first minutes asking. For the parking lot, Hello Interview picks a sample scope. There are three vehicle types: motorcycle, car and large vehicle. Entry gives a free, compatible spot and a ticket. Exit takes the ticket, works out the fee and frees the spot. The price is hourly, rounded up. Payments, gate hardware, cameras, the UI and reservations are out of scope. Say that list out loud. It protects your time. 2. Find the core objects and their responsibilities Pull out the meaningful nouns from your requirements. For the parking lot: lot, spot, ticket, vehicle. But "don't turn every noun into a class. Some things are just data." Give each object one job, in one sentence: ParkingLot: takes cars in and out, and owns the spots and the active tickets. Spot: knows its size and whether it is taken. Ticket: records which vehicle is in which spot, and since when. Vehicle: just data, a plate and a size. The framework's rule: "keep rules with the entity that owns the relevant state." Fowler calls the same habit tell-don't-ask: "rather than asking an object for data and acting on that data, we should instead tell an object what to do." So the lot tells a spot "take this ticket". It does not read a taken flag and set it from outside. 3. Choose the relationships The lot has spots. That is composition: spots belong to the lot. A ticket refers to a spot and a vehicle. That is association: it points at them but does not own them. Should Car and Truck be subclasses? Only if they behave differently. Here they differ only in size, so a size field is enough. Gamma calls inheritance "a cool way to change behavior", but brittle. A subclass "can easily make assumptions" about when the parent calls the methods it overrides. Here the variants have no behaviour to change. He still backs the GoF advice to favour composition, ten years on. 4. Write the interfaces and the few methods that matter You have about 10 minutes for code. Start with the happy path, then the edge cases. Ask whether they want real code or pseudo-code. Two methods matter here: enter and exit. Like a deep module, they hide the hard parts. // imports: java.time.*, java.util.*, java.util.concurrent.*, java.util.concurrent.atomic.* enum Size { SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE } record Vehicle(String plate, Size size) {} record Ticket(String id, Vehicle vehicle, Spot spot, Instant in) {} final class Spot { private final Size size; private final AtomicReference<Ticket> holder = new AtomicReference<>(); Spot(Size size) { this.size = size; } boolean fits(Vehicle v) { return size.compareTo(v.size()) >= 0; } boolean tryTake(Ticket t) { return holder.compareAndSet(null, t); } void release(Ticket t) { holder.compareAndSet(t, null); } }Spot has no public setter. Callers cannot put it into a bad state. 5. Add a pattern only where a change is coming A common follow-up asks for different prices by vehicle type. Now pricing has a real reason to change, so it earns a small interface: interface PricingPolicy { long feeCents(Ticket t, Instant out); } final class ParkingLot { private final List<Spot> spots; private final Map<String, Ticket> active = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private final PricingPolicy pricing; private final Clock clock; // constructor that sets all four is left out Ticket enter(Vehicle v) { for (Spot s : spots) { if (!s.fits(v)) continue; Ticket t = new Ticket(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), v, s, clock.instant()); if (s.tryTake(t)) { active.put(t.id(), t); return t; } } throw new IllegalStateException("no free spot for " + v.size()); } long exit(String ticketId) { Ticket t = active.remove(ticketId); if (t == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown or used ticket"); t.spot().release(t); return pricing.feeCents(t, clock.instant()); } }This is the Strategy pattern from the patterns lesson, used for one known need. Before the interviewer asked, a plain hourly method on the lot was enough. Hello Interview warns against a pricing engine with surge prices and discounts "unless they explicitly ask for it". The Clock is passed in, so a test can fix the time. The testing strategy lesson shows why that matters. 6. Handle state and concurrency Two gates means two threads. Hello Interview describes the classic race for a seat: "Both users checked availability before either completed their booking." The check and the action "happened as two separate steps". This bug is called check-then-act. The code above makes them one step. compareAndSet sets the new value only if the current value is still the expected one. It returns false if another thread got there first. So one gate wins spot 14. The other moves on to the next spot. Exit has the same risk. Someone might use one ticket twice. All ConcurrentHashMap operations are thread-safe, and remove returns the old value or null. So only one exit gets the ticket back. Locks, atomics and deadlocks are covered in depth in locks, atomics and deadlocks. 7. Answer the extensibility questions Expect follow-ups such as many floors, prices by vehicle type, or many entrances. Their goal is to show "that your initial design is extensible and robust". Answer each one by naming the class that changes. Many floors: ParkingLot holds floors, and each floor holds spots. A new price: a new PricingPolicy. If one answer touches five classes, say so and propose a fix. Choice Easy to change? Cost Use it when A field or enum for the variant (Size) Yes A new size is one value. No place for behaviour that differs. Variants differ only in data. Subclass per variant (Car, Truck) No Subclasses depend on the parent's details. More classes, brittle hierarchy. Variants really behave differently, and the parent's contract is stable. Interface plus implementations (PricingPolicy) Yes A new rule is a new class. One more name to learn. You can name a second rule, or the interviewer asks. Logic in one manager class Yes, at first. It grows into a god class. Every change touches it. A first sketch only. Split it before you finish. Atomic step on the object (tryTake) Yes You must think about which steps must be one. Two callers can change the same object. One lock around the whole lot Yes All gates wait for each other. Low traffic, or a quick first answer you then improve. In a design review or a pull request, ask each new class "What is your one job?" If the answer has "and" three times, it needs a split. Watch for a god class: a manager or service that keeps growing. Refactoring.Guru notes that classes "usually start small" but bloat as the program grows. Split it with Extract Class. Look for objects that are only getters and setters, with all rules in a service. Fowler calls this an anemic domain model. He calls it "really just a procedural style design". Move the rule next to the data it reads. Do not chase getters everywhere, though. Fowler himself says, "personally, I don't use tell-dont-ask". He still puts data and behaviour together, but he has seen the rule push people to remove every getter. When you see a new abstract base class, ask what behaviour the subclasses change. If none, suggest a field. When you see a new interface, ask for the second implementation. If nobody can name it, wait. Hello Interview says: "Build what you need now, not what you might need later." For every shared object, ask: "What if two requests call this at once?" Look for a read, a decision and a write as three separate lines. "Here is my parking lot spec and its out-of-scope list. Propose the classes, with one sentence of responsibility each. Do not add any design pattern I did not ask for." "In this class design, find every place where code reads a value, decides, then writes it back in a separate step. For each, say what two threads could do to break it." "List the classes in this diff that only have getters and setters. For each, name the service method that holds its rules." What to ask the agent The agent did not turn every noun into a class or add subclasses that change no behaviour. Every pattern it added solves a change you can name. The concurrency fix makes the check and the action one atomic step. A synchronized method that only wraps the check is not a fix. The code compiles and a test with two threads passes many times in a row. What to check yourself Before this: SOLID, coupling and cohesion and design patterns that still matter. Related: complexity and deep modules, locks, atomics and deadlocks, testing strategy, the system design interview method and big tech interview loops.

title: Evals for LLM systems
text: Test LLM features with a fixed set of cases, a grader and a score, and run it on every prompt or model change.
body: On 25 April 2025, OpenAI finished rolling out an update to GPT-4o in ChatGPT. It made the model "noticeably more sycophantic". It aimed to please users: it validated doubts, fuelled anger and urged impulsive actions. The update combined several changes that each looked good on its own. One was a new reward signal from users' thumbs-up and thumbs-down clicks. OpenAI believes that, together, these changes weakened the signal that had kept sycophancy in check. Why did the checks miss it? The offline evals "generally looked good". Users in a small A/B test seemed to like the model. There were no deployment evals that tracked sycophancy. Some expert testers said the model "felt" slightly off, but OpenAI launched anyway. It later called this "the wrong call". OpenAI began the rollback on 28 April. It is adding sycophancy evals to its deployment process. Behaviour issues now block a launch, even when A/B tests look good. It also plans to value hands-on testing more. It is expanding its evals to find issues beyond sycophancy. The lesson for you: an eval set only catches what it tests. A good score says nothing about a failure that has no test case. Normal unit tests compare output with one expected value. That works when code is deterministic: the same input always gives the same output. LLM features are different in two ways. The output changes between runs. Anthropic runs several trials of each task "because model outputs vary between runs". There are many correct answers. "Delivery takes 3 to 5 days" and "You will get it in 3 to 5 working days" are both right. A test that checks for one exact string fails on the other. OpenAI's guide says this variability makes traditional software testing methods not enough on their own. An eval fixes this with three parts: A test set. Saved inputs, each with a note about what a good answer must do. A grader. Logic that scores one output. It can be code, a model or a person. A score you track. For example, 37 of 40 cases pass. You compare it with the last good version, the baseline. The key idea. An eval is a unit test for an LLM feature. It does not ask "is this output equal to X?". It asks "does this output meet our rules?", over many cases, every time you change something. Step through one prompt change with Next and Back. The support bot in this example is made up. Build the test set Start small. Anthropic says 20 to 50 simple tasks drawn from real failures is a great start. Turn bug reports and the checks you already do by hand into test cases. Mix three kinds of cases: Real user cases. Take them from logs and support tickets. OpenAI advises you to log as you build, so you can mine the logs for good eval cases. The set should look like your real traffic. Edge cases. Anthropic lists missing or irrelevant input, very long input, harmful user input, and cases where even humans would disagree. Add questions where the right answer is "I don't know". Adversarial cases. Inputs that try to break the feature on purpose. See the safety section below. Write down what "good" means for each case. Vague cases give noisy scores: "Ambiguity in task specifications becomes noise in metrics". If a case fails every time, check the case first. Anthropic says a 0% pass rate is most often a sign of a broken task. Choose graders Anthropic's advice is to choose the fastest, most reliable and most scalable method that works for each check. Code checks. Exact match, "contains this phrase", valid JSON, length limits. They are the fastest and most reliable, but lack nuance for complex judgments. Hamel Husain runs these assertions on every code change. Reference comparison. Compare the output with a saved good answer, for example with ROUGE-L for summaries. Model graders (LLM-as-judge). A second model reads the output and grades it against a rubric. It is fast, flexible and suits complex judgment, but test it for reliability before you scale it. Give it a detailed rubric, ask for a simple result such as "correct" or "incorrect", and let it reason before it scores. Anthropic's examples say it is generally best to use a different model from the one that wrote the output. Human review. The most flexible and highest quality, but slow and expensive. Anthropic advises avoiding it where possible. Save systematic human studies for calibrating model graders. Know the biases of model graders Zheng et al. studied strong models as judges. They report position bias (favouring an answer because of its place in the list), verbosity bias (favouring longer answers) and self-enhancement bias (maybe favouring its own answers; their data could not confirm this one). In one test with two similar answers to each MT-Bench question, GPT-4 gave the same verdict in both orders only 65% of the time. Their fix: ask twice with the order swapped, and count a tie when the verdicts disagree. Still, on their MT-Bench data, GPT-4's pairwise verdicts agreed with human experts 85% of the time, on votes that were not ties. Two humans agreed 81% of the time. But that is their benchmark, not your feature. Hamel Husain advises you to track how well your model grader matches human judgment. Offline evals, online monitoring and A/B tests An offline eval runs on saved cases before you ship. It cannot show what real users will do. Use three layers: Offline evals on every change. Production monitoring after launch, for the truth about real behaviour. Read real user traces, and sample more as volume grows. A/B tests for big changes, once you have enough traffic. They cost the most, so run them the least often. Regression evals in CI Anthropic separates two kinds of evals. Capability evals measure what the feature cannot do yet, so they start with a low pass rate. Regression evals check that old tasks still work, and should have a nearly 100% pass rate. Our advice: run the regression set in CI for every change to the prompt, the model version, the retrieval settings or the tools. Show the result case by case, not only the total. A total of 34 can hide four new failures behind one new fix. Block the merge when a case that passed before now fails. Measure cost and latency too Anthropic lists latency and price as success criteria. Latency, token usage and cost per task can be tracked on the same fixed set of tasks. A new model that scores 2% higher but doubles your cost may be the wrong choice. Do not overfit the test set If you tune a prompt against the same 40 cases for months, the score can go up while real users see no change. This is overfitting. Our advice: Keep a held-out set that you run, but never tune against. Add new cases from live traffic every month. When the set is fully passed, write harder cases. Anthropic says an eval at 100% still tracks regressions but gives no signal for improvement. Make graders hard to fool. The feature "shouldn't be able to easily 'cheat' the eval". Safety evals Add attack cases to the set, and run them like any other test. OWASP advises adversarial testing and attack simulations against prompt injection. Include direct attacks, where the user types the instructions. Include indirect attacks, hidden in a web page or file the model reads. For harmful output, Anthropic gives a measurable example: under 0.1% of outputs flagged for toxicity, out of 10,000 trials. OWASP also advises checking that the output matches the expected format with deterministic code. This table is our own summary of the cited sources. Grader Speed and cost Handles many correct answers Same result every run Use it for Code checks Yes Fast and cheap. No Too strict for open-ended text. Yes Format, JSON, banned words, required phrases, length. Model grader (LLM-as-judge) Fast, but costs more than code. Yes Good for tone, correctness, grounding. No It varies, and has position and verbosity biases. Open-ended answers, once you have checked it against human labels. Human review No Slow and expensive. Yes The highest quality. No Experts can disagree. Building the rubric, calibrating graders, reading samples of live traffic. Simple rule: use code where a rule is exact, a model grader where it needs judgment, and humans to check both. Before anyone changes a prompt, ask: "What is our eval set, and what is the baseline score?" If there is none, build 20 to 50 cases first. Turn every bug report about the LLM feature into a test case on the same day. Treat a model upgrade like a dependency upgrade. Run the full set and compare quality, cost and latency before you switch. Sample model-grader results each month and check that they still agree with human labels. Ship big changes behind a feature flag to a small share of users, and watch live metrics. See Safe deploys. "Here are 30 real support tickets. For each one, write what a good answer must include and must not include. Mark tickets where the right answer is 'I don't know'." "Write a script that runs our prompt on every case in evals/cases.jsonl, applies these code checks, and prints a table of cases that passed before and fail now." What to ask the agent The expected behaviour for each case is right. The agent may guess the policy, so check a sample by hand. The model grader agrees with your own labels on at least 20 cases before you trust it. The CI job compares per case with the baseline, and fails the build on a new regression. You never put held-out cases into a prompt you are tuning. What to check yourself Evals for retrieval, such as recall@k, are covered in RAG: retrieval-augmented generation. Safety and cost in production: Guardrails, cost and latency for LLM features.

title: LLM fundamentals for product engineers
text: Know what a model really does with your request, so you can design for cost, speed, limits and wrong answers.
body: On 1 March 2023, a New York lawyer filed a document in a court case against the airline Avianca. A colleague at his firm had researched and written it. It cited court decisions that did not exist, with fake quotes and fake citations. They had been made up by ChatGPT. The colleague later said he had "falsely assumed" ChatGPT was "like a super search engine". When doubts came up, he asked ChatGPT, "Is Varghese a real case". The chatbot said it had given "real" sources that could be found in the usual legal databases. The lawyers and their firm later admitted that six of the cited decisions were generated by ChatGPT and do not exist. On 22 June 2023, the judge found bad faith. The lawyers had kept standing by the fake cases after the court asked about them. He ordered a $5,000 penalty, to be paid jointly by both lawyers and their firm. They also had to write to their client and to each real judge falsely named as the author of a fake decision. The judge wrote that there is "nothing inherently improper" about using a reliable AI tool. But lawyers have a "gatekeeping role" to make sure their filings are accurate. The lesson for product engineers: a model writes likely text, not checked facts. Asking the model if it was right is not a check. Our advice: check the output in code, against a real source of truth. A large language model (LLM) is first trained to predict the next word, given the text before it. On its own, it does not look up facts. It writes text that is likely to come next. The model does not read words. It reads tokens: words, parts of words, characters or bytes. You pay per token, limits are counted in tokens, and speed depends on tokens. The model writes its reply one token at a time. Then your code must decide if the reply can be trusted. The key idea. Treat the model like a fast, smart, unreliable dependency. It can be slow, rate-limited, down, or confidently wrong. Design for all four, as you would for any external service. Step through one API call with Next and Back. Tokens How many characters make a token depends on the model and the language. Anthropic's glossary says Claude 4.7 and later models use a newer tokenizer. It makes about 30% more tokens for the same text than earlier models. So use the provider's token counter with the exact model you plan to use. Language matters too. One study found that the same text, translated, can need up to 15 times more tokens in some languages than in others. If your users write in Hindi or Thai, measure your own token counts before you estimate cost. The context window The context window is everything the model can see for one response. It includes the system prompt, all messages, tool definitions, and the output itself. If the input alone is too long, the API rejects the request. Each model has its own limit, and limits change, so read the provider's model table. More context is not always better. Anthropic says accuracy and recall degrade as the token count grows. Send what the model needs, not everything you have. For large document sets, see RAG. Temperature: why outputs vary At each step, some next tokens are more likely than others. The temperature setting controls how random the choice is. Higher values give more varied output. Lower values stick to the most likely words. Even at temperature 0, outputs are not fully deterministic. So never write a test that expects one exact string. Use evals instead. Hallucination Models sometimes write plausible but false statements. One paper argues that training and tests reward guessing over saying "I don't know". OWASP says models fill gaps in their training data with statistical patterns. It also warns about overreliance: users trust output without checking it. Our advice: give the model the facts in the prompt, let it say "I don't know", and check key fields in code. System prompts and prompt structure The system prompt holds the rules for every request. A role there, even one sentence, focuses the model's behaviour. Wrap each kind of content in its own XML tag, such as instructions, context and input. Put long documents first and the question last. Anthropic says putting the question at the end improved quality by up to 30% in tests. Three to five examples help with format and tone. Structured output and tool use Free text is hard to parse. With structured outputs, the API forces the reply to match your JSON schema. There are exceptions. A refusal, or a reply cut off at max_tokens, may not match the schema. Even the capital letters of a fixed list value can differ. And valid JSON can still hold a wrong value. Tool use (also called function calling) lets the model ask your code to run a function. The model returns a structured call. Your app runs it and sends back the result. The model never runs your code itself. So your code decides what is allowed. Tool definitions also count as input tokens. More in Tool use and agents. Latency and streaming Time to first token (TTFT) is how long the user waits before anything appears. OpenAI says generating tokens is almost always the slowest step. Halving output tokens may cut about half the time; halving the prompt may save only 1 to 5%. OpenAI calls streaming the most effective way to make users wait less. With streaming, tokens arrive as server-sent events. An error can still arrive after the stream has started, so handle it in the stream code. Cost and prompt caching You pay for input tokens and output tokens, and tool definitions add input tokens. Prompt caching lets the provider reuse a fixed start of your prompt. The cached part must match exactly, so put fixed content first. As of October 2026, Anthropic prices 5-minute cache writes at 1.25 times the normal input price. Cache reads cost 0.1 times on most models, and less on a few of the newest ones. The default cache lives 5 minutes, and each use refreshes it. Prices change, so read the current table. Choosing a model size Anthropic frames the choice as capability against speed and cost. One approach is to start with a small, fast model and upgrade only if your tests show a gap. It calls a good evaluation set "the most important step". Rate limits Providers cap requests and tokens per minute. Go over, and you get a 429 error. When there is a retry-after header, wait that many seconds. For most Claude models, cached input tokens do not count toward the input limit. Prompt injection Text the model reads can contain instructions that change what it does. OWASP lists this first in its Top 10 for LLM Applications. It says it is unclear if it can be fully prevented. Its advice includes least privilege, human approval for risky actions, and marking outside content as untrusted. A system prompt is not a secret and not a security control: keep keys out of it, and enforce access in code. See OWASP Top 10 and secure coding. Privacy Everything in the prompt goes to the provider. OWASP advises cleaning sensitive data, and clear terms of use that tell users how their data is used. Read each provider's data policy. OpenAI says API data is not used for training unless you opt in, and keeps abuse monitoring logs for up to 30 days by default. Anthropic offers zero data retention by arrangement, for eligible features only. Treat the model as an unreliable dependency Anthropic's SDK retries connection errors, 429s and server errors twice by default, with exponential backoff. Anthropic also advises streaming for long requests. Our advice for the rest: Set a timeout that fits your feature, not the SDK default. See Idempotency, retries and timeouts. Validate every reply. If it fails, retry once, then fall back: a smaller model, a saved answer, or a human. Log input and output tokens per request, so you can see cost by feature. Run your eval set before any prompt or model change. This table is our own summary, except where a source is cited. Option Quality on hard tasks Cost and latency Effort to change Use it when Smaller, faster model Often enough. Test it on your evals first. Yes Cheaper and faster. Low. Change one setting. High volume, simple tasks, tight latency. Larger model Higher. No Slower and costs more. Low. Complex reasoning, where accuracy matters more than cost. Prompt only Good if the model already knows enough. Yes One call. Low. Edit text and run evals. Your first version, almost always. Prompt plus RAG Better on your own, fresh data. Extra search step and more input tokens. Medium. You run an index. Answers must come from your documents. See RAG. Fine-tuning Can change style and format. A training run for each change. High. Prompting and RAG have failed on a measured eval. Simple rule: start with a prompt and a small eval set. Change the model or add RAG only when the numbers say so. Before building, ask: "What happens when the model is slow, down, or wrong?" Write the fallback into the design. Keep fixed content at the top of the prompt, so caching works. Never let the model decide who may do what. Check permissions in your code. Read the provider's data policy with your security team before sending user data. "Here is our prompt and 20 sample inputs. Count the input and output tokens for each with the provider's token counter, and estimate monthly cost at 50,000 requests a day." "Wrap this LLM call with a timeout, retries that respect retry-after, JSON schema validation, and a fallback to the human queue. Add a test for each failure path." "Review this prompt. Mark every place where user or retrieved text could be read as instructions." What to ask the agent The token counts come from the real counter for your model, not a rough rule of characters per token. The retry code does not retry errors that will never succeed, such as a 400. Validation checks values against your own data, not only the JSON shape. No secret or API key is in any prompt. What to check yourself Next lessons: Evals for LLM systems, RAG: retrieval-augmented generation, Tool use and agents in products, and Guardrails, cost and latency for LLM features.

title: Load balancing
text: A load balancer decides which server gets each request. Learn to pick the rule, check health and remove servers without dropping users.
body: This story is made up, but it is common. A food delivery app runs six API servers behind one load balancer. The load balancer uses round-robin: each server gets one request in turn. On a Friday evening, one server starts to read from a failing disk. Its requests take 3 seconds instead of 80 ms. Its health check is a simple /health page, and it still answers "OK" in 2 ms. The load balancer sees a healthy server. It keeps sending it one request in six. Users who land there wait, give up and tap "Order" again. The dashboards show normal average latency, because five servers are fine. But p99 latency is over 3 seconds, and support gets angry messages. It takes the team an hour to find the one bad server. Nothing was down. The load balancer did exactly what it was told. It just did not know that "healthy" and "fast" are not the same thing. A load balancer is one address in front of many servers. Clients talk to the load balancer. For each new connection or request, it picks a server. It has three jobs: Pick a server. Follow a rule, such as "next in turn" or "least busy". Skip bad servers. Use health checks to stop sending traffic to servers that fail. Change the pool safely. Add and remove servers without breaking requests that are still running. The key idea. The goal is not to spread requests evenly. The goal is that no server is overloaded and no user waits on a failing server. Equal counts are not equal work. L4 or L7 A layer 4 (L4) load balancer sees TCP connections, not HTTP requests. AWS's Network Load Balancer works this way. It picks a server with a hash of the protocol, addresses, ports and TCP sequence number. Each TCP connection stays on one server for its whole life. It is fast and simple, but it cannot read URLs or headers. A layer 7 (L7) load balancer reads each HTTP request. AWS's Application Load Balancer can send /api to one group of servers and /images to another, by path, host or header. It does more work per request, but it can balance requests, not just connections. This matters with HTTP/2 or gRPC, where one connection carries many requests. Choosing a server Round-robin gives each server the next request in turn. It is the default on the AWS Application Load Balancer. It works well when requests cost about the same. In practice they often do not. Google found that the most expensive requests can use 1,000 times more CPU than the cheapest. Round-robin gave a spread of up to 2x in CPU use between the least and most loaded servers. Least connections sends the request to the server with the fewest requests in progress. AWS calls this "least outstanding requests". It suggests it when requests vary in cost or servers vary in power. Step through what happens to one slow server under each rule. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Least connections has one trap. A broken server that returns errors very fast has few open requests. So it looks "least busy" and gets even more traffic. Google calls this a sinkhole. Its fix was to count recent errors as if they were open requests. Power of two choices (P2C) picks two servers at random and sends the request to the less busy one. Mitzenmacher showed that two random choices are far better than one, while a third choice helps only a little. Envoy uses this for its least request balancer. Its docs say it is nearly as good as checking every server. It is cheap, because it looks at only two servers per request. Consistent hashing sends the same key, such as a user ID, to the same server. A simple hash mod N breaks when N changes: almost every key moves to a new server. With consistent hashing, adding or removing a server moves only a small share of keys. Envoy offers it as "ring hash" and "Maglev". Use it when a server keeps a local cache per key. Health checks The load balancer tests each server on a schedule. On an AWS Application Load Balancer, the defaults are a check every 30 seconds, with a 5 second timeout. Two failures in a row mark a server unhealthy. Five passes in a row bring it back. With those defaults, a dead server fails two checks 30 seconds apart. So it can get traffic for about a minute before it is removed. Our advice: shorten the interval for important services. What should the check test? A shallow check ("the process is up") misses the slow disk in our story. A deep check that calls the database can mark every server unhealthy at once when the database has a short problem. Our advice is a middle path: check the server's own parts, and watch latency and errors with alerts. Health checks can also hurt you. If every target fails, an Application Load Balancer "fails open" and sends traffic to all of them anyway. In October 2025, health checks for AWS's Network Load Balancer in us-east-1 kept flipping between failing and healthy. Healthy capacity was removed, and customers saw connection errors. Engineers turned off automatic health check failover to stop it. Connection draining You remove servers all the time: deploys, scale-in, repairs. If you cut a server off at once, its open requests fail. Connection draining fixes this. The load balancer stops sending new requests to the server, but lets open ones finish. On an AWS Application Load Balancer, this is the "deregistration delay", and the default is 300 seconds. If the server closes connections before the delay ends, clients get 500-level errors. Google's version is a "lame duck" state: the server still serves, but asks clients to stop sending new requests. New servers can need the opposite: a slow start. AWS can raise traffic to a new target step by step, so it can warm up first. Sticky sessions, and why to avoid them Sticky sessions send all requests from one user to the same server, often with a cookie. On AWS, the load balancer's own cookie is named AWSALB, and it skips the normal algorithm after the first request. This is useful when a server keeps session data in memory. But it has costs. If that server dies, those users lose their session. Load becomes uneven: AWS warns that after a big scale-up, stickiness can spread load unequally. Deploys get slower, because you must drain long sessions. The better fix is to make servers stateless. Keep sessions in a shared store, such as Redis or a database, so any server can serve any user. Global load balancing To spread users across regions, you balance before traffic reaches any one data centre. DNS. The DNS server returns a different IP address for each region. It is simple, but slow to change. Resolvers cache answers for the TTL, and not all resolvers respect it. The DNS server also sees the resolver's address, not the user's, so it can guess the user's location wrong. Anycast. Many sites announce the same IP address. The network sends each user to the nearest one. Google's book describes giving DNS servers an anycast address, so DNS queries flow to the closest one. Rule Handles a slow server? Cost Use it when Round-robin No Every server gets the same share. Almost none. Requests cost about the same and servers are the same size. Least connections Yes Busy servers get less. Must track open requests. Watch for fast-failing sinkholes. Request cost varies a lot. Power of two choices Yes, mostly. Checks only two servers per request. Many load balancers or proxies, each with its own view. Consistent hashing No The key decides, not the load. Hot keys can overload one server. Each server caches data per key. Sticky sessions No Users stay on the same server even when it is busy. Lost sessions when a server dies. Uneven load. Old apps that keep state in memory, while you move it out. Simple rule: start with least connections or P2C for HTTP services. Use hashing only when local data needs it. Ask: "What does our health check really test?" A check that passes while users wait is not a health check. Watch p99 latency and errors per server, not just the average. One bad server hides inside a good average. Set the draining time longer than your slowest normal request. Make sure the app stops cleanly on SIGTERM, the signal that asks a process to shut down. Know what happens when every server fails its check. Does the load balancer fail open, or send nothing? Remove sticky sessions when you touch old code. Move session data to a shared store. For long-lived connections, like gRPC or WebSockets, check that load is spread by request, not just by connection. Test it: kill one server during a load test, and slow one down. Watch what the users see. "Read this load balancer config. List the algorithm, health check path, interval, thresholds and draining time. Point out anything that could keep a slow server in the pool." "Change our /health endpoint so it fails when the local disk or thread pool is unhealthy, but not when a shared database is slow. Explain each check." "Write a shutdown handler for this service: on SIGTERM, fail the health check, stop taking new requests, finish open ones within 30 seconds, then exit." What to ask the agent The health check is cheap and fast, and cannot overload the server itself. A shared dependency failure does not mark every server unhealthy at once. The draining delay in the load balancer matches the shutdown timeout in the app. Any change to sticky sessions or hashing was tested with servers added and removed. The agent did not invent config keys. Check them against the docs for your load balancer. What to check yourself Related lessons: DNS and service discovery, API gateways, Sharding and consistent hashing and Multi-region. How a cluster decides a node is dead, beyond simple health checks: Failure detection and membership.

title: Load shedding and graceful degradation
text: When more work arrives than you can finish, drop the least important part early and cheaply, so the important part still works.
body: In 2019, Netflix had an outage. A sizable share of members could not play for a period of time. Netflix lists many things that can overload its systems. A client bug can trigger a retry storm. A backend can be under-scaled. A deploy can be bad, or the network or cloud provider can have problems. Each of these had stopped members from playing at some point. At the time, Netflix had on/off circuit breakers. It had "no progressive way to shed load". So the team built one into Zuul, its API gateway. Each request gets a priority. When things go wrong, low-priority requests are dropped first. In 2020, days after the change went live, a similar problem hit. It had the same potential impact as the 2019 outage. This time Zuul shed traffic until the service was healthy again, "without impacting members' ability to play at all". The problem was just as serious. The difference was that the system chose what to drop. Every server has a limit. When more work arrives than it can finish, some work will fail. You cannot avoid that. You can only choose which work fails, and how. Without a plan, the server tries to do everything. Then nearly everything fails. With load shedding, the server rejects some requests early and finishes the rest in time. You already know rate limiting and circuit breakers and bulkheads. The difference matters: A rate limit is usually a fixed quota per client. It stops one client from taking more than its share. Load shedding is the server protecting itself. It looks at its own state, such as CPU or requests in flight, whoever the traffic comes from. Graceful degradation goes one step further. It cuts the work per request, for example by serving a slightly stale local copy of the data. The key idea. Overload means some work will fail. Decide in advance which work that is. Drop it early, cheaply and on purpose, so the important work still finishes in time. What overload does Step through a server under rising load. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. The trap is that the server looks busy and healthy. It finishes as many requests as ever. But the client has already timed out, so the work is wasted. Amazon calls the useful part goodput: requests handled without errors and fast enough to use. If median latency equals the client timeout, half the requests time out, so availability is 50%. The Tail latency and queueing lesson showed why queues explode near 100% busy. Load shedding is what you do about it. It lets a server "maintain its goodput". Shed early and cheaply A rejection must cost much less than real work. Amazon says early rejection "is the cheapest place to drop excess traffic". So check before you parse the body, open a transaction or call another service. Google warns that rejecting is not always cheap. For a simple memory lookup, rejecting costs almost as much as serving. Shedding has limits, so you still need capacity. A simple server-side signal is the number of requests in flight. Over a limit, return HTTP 503 to new requests. Google also uses CPU and rejects by criticality as use nears a threshold. Decide what to drop Not all requests are equal. Netflix sorts its traffic into three classes: NON_CRITICAL: logs and background requests. They do not affect playback, but they are a large share of load. DEGRADED_EXPERIENCE: features like viewing history and pause markers. Users notice, but can still play. CRITICAL: if this fails, the user sees an error when they press play. Zuul gives each request a score from 1 to 100 as its first step. Under overload it drops requests below a moving threshold. A cubic curve moves the threshold slowly at first, then sharply. At 35% overload the threshold is still in the mid-90s. At 80% it reaches 50. Google uses four levels: CRITICAL_PLUS, CRITICAL, SHEDDABLE_PLUS and SHEDDABLE. Amazon adds useful hints. The load balancer's health check is "the most important request" a server gets. Requests that finish work already started beat requests that start new work. In a shop, that could mean: payment and checkout first, product pages next, then prefetch, recommendations and batch jobs. Move batch work to a queue, so it can wait. Here is a sketch of a server-side check. Lower classes get lower limits, so they are shed first: LIMITS = {"critical": 200, "degraded": 150, "sheddable": 100} def admit(req, in_flight): if req.deadline_left_ms() <= 0: return reject(503) # the caller has given up if in_flight >= LIMITS[req.priority]: return reject(503, retry_after_s=5) return None # accept the requestDrop work nobody waits for A request whose caller has gone is pure waste. Amazon suggests clients send a timeout hint, so the server can "drop doomed requests at little cost". Google says to check the time left at each stage, before more work. You met deadline propagation in Backoff, jitter and retry budgets. Keep queues small. For steady traffic, Google suggests 50% of the thread pool size or less. Amazon also caps how long a request may wait in a queue. Queue order: controlled delay and adaptive LIFO Facebook found that "many of our worst incidents" had large numbers of requests waiting in queues. In 2015, Facebook described using two ideas together. Controlled delay, a variant of the CoDel algorithm from network research. If the queue has not been empty in the last 100 ms, a new request may wait only 5 ms. Otherwise it may wait up to 100 ms. Short bursts still queue, but a standing queue cannot form. Facebook found these values work well for most services, without tuning for each one. Adaptive LIFO. In a long queue, the oldest request's user may have already left. So the server uses FIFO normally, then switches to LIFO when a queue starts to form. The newest requests then have the best chance to finish in time. Clients can help: adaptive throttling A rejected request still costs the server something. So Google's clients throttle themselves. Google calls this adaptive throttling. Each client counts requests (attempts) and accepts (accepted by the backend) over the last 2 minutes. Once requests passes K times accepts, the client starts rejecting some new requests locally, without sending them. The chance grows as the backend accepts less: K = 2.0 # Google's usual choice def reject_chance(requests, accepts): # counts from the last 2 minutes; requests includes local rejects return max(0.0, (requests - K * accepts) / (requests + 1))A lower K throttles harder. Facebook's clients also cap requests in flight to each service and fail extra ones at once. Send the right signal Use 503 for "I am overloaded". It means a temporary overload, and the server may add Retry-After. Keep 429 for a client that sent too many requests, as in the rate limiting lesson. The signal must calm clients down, not cause a retry storm. When Zuul sheds, it tells devices how many retries they may make, and in what time window. Google advises not to retry when many backend tasks are overloaded. Let the error go back to the caller. Degrade gracefully Shedding drops whole requests. Degradation does less work per request. Google's examples: search a smaller in-memory set instead of the disk, or use a cheaper ranking. Its example service stops returning pictures and small maps when capacity runs short. Other choices: serve stale cached data, as in Caching and cache stampedes. Or turn off optional features with a kill switch. Degraded modes should rarely run. Exercise them anyway, and alert when many servers use them. Test it Amazon's rule is direct. If you have not load tested "far beyond the point where it breaks", expect the worst way of failing. The ideal result: goodput levels off near full use, instead of falling. Netflix also tests what users see when traffic is shed. In production experiments, a small group of users has a range of priorities throttled for 45 minutes. The first run found a race condition on Android and iOS, in a low-priority request that caused playback errors. Option Protects goodput? Cost Use it when No limit, unbounded FIFO queue No Goodput falls close to zero. Nothing until the spike. Never for user-facing services. Bounded queue, reject when full Yes, partly. Drops at random, not by importance. A first, simple step. In-flight limit per priority class Yes You must label every request and keep labels right. Mixed traffic, like checkout and prefetch. Deadline checks Yes Removes wasted work. Clients must send a deadline or timeout hint. Long call chains. Controlled delay + adaptive LIFO Yes Newer requests overtake older ones. Server queues under bursty load. Client adaptive throttling Yes Saves the cost of rejecting. Some requests fail without trying. Many clients call one backend. Graceful degradation Yes Less work per request. Users get less. Rare code paths can break. Optional parts of a response. Simple rule: a small bounded queue, an in-flight limit per priority class, and deadline checks. Add degradation for optional features, and test it all with load tests. Ask of every service: "At twice our peak, what fails first? Did we choose that?" Write down the priority class of each endpoint with the product owner. Payment is not the same as a recommendations widget. Watch goodput, not only throughput. Count requests that finished in time and without error, and tie it to your SLOs. Count shed requests by class and alert when critical traffic is shed. Load test past the breaking point before big events. Check that goodput levels off. Review client retry rules. They should honor Retry-After and stop when most calls fail. "Add an admission check to this service. Count requests in flight. Read a priority from the X-Priority header (critical, degraded, sheddable). Reject over a per-class limit with 503 and Retry-After, before parsing the body." "Propagate the client deadline through every call in this handler. Before each downstream call, drop the request if less than 50 ms is left." "Write a load test that ramps from 50% to 300% of measured capacity. Plot throughput, goodput and p99 latency per priority class." What to ask the agent The rejection happens before any expensive work: no body parsing, database call or downstream call. Shed requests get 503, and the client code honors Retry-After. Health checks are never shed. Every endpoint has a priority, and unknown traffic gets a low class, not critical. The load test shows checkout latency staying flat while low-priority traffic is shed. What to check yourself Related lessons: Rate limiting, Circuit breakers and bulkheads, Tail latency and queueing, Backoff, jitter and retry budgets and Caching and cache stampedes.

title: Mechanical sympathy: CPU caches and memory
text: The same loop can run ten times faster or slower depending on how its data sits in memory. Learn how CPU caches work, so you can lay out data the way the hardware likes it.
body: This is a made-up example. A team runs a Java service that counts events. One thread did all the counting. It was too slow, so they split the work across 4 threads. To avoid locks, each thread got its own counter. They used an AtomicLongArray of size 4. Thread 0 adds to slot 0, thread 1 to slot 1, and so on, once per event. The main thread sums the slots at the end. No thread touched another thread's counter. But with 4 threads, the job ran slower than with 1. The cause was not in the code. It was in the hardware. The four counters took 32 bytes, side by side. A CPU cache moves memory in blocks of 64 bytes on most machines. So the four counters shared one block, or at most two. Each write by one core took the block away from the other cores. The fix was to space the counters 128 bytes apart. The code did the same work, and now it scaled with the number of threads. Martin Thompson shows the same effect in a short Java benchmark. Mechanical sympathy means writing code that suits how the machine really works. Martin Thompson took the term from the racing driver Jackie Stewart. Stewart's point was that a great driver knows how the car works, not only how to steer it. For you, the "car" is the CPU and its memory. A modern CPU is very fast. Main memory is slow next to it. To hide that gap, the CPU keeps small, fast caches close to each core. The hardware decides what goes in the caches. But your data layout and access order decide whether they help or hurt. The key idea. Memory is not one flat, equal-speed array. Data that is close together and read in order is fast. Data that is scattered, or written by many cores at once, is slow. The same algorithm can run ten times faster or slower because of this. The memory hierarchy A CPU has several levels of cache. L1 is the smallest and fastest. L2 is bigger and slower. Many CPUs also add a third level, L3. Behind them all is main memory (DRAM). The table below is old. It shows Intel's figures for the Pentium M, a laptop CPU from the early 2000s, as given in Drepper's 2007 paper. Newer CPUs differ, so read them as orders of magnitude only.
