Where the data is About how long Register 1 cycle or less L1 data cache 3 cycles L2 cache 14 cycles Main memory 240 cycles This chip had no L3. Most CPUs today have an L3 between L2 and main memory. So a read from main memory can cost as much as about 80 reads from L1. The latency numbers lesson puts a main memory read at about 100 ns. Cache lines The cache does not load single bytes. It loads a whole cache line. Early caches used 32-byte lines. The norm is now 64 bytes. Some CPUs use 128 bytes, such as Apple's M1. When you read one 8-byte long, you also get the 56 bytes around it. This rewards spatial locality: data you use together should sit together. It also rewards temporal locality: data you used a moment ago is probably still in the cache. Prefetching: why sequential beats random When you read memory in order, the CPU notices. It loads the next cache line before you ask for it. This is hardware prefetching. Walking an array has a fixed stride, so the CPU can predict it. Drepper measured this on a Pentium 4. He walked a large list of small elements, bigger than every cache. In memory order, each element cost about 9 cycles, thanks to prefetching and because 8 elements fit in one line. In random order, it cost 450 cycles and more. That is about 50 times slower, for the same work. Arrays versus linked structures A linked list, tree or hash map with chained nodes puts each node somewhere in memory. To find the next node, the CPU must first load the current one. This is pointer chasing. The CPU cannot fetch ahead, because it does not know the next address yet. The Disruptor paper says this can make memory access "more than 2 orders of magnitude less efficient". That is one reason the LMAX team built the Disruptor on a pre-allocated ring buffer, not a linked list. Array of structs versus struct of arrays A worked example: say each Order object has 10 fields, about 80 bytes. A report sums only price. With an array of Order objects, each 64-byte line brings in at most one price. The other 56 bytes are wasted. In Java, an array of objects holds references, so each item also costs a pointer hop. Now store each field in its own array: double[] prices, long[] ids, and so on. One line now holds 8 prices. The loop touches about 8 times fewer lines. This is a struct of arrays. Drepper gives a related example. A loop needs only two fields of an order struct, but the other fields are loaded too. He says the program could run "up to 5 times worse than it could". His advice is to split the struct. The order of the loop matters as much as the layout. In Drepper's matrix multiplication, changing the order of memory reads alone cut the run time to 23.4% of the original. With blocking and vector instructions too, it reached about 10%. That is a ten-times gain with the same maths. False sharing and padding Step through the bug from the story. Each core can keep its own copy of a cache line in its cache. Before a core writes to a line, the other cores' copies are marked invalid. So if two threads write two different variables in one line, the line moves between the cores on every write. This is false sharing. The fix is padding: unused bytes that push hot variables onto separate lines. The JDK pads by 128 bytes by default, not 64. In the story, the fix looks like this: // 16 longs = 128 bytes between slots; the first block stays empty AtomicLongArray counts = new AtomicLongArray((threads + 2) * 16); // thread i: counts.incrementAndGet((i + 1) * 16)A Java array is not aligned to a cache line. Slot 0 sits next to the array header, so the code leaves the first block empty. The JDK uses an internal annotation for this, @Contended. Its docs warn that it "will nearly always add significant space overhead to objects". By default, the JVM obeys it only in trusted JDK classes. Your own code needs the flag -XX:-RestrictContended. In everyday Java, use LongAdder for a shared counter. It keeps a table of counter cells, each padded with @Contended. Branch prediction and NUMA, briefly CPUs "invest heavily in branch prediction". They guess which way an if will go and start work early. A wrong guess wastes that work. If a branch goes one way or the other at random, the CPU often guesses wrong, and a hot loop slows down. Large servers have several CPU sockets, each with its own memory. This is NUMA. Reading memory attached to another socket costs more. In Drepper's test, reading memory one hop away was about 20% slower. Bigger machines have more hops, so the cost can be higher. Measure, do not guess Count the events with perf stat. Brendan Gregg shows commands such as: perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-references,cache-misses ./appWith cycles and instructions, perf also prints instructions per cycle (IPC). Low IPC with many cache misses usually means the CPU is waiting for memory. Many hardware counters may not be available inside a virtual machine. Compare layouts with a real benchmark harness: JMH for Java , or Criterion.rs for Rust. JMH's own README says a good harness does not free you from benchmarking pitfalls. Choice Good for Cost Watch out for Array, read in order Fast scans. The CPU prefetches. Inserting in the middle is slow. Fixed size or costly resizing. Linked list or tree Cheap inserts and deletes. Pointer chasing. Each step may wait for memory. Fine for small or cold data. Struct of arrays Loops that read a few fields of many items. Code is harder to read. One item is spread across arrays. Only worth it on hot loops you measured. Padding hot fields Stops false sharing between threads. More memory per object. Pad only fields that different threads write often. Ignore layout Simple, readable code. Can be many times slower on hot paths. Fine for most code. Measure first. Ask "is this on the hot path?" first. Most code is not. Do not trade clarity for cache tricks there. Run perf stat on the real workload before you change layout. Check cache misses and IPC. When adding threads makes a job slower, suspect false sharing. Look for counters, flags or indexes that different threads write, sitting side by side. In Java, try LongAdder for hot shared counters before you pad an array by hand. Prefer arrays for big collections you scan often. For big scans, ask which fields the loop really reads. Move cold fields to a separate object. Prove each change with a benchmark on hardware like production. "Here is our hot loop and the class it reads. List each field the loop uses. Suggest a layout that puts those fields in fewer cache lines, and explain the trade-off." "Write a JMH benchmark that compares an array of objects with a struct of arrays for summing one field over 10 million items. Include warm-up and use a Blackhole." What to ask the agent Every speed claim the agent makes is backed by a benchmark you ran, not by reasoning alone. The benchmark uses JMH or criterion, with warm-up and several runs. A loop timed with System.nanoTime() is not enough. Any padding uses at least 128 bytes between hot fields, like the JDK default, and is limited to fields that really cause contention. What to check yourself OS essentials for backend engineers Tail latency and queueing Latency numbers and back-of-envelope maths Locks, atomics and deadlocks Next on this track: lock-free programming and memory models, and the LMAX Disruptor and the single-writer rule.

title: Mentoring and sponsorship
text: Grow other engineers by asking more than you tell, and use your name to open doors for them.
body: This story is made up, but it happens on many teams. Meera was the senior engineer everyone asked. Karan, a new engineer on her team, asked her about ten questions a day. She was kind and fast. She would roll her chair over, take the keyboard and fix the problem in two minutes. Karan shipped a lot. In his first six months, he merged more pull requests than anyone else. Meera thought she was a good mentor. Then Meera took two weeks of leave. The payment retry job Karan "owned" started to send double emails. Karan opened the code. Most of the tricky parts were lines Meera had typed. He did not know why they were there. The fix took him three days, and he was afraid to touch the code the whole time. At her own review, Meera's manager asked one question: "Who can do your work when you are away?" She had no good answer. She had helped Karan finish tasks. She had not helped him grow. There are three different ways to help someone grow. Neha Batra, a former engineering leader at GitHub, gives short definitions: Mentoring is sharing your own experience, so the engineer can use it. Coaching is "asking the right questions to help an engineer reach a solution that works for them". Sponsoring is "giving stretch projects or opportunities to help an engineer grow". Most of us only give advice, because it is quick. Sponsorship is the one people forget. Lara Hogan describes it as feeling "on the hook" to help someone get promoted. She adds that it "is not just giving advice and mentorship". She writes that what people from groups that are less represented in tech often need most is "opportunity and visibility, not advice". Batra calls failing to sponsor "the biggest missed opportunity in leadership". The key idea. Advice helps someone finish today's task. Questions help them think on their own. Sponsorship gives them a chance to show what they can do. A good mentor uses all three. Step through one full mentoring cycle with Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Run 1:1s the mentee owns A 1:1 is a regular private talk between two people. Meet every week or two. Let the mentee bring the list of topics. If they come with nothing, that is a sign to ask more, not to fill the time with your stories. (This is our advice.) A simple way to start is to ask, "What do you think?" Batra used this question when she first added coaching to her 1:1s. Her article gives more examples. One is "What do you think you're doing well in and what do you think needs improvement?" Another is "Given your past few projects, what did you learn that could help someone like you six months ago?" Ask before you answer When your mentee is stuck, try questions first: "What did you expect to happen, and what happened?" "What have you ruled out?" "Where would you look next, and why?" Give the answer when time is short, the risk is high, or the mentee is upset. Batra says she leans toward mentoring, not coaching, when time, connection or trust are low. Google's review guide makes the same point about code. Pointing out a problem and letting the developer decide "often helps the developer learn". But sometimes direct instructions or even code are more helpful. Give feedback with SBI The Center for Creative Leadership teaches the SBI model. Situation. Say when and where. "In this morning's design review…" Behaviour. Describe what the person did that you could see or hear, with no judgement. "You interrupted me", not "You were rude". Impact. Say what it caused. CCL adds a fourth step: ask about intent. "What were you hoping to accomplish with that?" This turns feedback into a conversation. Your guess about why they did it may be wrong. Radical Candor gives one more test: care personally and challenge directly, at the same time. Its name for feedback that is kind but never honest is "ruinous empathy". Holding back a hard truth to be nice does not help anyone grow. Praise counts as feedback too. Google's guide says it is sometimes more valuable for mentoring to tell a developer what they did right. Use SBI for praise as well, so the person knows exactly what to repeat. Delegate stretch work with a safety net A stretch assignment is work just above someone's current level. It can help someone grow fast, but it is also an easy way to fail in public. So build a safety net before you hand it over (this list is our advice): Agree on the goal and the limits. What does "done" mean? What may they decide alone? Set check-in points. For example, review the design before any code, and review the rollout plan before launch. Keep it reversible. Ship behind a feature flag, so a mistake can be turned off. Say when to call you. "If customer data might be wrong, call me at once." Do not take the keyboard. If they go the wrong way, ask a question. Step in only to prevent real harm. Use pairing and review to teach Pairing works best when the mentee types and you talk. If you type, they only watch. (This is our advice.) Code review is also a teaching tool. Google's guide says a secondary goal of review is "improving the skills of developers so that they require less and less review over time". For how to review well, see Reviewing human and AI code. Write it down once If three people ask you the same question, write the answer down. Next time, send a link and spend your time on the follow-up questions. One page can help many people at once, including people you will never meet. (This is our advice. See Clear technical writing.) Why this counts for your level Career ladders write this down as an expectation. Dropbox's IC3 and IC4 levels both say: "I actively level up less-experienced members of my team by helping them with their craft." IC3 also says: "I actively look for opportunities to mentor new hires, interns and apprentices." CircleCI writes that as engineers grow, their focus shifts "from execution to include facilitating, guiding, and mentoring others". So growing others is part of the job at senior level, not extra work. See What senior really means. Way to help Fast today? Builds independence? Best when Give the answer (mentoring) Yes The task moves at once. No, not on its own. Time is short, risk is high, or the mentee is new to the topic. Ask questions (coaching) No It takes longer. Yes They learn to find answers. Trust is strong and the cost of a slow answer is low. Sponsor them No Results take months. Yes They get real chances and visibility. They are close to ready for the next level. Take over the work Yes No It teaches them to wait for you. Only in a live incident with real customer harm. Simple rule: answer the question, but ask one question back each time. Before you answer, ask: "Do they need the answer, or do they need to learn to find it?" Keep a short note per mentee: their goal, the last feedback you gave, and the next stretch task. In each 1:1, let them set the agenda. Ask at least one open question before you give advice. Give feedback within a day or two, using situation, behaviour and impact. Ask about intent before you decide why. Sponsor in small ways every week. Name your mentee when work is assigned. Ask them to present their own project. Credit them by name in public. When you get the same question twice, write the answer down and share the link. Ask yourself every quarter: who can run each system I own when I am away? If the answer is "nobody", start there. Juniors can now ship working code with an agent before they understand it. That makes mentoring more important. Anthropic ran a randomized study with 52 mostly junior engineers learning a new Python library. The group with AI help scored 50% on a quiz afterwards. The group without AI scored 67%. The biggest gap was in debugging. People who asked the AI for explanations or concepts scored 65% or more. People who handed over the work scored under 40%. These groups were tiny, and the authors say the patterns do not prove cause. The sample was small and the quiz came right after the task. The authors advise managers to build in "systems or intentional design choices that ensure engineers continue to learn as they work". For a mentor, that means: Ask your mentee to explain their agent's diff, line by line, before you review it. For some tasks, ask them to write and debug the code first, then compare with the agent. Review their prompts and plans, not only their code. See Working with coding agents. "I am mentoring a junior engineer on this pull request. List three questions I could ask them that would help them find the bugs themselves. Do not tell me the bugs." "Turn these notes from a 1:1 into feedback using situation, behaviour and impact. Remove any judgement words and keep it under 100 words." "My mentee keeps asking how our deploy works. Draft a one-page guide from this pipeline file, and list anything you are unsure about." What to ask the agent The feedback describes behaviour you saw yourself. An agent cannot know what happened in the room. The questions fit this person. You know their level, and the agent does not. Every fact in the drafted guide is true for your system. Test the steps before you share it. The sponsorship is real. Only you can say a name in the meeting where work is assigned. What to check yourself Before this: What senior really means. Next: Influence without authority and Getting promoted.

title: Money and double-entry ledgers
text: Why money must never be a float, and how a ledger where every entry sums to zero keeps every rupee accounted for.
body: This story is made up, but each part of it happens in real companies. A small wallet app gives users cashback. Each user has one row in a table with a balance column of type float. Every payment runs balance = balance + amount. For months it looks fine. Then the finance team adds up all user balances and compares the total with the money in the bank. The numbers do not match. They are off by ₹38,412.07. The team looks for the cause and finds three problems. Small float errors on millions of cashback payments do not add up to clean paise. A retry bug added some cashback twice. And one engineer fixed a support ticket by changing a balance by hand. Nobody can say which part of the ₹38,412.07 came from which problem. The table only holds the current balance. It has no history. The money is gone from the records, and so is the story of how it moved. Two rules prevent almost all of this. Rule one: never store money as a float. A float stores numbers as binary fractions. Most decimal amounts, like 0.1, cannot be written exactly in binary. So 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1 == 0.3 is false in Python and most other languages. The error is tiny, but money systems add millions of numbers, and the errors stay. Instead, store money as an integer in minor units. A minor unit is the smallest unit of a currency: paise for rupees, cents for dollars. ₹10.50 becomes 1050. Stripe's API works this way: you send 1000 to charge 10 US dollars. Another option is an exact decimal type, like NUMERIC in Postgres or Decimal in Python. Python's docs suggest its decimal module for accounting. Always keep the currency next to the amount. 1050 means nothing without "INR". And currencies differ. The official ISO 4217 list says the Indian rupee has 2 decimal places, the Japanese yen has 0, and the Kuwaiti dinar has 3. Rule two: record every movement of money as double-entry. Money never appears or disappears. It always moves from somewhere to somewhere. So every movement is written as at least two entries: one that takes money out of an account and one that puts it into another. In this lesson we write money leaving an account as minus and money arriving as plus. Accountants call the two sides debit and credit. Which side means "more" depends on the type of account. The rule that matters is the same in both styles: the entries of one transaction must sum to zero. The key idea. Never change a balance directly. Write balanced entries that never change, and calculate every balance from those entries. Step through a ₹1,000 card payment to a shop, with a ₹20 platform fee. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. A ledger has three parts: Accounts. One for each place money can sit: a customer, a merchant, your fee income, money held for a short time. Entries. One line each: account, amount in minor units, currency, and a sign. Transactions. A group of entries that happen together and sum to zero. Many teams also call this a journal entry. Entries never change The ledger is append-only. You add new entries. You never update or delete old ones. Square's ledger, Books, works this way: its entries are effectively append-only and immutable once stored. Stripe describes its Ledger as "an immutable log of events". So how do you fix a mistake? You post a reversal: a new transaction with the same entries and opposite signs. Then you post the correct one. TigerBeetle, a ledger database, follows the same rule: once transfers are recorded, they cannot be erased. The wrong entry stays in the history, next to its fix. An auditor can see what happened, when, and why. Martin Fowler notes that some systems let an entry change while it is still "open", then lock it once it is booked. Payment systems often use the same idea as pending and posted entries. Balances come from entries A balance is the sum of all entries for one account. Square describes a balance as "essentially summing up all of the changes" to that account. Summing millions of rows on every read is slow, so real systems also store a cached balance. They update it in the same database transaction as the new entries. The entries stay the truth. If the cache is ever wrong, you rebuild it from the entries. Retries must not post twice A ledger has the same retry problem as a payment API. If the "post transaction" call times out and the caller retries, you can post the same money twice. Give every ledger transaction a unique key from the event that caused it, such as the payment id. Make that key unique in the database, so a repeat is rejected. This is the idea from Idempotency, retries and timeouts, applied to money. Reconciliation: check against the outside world Your ledger can be perfectly balanced and still be wrong. It may miss a payment that the bank processed. Reconciliation means you regularly compare your ledger with outside records, such as bank statements and payment provider reports. Every difference is a missing, late or wrong entry that someone must explain. Stripe uses a neat trick inside its ledger. Money that is "on the way" sits in a clearing account. When all steps finish, that account should go back to zero. A balance that is not zero points to a missing, late or wrong transaction. Stripe also checks that every id in the source systems has a matching ledger event. Rounding Integers do not remove rounding. They make it visible. Split ₹100.00 between three people and you get 3,333 paise each, with 1 paisa left over. Decide where the leftover goes, for example to the first person, and write it as an entry. Pick one rounding rule and use it everywhere. A common choice is "round half to even": a tie goes to the nearest even digit. It is the default in Python's Decimal. Write it down in the code, not in someone's head. Approach Exact? Cost Use it when Float for amounts No Small errors build up. Easy at first, painful later. Never for money. Fine for charts and estimates. Integer minor units + currency Yes You must know each currency's decimal places and convert for display. Most payment and wallet systems. Simple and fast. Decimal type (NUMERIC, Decimal) Yes, if you create it from strings, not floats. Slower, and every language handles it a bit differently. You need fractions of a minor unit, like interest or FX rates. One balance column, updated in place No history, so you cannot prove it. Cheap to build. Toy projects only. Double-entry ledger, balances derived Yes, and every change is explained. More rows, more design work, and busy accounts can slow writes. Any system that holds or moves real money. Simple rule: integers in minor units with a currency code, in an append-only, double-entry ledger. Add a cached balance only when reads get slow. One cost needs a warning. Some accounts, like the platform's own fee account, appear in almost every transaction. Many writes then wait on the same balance row. Modern Treasury calls this the "hot account" problem, and handles it by batching entries for that account. This breaks the same-transaction rule on purpose. The cached balance can be a little behind: Modern Treasury targets 60 seconds. In practice, nine in ten entries are processed within 1 second. In design reviews, search for float and double near any money field. Ask: "Where is the currency?" Ask: "Where does this money come from, and where does it go?" If nobody can name both accounts, the design is not ready. Add a check in code that refuses any transaction whose entries do not sum to zero. Treat a failure as a bug, never as a warning. Ban UPDATE and DELETE on the entries table. Use database permissions, not only a team rule. Give every ledger transaction a unique key from the event that caused it, so retries cannot post twice. Run reconciliation every day. Give every difference an owner and a deadline. Keep accounts that should return to zero, like money that has been sent but has not arrived yet. Alert when they do not return to zero. Use the same pattern for things that are not money: reward points, credits, gift cards, even stock in a warehouse. "Search this codebase for money stored or calculated as float or double. List every place, with the file and line, and how you would change it to integer minor units." "Write a property-based test: generate random ledger transactions and assert that every posted transaction sums to zero, and that every account balance equals the sum of its entries." "Split ₹100.00 between 3, 7 and 9 people. Show the paise each person gets, and prove that nothing is lost or created." What to ask the agent Amounts are integers or exact decimals in every layer: database, code, API and JSON. A float in the middle breaks the whole chain. Decimal values are created from strings, not from floats. The currency travels with every amount, and the code uses each currency's correct decimal places. The agent did not add an UPDATE to "fix" a balance. Fixes are new entries. The entries and the cached balance change in the same database transaction (except for hot accounts, as above). Tests cover a retry of the same transaction and a split with a leftover paisa. What to check yourself Next on this line: Reconciliation and The payment lifecycle. If you have not read it yet: Idempotency, retries and timeouts. For a ledger stored as a stream of events, see Event-driven architecture and event sourcing.

title: Monolith, modular monolith or microservices
text: Microservices let teams ship on their own, but every network call has a cost. Learn what each style buys, what it costs, and why a modular monolith is often the best start.
body: This story is made up, but the pattern is common. A shop has one large app and 40 engineers. Deploys queue up, and one team's bug can block everyone's release. So the company decides to "move to microservices". In six months, the app becomes nine services. But the services still read and write the same database tables. A new checkout feature needs changes in five services. The five teams must deploy them in the right order, on the same night. Then a customer is charged, but gets no order. The request crossed four services. Each one has its own logs, and nothing ties them together. It takes two days to find a timeout between two of them. The team kept the old pain, the shared release. They added new pain: network calls, partial failures and lost traces. They split the code, but not the ownership or the data. A monolith is one application that you build and deploy as one unit. Lewis and Fowler point to two limits. Change cycles are tied together, so a small change means you build and deploy the whole app. And you must scale the whole app, not just the part that needs more resources. Microservices build one application as a set of small services. Each service can be deployed and scaled on its own. A modular monolith sits between them. Shopify describes it as one application in which "there are strictly enforced boundaries between different domains". You get clear parts, but still one deploy. The key idea. Microservices mostly buy independence for teams: each team deploys and scales its part on its own. You pay for it with network calls, data spread across databases and more to run. Pay only when the independence is worth more than the cost. What microservices cost Step through one order request in both styles. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Network calls. A function call in memory becomes a request over the network. Shopify lists this as one reason they did not pick microservices. Network calls add latency and reduce reliability. Lewis and Fowler say services must be designed to cope when other services fail. So every call needs a timeout, retries and idempotency. Data and transactions. Each service usually owns its data. Lewis and Fowler write that distributed transactions "are notoriously difficult to implement". So microservice systems tend to accept eventual consistency and fix problems with compensating operations. In practice, that means sagas, outbox and CDC. Running it. Fowler calls this the "microservice premium". The style adds cost and risk that "often gets projects into serious trouble". You need deployment automation, monitoring, failure handling and a way to deal with eventual consistency. Shopify also lists a test and deploy pipeline for each service, and infrastructure for each one. Large changes across services need coordinated deploys. To follow one request across services, you also need good observability, with traces that cross every hop. Conway's law In 1968, Melvin Conway argued that organisations which design systems are "constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations". This is Conway's law. Lewis and Fowler give an example. When teams are split by technical layer, such as UI, server and database, even simple changes become projects across teams. They call this "Conway's Law in action". Their answer is cross-functional teams and services organised around business capabilities. Our advice: draw the team chart next to the service map. If one team owns six services, it gets all the costs and little of the independence. If one service needs three teams to change it, its boundary is wrong. The lesson on team topologies and Conway's law goes deeper. The modular monolith: a common middle path Shopify runs "one of the largest Ruby on Rails codebases in existence". More than a thousand developers have worked on it for over a decade. They judged that microservices "would bring their own set of challenges". So they kept one app and changed how the code was organised. They moved from folders by software type (models, views, controllers) to components by business area, such as orders, shipping, inventory and billing. A tool records the calls made while tests run in CI. An internal tool called Wedge uses this data to flag calls that cross component boundaries. Calls are allowed only to things a component makes public. Fowler gives the same default. Do not even consider microservices unless the system is too complex to manage as a monolith. Build most systems as one application with good internal modularity. Monolith first, then the strangler fig Fowler noticed that "almost all the successful microservice stories have started with a monolith that got too big and was broken up". Systems built as microservices from scratch often "ended up in serious trouble". One reason: even experienced architects find it hard to get boundaries right at the start. He also notes that this view is not shared by everyone. When it is time to split, do not rewrite everything at once. Fowler's strangler fig approach grows the new system around the old one. You add new parts next to the old code, then move behaviour across one piece at a time. Each step is small, so the risk is lower and value arrives sooner. Sam Newman's book covers this pattern, and how to split the database when you break up a monolith. It also asks a harder question: should you migrate at all? Going back is allowed In 2023, a Prime Video team wrote about a monitoring service built from distributed serverless parts. The way the team used some components hit a hard scaling limit at about 5% of the expected load. Its orchestration and the data passed between parts cost the most. The team moved all the parts into one process, so data moved in memory. The infrastructure cost of this one service fell by over 90%. The post adds that the choice between microservices and a monolith "has to be made on a case-by-case basis". Segment had over 140 small services. Three full-time engineers spent most of their time keeping the system running. They merged the services into one. Deploys and tests became much faster. The post is honest about the cost: one bad part can now crash the whole service. When to split, and signs you split too early Our rules for when one part should become its own service: A separate team owns it, and the shared release truly blocks that team. It needs very different scaling, hardware or reliability from the rest. Its boundary is already clean inside the modular monolith, with few calls across it. Signs you split too early: Most features change several services, which must deploy together. Services share database tables. You have more services than teams. Nobody can follow one request from end to end. Option Independent deploys? Main cost Use it when Monolith No Change cycles are tied together. Shared release. You scale all of it. A small team, a new product, a domain still being learned. Modular monolith No, but teams work in clear parts. You must check the boundaries, for example with a CI tool. The default for most growing teams. Microservices Yes Each can deploy and scale on its own. Network calls, no shared transactions, more to run. Many teams that block each other, or parts with very different needs. Services with shared tables and lockstep deploys No All the costs of microservices, with few of the gains. Never on purpose. Merge back or fix the boundary. When someone says "let's use microservices", ask: "Which team will deploy on its own because of this, and what does it stop waiting for?" Start with a modular monolith. Make each module own its tables, and check the boundaries in CI. Before you extract a service, count the calls across that boundary. If it is chatty, it is not ready. Split one service at a time, with the strangler fig approach. Keep a way to send traffic back. Give each service one owning team. More services than teams is a warning. Budget the premium: tracing, dashboards, on-call, a pipeline for each service, and a plan for data that crosses services. "Here is our module list and the calls between modules from the last month. Group modules that call each other a lot. Suggest boundaries where cross-module calls are rare." "We want to extract the Payments module into a service. List every database table it reads or writes that other modules also use, and every call into it. What must change first?" "Act as a skeptical staff engineer. Argue against splitting this app into services. What new failures and costs would we take on?" What to ask the agent The call data is real, from traces or code analysis, not guessed by the agent. Every table in the split plan has one owner. No two services write the same table. Every new network call has a timeout, a retry rule and an idempotency key where it changes data. The plan says which team owns each new service, and who is on call for it. Claims about a tool's limits come from its official docs. What to check yourself Before this: domain-driven design. Next: evolutionary architecture and the strangler fig, sagas, outbox and CDC, and making architecture trade-offs.

title: Multi-region systems and data locality
text: A second region buys speed, survival and legal room. You pay in money, in lag between copies, and in a failover you must practise.
body: On 2 November 2023, between 11:44 and 12:01 UTC, a data centre near Hillsboro, Oregon, lost all power. It was called PDX-04. Cloudflare ran its control plane (the dashboard and APIs) and analytics mainly across three data centres in that area. They were built so that the control plane would keep running if any one of them failed. In Cloudflare's words, "The three data centers are independent of one another". The buildings were independent. Some of the software was not. Some services that were meant to survive still used Kafka and ClickHouse clusters that ran only in PDX-04. Some services, mostly for newer products, had not moved to the shared, highly available setup yet. At 13:40 UTC the team chose to fail over to its disaster recovery sites in Europe. The first services came up 3 minutes later. Then the API calls that had been failing all arrived at once, so the team added rate limits. A few newer products did not start properly in Europe. The services that did move were stable by 17:57 UTC. But some log processing stayed down, and every service was back only on 4 November. Two lines from the report stand out. "Throughout the incident, Cloudflare's network and security services continued to work as expected." And: "we had never tested fully taking the entire PDX-04 facility offline." The traffic part was spread across the world. The control part was not. A cloud region is a group of data centres in one area, such as Mumbai or Frankfurt. Running in more than one region gives you three things: Speed. Users near a region get faster answers. Survival. If a whole region fails, another can serve. Data residency. Some laws say certain data must stay in a country. A later lesson on privacy covers this. The price is real. You run and pay for two or more copies of everything. Each copy of the data lags behind the others. And the failover that should save you is a rare, risky event that nobody has practised. The key idea. The network between regions is slow, and sometimes it breaks. So for each piece of data, decide which region owns its writes, and what users see while the copies disagree. The speed-of-light floor ITU's planning value for optical fibre is 5 µs per km, one way. That works out to about 200 km per millisecond. So every 100 km of cable adds about 1 ms to a round trip. No code change can beat this. Real paths are longer than a straight line. Azure publishes measured median round-trip times between its regions. These are for the 30 days to 30 July 2026, in both directions: Region Region Median round trip East US East US 2 8–9 ms East US West US 67–69 ms Central India Southeast Asia 53 ms East US West Europe 83–85 ms Central India West Europe 139–140 ms Central India East US 198–201 ms These are medians. Your slow requests pay more. Now count the round trips. A page that makes 3 database calls in a row, from India to US East, waits about 600 ms before it does any work. Cross-region calls must be few, and never inside a loop. Active-passive or active-active In active-passive, one region serves all traffic. The other keeps a copy of the data and waits. Failover is simple to reason about, but you pay for a region that does little, and you only learn if it works on the bad day. In active-active, every region serves users all the time. Each region is tested by real traffic every day. But now writes can happen in two places, and you must handle conflicts. The disaster recovery lesson lists the steps in between, like pilot light and warm standby. Routing users to a region DNS is the usual tool. Amazon Route 53, for example, can answer with the region that gives the best latency, by the user's location, or by a failover rule that switches from active to passive. DNS answers are cached, so some clients keep using the old region for a while after a change. Anycast is the other tool: many sites announce one IP address, and the network picks the nearest. See load balancing for how it works. A CDN uses the same idea to serve cached files near users. Where the writes go This is the hard part. You have four main choices. One writer region, read copies elsewhere. Aurora Global Database has one primary region for writes and up to 10 read-only regions. Copies are typically under a second behind. Reads are local and fast. Writes from far away pay the long round trip. All the lag bugs from replication come back, now with bigger numbers. A home region per user or tenant. Each user's data lives in one region, often the one nearest to them. All their writes go there. A user in Delhi writes to Mumbai. A user in Berlin writes to Frankfurt. No row has two writers, so there are no conflicts. The cost: you need a lookup from user to region, and moving a user is a data migration. The multi-tenancy lesson shows the same idea with cells. Many writers, conflicts resolved later. DynamoDB global tables accept writes in every region. In the default mode, changes reach other regions "typically within a second or less". If two regions change the same item at once, the one with the latest internal timestamp wins. AWS calls this "last writer wins". The other write is silently gone. Other surprises follow. A strongly consistent read may return stale data if the item last changed in another region. A conditional write checks only the local copy. A transaction is atomic only in the region that ran it. One logical database with cross-region quorums. DynamoDB also has a strong mode. It runs in exactly three regions: three copies, or two copies and a "witness" that only votes. Each write is copied to at least one other region before it returns. Spanner works in a similar way. Each write needs a majority of five voting copies, one of them in the leader region, so every write crosses at least two regions. No write is silently lost. In DynamoDB, a write that clashes with one in another region fails and must be retried. Every write waits for regions to talk. Spanner advises putting write-heavy work in or near the leader region. This is the PACELC trade, paid on every write. Conflicts in active-active Picture a stock count of 5. A buyer in Mumbai takes 1 and writes 4. At the same moment, a buyer in Singapore takes 1 and writes 4. With last write wins, the final count is 4, but two items left the shelf. Neither region saw an error. The quorums lesson explains why timestamps make this worse when clocks drift. There are three common fixes. Send all writes for one item to one region. Store changes, like "minus 1", that can be added up in any order. Or use the strong mode for the few items that need it. Failing over and failing back Step through a region failover. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Aurora's docs show the real costs. An unplanned failover "can result in a loss of write transaction data" that had not been copied yet. The RPO is "typically measured in seconds". Aurora tries to stop writes in the old region, but this is best effort. Writes may still land there, which gives split-brain. So Aurora asks you to take apps offline first, and to keep DNS cache times short, such as 5 seconds. Failing back is a separate step. With a managed failover, Aurora adds the old region back as a copy. It first tries to snapshot the old data, so you can look for lost writes. Copy that snapshot if you need it longer than the backup retention period. Later you run a switchover, which waits until the copies match, so no data is lost. Capacity matters too. The surviving region must take all the traffic, plus a burst of retries. Cloudflare hit this. When its services came up in Europe, the API calls that had been failing all arrived at once, and it had to add rate limits. Keep regions from sharing fate Regions only help if they fail alone. A global control plane can tie them together without anyone noticing. AWS says some global services have their control plane in one region, while their data plane runs everywhere. IAM, Route 53 and CloudFront have their control planes in us-east-1. AWS advises you to keep these control planes out of your recovery path, so that recovery uses only data plane actions. It calls this being statically stable. Shared data can do the same. In June 2025, Google Cloud's Service Control ran in each region, with its own regional datastore. But a bad quota policy "was replicated globally within seconds", and the crash spread with it. Copy config and policy to one region at a time, as safe deploys explains. Design Conflicts? Write latency Data lost on region failure Use it when One writer region, read copies No Far users pay a long round trip. Yes The last seconds of async writes. Most apps that go global first for reads or survival. Home region per user or tenant No Each row has one writer. Low for users near home. Yes, for that region's recent writes. Users or tenants map cleanly to a place. Many writers, last write wins Yes One write is dropped. Low everywhere. Small. Seconds of writes not yet copied. Data where losing one of two writes at once is fine, like settings or sessions. Cross-region quorum (Spanner, strong mode) No silent conflicts. A clashing write fails and you retry. Higher. Every write waits for other regions. How much depends on how far apart they are. No Money, stock and unique names, and you accept slower writes. Simple rule: start with one writer region and read copies. Move to home regions when far users complain about write speed. Allow many writers only for data you have checked can lose a write. Ask first: "Which problem are we solving: speed, survival or law?" Each one leads to a different design. For every table, write down which region owns its writes and what a conflict does. Count cross-region round trips per request, and multiply by the real numbers for your regions. Run a failover drill each quarter. Turn off each whole site or region in a test, not one server. Cloudflare had switched off its other two sites in tests, but never the whole of PDX-04, the one that failed. Before a drill, check that the standby region has quotas and capacity for full load, plus retries. List every dependency your failover runbook calls. Remove any that run in only one region. Alert on replication lag between regions. It is your RPO, moving in real time. "Here is our request handler and its database calls. Our users are in India and our database is in US East. Count the sequential cross-region round trips per request, and estimate the latency with a 200 ms round trip." "We use DynamoDB global tables in two regions. List every write in this service that could conflict if two regions change the same item, and say what last-writer-wins would drop." "Write a failover runbook for our Aurora global database. Fence writes first, then fail over, then update DNS. Mark every step that calls a control plane in another region." What to ask the agent The latency numbers come from your provider's measured tables, not a guess. The runbook fences the old writer before it promotes the new one. No step in the recovery path needs a console or API that lives only in the failed region. Any code that checks then writes, like "is stock above zero?", runs in one region only. The test really cuts a whole region, including its queues and caches. What to check yourself Before this: Database replication and CAP, PACELC and consistency models. Related lessons: Disaster recovery and backups, Quorums and leaderless replication, DNS and service discovery and CDN and HTTP caching. DynamoDB global tables in more detail: DynamoDB in depth. Case study: the Cloudflare outage.

title: Multi-tenancy and noisy neighbours
text: Many customers share one system. Learn to keep their data apart and stop one busy customer from slowing down everyone else.
body: This story is made up, but it is common. A small company sells invoicing software to 400 businesses. All of them share one set of app servers and one Postgres database. This is cheap and easy to run. On the last day of the year, the biggest customer starts a full export of five years of invoices. It runs as hundreds of heavy queries at once. The database CPU goes to 100%. Every other customer now waits 20 seconds to open an invoice. Support gets messages from 399 businesses that did nothing wrong. The on-call engineer sees "database slow" on the dashboard, but nothing says which customer is causing it. It takes an hour to find the export and stop it. Then a second question comes: "Could a slow query ever return another customer's invoices?" Nobody is sure. Every query has WHERE tenant_id = ?, but only because developers remembered to add it. A tenant is one customer organisation, such as one company. Multi-tenancy means one running system serves many tenants. The tenants share code, servers and often databases, but each must feel like it has the system to itself. You must keep tenants apart in two ways: Data. A tenant must never see another tenant's data. A 2020 AWS whitepaper calls crossing this line "a significant and potentially un-recoverable event" for a SaaS (software as a service) business. Performance. One tenant must not make the system slow for the rest. This is the noisy neighbour problem: one user puts so much load on shared resources that other users suffer. The key idea. Sharing makes SaaS cheap. Every shared thing is also a path for a leak or a slowdown. Decide what to share on purpose, and isolate each shared thing. Silo, pool and bridge AWS names three models. Silo model. Each tenant gets its own resources, such as its own database or even its own full stack. Pool model. Tenants share resources. This is classic multi-tenancy, and it lowers the cost per tenant as you grow. Bridge model. A mix. Some services are siloed and others are pooled. Strict data rules or noisy load can push one service to silo. Cost and agility can push another to pool. The pool is cheapest, because it scales with the real load of all tenants. The same 2020 whitepaper lists its costs too: noisy neighbours, harder cost tracking per tenant, and a bigger blast radius. One outage will likely hit every tenant. You can mix models by price tier. Basic tenants share a pool, and premium tenants pay for their own stack. A 2022 AWS whitepaper (now archived) adds a warning: every silo should run the same version and setup as the pool, with no one-off changes. If you skip this, you end up running many different products. Tenant id everywhere In a pool, the tenant id is the only thing that keeps data apart. Our advice: Put tenant_id on every row of every tenant table, and in every index that starts a lookup. Read the tenant from the login token once, at the edge. Pass it down in a request context. Never trust a tenant id from the request body. Put the tenant id in every log line, metric label, cache key, queue message and file path. A cache key like invoice:991 can leak data between tenants. Use tenant:42:invoice:991. Row-level security Remembering WHERE tenant_id = ? in every query is not enough. One missed filter leaks data. Row-level security (RLS) moves the rule into the database. In PostgreSQL, you turn on RLS for a table and add a policy. If RLS is on but no policy exists, the default is to deny: no rows are visible. A common tenant policy reads the current tenant from a session setting: ALTER TABLE invoices ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON invoices USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.current_tenant')::uuid);The app sets app.current_tenant at the start of each request. Now the database adds the filter to every query. Know the traps: Superusers and roles with BYPASSRLS always skip the policies. The table owner usually skips them too, unless you use FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. So the app must connect as a role that does not own the tables. Session settings may not work with a connection pooler such as PgBouncer, which can share session state. Our advice: set the tenant inside each transaction, for example with SET LOCAL, and test it. Noisy neighbours and per-tenant limits The first wall is a per-tenant limit. Amazon describes fairness as giving every client "a single-tenant experience". Its services set quotas per tenant. A common way to enforce them is a token bucket. See rate limiting for how a token bucket works. Not all requests cost the same. Amazon notes that the cost of a call is not always known up front, and some services count large responses as several requests. Our advice: limit the costly things separately. Cap each tenant's concurrent exports, background jobs and database connections, not just requests per second. Tell tenants about their limits. Amazon's services show clients their quota and how close they are to it. Cells Limits stop one tenant from using too much. Cells stop one failure from reaching everyone. A cell is a full, independent copy of your workload. It shares no state with other cells and serves only some of the tenants. A thin cell router sends each request to the right cell, using a partition key such as the customer id. With 10 cells, a failure in one cell leaves 90% of requests unaffected. Shopify does this with pods. Each pod is a set of shops on its own fully isolated datastores. Sorting Hat, software in Shopify's load balancers, sends each request to the right pod. This keeps one shop from "sucking up database time across the platform". Shuffle sharding Shuffle sharding goes one step further. Amazon's example has 8 workers. With no sharding, a bad customer can crash all 8 workers. Everyone is down. With 4 fixed shards of 2 workers, a bad customer crashes one shard. That is 25% of customers. With shuffle sharding, each customer gets a random pair of workers. There are 28 possible pairs. A bad customer crashes its own pair. Only customers with that exact pair lose everything. The impact drops to 1/28, which Amazon calls 7 times better than plain sharding. Every other customer shares at most one worker with the bad customer. They keep working if their clients retry on the other worker. Route 53 uses 2,048 virtual name servers and gives each domain 4 of them. That makes about 730 billion possible shuffle shards. Step through it with Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Big tenants and observability Some tenants are much bigger than the rest. Our advice: give them their own cell or silo, as a paid tier, before they become a problem. Move them in a planned migration, not during an incident. Amazon puts the throttle key and the rate limit in its request log on every request. Build dashboards for the top tenants by requests, CPU time and errors. Your first question in an incident should be "Which tenant?", and the answer should take seconds. Model Data isolation Noisy neighbour risk Cost per tenant Use it when Silo Yes Separate resources. No Its resources are its own. High. Idle capacity, many copies to run. Strict data rules, or big tenants who pay for it. Pool Only by tenant id and RLS. Yes Needs per-tenant limits. Low. Scales with real load. Many small tenants. Bridge Mixed, per service. Mixed. Medium. Some data or services need a silo, the rest do not. Cells Yes, between cells. Only inside one cell. Medium. Needs a router and a system to manage the cells. You must limit how many tenants one failure can hit. Shuffle sharding Not by itself. Rarely shared fully. Low to medium. Many tenants, and clients that can retry on another worker. Our simple rule: start with a pool, RLS and per-tenant limits. Add cells when one failure would hurt too many tenants. Give the biggest tenants a silo as a paid tier. In every design review, ask: "Where is the tenant id here, and what stops a query without it?" Write a test that logs in as tenant A and tries to read tenant B's data through every API. Run it in CI. Ask: "What is the most one tenant can use?" Check requests, connections, jobs, storage and export size. Put tenant id on every log line and metric, so on-call can see who is noisy and who is hurt. Keep a list of your largest tenants and their growth. Plan their move to a bigger tier early. Keep every silo on the same version as the pool. Treat a "special build for one customer" as a warning sign. Before an incident, know your blast radius: how many tenants share each database, cell and queue. "Add PostgreSQL row-level security to these tables. Use a policy on tenant_id that reads current_setting('app.current_tenant'). The app role must not own the tables." "Find every query, cache key and queue message in this service that does not include the tenant id. List them by file and line." "Write an integration test: log in as tenant A, then call every read endpoint with ids that belong to tenant B. Every call must return 404 or 403." "Add a per-tenant limit on concurrent export jobs, 2 per tenant, stored in Redis. Log the tenant id and the limit when a job is rejected." What to ask the agent The app connects as a role that does not own the tables and does not have BYPASSRLS. Otherwise RLS does nothing. The tenant id comes from the auth token, not from a header or body the client controls. The tenant setting is set per transaction and cannot leak to the next request on a pooled connection. Cache keys, file paths and search indexes include the tenant id, not only database rows. Limits are per tenant, not global. A global limit lets one tenant use it all. What to check yourself Related lessons: Sharding, Rate limiting, Cell-based architecture and Load shedding.

title: Negotiation and compensation
text: Read every part of a tech offer, know what equity and CTC really mean, and ask for more honestly, with data and without fear.
body: This story is made up. Asha and Vikram, backend engineers with three years of experience, pass the same loop at the same company. Each gets the same offer by phone: base salary, a bonus and "some stock". Vikram is relieved and says yes on the call. He sees nothing in writing until the joining date. Asha thanks them and asks for the offer by email. Then she asks: which level is this? What kind of stock is it, and how does it vest? Is there a sign-on bonus? The stock vests over four years, with nothing in the first year. The level is one below the role she applied for. Asha asks what it was based on, and points to the design round she led. The level stays, but the company adds a sign-on bonus and more stock. A year later, Vikram learns the difference. Same loop, same skills, different pay. He just never asked. An offer is a set of parts, not one number. Each part has its own rules, risks and room to move. Negotiation is a normal, polite talk about those parts. The key idea. Get the offer in writing, understand each part, and ask for what you need with real data. Never lie about other offers. This lesson explains how offers work. It is not financial or tax advice. For big decisions, ask a qualified advisor. The parts of a tech offer Base salary. Fixed pay, every month. It is the safest part. Bonus. Often a yearly target percentage of base. It depends on results, so it may not be paid in full. Equity. A share in the company, as RSUs or stock options. See below. Sign-on bonus. A one-time payment for joining. Ask if you must pay it back if you leave early. Benefits. Health insurance, leave and retirement plans. RSUs and stock options An RSU is a right to receive shares once vesting conditions are met. You own no shares on the grant date. A stock option is the right, but not the duty, to buy shares at a fixed price, the strike price, after a vesting period. Startups often give options to employees as part of pay. Both usually vest over time. GitLab's handbook describes a four-year schedule for new-hire stock options, with a one-year cliff. It says that "at most companies, including GitLab", the cliff is generally one year. There, RSUs vest over two to four years from the grant date, and refresh grants have no cliff. Step through a made-up option grant below. At GitLab, unvested RSUs and options are lost when you leave. Vested options must be bought within 90 days of leaving. Read your own grant agreement. Why options can be worth nothing. For traded options, Investor.gov explains that a call option is "out-of-the-money" when the strike price is above the share price. Employee options are not traded, but in our reading the same sums apply. If the share price stays at or below your strike price, buying at that price gains you nothing. Private shares add a second risk. An SEC staff explainer says startup shares are "often illiquid": you cannot easily sell them. Money usually comes at an exit, such as an IPO or an acquisition. If a startup winds down, it pays its debts first. What is left goes to shareholders in order of liquidation preference. So in your sums, count startup options as uncertain and possibly worth zero, not as salary. This is our advice. In India: CTC versus in-hand pay Indian offers often show CTC, the cost to company: the total the employer spends on you, not what reaches your bank. It often includes: Variable pay. A bonus target that may be paid in part or not at all. Employer PF. EPFO says both employee and employer contribute 12% of basic wages plus dearness allowance. In our experience, most offers put the employer's 12% inside CTC. Your own 12% comes out of your salary. Gratuity. A lump sum paid when you leave. Most permanent staff qualify only after five years of continuous service. The Code on Social Security, 2020 waives this for death, disablement or the end of a fixed-term contract. Fixed-term staff qualify after one year. The amount is 15 days' wages per year of service. For monthly pay, that is monthly wages ÷ 26 × 15. These rules apply from 21 November 2025. It may sit in CTC each year, but you get it only if you qualify. Here is a made-up example. "Wages" here means basic pay plus dearness allowance. Under the new codes, if other pay is more than half the total, the excess counts as wages. So assume wages of ₹12,00,000 a year, about half the pay. CTC: ₹24,00,000 a year. Variable pay: ₹2,40,000. Employer PF: 12% × ₹12,00,000 = ₹1,44,000. Gratuity: ₹1,00,000 ÷ 26 × 15 ≈ ₹57,700. Insurance: ₹12,000. Fixed pay: 24,00,000 − 2,40,000 − 1,44,000 − 57,700 − 12,000 = ₹19,46,300. After your own PF of ₹1,44,000: ₹18,02,300, about ₹1,50,000 a month before income tax. EPFO makes contributions mandatory when basic pay plus DA is up to ₹15,000 a month, and voluntary above. So employers calculate PF in different ways. Ask for a full salary breakup. Where to find market data As of 2026, these are common sites. In our experience: levels.fyi shows pay by company and level, shared by users. Glassdoor has salaries and company reviews posted by employees and job seekers. Blind is an anonymous forum where tech workers discuss pay and offers. All three are mostly self-reported. We think people with high or unusual pay may post more often. Data can be old. Use a range from several sources. Three ideas from negotiation research BATNA. Your Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement is what you will do if this deal fails. PON says a deal should beat your BATNA, and interviewing at several firms makes it stronger. Anchoring. PON describes the anchoring effect: the first number tends to pull later offers towards it. Employers often name the first number, so plan for it. Research your range before the call. Interests, not positions. A position is a fixed demand; an interest is the need behind it. In PON's job example, the company cares about its budget. A signing bonus instead of a raise, or a salary review tied to milestones, can still meet your need. The script Our suggested script: Thank them and get it in writing. "Thank you, I'm excited about this team. Could you email me the full offer?" Ask for time. "I'd like a few days to review it. Can I reply by Friday?" Ask about every part. Level, base, bonus target, equity type and vesting, sign-on, benefits, and in India the CTC breakup. Ask about the level. Level sets your pay band. The interview loops lesson explains how it is set. Make one clear request. "Based on market data and how my design round went, I'd ask for ₹X base. If base is fixed, could we look at the sign-on bonus?" Use competing offers honestly. Name a real offer only if you have it. Be ready to show it. Never lie about another offer. Companies may ask for the letter. A lie can end a real offer, and it is wrong. What is usually negotiable In our experience, sign-on bonus and equity move most often. Base moves within the band for your level. The level itself moves only with evidence. Benefits and bonus percentages are usually fixed by policy. Exploding offers An exploding offer has a very short deadline, such as 24 hours. Our advice: politely ask for a few more days. If they refuse, still read every term before you decide. Pay transparency laws As of 2026, Colorado's Equal Pay for Equal Work Act requires employers to disclose pay in all job postings, internal and public. It also bans asking about your pay history. Since 1 November 2022, New York City has required a "good faith pay range" in all job ads for work done in the city. A posted range is useful data. But PON warns that an advertised range can anchor talks in the employer's favour, so do your own research too. Raises and promotions inside your company Internal pay follows your company's levels and review cycle. Career ladders and level expectations covers it. Approach Honest? Risk Use it when Accept on the call Yes Less pay or a lower level than you could get. Almost never. Counter with market data Yes Low. The answer may be no. Usually. Counter with a real competing offer Yes They may decline to match. You would really take the other offer. Bluff about an offer you do not have No You can lose the offer and your name. Never. Simple rule: understand every part, know your alternative, ask once with evidence, and stay honest. Before a job search, write your BATNA in one line. "If this fails, I stay and aim for promotion in March." Compare offers in the same terms. Turn equity into a yearly value, and mark private equity as uncertain. As an interviewer, write clear level evidence. It helps candidates get the right level. "Act as a polite but firm recruiter. Role-play the call while I ask about the level, vesting and a sign-on bonus. Then tell me where I was unclear." "Here is my offer letter with names removed. List every pay component, the vesting schedule, any cliff, and any clause about paying back a bonus. Quote the exact lines." What to ask the agent Every number the agent reads from your letter, against the letter itself. Tax and legal claims. Confirm them with official sources or an advisor. Your script. Never ask the agent to invent a competing offer or fake data. Privacy. Remove names, IDs and salary account details before you paste. What to check yourself Before this: big-tech interview loops and behavioural interviews. Also: what senior really means. Next: career ladders.

title: Data modelling for NoSQL
text: In DynamoDB and Cassandra you design keys around the questions your app asks. List them first, then shape the data so each one is a single cheap read.
body: Discord's 2017 post tells how it moved chat messages from MongoDB to Cassandra. Every query read one channel, so channel_id became the partition key. Messages inside it were sorted by message_id, a time-ordered ID. The first import showed a problem at once. Cassandra logged warnings about partitions over 100 MB. Under one key, a busy channel's messages would grow without end. Discord wrote that big partitions add heavy garbage collection pressure, and cannot be spread across the cluster. So they changed the key. They added a time bucket to the partition key: ((channel_id, bucket), message_id). They looked at the largest channels and chose about 10 days per bucket. They expected that to keep partitions comfortably under 100 MB. The model still had a sharp edge. In one public server, someone deleted millions of messages with the API. One message was left in the channel. To return it, Cassandra scanned millions of delete markers, called tombstones. The garbage collector ran 10-second stop-the-world pauses again and again. The fix was in table settings and the read path. Discord cut the tombstone lifetime from 10 days to 2. That was safe only because they ran repairs every night. The query code now remembers empty buckets and skips them. Nothing here was a bug in Cassandra. The key decided how big each partition could grow, and how much work one read could cause. In a relational database, you normalise first and write queries later. The data models lesson covers that. DynamoDB and Cassandra flip the order. AWS says it plainly: you should not design a DynamoDB schema "until you know the questions it will need to answer". Cassandra's docs say the same: "data modeling is query-driven". The reason is the trade. These stores answer a few kinds of query very fast at any size. Other queries can be "expensive and slow". You choose which queries are fast when you choose the keys. The key idea. Write the list of access patterns before you draw a table. Then pick a partition key and sort key so each pattern is one request to one partition. Copy data where a pattern needs it. Two keys The primary key has two parts. The partition key is hashed to decide which partition, and so which node, stores the item. The sharding lesson explains how the hash ring works. The sort key orders items inside one partition. Cassandra calls it the clustering key. In DynamoDB, all items with the same partition key form an item collection. They are stored together. One Query reads them in sort-key order. A sort key can also hold a path. AWS shows [country]#[region]#[state]#[county]#[city]#[neighborhood]. With begins_with you can read any level of that tree in one range query. Step through one small table. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Denormalise per query Neither store has joins. Cassandra's docs say all fields a query needs must sit in one table. Each query gets its own table, so the same data is copied into several tables. That copying is denormalisation. In DynamoDB you copy into item collections and indexes instead. In the diagram, the club's name is copied onto each membership item. The "my clubs" screen then needs one read, not one per club. The cost is that a club rename must update every copy. One-to-many and many-to-many One-to-many is the easy case. Put the parent and its children under the parent's partition key. Give the children a sort key prefix like ORDER# and read them with begins_with. Many-to-many needs two directions. AWS calls the usual answer an adjacency list. Each entity is a partition. Each link is an item in that partition, with the target's ID as the sort key. AWS's example is invoices and bills. One Query reads all bills on an invoice. For the reverse, "which invoices contain this bill?", you add a global secondary index (GSI) on the sort key. People call this flipped index an inverted index. A GSI is not free. It is updated asynchronously, usually "within a fraction of a second". A query on it can return stale results. Each GSI also adds write cost, and a GSI short of write capacity throttles writes to the table. Keep partitions bounded A partition key with a few huge values is a trap. In DynamoDB, each partition can serve at most 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second. Cassandra suggests under 100,000 values and under 100 MB per partition. Its hard limit is 2 billion cells, but it gets slow well before that. The fix is the one Discord used. Add a column to the partition key, such as a month or a date. Here is the simplified schema from Discord's post. It keeps the newest messages first. The real table has about 10 more columns. CREATE TABLE messages ( channel_id bigint, bucket int, message_id bigint, author_id bigint, content text, PRIMARY KEY ((channel_id, bucket), message_id) ) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_id DESC);The bucket must be computable from the ID or a timestamp. Reads then walk buckets from now backwards until they have enough rows. The cost lands on quiet channels: they may need several queries to fill one page. Pick the bucket size from your biggest key, not your average one. Single-table design, and its critics AWS's general advice is to keep "as few tables as possible". Single-table design goes further. It stores many entity types in one table, so one Query can return a user and their orders together. AWS also lists the costs. It has a steep learning curve. All entities share one backup, one encryption setting and one stream. AWS says multiple tables are "good and sufficient" when you never query entities together. Alex DeBrie, who recommends it for most apps, gives the main reason: fetching several item types "using a single request". He lists the downsides too. New access patterns are hard to add, and analytics need extra work. He would skip it for GraphQL, and for new apps that value flexibility. Pete Naylor, who worked at Amazon, pushes back harder. He says: "Do NOT start with exactly one table as a design constraint…" He agrees the best answer might be one table, but says it often will be more. Items in one table but different partitions are no cheaper to read than items in two tables. The real win is the item collection. So treat the number of tables as an outcome of the modelling. What you give up Ad-hoc queries. A question that the keys do not answer needs a Scan of the whole table, or a new index. Joins. Cassandra has none, so you copy data instead. Big transactions. A DynamoDB transaction holds up to 100 distinct items and 4 MB, in one account and Region. Each item costs two writes: one to prepare and one to commit. Choice Fast reads Easy to change later Watch out for One table per entity (normalised) No Several requests per screen. Yes Code that joins in memory. Single-table design Yes, when items share a partition key. No New patterns are hard to add. Shared backups, streams and encryption. Denormalised copies Yes One read per screen. No Each copy needs an update path. Copies that disagree. GSI for the reverse lookup Yes One Query. Yes You can add one later. Stale reads and extra write cost. Time-bucketed partition key Yes, for recent data. Partly. Bucket size is hard to change. Quiet keys need several queries. Simple rule: if you cannot list the access patterns yet, you are not ready for these stores. Start with a relational database and come back. Here is a worked example: a small sports club app. First, the access patterns. Then the keys. Each row is one request. Access pattern Request PK SK Show a member's profile GetItem MEMBER#m1 PROFILE List a member's clubs Query, begins_with MEMBER#m1 CLUB# List a club's members Query on GSI1 CLUB#c1 (GSI1PK) MEMBER# (GSI1SK) Show one court's slots for a day Query COURT#c7#2026-11-20 SLOT# List a member's upcoming bookings Query, between MEMBER#m1 BOOKING#2026-11-20 to BOOKING#9999 The bookings query needs an upper bound. A plain >= would also return the CLUB# and PROFILE items, because they sort after BOOKING#. The court partition is bucketed by day, so it holds at most one item per slot. Booking writes two items in one transaction. The condition stops a double booking. await ddb.send(new TransactWriteCommand({ TransactItems: [ { Put: { TableName: "Club", Item: { PK: "COURT#c7#2026-11-20", SK: "SLOT#18:00", member: "m1" }, ConditionExpression: "attribute_not_exists(PK)" } }, { Put: { TableName: "Club", Item: { PK: "MEMBER#m1", SK: "BOOKING#2026-11-20T18:00", court: "c7" } } }, ] }));Habits that go with it: Write each access pattern with its key, its sort order and its peak rate. AWS says to know data size, shape and velocity first. For each partition key, ask: "What is the biggest this partition can get?" If there is no answer, add a bucket. For every copied field, name the code that updates it. Ask: "Which question will product ask next year?" If you can't answer it with a new GSI, say so now. Load test with your biggest real tenant or channel, not average data. "Here are our 8 access patterns with rates. Propose a DynamoDB key design. For each pattern, show the exact GetItem or Query call, the PK and SK values, and how many items it reads." "For this Cassandra schema, estimate the largest partition using our biggest customer's data. Show the formula and the numbers." "List every field this design copies. For each one, show the code path that must change when the source changes." What to ask the agent Every access pattern maps to one request. None needs a Scan or a filter on a non-key field. No partition key value can grow without a limit. The agent did not add a GSI where the base table could already answer. Code that reads a GSI can handle a missing or stale item. Transactions stay under 100 items, and the agent counted the double write cost. What to check yourself Before this: Data models, Sharding and Secondary and composite indexes. Quorums and leaderless replication explains how Cassandra reads and writes replicas of each partition. Next: DynamoDB in depth and Cassandra in depth go deeper on each store.

title: Observability, SLOs and error budgets
text: Logs, metrics and traces show what your system does. SLOs and error budgets tell you when to act.
body: Meera's team runs the checkout API for an online shop. Their dashboard has 40 graphs. On Tuesday evening, every graph looks fine. Average latency is 120 ms. CPU is at 45%. At the same time, one in ten customers cannot pay. A new release broke payments for one card type. Those requests fail fast, so they even pull the average latency down. Nobody is paged. The team gets 200 alerts a week about CPU and disk, so they have learned to ignore the alert channel. The problem is found the next morning, from angry messages to support. The team had a lot of data, but no clear answer to one question: "Are our users getting what they need right now?" (This story is made up, but the pattern is common.) Observability means you can understand what your system is doing from the data it sends out. Most of that data comes in three kinds. OpenTelemetry lists these three, plus other signals such as baggage, which carries context between them : Metrics: numbers measured over time, like requests per second or error rate. Cheap to keep, good for graphs and alerts. Logs: a record of one event, like "payment 7f3a failed: card declined". Rich in detail, but large. Traces: the path of one request through many services. A trace is made of spans, one for each step, with its timing. Data alone does not tell you when to act. For that you need a target that matches what users feel: An SLI (service level indicator) is a measure of service, best written as good events ÷ total events . In practice, count only valid events: leave out calls like health checks. For example: the share of checkout requests that succeed in under 500 ms. An SLO (service level objective) is the target for that SLI over a time window. For example: 99.9% over a rolling 4 weeks . The alerting maths below uses a 30-day window instead, as the alerting chapter does . An SLA (service level agreement) is a contract with customers that has a penalty, often money, if you miss it . The error budget is the part you are allowed to fail: 100% minus the SLO . With a 99.9% SLO and 1 million requests, you can fail 1,000 of them. The key idea. Never aim for 100%. It is not realistic . A user on a phone that works 99% of the time cannot tell 99.99% from 99.999% . Pick a target, then spend the error budget on purpose. When some budget is left, ship. When it is gone, fix reliability first . Availability maths: the nines Each extra "nine" cuts the allowed downtime by 10 : 99%: about 7.2 hours a month. 99.9%: about 43 minutes a month. 99.99%: about 4.3 minutes a month. 99.999%: about 26 seconds a month. Services that depend on each other multiply. If checkout needs three services in a row, each 99.9%, the best it can do is 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 99.7%. This assumes they fail independently. Two copies in parallel help: if each copy is 99% and they really fail independently, both are down only 0.01 × 0.01 = 0.01% of the time. In real life, copies often fail together, for example after one bad config change.
