What to measure Google's SRE book suggests four golden signals for any service: latency, traffic, errors and saturation (how full the service is) . It also warns that averages hide slow requests. A service with an average latency of 100 ms can still have 1% of requests take 5 seconds . So use percentiles, like p99, in your SLIs. Burn-rate alerts The burn rate is how fast you spend the error budget, compared with the speed that would use it up exactly at the end of the window . At burn rate 1, the budget lasts 30 days. At burn rate 10, it is gone in 3 days . Step through a bad deploy and see how a burn-rate alert reacts. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. The Site Reliability Workbook recommends three alerts for a 99.9% SLO : Page if the burn rate is above 14.4 over the last hour and the last 5 minutes. That is 2% of the 30-day budget in one hour. Page if it is above 6 over the last 6 hours and the last 30 minutes. That is 5% of the budget. Open a ticket if it is above 1 over the last 3 days and the last 6 hours. That is 10% of the budget. The long window proves the problem is real. The short window makes the alert stop a few minutes after the problem stops . Approach Catches real user pain? Noise Use it when Alert on causes (CPU, disk, memory) No Users can suffer while CPU is fine. High. Many alerts need no action. Only as tickets or dashboards, to help find a cause. Alert on any error Yes, but too early. Very high. Every short error pages someone. Almost never for paging. Simple SLO threshold (error rate above 0.1% for 10 minutes) Yes Medium. Short spikes can still page. A first step, while you learn your traffic. Multiwindow, multi-burn-rate SLO alerts Yes Fast for big outages, slower for small, steady error rates. Low. Most user-facing services, once SLOs exist. Simple rule: page a human only for symptoms that users feel. Keep cause metrics for debugging . Start from the user's journey: "Can a customer pay?" Write the SLI as good events ÷ valid events. Then add the SLO. Choose the SLO with the product owner. Use past data, and do not promise more than your dependencies give you. Write an error budget policy before you need it. For example: if the budget for 4 weeks is spent, stop feature launches and work on reliability until the service is back within the SLO . Put a trace ID in every log line. Then you can jump from a slow trace to the logs of that exact request. Keep monitoring separate from what it watches. In 2021, Roblox was down for 73 hours, and its monitoring depended on Consul, the system that was failing. That slowed the team's diagnosis . Slack's dashboards and alerts also failed in its January 2021 outage, because they reached their databases through the overloaded network . Delete or fix every alert that pages without needing action. Alert noise trains people to ignore the real alert. "Write a Prometheus recording rule for the checkout SLI: the share of requests that return a non-5xx status in under 500 ms. Then write burn-rate alerts for a 99.9% SLO, with 1 hour and 5 minute windows at 14.4, and 6 hour and 30 minute windows at 6." "Add OpenTelemetry tracing to this HTTP handler. Add the trace ID to every log line it writes." What to ask the agent The SLI counts only valid requests. Decide on purpose whether health checks and 4xx errors from bad user input count. The burn-rate maths matches your SLO. A burn rate of 14.4 for a 99.9% SLO means an error rate of 1.44%. Each alert uses both a long and a short window. The latency SLI uses a percentile or a threshold count, never an average. Logs do not contain passwords, card numbers or other personal data. What to check yourself Next on this line: Alerting and on-call explains how to page humans only for what matters.

title: OS essentials for backend engineers
text: Processes, threads, memory, files and system calls are where your code meets the machine. Know them, and many "random" production failures stop being random.
body: This is a made-up example, but each part of it is common. A team moves a Java order service into Kubernetes. The container gets a 512 MiB memory limit. To be safe, they set the JVM heap to 512 MiB too. Under load, the pod restarts every few hours. kubectl get pod shows the status OOMKilled. The last state has exit code 137. The Kubernetes docs show exactly this pattern: a container goes over its limit, gets killed, restarts, and gets killed again. The team looks at the JVM dashboard. Heap use is at 400 MiB, well under 512 MiB. So who used the memory? The answer is: the operating system counted more than the heap. The limit applies to the whole container. It counts every thread stack and every native buffer. It even counts file pages in the page cache, but the kernel can free those first. Stacks and native memory cannot be freed that way. A week later, the same service fails in a new way. Logs fill with "too many open files". A client library forgot to close sockets. This lesson explains both failures, and the OS ideas behind them. Your program cannot use devices such as disks and network cards directly. The kernel sits in between. It shares the CPU, memory and disks among many programs. A process is a running program with its own private memory. A thread is one line of execution inside a process. Threads in one process share memory and open files. Each thread has its own stack. When your code needs the kernel, for example to read a file or send bytes on a socket, it makes a system call. That call costs time. The kernel also keeps limits. It limits how much memory a group of processes may use, and how many files one process may hold open. Some limits are hard. When you hit the memory limit or the open-file limit, the kernel does not slow down politely. It kills the process, or the call fails. The key idea. Your runtime shows you a small part of the picture, such as the heap. The kernel counts much more: almost all memory, every open file and socket, and time spent waiting. Limits and costs come from the kernel's view, not your runtime's view. User mode, kernel mode and system calls Your code runs in user mode. In user mode it cannot do I/O or other privileged operations. The kernel runs in kernel mode, with full access to the machine. To ask the kernel for something, a program runs a special trap instruction. The CPU jumps into the kernel, which does the work and then returns to user mode. read, write, open, accept and fsync are all system calls. Context switches The kernel shares each CPU among many threads. It runs one for a while, then switches to another. To switch, it saves the registers of the running thread and restores those of the next one. This is a context switch. Both steps cost time. In 1996, on a 200 MHz CPU, a system call took about 4 microseconds and a context switch about 6. OSTEP says modern 2–3 GHz systems reach sub-microsecond results. These are the direct costs. OSTEP also notes that many OS operations depend on memory speed, which has not improved as fast as CPUs. A few microseconds is cheap once. It is not cheap 100,000 times per second, so reading a file 1 byte per call is slow. Virtual memory Every process gets its own address space. It looks like a large, private block of memory. The OS and hardware map each address to a real place in RAM. So every address your program prints is a virtual address. Two processes can use the same address and never see each other's data. This is how the OS keeps one buggy process from damaging another. The page cache The kernel keeps recently read and written file data in RAM. This is the page cache. In /proc/meminfo you see it as Cached. The page cache is why the second read of a file is often much faster than the first. It is also why free on a busy server can show little free memory. The useful number is MemAvailable: how much memory new programs can get without the system swapping. Memory limits and the OOM killer The container runtime puts the processes of each container in a control group, or cgroup. Kubernetes uses it to enforce the container's memory limit. In cgroup v2, memory.max is the hard memory limit. The cgroup counts the page cache, anonymous memory such as heaps and stacks, and some kernel memory, such as TCP socket buffers. When usage reaches memory.max and the kernel cannot reduce it, it runs the OOM killer inside that cgroup. The OOM killer ends a process to get memory back. memory.events counts these events. oom counts how often the limit was reached, and oom_kill counts processes killed. There is also a softer limit, memory.high. Going over it slows the processes down, but it never calls the OOM killer. In Kubernetes, a container may use more than its request if the node has room, but never more than its limit. Files and file descriptors When you open a file, the kernel returns a file descriptor. It is a small number, starting from 0, that points into your process's table of file descriptors. A new socket gets a file descriptor too. So do pipes. Each process has a limit, RLIMIT_NOFILE. Calls such as open, pipe and dup that go over it fail with EMFILE. The open(2) man page describes EMFILE as the per-process limit on open file descriptors. Your logs show it as "Too many open files". There is also a system-wide limit, which gives ENFILE. The limit has a soft value, which the kernel enforces, and a hard value, which caps the soft one. A child process inherits its parent's limits. All threads in a process share one descriptor table and one limit. A leak in one library can starve the whole service. Writes, fsync and durability Step through one write, with the ← and → keys or the buttons. A successful write() does not mean the data is on disk. For normal, buffered writes, the kernel only copied it into the page cache. /proc/meminfo calls this data Dirty: memory waiting to be written back to disk. fsync() sends the file's changed data to the storage device. It blocks, and returns only after the device confirms it has stored the data. If you created a new file, you also need an fsync() on its directory to be sure the entry is on disk. Errors can come late, too. If the kernel fails to write the data back, fsync() reports it. On some filesystems, such as NFS, an error may show up only at a later write(), fsync() or even close(). Always check the return value of fsync(). This wait is real. PostgreSQL waits for its log records to reach permanent storage before it reports a commit. For short transactions, the docs call this delay "a major component of the total transaction time". Seeing it on a real server Brendan Gregg's USE checklist names the tools for each resource. free -m and vmstat 1 for memory use. vmstat columns si and so show swapping. dmesg | grep killed to find OOM kills. /proc/sys/fs/file-nr for system-wide open files. strace to catch calls that fail with EMFILE. Choice Good for Cost Watch out for Many threads in one process Sharing memory cheaply. Each thread needs its own stack. Locks for shared data. One bad thread can corrupt shared memory or leak shared descriptors. Many processes Isolation. A crash stays in one process. More memory. Sharing data needs sockets, pipes or shared memory. Each process has its own limits. write() without fsync() Fast writes. No Data may be lost on a power cut. Fine for caches and logs you can lose. fsync() on every commit Durable data. Every commit waits for the device. Check its errors. A new file also needs a directory fsync(). Postgres asynchronous commit Much faster small transactions. The last few transactions can be lost in a crash. Data loss, but not corruption. Memory limit = heap size Nothing. OOM kills under load. Leave room for stacks and native memory. When a pod restarts, check the last state first. The reason OOMKilled means the container hit its memory limit. The cause can be a limit that is too low, or a memory leak. Trust the reason, not the exit code alone. Set the memory limit above the heap. Measure total container memory under load, not only heap graphs. Watch memory.events. Rising high or max counts warn you before a kill. Any oom_kill means a process already died. Treat "too many open files" as a leak until proven otherwise. Raising the limit only buys time. Count open descriptors per process in your dashboards, next to memory. Ask "where does this write become durable?" in every design review that stores data. "Here is our Kubernetes deployment and JVM flags. Estimate total container memory: heap, thread stacks, metaspace and native buffers. Tell me if the memory limit leaves enough room." "Search this Go service for every place we open a file, socket or HTTP response body. For each, show where it is closed, and list paths where it is not." "This code writes an order to a file and then replies 'saved'. Explain which crash could lose the order, and show the smallest fix with fsync." What to ask the agent Every memory number the agent gives is labelled heap, stack or native. Totals that add only the heap are wrong. Each close happens on error paths too, for example in defer or finally. The fsync fix checks the return value, and a new file also gets a directory fsync. What to check yourself Locks, atomics and deadlocks: what to do once two threads share memory. Kubernetes and runtime basics: requests, limits and how pods are scheduled. Garbage collection and runtime tuning: heap sizing inside a container limit. Next steps on this track: mechanical sympathy (CPU caches and memory), I/O models (blocking, epoll, zero-copy), and storage engine internals.

title: OWASP Top 10 and secure coding
text: The few web security bugs that cause most damage, and the plain coding habits that stop them.
body: On 8 March 2017, a US government security team publicly warned about a flaw in Apache Struts. Struts is a widely used, open-source framework for web apps. The flaw let an attacker run commands on the server. Two days later, someone scanned Equifax's systems for it. They found an online dispute portal still running the old version, broke in, and confirmed they could run commands. They took no data that time. Equifax did send the warning to its system administrators. But the list of people was out of date, so the people who should install the patch never got it. A scan a week later also missed the flaw. From 13 May 2017, attackers used the portal again. They found a store of usernames and passwords kept unencrypted. With those, they reached 48 more databases. They ran about 9,000 queries, far more than normal work needs, and nothing limited them. A device that inspected network traffic should have seen this. But its digital certificate had expired about 10 months before the breach, so it was not inspecting encrypted traffic. On 29 July 2017, an administrator replaced the certificate and saw the attack. It had lasted about 76 days. The attackers reached personal data of at least 145.5 million people in the US. One unpatched framework let them in. Plain-text passwords, databases that were not separated and blind monitoring did the rest. This lesson covers the habits that stop each of these. The OWASP Top 10 is "a standard awareness document" about the most critical security risks to web applications. Treat it as a list of bug types to learn, not a full checklist. The current edition is OWASP Top 10:2025, the eighth one. For it, OWASP used data from over 2.8 million applications. Eight categories come from testing data and two from a survey of practitioners. # 2025 category A01 Broken Access Control A02 Security Misconfiguration A03 Software Supply Chain Failures A04 Cryptographic Failures A05 Injection A06 Insecure Design A07 Authentication Failures A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions Two changes since 2021 matter for daily work. Server-side request forgery is now part of A01. A03 grows the old "Vulnerable and Outdated Components" to cover builds and distribution too. The key idea. Many of these bugs happen when your code trusts something it should not: user input, a library, a default setting or its own network. Check on the server, keep data apart from code, and give each part the least power it needs. Here are six to start with, each with one example and one fix. Broken access control (A01) A user changes /accounts/123 to /accounts/124 and sees someone else's account. The server never checked ownership. OWASP found some form of broken access control in 100% of the applications tested. Fix: deny by default, write the check once and reuse it everywhere, and enforce record ownership. Add access control cases to your unit and integration tests. The full story is in Authentication and authorization. Injection (A05) Injection happens when untrusted input reaches an interpreter, such as a SQL database, as part of a command. Step through the classic attack. Fix: use a parameterized query. With it, "the database will always distinguish between code and data". Most drivers and ORMs support it. # Wrong: input becomes part of the SQL cur.execute("SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id = '" + acc_id + "'") # Right: a placeholder, so the driver passes input only as a value cur.execute("SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id = %s", (acc_id,))Placeholders cannot hold table or column names. For a "sort by" field, map the user's choice to a fixed list of allowed names. Also, never give your app's database account admin rights. Security misconfiguration (A02) Examples: an admin console with its default password, sample apps left on a production server, or stack traces shown to users. At Equifax, an expired certificate left a traffic monitor misconfigured, so it missed the attack. Fix: build each environment from a script, with the same hardened settings everywhere and different credentials in each. Remove features and samples you do not use. Add one central setting that stops detailed error messages from reaching users. Software supply chain failures (A03) Your app is mostly other people's code. You are exposed if you do not know every version you run, including dependencies of dependencies, or you do not scan them regularly. OWASP lists a 2017 Apache Struts 2 flaw, CVE-2017-5638, and Log4Shell among its example attacks. A CVE is the public ID of one known flaw. Fix: keep a software bill of materials (SBOM), remove unused packages, and watch for new flaws in what you use all the time. A tool like Dependabot compares your dependency list with a database of known flaws. It alerts you when a new flaw is published for a version you use. Server-side request forgery (part of A01) Your app has a feature "import an image from a URL". An attacker gives http://169.254.169.254/, a cloud metadata address. Your server, which sits inside your network, fetches it. SSRF often aims at such endpoints to steal cloud credentials. Fix: if you know the target hosts, use an allow-list. Do not accept full URLs from users, and turn off redirects. If you must call any address, block private, loopback and link-local ranges and metadata endpoints. Check the address the name resolves to, and connect only to that address. On AWS, move to IMDSv2. Logging and alerting failures (A09) "Without logging and monitoring, attacks and breaches cannot be detected." A common gap is logging only successful logins, so failed attempts go unseen. Fix: log security events, including failures, with enough user context. Encode log data so attackers cannot inject fake lines. Keep personal data and secrets out of logs, and set alerts that people act on. Input validation versus output encoding These two are often mixed up. Input validation checks data when it arrives. Use allow-lists ("this field is 1 to 64 letters"), not lists of bad strings. Always validate on the server, because browser checks can be skipped. Output encoding changes data when you display it, so the browser shows it as text and does not run it. HTML, JavaScript, URLs and CSS each need their own encoder. Validation alone does not stop SQL injection or cross-site scripting. You still need parameterized queries and output encoding. Modern frameworks help by escaping output automatically. Escape hatches like React's dangerouslySetInnerHTML skip that protection. Secrets out of code, and least privilege Never put passwords or API keys in code, config files or Docker ENV lines. Load them at run time from a secrets manager, like AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault. Run a secret scanner in a pre-commit hook. If a secret leaks: revoke it, rotate it, then delete it from code and logs. Give each service the smallest access it needs. Equifax's attackers jumped to 48 more databases because they were not separated, and plain-text credentials let them in. Defense Stops Does not stop Cost Parameterized queries Yes SQL injection through values. Bad table or column names. Use an allow-list. Low. Most libraries support it. Escaping input by hand Some injection. No OWASP calls it fragile and strongly discourages it. Low to write, high to get right. Allow-list input validation Bad formats, wrong values. No It does not replace parameterized queries or output encoding. Low. Output encoding Most XSS when you show user data. Not every case. "Output encoding is not perfect." Low with a framework. SSRF allow-list Calls to any host you did not list. Features that must call any URL. Medium. You keep the list. SSRF block-list Known private ranges and metadata. Tricks like DNS rebinding, unless you connect to the address you checked. Medium. A last resort. Dependency scanning Known flaws in versions you use. Flaws not yet in the advisory database. Alerts cannot catch every issue. Low to start. Ongoing work to update. Simple rule: prefer the defense that makes the bug impossible, like a parameterized query or an allow-list. Use filters and block-lists only as extra layers. In review, ask of every new endpoint: "Who may call this, and where do we check it?" Search the diff for string-built SQL, shell commands and HTML. Each one needs a parameter, an argument list or an encoder. For any feature that fetches a URL, ask: "Which hosts may it reach?" Write the answer as an allow-list. Keep dependency alerts at zero open critical items. Agree on a patch deadline with your team, and track it like a bug. Give each service its own database user with only the tables it needs. Check that failed logins and access denials are logged and alerted. Ask: "Would we notice this attack within a day?" Treat certificates, keys and secrets as things that expire. Put their dates in monitoring. "Find every place in this repo that builds SQL, shell commands or HTML with string concatenation or f-strings. For each, show the safe version." "List every endpoint that fetches a URL given by the user. For each, say which hosts it can reach, and whether it follows redirects." "Scan the repo and its history for hard-coded secrets. List each one with file and commit, but do not print the secret." What to ask the agent Every query uses placeholders. Table and column names come from a fixed list. An AI agent may add packages to fix a problem. Check that each new package is real, maintained and pinned, and that it shows up in your scanner. No secret appears in code, test fixtures, prompts or logs that the agent wrote. New handlers have the ownership check, not only the login check. Read the agent's SSRF fix. A check on the host name alone is not enough. It must check the resolved address and connect to that same address. What to check yourself Authentication and authorization: A01 and A07 in depth. More on this line: Secrets and key management, Dependency and supply-chain security and Threat modelling and zero trust.

title: API pagination and filtering
text: Offset and cursor pagination, stable sort orders, filters and page sizes, and why deep offsets get slow on big tables.
body: A shop has an admin page for orders. It calls GET /orders?page=1&per_page=50, and the server runs OFFSET (page - 1) * 50. In the first year, the table holds 20,000 orders, and every page loads fast. Two years later, the table holds 30 million orders. A finance tool walks through all orders every night, page by page. The first pages take a few milliseconds. Page 100,000 takes seconds, and the whole job never ends before morning. The support team reports a second problem. During a sale, they scroll the list of new orders. Some orders appear twice, and some never appear at all. New orders arrive every second and push the rest down. The team moves to a cursor that remembers the last order seen. Every page is now fast, and nothing repeats. This story is made up. Slack, however, left offsets for the same two reasons. You never return a whole list in one answer. You return it in pages. The REST API lesson explains why to add paging from day one. This lesson is about how to do it well. There are two main ways. Offset pagination says "skip 40 rows, then give me 20". The client counts positions. Keyset pagination, also called the seek method, says "give me 20 rows after the last one I saw". Most APIs hide the "last one I saw" inside a token called a cursor. The key idea. An offset remembers a position, and positions move when data changes. A cursor remembers a row, and a row stays where it is. Step through two pages of a list, with a new row between them. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Offset, and why deep pages get slow. In SQL, LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40 skips 40 rows and returns the next 20. PostgreSQL's docs say the skipped rows "still have to be computed inside the server", so a large offset can be slow. Markus Winand shows the same thing. The database must count all rows from the start until it reaches the page, so later pages take longer. Page 1 is cheap. Page 100,000 reads millions of rows to throw them away. Offsets also drift. When a row is inserted above the reader's position, the next page starts one row too early and repeats a row. When a row is deleted, the next page starts one row too late and skips one. Slack's example: you read 10 messages, 10 new ones arrive, and page two shows the same messages again. Keyset pagination. Instead of a position, send the sort values of the last row. If the list is sorted by created_at DESC, id DESC, the next page is: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;The (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) part is a row value comparison. With an index on (created_at, id), the database jumps straight to the right place. Deep pages stay fast, while offset pages get slower the further you go. New rows do not move your place, so results stay stable. The cost: you cannot jump to page 7. You can only go next or back, and going back means you reverse the comparison and the sort. There is also no total page count. A stable sort needs a tie-breaker. Many orders share the same created_at. PostgreSQL warns that without an ORDER BY that gives a unique order, you get an unpredictable subset of rows. Different LIMIT and OFFSET values can even give inconsistent results. So always end the sort with a unique column, usually the primary key. Winand's advice is the same: add a unique column and extend the index. This applies to offsets and cursors alike. Opaque cursors. Do not ask clients to build the cursor from raw fields. Encode it, and say in the docs that clients must not read it. Slack's cursors are Base64 text. One decodes to user:W07QCRPA4, which means "start after this user". Slack also shows how one cursor could hold a position for each shard when data is spread over shards. Clients never read the cursor, so they would not see that change. Google's AIP-158 says page tokens must be opaque and must not be user-parseable. Plain Base64 is not enough to hide what is inside, so Google says to do more than that. It also says a token only marks where to continue. It never grants access, so check permissions on every request. Cursors can expire. Slack tells clients not to keep cursors for hours or days. Google says tokens may expire after a reasonable time and suggests about three days. Filtering and sorting. Filters and sort order are query parameters, for example GET /orders?status=paid&sort=-created_at. Our advice: only allow sorts that have an index. Without one, each page may need to sort the whole table. Google says the other parameters must stay the same while a client follows page tokens, and the API should return an error if they change. Only the page size may change. Put the filter and sort inside the cursor too, so the server can check them. Page size limits. Always cap the page size. Google says the page size must be optional. If it is too large, the API should lower it to the maximum, and a negative size is an error. Stripe's limit goes from 1 to 100, with a default of 10. Slack recommends 100 to 200 results and allows at most 1,000. A page can hold fewer items than the limit and still have more after it. So clients must check the "more" signal, not the item count. Total counts are expensive. "Page 3 of 912" needs an exact count. In PostgreSQL, count(*) must walk through all rows to check which ones the current transaction can see. Estimates are much faster. Google makes total_size optional, and allows an estimate if the API documents it. GitHub search returns at most 1,000 results per search, at most 100 per page. Ask product: does the screen need "912 pages", or just "more"? How well-known APIs name things. Stripe: limit, starting_after and ending_before. The answer has data and has_more. The cursor is just an object ID, and lists are newest first. GitHub REST: per_page and page, with up to 100 per page on most endpoints. The Link header gives next, prev, first and last URLs. Some endpoints use before and after instead. Slack: cursor and limit. The answer has response_metadata.next_cursor, which is empty at the end. Google: page_size, page_token and next_page_token. GraphQL. The Relay cursor connections spec is the common pattern. A connection has edges and pageInfo. Each edge has a node and a cursor. You page forward with first and after, and back with last and before. pageInfo has hasNextPage, hasPreviousPage, startCursor and endCursor, and clients should treat cursors as opaque. The spec has no total count. Add totalCount yourself only if you can afford it. Option Speed on deep pages Stable while rows change? Jump to page 7? Use it when Offset and limit No Gets slower as the offset grows. No Rows can repeat or be skipped. Yes Small admin tables, or lists that rarely change. Keyset or cursor Yes Stays fast on deep pages, with the right index. Yes No Only next and back. Feeds, logs, exports, public APIs, any large list. Exact total count No Must walk the rows. Not applicable. Not applicable. Small tables, or when the screen truly needs it. Estimated or no count Yes Not applicable. Not applicable. Large tables. Show "more" instead of "page 3 of 912". Simple rule: use opaque cursors over a unique, indexed sort. Cap the page size. Skip exact counts unless a user really needs them. Ask: "How big will this list be in two years?" Design for that size, not for today's. Check every list query with EXPLAIN. Look for a sort that uses an index, not a sort over the whole table. Make sure every sort ends with a unique column. Ask: "What happens when two rows have the same value?" Keep cursors opaque from version one. You can then change what is inside them, for example after sharding. Test with inserts and deletes between page requests. Then count duplicates and gaps. Push back on "page X of Y" for big tables. Offer "load more", or an estimate. For big exports, do not use the public paging API at all. Use a background job or a database snapshot. "Change this offset-based /orders endpoint to keyset pagination. Sort by created_at DESC, id DESC. Return an opaque cursor that also holds the filters. Add an index for it." "Write a test that inserts and deletes rows between page 1 and page 2, then checks that no order is repeated or missed." "Design a Relay connection for orders in GraphQL, with first, after, last and before. Explain how the cursor is built and checked." What to ask the agent The sort ends with a unique column, and the cursor holds every sort column, not only the id. The WHERE comparison matches the sort direction. One flipped < repeats or skips rows. An index matches the filter and sort. Run EXPLAIN on a big table. The server caps the page size, and rejects negative values. The server checks permissions on every page. A cursor is not a key to the data. Agents often add COUNT(*) to every list call. Remove it unless the screen needs it. What to check yourself REST API design: resources, status codes, and adding paging from day one. B-tree vs LSM-tree: why an index lets keyset pagination jump straight to a row. Search and inverted indexes: ranked results and why search APIs cap deep pages. Scaling reads: caches and replicas for heavy list endpoints.

title: The payment lifecycle
text: What really happens after the customer taps "Pay", and the states your code must track until the money is in your bank.
body: This is a made-up example, but each rule in it comes from processor docs. Meera's team runs an online furniture shop in India. To avoid refunds for items that are out of stock, the shop takes card payments in two steps. At checkout it only places a hold on the card. When a sofa ships, a job captures the money. In one busy month, some sofas shipped late, 9 or 10 days after checkout. The capture job logged "error" for those orders, and nobody read the log. The sofas went out anyway. Their processor's rule was simple. For many online card payments, a hold lasts about 7 days. If you do not capture before it expires, the funds are released and the payment becomes canceled. The shop gave away the sofas for free. Nobody saw it for weeks. The order table said "paid" because the hold had worked. The team found it only at month end. The money in the bank was lower than the sum of "paid" orders, and finance asked why. Three bugs, one root cause. The team treated a payment as one event, "paid". It is really a series of states over many days, and each state can fail. A card payment has several parties. Customer: the person who pays with a card. Merchant: your business. Payment processor or gateway: a company such as Stripe or Adyen that your code talks to. Acquiring bank: processes card payments for merchants. It sends the authorization request to the customer's bank through the card networks. Card network: the network of a card brand, such as Visa or Mastercard. Issuing bank: the bank that gave the customer the card. The payment then moves through states. Your code must track each one. Authorization: the issuing bank checks that funds are there and holds the amount. Capture: the money moves from the issuing bank toward you. Settlement: the customer's bank transfers the funds to the processor. Adyen marks a payment Settled at this point. Payout: the processor sends money from your available balance to your bank account. The key idea. "Paid" is not one moment. A payment is a state machine that runs for days. Store each state, learn about changes from verified webhooks, and check the final money against the processor's report. Step through one ₹1,000 card payment. Authorize, then capture You can capture right away. You can also authorize and capture in two steps, with the capture later. Hotels, for example, often authorize the full amount before a guest arrives and capture at checkout. With Stripe, you set capture_method=manual. After authorization, the payment's status becomes requires_capture. You can capture less than you held, and Stripe releases the rest automatically. The hold does not last forever. Stripe says an online card authorization is usually valid for 7 days. For Visa payments that you start without the customer, the table says 5 days, and the exact window is 4 days and 18 hours. Other payment methods have their own windows. If the hold expires before capture, the funds are released and the payment is canceled. On Stripe, the charge's capture_before field shows when the hold expires. Build an alert for holds that are about to expire. If you no longer want the money, cancel before capture. At Stripe, canceling costs nothing, while a refund after success might cost a fee. 3-D Secure Sometimes the issuing bank wants proof that the real cardholder is paying. With 3-D Secure (3DS), the bank may ask for a password, a one-time code sent to the phone, or a biometric check. Rules in the EEA, the UK, India, Japan and Australia may require it for card payments. On Stripe, the payment waits in the requires_action status until the customer finishes this step. Settlement takes days Capture is not cash. The money still has to travel between banks. Stripe gives settlement timing per country as "T+X" days. "T" is when the payment was confirmed or captured. Stripe's table has an "initial settlement timing" column, which applies to your first payout. There it lists 2 business days for the United States. For India, it lists 2 business days for domestic charges and 5 for international ones. Later payouts follow a default timing, which can differ. Your processor and contract may differ too, so read your own terms. Then a payout sends the money to your bank. Stripe's payout.paid event means the payout is expected to arrive. If it then fails, a payout.failed event comes later. Refunds and chargebacks A refund is started by you. At Stripe, you can refund part or all of a payment, but never more than the original charge. It is not instant. Stripe says the customer sees the credit about 5 to 10 business days later, depending on the bank. A refund can also fail, for example on a closed bank account. A chargeback, also called a dispute, is started by the cardholder with their issuer. The network reverses the payment at once. Stripe then takes the amount and a dispute fee from your balance. On Stripe, you usually have 7 to 21 days to respond, depending on the card network. If you miss the deadline, you lose. If you counter the dispute, the cardholder's bank decides the outcome. Stripe says this can take up to 3 months. So money you counted can leave your account weeks after a "successful" sale. Your ledger needs entries for refunds, disputes and fees, not only sales. Webhooks: verify, then dedupe Many results arrive later, for example when a bank confirms a payment or a customer disputes a charge. The processor tells you with a webhook. Treat each one with care. Verify the signature. Without it, an attacker could send a fake "payment succeeded" event and get free goods. Stripe signs each event with HMAC-SHA256 in the Stripe-Signature header. Verify it on the raw request body. Reject old events. The signed timestamp stops replay attacks. Stripe's libraries allow 5 minutes by default. Dedupe. The same event can arrive more than once. Save the event IDs you have processed and skip repeats. This is the same idea as in Idempotency, retries and timeouts. Do not trust order. Events can arrive out of order. If one is missing, fetch the object from the API. Answer fast. Return 2xx before slow work, and process from a queue. Stripe retries failed deliveries for up to three days in live mode. Reconcile with the settlement report Webhooks can be late or lost, and your code has bugs. So once a day, compare your records with the processor's. For automatic payouts, Stripe's payout reconciliation report lists every payment, refund, dispute and fee inside each payout. Match each line to your ledger and explain every difference. Meera's team would have seen the missing money in the first daily check. PCI DSS scope PCI DSS is the security standard for anyone who stores, processes or transmits card data. If your servers handle raw card numbers, you may face more than 300 security controls. Most teams avoid that. They use hosted fields or a hosted checkout page, so the card number goes straight from the browser to the processor. It never passes through your servers. You may still store the card brand, the last four digits and the expiry date. Your scope shrinks, but you still must attest to PCI compliance every year. Option Customer sees Risk Use it when Capture at once One charge. Refunds for items you cannot deliver. Refunds can cost fees. Digital goods and in-stock items that ship the same day. Authorize now, capture later A hold, then a charge. Some statements do not show the difference. The hold expires before capture, and the payment is canceled. Stock checks, hotels, rentals, or a final amount that may drop. Trust webhooks only Nothing. Missed or late events leave orders in the wrong state. Never alone. Webhooks plus daily reconciliation Nothing. More work for your team. Always, for real money. Your own card form Your design. Raw card data on your servers, and a much larger PCI scope. Rarely. Only with a strong reason and a security team. Hosted fields or checkout The processor's fields in your page. Less control over the look. The default for most teams. Simple rule: store every payment state, verify and dedupe every webhook, and reconcile every payout. Draw the payment state machine for your product, with every state and every exit, before you write code. Ask: "What happens if this webhook never arrives? If it arrives twice? If it arrives before the one before it?" Store the processor's payment ID and status next to your order. Never mark an order "paid" from the browser's redirect alone. Alert on holds close to expiry, captures that fail, refunds that fail and new disputes. Run reconciliation daily, and give someone the job of explaining each difference. Keep card numbers out of your systems, including logs and support tools. Use the processor's hosted fields. "Draw the state machine of a payment in our code: every status, every event that changes it, and every place we write it. Mark any state with no exit." "Review our webhook handler. Does it verify the signature on the raw body, reject old timestamps, dedupe by event ID and return 2xx before slow work? Show the line for each." "Write a daily job that matches each payout line in the processor's report to our ledger. List rows found on only one side." What to ask the agent The handler uses the processor's official library to verify signatures. AI agents sometimes parse the JSON first, which breaks the raw-body check. The dedupe check and the business update happen in one database transaction. No settlement days, hold windows or fees are hard-coded from memory. They must match your processor's docs and contract. Amounts are integers in minor units, as in Money and double-entry ledgers. Test cards and test webhooks run in CI for capture failure, refund failure and a dispute. No card number or CVC appears in logs, prompts or test data. What to check yourself Money and double-entry ledgers: how to record each state as balanced entries. Idempotency, retries and timeouts: safe retries for capture and refund calls. Coming next on this line: Reconciliation, PCI-DSS and tokenisation and Payment rails: UPI and card networks.

title: PostgreSQL in depth
text: Learn how Postgres stores, cleans, indexes and copies your rows, so it does not stop taking writes on a Monday morning.
body: At 05:35 UTC on 4 February 2019, one database stopped taking writes at Mandrill, Mailchimp's email service for apps. The database was a Postgres shard called shard4. It went into "safety shutdown mode". The cause was transaction ID wraparound. Postgres gives each writing transaction a 32-bit ID. Autovacuum must clean up old IDs in time. On shard4 it had fallen behind or failed, and the IDs hit their limit. The team had seen it coming. In November 2018 they found the IDs at about half their limit during peak load. They added a ticket to set up more monitoring. The fix was slow. Vacuuming the whole shard was estimated to take up to 40 days. Two tables were terabytes in size. Mandrill deletes queued mail after 48 hours, so time mattered. At 19:12 UTC on 5 February, the team truncated those large tables. The vacuum finished about an hour later. Service came back after about 40 hours. By 22:40 they had alerts for wraparound. Sentry had the same outage in 2015. It too ended by truncating one large table. Postgres does not change a row in place. An UPDATE writes a new row version and leaves the old one behind. The concurrency control lesson showed why: readers with an older snapshot still need it. So every busy table creates garbage all the time. An old version that no transaction can see is a dead tuple. VACUUM finds dead tuples and frees their space. VACUUM has a second job that people forget. It marks old rows as "frozen", so their transaction IDs can be reused safely. Skip the first job and you get bloat. Skip the second and Postgres stops writes. The key idea. In Postgres, every update and delete leaves work for VACUUM. Your job is to keep autovacuum fast enough, and to make sure nothing stops it. Step through one update, from new row version to cleanup. Autovacuum and when it falls behind Autovacuum vacuums a table after enough rows have changed. By default the trigger is 50 rows plus 20% of the table. On a table with 100 million rows, that means about 20 million dead tuples before it starts. By default, 3 workers share the whole server. When it falls behind, dead tuples pile up and the table bloats. Scans read more pages. A long open transaction or a forgotten replication slot can also stop cleanup. Watch n_dead_tup and last_autovacuum in pg_stat_all_tables. Transaction ID wraparound, precisely Transaction IDs (XIDs) are 32 bits. Postgres compares them in a circle: for each ID, two billion are "older" and two billion are "newer". An unfrozen row older than that would suddenly look like it is from the future. So every table must be vacuumed at least once every two billion transactions. Here are the steps, from the current docs: A table with unfrozen rows older than autovacuum_freeze_max_age gets an anti-wraparound autovacuum. The default is 200 million. This runs even if autovacuum is off. When the oldest XIDs are 40 million transactions from wraparound, PostgreSQL 18 logs WARNING: database "mydb" must be vacuumed within ... transactions. From version 19 this warning starts at 100 million. At 3 million left, it refuses to start new transactions that need an XID. Reads still work. Writes fail. To recover, the docs say: end old transactions, resolve prepared ones, drop stale slots, then run a plain VACUUM as a superuser. Single-user mode is usually not needed any more. The one exception: you want to TRUNCATE or DROP a large table instead of vacuuming it. Check how close each database is: SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) FROM pg_database ORDER BY 2 DESC;On a healthy server the age stays below about 200 million, because the anti-wraparound autovacuum starts there. Alert when it stays well above that, for example at 500 million. That is long before the warning. Mandrill's monitoring ticket sat in the backlog. HOT updates In the diagram, the update was a HOT update (heap-only tuple). It needs two things. No column used by an index changes (BRIN indexes do not count), and the new version fits on the same page. Then no index needs a new entry, though a BRIN summary may be updated. Every B-tree, GIN or GiST index you add makes HOT less likely. To leave room on pages, lower the table's fillfactor: ALTER TABLE orders SET (fillfactor = 80);This applies to pages written from now on. Existing full pages get no room until the table is rewritten. Compare n_tup_hot_upd with n_tup_upd to see your HOT rate. Picking an index type The indexes lesson covers composite, partial and expression indexes. Here is when to leave the B-tree. B-tree: the default. Equality and ranges on sortable values. GIN: an inverted index for values with many parts, like arrays. It also serves jsonb containment (@>) and key checks. It is the preferred index for full text search. GiST: a framework for geometric data and "nearest-neighbor" queries. BRIN: small summaries of block ranges. Best when a column follows the physical row order, like created_at in an append-only log. CREATE INDEX events_payload_gin ON events USING GIN (payload jsonb_path_ops); CREATE INDEX events_created_brin ON events USING BRIN (created_at);jsonb_path_ops is usually much smaller than the default class. But it does not support the key-exists operators like ?. Reading EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and shows real times and row counts next to the estimates. Three checks catch most problems: Estimated vs actual rows. The docs call this the most important thing to look for. A big gap means the planner guessed wrong. Loops. Times and rows are per loop. Multiply by loops for the total. Buffers. From PostgreSQL 18, ANALYZE turns on buffer counts too. On older versions, add BUFFERS. A "hit" means a read was avoided because the page was already in the cache. A "read" had to ask the operating system, from disk or its cache. Our advice: many buffers (hit plus read) for a few rows often point to bloat or a missing index. Many reads but few hits just mean the data was not in cache. ANALYZE really runs the statement. Wrap an UPDATE in BEGIN and ROLLBACK. WAL and checkpoints You met the write-ahead log before. Postgres also runs checkpoints. At a checkpoint it flushes all changed pages and records that point in the WAL. After a crash, it replays only from there. A checkpoint starts every 5 minutes, or sooner when the WAL nears max_wal_size (default 1 GB). After each checkpoint, the first change to a page writes the whole page to the WAL. So frequent checkpoints mean more WAL. By default, Postgres logs a hint when checkpoints caused by WAL volume come less than 30 seconds apart (checkpoint_warning). Physical vs logical replication Physical streaming replication sends WAL records to a standby as they are made. It copies exact disk blocks, so the standby is a copy of the whole server. It cannot run a different major version. Logical replication sends row changes by table and key, through publications and subscriptions. It can copy a subset of the data, and works across major versions. But it does not copy schema changes. It also does not keep sequence values in step, though version 19 can sync them on request. Both can use a replication slot. A slot that nobody reads can keep WAL until the disk fills. It also holds back VACUUM. One process per connection Postgres starts a new backend process for every connection. The default max_connections is about 100. Raising it allocates more shared memory. So thousands of app connections usually go through a pooler like PgBouncer. Database connection pooling covers this. Choice Gain Cost Use when Default autovacuum No tuning work. Starts late on huge tables. 3 workers in total. Small and medium tables. Per-table autovacuum settings Vacuums big, busy tables early. More vacuum I/O, and settings to maintain. Tables with many millions of rows and frequent updates. Lower fillfactor More HOT updates, fewer index writes. Bigger table on disk. Rows updated often on non-indexed columns. GIN on jsonb Fast containment and key search. Updating it tends to be slow. You filter on fields inside documents. BRIN Very small index. Poor when values do not follow row order. Append-only time data. Physical replica Exact copy, simple failover. Same major version, whole server only. High availability and read scaling. Logical replication Chosen tables, across versions. No schema changes. Sequences only from version 19. Upgrades and feeding other databases. Simple rule: keep the defaults, but watch dead tuples and XID age from day one. Alert on age(datfrozenxid) per database. Treat a rising number as a ticket for this week, not the backlog. Mandrill's monitoring ticket waited there. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout. An idle open transaction holds back VACUUM and causes bloat. Set statement_timeout per app role or session, not in postgresql.conf, which affects every session. Set lock_timeout in every migration, as in the schema migrations lesson. Turn on pg_stat_statements. It needs shared_preload_libraries and a restart, so do it early. Sort by total_exec_time to find what costs most. Check pg_replication_slots for inactive slots after every replica or CDC change. For big, busy tables, tune autovacuum per table. Sentry raised workers and removed the cost delay after its outage. Know which large tables you could truncate in an emergency. Both Mandrill and Sentry recovered that way. Once writes have stopped, truncating needs single-user mode. "Write SQL that lists, for each table, dead tuples, the last autovacuum time, the HOT update rate and the age of relfrozenxid. Sort by the worst." "Here is our EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) output. Find the node where estimated and actual rows differ most, and explain why." "We query payload->>'country' and payload @> '{\"tier\":\"gold\"}' on a jsonb column. Propose indexes for each and explain the difference." What to ask the agent Every number the agent gives for wraparound matches the docs for your version: 200 million, 40 million (100 million from version 19) and 3 million. Old blog posts give older advice. The agent did not suggest VACUUM FULL as a fix for wraparound. The docs say not to use it there. A proposed GIN index actually supports the operator in the query. Timeouts are set per role or session, with a longer limit for migrations and reports. EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a write runs inside a transaction that rolls back. What to check yourself Before this: Transactions and isolation levels and Replication. Related: Concurrency control in practice, Secondary and composite indexes and B-trees and LSM-trees. Next: Database connection pooling.

title: Presence and real-time fan-out
text: How to show who is online and typing, and push each change only to the people who need it, without the cost growing out of control.
body: In 2017, Discord had nearly five million users online at the same time. Each user had one session process. Each Discord server, called a guild, had its own process. Anything that happened in a guild was sent to every session connected to it. Discord was first built for groups of 25 or fewer. Then some guilds grew to 30,000 users online at once. At peak hours, the guild processes could not keep up with their message queues. The team had to turn off features that created messages, by hand. They measured why. One send call took 30 to 70 microseconds, because Erlang could pause the sending process. A large guild had to send one event to every connected session. So one event could take from 900 milliseconds to 2.1 seconds to publish. Six years later, the same team explained the core problem. The work for a server grows with the square of its size. If 1,000 people are online and each sends one message, that is 1 million notifications. With 10,000 people it is 100 million. With 100,000 people it is 10 billion. Presence is the small status next to a name: online, away, or "typing…". Slack, for example, has two presence values, active and away. A user becomes away after 10 minutes with no activity. Presence looks cheap, because each change is tiny. But each change goes to everyone who watches that user. If N people each watch M people, every change creates work for many screens. When a team grows, both N and M grow, so total work grows with the square of the size. Real-time fan-out means taking one event and sending a copy to every open connection that needs it. A chat message, a presence change and a "typing" signal all need fan-out. The key idea. Presence is cheap to store and expensive to send. Most of the design is about sending each change to fewer people, less often. Step through one user going offline. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Connection servers. Clients hold a WebSocket to a connection server. Slack calls them gateway servers. They keep user data and the list of channels each client subscribed to. They are the only Slack servers spread across many regions. Keep these servers thin. They hold sockets and pass messages on. Heartbeats and timeouts. A phone in a tunnel does not say goodbye. Its connection just goes quiet. So the client sends a small heartbeat on a fixed interval. Discord's gateway sends the client an interval, for example 45,000 ms. The client waits a random part of that interval before its first heartbeat, so clients do not all beat at the same moment. The server answers each heartbeat with an ACK. If a client misses a heartbeat, Discord closes the connection. If the client gets no ACK, it should treat the connection as dead, close it and reconnect. Discord calls this a "zombied" connection. Pick the timeout with care. A short timeout marks people offline every time a train enters a tunnel. Status then flickers on everyone's screen, and each flicker is one more fan-out. A long timeout shows people as online after they left. The 30 seconds and 90 seconds in the diagram are only an example. One owner per user. Slack hashes each user to one presence server, and those servers keep in memory who is online. One owner means one place decides "Asha is offline". Also make one rule for many devices. For example, a user is online if any device is connected. Pub/sub and sharding. Every user, channel or team gets a channel in a pub/sub layer. Connection servers subscribe for their own clients. Slack's channel servers each own a share of channels, found by consistent hashing. The word "channel" there covers users, teams, files and huddles too. Sharding by channel or user spreads the load. One hot channel still lands on one owner, so watch for it. Fan-out on write or on read. There are two ways to deliver an event. Push (fan-out on write): when the event happens, send it to every watcher at once. Reads are cheap, but one event to a huge audience is very costly. Pull (fan-out on read): store the event once. Each client asks for it when it opens the screen. Writes are cheap, but each open screen pays a little. Many systems mix the two. Our advice for presence is the same mix: push to people who are looking right now, and let everyone else pull a fresh snapshot when they open the screen. This is this lesson's own advice, not a rule from one source. Discord's passive sessions, below, are close to this idea. Limit presence to what the user can see. This is the biggest win. In Slack, clients get presence updates only for users visible on the screen at that moment. Slack's API works the same way. A client sends a presence_sub message with the full list of user IDs it wants. Since January 2018, presence_change events are not sent without these subscriptions. Discord found the same at its scale. Some users are in many guilds and may never open some of them. Discord moved those connections to a separate "passive" list that does not get every event. Around 90% of user-guild connections in large servers were passive, so fan-out work dropped by about 90%. Bots must even opt in to presence. Discord's GUILD_PRESENCES intent is privileged and off by default. Batch the updates. Instead of one message per change, send a few changes together. Slack's API batches presence updates into one presence_change event with a users array, when the client asks with batch_presence_aware=1. You can also merge updates for the same user. If Asha goes offline and back online within one second, send only the latest state, or nothing. Spread the sending work. One process that sends to a million connections becomes the bottleneck. Discord built Manifold. It groups the target processes by remote machine, so the sender makes at most one send per machine, and workers there finish the job. It also cut network traffic between machines. Later, Discord added relays between a guild and its sessions. Each relay handles up to 15,000 connected sessions and does the fan-out and permission checks, so one guild can use many machines. Protect yourself from slow parts. When the fan-out falls behind, queues grow. Discord's session processes once grew their message queues until the whole Erlang VM ran out of memory. Give each connection a bounded queue. For presence, dropping an old update is fine, because only the newest state matters. See Backpressure and flow control. Option Cost per change Freshness Use it when Push to every watcher High. One message per watcher, and it grows with the square of group size. Instant. Small groups, like a 1:1 chat or a team of 50. Push only to what is on screen Low. Only active subscribers get it. Instant for what you see. Others refresh when they open. Big teams and servers. This is the usual default. Pull when a screen opens Very low on write. Each open screen pays one read. As fresh as the last read. Member lists and huge groups where status is a nice extra. Batch and merge updates Fewer, larger messages. Slightly late, by the batch window. Busy groups where status changes often. Short heartbeat timeout More traffic and more flicker. Fast to show "offline". Calls and games, where a gone user matters at once. Long heartbeat timeout Less traffic. Slow to show "offline". Chat, where a few minutes of error is fine. Simple rule: never send presence to everyone. Send it to what is on screen, batch it, and let the rest pull. Do the multiplication first. Ask: "How many watchers per change, and how many changes per second?" Multiply them before you pick a design. Ask: "Who actually sees this status right now?" Design subscriptions around the screen, not around the team list. Treat presence as soft state. It can be a few seconds late or wrong after a crash. Discord's presence services once crashed, and sessions stayed up while presence rebuilt in minutes. Keep presence apart from messages. Never let a burst of "typing" signals delay real chat messages. Set heartbeat and timeout from data. Measure how often your users lose signal for 10, 30 and 60 seconds. Load test the biggest group you have, with everyone online. Tests with many small groups hide the square growth. Add a kill switch for "typing" and presence in huge groups. Discord had to turn off message-making features by hand when guilds fell behind. "We have 5,000-person teams. Estimate presence messages per second if each user changes status 20 times a day and every member watches every other member. Then estimate again if only users on screen are watched." "Write a WebSocket gateway in Node that keeps a set of presence subscriptions per client, sends updates only for those users, and batches them every 500 ms with only the latest state per user." "Review this heartbeat code. Does it add jitter to the first beat, detect missing ACKs, and close zombied connections?" What to ask the agent The code does not loop over all team members for each change. Agents often write exactly that. Subscriptions are removed when a client disconnects, or the server keeps sending to ghosts. A user is offline only when all devices are gone, not when one tab closes. Each connection has a bounded queue, and old presence updates are dropped first. The server checks that the client may see each user it subscribes to. What to check yourself WebSockets, SSE and long polling: how the open connections work. Fan-out on write vs read: the same choice for news feeds and timelines. Sharding and consistent hashing: how channels are spread over servers. Queues vs logs: when an event must not be lost, unlike presence.

title: Project memory: CLAUDE.md and rules files
text: Write down what the agent cannot guess, keep it short, and review it like code.
body: This story is made up, but you may know it. Sana's team moved their tests from Jest to Vitest last spring. The agent did not know. Every few days it wrote a new test file that imported from @jest/globals. The tests failed, Sana typed "we use Vitest, not Jest", and the agent fixed it. The next morning, a new session started. The agent made the same mistake again. Two weeks later, a teammate found the same error in a pull request. Each person had corrected the agent many times, but the correction lived only in old chat sessions. Then Sana opened the project's CLAUDE.md and added two lines: - Tests use Vitest. Import from `vitest`, never from `@jest/globals`. - Run one file with `pnpm vitest run path/to/file.test.ts`.She committed it, and the team reviewed it like any other change. The mistake stopped, for everyone, in every session. A coding agent does not remember yesterday. Claude Code's docs say it plainly: "Each Claude Code session begins with a fresh context window." Your corrections, your team's habits and the trap you found last week are gone. A memory file fixes this. It is a plain Markdown file that the tool loads at the start of every session. Think of it as the note you would give a new teammate on day one: how to build, how to test, and what not to touch. Every major tool has one. The names differ: Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md. GitHub Copilot reads .github/copilot-instructions.md. Cursor reads rules from .cursor/rules/. AGENTS.md is a shared format that many tools read. Its site calls it a "README for agents". The key idea. A memory file is context, not a law. It makes good behaviour more likely, but it does not force it. Keep it short, so the important lines are not lost, and put hard rules in code. Step through one session with Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Where the files live in Claude Code As of October 2026, Claude Code reads memory files from several places, from broad to specific: File Scope Shared with ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md You, in all projects Only you ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md This project The team, through git ./CLAUDE.local.md You, in this project Only you (add it to .gitignore) CLAUDE.md in a subfolder One part of the project The team, through git An organization can also install a managed file for every user on a machine. It loads first, before your user file. At launch, Claude Code loads the files in your working folder and in every folder above it. Files in subfolders load later, when the agent reads, writes or edits a file in that subfolder. The files are joined together, not replaced. Instructions closer to your working folder are read last. If two files disagree, the agent may follow either one. So do not let them conflict. Useful commands and tricks /init looks at your codebase and writes a first CLAUDE.md with build commands and conventions it finds. /memory lists your memory files and opens one in your editor. /context shows which memory files actually loaded. @path/to/file inside CLAUDE.md imports another file, up to four levels deep. Imports help you organize, but the imported text still loads at launch, so it still costs context. Files in .claude/rules/ can have a paths field with a glob pattern such as src/api/**/*.ts. That rule loads only when the agent works on matching files. The same idea in other tools GitHub Copilot reads .github/copilot-instructions.md for the whole repository. You can add NAME.instructions.md files in .github/instructions/, each with an applyTo glob for certain paths. Copilot also reads AGENTS.md, and the nearest one in the folder tree wins. Personal instructions have the highest priority, then repository, then organization. Cursor keeps project rules as .mdc files in .cursor/rules/. Each rule can apply always, when the agent thinks it is relevant, for matching files, or only when you mention it. Cursor also has user rules and team rules, and it reads AGENTS.md. AGENTS.md goes in the repository root. In a monorepo, you can add one per subproject, and the closest file takes precedence. As of October 2026, Claude Code reads AGENTS.md too, from version 2.1.277. By default it does this only when there is no CLAUDE.md in your folder or above it. On older versions, put the line @AGENTS.md in a CLAUDE.md to import it. What goes in, what stays out Anthropic's guide gives a clear test for each line: "Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?" If not, cut it. Put it in Leave it out Commands the agent cannot guess Anything it can learn by reading the code Style rules that differ from the defaults Standard language conventions How to run tests, and which runner Long API docs (link to them instead) Branch and pull request rules Facts that change often Project-specific design decisions Long tutorials Environment quirks and known traps "Write clean code" This table follows the guide. Two more things never go in: secrets, because the file is shared and read by a model, and stale facts, because a wrong rule is worse than no rule. (This is our advice.) Write rules that can be checked. "Run npm test before committing" is better than "Test your changes". Aim for under 200 lines per file. Longer files cost more context and the agent follows them less well. Cursor's docs suggest keeping each rule under 500 lines. Context, not a lock Claude Code treats memory files "as context, not enforced configuration". If an action must be blocked every time, use a hook or a permission rule. Write the reason in the memory file, and put the lock in code. Extending agents covers hooks. Memory files are an attack path The agent reads memory files as trusted instructions. That makes them a target. OWASP describes indirect prompt injection as an attack where a model "accepts input from external sources, such as websites or files". In March 2025, Pillar Security showed an attack on rules files. They called it the "Rules File Backdoor". They hid instructions in the file using invisible Unicode characters, such as zero-width joiners. In their demo, a Cursor agent asked for a simple HTML page added a script from an attacker's site, and did not mention it. The researchers say the hidden characters also stayed invisible in GitHub pull request reviews at the time. In May 2025, GitHub added a warning for files with hidden Unicode text. In an interactive session, Claude Code shows a trust dialog when you start it in a folder you have not trusted before. It also asks before it loads imports that point outside the project, to protect you from files other people commit. These help, but they do not replace reading the files yourself. Approach Agent follows team rules? Cost Use it when No memory file No You repeat yourself every session. Free today, slow every day. One-off scripts. Short root file (under 200 lines) Yes, most of the time. A few minutes to write and review. Almost every project. Root file plus path-scoped rules or nested files Yes, with less noise per task. More files to keep in sync. Large repos and monorepos. One huge file with everything No Real rules get lost. High context cost every session. Never. Split or cut it. Hooks and permission rules Yes, every time. You must write and test code. Rules that must never be broken. Simple rule: advice goes in memory, locks go in code. Add a line when the agent makes the same mistake twice, or when a code review catches something the agent should have known. Commit the project file to git and treat it like code. Review every change to it in a pull request, like a change to a CI script. (This is our advice.) Prune it regularly. For each line, ask "Would removing this cause mistakes?" Run /context to see which files loaded. If the agent keeps skipping one rule, add "IMPORTANT" to that line alone. If many lines are marked important, none stands out. Keep personal habits in your user file or CLAUDE.local.md, not in the team file. Before you run an agent in a repo you did not write, read its CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursor/rules/ and .github/ instruction files first. (This is our advice.) If your team uses more than one tool, keep one shared AGENTS.md. Import it into CLAUDE.md with @AGENTS.md if you also need Claude-only rules. "Read this repo and draft a CLAUDE.md under 60 lines. Include only build and test commands, non-default style rules and known traps. For each line, tell me which file proved it." "Here is our CLAUDE.md. Mark each line as keep, cut or move. Cut lines you can learn from the code. Move lines that only matter for one folder." "You used Jest again in this session. Write one short rule for CLAUDE.md that would have prevented it." "Scan every memory and rules file in this repo for hidden Unicode characters, instructions to fetch URLs, or instructions to hide changes from me. Report them, do not change anything." What to ask the agent Every command in the file runs today. Try each one. No secret, token or internal URL that should stay private is in a shared file. No line conflicts with another file in a parent or child folder. After a change, the agent's behaviour actually changed. Test it in a fresh session. You read the rules files of any new repo before letting an agent act there. What to check yourself Before this: Working with coding agents. Next: Extending agents: skills, hooks and MCP and AI code security risks.

title: Prompt and context engineering
text: Build prompts and context that give the same good result on the ten-thousandth request, and change them as safely as code.
body: A team runs a support tool. An LLM reads each new ticket and returns a category and a one-line summary. It works well for three months. On a Friday, a developer adds five examples to the prompt to fix the summary style. All five happen to be billing tickets. The tests pass, because the tests only check that the JSON parses. On Monday, the billing queue is full. About a third of all tickets now say "billing", including login problems. The model copied the pattern in the examples, not only the style. Nobody can say which prompt is live. It was edited in a web console, not in the repo. There is no list of past versions and no test set to compare against. Rolling back takes a day of guessing. This story is made up. Each failure in it is common, and each one has a known fix. You already know from LLM fundamentals that the model only knows what is in the request. Prompt engineering is writing the instructions in that request. Context engineering is the larger job: choosing everything the model sees, and in what order. In a product, the prompt is code. It has inputs, outputs, bugs and versions. It needs review and tests like any other code. The key idea. A good prompt is clear to a smart new colleague. Fixed parts come first. User text is fenced and treated as data. Every change runs through an eval set. Step through the parts of one request, in the order a careful team builds it. Use Next and Back. Clear instructions and a role Anthropic suggests a simple test. Show your prompt to a colleague who does not know the task. If they would be confused, the model will be too. Say the exact output format and limits you want. Use numbered steps when order matters. Give the reason behind each rule. "Never use ellipses" works less well than "The reply is read aloud by a speech engine, so never use ellipses." The model can then apply the reason to cases you did not list. A role in the system prompt, even one sentence, focuses the model's behaviour and tone. OpenAI's API has a developer role for your instructions, which ranks above user messages. Aim for what Anthropic calls the "right altitude". Avoid long, brittle if-else logic, and avoid vague advice. Start with a short prompt, then add rules only for failures you have seen. Examples (few-shot prompting) Anthropic finds that examples work very well for controlling format, tone and structure. Anthropic suggests 3 to 5 examples. Make them relevant, varied, and wrapped in <example> tags. Google goes further and recommends always including examples. Two warnings. With too many examples, the model may copy them too closely. And examples that all look alike teach a pattern you did not mean, as in the story. Keep every example in exactly the same format. Delimiting input, and why it does not stop injection Wrap each kind of content in its own tag, such as <instructions>, <context> and <input>. This helps the model tell them apart. OpenAI suggests Markdown headings or XML tags for the same reason. Tags are not a security wall. In September 2022, Simon Willison wrote about an early example found by Riley Goodside. A translation prompt obeyed "Ignore the above directions" written inside its input. A warning in the prompt did not stop it, and neither did quoting the input as a JSON string. OWASP still lists prompt injection first. It says it is unclear if there are fool-proof ways to prevent it. Injection can also be indirect: hidden in a web page or file the model reads. The danger grows with power. If an email assistant can send mail, an email it reads can tell it to. So use layers. OWASP lists them: constrain the model's behaviour, validate output formats, filter input and output, apply least privilege, ask a human before risky actions, mark outside content, and test with attacks. In our view, the strongest layer is in your code: the model cannot do what its tools do not allow. Structured output Ask for JSON that matches a schema, not free text. With structured outputs, the API constrains the reply to your JSON Schema. OpenAI recommends Structured Outputs over plain JSON mode, because only Structured Outputs follow the schema. Use a tool call when the model should trigger your code. Use a response format when you only want a shaped reply. The guarantee has limits. A refusal, or a reply cut off at max_tokens, may not match the schema. Claude's structured outputs do not support numerical limits such as minimum and maximum. So check ranges, IDs and allowed values in your own code. What goes in the context, and in what order Context is a limited budget. Anthropic calls it "a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns". As the token count grows, the model recalls facts less accurately. This is called context rot, and tests show it in all models. A very large window does not mean you should fill it. Put in only what this request needs: the rules, a few examples, the top search results, and recent history. For agents, Anthropic suggests loading data only when it is needed, using file paths or saved queries. Retrieval is its own skill: see RAG. For long inputs (Anthropic says 20,000 tokens or more), put the documents before the question. Anthropic says a question at the end improved quality by up to 30% in tests. Google gives the same advice. Anthropic would also put documents above the examples. If you cache a fixed prefix of rules and examples, you trade a little of that for cheaper calls. Prompt caching The provider can reuse the work on a fixed start of your prompt. On Claude, the cache is built in this order: tools, then system, then messages. A hit needs a 100% identical prefix. So put fixed parts first and anything that changes after them. OpenAI gives the same advice. Writing to the cache costs a little more than normal input. Reading from it costs a small fraction of the normal input price. Prices differ by model and change often, so check the current pricing table. The default cache lives 5 minutes, and each hit refreshes it. A timestamp at the top of your system prompt breaks every cache hit. Version prompts like code and test them with evals OpenAI now says: store production prompts in your application code. It is shutting down its stored-prompt API, v1/prompts, on 30 November 2026. Code-managed prompts get typed inputs, code review, tests and normal deploys. OpenAI also advises pinning production apps to a model snapshot, and building evals that measure prompt behaviour. Then a prompt change is a pull request with an eval score, as in Evals for LLM systems. A model upgrade is a separate change, with its own eval run. This table is our own summary, except where a source is cited. Option Reliability gain Cost Use it when Clear rules with reasons Yes Fewer vague failures. A few hundred tokens. Always.
