Few-shot examples Yes Strong control of format and tone. More input tokens. Can skew output if they all look alike. The output has a set style or format. Structured output Yes The shape is fixed in most cases. Values still need checks. Some schema features are missing. Code reads the reply. More context Only up to a point. Recall drops as it grows. More tokens and latency. Each added part answers a real failure. Prompt caching No change to quality. Lower. Cached input is cheaper and faster. Large fixed prefix, many calls. Input tags and warnings Some. The model can tell parts apart. Almost free. Always, but never as the only injection defence. Simple rule: start short and clear. Add examples, context and rules only when an eval shows a failure. Keep the prompt in the repo, next to the code that calls it. One file per prompt, reviewed in pull requests. Log the prompt version and model snapshot with every request. Then you can link a bad answer to a change. Ask: "Which eval cases did this prompt change move?" Never merge on "it looked better on three tries." Ask: "If this input is hostile, what is the worst the model can do?" Then remove that power from its tools. Keep the fixed prefix stable. Move dates, user names and IDs to the end. When you add a rule, add an eval case for the failure that caused it. For coding agents, the same ideas apply to project memory files. "Here is our system prompt. Rewrite it so each rule has its reason. Put fixed parts first and anything that changes per request last. List what you removed and why." "These are our five few-shot examples. Check them for variety. Point out any pattern they share that the model might copy by mistake." "Write a validator for this JSON schema output. Check ranges, allowed values and IDs against our database, and handle refusals and cut-off replies." "Write 20 eval cases for this prompt, including five prompt injection attempts hidden in the user input and in retrieved documents." What to ask the agent The agent did not paste user text into the system prompt, outside any tag. Nothing that changes per request, such as a date, sits before the cached prefix. The validator checks values, not only that the JSON parses. The eval set has cases from every category, not only the easy ones. No tool lets the model take a risky action without a check in code. What to check yourself LLM fundamentals: tokens, the context window, and cost. Evals for LLM systems: how to build the test set that every prompt change runs through. RAG: retrieval-augmented generation: how to choose which documents go into the context. Tool use and agents in products: giving the model tools, and limiting what they can do. Project memory: CLAUDE.md and rules files: context engineering for coding agents.

title: Queues vs logs and delivery guarantees
text: A queue forgets a message once it is done. A log keeps it. Know which one you have, and what "delivered once" really means.
body: A billing service puts one message on an Amazon SQS queue for each invoice. A worker takes the message, builds a PDF, emails it to the customer, and deletes the message. For most customers this takes 5 seconds. For a few large customers, the PDF has thousands of lines and takes 50 seconds. The queue uses the default visibility timeout of 30 seconds. At second 30, the message for a large customer becomes visible again. A second worker takes it and starts the same invoice. At second 50, the first worker sends the email and deletes the message. At second 80, the second worker sends the same email again. The biggest customers, the ones the company cares about most, get every invoice two or three times. Their finance teams start asking if they were charged twice. Nothing in the logs shows an error. Each worker did exactly what it was told. Both queues and logs let one service hand work to another without waiting. The sender is called the producer. The service that does the work is the consumer. A server in the middle, the broker, holds the messages. A queue, like SQS or RabbitMQ, hands each message to one consumer. When the consumer says "done", the broker deletes the message. Many workers can share the load. A log, like Kafka, is a file you only add to. Each message gets a number, its offset. Consumers do not delete anything. Each consumer just remembers how far it has read. Messages stay until a time limit you set, so you can read them again later. You can also set a size limit for each partition. The key idea. In a queue, "done" deletes the message. In a log, "done" moves a bookmark. Either way, a crash between doing the work and saying "done" means the work runs again. Step through a worker crash in both systems. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. The queue: acks and visibility timeout In SQS, a received message is not removed. It is hidden from other consumers for the visibility timeout, 30 seconds by default. If you do not delete it in time, it becomes visible again, and any worker can receive it. That is the invoice bug. The fix is to set the timeout above your slowest normal job. For long jobs, call ChangeMessageVisibility from time to time, like a heartbeat, to keep the message hidden. The total is capped at 12 hours from the first receive. RabbitMQ works in a similar way with acks. With manual acks, if a consumer's channel or connection closes before it acks, RabbitMQ puts the message back in the queue. It marks it as redelivered. With automatic acks, RabbitMQ counts a message as delivered as soon as it sends it. The docs call this mode unsafe, because a crash can lose the message. The log: partitions, offsets and consumer groups A Kafka topic is split into partitions. Messages with the same key, such as a customer ID, always go to the same partition. Inside one partition, every consumer reads messages in the order they were written. Do not count on any order across partitions. A consumer's position in a partition is a single number: the offset of the next message to read. The consumer commits this number to save its progress. It can also rewind to an old offset and read again, for example after you fix a bug. Consumers that share the work join a consumer group. Each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group at a time. So a topic with 6 partitions can keep at most 6 consumers busy in one group. Other groups, like an analytics job, read the same messages with their own offsets. Three delivery guarantees The Kafka docs give three meanings. At-most-once. Messages may be lost, but never run twice. You get this if you save your position before you do the work. At-least-once. Messages are never lost, but may run twice. You get this if you do the work, then save your position. Kafka gives this by default. Exactly-once. Each message is processed once and only once. SQS standard queues are at-least-once too. AWS says more than one copy of a message might be delivered, and order is only best effort. Why "exactly once" usually means "at least once, plus idempotency" Your work and your "done" are two separate steps. A crash can always fall between them. So the broker must either skip the message or send it again. Kafka gives exactly-once when you read from Kafka topics and write to Kafka topics, for example in Kafka Streams. It uses transactions, so the output and the new offset are saved together. But for an outside system, like a database or an email API, the docs say this "generally requires cooperation" from that system. One way is to store the offset in the same database as the result, in one transaction. SQS FIFO queues promise "exactly-once processing". Read the details. It means SQS will not add a duplicate if you retry a send within a 5-minute window. It cannot stop your worker from crashing after it emails and before it deletes. The practical answer: accept at-least-once, and make the handler idempotent. Save a message ID or an idempotency key with the result. Skip any message you have already done. The lesson on idempotency, retries and timeouts shows how. Dead-letter queues Some messages fail every time, for example because of bad data. Without a limit, they come back forever. In SQS you set maxReceiveCount. After that many receives without a delete, the message moves to a dead-letter queue, where you can inspect it. On a standard queue, a moved message keeps its first enqueue time. So set the dead-letter queue's retention longer than the main queue's, or messages may expire before you look. And on a FIFO queue, moving one message aside breaks the strict order of the rest. Backpressure If producers are faster than consumers, the backlog grows. Kafka consumers pull messages, so a slow consumer just falls behind and catches up later. It is not flooded. RabbitMQ's prefetch setting limits how many unacked messages one consumer can hold. Watch the backlog, or consumer lag in Kafka (how far a consumer is behind the newest message), and alert when it keeps growing. See backpressure and flow control. Option Replay old messages? Order Best for Queue (SQS standard, RabbitMQ) No A message is deleted after the ack. Best effort only. Jobs: send email, resize an image. Add workers to go faster. SQS FIFO queue No Yes, inside a message group (messages with the same group ID). Jobs where order matters per customer or per order, at lower throughput. Log (Kafka) Yes, until retention ends. Yes, inside a partition. Events that many teams read, rebuilding data, audit trails, stream processing. At-most-once n/a n/a Metrics or logs where losing a few is fine. A failed message is not retried. At-least-once + idempotent handler n/a n/a Almost everything else, including payments. A failed message runs again, so the handler must be safe to repeat. Simple rule: use a queue for "please do this job". Use a log for "this happened", when more than one reader needs it or you may want to replay. Either way, design for at-least-once. For every consumer, ask: "What happens if this message runs twice?" If the answer is "a customer is charged twice", fix the handler before launch. Set the visibility timeout from the slowest normal job, not the average. Add a heartbeat for long jobs. Pick the Kafka key on purpose. It decides order and load. A hot key fills one partition while the others sit idle. Count partitions before you scale consumers. More consumers than partitions in one group means some sit idle. Give every queue a dead-letter queue and an alert on it. A dead-letter queue nobody watches is lost data. Write down the guarantee for each topic in its README: at-least-once, the key, and where order holds. "Here is our SQS consumer. Find every point where a crash would cause a message to run twice or be lost. Then make the handler idempotent using the message ID." "Our longest job takes up to 3 minutes. Add a heartbeat that extends the SQS visibility timeout every 60 seconds while the job runs, and stops when it ends." "Write a test that kills our Kafka consumer after it processes a message but before it commits the offset. Assert that the restarted consumer does not create a duplicate row." What to ask the agent Offsets are committed, or messages deleted, only after the work is saved. Look for auto-commit settings that commit on a timer. The idempotency check and the result are saved in one transaction. A check in one step and a write in another can still race. The test really crashes the process between the work and the ack. A clean shutdown proves nothing. The agent did not "fix" duplicates by turning off retries. That only swaps duplicates for lost messages. Ordering code does not assume order across partitions or message groups. What to check yourself Before this: Idempotency, retries and timeouts. Next: Kafka internals, and sagas, the outbox pattern and CDC for writing to a database and a queue together. Schema evolution and encoding covers changing the format of messages that are already in the log. Exactly-once and effectively-once shows how to process each message once, and event-driven architecture and event sourcing when to keep events as the source of truth.

title: Quorums and leaderless replication
text: In a leaderless store, you choose how many copies must answer each read and write. Learn what that number buys you, and the cases where it still returns the wrong data.
body: On 29 July 2019, at about 13:10, some Monzo customers could not log in. Some could not send or receive payments. Some saw wrong balances. Monzo kept its data in one Cassandra cluster of 21 servers. Every piece of data had 3 copies. Every read and write used quorum, so at least 2 of the 3 copies had to answer. That day, the team added 6 servers for more capacity. A setting, auto_bootstrap, was false. The team believed the new servers would wait, inactive, until data was copied to them. Instead, they took ownership of some keys at once and started answering queries. They held none of the data. For some keys, two or three of the three copies now lived on empty servers. A quorum read could then get both of its answers from empty servers. To the app, the data looked missing. Monzo had tested the change, but with one new server, not six. With one empty server, the other two copies still formed a quorum. In their words, "What we failed to account for was quorum". Most customers were working again by 15:08, after the team removed the new servers one by one. All were fixed by 23:00. In replication you met the leader model, and leaderless replication in one paragraph. Here is the full picture. In a leaderless store, there is no single node that orders writes. Each key lives on N nodes. A coordinator node sends every write to all N copies and waits for W of them to say yes. A read waits for R answers. Cassandra keeps the one with the newest timestamp. Dynamo can return several versions (more below). If W + R > N, the copies you read and the copies you wrote must share at least one node. So the read sees the write. Amazon's common setting was N = 3, R = 2, W = 2. The key idea. W + R > N only says the two sets of nodes overlap. It does not say those nodes hold the right data, or that everyone agrees on what "newest" means. A quorum is a counting rule, not a promise of linearizability. Step through a write, a read, and four ways a quorum still goes wrong. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Why not a strict quorum? Dynamo was built so that a shopping cart could always take writes. A strict quorum would fail writes when replicas are down or cut off. So Dynamo uses a sloppy quorum. It writes to the first N healthy nodes it can reach, even if they are not the key's usual home. A stand-in node keeps the copy with a hint that names the real owner. When the owner comes back, the stand-in sends the copy over. This is hinted handoff. The cost is clear from the diagram: a reader that reaches only the usual owners can miss the write. Cassandra also stores hints for a replica that is down, for up to 3 hours by default. Its docs say hints are best effort, not a guarantee. Its weakest write level, ANY, accepts a stored hint in place of a replica. At every other level, only real replicas count toward the quorum. Hints just help a replica catch up later. Where else quorums leak A failed write may still be there. A write that reaches only one replica returns an error, but nothing rolls it back. Cassandra's docs say such a write "may be visible in one read, and then disappear" if read repair is off. Concurrent writes. Two clients write the same key at once. Each write reaches a quorum. Someone must now pick a winner, and that rule decides what you lose. Clocks. Cassandra picks the winner by timestamp: last write wins. The timestamp comes from a client clock or the coordinator's clock, so correctness depends on synced clocks. Time, clocks and ordering shows how skew lets an older write win. Membership changes. At Monzo, some keys had two of their three replicas on new, empty servers. The count was right, but the data looked missing. Read repair When a read finds that replicas disagree, the coordinator writes the newest value back to the stale ones. Dynamo calls this read repair. Cassandra does it in the foreground by default. The client waits until the repair is done. The timing matters. Blocking repair gives "monotonic quorum reads": a second quorum read will not return something older than the first. But read repair only fixes keys that someone reads. Cold keys stay out of sync. Anti-entropy with Merkle trees For everything else, replicas compare their data in the background. This is anti-entropy repair. Comparing every key would be slow, so Dynamo uses Merkle trees. A Merkle tree is a tree of hashes. Each leaf is the hash of one key's value. Each parent is the hash of its children. Two nodes swap the root hashes for a key range. If the roots match, the range is in sync. If not, they compare children and walk down only the branches that differ. Cassandra does not run repair for you. You run nodetool repair. Its docs suggest incremental repair every 1–3 days and a full repair every 1–3 weeks as a starting point. Deletes add a hard deadline. With the default 10-day grace period, repair every node at least once every 7 days. Otherwise deleted data can come back. Tunable consistency in Cassandra Cassandra turns R and W into named consistency levels that you set per query. With a replication factor of 3: -- in cqlsh CONSISTENCY QUORUM; -- 2 of 3 replicas must answer SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 42;ONE: one replica answers. Fastest, and it works if any single replica is up. QUORUM: a majority of all replicas, n/2 + 1. QUORUM for both reads and writes gives overlap. LOCAL_QUORUM: a majority in the coordinator's data centre. Reads see the latest write made from the same data centre. ALL: every replica must answer. ScyllaDB rates it highest in consistency and lowest in availability. The write is sent to every replica at any level. The level only sets how many answers the coordinator waits for. Waiting for more answers means waiting for a slower node. Dynamo's paper says latency is set by "the slowest of the R (or W) replicas". Lower levels are faster and keep working with more nodes down. But fewer copies have confirmed the write when you hear yes, so you get weaker consistency and durability. Last write wins or versions? Last write wins keeps one value and drops the others, with no error. If two clients each read a value, change it and write it back, the write with the lower timestamp is lost. Jepsen showed acknowledged writes being lost this way. Early on, Cassandra chose this for speed. Vector clocks usually need a read before each write. Dynamo kept vector clocks instead. When versions are concurrent, it returns all of them and the app merges. A cart then never loses an added item, but deleted items can come back. In practice this was rare. Over 24 hours, 99.94% of requests to the cart service saw exactly one version. With N = 3 replicas. The failure counts are our arithmetic. Choice Survives replicas down Latency What you get W = 1, R = 1 (ONE/ONE) Yes Up to 2. Lowest. One answer each. No overlap. Reads can be stale. W = 2, R = 2 (QUORUM/QUORUM) Yes 1. Waits for the slower of two replicas. Overlap. Still not linearizable. W = 3, R = 1 (ALL/ONE) No for writes. A single node down blocks writes. Writes wait for the slowest replica. Overlap with fast reads. LOCAL_QUORUM, two data centres Yes A whole remote data centre. No cross-region wait. Overlap inside one data centre only. Sloppy quorum Yes Writes rarely fail. Low. Reads can miss writes held by stand-in nodes. Simple rule: start with QUORUM or LOCAL_QUORUM for both reads and writes. Drop to ONE only for data you can afford to see stale. For a true check-and-set, use something built for consensus, like Raft. Write down N, W and R for every table, and the reason. Check what your driver actually sends. Defaults differ; cqlsh uses ONE. Treat a timeout as "unknown", not "failed". Make writes idempotent so a retry is safe. Ask, "What happens if two clients write this key at once?" If the answer is "one is lost", use a version check, a merge, or a new key per change. Check that repair runs, and finishes, inside the tombstone grace period. Alert when it does not. Treat adding or removing nodes as a risky change. Rehearse it at production scale, and watch "row not found" rates while it runs. After its outage, Monzo planned alerts on sharp shifts in "row not found". Monitor clock offset on every node. Last write wins trusts those clocks. "Here is our Cassandra data access code. For each query, list the consistency level it really uses, including driver defaults. Flag any read and write pair where W + R is not more than the replication factor." "Write an integration test with a 3-node Cassandra cluster. Stop one node, write at QUORUM, start the node, and check that a QUORUM read returns the new value." "This code does read-modify-write on a Cassandra column. Show me how concurrent requests can lose an update, and rewrite it to use a lightweight transaction or a new row per change." What to ask the agent The consistency levels the agent quotes match your Cassandra or ScyllaDB version's docs, and your multi-region layout. Retries after a timeout are safe to repeat. A timed-out write may already be stored. A test that "proves" consistency also covers a stopped node, a slow node and two concurrent writers. One happy run proves nothing. Repair is scheduled, and someone gets alerted if it fails. Any claim that quorums make reads linearizable is removed. They do not. What to check yourself Before this: Replication and Sharding and consistent hashing, which explains the ring that decides where each key lives. Related: CAP, PACELC and consistency models and Time, clocks and ordering. Next: Cassandra in depth, and CRDTs and coordination avoidance.

title: Consensus and Raft
text: Raft lets a small group of servers agree on one list of changes, even when some of them fail. Learn how it works and what it costs.
body: A payouts service runs on two servers. Only the active one may send money to sellers each night. Every second, it writes "I am alive" to a shared table. If the standby sees no update for 10 seconds, it takes over. One night the active server freezes for 15 seconds in a long garbage collection pause. The standby takes over and starts sending payouts. Then the old server wakes up. Nothing tells it that it lost its job, so it carries on. About 300 sellers get paid twice. Each server decided "I am in charge" on its own. This is a split-brain. This story is made up, but the pattern is common. A better timeout will not fix it. The servers need to agree, by majority, on who is in charge. That is consensus. The old server must also check that it is still in charge before it acts. Many systems need one agreed answer: who is the leader now, or which config is current. A consensus algorithm gives it. It lets a group of machines act as one, even if some of them fail. Once the group decides something, the decision is final. The usual shape is a replicated state machine. Each server keeps a log of commands, and every log holds the same commands in the same order. Each server runs them on the same deterministic code, so all end up with the same state. Raft is a consensus algorithm built to be easy to understand. It is equal to Paxos in fault tolerance and speed. The key idea. One leader decides the order. A change counts only when a majority of servers has stored it. Any two majorities share at least one server, so the group can never decide two different things. Roles and terms Each Raft server is in one of three states: leader, follower or candidate. In normal work there is exactly one leader and the others are followers. Followers only answer the leader and candidates. The leader handles all client requests. Raft splits time into numbered Raft terms. Each term starts with an election. If a candidate wins, it is the leader for the rest of that term. There is at most one leader per term. Terms work like a clock that every server can read. Servers send their term in every message. A server that sees a bigger term takes that number, and a leader or candidate goes back to being a follower at once. A request with an old term is rejected. This is how an old leader that wakes up learns that it lost its job. The basic algorithm needs only two kinds of messages. RequestVote is sent by candidates. AppendEntries is sent by the leader to copy log entries. An AppendEntries with no entries is a heartbeat. Elections The leader sends heartbeats to every follower. If a follower hears nothing for one election timeout, it assumes there is no leader. It moves to the next term, becomes a candidate, votes for itself, and sends RequestVote to all other servers. A candidate wins if a majority of the full cluster votes for it in that term. Each server votes for at most one candidate per term, first come, first served. So two candidates cannot both win the same term. The winner sends heartbeats at once to stop new elections. What if two followers time out together and split the votes? Nobody wins, and they try again in a new term. To make this rare, Raft picks each election timeout at random from a fixed range. The paper uses 150–300 ms as an example. Usually one server times out first, wins and sends heartbeats before the others time out. Step through an election. Now stop the leader yourself and watch a follower take over. Copying the log A client sends a command to the leader. The leader adds it to its log, then sends AppendEntries to all followers at the same time. Each log entry stores the command, its position (the index) and the term in which the leader got it. An entry is committed once the leader that created it has stored it on a majority of servers. Then it is safe to run on the state machines. The leader sends its commit index, the highest committed index, in every AppendEntries, so followers learn which entries they may apply. Each AppendEntries also carries the index and term of the entry just before the new ones. If the follower does not have that exact entry, it refuses. The leader then steps back one entry and tries again, until the two logs match. The follower deletes anything after that point and takes the leader's entries. This check gives the Log Matching rule: if two logs share an entry with the same index and term, they match up to that point. The safety rule What stops a server with an old log from becoming leader and deleting committed entries? The vote itself. RequestVote includes the candidate's last log index and term. A server refuses to vote for a candidate whose log is less up to date than its own. "More up to date" means a later term on the last entry. If the last terms are equal, the longer log wins. A candidate needs a majority, and every committed entry lives on a majority. So at least one voter has every committed entry, and that voter blocks a candidate that lacks one. A new leader cannot treat an old entry as committed just because a majority holds it. It counts majorities only for entries from its own term. 3 servers or 5 A Raft group works while a majority of its servers are up and can talk, so five servers survive any two failures. If more fail, the group stops making progress, but it never gives a wrong answer. Servers Majority Failures you survive 3 2 1 4 3 1 5 3 2 7 4 3 A 4th server adds no failure tolerance. etcd recommends an odd number of members, and probably no more than seven. Consul recommends 3 or 5 servers. What it costs In the normal case, a command finishes after one round of messages to a majority. Each of those messages usually waits for a disk write. The paper says this round trip may take 0.5–20 ms, based on the storage. Servers in different data centres make each request slower. More members also make writes slower, because data goes to more machines. When the leader crashes, the group is unavailable for about one election timeout. Reads need care too. A leader that answers from memory may already be replaced, so for fresh reads it first checks with a majority. Our advice: put small, important data in Raft, like leaders, config, locks and metadata. Not every user event. Where it runs etcd is built on Raft. Its leader handles all requests that need consensus. Consul servers use Raft. The log holds changes like new nodes, registered services and key-value updates. CockroachDB splits data into ranges. Each range has three or more copies, and they run their own Raft group. TiKV splits data into Regions. The copies of each Region form a Raft group. Kafka used to rely on ZooKeeper's consensus protocol. Its replacement, from KIP-595, is "a sort of Raft dialect": Kafka's own log copying plus Raft's leader election. In KRaft mode, a quorum of controllers keeps the metadata. With 3 controllers it survives 1 failure, and with 5 it survives 2. Paxos and FLP, briefly Paxos, by Leslie Lamport, is the older consensus algorithm. Proposers suggest values and acceptors accept them, in two phases that each need a majority. One run picks one value. For a log, you run one instance per log position, with a leader as the only proposer. Raft gives the same result as this multi-Paxos, but is easier to learn. In 1985, Fischer, Lynch and Paterson studied consensus in an asynchronous system, where messages can take any amount of time. They proved that every protocol for it might never finish, even if only one process is faulty. This is called the FLP result. Because of it, a reliable way to elect a leader must use randomness or real time, such as timeouts. In Raft, safety never depends on timing. Only availability does. Option Lose committed writes? Cost Use it when Single leader + async replication Yes A primary crash can lose recent commits. Fast writes. Failover needs a safe way to choose one leader. Most app databases. It is the Postgres default. Raft group (3 or 5 servers) No, while a majority survives. Every write waits for a majority and a disk write. No writes without a majority. Leaders, config, locks, metadata, and databases built on Raft. Leaderless quorums No single order. Apps may need to merge conflicting versions. Any node takes writes. You must design conflict rules. You need writes to always work, like a shopping cart. External coordination service (etcd, Consul, ZooKeeper) No, for data stored in it. Your own database is not protected. One more system to run. Many services may depend on it. You need leader election or locks but do not want to write Raft yourself. Simple rule: do not write your own consensus. Use a tested Raft library or a coordination service. When a design says "only one worker does X", ask: "Who decides that, and what happens to the old one if it wakes up?" If the answer is a timestamp in a table, you have the payouts bug. Run 3 or 5 servers, never 2 or 4. Place them in different failure zones so one outage cannot take a majority. Know what Raft protects. At GitHub in 2018, Orchestrator used Raft for its own decisions. After a 43-second network cut, it still failed MySQL primaries over to the US West Coast. Both coasts ended up with writes the other did not have. Consensus in the tool did not make the database safe. Watch the blast radius of the coordination cluster. Roblox used one Consul cluster for service discovery, health checks, session locking and key-value data. When it failed, Roblox had a 73-hour outage. Measure write latency on the Raft group, and alert on leader changes. If the leader changes often, check disk speed and the network first. "Our cron job runs on 3 pods, and only one may run each night. Show me how to use an etcd lease and election so only the leader runs it. Explain what happens if the leader pauses for 30 seconds." "Here is our Raft cluster config. List the election timeout and heartbeat interval, and check that the heartbeat is much shorter than the election timeout." What to ask the agent The code stops doing leader work as soon as it loses the lease or sees a newer term. It must not finish the batch "just this once". The cluster has an odd number of nodes, spread across failure zones. Any Raft code comes from a tested library. A "simple Raft" from scratch will miss edge cases, like the rule on older-term entries. Reads that must be fresh go through the leader's majority check, not a local read from any member. Monitoring and alerts do not depend on the same coordination cluster they watch. What to check yourself Before this: database replication, failure detection and membership and leader election and leases. Next: ZooKeeper, etcd and coordination, and CAP and consistency models.

title: RAG: retrieval-augmented generation
text: Ground answers in your own documents, check who may read them, and measure retrieval before you blame the model.
body: In November 2022, Jake Moffatt's grandmother died. The same day, Moffatt went to Air Canada's website to book a flight at its lower bereavement fares. Moffatt asked the website's support chatbot about these fares. The chatbot said a passenger who had already travelled could ask for a reduced bereavement rate within 90 days of the ticket date. The words "bereavement fares" in its answer linked to the airline's own policy page. That page said the policy does not apply to requests made after travel is completed. Moffatt trusted the chatbot, booked two flights, and applied for the lower rate within the 90 days. Air Canada staff then said the airline did not allow requests after travel. In an email, an airline representative admitted the chatbot had used "misleading words". At the tribunal, Air Canada argued that it could not be held liable for what its chatbot said. The tribunal said this treats the chatbot as a separate legal entity, and called it "a remarkable submission". It said the airline is responsible for all the information on its website, whether it comes from a static page or a chatbot. It also asked why a customer should have to double-check one part of a website against another. The airline had to pay $812.02: $650.88 in damages, plus interest and tribunal fees. Air Canada gave no information about how its chatbot worked, and the decision does not say how it was built. But the lesson for anyone who ships one is clear. The answer and the policy page disagreed. Our advice: your system must answer from the real policy text, and show the user where the answer came from. A language model alone is not enough for questions about your data. There are three reasons. It has a knowledge cutoff. Every model has a date after which its knowledge is not reliable. Anthropic lists this date for each Claude model. Your price change from last week is not in it. It has never seen your private data. Your policies, tickets and contracts were not in its training data. It can hallucinate. Models sometimes write text that is false, or that does not match the text you gave them. The RAG paper of 2020 described the core problem. When knowledge is stored only in model weights, it is hard to update, and hard to show where a fact came from. Its answer was to add a second memory: a vector index of Wikipedia that the model reads from at answer time. So RAG works like an open-book exam. Your app searches your documents, puts the few passages that matter in the prompt, and the model answers from them with citations. The key idea. In RAG, the model can only be as good as the text you give it. When an answer is wrong, first check whether retrieval found the right text. So treat retrieval as the main part of the system, and measure it. Step through one request with Next and Back. Before any question: index your documents Chunk. Split each document into small pieces. Anthropic says chunks are usually no more than a few hundred tokens. Embed. An embedding model turns each chunk into a vector, a list of numbers. The distance between two vectors measures how related the texts are. Store. Save each vector with its text, its source link, and who may read it. A vector database does this. So does Postgres with pgvector, which supports exact and approximate nearest-neighbour search. At question time Retrieve. Embed the question the same way, and find the top k chunks with the nearest vectors. For how search indexes work in general, see Search systems and inverted indexes. Filter. Drop every chunk the user may not read. Prompt. Put the allowed chunks into the prompt, each with a number. Tell the model to use only these sources and to cite them. Let it say "I don't know" when the sources do not answer. Anthropic's guide lists all three methods to reduce hallucinations. Answer. Show the answer with links to the cited chunks, so the user can check. Hybrid search and re-ranking Vector search finds text with a similar meaning. But embeddings can miss exact matches, such as an error code like "TS-999". BM25 is a keyword ranking function that finds exact words and phrases. Hybrid search runs both and merges the two lists. One way to merge them is reciprocal rank fusion (RRF). Each result gets 1 / (k + rank) from each list, and the points are added up. Elasticsearch uses k = 60 by default. RRF needs no tuning, and the scores from the two lists do not need to be related. For hybrid search, pgvector suggests Postgres full-text search, merged with RRF or a re-ranking model. Re-ranking adds one more step. A re-ranking model scores the top results again, and only the best ones go into the prompt. It adds some latency, and you trade more re-ranked chunks against speed and cost. Chunking choices Chunk size, chunk borders and overlap all change what retrieval finds. A small chunk can lose its meaning. Anthropic's example is a chunk that says revenue grew by 3%, without saying which company or which quarter. Its fix, "contextual retrieval", adds a short note about the whole document to each chunk before indexing. Anthropic measured this on codebases, fiction, ArXiv papers and science papers. The failure rate is the share of relevant chunks missing from the top 20, averaged over these sets. Contextual embeddings plus contextual BM25 cut the top-20 retrieval failure rate by 49%, from 5.7% to 2.9%. Adding re-ranking cut it by 67%, to 1.9%. These are their numbers on their data. Your data will differ, so measure your own. Evaluation: measure, don't guess Test the two halves apart. Retrieval quality. For each test question, write down which chunks should come back. Then measure recall@k: the share of those chunks that appear in the top k. Anthropic's study uses exactly this kind of metric. Answer quality. Is the answer correct, and is every claim backed by a cited chunk? Anthropic's eval guide says to mirror your real task mix, include edge cases, and grade automatically where you can. If a model grades the answers, it suggests using a different model from the one that wrote them. Our advice: start with 30 to 50 real questions from users or support tickets. Add questions where the right answer is "I don't know". Run the set after every change to chunking, the embedding model, top-k or the prompt. Common failures Wrong chunk retrieved. The answer sounds right but cites the wrong policy. Look at the retrieved chunks first. Stale index. The document changed, but the old chunks are still in the index. Re-index on every change, and delete chunks of deleted documents. Prompt injection from documents. A retrieved page can contain hidden instructions. OWASP calls this indirect prompt injection, and says RAG does not fully remove the risk. Mark retrieved text clearly as untrusted data, and give the model only the access and tools it needs. Leaking documents. If the index holds documents for different users, weak access control can leak them. OWASP advises permission-aware vector stores. Filter at retrieval time, not in the prompt. One trap: with approximate indexes in pgvector, a WHERE filter runs after the index scan, so you may get fewer results than you asked for. Cost and latency Each request adds steps: embed the question, search, maybe re-rank, then a longer prompt. More chunks mean more input tokens. Re-ranking costs time but can lower model cost, because the model reads less text. If your whole knowledge base is under 200,000 tokens (about 500 pages), Anthropic suggests you may not need RAG at all. Put it all in the prompt and use prompt caching. This table is our own summary, except where a source is cited. Approach Fresh data Can cite its source Cost and latency Use it when Whole knowledge base in the prompt Yes Edit the text and it is live. Yes More tokens per call. Caching helps. The data is small, under about 200,000 tokens. RAG with vector search Yes, if you re-index on change. Yes Embedding and a search per question. Users ask in their own words, and data is large. RAG with keyword search (BM25) Yes Yes Cheap and fast. Users search for exact codes, names or IDs. Hybrid search plus re-ranking Yes Yes The most steps and the slowest. Both kinds of question, and quality matters most. Fine-tuning No Facts in model weights are hard to update. No The paper calls tracing facts in weights an open problem. Our view: a training run for every change. Our view: to change style or format, not to add facts. Simple rule: start with the simplest design that passes your test set. Add hybrid search or re-ranking only when the numbers show you need it. When an answer is wrong, first ask: "Was the right chunk retrieved?" Log the retrieved chunk IDs for every request so you can answer this. Build the test set before you tune anything. Keep it in the repo and run it in CI. Treat permissions as part of retrieval. Store the access rules next to each chunk, and filter in the query. When a policy changes, re-index it the same day and add a test question for it. Show citations in the user interface. If the model cannot cite a source, it should say it does not know. Ask your team who owns the bot's answers. The tribunal's view was clear: the company does. "Here are 20 real user questions and our docs folder. For each question, list the document sections that should be retrieved. Mark any question our docs cannot answer." "Write a script that runs our RAG pipeline on this test set and prints recall@5 and the retrieved chunk IDs for each question that failed." "Review this retrieval code. Show me every path where a chunk can reach the prompt without the user's permission check." What to ask the agent The expected chunks in the test set are right. Check a sample by hand, because the agent may guess. The permission filter runs inside the search query, before the prompt is built, and a test proves it. The test set includes questions that should get "I don't know". Retrieved text is marked as data in the prompt, and the model has no tools it does not need. You compared numbers before and after each change, not only a few examples. What to check yourself Related lessons: Vector databases and ANN search, Search systems and inverted indexes, Evals for LLM systems, and Guardrails, cost and latency for LLM features.

title: Rate limiting
text: A rate limit says no early and cheaply, so one noisy client cannot take your service down for everyone else.
body: This story is made up, but it is common. A small company sells a public API for sending text messages. Most customers send a few requests a second. One Monday, a new customer starts a data import. Their script has a bug: when a request is slow, it retries at once, in a loop, with no wait. Soon this one customer sends 3,000 requests a second. The API servers pass every request to the database. The database slows down, so requests get slower. Slower requests make the script retry even more. Within ten minutes, every customer sees timeouts. The team blocks the customer by hand, and things recover. Then the next question comes: "Why could one customer do this at all?" There was no rate limit. The service said yes to every request until it could not say anything. A rate limit is a rule like "each API key may make 100 requests a minute". The service counts requests. When a client goes over the limit, the service rejects the extra requests at once, before doing any real work. A rate limit protects you in three ways: Safety. One client, a bug or an attack cannot use all your capacity. Fairness. Every customer gets their share. Cost. You do not pay for work that nobody planned for. The key idea. A fast, cheap "no" is better than a slow "yes" that ends in a timeout. Rejecting early keeps the service healthy for everyone else. Token bucket Picture a bucket of tokens for each client. Each request takes one token. Tokens drip back in at a fixed rate, up to the size of the bucket. If the bucket is empty, the request is rejected. Two numbers set the rule. The bucket size sets the biggest burst. The refill rate sets the average. Stripe uses a token bucket for its main limiter, with the buckets stored in Redis. Step through a burst. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Now try it yourself. Change the bucket size and refill rate, then send a burst. Leaky bucket A leaky bucket smooths traffic instead of allowing bursts. Requests join a queue, and the queue drains at a fixed rate. When the queue is full, new requests are rejected. NGINX's limit_req module uses this method. With rate=1r/s burst=5, NGINX lets through 1 request a second on average. Up to 5 extra requests wait in line, and more than that get an error. With nodelay, the queued requests are not delayed. By default the error is 503, but you can change it with limit_req_status. Set it to 429, so clients know they hit a limit. Fixed window Count requests per client per minute. The key could be user42:12:01. When the minute ends, start a new counter. In Redis this is a few lines: INCR the key and set it to expire. It is cheap and easy to explain to customers. But the edges are weak. With a limit of 100 a minute, a client can send 100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 more at 12:01:00. That is 200 requests in two seconds. Sliding window A sliding window log stores the time of every request. To decide, it counts the times in the last 60 seconds. It is exact, but it stores one entry per request, which uses a lot of memory for busy clients. A sliding window counter keeps only two counters: this minute and last minute. It guesses the rate by weighting last minute's count by how much of it is still inside the window. Cloudflare gives an example. The limit is 50 a minute. Last minute had 42 requests, and this minute has 18 so far, 15 seconds in. The estimate is 42 × 0.75 + 18 = 49.5, just under the limit. It is only an estimate. But on 400 million requests, Cloudflare found just 0.003% were wrongly allowed or wrongly limited. Limits across many servers If each server counts in its own memory, the limit multiplies. With 20 servers and a limit of 100, a user can make up to 2,000 requests. So most teams keep counters in a shared store like Redis. Be careful with races. If you INCR a key and set its expiry in a separate step, a crash between them can leave the key with no expiry. Redis suggests MULTI/EXEC or a small Lua script, so both happen together. A shared store adds a network call to every request, so it can become a bottleneck. Envoy's answer is a separate rate limit service, plus a local token bucket on each proxy. Its reference service uses Redis. The local limit absorbs large bursts and cuts the load on the shared service. What if the limiter itself fails, because of a bug or because Redis goes down? Stripe's advice is to fail open: catch errors at all levels and let the request through. The limiter should never become the outage. Where to enforce it At the edge or API gateway. Reject by IP address or API key before any real work. This is cheap and stops floods early. In the service. The service knows the user, their plan and how costly each call is. A search can cost much more than a read by ID. Our advice is to use both: a coarse limit at the gateway and finer limits in the service. Per-user and global limits A per-user limit keeps things fair. A global limit protects a shared resource, such as the database, whoever the traffic comes from. Stripe runs four kinds. A request rate limiter caps each user's requests per second. A concurrent requests limiter caps how many requests can run at once, such as 20. Two load shedders protect the whole system: one keeps capacity for critical requests, and the other sheds traffic when workers are overloaded. Telling the client The HTTP status for this is 429 Too Many Requests. The response may include a Retry-After header that says how long to wait. Retry-After can be a number of seconds, like Retry-After: 120, or a date. Tell clients their budget too. GitHub's REST API sends headers like x-ratelimit-remaining and x-ratelimit-reset. A logged-in user gets 5,000 requests an hour. After a primary limit, GitHub says to wait until the reset time. After a secondary limit, wait for retry-after if sent. Otherwise wait for the reset time, or at least one minute. Algorithm Allows bursts? Memory per client Accuracy Use it when Token bucket Yes, up to the bucket size. Two numbers. Good. Most APIs. Clients are bursty but you want a fair average. Leaky bucket No Output is smooth. A queue. Good. You must protect a backend that needs a steady rate. Fixed window Yes, up to 2x at window edges. One counter. Weak at the edges. Simple limits, like daily quotas. Sliding window log Up to the limit, never more in any window. One entry per request. Exact. Low limits where exactness matters, like login attempts. Sliding window counter Up to about the limit. Two counters. Close estimate. High traffic, many clients. Our simple rule: use a token bucket per API key in a shared store, plus a coarse limit at the gateway. Ask about every public endpoint: "What stops one client from using all of it?" Choose the key with care: API key, user, account or IP address. Many users can share one office IP address. Dark launch a new limit first. Log who would be blocked, then turn it on. Stripe does this, and adds a kill switch. Put limits in your API docs. Send 429 with Retry-After, and headers that show what is left. Alert when limits fire a lot. It can mean an attack, a client bug or a limit that is too low. Treat limiting a customer as a product decision, with an owner and a clear process. In 2023, an unapproved throttle applied by hand made one Cloudflare customer's site unusable. It stayed on for almost 13 hours. Afterwards, Cloudflare said such actions would need several levels of approval. See the incident. Check your own clients: they should back off with jitter, not retry in a loop. "Add a token bucket rate limiter to this API, per API key, stored in Redis. Use a Lua script so the check and the update happen together. Return 429 with Retry-After." "Write tests for the limiter: a burst up to the bucket size passes, the next request gets 429, and one request passes after one refill interval." "Make the limiter fail open if Redis is down or slow for more than 20 ms. Log and count every fail-open." What to ask the agent The read and the update of the counter happen in one atomic step, not two. Every Redis key has an expiry, so idle clients do not fill memory. The limit key is right: per API key, not per server, and not shared by accident. Retry-After is in seconds and matches when a token will really be free. The agent did not use the server's local clock in a way that breaks across many servers. What to check yourself Related lessons: API gateways, Load shedding, Backoff and jitter and Redis in depth.

title: WebSockets, SSE and long polling
text: How a server can push live updates to apps, and how to pick between long polling, Server-Sent Events and WebSockets.
body: A food delivery app adds live order tracking. When the restaurant marks an order as "cooking" or the rider moves, the phone should update at once. The team picks WebSockets and builds it in two weeks. On a laptop, it works well. In production, two problems appear. First, many phones show "Reconnecting…" again and again. The team finds that their nginx proxy closes any connection that is quiet for 60 seconds. A cooking order can be quiet for ten minutes. Second, some users never see "rider picked up". The team runs four WebSocket servers. The update is created on server 1, but the user's phone is connected to server 3. Server 1 has no idea that server 3 holds the user. The fix takes another two weeks: ping frames every 30 seconds, and a Redis pub/sub channel per order. This story is made up, but both problems are real and well documented. Normal HTTP is request and response. The client asks, and the server answers. The server cannot speak first. For live updates, like chat, scores or a rider on a map, you need the server to push. There are four common ways to do this: Short polling: the client asks "anything new?" every few seconds. Simple, but most answers are empty, and updates wait until the next ask. Long polling: the client asks, and the server holds the request until there is news or a timeout. Then the client asks again. Server-Sent Events (SSE): the client opens one HTTP response that never ends. The server keeps writing events into it. Data flows only from server to client. WebSocket: the client starts with an HTTP request and asks to "upgrade". After that, one connection stays open, and each side can send at any time. The key idea. Pushing data means holding a connection open for every user. The hard part is not the protocol. It is keeping millions of open connections alive, routed and fed at the right speed. Step through one chat message, delivered three ways. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Long polling. The server answers only when an event happens or a timeout ends. The client then sends a new request, usually at once. Every poll is a full HTTP message with headers. In the worst case, a message waits more than three network trips, because it can arrive just after a response left. RFC 6202 says a timeout of about 30 seconds is safer than longer ones, which proxies may cut. SSE. The browser calls new EventSource("/events"). The server answers with the type text/event-stream and writes lines like data: hello, with a blank line after each event. Each event can carry an id. If the connection drops, the browser reconnects by itself and sends the last id in a Last-Event-ID header. The server can then send what the client missed. The client cannot send events on this connection. To send data, use normal requests, such as POST. WebSocket. The client sends an HTTP Upgrade request. The server answers 101 Switching Protocols, and from then on, either side can send frames at any time. RFC 6455 leaves reconnecting to the client. It says clients should wait a random time before the first reconnect, then use backoff. There is also no built-in "what did I miss", so you design that yourself. Proxies and load balancers. Anything between the app and your server can break a long-lived connection. Upgrade is a hop-by-hop header, so a reverse proxy does not pass it on by default. In nginx you must set the Upgrade and Connection headers yourself. nginx closes a proxied connection if the server sends nothing for 60 seconds. You can raise proxy_read_timeout, or send ping frames. Some old proxies drop quiet HTTP connections too. The SSE spec suggests a comment line, starting with :, about every 15 seconds. Proxies may also buffer a whole response before they send any of it, which breaks streaming. Heartbeats. A WebSocket ping frame can work as a keepalive or as a check that the other side still answers. The other side must reply with a pong. Heartbeats do two jobs: they keep proxies from closing quiet connections, and they find dead connections, so you can free their memory. HTTP/2. Without HTTP/2, MDN says a browser allows only 6 SSE connections per domain, across all tabs. So a few open tabs can use them all up. Over HTTP/2, the browser and server agree on a stream limit, and the default is 100. RFC 8441 lets a WebSocket run on one HTTP/2 stream instead of its own TCP connection. Scaling many open connections. Each user now holds a connection to one server. Two things follow. Routing. A WebSocket stays on the server where it started. Long polling sends many separate requests, so they need sticky sessions to reach the server that holds the client's state. Fan-out. One event must reach every user who cares, but those users sit on many servers. You put a pub/sub layer in the middle. Each server subscribes to the topics of its own users, and passes messages down their connections. Socket.IO calls this an adapter, and Redis is one option. Slack does this at large scale. Gateway servers in many regions hold the users' WebSockets. A channel server, found by consistent hashing, sends each message to every gateway with a subscriber. Each gateway then sends it to its own clients. At Discord, each WebSocket gets its own session process. Anything published in a guild goes to every session connected to it. Backpressure for slow clients. A phone on a weak network reads slowly. If the server keeps sending, messages pile up in memory. MDN says the plain browser WebSocket interface has no backpressure. Fast messages can fill memory or use all the CPU. On the sending side, bufferedAmount shows the bytes queued by send() that are not yet on the network. Watch your server's queue per connection. When it grows too large, drop old updates, merge them, or close the connection and let the client resync. Discord learned how slow parts spread. During peak hours, some guild processes could not keep up with their message queues. In another case, session processes grew their message queues until the whole Erlang VM ran out of memory. Option Direction Reconnect and missed events Proxies and load balancers Use it when Short polling Client asks Yes Each ask is fresh. Easy. Plain requests. Updates are rare, and a delay of seconds is fine. Long polling Server to client, one answer per request Yes Next request picks up. Needs sticky sessions with many servers. Header cost on every message. A fallback for networks that block other options. SSE Server to client only Yes Built in, with Last-Event-ID. Plain HTTP. Use HTTP/2, or six tabs can use up the browser limit. Feeds, scores, notifications, streaming AI answers. WebSocket Both ways No You build reconnect and catch-up. Proxy must pass Upgrade. Idle timeouts need pings. Chat, games, shared editing: the client sends often too. Simple rule: if only the server talks, start with SSE. Choose WebSocket when the client also sends often. Keep long polling as a fallback. Ask first: "How fast must the update arrive, and who talks?" A ten-second delay may be fine with plain polling. Plan "what did I miss" from day one. Give events an id, and let the client ask for everything after its last id. Check every hop: CDN, load balancer, proxy. Ask: "What is the idle timeout here?" Set your heartbeat below the smallest one. Treat connections as a resource. Count open connections per server, and alert on sudden drops. After a deploy or outage, every client reconnects at once. Add random jitter to reconnect delays. Keep connection servers thin. They hold sockets and forward messages. Business logic lives in normal services. Load test with real numbers of idle connections, not only with requests per second. "Write an SSE endpoint in Node for order status. Send an id with each event, support Last-Event-ID, and send a comment line every 15 seconds." "Review this WebSocket client. Does it reconnect with backoff and jitter? Does it fetch missed events after a reconnect?" "We run 6 WebSocket servers behind a load balancer. Design the pub/sub layer with Redis so a message reaches users on any server." What to ask the agent The proxy config passes Upgrade and Connection, and the idle timeout is longer than the heartbeat. The server sends heartbeats, and closes connections that stop answering. Reconnect has a limit, backoff and jitter. A loop with a fixed one-second delay can flood your servers after an outage. Each connection has a send queue with a maximum size. Agents often write socket.send() in a loop with no limit. The client sends an auth token on connect, and the server checks that the user may see each topic. What to check yourself HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC: why many streams on one connection matter. Presence and real-time fan-out: sending one event to millions of users. Backpressure and flow control: what to do when a reader is slower than a writer.

title: Reconciliation
text: How to match your ledger against provider reports and bank statements, sort every difference, and fix it without rewriting history.
body: In May 2024 thousands of people suddenly could not touch their money. According to a later complaint by the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), some waited more than eight months. They used apps built on Synapse, which connected fintech apps to the banks that held the money. The complaint describes the setup. Synapse told several partner banks where to move customer money. According to the CFPB, Synapse was responsible for tracking where each customer's money was. It also had to make sure its records matched the banks' records. The complaint says they did not match. As early as September 2023, one bank held less money than Synapse's records said it should. The bank and Synapse blamed each other for the gap. Synapse filed for bankruptcy in April 2024. In May 2024, the complaint says, Synapse stopped sending one bank the daily ledger reports it used to send. The bank also lost access to a dashboard of customer balances. On 11 May that bank froze all activity for end users. According to the complaint, the banks together held less money than Synapse's records showed. The court-appointed trustee estimated the gap at $60 to $90 million. Two banks hired outside help to reconcile and confirm each balance. They used their own records, Federal Reserve records and records from the trustee. The CFPB alleged that Synapse failed to keep adequate records of where consumers' money was. It also alleged that Synapse failed to make sure those records matched the banks' records. The case was settled when the court entered an order on 12 September 2025. Synapse's bankruptcy trustee agreed to it without admitting or denying the allegations. Records that nobody compares can drift apart for months. This lesson is about the daily check that catches the gap early. Your system keeps its own record of money: orders, payments and a ledger. But you do not hold the money. A payment provider and a bank do. They keep their own records. Reconciliation means comparing your records with theirs, line by line, and explaining every difference. A difference is called a reconciliation break. Usually you compare three sides: Your ledger. What you think happened. The provider's report. What Stripe, Adyen or another provider says it processed, and what it kept as fees. The bank statement. What actually arrived in your bank account. Each pair must agree. If two agree and the third does not, you know where to look. The key idea. Your ledger is only a claim. Reconciliation proves the claim against outside records every day. Every break gets a type, an owner and an age, and you fix it with new entries, never by editing old ones. Step through one day of card payments. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Step 1: Load the outside files Providers send settlement reports. Stripe's payout reconciliation report lists every payment, refund, dispute and fee inside each payout. You can get the same list from the API: list balance transactions and filter by the payout id. Adyen creates a settlement details report, by default one per merchant account per batch. Banks send statements. Many US banks send BAI2 files. Banks usually send one every day with posted transactions, and more during the day with pending ones. Another standard format is camt.053, the ISO 20022 XML bank-to-customer statement. Adyen and Circle, for example, provide statements in it. Turn every file into one shape: id, amount in minor units, currency, date, type. Watch the units. Stripe's report gives amounts in major units, like dollars, not cents. Step 2: Match on keys Match on exact ids first. Store the provider's id on your payment row when you create it. Adyen's PSP reference is a 16-character, globally unique id. Its report also carries your own merchant reference from the payment request. Stripe's itemised report has balance_transaction_id by default. You can add columns such as payment_intent_id and charge_id. The payout must then match the bank deposit. Stripe's report can include a trace_id, which banks use to find a transfer. It can also include a reference that appears on your bank statement. Some money arrives with no id you know, like a customer's bank transfer. Then you match on amount, currency and a date window. Modern Treasury's "expected payments" work this way. You give an amount range and a date range, and the date range can be at most 75 days (200 for cheques). Keep windows tight, or you get false matches. Step 3: Compare amounts, then sort the breaks A matched pair can still disagree. Compare gross, fee and net separately. In Adyen's report, the commission should be the difference between the gross and net amounts. For some acquirers it is split into markup, scheme fee and interchange columns instead. Your ledger should record the fee as its own entry, so the net is never a surprise. Common break types: Missing on your side. The provider has a payment your ledger never recorded. A lost webhook is a common cause. Missing on their side. You recorded a payment the provider does not show. Amount or currency mismatch. Same id, different numbers. Duplicate. The same id appears twice on one side. A retry without an idempotency key is a common cause. Timing. The item will appear, but in the next file. Stripe groups a payout by its estimated arrival date, not by the date your bank posts it. Report data can also be ready after the money arrives. Fees and other provider entries. Disputes and failed payouts show up as their own balance transactions. FX. Adyen's report has an exchange rate column. It is 1 when you process and settle in the same currency. Finally, check the statement against itself. The opening balance plus all entries must equal the closing balance. If it does not, something is wrong. The file may be incomplete, or your parser may have read it wrongly. Do not reconcile against it. Step 4: Work the break queue Put every break in a queue with a type, an owner and an age. Many breaks follow known patterns, so write auto-fix rules for them. A timing break can wait one cycle. A missing fee can post a fee entry. Everything else goes to a person. Stripe's Ledger team tracks "Aging Balances" for problems that persist over time. Its tooling lets people move a problem to the right owner. Stripe also checks that every id in a source system has a matching ledger event. The fix is always a new ledger entry: an adjustment or a reversal, linked to the break. You never edit or delete history. Money you cannot explain yet sits in a suspense account with an owner, not in revenue. Option Catches problems Cost Use it when Daily batch recon on final files Yes, but up to a day late. Low. Simple jobs on files that do not change. Always. This is the base layer. Near real-time recon on webhooks and intraday data Yes Within minutes. Higher. Data is pending and may change, so you get more false breaks. High volume, instant payouts, or tight cash. Exact id matching Yes Very few false matches. You must store provider ids on day one. Card and provider payments. Amount and date window matching Partly. Can match the wrong item. Needs tuning and manual review. Bank transfers with no shared id. Manual payouts Only if you do the work. Stripe cannot tell you which transactions a manual payout covers. Rarely. Prefer automatic payouts if you can. Simple rule: reconcile every day on final data, match on stored ids, and treat any break older than its window as an incident. Real-time recon helps, but it does not replace the daily run, because final statements still arrive once a day. Circle, for example, delivers one camt.053 file per UTC day, by 06:00 UTC the next day. Stripe sends a reporting.report_type.updated webhook when new report data is ready. Use that event to start the job, not a fixed clock. In a design review, ask: "Which provider id do we store on this row, and when?" If the answer is "we look it up later", ask for the id to be stored when the row is created. Ask: "What are the three sides here, and who owns each one?" A missing side is a missing control. Write the expected window for each break type in the code: timing breaks may wait one cycle, missing payments must not. Alert on the count and value of breaks older than their window, per currency. Also alert when an expected file does not arrive. Require a second person to approve manual adjustments above a set amount. Log who approved each one. After any bug fix that touched money, run the full recon again. Old breaks should close, and no new ones should open. "Write a parser for this Stripe itemised payout reconciliation CSV. Convert amounts from major units to integer minor units using each row's currency. Add tests for a zero-decimal currency." "Given these two tables, ledger_entries and provider_report_lines, write SQL that lists rows found on only one side, rows with the same id but different amounts, and ids that appear twice." "Design a break queue table with type, owner, age, status and a link to the fixing ledger entry. Explain how a break is closed." What to ask the agent Amounts are integers in minor units after parsing. No floats. The matcher uses exact ids before any fuzzy rule. Fuzzy windows are small and logged. Duplicates are found, not silently merged. Fixes create new ledger entries. The agent did not write an UPDATE on old entries. Timezones and cut-off times match the provider's and bank's files. A missing or empty file raises an alert. It must not count as "zero breaks". What to check yourself Money and double-entry ledgers: entries, reversals and clearing accounts that should return to zero. The payment lifecycle: authorization, capture, settlement and payout, the steps that create the files you reconcile. Idempotency, retries and timeouts: how to stop the duplicates before they become breaks.

title: Redis in depth
text: Redis runs your commands one at a time on one thread. Learn what that buys you, what it costs, and what Redis can lose.
body: On 20 March 2023, OpenAI took ChatGPT offline. Some users could see titles from another active user's chat history. Later it found something worse. In the hours before the shutdown, some users could see another active Plus user's name, email address, payment address and the last four digits of their card. OpenAI says this may have affected 1.2% of Plus subscribers active in a nine-hour window. ChatGPT cached user data in Redis Cluster. Its Python servers used the asyncio version of the redis-py client, with a shared pool of connections. If a request was cancelled after it was sent, but before its reply was read, the connection kept that reply. The next, unrelated request on the connection read it instead. Usually this caused an error. Sometimes the data looked valid, so one user got another user's cached data. The bug report shows the same thing: after a cancelled GET foo, the next GET bar returned foo's value. At 1 a.m. Pacific time that day, a server change caused a spike in cancelled Redis requests. One fix OpenAI added: check that data from the cache belongs to the user who asked. The bug was in the client library, not in the Redis server. To use Redis well, you need to know exactly what it promises, and what it doesn't. Redis keeps your data in memory and runs one command at a time. That one rule explains most of its strengths and its traps. Fast and simple. Each command runs alone, so a single command is always atomic. INCR never loses an update. Fragile under slow commands. If one command takes two seconds, every client waits two seconds. Memory first, disk second. Data reaches disk later, by your choice of settings. A crash can lose recent writes. Copies are late. Replicas get writes after the primary replies. A failover can lose writes that clients saw succeed. The key idea. Redis is safe for one command and fast for small ones. Ask of every use: how long does each command take, and what happens to my data if this node dies right now? One thread runs every command The docs call Redis "mostly single threaded". One main thread serves all requests, one after another, using an event loop. Normal commands like GET, SET and LPUSH take a tiny, constant time. Commands that touch many elements do not. Step through what one slow command does to everyone else. The usual suspects: KEYS. The docs call it "a VERY common source of latency" in production. Use SCAN, which walks the keys in small steps. Deleting a huge key. DEL frees memory on the main thread. For a value with millions of elements, it "can block for a long time (even seconds)". UNLINK frees it in the background instead. Long scripts. A Lua script blocks every other client while it runs. More on that below. Forking for persistence. Saving a snapshot needs a fork(). On a big dataset, Redis may stop serving clients for milliseconds, or even a second. Find them with the slow log (SLOWLOG GET). What about I/O threads? Since Redis 6.0, I/O threads can read requests, parse them and write replies. The main thread still runs every command. Redis kept this rule on purpose, to avoid races. They are off by default. The config file suggests them only on machines with 4 or more cores, and only if you have a real performance problem. I/O threads help with many busy connections. They do nothing for one slow command. Atomic groups: MULTI/EXEC, WATCH and scripts MULTI/EXEC queues commands and runs them together. No other client's command runs in the middle. But there is no rollback. If one command fails at run time, the others still run. In Redis, atomic means nothing else runs in the middle. It does not mean that failed work is undone. WATCH adds a check-and-set. If a watched key changes before EXEC, the whole transaction aborts and EXEC returns null. You retry. This is the optimistic locking from the concurrency control lesson, in Redis form. Lua scripts can read, decide and write in one atomic step. The docs say a script is usually "both simpler and faster" than a transaction. Here a script takes stock only if enough is left: -- KEYS[1] = stock key, ARGV[1] = amount local left = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0') if left < tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return -1 end return redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])Pass every key name in KEYS. Never build key names inside the script. Redis needs this to run scripts correctly, and Redis Cluster needs it most. Since Redis 7.0, functions let you load scripts into the server as named, first-class code. The price of atomic is blocking. A script past the busy limit (five seconds by default) is not stopped. Other clients get BUSY errors. If the script has already written, only SHUTDOWN NOSAVE ends it. So no loops over big data inside scripts. Pick the structure that fits Sorted sets keep members ordered by score. The docs list leaderboards and sliding-window rate limiters as uses. Adding or updating a member costs O(log N). Streams act like an append-only log, for events in order. For when to pick a log over a queue, see queues vs logs. HyperLogLog estimates unique counts, like unique visitors, in at most 12 KB, with a 0.81% standard error. What a crash can lose Redis has two ways to reach disk. An RDB snapshot is a point-in-time copy, written by a forked child. You usually save one every few minutes, so be ready to lose "the latest minutes of data". The append-only file (AOF) logs every write. Its appendfsync setting decides how often Redis calls fsync: always, everysec (the default) or no. With everysec you may lose 1 second of data. With no, Linux usually flushes every 30 seconds. If the disk is slow, everysec can lose up to about 2 seconds. The docs suggest both together if you want safety close to PostgreSQL. When memory is full maxmemory caps the data size. On 64-bit systems the default is 0, which means no limit. The default policy, noeviction, returns an error for writes that would add data when memory is full. Reads still work. For a cache, allkeys-lru is a good default, as in caching stampedes. The volatile-* policies only evict keys with a TTL, so with no TTLs they act like noeviction. Replication and AOF buffers are not counted, so leave some RAM free. Copies, failover and shards Replication is asynchronous. The primary replies to you, then sends the write to replicas. WAIT n timeout blocks until n replicas acknowledge your earlier writes, or until the timeout. It returns how many did, so check that number. It "does not make Redis a strongly consistent store". A write that reached replicas can still be lost in a failover. min-replicas-to-write, with min-replicas-max-lag, limits the loss window to a few seconds. It does not remove it. Sentinel watches a primary and its replicas. It promotes a replica when the primary fails, and tells clients the new address. Run at least three Sentinels. The docs describe the result as "last failover wins": there is always a window for losing acknowledged writes. Redis Cluster also shards data. Each key maps to one of 16,384 hash slots: CRC16 of the key, modulo 16384. Multi-key commands, transactions and scripts work only if all keys share a slot. A hash tag forces this: user:{123}:profile and user:{123}:account land together. Cluster can also lose acknowledged writes, through async replication or a network partition. Locks in Redis, and the Redlock debate The simple lock is one command: SET lock:job42 <random-value> NX PX 30000. Release it with a script that deletes the key only if the value is still yours. On one primary with a replica, a failover can hand the same lock to two clients. The write may not have reached the replica yet. Redlock answers this. A client takes the lock on a majority of, say, 5 independent primaries, within the lock's validity time. Martin Kleppmann argued that Redlock depends on timing assumptions: bounded network delay, process pauses and clock error. A clock jump can let two clients hold the lock. His advice: for efficiency, one Redis node is enough. For correctness, use fencing tokens and a consensus system such as ZooKeeper. The locks lesson covers the pause problem. Salvatore Sanfilippo (antirez), who wrote Redis, replied. If your storage can check tokens, he says, "you probably don’t need a distributed lock at all". A unique random token with check-and-set can work too. He pointed out that Redlock checks the time again after it gets the majority. He also said pauses after that point hurt "all the distributed locks implementations". On clocks, he replied that Redlock does not need synchronized clocks. Processes only need to count time at about the same speed. He said ops teams can avoid big clock jumps: don't set clocks by hand, and use an ntpd that spreads changes out. He did agree Redis should move to monotonic time. But he found no other point that broke Redlock's safety, and he rejected the advice to stop using it. Today the Redis docs point readers to both posts. They tell you to use fencing tokens, and warn that TTLs do not use a monotonic clock. Persistence setting What a crash can lose Cost Use it when None Everything. Fastest. A restarted empty primary can wipe its replicas. A pure cache you can rebuild.
