RDB snapshots only Minutes of writes. A fork per save, which can pause Redis. Losing a few minutes is fine. AOF, everysec About 1 second of writes. Bigger files, some disk I/O. The usual choice for data you care about. AOF, always Very little. "Very very slow." Rarely. If every write must be on disk, a disk-first database may fit better. RDB + AOF About 1 second, plus easy backups. Both costs. You want safety close to PostgreSQL. Sources: and, for the empty-primary trap, . Ask of every Redis use: "Is this a cache, or the only copy?" Settings for the two are very different. Rename or block KEYS and FLUSHALL for app users with ACLs. Use SCAN and UNLINK in tools and scripts. Watch the slow log and the latency monitor. A CPU-busy Redis with low traffic usually means slow commands. Keep values and collections small. A 5-million-member set is a slow command waiting to happen. Set maxmemory and a policy on purpose. Alert on evictions and on rejected writes. Never turn off persistence on a primary that restarts by itself. It comes back empty, and replicas copy the empty set. For locks, ask: efficiency or correctness? For correctness, the database must check a token or a version. Treat client connections as stateful. On a cancel or timeout, drop the connection. Don't return it to the pool. "Find every Redis call in this repo that is O(N) on a large key or keyspace: KEYS, SMEMBERS, HGETALL, LRANGE 0 -1, DEL on big keys. Suggest SCAN, paging or UNLINK for each." "Rewrite this read-then-write Redis code as one Lua script. Pass all key names in KEYS. Add a test with 50 parallel clients." "Review our Redis config for a cache: maxmemory, maxmemory-policy, persistence and io-threads. Explain each choice for a 16 GB, 4-core machine." What to ask the agent No script loops over a whole collection. Scripts must stay short. Every key the script uses is passed in KEYS, and multi-key operations use hash tags in Cluster. The code checks for a null EXEC and retries. Any lock has a TTL, a unique value, and a safe release. Correctness still rests on a fencing check. A cancelled or timed-out request closes its connection. Nobody assumes WAIT makes a write safe from failover. What to check yourself Before this: Caching stampedes, Rate limiting and Locking and MVCC in practice. Related: Batching and pipelining, Database replication, Sharding and consistent hashing and Consensus and Raft. See also Leader election and leases. Coming later: Leaderboards and live ops.

title: Replication
text: Copies of your data make reads fast and keep you running. They also make users see the past, unless you plan for it.
body: Ravi changes his delivery city from Pune to Delhi in a shopping app. He taps Save and sees "Saved". The page reloads, and the city still says Pune. He taps Save again. Same result. He writes to support: "Your app does not save my address." Five seconds later he refreshes once more, and now it says Delhi. Nothing was lost. The write went to the leader, the one database that takes writes. The page read came from a copy that was 3 seconds behind. The team had added copies last month to handle more reads. Nobody had asked what users would see while a copy catches up. This bug is common, hard to reproduce on a laptop, and easy to prevent once you know its name. Replication means keeping the same data on several machines. You do it for three reasons. Reads can be spread across many machines. A copy can take over if one machine dies. And a copy near the user can answer faster. The most common setup has one leader and some followers. All writes go to the leader. The leader sends each change to every follower, and the followers apply the changes in the same order. Reads can go to the leader or to any follower. The key idea. A follower is a copy of the past. How far in the past is the replication lag. Every read from a follower must be fine with seeing that past. Most of the time the lag is small. Postgres says it is typically under one second when the standby can keep up. But that is not a promise. Our advice: plan for the lag to grow much larger under heavy load, a long query, or a network problem. Step through Ravi's bug. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Now try it yourself. Move the sliders to change the lag and the moment you read. Sync or async The big choice is when the leader says "done" to the client. With synchronous replication, the leader waits until a follower confirms it has the change. By default, Postgres waits until the commit is written to disk on both servers. The cost is at least one network round trip on every commit. With asynchronous replication, the leader says "done" at once and sends the change later. Writes are fast. But if the leader crashes, its newest commits may never have reached a follower. Postgres and MySQL both replicate asynchronously by default, and both docs warn about this data loss. MySQL also has a middle option, semisynchronous replication: the leader waits until at least one replica has received and logged the change. If no replica answers before a timeout, it falls back to async. Lag bugs, and their names Two lag bugs come up again and again. Read-your-writes. After you save something, your own next read should show it. Ravi's bug breaks this. Other users may see the change a bit later, and that is usually fine. Monotonic reads. Your reads should never go back in time. Imagine you refresh twice. The first read hits a fresh follower and shows a new comment. The second hits a slow follower, and the comment is gone. Common fixes: read a user's own recent data from the leader for a short time after they write. Send all of one user's reads to the same follower. Or make the client remember the last version it saw, and skip followers that are behind it. Failover and split-brain When the leader dies, a follower must become the new leader. This is failover. It sounds simple, but each step can go wrong. First, you must decide the leader is dead. You usually use a timeout. Too short, and a slow leader gets replaced for no reason. Second, you pick the follower with the most data. With async replication, some recent writes may be missing. Third, every client must send writes to the new leader. The worst case is split-brain: the old leader is still alive and still takes writes. Now two nodes think they are the leader. Their data goes in two directions. This happened to GitHub in October 2018. A network cut lasted 43 seconds. In that time, their failover tool made database servers on the US West Coast the new leaders. Several seconds of writes on the East Coast never reached the West. Then the West took writes for nearly 40 minutes. Both sides now had writes the other did not have. GitHub chose to keep user data correct over coming back fast. The site was degraded for 24 hours and 11 minutes while they put the data back together. Two other shapes, briefly Multi-leader. Each data centre has its own leader, and the leaders copy to each other. Writes are fast everywhere. But two people can change the same row in two places, and you must resolve the conflict. Leaderless. The client writes to several copies and reads from several copies. Amazon's Dynamo made this popular, and Cassandra works this way. With n copies, you write to w of them and read from r. If w + r > n, at least one copy you read has the latest write. With 3 copies, w = 2 and r = 2 is a common quorum. Setup Lose writes on crash? Cost Use it when Leader + async followers Yes The newest commits may be lost on failover. Fast writes. Stale reads from followers. Most web apps. It is the default in Postgres and MySQL. Leader + one sync follower No, unless both crash at once. Every commit waits for a round trip. If the sync follower is down, writes can stall. Money, orders, anything you must not lose. Multi-leader Yes Conflicts can drop one side's change. You must design conflict rules. Several regions must accept writes, or apps must work offline. Leaderless with quorums Depends on w and r. More copies per request. Edge cases with lag still exist. Very high write volume, and you can live with some stale reads. Simple rule: start with one leader and async followers. Then decide, for each read, whether it may see stale data. For every new read path, ask: "What does the user see if this read is 5 seconds old?" If the answer is "a bug report", read from the leader. Watch replication lag on a dashboard, and alert on it. A follower that is minutes behind is a quiet incident. After a write, send that user's reads to the leader for a short window. Make the window longer than your normal lag. Ask how failover works before you need it. Who decides the leader is dead? What stops the old leader from taking writes? Practise failover in a test environment. Measure how many writes you lose and how long clients take to find the new leader. Know your settings. "Async by default" means a crash can lose your last commits. "We read profiles from a Postgres read replica. Change the code so that for 10 seconds after a user updates their profile, that user's reads go to the primary." "Write an integration test with a primary and a replica where replication is paused. Assert that a user's own profile read after a save shows the new value." "List every query in this service that reads from a replica. For each, tell me what goes wrong if the data is 30 seconds old." What to ask the agent The "read from leader" window really covers your worst normal lag, not just the average. A connection pool or ORM (a library that maps code objects to database rows) did not quietly send writes, or reads inside a transaction, to the replica. Reads that check a rule before a write, like "is the coupon still unused?", go to the leader. The test really pauses or slows replication. A test with zero lag proves nothing. Failover scripts stop the old leader from taking writes before they promote a new one. What to check yourself Next: Transactions and isolation levels. It covers bugs inside one database, even with no copies at all. For how one database does this in practice, see PostgreSQL in depth.

title: Requirements and non-functional needs
text: Ask the questions that turn "fast" and "always up" into numbers for scale, latency, availability, consistency, durability, security and cost, then write them down before you design.
body: A food delivery team got a request from its product manager (PM). Build a live order status page. It "must be fast and always up". Nobody asked what those words meant. The team wrote no numbers down. In testing, the page answered in 120 ms on average. The team used one Postgres database, with a nightly 20-minute maintenance window. It seemed fine. On the first Friday night, traffic was eight times the test load. The average was still under 400 ms. But one request in a hundred took over 6 seconds. Those users refreshed again and again, which added more load. Then a restaurant owner called at 2 a.m. Her kitchen tablets used the same page, and they went blank every night during maintenance. To the PM, "always up" had meant "up whenever a restaurant is open". Some restaurants never close. The fix took a month. It needed a read replica, a cache and a new way to run maintenance. Three questions in the first week would have changed the first design. This story is made up, but each part of it is common. Functional requirements say what users can do: "see the status of my order". Non-functional requirements say how well the system must do it: how fast, for how many people, how often it may fail, and what it may cost. The functional list tells you which parts to build. The non-functional list tells you how to build them. The same feature can be one server or fifty, depending on these numbers. People rarely give you these numbers. They give you words like "fast", "scalable" and "always up". Your job is to turn each word into a number that you can design for and later measure. The key idea. A need you cannot measure is a wish. Ask questions until each one has a number, a way to measure it and a person who agreed to it. Then design for those numbers, and no more. Step through how one vague ask becomes numbers. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Start with the functional requirements, as in the system design method. Then go through the qualities below. Hello Interview gives a checklist of eight areas, including latency, scalability, durability, security and compliance. It advises picking the top 3 to 5 for your system. ISO/IEC 25010:2023, a standard model of software quality, lists nine quality characteristics with sub-characteristics. You do not need all of them. Use them as a list of questions you might forget. Scale Ask: how many users, how many requests per second at the busiest time, and how much data after a year? Ask for the peak, not the daily average. ISO 25010 calls this "capacity": how well the system's maximum limits, such as users or data size, meet the requirements. To turn users into requests per second, see latency numbers and estimation. Latency, as percentiles "Fast" needs a percentile, a load and an operation. An average hides the slow requests. In one example from the Google SRE book, a typical request takes about 50 ms, but "5% of requests are 20 times slower!" A high percentile, such as the 99th, shows "a plausible worst-case value". So write: "99% of GET /orders/:id calls answer in under 300 ms, at 2,000 requests per second". The book's own example has this shape: "99% of Get RPC calls will complete in less than 100 ms." Hello Interview makes the same point. "Low latency" alone is not useful. "Low latency search, < 500ms" names the part and the target. Availability, as nines "Always up" is not a real target. The SRE book calls it "unrealistic". A system that comes close would be slow to build and expensive to run. Ask instead how much downtime users can live with. Count it per month. A month is a common period for availability targets, and a number of minutes per month is easy to picture. These numbers are simple maths over a 30-day month: Target Downtime allowed per month 99% about 7 hours 12 minutes 99.9% about 43 minutes 99.95% about 22 minutes 99.99% about 4 minutes 19 seconds 99.999% about 26 seconds AWS gives example uses for each level: internal tools at 99.9%, online shops at 99.95%, and ATM transactions at 99.999%. Its own table shows downtime per year. AWS also advises that planned maintenance should count as downtime, because users may want the service then. Two more facts change designs. First, hard dependencies multiply. A 99.99% service that needs two other 99.99% services can reach only about 99.97%. Second, more reliability gets expensive fast. The SRE book warns that each improvement in reliability "may cost 100x more than the previous increment". It suggests asking what users expect, whether the service ties to revenue, and whether it is free or paid. To measure availability over time, see observability, SLOs and error budgets. Consistency Ask: after a write, who must see it at once, and who can see old data for a few seconds? A seat sold twice is a real failure. A follower count that is 5 seconds old is not. Hello Interview puts this as the first item on its list: should the system prefer consistency or availability? Answer it for each part, not for the whole system. See CAP, PACELC and consistency models. Durability and recovery Durability is not the same as availability. Amazon S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% durability but 99.99% availability over a year. Your data is very safe, but you may not reach it for a while. For disasters, ask for two numbers. The RPO is the most data, in time, you accept to lose. The RTO is the longest you accept to be down. AWS says the organization defines both, so ask the business, not only engineers. In 2017, GitLab lost about six hours of database changes. Most of its backup methods were broken or never set up, and nobody had noticed. It recovered from a copy made six hours earlier for another purpose. See the GitLab incident. Security and compliance ISO 25010 splits security into parts such as confidentiality, integrity and accountability. Turn each into a question. Who may read this data? Must every change be traced to a person? Is there personal or card data, and which laws apply? Hello Interview lists compliance as its own area. Cost Ask for a budget, even a rough one: "under $2,000 a month in cloud costs". AWS warns that higher availability needs more testing, more automation and slower releases. It advises finding the "true availability needs" before you design. Write them down Put each need in one row: the need, the number, how you will measure it, and who asked for it. Start with a loose target you can tighten later. The SRE book says this is better than a strict target you must relax. Put the table near the top of the design doc. In an interview, the requirements step takes about 5 minutes. Say 3 to 5 needs out loud, each with a number, and write them on the board. Way to state a need Easy to agree? Guides the design? Cost Use it when A word: "fast", "always up" Yes No Rework later, when the words mean different things. Never as the final version. An average: "200 ms on average" Yes Partly. Hides the slowest requests. Only for batch jobs, where the total matters. A percentile at a load: "p99 < 300 ms at 2,000 req/s" Needs a talk. Yes You must measure it in production. Any user-facing request path. A very high target: 99.99% or more Hard. Yes Each nine costs far more. Releases get slower. Payments, or when the business proves it needs it. A loose target you tighten later Yes Yes You may need to rebuild some parts as targets rise. New systems with no traffic data yet. Simple rule: every need gets a number, and every number gets a reason from a user or the business. Ask "what happens to the user if this is slow, or down for 10 minutes?" The answer sets the target better than any guess. Ask for peak load, not average. Ask when the peak happens, such as Friday dinner or a sale at noon. Ask what "always" means. Does it include nights, weekends and planned maintenance? Split the system. The checkout can need 99.95% while the reports page needs 99%. List every hard dependency and its availability. Your target cannot be higher than what they allow. Ask the business for the RPO and RTO. Then test a restore, because a backup you never restored may not work. Write "out of scope" needs as non-goals, for example "no multi-region in version 1". In a review, ask "which need does this part serve?" A cache or a queue with no need behind it is extra cost. "Here is a feature request from my PM. List the questions I should ask about scale, latency, availability, consistency, durability, security and cost. Mark which answers would change the design." "Turn these vague needs into measurable ones. For each, give a number, the operation it applies to, the load, and how I would measure it in production." "My service needs 99.95% and calls these four services. Their targets are listed below. Can my target be met? Show the maths." What to ask the agent Every number came from a person or from data, not from the agent. An agent may invent targets that look plausible. Latency targets name a percentile, an operation and a load, not only an average. The monthly downtime maths is right. Check one row by hand: 43,200 minutes × 0.1% = 43.2 minutes. Durability, RPO and RTO are separate from availability in the list. The list is short. Three to five strong needs beat fifteen weak ones. What to check yourself Before this: the system design method. Next: latency numbers and estimation, observability, SLOs and error budgets, design docs and RFCs and tail latency and queueing.

title: Circuit breakers, bulkheads and fallbacks
text: One slow service can take down every service that calls it. Here is how to keep the damage small.
body: On 12 June 2025, Cloudflare's Workers KV started to fail. KV is a key-value store, and Cloudflare calls it "a critical dependency for many Cloudflare products". Part of the storage behind KV ran on a third-party cloud, and that cloud had its own outage. About 90% of KV requests failed. Reads that hit a cache still worked. The failure did not stay inside KV. Access, Cloudflare's login gate, failed every identity-based login. Dashboard logins failed, and Workers AI could not run models at all. Cloudflare wrote that the cascading impact from KV "significantly broadened the blast radius." Each product's design decided what happened when KV failed. Access and Gateway are designed to fail closed, so they blocked users instead of skipping customer rules. Turnstile turned on kill switches that switch off those failing calls. Users could get through, but a token could be used more than once. At 19:32 UTC, Access and Device Posture dropped requests on purpose to take load off KV. Impact ended at 20:28 UTC. One fix is a tool to bring KV back step by step, without "a denial-of-service against our own infrastructure as caches are repopulated." Every service you call can fail or get slow. If you do nothing, its problem becomes your problem, and then your callers' problem. Four tools keep the damage small: A timeout limits how long one call waits. A circuit breaker stops calling a service that keeps failing, for a short time. A bulkhead limits how many of your threads one dependency can use. Graceful degradation decides what the user gets when the call fails: old data, a default, or a page without that feature. The key idea. A dead dependency fails fast. A slow one holds on to your threads until you have none left. Put a limit on every call: how long it waits, how many calls wait at once, and how long you keep calling a service that is failing. Why slow is worse than dead If a service is down and its machine refuses the connection, you get an error in milliseconds. (If the whole machine is gone, you wait for the connect timeout.) If it is slow, each call holds memory, a thread and a connection while it waits. New requests keep coming, so waiting calls pile up. Say you get 200 requests a second and each makes one call. At 50 ms per call, about 10 calls wait at any moment. At 5 seconds per call, about 1,000 wait. A pool of 200 threads is full in about one second. The Hystrix wiki says that under high traffic, "a single backend dependency becoming latent can cause all resources to become saturated in seconds on all servers." Now your service is slow too, and your callers start to pile up. Fowler calls the result "cascading failures across multiple systems." Timeouts come first You met timeouts in Idempotency and retries. Every remote call needs one. Amazon picks an acceptable rate of false timeouts, such as 0.1%. It then uses that percentile of the downstream latency: the 99.9th percentile. A timeout caps one call. It does not stop you from sending the next call to the same slow service, and the one after that. That is the job of the circuit breaker. The circuit breaker Michael Nygard made this pattern popular in his book Release It!. Martin Fowler's short article describes it well. You wrap the remote call in a breaker object that watches for failures. It has three states: Closed. Calls go through. The breaker counts failures, and a timeout counts as a failure. Open. When failures reach a threshold, the breaker trips. Every call now gets an error at once, and the service is not called at all. Half-open. After a wait, the breaker lets a trial call through. If it works, the breaker closes. If it fails, the breaker opens and waits again. Step through a breaker in front of a ratings service. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Real libraries judge a rate, not a simple count. Hystrix trips only when there are enough requests and the error percentage is over a threshold. After a sleep window, it lets one request through as a test. Resilience4j records the last N calls, or the calls in the last N seconds. It can also trip when too many calls are slow, not only when they fail. That matters, because slow is the dangerous case. An open breaker rejects calls with a CallNotPermittedException. Here is the diagram's setup in Resilience4j. The slow-call setting does not stop a call, so you still need the timeout: // The 1 s timeout is set on the HTTP client (or a TimeLimiter). // The breaker counts the timeout exception as a failure. CircuitBreakerConfig config = CircuitBreakerConfig.custom() .slidingWindowType(SlidingWindowType.COUNT_BASED) .slidingWindowSize(20) // judge the last 20 calls .minimumNumberOfCalls(10) // but only after 10 calls .failureRateThreshold(50) // open at 50% failures .slowCallDurationThreshold(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) .slowCallRateThreshold(50) // or at 50% slow calls .waitDurationInOpenState(Duration.ofSeconds(30)) .permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState(3) .build();The defaults are larger: a window of 100 calls, at least 100 calls before it judges, a 60-second wait and 10 trial calls. A call counts as slow only after 60 seconds, and the breaker trips on slow calls only if all of them are slow. So set both slow-call values yourself. Check them against your traffic. A breaker that needs 100 calls may never trip on a quiet endpoint. Log every state change, and show the breaker's state on your monitoring. Breakers have a cost, as you saw in Error handling. They add a second mode of working, which "can be difficult to test", and they can slow recovery. Amazon limits retries locally instead, as in Backoff, jitter and retry budgets. Bulkheads A ship's hull is split into sealed sections. If one section floods, the others keep the ship afloat. A bulkhead in software does the same for your threads. Give each dependency its own small pool. Hystrix ran a separate thread pool per dependency, so a slow dependency filled only its own pool. Each Netflix API server had more than 40 thread pools, with 5 to 20 threads each, and most had 10. A lighter option is a semaphore: a counter of calls in flight. It costs less than a thread pool. But the caller cannot time out and walk away from a call that hangs. Resilience4j offers both kinds. Its semaphore bulkhead allows 25 calls at once by default, and it does not wait for a free slot. Here is the effect. Your service has 200 threads, and the ratings call gets a bulkhead of 20. When ratings gets slow, 20 calls wait and the 21st is rejected at once. The other 180 threads keep serving other pages, such as checkout. Fallbacks and graceful degradation When a call fails, you still have to send the user something. Serving less instead of failing is graceful degradation. Common choices: Stale data. Show the last cached ratings. A default. Show a safe value from config, such as the standard delivery time. Hide the feature. Show the product page without ratings. Fail. Return a clear error. Cloudflare's Access chose this on purpose, to avoid letting in users it could not check. Hystrix calls code like the first three a fallback. Its advice: a fallback should avoid network calls, and "It is a poor practice to implement a fallback implementation that can fail." Amazon uses the word fallback in a narrower sense: a different mechanism that does the same job. Its example is web servers that read from a database when their cache fails. Amazon almost never uses that kind, because it rarely runs, is hard to test and can make an outage worse. Error handling tells the story of the outage behind this view. Amazon prefers to make the main path more reliable. Two of its other options: push data out ahead of time, as when EC2 instances get IAM role credentials that stay valid for hours. Or run both paths all the time, for example by picking at random between their answers, so neither path is rare. Amazon's warning is about a second mechanism for the same job. The same logic applies to any degraded mode, though: code that rarely runs needs tests. The Turnstile kill switch shows the trade: users kept moving, but tokens could be reused. Decide each trade with your product owner before the outage. Where these live In your code, as a library. Resilience4j is one Java library for this. Hystrix is in maintenance mode, and Netflix suggests resilience4j for new projects. In a proxy next to each service, as in a service mesh. Envoy calls its per-cluster limits "circuit breaking": maximum connections, pending requests, requests and active retries. These act like bulkheads, and you write no app code. Removing hosts that fail more than their peers is a separate Envoy feature, outlier detection. At the gateway, to guard your services from outside traffic. The server can protect itself too, by rejecting work it cannot finish in time. That is load shedding, the topic of load shedding and graceful degradation. Test them A breaker or fallback that never ran is like any rare code path: it may not work. Make a dependency slow in a test environment. Check that the breaker opens, the bulkhead rejects and the page still renders. Chaos engineering and game days shows how to do this safely in production. Option Protects your threads? Cost Use it when Timeout only Partly. Each call is capped, but slow calls still pile up. Almost nothing. Always. It is the minimum. Circuit breaker Yes An open breaker fails fast. A new mode that is hard to test. It can slow recovery. A dependency fails or slows for minutes, not milliseconds. Thread-pool bulkhead Yes Each dependency has its own pool. More threads and a thread switch on each call. Blocking calls to several dependencies of different health. Semaphore bulkhead Yes, it caps calls in flight. You cannot walk away from a hung call. Non-blocking clients, or calls with their own timeout. Stale data or a default Yes, if it needs no network call. Users may see old or wrong data. Old data is clearly better than none. Hide the feature Yes Users lose that part of the page. The feature is optional. Fail closed with an error Yes Users are blocked. Security checks, payments, anything unsafe to guess. Simple rule: a timeout on every call, a bulkhead per dependency, a breaker where failures last, and a fallback only if you test it often. List every dependency of your service. For each one, ask: "If this takes 10 seconds, what happens to our threads?" Mark each dependency as critical or optional. Optional ones get a bulkhead and a planned degraded mode. Size bulkheads with numbers: calls a second × normal latency, plus room for spikes. Put breaker state on a dashboard and alert when a breaker stays open. Agree with the product owner on fail open or fail closed, feature by feature. "List every outgoing call in this service. For each, show the timeout, retry policy, circuit breaker and bulkhead settings, and what the caller gets on failure. Mark calls with none." "Wrap the ratings client in a Resilience4j circuit breaker and a semaphore bulkhead of 20 calls. On CallNotPermittedException or BulkheadFullException, return an empty ratings list. Do not make network calls in the fallback." "Write a test where the ratings service answers after 5 seconds. Assert that the breaker opens, that checkout still answers in under 300 ms, and that the page renders without ratings." What to ask the agent Every remote call has a timeout, and the breaker counts a timeout as a failure. Thresholds fit your real traffic, not the library defaults. No fallback calls another remote service, especially a shared database. Fail open or fail closed was a decision, not an accident. A test makes the dependency slow, not just down. What to check yourself Related lessons: Backoff, jitter and retry budgets, Error handling, Tail latency and queueing and Why distributed systems are hard. Read the Cloudflare Workers KV incident and the Shopify payments case.

title: REST API design
text: Nouns, methods, status codes and errors that clients can trust, and changes that never break an app already in use.
body: A food delivery app has an orders API. The mobile app shows a list of past orders with a price on each one. The API returns each order with a field called total. A backend developer tidies up the code. He renames total to total_amount, because it is clearer. The web app is updated in the same release. All the tests pass. The next morning, support gets angry messages. On the Android app, every order shows a price of ₹0. Some old iPhone versions crash on the orders screen. The team checks the data. Many users had not updated the app in months. Those versions still read total, and now the field is gone. The team cannot force an update on every phone, so they put total back and send both fields. This story is made up, but the mistake is common. A web page updates on every reload. A mobile app on a phone may be months old. Your API must serve all of them. A REST API is built around resources: the nouns of your product. Orders, users and payments are resources. Each one has an address, like /orders/42. A group of them, like /orders, is a collection. You act on resources with a few standard HTTP methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE. You do not invent a new URL for every action. Google's guide says APIs should prefer standard methods over custom ones. The server answers with a status code that tells the client what happened. When something goes wrong, it sends an error body in one fixed shape. The key idea. An API is a promise to every client that uses it, including old ones you cannot update. Design it so you can add to it for years without breaking that promise. Step through one order, from creation to an error. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Methods. RFC 9110 defines GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE as safe: the client does not ask for any change. PUT, DELETE and the safe methods are also idempotent: sending the same request twice has the same intended effect as sending it once. POST is neither. PATCH is not idempotent by default either. This matters for retries. RFC 9110 says a client should not retry a non-idempotent request automatically, unless it has some other way to know it is safe. For POST, that way is an idempotency key. In its v1 API, Stripe accepts an Idempotency-Key header on every POST. If the same key comes with different parameters, it returns an error. Status codes that matter. These cover most APIs. 200 OK: it worked, here is the result. 201 Created: a new resource exists. The Location header points to it. 204 No Content: it worked, and there is no body. 400 Bad Request: the request is broken, for example bad JSON. 401 Unauthorized: no valid login. 403 Forbidden: the server understood the request but refuses it, for example because the user lacks permission. 404 Not Found: no such resource. A server may also use it to hide a resource the user may not see. 409 Conflict: the request clashes with the current state, for example cancelling an order that has shipped. 422 Unprocessable Content: the syntax is fine, but the content makes no sense, like quantity -1. 500 Internal Server Error: a bug or surprise on the server. 503 Service Unavailable: overloaded or in maintenance, try later. There is one more: 429 Too Many Requests means the client sent too many requests in a given time. It may carry a Retry-After header. See Rate limiting. One error format. RFC 9457 defines "problem details": a JSON body with the media type application/problem+json. It has five standard fields: type: a URI that names the kind of problem. title: a short label for that kind of problem. status: the HTTP status code. detail: an explanation of this case, to help the client fix it. instance: a URI for this one occurrence. You may add your own fields, and clients must ignore fields they do not know. Pick one format and use it on every endpoint. Then clients write the error handling once. Pagination and filtering. Never return a whole collection in one answer. Stripe uses cursor pagination: you send limit and starting_after, and the answer has has_more. Google uses page_size, page_token and next_page_token, and its page tokens must be opaque. Filters are query parameters, like GET /orders?status=shipped. Add pagination from day one. Both Google and Microsoft say adding it later is a breaking change. Versioning and compatibility. Adding something new, like a field or an endpoint, is usually safe. Removing a field breaks clients. Google treats renaming as "remove and add", so it breaks them too. Changing a field's type also breaks them. When you must break something, release a new version and deprecate the old one slowly. Stripe puts /v1/ in the URL and sets a dated version per account. A client can choose another one with the Stripe-Version header. Since September 2024, its monthly versions have no breaking changes, and breaking ones come only twice a year. Microsoft uses a required api-version query parameter with a date, like 2021-06-04. Naming. Use plural nouns for collections, like /orders. Pick one style for field names and keep it everywhere. Microsoft uses camelCase for JSON fields. Stripe uses snake_case, like has_more. Both work. Mixing them does not. Document it. The OpenAPI Specification is a standard way to describe an HTTP API in a file. People and tools can then understand the API without reading its code. Tools use the file to generate docs, client and server code, and tests. When not REST. REST is a good default for public and mobile APIs, but not the only choice. gRPC: calls a method on another server as if it were local, with Protocol Buffers as the contract. It suits calls between your own services. GraphQL: the client asks for exactly the fields it needs, often in one request. It suits screens that need data from many resources. Webhooks: the server pushes events to your HTTPS endpoint when they happen. It retries failed deliveries, and the same event can arrive twice, so handle duplicates. See webhooks and async APIs. Pagination How it works Jump to page 7? Stable while rows are added? Use it when Offset (?offset=40&limit=20) Skip 40 rows, return the next 20. Yes Easy page numbers. No Items can repeat or be skipped. Deep pages get slow, because the database still reads the skipped rows. Small lists that rarely change, like an admin table. Cursor (?cursor=c_7Hq&limit=20) Return 20 rows after the item the cursor marks. No You can only go next or back. There is no total page count. Yes The window does not move when new rows arrive. Feeds, messages, orders, any large or busy list. Simple rule: start with cursors and opaque tokens. You can always add filters later. You cannot easily switch a public API from offset to cursor without a new version. Design the API from the client's screens first. Ask: "What does the app need to show, and in how many calls?" Treat every response field as a promise. Before you remove or rename one, ask: "Which app versions still read it?" Make new request fields optional. Google says new required fields must not be added to existing requests. For every POST that creates something or moves money, ask: "What happens if this runs twice?" Then add an idempotency key. Return 4xx for client mistakes and 5xx for server faults. Alerts on 5xx then mean real server problems. Use one error format on every endpoint. Put a stable error type in it, so clients never parse the message text. Write the OpenAPI file in the same pull request as the code. Review the file like code. Plan deprecation: tell clients early, measure who still calls the old version, and remove it only when traffic is near zero. "Write an OpenAPI spec for an orders API: create, get, list with cursor pagination, and update. Use RFC 9457 problem details for every error. Use camelCase field names." "Compare this OpenAPI file with the version on main. List every change that could break an existing client, like a removed, renamed or retyped field." "Add an Idempotency-Key header to POST /orders. Store the key with the order in one transaction, and reject a reused key with a different body." What to ask the agent Field names, casing and plural collection names are the same on every endpoint. Every error uses the same problem details shape, with the right status code. No 200 with "error": true in the body. POST endpoints that create things take an idempotency key. GET never changes data. List endpoints are paginated, with a limit and a maximum page size. Nothing was removed, renamed or made required compared with the last version. An agent may "tidy up" names, just like the developer in the story. The status codes the code really returns match the ones in the OpenAPI file. What to check yourself Idempotency, retries and timeouts: how one retry can charge twice. Rate limiting: what to do before you send 429. Coming next on this line: API pagination and filtering and API versioning and lifecycle.

title: Runbooks and reducing toil
text: Write runbooks that work at 3 a.m., measure the repeat work your team does by hand, and automate it step by step with safety limits.
body: On 28 February 2017 at 9:37 a.m. PST, an S3 engineer at AWS was debugging a slow billing system. They used "an established playbook" and ran a command to remove a few servers. AWS wrote: "one of the inputs to the command was entered incorrectly". The command removed more servers than intended. Those servers ran two S3 parts. One knows where every object is stored, and every request needs it. The other picks where new objects go. Both had to restart fully. S3 was not fully back until 1:54 p.m. The engineer followed a written runbook. AWS's fixes were not to the runbook or the person. They were to the tool, which AWS said "allowed too much capacity to be removed too quickly". AWS changed the tool to remove capacity more slowly. It also refuses to take any subsystem below its minimum capacity. AWS said it was also auditing its other operational tools for similar safety checks. This lesson is about that path: from a written runbook, to a script, to automation. Each step saves time. Each step also needs limits. You met runbooks in Alerting and on-call. This lesson is about the work behind them. Google's SRE book defines toil as "the kind of work tied to running a production service" that has six properties. Not every toil task has all six. The more of them a task has, the more likely it is toil. Manual. Running a script by hand still counts. Your hands-on time is toil, not the time the script runs. Repetitive. The first or second time is not toil. Doing it again and again is. Automatable. A machine could do it as well as you. If it needs human judgement, it is probably not toil. Tactical. It is driven by interrupts, not by a plan. Handling pages is toil. No lasting value. After the task, the service is in the same state as before. Grows with the service. Twice the traffic or users means twice the work. Some work is not toil. Meetings, goal setting and HR paperwork are overhead. Hard cleanup that makes the service better for good is not toil either. Google's SRE teams aim to keep toil below 50% of each person's time. In Google's quarterly surveys, the average was about 33%. Some people reported 0% and some 80%. The book warns that too much toil leads to burnout, boredom and discontent. The key idea. A good runbook makes manual work fast and safe. Then measure that manual work, and turn the biggest pieces into code, one step at a time. Give every piece of automation limits, so one mistake cannot spread. 1. Write a runbook people can follow at 3 a.m. Google found that a written "playbook" gives "roughly a 3x improvement" in time to repair, compared with "winging it". As you saw in the alerting lesson, PagerDuty says alerts with neither steps nor a runbook link "are useless". Our advice: a runbook needs these parts, in this order. # Runbook: DiskFull on app workers Owner: payments-platform Last tested: 2026-10-14 (game day) Impact: uploads fail on this host. Users see "try again". Quick check (30 s): ssh <host> df -h /var/log If use < 90%: the alert was a blip. Stop. Fix: 1. ssh <host> 'sudo find /var/log/app -type f -exec du -h {} + | sort -h | tail -5' 2. If the biggest files are old *.gz logs: ssh <host> 'sudo find /var/log/app -type f -name "*.gz" -mtime +7 -delete' 3. Else: do not delete. Escalate to #payments-oncall. Undo: you cannot undo the delete on the host. Copies of these logs stay in the log store for 30 days.Impact first. The reader learns how bad it is before anything else. A quick check. It tells the reader if they can stop. Commands you can copy and paste. No "check the disk somehow". Decision points. Say what to do in each case, including "stop and escalate". Rollback. Say how to undo each step, or say clearly that you cannot. Owner and last-tested date. A runbook with no owner goes stale. 2. Keep runbooks alive Runbooks rot. Commands change, hosts get new names, dashboards move. Google's automation chapter calls this "bit rot" when it happens to automation kept apart from its system: the system changes and the automation does not. A runbook kept apart from the system has the same risk. Our advice: test runbooks on a game day. Break a test system on purpose and let a new team member follow the runbook alone. Fix every step where they get stuck. Google also uses practice exercises, such as the "Wheel of Misfortune", to prepare engineers for on-call. 3. Measure toil before you fix it Google's workbook says intuition is not "repeatable, objective, or transferable". So measure. Pick a unit. Minutes and hours are the natural choice. Count the cost of context switching too. Track it over time. Measure before, during and after a fix. Rank it. Google SRE teams often track toil in bugs and rank it by "the cost to fix it and the time saved". The workbook also says eliminating toil "isn't always the best solution". Sometimes the best first move is to reject the task. Or batch it, to cut interrupts and see patterns. 4. Climb the automation ladder The ladder below is our own framing. Google's SRE book describes a different five-step path. It is about where automation lives: from "No automation", through scripts kept outside the system, to "Systems that don't need any automation". Doc to script. Google's workbook says runbook steps are "essentially pseudocode" to a software engineer. A good first script is a do-nothing script. Dan Slimmon describes it as a script that puts each step of a manual task in a function. At first, each function only prints the step and waits. #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Do-nothing script: free disk space on an app worker. Each step only prints what to do, then waits for you.""" def check_disk(host): print(f"1. Run: ssh {host} df -h /var/log") print(" If use is below 90%, stop here.") def find_big_logs(host): print(f"2. Run: ssh {host} 'sudo find /var/log/app -type f -exec du -h {{}} + | sort -h | tail -5'") def delete_old_logs(host): print("3. Only if the biggest files are old *.gz logs. Otherwise do not delete: escalate to #payments-oncall.") print(f" Run: ssh {host} 'sudo find /var/log/app -type f -name \"*.gz\" -mtime +7 -delete'") def main(): host = input("Host name: ") for step in (check_disk, find_big_logs, delete_old_logs): step(host) input(" Done? Press Enter to continue, or Ctrl+C to stop. ") if __name__ == "__main__": main()It looks useless, but you lose your place less often. And you can replace one step at a time with real code. Slimmon says it "lowers the activation energy for automating tasks". Script to self-service. Let other teams run the task themselves. The workbook suggests a web form, script, API or documented pull request. Self-service to auto-remediation. The alert runs the fix with no human. Our view: this step removes the most human time, and it carries the most risk. The diagram leaves out self-service, because it moves the work to other teams rather than removing it. Fix the cause. The workbook calls removing toil at its source "the optimal strategy". 5. Give automation limits Automation repeats a mistake as fast as it repeats a fix. Google's SRE book tells a story from its own CDN. A disk-erase job got an empty list of machines. The empty list was read as "everything". "Within minutes", it wiped the disks of all machines in Google's CDN. Afterwards, Google added more sanity checks, including rate limiting, and made the workflow idempotent. The workbook gives clear rules: Check input carefully, even input from other systems. Add safeguards, such as timeouts or checks of current metrics. "Automation should default to human operators if it runs into an unsafe condition." AWS's fix after S3 follows the same idea: go slowly, and refuse to go below a minimum. Step Human time per run Cost to build Main risk Runbook High. Low. Goes stale. People skip or mistype steps. Do-nothing script Same as the runbook. Very low. Feels like no progress, so people stop. Script run by a person Low. Medium. One wrong input acts on many hosts, as in the S3 outage. Self-service tool None for your team. Medium to high. Other teams use it in ways you did not plan for. Auto-remediation None, unless it pages a person. High. It hides a growing problem, or repeats a mistake at machine speed. Fix the cause None. The task is gone. Often highest. Takes the longest, so the toil continues until it ships. Link a runbook from every page. If an alert has no runbook, write one in the next postmortem. Put an owner and a "last tested" date at the top. Our advice: treat a runbook not tested in 6 months as untrusted. Keep a toil log for a month. Each entry has the task, minutes spent and what triggered it. Rank the log by minutes per month and by cost to fix. Bring the top three to planning. Ask "can we stop doing this?" before "can we automate this?". The workbook puts rejecting the task first. In code review of any automation, ask: what is the most it can change at once? What happens with empty or wrong input? When does it stop and page a person? Watch for growth. If a task doubles when traffic doubles, it will not wait for you to have time. "Here is our Slack thread and timeline from last night's DiskFull incident. Draft a runbook with: impact, a 30-second quick check, copy-paste commands, decision points, rollback, owner and a last-tested field. Mark any command you are not sure about." "You are on call with read-only access. For the alert DiskFull on worker-7, run only read commands: df, du, ls, journalctl. Show me each command and its output. Propose a fix, but do not run any command that changes or deletes anything." "Turn this runbook into a do-nothing script in Python. Each step is a function that prints the exact command and waits for Enter." What to ask the agent Run every command the agent wrote on a test host first. Agents can invent flags or paths. Check that "read-only" is enforced by permissions, not only by the prompt. Our advice: give the agent a read-only account, and approve every change yourself. Check delete and restart commands for limits: a path, an age, a host list, never "all". Make sure the runbook says how to undo each step. See Working with coding agents for permission settings and review habits. What to check yourself Before this: Alerting and on-call covers which alerts should page and how to run a fair rota. Related: Incident response covers the team side of an incident, and postmortem action items are a good source of toil to remove. Safe deploys applies the same "go slowly, with limits" idea to changes. Observability and SLOs helps you decide which work actually matters to users.

title: Safe deploys and config changes
text: Most outages start with a change. Learn to ship code and config in small, watched steps, and to undo them fast.
body: On 2 July 2019 at 13:42 UTC, a Cloudflare engineer deployed a small change to a firewall rule. The rule was meant to catch cross-site scripting attacks. It had passed its automatic tests. Within seconds the rule was on every Cloudflare server in the world. It contained a regular expression that backtracked badly. CPU use on the servers that handle web traffic jumped to nearly 100%. Visitors to Cloudflare sites got 502 errors, and Cloudflare lost about 80% of its traffic. The rule was in "simulate" mode, so it was not meant to block anything. But even in that mode the rule still had to run, and running it was the problem. Why did one rule reach everyone at once? Normal Cloudflare code went through staged rollouts. Firewall rules did not, by design, so that the team could respond fast to new attacks. At 14:07 the team used a "global terminate" to switch off the firewall everywhere. Traffic came back at 14:09. One of the fixes they listed was to move rule changes to staged rollouts, like code. Most outages do not start on their own. They start with a change. Google's SRE team writes that, in its experience, most incidents are triggered by binary or configuration pushes. The key idea. Config is code. It changes how running systems behave, so it needs the same checks, the same slow rollout and the same fast undo as code. A safe deploy has three parts: Check before you ship. Validate the change before it reaches any real server. Ship to a few first. Send the change to a small group, watch it, then go wider in steps. Undo fast. Make rollback one click or fully automatic, and practise it. The goal is a small blast radius. If a change is bad, only a few users should see it, and only for a few minutes. Step through a bad config change. Path A pushes it everywhere at once. Path B uses a staged rollout. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Now try it yourself. Push the same bad change both ways, and change how fast alerts notice. Validate the change first Before any rollout, a machine should check the change. Does the file parse? Does it match the schema? Is it a normal size? Does a quick test on sample traffic stay fast? After the outage, Cloudflare planned speed tests for every firewall rule. It also planned to switch to a regex engine with run-time guarantees. Validation catches simple mistakes. It does not catch every bug, so you still need the next steps. Canary, then waves A canary is a small part of the fleet that gets the change first. The rest of the fleet is the control. You compare the two: error rate, latency, CPU. If the canary looks healthy, you go wider in waves. AWS describes a real pipeline: first one box in one zone, then one region, then groups of regions that get bigger each time. In the first wave, AWS deploys to only one Availability Zone at a time. An Availability Zone is one of several separate locations inside an AWS region. Its top goal is to never hurt more than one region at once. A simple percentage rollout follows the same idea: 1%, then 10%, then 50%, then 100% of servers or users. Bake time and health checks Bake time is how long you wait at each stage before going wider. Some bugs need time or real traffic to show up. The AWS pipeline waits at least one hour after each one-box stage. It waits at least 12 hours after the first wave of regions. During bake time, automated health checks watch the metrics. If an alarm fires, the system rolls back on its own. No human has to wake up and decide. Feature flags and kill switches A feature flag lets you turn code on or off without a new deploy. Ship new code switched off, then turn it on for 1% of users, then more. If it breaks, turn it off in seconds. Flags also act as kill switches. On 29 May 2025, Google Cloud added new quota-checking code with no feature flag and no proper error handling. Nothing used it until 12 June. Then a policy with blank fields spread to every region within seconds. The code crashed on it. The team needed about 40 minutes to finish rolling out its "red button" fix. Afterwards, Google said changes to critical binaries must be behind a flag that is off by default. It also said policy data must roll out in steps, with time to check each step. Flags have a cost. Each one adds a branch to test. Remove a flag once the feature is fully on. Approach Small blast radius? Speed to reach everyone Use it when Global push No Every user at once. Seconds. A real emergency, like an active attack, and you accept the risk. Canary, then waves Yes A small group sees a bad change first. Hours to days. Most code and config changes. Percentage rollout behind a flag Yes You choose the share of users. Minutes to days, your choice. New features and risky code paths. Blue-green (two full copies, switch traffic) No All traffic moves at once. Minutes. You need a very fast undo, and you can pay for two copies. Simple rule: keep a fast global path only for emergencies, and make the slow staged path the default. Cloudflare's planned fix did the same: staged rollouts for rule changes, and a global push kept only for active attacks. Ask about every change: "How do we undo this, and how long does it take?" If nobody knows, the change is not ready. Treat config, feature flags, firewall rules and data files as code. They need review, validation and a staged rollout. Ask "what is the blast radius?" A change that touches every region at once needs a very good reason. Name the metric that decides go or no-go before you deploy. Write it in the change ticket, for example "5xx rate above 0.5% on the canary means rollback". Make rollback automatic where you can. Test it on a normal day, not for the first time during an outage. Check that the tools you use to roll back do not depend on the system you are deploying. During the 2019 outage, Cloudflare engineers had trouble reaching internal tools. Ship big changes as many small ones. A small change is easier to check and easier to undo. "Here is our deploy pipeline config. List every way a change can reach all production servers at once, including config and feature flags." "Write a validation script for this config file. Check the schema, the size limits and the allowed values. Fail the build if any check fails." "Add a canary stage to this pipeline: deploy to 1% of hosts, wait 30 minutes, and roll back if the 5xx rate or p99 latency rises." What to ask the agent The canary gets real traffic, and enough of it to show a problem. The rollback trigger uses metrics you trust, with clear thresholds. Rollback was tested, and it works when the new version is crashing. Config and data files go through the same stages as code, not a side path. New flags are off by default, and each has an owner and a plan to remove it. What to check yourself Related lessons: Feature flags, CI/CD and Incident response.

title: Sagas, outbox and CDC
text: When one order touches three services, there is no single "undo". Learn to undo step by step, and to send events that never get lost.
body: A shop splits checkout into three services: Orders, Inventory and Payments. Each one has its own database. A new engineer writes the order flow in the Orders service. It creates the order, calls Inventory to hold the item, and then calls Payments to charge the card. If the charge fails, it marks the order "failed". It looks fine in testing. In production, cards fail every day. Each time, the order is marked "failed", but the held item stays held. Nobody tells Inventory to let it go. After a month, popular items show "out of stock" on the site. The warehouse has them on the shelf. Hundreds of units are held for orders that will never ship. A second bug hides in the same code. Orders saves an order, then sends an "OrderPlaced" event to Kafka. One night the service restarts between those two steps. Thirty orders exist, but the warehouse never hears about them. Customers wait for parcels that nobody packs. Inside one database, a transaction gives you "all or nothing". Across three services with three databases, you do not get that for free. The classic tool for "all or nothing" across databases is two-phase commit, or 2PC. A coordinator asks every database to prepare, then tells all of them to commit. AWS says 2PC is not an option in a database-per-service design. There is no single controller that can coordinate the services that way. Message brokers add another gap. You cannot have one transaction that spans your database and Kafka. So teams use a saga. A saga is a chain of small local transactions. Each step commits on its own. If a later step fails, the saga runs a compensating transaction for each earlier step, to undo its effect. The idea comes from a 1987 paper by Garcia-Molina and Salem. They split long database transactions into short ones, with compensations that undo a partial run. Each step must also tell the next service what happened. Writing to your database and to a broker in two calls is the dual-write problem. The transactional outbox fixes it. You save the event in your own database, in the same transaction as your data. A separate relay publishes it later. The key idea. Across services, you cannot roll back. You can only move forward with new actions that undo old ones. And you never write to two systems at once: write to one, and copy from it. Step through an order saga that fails at payment. Then see how the outbox sends each event. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Choreography or orchestration There are two ways to run a saga. Choreography. No one is in charge. Each service listens for events and reacts. Orders emits "OrderPlaced". Inventory hears it, holds stock, and emits "StockReserved". Payments hears that, and so on. Orchestration. One component, the orchestrator, tells each service what to do next. It keeps the state of the whole saga in one place. AWS lists the costs of each. Choreography has no central part to fail. But as services grow, the flow gets hard to follow, and services can end up depending on each other in a cycle. Timeouts and retries must be built into every service. An orchestrator keeps the flow in one place, but it can become a single point of failure. The AWS guide shows an orchestrator built on Step Functions. It undoes payment, inventory and the order when a step fails. Writing good compensations A compensation is not a database rollback. The first step already committed, and other people may have seen it. So the compensation is a new business action: "release the item", "refund the charge", "cancel the order". Sagas also have no isolation. Two sagas can run at the same time and see each other's half-done work. For example, a customer may see stock as held for a minute, then free again. Design for this. Show states like "pending" to users, and do the steps that are hard to undo, like shipping, last. Compensations can fail and run twice too. Make every step and every compensation idempotent, so a retry does no harm. See idempotency, retries and timeouts. The outbox, step by step In the same database transaction, you insert the order row and one outbox row. The outbox row holds the event: an ID, the aggregate type and ID (here, the order and its ID), an event type like "OrderCreated", and a payload. If the transaction commits, both rows exist. If it rolls back, neither does. So the event is sent if and only if the data was saved. A relay then moves outbox rows to the broker. There are two common ways. Polling. A job reads new rows from the outbox table every second or so, publishes them, and marks them as sent. Log tailing. A tool reads the database's own change log and publishes every new outbox row. Change data capture Log tailing is a kind of change data capture, or CDC. Most databases keep a log of changes so it can recover from a crash. In Postgres this is the WAL. The Debezium Postgres connector reads it through logical decoding and a replication slot. Logical decoding turns the WAL into plain row changes. A slot is a stream of those changes that Postgres keeps until the reader has them . After a restart, the connector carries on from where it stopped. Debezium lists the benefits over polling. It captures every change, with very low delay. It needs no "last updated" column. It can also see deletes. With CDC, you can even delete each outbox row right after you insert it. The insert is already in the log, so the table stays empty. The inbox: dedup on the consumer side The relay can publish a message more than once. For example, it might crash after it publishes but before it records that fact. So every consumer must expect duplicates. The fix is an inbox. The consumer keeps a table of event IDs it has already handled. In one transaction, it does the work and saves the ID. If the ID is already there, it skips the event. This is at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent handler, the same pattern as in queues vs logs. Order matters too. By default, Debezium uses the outbox row's aggregate ID as the Kafka message key, so events for one order stay in order inside a partition. Option One place to see the flow? Main risk Use when 2PC across services Yes Every service must support it and wait on a coordinator. Rarely. Only inside one system that supports it well. Saga with choreography No The flow is spread across services. Hard to trace, cycles between services. Two or three steps with a simple flow. Saga with orchestration Yes The orchestrator is critical and must be reliable. Many steps, timeouts, human steps, frequent changes. Outbox with a polling relay n/a Delay and load from polling the table. A simple start, with no CDC tooling. Outbox with CDC (Debezium) n/a More systems to run and watch. High volume, low delay, a team that can run Kafka Connect. Dual write (DB, then broker) n/a Lost or phantom events after a crash. Never for events that matter. Simple rule: start with an orchestrated saga and an outbox. Move to choreography only for short flows where each team owns its part. For every multi-service flow, write the table: step, compensation, and "can this be undone?". Put steps that cannot be undone, like shipping or sending money out, last. Search the code for "save, then publish". Each one is a dual write. Replace it with an outbox. Give every event a unique ID, and make every consumer store the IDs it has handled. Make the saga's state visible. Store it in a table or a workflow engine, with a dashboard of stuck sagas older than, say, 15 minutes. Add a timeout to every saga step. A step that never answers must lead to a compensation, not a forever "pending". Watch the relay. Alert on outbox rows that are old and still unsent, or on CDC lag. "Here is our checkout flow across Orders, Inventory and Payments. List each step, what commits where, and what compensation undoes it. Mark any step with no compensation." "Find every place in this service where we write to the database and then publish to Kafka. Replace each one with an insert into an outbox table in the same transaction." "Write a consumer for OrderCreated that stores the event ID and its result in one transaction, and skips IDs it has seen. Add a test that delivers the same event twice." What to ask the agent The outbox insert really is inside the same transaction as the business write. Check the transaction boundaries, not just the function name. Every compensation is idempotent. Run it twice in a test. Compensations run in reverse order, and a failure in a compensation is retried or raised to a person. It is not silently logged. The agent did not add a "publish directly if the outbox is slow" shortcut. That brings the dual write back. The consumer's dedup check and its work share one transaction. What to check yourself Before this: queues vs logs and idempotency, retries and timeouts. Next: checkout and the order state machine. Related: event-driven architecture and event sourcing, exactly-once and effectively-once, and distributed transactions and two-phase commit, the approach sagas replace across services.

title: Scaling reads
text: Most apps read far more than they write. Learn the order of steps that serves many more reads without breaking what users see.
body: This is a real case, from a paper Facebook published in 2013. Facebook's users read an order of magnitude more content than they create. So the work was mostly reads, and Facebook put a large cache, memcache, in front of MySQL and other data stores. Loading one popular page fetched an average of 521 different items from that cache. Facebook ran hundreds of cache servers in one cluster. Every web server talked to every cache server, and that caused two problems. Replies that arrived all at once could overload the network switches. And one busy cache server could slow down many web servers. Simply buying more servers did not fix everything. The paper says popular items only become more popular as you add web servers. It also notes that a single key can be 20% of one cache server's requests. Then Facebook added data centres in other regions. One master region kept the other regions up to date. Those regions read from local copies of the database, which can lag behind. When lag was large, a user's next page could be missing the change they had just made. There was no single outage. The read path worked at one size and needed new fixes at the next. A read path is the route a read takes, from the user's phone to the data. Scaling reads means answering each read as close to the user and as cheaply as you can. Keep the primary database for work only it can do. Think of it as a ladder. Climb one step at a time, only when your numbers say so. Each step adds a new way for data to be stale. The key idea. Every read you answer higher up is a read your database never sees. But every copy of data can be out of date. Choose, for each kind of read, how stale it may be. Step 0: measure the read/write ratio First, count reads and writes per second, and find the queries that use the most total time. In PostgreSQL, the pg_stat_statements module, once enabled, tracks planning and execution statistics for every SQL statement. These include how often each one ran and its total time. Facebook's numbers made the choice clear. In a sample of 6.5 million requests to TAO, its graph store, 99.8% were reads and 0.2% were writes. If your mix is closer to half and half, read-side tools will help much less. See Scaling writes instead. Step 1: fix the query and the index Many "we need replicas" problems are one slow query. EXPLAIN shows the query plan the database chose. EXPLAIN ANALYZE really runs the query and shows true row counts and times. So for an UPDATE or DELETE, wrap it in a transaction and roll it back. Look for a full table scan where you expected an index. This step is cheap, and it never shows stale data. Do it first. Step 2: cache Keep hot results in memory. The common pattern is cache-aside: read the cache, and on a miss read the database and fill the cache. On a write, Facebook deletes the cached key instead of updating it, because deletes are idempotent. The caching lesson covers TTLs, invalidation and stampedes. Step 3: read replicas Send reads to copies of the database, and writes to the primary. This adds read capacity, but replicas lag. TAO measured the lag of its replica databases in other regions. It was under 1 second 85% of the time, under 3 seconds 99% of the time, and under 10 seconds 99.8% of the time. So plan for seconds, not zero. The replication lesson explains lag in depth. The bug users notice is read-your-writes: "I saved it, and it is gone." Facebook's fix was a "remote marker". When a web server in a non-master region writes, it first sets a marker for that key. On a cache miss, if the marker exists, the read skips the local replica and goes to the master region. TAO has a similar idea: a read can be marked "critical" and sent to the master region. The paper's example is a login check, so old credentials are not used. Our advice: most reads go to replicas. A user's own data, just after they write it, goes to the primary. Step through one read falling through the layers. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Step 4: denormalise and precompute Denormalise. Store a copy of data where it is read. For example, keep comment_count on the post row, instead of counting comments on every page view. You now have two places to update. Materialized views. PostgreSQL can store the result of a query in a table-like form. Reads are often much faster than querying the base tables. The cost: the data is not always current. You update it with REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW. A plain refresh can block readers. With CONCURRENTLY, readers are not blocked. But the view needs a unique index on plain columns that covers all rows. Step 5: read models fed by change data capture When one database cannot serve every kind of read, build separate read models. This is the idea behind CQRS: one model for updates and a different model for reads, maybe in a different database. In this lesson, a feed table, a search index and a cache can all count as read models. CQRS and read models goes deeper. Feed them from the database's change log, with change data capture (CDC). The sagas, outbox and CDC lesson shows how. Facebook used a similar idea to keep its caches correct. Daemons read the SQL that each database committed and sent the cache deletes to every frontend cluster in the region. Lost deletes could be replayed from that reliable log. Be careful. Fowler warns that for most systems CQRS adds risky complexity, and should be used only on parts of a system. Separate models also make eventual consistency likely. For a few heavy queries, he suggests a simpler option: a separate reporting database. Step 6: search indexes for complex reads Send full-text search and complex filters to a search index: another read model, with its own lag. See Search systems. Step 7: CDN and edge caches for public reads Reads that are the same for everyone, like product pages or images, can be answered by a CDN near the user. See CDNs and HTTP caching. Slack's Flannel caches data about users, channels and more at its edge locations, so clients load it only when needed. For a team of 32,000 users, the startup data clients needed became 44 times smaller. Hot keys A hot key is one key that gets a huge share of reads. Hashing spreads keys, not reads of one key, so more servers do not help. Facebook copies a small, very busy set of keys to several servers in a pool. Its example: one server holds 100 keys and answers 500,000 requests a second. Each request needs all 100 keys, and 1 million requests arrive each second. Split the keys over two servers, and each server still gets 1 million requests. Copy all keys to both, and each gets 500,000. The cost: every delete must reach every copy. Other ways to spread a hot key, from our experience: Cache it inside each app server for a few seconds. Split it into copies like post:42#1 … post:42#8, and read one at random. Collapse many misses for one key into one database read. Step Read capacity gained Staleness Cost and new risks Query and index tuning Often large, for the queries you fix. None. Indexes slow writes a little and use disk. Cache Very large for hot data. Until the TTL or delete arrives. Invalidation bugs, stampedes, hot keys. Read replicas Roughly one database per replica. Replication lag, sometimes several seconds. Routing logic for read-your-writes. Denormalise or materialized view Large for joins and counts. Until you update or refresh. Two copies to keep in step. Read model fed by CDC Large, and each read shape gets its own store. Pipeline lag. A new pipeline to run, watch and replay. Search index Makes complex queries possible. Indexing lag. Another system and its own operations. CDN Huge for public reads. Until the cache rules say it expires. Only safe for data that is the same for many users. Our simple rule: climb the ladder in order, and stop at the first step that meets your target. Start with numbers: reads per second, writes per second, and the top ten queries by total time. For each kind of read, ask: "How stale may this be?" Write the answer in the design doc. A bank balance and a like count get different answers. Decide who reads from the primary. Make it a rule in one place in the code, not a choice in each query. Watch replica lag and alert on it. Reads that "sometimes show old data" are often lag. Before a launch or a sale, ask which item everyone will open at once. "Here is the output of pg_stat_statements for our top 20 queries, and our schema. For each query, say if an index would help, and write the CREATE INDEX statement. Do not suggest caching yet." "Add read routing to this data layer. Reads go to a replica by default. For 10 seconds after a user writes, that user's reads go to the primary. Show where the 10 seconds is set." "Design a materialized view for this dashboard query. Add the unique index it needs for REFRESH CONCURRENTLY, and a job that refreshes it every 5 minutes." What to ask the agent The new index matches the real WHERE and ORDER BY, and EXPLAIN shows the plan uses it. The agent did not run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on an UPDATE or DELETE outside a rolled-back transaction. The read-your-writes window is longer than your real replica lag at p99, not your average. Every cache or read model has a way to be rebuilt, and someone owns it. Hot keys are spread, and the agent did not add a cache that all servers miss at once. What to check yourself Read the TAO case and the Slack Flannel case. Related lessons: Distributed caches, Replication and Scaling from zero to millions.

title: Scaling writes and hot keys
text: Reads can be copied, but every write must land on the one place that owns its key. Learn to spread writes, split hot keys and smooth bursts, and know what each fix costs.
body: Amazon DynamoDB lets you buy write throughput for a table. In its early years, DynamoDB split that throughput evenly over the table's partitions. The paper's example: one partition can take at most 1,000 write units. A table bought with 3,200 got four partitions of 800 each. This works only if your app writes to all keys evenly. Real apps do not. Amazon found that workloads "frequently have non-uniform access patterns", over time and over keys. A few busy items sat on one partition. That partition hit its 800, and DynamoDB rejected the extra writes. This is called throttling. It happened even when the whole table had enough capacity. To customers, it looked like downtime, "even though the service was behaving as expected". Customers worked around it by buying more capacity than they used, just to give the hot partition enough. Amazon added fixes over time. Partitions could borrow unused capacity for short bursts. Adaptive capacity raised the limit on hot partitions and removed over 99.99% of the throttling caused by skew. Later, busy partitions were split automatically. But one case was left. A partition "receiving high traffic to a single item" does not gain from a split. Today each partition still takes at most 1,000 write units a second. The database can spread many keys. Only you can spread one key. Reads are easy to copy. You can add replicas and caches, and each copy serves its own share of reads. Writes cannot be copied away. Each write must reach the one place that owns its key. Every replica must then apply that write too. So adding replicas does not add write capacity. When writes are the bottleneck, you have five moves: A bigger machine. Simple, and it buys time. Spread keys over shards, so each machine owns part of the writes. Split a hot key into many sub-keys. Write less often, by combining many small writes into one. Smooth bursts with a queue, so the database sees a steady rate. The key idea. One key lives in one place, so its write rate is capped by that place. To go faster, you must change the key, or send fewer writes to it. Every fix moves cost somewhere else: to reads, to freshness, or to correctness. First, check that writes are the problem Look at the primary database, not the replicas. Signs of a write bottleneck are a busy disk, a long write queue, and transactions waiting on row locks. Replicas that lag behind are another sign, because each replica must apply every write. Then try the cheap fix: a bigger machine with faster disks. It needs no code change.
