Do this before you shard, as in Sharding and From zero to millions. Shard by a key that spreads writes If one machine is not enough, shard. For writes, the shard key must have many values, and new writes must spread over all of them. A user ID or tenant ID usually works. A date is a bad write key. All of today's writes go to the shard that owns today. The DynamoDB docs use exactly this example of a hot key. Split a hot key: write sharding Some keys are hot by nature: a celebrity's post, a flash-sale product, a global counter. No shard key fixes them. So you split the key itself. Step through it. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. The DynamoDB docs call this write sharding. Their example adds a random number from 1 to 200 to a date key, such as 2014-07-09.1 to 2014-07-09.200. Writes spread across partitions. To read the whole day, you query all 200 keys and merge the results. If you need to find one item again, use a calculated suffix instead. Compute the suffix from something you know, such as a hash of the order ID. For a counter, this is called a sharded counter. Firestore's docs describe a pattern you build yourself: each counter gets a set of shard documents. A write adds 1 to a random shard. A read sums all the shards. Here it is in Python with Postgres: import random N = 40 # sub-keys per hot counter def add_like(conn, post_id): # conn: a psycopg 3 connection with autocommit=True conn.execute( """INSERT INTO like_shards (post_id, shard, n) VALUES (%s, %s, 1) ON CONFLICT (post_id, shard) DO UPDATE SET n = like_shards.n + 1""", (post_id, random.randrange(N))) def like_count(conn, post_id): return conn.execute( "SELECT COALESCE(SUM(n), 0) FROM like_shards WHERE post_id = %s", (post_id,)).fetchone()[0]The table has the primary key (post_id, shard). In one Postgres, the 40 rows let 40 writers hold row locks at once, not one. In a sharded store, if the shard key includes the sub-key, the rows also land on different machines. The read sums whatever rows exist, so you can raise N later without moving data. Choose N from numbers. Firestore says write throughput grows linearly with the number of shards. So does the cost of each read. For 20,000 writes a second and a limit of 1,000 per key, you need at least 20. Add headroom, and stop there. Only split the keys you have measured as hot. For busy pages, add a roll-up. A job sums the shards every few seconds and stores one total. Firestore suggests this too, at the price of a total that lags. The deep dives lesson walks through this choice for a like counter. Write less often: combine, then flush You can also stop sending every write to the hot row. This part is our advice. Each app server keeps a running total per key in memory. Once a second, it writes the total as one UPDATE ... SET n = n + 37. With 50 servers, the row gets at most 50 writes a second, whatever the traffic. The risk: a crash loses the totals not yet written. And a retried flush can add the same total twice. So use it only for counts where a small loss is fine, such as views. A safer form keeps every event in a queue and applies them in batches. Modern Treasury had a "hot account" in its ledger: a ledger account that was "present on most Transactions". Contention on its single balance cache row made write latency spike. Its fix lets a client mark an entry as safe to process later. Those entries go to an AWS SQS queue. A scheduled job takes them from the queue in batches. The target is 60 seconds; in practice, the p90 is 1 second. Modern Treasury still keeps every entry, because all money movement must be recorded immutably. The balance still lives in one cached row. The batch job simply writes to that row far less often than once per entry. Wait too little between batches, and contention comes back. Money and ledgers shows why ledgers work this way. Smooth bursts with a queue A database has a steady rate it can handle. Traffic arrives in spikes. Put a log or queue in front, and let consumers write at the rate the database can take. During a spike, you get lag, not errors. Queues vs logs covers delivery, and backpressure covers what to do when the queue fills. A consumer can also write in batches, such as 500 rows per statement. That shares the fixed cost of each round trip and each disk flush. See batching and group commit. Each write costs more than one write Every index on a table is extra work for every write. In DynamoDB, a write that changes an attribute the index stores also uses the index's write units. Changing an indexed key costs two index writes: a delete and a put. If an index lacks capacity, writes to the table itself are throttled. Postgres had its own form of this in 2016. Uber wrote that every index pointed to the row's location on disk. When that location changed, all indexes had to be updated. The write-ahead log grew too, so replication carried more data. Storage engines add more: an LSM-tree rewrites data during compaction. See B-trees vs LSM-trees. Before you scale writes, remove the indexes nobody uses. Option Write gain Cost on reads Other costs Bigger machine Some. One step, then a ceiling. None. Price. Still one machine. Shard by a spread-out key Yes Grows with shards. Queries without the key hit every shard. Cross-shard transactions get hard. Split a hot key into N sub-keys Yes About N times for that key. N reads, or a roll-up that lags. A rule like "stock ≥ 0" no longer lives in one row. Combine in memory, then flush Yes One write per server per interval. Count lags by the interval. A crash loses the pending totals. Queue events, apply in batches Yes The shared total row is written once per batch. Total lags by the batch interval. A queue and a batch job to run and watch. Queue in front of the database Smooths peaks only. Reads lag behind the queue. The queue needs a limit and an alert. Simple rule: go bigger first, then shard by a key that spreads writes. Split or combine only the few keys you have measured as hot. Ask: "What is our peak write rate per key, not per table?" Averages hide the one hot key. Find the limit of one key in your store, and divide. The answer tells you if a key needs splitting. Log the top keys by write count on each partition. Alert when one key takes a big share. Decide how stale each count may be, and get product to agree. It picks between sub-keys, a roll-up and in-memory totals. Before splitting stock or balances, check the rules that need one row, such as "never below zero". See inventory and flash sales. Count the indexes on write-heavy tables. Each one needs a reason. Load test with real skew: one key with a large share of the writes, not keys spread evenly. "Here is our schema and a sample of write logs. Find the 10 keys with the most writes per second at peak, and say which ones exceed the per-key limit of our database." "Convert this single-row counter to 40 sub-keys with a random suffix. Keep the read API the same, and add a job that stores the total every 5 seconds." "List every index on these tables, how often each is used by queries, and how many extra writes each adds per insert." What to ask the agent The sub-key is picked at random, or from a hash, never from a value that is the same for every write. The read sums every sub-key that exists, not just 0 to N − 1 of today's N. In-memory totals are only used where losing a few seconds of writes is acceptable. The queue in front of the database has a limit and an alert on lag. The load test sends a large share of writes to one key. What to check yourself Before this: Sharding and consistent hashing and Queues vs logs. For the read side of hot keys, see Distributed caches. Each store in depth: DynamoDB and Cassandra.

title: Schema evolution and encoding
text: Change the shape of your data so that old code can read new data, and new code can read old data, while both run at once.
body: On 19 July 2024, Windows machines running CrowdStrike's Falcon sensor crashed. The cause was not new code. It was new data that the sensor code could not safely read. In February 2024, sensor version 7.11 added a new template type for IPC (named pipes). Content files for it arrive from the cloud as Channel File 291. Both parts were built at the same time, and they disagreed from day one. The template's definition said each check had 21 input fields. The sensor code supplied only 20. For months, nobody noticed. The tests and the first live content used a wildcard for the 21st field, so the sensor never had to look at it. Then two new content entries were sent. One had a real value for the 21st field. The content validator approved it, because it also assumed 21 inputs. The sensor tried to read input 21 from an array of 20. That out-of-bounds read crashed the system. The data and the code that read it disagreed about the shape, and the code did not check the array size. Among its fixes, CrowdStrike now checks the number of fields when it builds the sensor. It also added a bounds check that runs on the machine. This lesson is about that gap between writer and reader, and how data formats help you close it. Every time you send or store data, you encode it into bytes. Later, some other code decodes it. That other code may be older or newer than the code that wrote it. This happens all the time, not only in rare cases: Rolling deploys. Kubernetes scales up the new pods while it scales down the old ones. For a few minutes, v1 and v2 talk to each other. Messages in a queue or log. A message written yesterday by v1 is read today by v2. In a log, it may be read again in a year. Stored data. A database row or a file written three years ago is still read by today's code. So you need two promises: Backward compatibility: new code can read data written by old code. Forward compatibility: old code can read data written by new code. Forward is the harder one. Old code cannot know what you will add later. So it must be built to skip what it does not know. The key idea. Old and new code always overlap. Change your data so both can read it: add optional fields, never change the meaning of an existing one, and never reuse an old name or number. JSON: no schema, so the rules live in your code JSON carries field names, so a reader can find fields in any order. But nothing checks the shape. Two habits keep JSON safe: Ignore unknown fields. Then new fields do not break old readers. Some parsers reject them by default. ProtoJSON parsers do, for example. Check yours. Treat missing fields as normal. Then new readers can read old data. Numbers are a trap. RFC 8259 lets parsers limit precision. Only integers between −(2^53 − 1) and 2^53 − 1 are safe to exchange. JavaScript stores every number as a double, so bigger integers get rounded. JSON.parse('{"id": 9007199254740993}').id // 9007199254740992 — a different id, and no errorSend big ids, such as 64-bit database keys, as strings. Protobuf's own JSON format does this for all 64-bit integers, for the same reason. Protocol Buffers: the field number is the contract In Protobuf, each field has a field number. The bytes on the wire carry that number, not the field name. So you can rename a field, but you can never change its number. syntax = "proto3"; // v2 message Order { int64 id = 1; int64 amount = 2 [deprecated = true]; // rupees; v1 still reads it int64 amount_paise = 3; // new in v2 optional string currency = 4; // new in v2 }Later, when no reader needs field 2, v3 deletes it and adds reserved 2; and reserved "amount";. The rules that matter: Adding and removing fields is safe. Changing a field's number is not. Never reuse a number. Google's guide says it "messes up deserialization". When you delete a field, reserve its number. Also reserve the name, so no new field reuses it. JSON and text formats carry names, not numbers. Unknown fields survive. An old proto3 reader keeps fields it does not know, and writes them out again. They are lost if you convert the message to JSON. Missing means default. A missing string reads as empty, a number as zero, and a bool as false. So "zero" and "not sent" look the same. Use optional when "not sent" matters. Then you can check whether a value was set. Do not change a field's type. A few types are wire-compatible, such as int32 and int64. But a big value read as int32 is cut short with no error. No required fields. Proto3 has none. In proto2, never add one. Step through a rolling deploy that shares one queue. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Avro: the reader needs the writer's schema Avro has no field numbers. Binary Avro data has no field names or types either. So a reader needs the exact schema the data was written with: the writer's schema. The reader also has its own schema, the reader's schema. Avro matches the two by field name. A field only in the writer's schema is ignored. A field only in the reader's schema takes its default. If that field has no default, the read fails. So if both old and new readers must work, add or remove only fields that have a default. { "type": "record", "name": "Order", "fields": [ {"name": "id", "type": "long"}, {"name": "amount_paise", "type": "long"}, {"name": "currency", "type": ["null", "string"], "default": null} ] }In Avro before 1.12, a union default had to match the first type in the union. Version 1.12 accepts the first type that matches. Many tools still use the old rule, so put "null" first when the default is null. Where does the writer's schema come from? An Avro file stores it once in its header. For records stored one by one, such as rows in a database, each record carries a schema version or id. A schema registry maps that id to the full schema. With Confluent Schema Registry, each Kafka message begins with a version byte and a 4-byte schema ID. Schema registries and compatibility modes A registry also guards changes. Confluent Schema Registry checks each new schema against old ones before it accepts it. BACKWARD (the default): consumers on the new schema can read data written with the last schema. Upgrade consumers first. FORWARD: consumers on the old schema can read data written with the new schema. Upgrade producers first. Then make sure consumers no longer read old data. FULL: both. You can upgrade either side in any order. Each mode also has a _TRANSITIVE form. It checks against all older schemas, not only the last one. Confluent made BACKWARD the default so that consumers can rewind to the start of a topic. If your topic keeps data for a long time, a transitive mode is safer. What no format can catch Every check above looks at names, numbers and types. None of them looks at meaning. Say you keep int64 amount = 2, but start to send paise instead of rupees. The schema is the same, so every check passes. Old readers now show prices 100 times too high. So a change of unit or meaning is a new field, with a new name and a new number. That is why the example above added amount_paise instead of changing amount. Format Schema needed to read? New fields and old readers Main risk Use it when JSON No Names are in the data. Yes, if readers ignore unknown fields. Nothing checks shape. Big numbers lose precision. Public APIs, webhooks, browsers. Protobuf Yes, to know names. Unknown fields can still be skipped. Yes Old code skips them. A reused field number gives wrong data, silently. Calls between your own services, such as gRPC. Avro Yes The exact writer's schema. Yes Old readers ignore it. A default lets new readers read old data. Lost or wrong writer's schema means unreadable data. Kafka topics and data files, with a registry. Simple rule: pick the format your readers can handle. Then put a compatibility check in CI, not in a reviewer's memory. For every data change, ask: "Who reads this, and how old can their code be?" Count queue backlog, log retention and stored rows, not only live services. Add new fields as optional, with a safe default. Never make a new field required. Never change the meaning or unit of a field. To move from rupees to paise, add amount_paise and keep amount until nobody reads it. Deprecate before you delete. Stop writing the field, wait until no reader needs it, then delete it and reserve its number and name. Run a schema check in CI. For Protobuf, a breaking-change linter. For Kafka, the registry's compatibility mode. Make readers fail safe on bad input. CrowdStrike's fix was a bounds check at runtime as well as a check at build time. For changes to public HTTP APIs, use API versioning and lifecycle. For database columns, use zero-downtime schema migrations. "Compare this .proto file with the one on main. List every change that breaks old readers or old writers: changed or reused field numbers, changed types, removed fields without reserved, and new required fields." "Here is our Avro schema and the new version. Would Confluent Schema Registry accept it in BACKWARD mode? In FORWARD mode? Explain each field." "Find every place our JavaScript code parses JSON ids that can be larger than 2^53 − 1. Change them to strings end to end." What to ask the agent No field number was reused or renumbered. An agent may "tidy up" numbers so they run 1, 2, 3. Every deleted Protobuf field has its number and name in reserved. Every new Avro field has a default, and a union default matches the first type, for older Avro tools. No field kept its name but changed its unit or meaning. A linter cannot catch that. The plan says which side deploys first, and it matches the registry mode. What to check yourself Queues vs logs: why old messages stay around to be read again. Webhooks and async APIs: JSON events that your customers decode with code you cannot update. Safe deploys and config changes: rolling out content and config as carefully as code. Kafka internals: how the messages you encode are stored and replicated. Coming later: RPC and gRPC, and contract and integration tests.

title: Schema migrations without downtime
text: Change a live database schema in small steps that old and new code can both survive, with a way back at every step.
body: GoCardless is a payments company. Its team wrote about a schema migration that went wrong. It renamed some invoicing tables and dropped and recreated their foreign keys. The tables were empty, and no production code used them yet. Just after the migration started, alerts fired: API requests were timing out. This lasted about 15 seconds. Then the migration finished and the API came back. The strange part: the same migration, run on a copy of the database, took a few hundred milliseconds. The ALTER TABLE itself was fast. The cause was a lock. On their Postgres version, adding the foreign key needed an AccessExclusive lock on both tables. That included the busy parent table. A long-running read query was already using it. So the ALTER waited. And every normal query that arrived after it waited behind the ALTER. Current Postgres docs list a weaker lock for this, SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE. It still blocks writes. For 15 seconds, the API's own reads and writes piled up, and clients timed out. The fix they suggest is short: set lock_timeout in migration scripts. "It's better to abort a deploy than take your application down." A schema change on a live database can hurt you in three ways. Locks. Many changes need a strong lock on the table. While they wait for it or hold it, other queries stop. Table rewrites. Some changes copy the whole table. On a big table that can take a long time and double the disk space. Two versions of code. During a rolling deploy, new pods start while old ones still run. Both versions must work with the schema at every moment. The fix is to never make a big change in one step. Split it into small steps that each keep old and new code working. This is called expand and contract, or parallel change: expand to support old and new, migrate the users, then contract to remove the old. Sato writes that most database refactorings follow this pattern. The key idea. Never change the schema and the code in a way that needs both to switch at the same moment. Add first, move slowly, remove last. Step through a column rename done safely across several deploys. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Know your locks In Postgres, ALTER TABLE takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock unless the docs say otherwise. That lock conflicts with every other lock mode. It is the only one that blocks a plain SELECT. By default, a statement waits for a lock with no time limit. So set lock_timeout in your migration session. It aborts a statement that waits too long for a lock. Its default is 0, which means no timeout. If the migration times out, retry it later. A failed deploy is better than a down API. Also find long-running queries and transactions before you migrate. GoCardless advises removing them, and splitting schema changes into smaller pieces. Adding a column In Postgres, adding a column with no default, or with a non-volatile default such as a constant, does not rewrite the table. A volatile default, such as clock_timestamp(), rewrites the whole table and its indexes. Even the fast form takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for a moment, so set lock_timeout. In MySQL 8.4, ADD COLUMN uses the INSTANT algorithm by default, with some limits. Our advice: add new columns as nullable or with a constant default. Old code that names its columns ignores them, so this step is safe on its own. Renaming and changing types Renaming a column in Postgres does not touch stored data. MySQL 8.4 can often rename a column instantly, if the type stays the same. But the fast rename is still a trap. Old pods ask for name the moment it becomes full_name, and they fail. So rename with the five steps in the diagram. The same goes for changing a type. In Postgres, most type changes rewrite the table and its indexes. In MySQL, a type change uses a full table copy with no writes allowed during it. Add a new column of the new type instead, then move the data. Adding NOT NULL and constraints SET NOT NULL normally scans the whole table while it holds its lock. But if a valid CHECK constraint already proves there are no nulls, Postgres skips the scan. So do it in three steps: Add CHECK (full_name IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID. This skips the check of old rows. It still needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for a moment. Run VALIDATE CONSTRAINT. It scans the table, but takes only a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock, so normal reads and writes continue. Run SET NOT NULL, which now skips the scan. You can then drop the CHECK. The current docs also allow NOT VALID on a not-null constraint itself. Check your version before you rely on it. Foreign keys work the same way: add them NOT VALID, then validate. Adding a foreign key locks both tables, so set lock_timeout here too. Adding indexes A normal CREATE INDEX in Postgres lets reads continue but blocks inserts, updates and deletes until it is done. On a busy table, that is an outage. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. It does not block writes. The cost: it scans the table twice, waits for older transactions, and takes much longer. It cannot run inside a transaction block. If it fails, it leaves an "invalid" index that still slows writes. Drop it and try again. In MySQL 8.4, adding a secondary index runs in place and allows reads and writes. For changes that MySQL cannot do online, tools like GitHub's gh-ost build a "ghost" copy of the table, copy rows over in small pieces and follow new changes from the binary log. It can pause, and you choose when it swaps the tables. Backfills and dual writes A backfill copies or fixes data in old rows. Our advice: do not run it as one giant UPDATE, which can hold row locks for a long time and make replicas fall behind. Instead, update a small batch of rows by primary key, commit, pause, and repeat. Make the job safe to stop and restart. Watch replica lag and slow it down if lag grows. While the backfill runs, the app writes both the old and new columns, so new rows stay correct. Stripe used this for hundreds of millions of objects: dual write, move reads, move writes, then remove the old data. It ran old and new reads side by side with GitHub's Scientist library and alerted when results did not match. Rollback plans and backups Our advice: give each step a way back. Until the contract step, rollback is easy: deploy the previous app version. The old column is still complete. After you drop a column, the only way back is a restore. So before the contract step, take a backup and know how long a restore takes. GitLab's 2017 outage shows why. Its pg_dump backups had been failing because of a version mismatch, and the failure emails were rejected. After an engineer deleted data on the primary by mistake, about six hours of data was lost, and the site was down for about 18 hours. A backup you have never restored is only a hope. Approach Downtime? Old and new code both work? Effort Use it when One big migration in a maintenance window Yes Planned. No Everything switches at once. Low. Small internal tools where a short outage is fine. Direct change with lock_timeout No, if it is metadata only and gets its lock fast. Yes, for adds. No, for renames and drops. Low. Adding a nullable column, or a concurrent index. Expand and contract No Yes, at every step. High. Several deploys over days. Renames, type changes, splitting tables, anything a running app reads. Online copy tool (gh-ost, similar) Mostly no. You choose when the final swap happens. Yes, if the change itself is compatible. Medium. Needs disk space and care. Big MySQL tables where the change would rebuild the table. Simple rule: if a change removes or renames something that running code reads, it needs expand and contract. Otherwise, a single small migration with a lock timeout is usually fine. For every migration, ask: "What lock does this take, and for how long?" Check the docs for that exact statement. Ask: "Does the code running right now still work after this migration? Does the next version work before it?" Keep schema changes and code changes in separate deploys. For an add, run the migration first. For a drop, deploy the code that stops using the column first. Set lock_timeout in every migration session. Also set statement_timeout, but raise it for slow steps like VALIDATE CONSTRAINT. Run big backfills as a job, not inside the migration. Batch, pause, and make it restartable. Test the migration on a copy of production data size, not an empty test database. Write the rollback plan in the pull request. Say when the point of no return is. Test a restore from backup on a schedule, and alert when a backup job fails. "Here is a Postgres migration. For each statement, tell me the lock it takes and whether it rewrites or scans the table. Quote the PostgreSQL docs." "Split this column rename into expand and contract steps. Give me the migrations and code changes for each deploy, and the rollback for each step." "Write a backfill job that copies name to full_name in batches of 1,000 rows by id, with a pause, a resume point and a progress log." What to ask the agent No migration renames or drops a column that the deployed code still reads. Index builds on big Postgres tables use CONCURRENTLY, outside a transaction. Some migration tools wrap each file in a transaction, so check yours. NOT NULL and foreign keys are added NOT VALID first, then validated. No volatile default on a new column, and no type change on a big table. lock_timeout is set. AI agents rarely add it unless asked. The backfill is batched, restartable and does not run inside the schema migration. There is a tested backup before any step that deletes data. What to check yourself Safe deploys: how to roll out the code side of each step. Transactions and isolation levels: what locks are and why they wait. Coming next on this line: Running large migrations, API versioning and lifecycle and Disaster recovery and backups.

title: Search systems and inverted indexes
text: A search engine does not scan your text. It looks words up in an inverted index, ranks the matches, and must be kept in step with your database.
body: This story is made up, but it is common. A small shop has a search box. The code runs SELECT * FROM products WHERE title ILIKE '%shoe%'. With 5,000 products, it answers fast. Two years later there are 3 million products. Each search now reads every row, because no normal index can help with a pattern that starts with %. During a sale, searches use most of the database CPU, and checkout slows down too. The results are also poor. A search for "running shoes" does not find "Shoe for runners". The results come back in no useful order. So the team adds Elasticsearch. The code saves each product to Postgres and then to Elasticsearch. One night the Elasticsearch call times out for some saves. The prices in search no longer match the real prices, and nobody notices for a week. Both problems have known fixes. This lesson explains them. The Postgres docs list three problems with LIKE search. It has no language support, so satisfies does not match satisfy. It does not rank results. And it tends to be slow, because there is no index support, so it must process every document for every search. A search engine fixes this in two steps. When you add a document, it splits the text into words, cleans each word, and records which documents contain it. When you search, it cleans the query words the same way, looks them up, and ranks the matching documents. The record from step 1 is an inverted index. A book index is a good picture: "replication, pages 40, 112, 305". You do not read the whole book to find a word. The key idea. Search is fast because the work happens when you write. Each document is broken into terms once, and each term points to its documents. A query reads only a few short lists. Step through three product titles, the index built from them, and one query. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Step 1: analysis (tokenize and normalize) Elasticsearch calls this text analysis. Tokenization breaks text into small pieces called tokens. Normalization makes near matches equal. It can lowercase Quick to quick, stem foxes to fox, and index the synonyms jump and leap as one word. Postgres does the same work with dictionaries. Its normalized words are called lexemes. Very common words, like "the", are stop words and are usually dropped. Elasticsearch can apply the same rules to the query text. Always do this. If the index holds shoe but the query asks for Shoes, nothing matches. Step 2: the inverted index Each Elasticsearch shard is a Lucene index. Lucene's docs call the inverted index its core. It is made of postings, which let you look up the documents for a given term. It can also store the positions of a term inside each document. Positions make phrase search possible, like "red shoes" as two words side by side. Postgres has an inverted index too. Its GIN index has one entry for each lexeme, with a compressed list of where it appears. The docs call GIN the preferred index type for text search. Step 3: ranking A query for "red shoes" may match 40,000 products. Which come first? The engine gives each match a score. The classic idea is TF-IDF. Lucene's docs explain its parts. A document that contains a term more often scores higher. Rarer terms add more to the score. And a match in a shorter field counts for more. So "jacket" in 10 products tells you more than "red" in 50,000 products. BM25 is a newer formula built on the same TF-IDF ideas, with built-in term frequency normalization. Lucene's BM25 class traces it to the Okapi system at TREC-3, in 1994. It is the default similarity in Elasticsearch. Its two main settings are: k1 (default 1.2) controls saturation: how fast extra repeats of a word stop adding score. b (default 0.75) controls how much document length affects the score. You rarely change these. Most relevance work is in the analyzer, the fields you search and the boosts you add. Near real-time: refresh New documents are not searchable the moment you write them. Elasticsearch collects them and, on a refresh, writes them to a new segment and opens it for search. A segment is similar to an inverted index. By default, Elasticsearch refreshes every second. It only does this for indices that got at least one search request in the last 30 seconds. You can ask a write to wait. refresh=true makes the change visible at once, but it creates tiny segments that cost more at index, search and merge time. refresh=wait_for waits for the next refresh instead. The docs say to use the default, refresh=false, unless you have a good reason. Shards and replicas An Elasticsearch index is split into shards. Each shard is a self-contained Lucene index with part of the documents. Each document belongs to one primary shard. A replica shard is a copy of a primary, for failover and for more read capacity. You choose the number of primary shards when you create the index, and you cannot change it later. You can change the number of replicas at any time. Each shard runs a search on one CPU thread. Too many small shards slow search and can make the cluster unstable. Elastic suggests shards between 10 GB and 50 GB. Keeping the index in sync The search index is a copy. Your database is the source of truth. The dangerous design is the one from the story: write to the database, then write to the search engine in the same request. If the second write fails, the copy is wrong, and nothing repairs it. Safer designs read changes from the database itself: Outbox. In the same transaction as the product change, insert a row into an outbox table. A worker reads it and updates the index. CDC (change data capture). A tool reads the database's change log and sends each change to the indexer. Both are explained in Sagas, outbox and CDC. Make index updates idempotent: send the full document with its ID, so a retry is harmless. Keep a script that rebuilds the whole index from the database, because you will need it after mapping changes. When Postgres is enough You may not need a second system. Postgres gives you tsvector, tsquery, stemming dictionaries and a GIN index. It can rank with ts_rank and ts_rank_cd. But ranking must read the tsvector of each matching document, so it can be slow when a query matches many rows. Start with Postgres when the data fits in one database and the search needs are simple. Move to a search engine when you need better relevance, typo tolerance, facets, or search load that would hurt your main database. Option Fast on big data? Good ranking? Extra cost LIKE '%x%' No Every row is checked. No None at first. Postgres full-text search + GIN Yes, for many workloads. Basic: ts_rank. Slow with many matches. Little. Same database and same transaction. Elasticsearch or OpenSearch Yes Shards spread the load. Yes BM25, analyzers, boosts. A second cluster to run and an index to keep in sync. Managed search service Yes Yes, with less tuning. Money and less control. Still needs sync. Simple rule: start with Postgres full-text search. Add a search engine when relevance or load needs it, and feed it from an outbox or CDC. When you see LIKE '%...%' on a growing table, ask: "How many rows will this read in a year?" Write down the analyzer for each field. Test it with real queries from your users, including plurals, accents and typos. Treat the search index as derived data. Ask in design review: "How do we rebuild it from scratch, and how long does that take?" Monitor sync lag: the time between a database change and when search shows it. Alert on it. Do not set refresh=true on every write to fix "I can't see my change". Use wait_for only where a user must see their own write. Pick shard counts from expected data size, not from a guess. The primary count is fixed, so changing it means building a new index. Keep a small set of test queries with the results you expect. Run it after each analyzer or scoring change. "Find every SQL query in this repo that uses LIKE or ILIKE with a leading %. For each, estimate the table size and suggest a full-text index or a search engine." "Add a Postgres full-text search on products.title and products.description, with a GIN index on a generated tsvector column, and rank with ts_rank." "Write an outbox worker that reads product changes and sends the full document to Elasticsearch by ID. It must be safe to run twice." What to ask the agent The query uses the same language config or analyzer as the index. Otherwise matches are missed. The agent did not add a direct database-then-search write in the request path. Index writes use the document ID, so retries replace instead of adding duplicates. No refresh=true on every write. Test with real queries, not just the one the agent picked. What to check yourself Related lessons: Secondary, composite and special indexes, Sagas, outbox and CDC, Product search and discovery and PostgreSQL in depth.

title: Secondary, composite and special indexes
text: Pick indexes that match your real queries, read the plan to prove it, and count what every extra index costs on writes.
body: On 6 January 2026, GitLab.com slowed down for 2 hours and 36 minutes. Merge requests were slow and CI pipelines started late. Customers opened emergency tickets. A background job queue grew to between 600,000 and 700,000 jobs. The PgBouncer connection pool in front of the primary database was 100% full from 07:12 UTC. Database CPU stayed high. The cause was one missing index. A migration after a deploy had removed index_ssh_signatures_on_commit_sha. That was a single-column index on ssh_signatures (commit_sha). Queries that looked up signatures by commit_sha became slow or timed out. They held connections for longer, so the pool filled up, and everything else waited. By 08:51 the team had found the cause and recreated the index by hand. Performance came back. One follow-up is the lesson of this page. GitLab updated its docs on the column order of composite indexes. The point: a query that uses only the trailing columns of a composite index is not covered by it. The review does not say why the index looked safe to drop. But here is the lesson for you. An index can look like a copy of another one. It can still be the only one that serves a query. A table stores its rows in one way. InnoDB keeps them sorted by primary key. Postgres keeps them in no particular order. A secondary index is an extra sorted copy of a few columns, with a pointer back to each row. It lets the database find rows by something other than the main key, like orders by customer. In PostgreSQL, every index is a secondary index. The rows live in a separate area called the heap. A normal index scan reads the index, then fetches each row from the heap. MySQL's InnoDB works differently. The primary key index (the clustered index) holds the rows themselves. Each secondary index entry stores the row's primary key. So a lookup finds the primary key first, then searches the clustered index for the row. That is why InnoDB advises a short primary key: it is copied into every secondary index. The key idea. An index is a promise to answer one shape of query fast. You pay for that promise on every write. Choose indexes from your real queries, check the plan, and remove the ones nothing needs. You already know how a B-tree stores sorted keys from the B-tree and LSM lesson. This lesson is about which keys to put in it. Step through one composite index and three queries. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Composite indexes and column order A composite index sorts by its first column, then by the second inside each value of the first, and so on. Think of a phone book: sorted by last name, then first name. PostgreSQL states the exact rule. Equality conditions on the leading columns, plus a range on the first column without equality, narrow the part of the index it reads. Conditions on later columns are only checked along the way. So put equality columns first, then the range column. Winand shows the same with a date range and a subsidiary ID: with the equality column first, the scan reads far fewer index pages. CREATE INDEX orders_customer_created_idx ON orders (customer_id, created_at); -- Uses the index well: equality, then range SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 AND created_at >= '2026-05-06'; -- Cannot narrow the scan: no condition on customer_id SELECT id FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-05-06';PostgreSQL 18 can sometimes "skip scan" past a leading column with no equality condition. It usually does this only when that column has few distinct values. With many values, the planner usually prefers a full table scan. The docs also say to use multicolumn indexes sparingly. Indexes with more than three columns rarely help. Covering indexes and index-only scans If the index holds every column the query needs, Postgres can skip the heap. This is an index-only scan. An index that holds every column a query needs is a covering index. You can add extra "payload" columns with INCLUDE. They are stored but are not part of the search key. CREATE INDEX orders_customer_created_cov_idx ON orders (customer_id, created_at) INCLUDE (status, total);There is a catch. Postgres must still check that each row is visible to your transaction. It skips the heap only for pages marked all-visible in the table's visibility map. VACUUM updates that map. On a table where many rows change, index-only scans may gain you little. Wide payload columns also make the index bigger. Partial, expression and unique indexes A partial index covers only rows that match a WHERE condition. It is small when most rows don't matter, like unbilled orders. The query's condition must clearly match the index condition. A parameter like x < $1 does not count. CREATE INDEX orders_unbilled_idx ON orders (created_at) WHERE billed = false;An expression index stores the result of an expression. A search on lower(email) can use it. The expression runs on each insert and on many updates, so writes cost more. Use one when fast reads matter more than fast writes. CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_lower_idx ON users (lower(email));Because it is UNIQUE, this index also blocks two emails that differ only in case. A unique constraint or primary key creates its unique index for you. Don't add a second one by hand. By default, a unique index allows many nulls. NULLS NOT DISTINCT changes that. Reading EXPLAIN EXPLAIN shows the query plan. EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs the query and shows real row counts and times. It really runs it, so wrap an UPDATE or DELETE in a transaction and end it with ROLLBACK. The scan nodes you will see most: Seq Scan: reads the whole table. Index Scan: walks the index, then visits the heap for each row. Index Only Scan: answers from the index, visiting the heap only for pages not marked all-visible. Bitmap Index Scan + Bitmap Heap Scan: first collects matching row locations, sorts them into physical order, then reads the pages. It skips pages with no matches, so it can beat a full scan. Here is a query that the covering index above can answer alone. Every column it uses is in the index. EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 AND created_at >= '2026-05-06';The plan below is illustrative: we made up the numbers, in the PostgreSQL 18 style. PostgreSQL 18 shows buffers by default and prints fractional row counts. The long lines are wrapped to fit a phone. Index Only Scan using orders_customer_created_cov_idx on orders (cost=0.43..8.61 rows=12 width=12) (actual time=0.031..0.044 rows=11.00 loops=1) Index Cond: ((customer_id = 42) AND (created_at >= '2026-05-06 00:00:00+00'::timestamp with time zone)) Heap Fetches: 0 Index Searches: 1 Buffers: shared hit=4 Planning Time: 0.112 ms Execution Time: 0.061 msHeap Fetches: 0 means no row needed a heap visit. A high number means many pages are not all-visible: rows changed recently, or VACUUM is behind. Also look for Rows Removed by Filter: rows read and then thrown away. What each index costs The database must keep every index in step with the table. That adds work to each insert, update and delete. Indexes also use disk and memory. Postgres has a cheaper kind of update that skips index work. More indexes make it happen less often. The docs say plainly: remove indexes that are seldom or never used. To find them, look at pg_stat_user_indexes. Its idx_scan column counts scans, and last_idx_scan (PostgreSQL 16 and later) gives the time of the last one. SELECT indexrelname, idx_scan, last_idx_scan FROM pg_stat_user_indexes ORDER BY idx_scan;A unique index can show zero scans and still be needed, because it enforces the constraint. Never drop one for a low idx_scan. Counters reset after a crash or a restore from backup. Each server, including each replica, keeps its own counters. A replica that serves reports may use an index the primary never touches. Dropping it on the primary removes it from the replicas too. So check every server first. Building an index on a live table A normal CREATE INDEX lets reads continue but blocks inserts, updates and deletes until it finishes. On a large table, the build can take a long time. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY does not block writes, but it is slower and can leave an invalid index if it fails. See schema migrations for how to ship this safely. Special index types in one line each GIN: an inverted index for values with many parts: arrays, jsonb and full text search. Fast to search, slow to update. See search systems. GiST: a framework for many index types, including geometric data and nearest-neighbour search ("the 10 closest shops"). BRIN: tiny summaries per block range. Use it for huge tables where a column follows the physical row order, like an order date in an append-only table. Hash: equality only. A B-tree also handles equality, so start with a B-tree. At scale: local and global secondary indexes When data is split across machines, an index can be local to each piece, or global. The sharding lesson explains both. DynamoDB makes the trade-off concrete. A local secondary index (LSI) keeps the table's partition key with a different sort key. It allows strongly consistent reads. But it must be created with the table, and all items with one partition key value, in the table and its local indexes together, are limited to 10 GB. A global secondary index (GSI) can use any key. It is updated asynchronously, usually "within a fraction of a second", so reads may be out of date. If a GSI lacks write capacity, writes to the table itself are throttled. Option Fast reads Write cost Use when No index No Full scan on each query. Lowest. Small tables, or queries that read most rows anyway. Single-column index Yes, for that column. One more write per row change. One column filters well on its own. Composite index Yes, if the query matches the leading columns. One write, larger entries. Queries filter on a few columns together: equality first, then range. Covering (INCLUDE) Yes Can skip the heap. Larger index. Hot queries on tables that change slowly. Partial index Yes, for matching queries only. Low. Only matching rows. Most rows are not interesting, like billed = false. Global index (GSI) Yes, by any key. Extra write on another partition. Eventually consistent. A distributed store needs a second access path. Simple rule: every index should name the query it serves. If you cannot name one, you probably don't need it. Start from the slow query log or pg_stat_statements, not from the schema. Index the queries that run most or cost most. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on a copy of production data. Small test data gives different plans. Choose column order by the queries: equality columns first, the range or sort column last. Before dropping an index, list every query that might use it, including ones that use only its trailing columns. GitLab's outage came from one drop. On write-heavy tables, count the indexes. Before you call one unused, watch pg_stat_user_indexes on every server for a full business cycle. Build indexes on live tables with CONCURRENTLY, and check afterwards that no invalid index is left behind. "Here is the table definition, its indexes, and our 10 most frequent queries with their counts. For each query, say which index serves it, or propose one. Explain the column order. List indexes that no query uses." "Here is the EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) output for a slow query. Explain each node in plain words. Say where the time goes, and whether a different index or query would help." "Write a migration that adds this index to a 200-million-row Postgres table without blocking writes. Include a check for an invalid index and a rollback step." What to ask the agent Run every index the agent proposes through EXPLAIN ANALYZE on realistic data. A plan that looks good on 1,000 rows can change at 100 million. Check that the column order fits equality first, then range. Before dropping an index, check pg_stat_user_indexes on every server yourself. Make sure the migration uses CONCURRENTLY and is not wrapped in a transaction. For a partial index, check that the app's queries match its condition exactly, not through a parameter. What to check yourself API pagination and filtering: keyset pagination needs a composite index that matches the sort. Data models and query languages: how the planner picks a plan. Data modelling for NoSQL: global secondary indexes in DynamoDB-style stores.

title: Secrets and key management
text: Keep secrets out of code, give them a short life, and be ready to rotate any of them in minutes.
body: On 4 January 2023, CircleCI told its customers to rotate every secret they kept in it. CircleCI runs build and deploy jobs. Teams store API keys, tokens and cloud keys there, so those jobs can deploy. The attack began on 16 December 2022. Malware on one engineer's laptop stole a valid single sign-on session. The session already had two-factor authentication behind it. So the attacker could act as the engineer from far away. That engineer could create production access tokens. With them, the attacker reached some production databases and stores. On 22 December, they copied customer data, including environment variables, tokens and keys. The data was encrypted at rest. But the attacker "extracted encryption keys from a running process", so they could potentially read it. On 29 December, a customer reported odd GitHub OAuth activity. From 31 December, CircleCI rotated customers' GitHub OAuth tokens. On 4 January, it told customers to "assume they have been accessed" and rotate their secrets. The next day it revoked Project API tokens. One laptop forced every customer into an emergency. The lesson for us: many secrets sat in one store, and the keys to decrypt them were in a running process. A secret is anything that gives access. OWASP lists database credentials, SSH keys, certificates and API keys. OAuth tokens, signing keys and TLS private keys count too. Three rules cover most of the work: Keep secrets out of code and build output. The Twelve-Factor App asks for "strict separation of config from code". Its test: could you open-source the code today "without compromising any credentials"? Make secrets short-lived and small. A stolen secret should work for minutes, not years, and reach one system, not all. Be able to rotate any secret fast. Leaks will happen. Rotation is how you recover. The key idea. Assume every secret will leak one day. Then design so a leak does little harm: short lifetimes, small scopes, an audit log, and a rotation you have already practised. How secrets leak Secrets leak through ordinary paths: Git commits. Deleting the line in a later commit does not help. The old commit still holds it. That is why GitHub's scanner checks "your entire Git history on all branches". Logs and CI output. A debug line prints a request with its Authorization header. Container images. OWASP says never to put secrets in Docker ENV or ARG lines. Client apps. Anything shipped inside a mobile app or a JavaScript bundle can be read by anyone who downloads it. Chat and AI tools. Someone may paste a config file into a chat or an AI prompt to get help. Environment variables: better than code, not the end The Twelve-Factor App says to put config in environment variables. They change per deploy without code changes, and they are unlikely to be committed by accident. OWASP adds a warning. Environment variables "are generally accessible to all processes and may be included in logs or system dumps". It does not recommend them unless the other methods are not possible. A better option is a file that the orchestrator mounts at run time, never one built into the image. A secrets manager A secrets manager, such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager or GCP Secret Manager, gives you four things: One central store. OWASP says to centralize and standardize secrets management. Access policy. Each service reads only its own secrets. This is least privilege, applied to machines. An audit log. It records who asked for which secret, and when. OWASP says the log must resist tampering. Rotation. The store can change the secret on a schedule. Short-lived credentials instead of stored keys The best secret is one that does not exist until you need it. Dynamic secrets. Vault's database engine creates a new database user when a client asks. Each user has a lease, for example 1 hour, which the client can renew up to a maximum, for example 24 hours. When the lease ends, Vault revokes the user. Every service gets its own username. So you can trace a strange query back to one service instance. OIDC from CI. A GitHub Actions job can deploy to a cloud with no stored cloud key. The job gets a signed token from GitHub's OIDC provider. The cloud checks it and returns an access token that "is only valid for a single job". jobs: deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: id-token: write # lets the job request an OIDC token contents: read steps: # <pinned-sha> stands for a full commit SHA - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@<pinned-sha> with: role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/deploy aws-region: eu-west-1The id-token: write line does not give write access to anything. It only lets the job ask for the token. OWASP gives the same advice for pipelines: avoid static bootstrap credentials and use short-lived OIDC tokens. Rotation with two valid versions A rotation has a risky moment. If the password changes before every app has the new one, some calls fail. For rotation by a Lambda function, AWS Secrets Manager offers two strategies for database secrets. "Single user" changes one password. AWS calls it the simplest, and fine for most cases. There is a short window when the database may deny calls, so retry. "Alternating users" keeps two users and changes them in turn. After a rotation, both users' credentials are valid. AWS says it fits apps that need high availability. The same idea works for API keys and signing keys. Add the new key. Move every client to it. Then remove the old one. Encryption keys: KMS and envelope encryption Encrypting data creates a new problem: you must protect the key. AWS defines envelope encryption as "encrypting plaintext data with a data key, and then encrypting the data key under another key". Google Cloud names the two keys. The data encryption key (DEK) encrypts the data. The key encryption key (KEK) wraps the DEK, and "the KEK never leaves Cloud KMS". Step through it: Why not send all the data to KMS? Cloud KMS's Encrypt and Decrypt calls accept at most 64 KiB, because the service was built to manage KEKs. Google also says to make a new DEK for every write, and never to share one DEK between two users. That fits multi-tenancy well. At the top sits a hardware security module (HSM). AWS KMS keys never leave the service's FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSMs unencrypted. OWASP says a dedicated HSM of your own is only needed when a law, contract or security policy demands it. KMS also holds asymmetric keys, for example for signing. Their private keys never leave AWS KMS unencrypted. Secret scanning Catch secrets before they land, and find the ones that already did. GitHub secret scanning checks all history. It is free and automatic on public repos. Private organization repos need GitHub Secret Protection. For partner secrets, GitHub tells the provider, which may revoke the credential. Push protection blocks a push that contains a secret. For users it is on by default for public repos. For repositories, it needs GitHub Secret Protection, and an admin must turn it on. Anyone with write access can bypass it by giving a reason. The bypass raises an alert. Gitleaks scans Git history with gitleaks git and folders with gitleaks dir. It also runs as a pre-commit hook. It is now in maintenance: security fixes only. When a secret leaks OWASP's order is: revoke, rotate, then delete the secret from the exposed system. Do not start with a history rewrite. GitHub says removing a secret from history is slow and often not needed once the credential is revoked. Then ask OWASP's questions: who had access, when was it used, and when was it last rotated? Assume it was used, as CircleCI told its customers. Treat it as an incident. Option Survives a Git leak? Rotation effort Main risk Use it when Hard-coded in code No History keeps it. High. A code change and a deploy. Anyone with the repo has it. Never. Environment variable or CI variable Yes, if never committed. Medium. Update and restart. Readable by other processes, logs and dumps. Small apps, with no better option yet. Secrets manager, static secret Yes Low. Scheduled rotation. The store itself, and its bootstrap credential. Third-party API keys and passwords you cannot make dynamic. Dynamic or OIDC credential Yes Low. Each credential expires on its own. Vault's own root credential still needs rotating. Setup work, and a new runtime dependency. Databases, cloud access and CI deploys. Simple rule: use short-lived credentials where the system supports them. Put everything else in a secrets manager with rotation. For every secret, ask: "If this leaks tonight, who can rotate it, and how long does it take?" Keep a list of secrets with owner, scope and last rotation date. Put expiry dates in monitoring. Replace stored cloud keys in CI/CD with OIDC. Delete the old keys after. Turn on push protection and a pre-commit scanner for every repo. On private organization repos, push protection needs GitHub Secret Protection. Practise a rotation of your main database password before you need it. In review, look for secrets in logs, test fixtures, Dockerfiles and front-end code. Give each service its own credentials. Shared credentials make audit logs useless. Coding agents read your files and run commands. Treat them like any tool that can see secrets. "Scan this repo and its Git history for hard-coded secrets. List file, commit and secret type. Do not print the secret values." "Rewrite this GitHub Actions workflow to use OIDC with AWS instead of stored access keys. Pin every action to a commit SHA." "Add envelope encryption for the ssn column using AWS KMS. Use a new data key for every write and store only the wrapped key." What to ask the agent No real secret appears in the prompt, in .env files the agent can read, or in its output. The agent did not log a secret while debugging, even "just for now". New code reads secrets at run time from the secrets manager, not from a constant. Envelope encryption code never writes the plain data key to disk or logs. OIDC trust policies limit which repo and branch can assume the role. If a secret was pasted into a chat, treat it as leaked and rotate it. What to check yourself Authentication and authorization: tokens, sessions and least privilege. OWASP Top 10 and secure coding: where secrets fit among the common flaws. Dependency and supply-chain security: trusting the code you did not write. Threat modelling and zero trust: finding what an attacker would target before you build it.

title: Service mesh and sidecars
text: A service mesh moves mTLS, retries, traffic control and metrics out of your code and into proxies. Learn what that buys you, what it costs, and when to say no.
body: On Friday 27 October 2017, at 14:10, Monzo deployed a change to a payments service. Current account payments started to fail. The team rolled the change back two minutes later. The errors did not stop . Monzo used linkerd to route and load balance the calls between its several hundred services. Linkerd learned where each service ran from Kubernetes. At 14:18, engineers found that linkerd was sending traffic to IP addresses of processes that no longer existed. It had stopped getting updates . At 14:26 they restarted all of the several hundred linkerd proxies. The new proxies could not start until the Kubernetes API servers were restarted too. By 15:13 every proxy was back, but no service got any traffic. Now the whole platform was down, including the app . At 15:27 the logs showed the real blocker. Linkerd crashed with a NullPointerException while it read service discovery data. A new service, deployed the day before and then scaled to zero copies, triggered a bug between the linkerd and Kubernetes versions. Deleting that empty service fixed it at 15:31 . The first fault was a bug in Kubernetes and its etcd client after an etcd cluster upgrade a week or two earlier. Monzo called the restart of every proxy a poor decision that made the outage worse . The proxy layer touched every call. So when it broke, everything broke. In microservices, every call between services needs the same things. It needs a timeout, a retry rule, encryption, a check of who is calling, and metrics. You can write these in every service, in every language. Or you can move them into a proxy. A service mesh is that proxy layer, plus a system that manages it. It has two parts : The data plane. Proxies that carry every request between services. In Istio these are Envoy proxies, often deployed as sidecar proxies . The control plane. A service that tells the proxies what to do: routes, endpoints, rules and certificates. In Istio this is istiod . The app calls http://payments as if the network were simple. The proxies do the hard parts. Because the proxy is a separate process, it works with any language, and you can upgrade it without changing app code . The key idea. A mesh does not remove network work. It moves that work out of your code into proxies that your team must now run. You trade code in many services for one more critical system. Step through one call from an orders service to a payments service. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. mTLS and workload identity In the TLS lesson you saw mutual TLS. A mesh makes it the default. Each workload gets a workload identity. In Istio, it comes from the workload's Kubernetes service account . An agent next to each proxy makes a private key and asks istiod to sign a certificate. It also renews that certificate before it expires . Nobody copies certificates by hand. On each call, the client-side proxy starts the mTLS handshake. It checks that the server's certificate names a service account allowed to run the target service . The server-side proxy can then apply rules such as "only orders may call payments" . To roll this out, start in permissive mode. It accepts both plain text and mTLS while you add proxies. Then switch to strict mode, which accepts only mTLS . Timeouts, retries and traffic splitting Mesh config sets timeouts and retries per service, with no app change. Check the defaults. In Istio, the HTTP timeout is off by default. Failed HTTP requests are retried twice before the error is returned . That default meets your own code. Say your HTTP client tries each call 3 times. Each of those tries can become 3 attempts in the proxy. So one call can hit a failing service 9 times. This is retry amplification. Linkerd warns that services under constant retries can be taken down by them, not given time to recover . Timeouts clash in the same way. Istio's docs give an example. The app has a 2 second timeout. The mesh has a 3 second timeout with one retry. The app gives up first, so the mesh settings have no effect . Mesh and app settings work on their own, and can conflict . Retry only safe requests. Linkerd says retrying a request that changes state each time "can be disastrous" . Use idempotency keys for the rest. The mesh can also split traffic by weight. Istio's example sends 75% of requests to version 1 and 25% to version 2, for a canary or an A/B test . You raise the weight in config, not with a new deploy. The same proxies give you per-host limits and ejection of bad hosts. The circuit breakers lesson covers those. Telemetry Every proxy reports metrics for the traffic it carries . So you get request count, errors and latency for every service, in every language, from day one. Proxies can send trace spans too . But your app must still pass the trace headers from each incoming request to its outgoing calls . The distributed tracing lesson explains why. What it costs Resources. The Istio project tested version 1.24 at 1,000 requests per second with 1 KB payloads. One sidecar used about 0.20 vCPU and 60 MB of memory . Multiply that by your pods. For 400 pods, 60 MB each is 24 GB of memory just for proxies. Real numbers depend on your hardware and config . Latency. In sidecar mode, each call passes through two extra proxies: one next to the caller and one next to the callee . Each hop adds a little time, and the TLS work adds more. Measure p99 latency before and after, on your own hardware. Operational complexity. The mesh is now on the path of every call. Its upgrades, config pushes and bugs can break every service at once. That is what happened at Monzo . Someone must own it, upgrade it and debug it at 3 AM. Confusing failures. An error may now come from a proxy, not from your app. Engineers must learn to read proxy logs and mesh config. Sidecar or sidecar-less Istio's own team listed the problems with sidecars. You must restart the app pod to add or upgrade a sidecar. Each sidecar is sized for its pod's worst case, so a lot of CPU and memory sits idle. And sidecars can break apps with non-standard HTTP code . Ambient mode is Istio's answer. A ztunnel proxy runs once per node, not once per pod. It handles mTLS, L4 authorization and telemetry, and it does not read HTTP . For L7 features like HTTP routing and L7 authorization, you add waypoint proxies. These are Envoy proxies that run outside your app pods and scale on their own . Ambient mode became generally available in Istio 1.24, in November 2024 . In the same test, ztunnel used about 0.06 vCPU and 12 MB of memory per node. A waypoint used about 0.25 vCPU and 60 MB . Ambient and sidecar workloads can share one mesh, so you can move step by step . Option mTLS between services Retries and routing Cost to run Use it when Shared client library No You build it yourself. Yes, in code. One version per language. Low. No new system. Few services, one or two languages. Sidecar mesh Yes Automatic, with rotation. Yes Per service, in config. High. A proxy in every pod, and restarts to upgrade. Many services and languages, and a team to own the mesh. Sidecar-less mesh (Istio ambient) Yes, from the per-node ztunnel. Only where you add waypoint proxies. Lower per pod. Still a system to run. You mainly need mTLS and metrics, or sidecar cost is the blocker. API gateway only No Only at the edge. Yes, for outside traffic only. Medium. One layer at the edge. Your main need is clients outside, not service-to-service calls. Simple rule: adopt a mesh for a need you can name, like mTLS everywhere or many languages. Do not adopt one because it is popular. Ask "Which problem does the mesh solve that we cannot solve in a library?" If the answer is only retries, use a library. Do not adopt a mesh when you have a few services, one language, no compliance need for mTLS, or nobody to own it. Pick one layer for retries. If the mesh retries, turn them off in the app, or the other way round. Write that rule down. Set a timeout in the mesh for every route. Make the app timeout a little longer than the mesh timeout × attempts. Roll out mTLS in permissive mode first. Watch for plain-text traffic. Then go strict. Treat a mesh upgrade like a database upgrade. Canary it on a few workloads, and have a rollback plan. During an incident, do not restart every proxy at once. Monzo's restart turned a partial outage into a full one . Alert on the control plane too: config push errors and stale endpoints, not only request errors. "Read our Istio VirtualService and DestinationRule files and our HTTP client config. For each route, list the app timeout, app retries, mesh timeout and mesh retries. Show the worst-case attempts per call." "We have 30 services in Go and Java. List what we would gain and lose by adopting Istio ambient mode instead of sidecars. Cite the Istio docs for each point." "Write a rollout plan to move these 5 namespaces to strict mTLS. Include how to find clients still sending plain text." What to ask the agent Retry counts match the docs for your mesh version. Defaults change between versions. Retries apply only to idempotent requests, such as GET, or requests with an idempotency key. The agent did not set the mesh timeout longer than the app timeout. Resource numbers come from your own load test, not from a blog post. Config keys exist in your mesh version. Run the mesh's own config check before you apply anything. What to check yourself Load balancing: the balancing rules each proxy uses. Circuit breakers and bulkheads: the limits a mesh can enforce. Backoff, jitter and retry budgets: how to keep mesh retries from piling up. Distributed tracing: what the mesh can and cannot trace for you. Sidecar and container patterns (coming soon): the sidecar pattern beyond meshes.

title: Sharding and consistent hashing
text: One machine cannot hold everything. Learn how to split data across many, and how to add a machine without moving it all.
body: A food delivery app keeps menus in a cache cluster with 3 servers. To find the right server, the code runs hash(key) mod 3. It worked well for a year. On a Friday evening, traffic grows and the cache servers become overloaded. An engineer adds a fourth server and changes the code to mod 4. The deploy takes two minutes. Within seconds, the cache hit rate drops from 95% to about 25%. Almost every request now looks for its menu on a different server than before. The menus are still in the cache, but on the wrong machines. Every miss goes to the database, which was sized for 5% of the traffic. The database slows down, then times out. The app is down for 40 minutes at dinner time. Adding capacity caused the outage. The fix they needed was not a bigger database. It was a better way to map keys to servers. Sharding means splitting one big dataset into smaller pieces, called shards, and putting them on different machines. You shard when one machine cannot hold all the data, or cannot handle all the reads and writes. Books often call the same thing partitioning. Every record needs a rule that says which shard it lives on. That rule uses a shard key, such as the user ID or the order ID. You choose it once, and it is hard to change later. Sharding is not the same as replication. Replication keeps full copies of the same data. Sharding gives each machine a different part. Real systems usually do both: each shard has a leader and some followers. The key idea. A good shard key spreads both data and traffic evenly. A good mapping from keys to machines lets you add a machine and move only a small part of the data. Two ways to split the data Key-range partitioning. Each shard owns a range of keys, like the volumes of a paper encyclopedia: A–F, G–M, and so on. Range queries, such as "all keys from A to C", are cheap, because nearby keys sit together. The risk is uneven load. If the key is a timestamp, every new write goes to the shard that holds "today". Hash partitioning. You run the key through a hash function, code that turns any key into a number that looks random. Then you use the hash to pick the shard. A good hash spreads keys evenly, even keys that look alike. The cost: range queries no longer work well, because nearby keys land on different shards. Why hash mod N breaks The simple way to use a hash is shard = hash(key) mod N, where N is the number of servers. It spreads keys evenly. The problem comes when N changes. Step through what happens when you add a fourth server. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. With mod N, a key stays on its server only if its old and new remainders match. Going from N to N + 1 servers, only about 1 key in N + 1 stays. The rest move, and many move between two old servers. The 1997 paper that named consistent hashing says it plainly: when the range of a classic hash changes, "almost every item would be hashed to a new location." Now try it yourself. Add a server and compare how many keys move with each method. Consistent hashing and virtual nodes Consistent hashing changes as little as possible when servers come and go. Amazon's Dynamo database made the ring version famous. Servers and keys are hashed to points on a circle. Each key belongs to the first server you meet when you walk clockwise from the key. When a server joins or leaves, only its neighbours are affected. The others keep all their keys. With N servers, a new one takes about 1/(N + 1) of the keys on average. One point per server is not enough. Random points make some arcs much longer than others, so some servers get more keys. Dynamo's fix is virtual nodes: each server gets many points on the ring. Small arcs average out. When a server dies, its load spreads over many servers, not just one neighbour. And a bigger machine can get more points. Hot keys: the celebrity problem A perfect hash cannot fix one very busy key. All requests for one key go to one shard, however many shards you have. Think of a celebrity with millions of followers. A post from them can send huge traffic to a single shard. Discord stores messages by channel and time window. Discord gives an example: a big announcement on a large server can send many users to the same channel at once. Discord wrote that a hot partition "frequently affected latency across our entire database cluster." Part of their fix was routing by consistent hash. All requests for one channel go to the same service instance. It then sends one database query for many users who want the same data. For writes, a common fix is to split the hot key. Add a random two-digit suffix, and one key becomes 100 keys on many shards. The cost: every read must fetch all 100 and combine them. So do this only for the few keys that need it. Rebalancing and routing Moving data between machines is called rebalancing. A common pattern is to create many more shards than machines from the start. When you add a machine, it takes whole shards from the others. Keys never change shards, only shards change machines. For example, you might start with 1,000 shards on 10 machines. Dynamo tried three ways to split its ring. The most even load came from this one: cut the ring into equal, fixed ranges, and give each node the same number of them. Some databases rebalance on their own. Kleppmann suggests it can be good to keep a human in the loop. Moving data uses a lot of disk and network. If a node is only slow, an automatic system may think it is dead and start moving data. That adds even more load. Something must also know which machine holds which shard. There are three common choices. A client can ask any node, which forwards the request. A routing layer can sit in front of all nodes. Or the client can know the map itself. Some systems keep this map in a coordination service: a small, very reliable store that many machines share. Apache Helix, for example, stores which node holds each partition in ZooKeeper. Secondary indexes Say you shard orders by order_id, but you also need "all orders of customer 42". There are two kinds of index. Local index. Each shard indexes only its own rows. Writes are simple. But a query by customer must ask every shard and merge the results. This is called scatter/gather, and it is as slow as the slowest shard. Global index. The index itself is sharded by the indexed value, so one shard holds all of customer 42's entries. Reads are fast. But one write may need to update several shards, so the index is usually updated in the background. DynamoDB's global secondary indexes work this way. The docs say updates usually reach the index "within a fraction of a second". Your app must still handle results that are not up to date. Choice Even load? Range queries? Adding a machine Key-range partitioning No Busy ranges, like "today", get hot. Yes Nearby keys sit together. Split a range in two and move one half. hash mod N Yes, for normal keys. No Most keys move. Avoid it for anything you will resize. Hash ring with virtual nodes Yes, more even with more virtual nodes. No Only about 1/(N + 1) of the keys move. Fixed number of shards (many per machine) Yes, if shards are similar in size. Depends on the hash or range inside. Whole shards move. You must pick the count up front. Simple rule: don't shard until one machine and its replicas truly cannot cope. When you must, pick the shard key from your top queries, and never use plain mod N for a cluster that will grow. Before sharding, ask: "Can a bigger machine, read replicas or a cache give us another year of room to grow?" Sharding adds cost to every future feature. Choose the shard key from the queries you run most. If most requests are "for one user", shard by user ID, so one request touches one shard. List every query that will not include the shard key. Each one is a scatter/gather or a global index. Decide which, on purpose. Look for hot keys before launch: big customers, celebrity accounts, "today" timestamps. Plan how to split them. Watch load per shard, not just the cluster average. One shard at 95% CPU is an incident, even if the average is 40%. Rehearse adding a node in a test environment. Measure how much data moves and how long it takes. "Here are our 10 most frequent queries and the table schema. Suggest a shard key. For each query, say if it hits one shard or all shards." "Find every place in this code that picks a server or shard with hash(...) % n. Show what breaks when n changes." "Write a script that loads 1 million fake keys, maps them to 10 servers with a hash ring of 100 virtual nodes each, then adds an 11th. Print the share of keys that moved and the load per server." What to ask the agent The shard key appears in your most common queries, and the agent did not pick it just because it is unique. The hash function is the same in every service and every language that routes requests. Two hashes mean two different maps. The test data has realistic skew, such as one customer with 10% of all rows. Uniform fake data hides hot keys. The rebalancing plan says what happens to reads and writes while data is moving. Any query without the shard key has a known cost, and someone agreed to it. What to check yourself Before this: Replication. Each shard is usually replicated too. Next: Quorums and leaderless replication, which builds on the Dynamo ring, and Distributed caches, which spread a cache across nodes the same way. For writes that pile onto one key, see Scaling writes and hot keys; for designing tables around one shard key, see Data modelling for NoSQL.

title: SOLID, coupling and cohesion
text: Learn what coupling, cohesion and the five SOLID principles really say, and when following them blindly makes code harder to change.
body: This story is made up, but both halves are common. Kiran's team runs the checkout service of a shoe store. The Checkout class creates an SmtpMailer and calls it to send order emails.
