Do not hide it, and do not ask for it separately each time. When someone proposes a rewrite, ask: "Can we replace one piece first and ship it?" After paying down an item, measure again. Show the PM that the change time dropped. "Here is the git log for the last 12 months as a list of files and change counts. Rank the 10 files that changed most, and for each one, list the size and the number of commits that mention 'fix' or 'bug'." "Read this module. List the duplicated logic and the riskiest parts to change. Suggest three refactoring steps, each small enough to ship alone with its own tests." "Turn this debt item into a short note for my PM: what it costs us each month, the fix in steps, and when it pays back." What to ask the agent The ranking uses real history, not guesses. Run the git command yourself and compare. Each refactoring step keeps behaviour the same. Tests must pass before and after every step. The agent did not "clean up" odd code that is really a bug fix. Check the commit history of strange lines before you delete them. The cost numbers in the PM note come from your team, not from the agent. An agent can rewrite a module fast. That does not make a rewrite less risky. Review it like any other large change. What to check yourself Before this: architecture trade-offs. Related: working with PMs and the business, refactoring and legacy code, estimation and planning under uncertainty and running large migrations.

title: Testing strategy that scales
text: Which tests to write at each level, how to keep a growing suite fast and trusted, and how to spot tests that check nothing.
body: A team runs an online shop. Its main test suite clicks through the site in a real browser: sign in, search, add to cart, pay. There are 300 of these tests, and the suite takes 40 minutes. Every week a few tests fail with no change to the code. A timeout here, a slow page there. The team learns a habit: when a test fails, press "re-run". Usually it turns green. One Friday, the payment test fails. A developer re-runs it twice, and on the third run it passes. He merges. The failure was real: a race in the new payment code that showed up only some of the time. Customers were charged twice over the weekend. This story is made up. But Google has seen the same thing: developers dismiss a failure as flaky and later find it was a real bug. The tests were not the problem. The strategy was. Tests are not there to find bugs once. They are there so you can change code with confidence, again and again, for years. A good suite tells you fast, and truthfully, if your change broke something. Tests come in three common scopes: Unit tests check one small piece, like a function or a class. Integration tests check a few parts working together, like your code and a real database. End-to-end tests run the whole system the way a user does. Lower tests are fast and cheap, and a failure points close to the cause. Tests through the UI are slow, brittle and expensive to write, but they see the real system. A strategy is the mix you choose, and the rules that keep it fast and trusted. The key idea. Write many small, fast tests and only a few large ones. In our view, a test that people do not trust does harm, because it teaches them to ignore red. Step through one change as it passes four layers of checks. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. The test pyramid. Mike Cohn made the pyramid popular in his 2009 book Succeeding with Agile. The bottom is many unit tests. The top is a few tests through the UI. Ham Vocke sums it up in two rules: write tests at different levels, and the higher the level, the fewer tests you should have. As a very rough guide, Google aims for about 80% unit, 15% integration and 5% end-to-end tests. The opposite shape is the ice cream cone: many end-to-end tests and few unit tests. Google says such suites tend to be slow, unreliable and hard to work with. The team in the story had an ice cream cone. The critics: the testing trophy. Kent C. Dodds draws a trophy instead. From the bottom, it has static checks, unit tests, integration tests and end-to-end tests. He builds on Guillermo Rauch's advice: "Write tests. Not too many. Mostly integration." His rule: "The more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you." He made it for JavaScript apps, mostly in one codebase. In our view, both shapes agree on the main point: keep end-to-end tests few. They differ on how much weight integration tests get. Size is not the same as scope. "Unit" and "integration" mean different things to different teams. So Google also sorts tests by the resources they use. Small: one process, no network, no disk, no sleep. Time limit 60 seconds. Medium: one machine. Network to localhost only, so a database in a container is fine. Limit 300 seconds. Large: anything, across many machines. Limit 900 seconds or more. Google cares most about speed and determinism, and size predicts both. A test that cannot touch the network cannot fail because the network was slow. Flaky tests. A flaky test passes and fails on the same code. In 2016, Google reported that about 1.5% of all its test runs gave a flaky result. Almost 16% of its tests had some flakiness. In post-submit CI, about 84% of pass-to-fail changes involved a flaky test. The book says tests begin to lose value as flakiness nears 1%. The real cost is trust. People ignore alarms that are often false, so real failures get dismissed. Google's tools re-run failing tests and quarantine very flaky ones. Quarantine has a cost: it can hide a real race in the code. Treat a flaky test as a bug with an owner, not as noise. Test data. Large tests need data that looks real. Data written by hand covers a narrow range of cases and reflects the author's biases. Copied production data is more real, and a sample of it keeps the size down. Google's book says tests should not depend on the order they run in, or on a shared database. So let each test create its own data. Contract tests between services. End-to-end tests across many services are slow and brittle. A contract test checks each service alone against a shared contract. In Pact, the consumer's tests generate the contract, so it holds only the requests the consumer really uses. The provider then checks that it can answer them. Testing in production. Some bugs appear only with real traffic, real data and real config. Google's book says config changes are the number one cause of its major outages. Unit tests alone cannot check them. So the last check runs in production. A prober is a test that checks production, usually with read-only actions. During a staged rollout, canary analysis compares the canary's health with the rest of the fleet. See Safe deploys and config changes for how a canary stops a bad release. Mutation testing. Line coverage only shows which code ran during tests. It does not show that a test would notice a bug. Mutation testing makes small changes to your code, such as flipping a condition, and runs the tests again. If a test fails, the change is "killed". If all tests still pass, the change "lived", and your tests missed it. It runs your tests many times, once per change. So we suggest you start with the code that matters most. See Property-based and mutation testing. What to test first. You cannot test everything, so start with risk. Ask: what costs the most if it breaks, and what changes most often? Money, auth, data loss and shared libraries come first. Google calls this the Beyoncé Rule: test everything you do not want to break. In its words, "If you liked it, then you shoulda put a test on it." Option Speed What it catches What it misses Keep it Unit (small) Fast. Run them on every change. Logic, edge cases, rounding. Points close to the cause. Wrong SQL, config, how parts fit together. Many. Most of the suite. Integration (medium) Slower. Limit 300 s per test. Real database, queues, serialisation. Other teams' services, the full user flow. A good number, for each boundary you own. Contract Each side runs alone, without the full system. Broken requests or responses between services. Whether the whole flow works for a user. One per consumer and provider pair. End-to-end (large) Slow. Often flaky. A broken user journey across the system. Exact cause of a failure. Few. Only key journeys, like sign-up and pay. Canary in production Slow. It waits for real traffic. Real data, real load, real config. Bugs that hit only rare users. Some users see errors. On every deploy. Simple rule: test each thing at the lowest level that can catch it. When a higher test finds a bug, add a lower test for it. Ask in design reviews: "How will we know this works, and how fast?" Plan the tests with the feature. Watch suite time. Ask: "How long from push to green?" If it grows, move tests down the pyramid. Track flaky tests on a list with owners. Fix or delete them. Do not let "re-run" become a habit. Use a real database in a container for data code. Use a test double for slow or paid services, like a payment provider. When a bug reaches production, write the lowest test that would have caught it, before you fix it. In reviews, read the assertions first. Ask: "If I broke this code, would this test fail?" "Write unit tests for applyDiscount. Cover zero, negative, rounding and the maximum value. Every test must assert the exact result." "Here is our test suite. Which tests are end-to-end checks of logic that a unit test could cover? List them with a lower-level replacement." "This test is flaky. Read it and list every source of non-determinism: time, order, randomness, network and shared state." What to ask the agent Every test has an assertion that would fail if the code were wrong. AI tools sometimes write tests that only call the code, or assert that a mock was called. See Reviewing human and AI code. The test does not copy the code's logic into the expected value. Then a wrong formula passes. Break the code on purpose, or run a mutation tool. If the tests stay green, they test nothing. No sleep calls, real clocks or real network in unit tests. The agent did not change or delete a failing test to make the build green. What to check yourself Flaky tests: finding and fixing the causes. Contract and integration tests: Pact and testing service boundaries. CI/CD and trunk-based development: where these tests run.

title: Threat modelling and zero trust
text: Find what an attacker would target in your design before you build it, and stop trusting a call just because it comes from inside.
body: On 16 June 2023, the US State Department told Microsoft about strange access to its email. A custom alert on mailbox access logs had fired. Microsoft found that an attacker it calls Storm-0558 was reading mail with forged login tokens. The tokens were signed with a Microsoft consumer account key from 2016. That key was only meant to sign tokens for consumer email, not enterprise mailboxes. It was also meant to be retired in March 2021. The key should never have opened enterprise mail. But Microsoft had built one shared endpoint that listed active signing keys for both consumer and enterprise systems. The libraries that check tokens were not properly updated to tell the two kinds of key apart. So mail accepted a token signed by either kind of key. The attacker reached the mailboxes of 22 organizations and 503 personal accounts. It downloaded about 60,000 emails from the State Department alone. Microsoft still did not know how the key was stolen when the Cyber Safety Review Board finished its review. The Board called the intrusion "preventable". The Board listed several errors. For example, the old key was never removed, and Microsoft did not detect the forged tokens itself. But it found that without the validation flaw, no enterprise customer would have been hit. In our reading, the missing check sat on a trust boundary between consumer and enterprise systems. A threat model asks at each such line: what if a token from the other side shows up here? The Board asked cloud providers to design identity systems "informed by a rigorous threat model". A threat model is a structured look at a design to find what could go wrong with its security and privacy. You do it before you build, and you keep doing it as the design changes. It comes down to four questions: What are we working on? What can go wrong? What are we going to do about it? Did we do a good enough job? Zero trust is a related idea. No user, device or service is trusted just because of where it sits on the network. Every request proves who it comes from and gets checked. The key idea. Draw where data crosses from one level of trust to another. Ask what could go wrong at each crossing. Then check identity and permission at every crossing, including the ones inside your own network. Draw the system and its trust boundaries Start with a data flow diagram. OWASP says a useful model shows trust boundaries, data flows, data stores, processes and external entities. These often mark the places attackers aim at. A trust boundary is where data or a call moves between parts you trust differently. Examples: the internet to your API, one tenant to another, a partner's webhook to your code, or a consumer system to an enterprise one. Step through a small design: an expense app where users upload receipts. Ask what can go wrong: STRIDE STRIDE is a list of six prompts. Each letter is a kind of threat, and each one breaks a security property. Letter Threat Breaks Receipt app example S Spoofing: using someone else's identity Authentication The body sends another user's userId, or a stolen session uploads. T Tampering: changing data you should not Integrity A user edits an expense total after it was approved. R Repudiation: denying an action with no proof Accounting A user says "I never uploaded that". I Information disclosure Confidentiality The bucket is public, or links never expire. D Denial of service Availability A 2 GB upload fills the worker's disk. E Elevation of privilege Authorization A crafted PDF exploits the parser, and the worker has database admin rights. Walk the list at each trust boundary. Spend most time where outside data enters. You will find ideas that are not on the list. That is fine. Choose what to do Rank each threat by how likely it is and how bad it would be. OWASP admits both are hard to measure, and that this ranking ignores the work to fix each one. So weigh the cost of the fix too. A simple high, medium or low for each is enough to start. Then pick one of four responses: Mitigate: lower the chance it happens. Lock an expense once it is approved. Eliminate: remove the feature. Maybe you do not need public receipt links at all. Transfer: give the cost to someone else, such as an insurer. This does not make the event less likely or less harmful. Accept: write down why, and who agreed. For the receipt app, a good list is short. Take the user from the verified session, not the body. Keep the bucket private and use links that expire in minutes. Log every upload with the user ID. Limit the file size. Run the parser with no database rights; it hands results to a small writer with insert-only access. Each fix should be testable. OWASP asks reviewers to check that agreed mitigations can be tested. Keep it lightweight The manifesto values "people and collaboration" over processes, methodologies and tools. It also values "continuous refinement" over a single delivery. Threat modelling should fit how your team already works, in small steps scoped to the part that changed. In practice: add a "Threats" section to each design doc. Spend 30 minutes with the people who know the design. Turn each decision into a ticket or a test. The fourth question checks the model itself. Does the diagram match the system? Does every threat have a response, and can each fix be tested? Ask it again after launch or after an incident. Zero trust: what it means The old model is a castle. Anything inside the wall is trusted. Google's BeyondCorp paper says that once the wall is breached, the attacker has easy access to the internal network. NIST's definition: zero trust "assumes there is no implicit trust granted to assets or user accounts based solely on their physical or network location". Two of its tenets matter most for daily work: Every connection is protected, wherever it comes from. A request from inside must meet the same rules as one from outside. Access is granted per session, with least privilege. Access to one resource does not grant access to another. At Google, every internal app sits behind an internet-facing access proxy. It checks the user, their groups, the device certificate and the device's state on every request. In a Google office, a laptop without a valid certificate lands on a network with very limited access. Zero trust for a service team You probably do not run the access proxy. You run services. For you, zero trust means three habits. Every caller has an identity. Each workload gets its own identity, proved with a short-lived certificate or token. SPIFFE names workloads with IDs like spiffe://acme.com/billing/payments, and rotates their keys often and automatically. A service mesh can do this for you. See Service mesh and sidecars. Every request is checked. Verify the caller's credential, then check what it may do. Never trust a header because the call came from inside. # Wrong: any pod that can reach us can claim to be any user user_id = request.headers["X-User-Id"] # Right: verify a signed token for this service, then read the user from it claims = verify_token(request.headers["Authorization"], audience="receipts-api") user_id = claims["sub"]Credentials are short-lived and narrow. Each service gets only the permissions it needs. How to issue and rotate them is in Secrets and key management. What zero trust does not mean It is not a product. NIST calls it a set of guiding principles. Moving to it is "a journey", not a swap of technology. It does not remove the firewall overnight. NIST expects most companies to run a hybrid of zero trust and perimeter controls for an indefinite period. It does not stop a valid account. An attacker with real credentials can still reach what that account may reach. Zero trust should stop it from moving further. It adds a critical part. If the policy service fails or is attacked, people may not reach anything. Run it in several places. Option What it catches Cost Main risk Use it when No threat model, code review only Bugs in single lines. None up front. No Design flaws, like a missing boundary check, ship. Small changes with no new data flow. 30-minute four-question session Many design flaws at trust boundaries. Low. One meeting per design. Shallow if the right people are not there. Every new feature, endpoint or integration. Full STRIDE per element, with a tool More threats, written down for audits. High. Days of work. It goes stale if nobody updates it. Identity, payments and other high-risk systems. Network perimeter as the main control Outsiders who never got in. Low. It already exists. No Once inside, an attacker moves freely. Only as one layer among others. Zero trust: per-request identity and policy Stolen access to one part reaching other parts. Medium to high. Identity for every workload and device. The policy service becomes critical. New systems, and step by step for old ones. Simple rule: threat model every design that adds a trust boundary. Make every service check its caller, whatever network the call comes from. In design review, ask: "Where are the trust boundaries, and what checks the data at each one?" Draw the data flow on the whiteboard first. Most missed threats hide in arrows nobody drew. Ask: "What if a valid token from the wrong tenant, environment or system shows up here?" That was the Storm-0558 question. Never accept "it is internal" as a reason to skip authentication. Ask who else can reach that network. Turn each threat into a ticket, a test or a written acceptance with an owner. A list in a doc is not a fix. Revisit the model when the design changes, not on a calendar. Prefer shared libraries for token checks. The Board found that many different token libraries made correct, uniform checks harder. "Here is our design doc. Draw a data flow diagram as a Mermaid chart. Mark every trust boundary and list the data that crosses each one." "For each trust boundary in this diagram, list STRIDE threats. For each, give likelihood, impact and one concrete mitigation. Mark the ones you are unsure of." "Search this service for code that reads user or tenant IDs from headers or request bodies without verifying a token. List file and line." What to ask the agent The agent's diagram matches the real system. Check it against your deploy config, not only the doc. Generic threats like "use strong passwords" add noise. Keep only threats tied to a flow in your design. Mitigations name a real place in your code or config. "Add validation" is not a mitigation. Each internal endpoint the agent writes checks the caller's identity, not just its IP address. The agent cannot judge business impact. You decide the ranking with your team. What to check yourself Authentication and authorization: how to check a user and their permission on every request. Authorization models: RBAC, ABAC and ReBAC: how to write the "what may this caller do" rules. Dependency and supply-chain security: threats that arrive in code you did not write. Design docs and RFCs: where your "Threats" section lives.

title: TLS and secure connections
text: Learn what TLS protects, how a client decides to trust a server, and how to stop certificate expiry from taking your service down.
body: On 27 July 2026, at 17:56 UTC, one certificate expired at Lucidworks. It covered several names, including platform.lucidworks.com and api.lucidworks.com. Users of the platform got certificate errors and could not open it . Data was lost too. Usage signals sent to the Beacon endpoint on api.lucidworks.com between 17:56 and 19:01 UTC were not stored. They cannot be recovered . The warning came in time. On 27 June, a monitoring check raised an alert 30 days before expiry. It went to an internal channel, and nobody acted on it. From 1 July, alerts also stopped reaching the incident management system, and nothing watched that path . The team made and installed a new certificate by hand. This took longer because they used a new certificate provider, so they first had to prove they owned the domains in DNS. Service was fully back at 19:24 UTC . Their action items: remove the manual renewal step, and send expiry alerts to a pager that needs a person to answer . A certificate fails on a date you know in advance. Seniors plan for that date. When your app calls https://api.shop.example, the data crosses Wi-Fi, ISPs and routers you do not control. TLS protects that path. TLS 1.3 gives three things : Confidentiality. Only the two ends can read the data. Integrity. Nobody can change the data without being noticed. Authentication. The server always proves who it is. The client proves who it is only if the server asks. The server proves its identity with a certificate. A certificate says "this public key belongs to api.shop.example", and is valid between two dates . A certificate authority (CA) signs it. Your app does not know every CA. It knows a small set of root certificates in its trust store. Roots sign intermediate certificates, and intermediates sign site certificates . This is the chain of trust. The key idea. TLS does two jobs: it agrees on secret keys, and it proves the server holds the private key for a certificate the client trusts. The outages in this lesson were not about cryptography. They were about a certificate that expired. A chain the client cannot follow fails the same way. Step through one TLS 1.3 handshake and a request. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. The TLS 1.3 handshake in plain words TLS runs on top of a TCP connection. Then: ClientHello. The client sends the options it supports and its part of a key exchange (a "key share") . ServerHello. The server picks the options and sends its own key share. From here, both sides can compute the same keys. Every handshake message after ServerHello is encrypted . Certificate and proof. The server sends its certificate chain. It also sends a signature over the whole handshake, made with the private key that matches the certificate . A thief who copied the certificate but not the private key cannot make this signature. Finished. The client checks everything and sends Finished. Now application data can flow . This takes one round trip, so RFC 9846 calls it the 1-RTT handshake . How the client checks the chain The client must check that the certificate is for the host it asked for . It then follows the chain. Each certificate must be signed by the next one up, and the top must be signed by a trust anchor, such as a root in the trust store . Each certificate must be valid now: the current time must be inside its dates . When the server sends its own certificate plus the intermediate, the client can check every signature up to a root it already trusts. It does not need to download anything else . If the check fails, an automated client must log the error and should close the connection . SNI: many sites on one address One IP address often serves many domains. The server must know which certificate to send before it can send one. So the client puts the host name in the ClientHello. This is Server Name Indication (SNI) . The ClientHello also lists the application protocols the client speaks, such as HTTP/2. This is ALPN . 0-RTT and replay When a client has talked to a server before, TLS 1.3 lets it send data in its very first message. This is called 0-RTT, or early data . It saves a round trip, but it has weaker protection. RFC 9846 says there are no guarantees of non-replay between connections . An attacker can copy that data and send it again. For HTTP, clients must not send unsafe methods, like POST, in early data . A server that does not want to risk a replay can answer 425 Too Early . Mutual TLS between services In normal TLS, only the server shows a certificate. With mutual TLS (mTLS), the server also asks the client for one . Now both sides know who they talk to. This is common between internal services. A service mesh such as Istio can do this for you. A proxy next to each service starts the mutual TLS handshake . Istio gives each workload a certificate and rotates keys and certificates automatically . Its permissive mode accepts both plain text and mTLS, which helps you move services over step by step . Then switch to strict mode. Expiry and automatic renewal Every certificate has an end date . Let's Encrypt certificates are valid for 90 days by default, and it suggests renewing them every 60 days . They are getting shorter. On 10 February 2027 the default becomes 64 days, and on 16 February 2028 it becomes 45 days . Let's Encrypt warns that a fixed schedule, like a job every 60 days, will then fail . ACME is the protocol that makes renewal automatic. Software proves it controls the domain and gets a certificate with no human involved . Before ACME, people often needed 1–3 hours to get and install one certificate . Automation still fails. At ImprovMX, a changed credential made renewals fail silently. An outside monitor gave no warning. The SMTP certificate expired, and sending mail failed for about six hours . Their fix: their own expiry checks, and alerts when a renewal fails . HSTS A user who types shop.example may first reach your site over plain HTTP. An attacker can act there. The Strict-Transport-Security header tells the browser to use only HTTPS for your site from now on . The browser then turns http:// links into https:// before it sends anything . It also stops users from clicking through certificate errors . The first visit is still exposed, and the preload list fixes that . Where TLS ends TLS protects one hop. Often it ends at the load balancer. An AWS Application Load Balancer uses its certificate to decrypt requests, then sends them to your servers . You can send HTTPS to the servers too. But the load balancer does not validate their certificates . AWS says this is safe inside the VPC, but traffic that leaves AWS needs more steps . To keep traffic encrypted until your server, AWS suggests a Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener, which passes TLS through . Option Encrypted until Who holds certificates Use it when End TLS at the load balancer The load balancer. Only the load balancer. Most web apps on a private network. Re-encrypt to servers The server, but its certificate is not checked by AWS. Load balancer and servers. Rules say all traffic must be encrypted. TLS passthrough (Network Load Balancer, TCP) The server. Only the servers. The load balancer must not see the data. Mutual TLS Both ends, both proven. Every service. Needs automatic rotation. Calls between your own services. 0-RTT Weaker. It can be replayed. Same as normal TLS. Only safe, repeatable requests like GET. Simple rule: end TLS at the edge for speed, add mTLS inside when services must prove who they are, and automate every certificate. Keep a list of every certificate: where it lives, who owns it, and when it expires. Shared certificates for many names make one expiry hit many services. Ask of each certificate: "What renews it, and what tells us when renewal fails?" Alert on the renewal, not only on the date. Send expiry alerts to the on-call pager, 30 days and 7 days ahead. A chat channel is not enough. Check certificates from outside too, with a probe that follows the full chain like a real client. When one client fails and another works, compare the chain each one receives and the trust store each one uses. Turn off 0-RTT for APIs that change data, unless every request is safe to replay. Never ship code that disables certificate checks, even "only in staging". "Write a script that lists every TLS certificate on these 40 hosts, with issuer, names and expiry date. Sort by expiry and flag anything under 30 days." "Review this nginx TLS config. Does it send the full chain? Is 0-RTT on, and is that safe for these endpoints?" "Our certificate renewal runs from cron every 60 days. Our CA is moving to 45-day certificates. Rewrite it to use ACME Renewal Information, and alert when renewal fails." What to ask the agent The agent did not add verify=False, InsecureSkipVerify or a similar switch to make an error go away. Expiry dates come from the real certificate the server sends, not from a file on disk that may be old. Lifetimes and dates match the CA's current docs. Let's Encrypt changes its lifetimes from 2026 to 2028 . The mTLS setup checks the client certificate, not only that one exists. HSTS is sent only over HTTPS, and includeSubDomains does not cover a subdomain that still needs HTTP. What to check yourself TCP/IP and the network stack: the connection TLS runs on. HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3: ALPN, and TLS inside QUIC. Authentication and authorization: who the user is, which TLS does not tell you. Secrets and key management: where private keys should live. Service mesh and sidecars: mTLS for every service.

title: Transactions and isolation levels
text: Your code is correct when it runs alone. Isolation levels decide what happens when it runs twice at the same moment.
body: A small shop sells concert T-shirts. The stock for size M is 10. A popular singer posts a link, and orders arrive many per second. The order code looks fine. It reads the stock, checks that it is above zero, works out stock minus one, and saves the new number. Each order runs inside a database transaction. Every test passes. After the sale, the warehouse counts the shirts. The database says 4 left, but the shelf is empty. The shop has sold 6 shirts it does not have. Now someone must email 6 customers and refund them. The code was correct for one order at a time. It was not correct for two orders at the same moment. Wrapping it in a transaction did not help, because of the isolation level. A transaction groups several reads and writes into one unit. The database makes four promises about it, called ACID. Atomicity: all or nothing. If anything fails halfway, the database undoes the whole group. Consistency: your rules, like "stock is never negative", still hold at the end. This one is mostly your job, not the database's. Isolation: transactions running at the same time should not get in each other's way. Durability: once the database says "committed", the data survives a crash. The surprise is in the "I". Full isolation is slow, so databases offer weaker isolation levels. Most apps run at a weak level without knowing it. The key idea. A transaction is not a lock. At the default level in Postgres and MySQL, two transactions can both read a value, both change it, and one change can vanish. Step through the T-shirt bug. Two orders, A and B, buy one shirt each. This is a lost update: two transactions read, change and write the same value, and the second write wipes out the first. The levels, from weak to strong Read committed. You never see data that another transaction has not committed yet. That rules out the dirty read. But each statement sees the newest committed data. So two reads in one transaction can return different answers. This is the Postgres default. Snapshot isolation (called Repeatable Read in Postgres). The transaction reads from one snapshot of the database, taken at its first statement. It does not see changes that others commit later. How does the database keep old and new versions at once? With MVCC. It keeps several versions of a row. Readers see the version that fits their snapshot, and writers add a new version. Readers and writers do not block each other. Serializable. The result must be the same as if the transactions had run one after another. Postgres builds this on top of snapshots. It watches for dangerous patterns and aborts one transaction when it finds one. What the defaults really do Names differ between databases, so check what your database does, not what the level is called. Postgres defaults to Read Committed. A lost update can happen here. In Postgres Repeatable Read, order B's write fails. It gets "could not serialize access due to concurrent update", and the app must retry the whole transaction. MySQL InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ. Plain reads use a snapshot from the first read. But Hermitage's tests found that this level does not prevent lost updates when you read with a plain SELECT. At Serializable, both databases prevent lost updates and write skew. Three ways to fix a lost update 1. Atomic update. Let the database do the math in one statement: UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 42 AND stock > 0;If no row changed, the shirt is sold out. In Read Committed, Postgres makes the second update wait. Then it checks the WHERE clause again on the new row. This is the simplest fix, and you should use it whenever the change fits in one statement. 2. Lock the row. Read with SELECT … FOR UPDATE. Other transactions that try to lock or change the row wait until you commit or roll back. In Read Committed, the waiting transaction then gets the new value, 9, not 10. Use this when the logic is too complex for one statement. 3. Stronger isolation. Use Repeatable Read or Serializable in Postgres, and retry when the database aborts a transaction. Every caller must handle the retry. Write skew: the harder bug Some bugs are not about one row. A hospital rule says at least one doctor must be on call. Two doctors are on call, and both feel ill at the same time. Each doctor's transaction checks: "Are at least 2 on call? Yes." Then each removes only their own row. No row is written twice, so no lock and no snapshot check fires. Both commit. Now nobody is on call. This is write skew. Repeatable Read does not stop it, in Postgres or in MySQL. Serializable does. You can also lock the rows you read with FOR UPDATE, so the second doctor waits and then sees only one on call. Level Stops lost update? Stops write skew? Cost Read committed (Postgres default) No Use atomic updates or FOR UPDATE. No Cheapest. Few aborts. Repeatable read, Postgres (snapshot) Yes One transaction fails and must retry. No The app must retry on errors. Repeatable read, MySQL (default) No, Hermitage says. No Cheap. But it does not catch the conflict for you. Serializable Yes Yes More aborts and retries under contention. In MySQL, plain reads take shared locks when autocommit is off. Simple rule: keep the default level. Make every read-change-write either one atomic statement or a FOR UPDATE read. Use Serializable for rules that span several rows, like the on-call check. In code review, look for this shape: read a value, change it in app code, write it back. Ask: "What if two requests do this at once?" Know your database's default level, and write it in the service README. Don't assume "repeatable read" means the same thing in MySQL and Postgres. Prefer SET x = x + 1 over reading and writing the value in app code. Turn business rules into constraints when you can: UNIQUE, CHECK (stock >= 0). The database then enforces them for every caller. If you use Repeatable Read or Serializable, wrap transactions in a retry helper. Postgres marks these failures with the error code (SQLSTATE) 40001. Keep transactions short. Never wait for a user or a slow network call while holding a row lock. Write a concurrency test. Run the same request 50 times in parallel and check the final count. "Find every place in this service that reads a row, changes a value in code, and writes it back. For each, tell me if two requests at once can lose an update." "Rewrite this stock decrement as one atomic UPDATE with a stock > 0 check. Return whether a row was updated." "Write a test that runs 20 parallel orders against a real Postgres with stock 10. Assert that exactly 10 succeed and stock ends at 0." What to ask the agent The test uses a real database with real parallel connections. Mocks and an in-memory map cannot show a lost update. The fix runs inside the same transaction as the rest of the order. A lock taken in one transaction and used in another protects nothing. Any retry repeats the whole transaction, not just the last statement. The agent did not "fix" it with a lock in app memory. That breaks as soon as you run two servers. Locks are taken in the same order everywhere, so two transactions don't wait for each other forever. What to check yourself Before this: Replication, which adds stale reads on top of these bugs. Next on this line: Concurrency control in practice. Across machines: Distributed transactions and two-phase commit.

title: Unique ID generation
text: Every row, request and event needs a name that no other has. Learn the main ways to create IDs, and what each one costs your database, your clocks and your security.
body: This story is made up, but each part of it is common. A shop app keeps orders in one PostgreSQL table. The id column is an auto-increment number. It has worked for three years. The table grows too big, so the team splits it into two shards. Each shard is a copy of the old schema, and each still counts its own IDs. On day one, both shards create order 1,000,001. Support searches for order 1,000,001 and finds two. A refund goes to the wrong customer. Payment webhooks carry only the order ID, so some payments are marked on the wrong order. There is a second problem. The order page URL is /orders/1000001. A curious customer changes the number by one and sees a stranger's address. The endpoint did not check who owns the order. Both bugs come from the same choice: an ID that was only unique inside one database, and easy to guess. An ID names one thing, forever. You use IDs as primary keys. You use them as idempotency keys, so a retried request is not done twice. You often sort by them, and you may use them as shard keys. A good ID scheme answers four questions. Can many machines create IDs without asking each other? Do IDs sort by time? How big are they? Can outsiders guess them? The key idea. Pick the ID scheme for the scale you will have, not the scale you have today. Changing it later means changing every table, API and URL that holds an ID. Auto-increment and sequences The database hands out 1, 2, 3 and so on. IDs are small, ordered and easy to read. In PostgreSQL, a sequence never takes a number back, even when the transaction fails. So you will see gaps, and you cannot use a sequence for "gapless" numbers like invoice numbers. The limit is that one database owns the counter. With two databases, you must split the number space. MySQL has two settings for this. auto_increment_increment is the step between values, and auto_increment_offset is the start. Flickr ran two MySQL ticket servers this way. Both used a step of 2. One started at 1 and gave odd IDs, the other started at 2 and gave even IDs. This works, but adding a third server means planning the numbers again. UUID v4: random A UUID is 128 bits. Version 4 fills 122 of them with random bits. The other 6 bits mark the version and variant. Any machine can make one, with no coordination. Random keys have a cost in a B-tree index. RFC 9562 says UUID v4 has "poor database-index locality". Each new key lands on a random page. InnoDB reports that keys inserted in order leave index pages about 15/16 full. Keys inserted in random order leave them between 1/2 and 15/16 full. UUID v7: time first UUID v7 keeps the UUID format but puts time first. The first 48 bits are the Unix time in milliseconds. Then come the version, 12 random bits, the variant, and 62 more random bits. A generator may put a counter in some of the random bits, to keep order within one millisecond. So new IDs sort after older ones, and new values sit near each other in the index. The RFC says this gives better database-index locality. It says the difference from random inserts "can be one order of magnitude or more". It also says implementations should use v7 instead of the older time-based versions, v1 and v6, if possible. PostgreSQL 18 has a built-in uuidv7() function, next to gen_random_uuid() for v4. Snowflake: 64 bits, built from parts In 2010, Twitter was replacing many MySQL systems with Cassandra or sharded MySQL. Neither had a built-in way to create unique IDs. Twitter needed tens of thousands of IDs per second, from a highly available service. So it chose an approach with no coordination. Each ID has three parts: a timestamp, a worker number and a sequence number. The README gives the sizes. The time takes 41 bits, in milliseconds from a custom epoch, which lasts 69 years. The machine ID takes 10 bits, for up to 1,024 machines. The sequence takes 12 bits, so it rolls over every 4,096 IDs per machine. That is 63 bits, so the ID fits in a signed 64-bit integer. Worker numbers were chosen at startup through ZooKeeper, or set in a config file. Step through how one ID is built. IDs from one machine sort by time, because time sits in the top bits. Across machines, the order is only rough. Twitter called its IDs "roughly sortable". The README says they are "k-sorted" within a bound: it promised 1 second and aimed for tens of milliseconds. ULID, in one paragraph A ULID is 128 bits, like a UUID: a 48-bit millisecond timestamp, then 80 random bits. It is written as 26 characters, not the 36 of a UUID, and the text sorts in time order. The spec says it allows 1.21e+24 unique IDs per millisecond. Within one millisecond, order is not guaranteed. An optional monotonic mode adds one to the random part instead. If that overflows, generation fails. In our view, UUID v7 now gives you most of the same benefits in the standard UUID format. Clocks can break your IDs Any time-based ID depends on the wall clock, and wall clocks can jump back. RFC 9562 lists clock rollbacks, leap seconds and counter rollovers as causes of out-of-order IDs. It says generators should check that each new ID is bigger than the last. Snowflake protects itself. If the clock goes back, it refuses to create IDs until the time passes the last time it used. Its README suggests running NTP in a mode that never moves the clock back. Do not hand out guessable IDs Sequential IDs in URLs invite people to try the next number. OWASP's example of this bug uses a "fairly predictable, perhaps sequential" ID. It is a form of insecure direct object reference. Random IDs make guessing harder, but OWASP says that is "generally not sufficient by itself". The fix is an access check on every request. See authentication and authorization. RFC 9562 also warns: do not assume UUIDs are hard to guess, and never use one as a secret that grants access. How likely is a clash? For UUID v4, think of 122 random bits. That is about 5.3 × 10^36 possible values. By our own arithmetic, with the standard birthday estimate, you would need about 2.3 × 10^18 IDs before the chance of even one clash reaches about 40%. RFC 9562 itself gives no numbers. It says true global uniqueness cannot be guaranteed without shared knowledge. It asks you to weigh what a clash would cost your application. Our view: in practice, a clash is far more likely to come from a bug, like a copied seed or a reused machine number, than from bad luck. Scheme Needs coordination? Sorts by time? Size Index-friendly? Auto-increment Yes One database owns the counter. Yes Small: one integer column. Yes Inserts go to the end. Ticket servers (odd and even) A little: you plan the offsets. Only roughly. The two servers drift apart. 64 bits. Yes UUID v4 No No 128 bits. No Poor locality. UUID v7 No Yes, by millisecond. 128 bits. Yes Snowflake-style Only to assign machine IDs. Yes, roughly. 64 bits. Yes ULID No Yes, by millisecond. 128 bits, 26 characters. Yes Simple rule: one database and private IDs? Auto-increment is fine. Many writers, or IDs created on clients? Use UUID v7. Need 64-bit IDs at very high rates? Use a Snowflake-style generator, and treat machine IDs and clocks as part of the design. Ask early: "Will this table ever live on more than one database?" If yes, do not depend on auto-increment. Separate the internal key from the public ID if you must. A table can keep a small integer key and also store a random public ID for URLs. Never let an ID replace an authorization check. Test that user A cannot read user B's object by changing the ID. For Snowflake-style IDs, write down how machine IDs are assigned and freed. Two generators with the same machine ID can create the same IDs. Alert when an ID generator refuses to work because of the clock. It means NTP or the host has a problem. Use 64-bit integer columns, or the database's UUID type. Do not store UUIDs as long strings without a reason. Never promise gapless IDs from a sequence. If finance needs gapless numbers, design that separately. "List every table in this schema with its primary key type. For each one, say whether it would still be unique if we split the table across two databases." "Find every API route that takes an ID from the URL or body. For each, show where the code checks that the caller may access that object. Flag any route without such a check." "Write a test for our ID generator. Make 1 million IDs on 8 threads, check that none repeat, and check that IDs from one thread always go up. Then move the fake clock back by 5 ms and show what happens." What to ask the agent The UUID version the agent's code produces is the one you want. Check the library docs, and do not assume. Any bit layout adds up to 64 or fewer bits, and the time part lasts long enough from your chosen epoch. The agent did not treat random IDs as security. Every object access still has an owner check. Generated IDs are not used as the only sort key across machines when exact order matters. Database functions, like uuidv7(), exist in the version you run in production. What to check yourself Before this: time, clocks and ordering. Related: B-tree vs LSM-tree for why key order matters, sharding for shard keys, and idempotency and retries for idempotency keys.

title: Web performance and Core Web Vitals
text: Measure how fast your pages feel to real users with LCP, INP and CLS, and fix the few things that matter most.
body: Vodafone had a landing page that people reached from paid ads: display, search, social, and iOS and Android. The team wanted to know if performance work alone would change sales. So they ran an A/B test. Half the traffic went to the old page and half to a faster one. The only difference was the Web Vitals work on the faster page. Each version got about 34,000 visits a day. The faster page did three things. It moved a widget's rendering from the browser to the server, so less JavaScript blocked rendering. It rendered the important HTML on the server. And it resized the hero image, made SVGs and PNGs smaller, and did not load images outside the screen. They measured real users with the browser's PerformanceObserver API. Largest Contentful Paint dropped from 8.3 seconds to 5.7 seconds, 31% better. Total sales rose by 8%. The lead-to-visit rate rose by 15%, and the cart-to-visit rate by 11%. Note one detail. An older metric, DOMContentLoaded, got 15% worse on the faster page. If the team had watched only that number, they could have rolled back a change that made money. You must measure what users feel. A page can be slow in three different ways. It can be slow to show its main content. It can be slow to react when you tap. Or it can jump around while you read. Google's Core Web Vitals give one number for each. Metric What it measures Good Poor LCP When the largest image, text block or video in view is shown ≤ 2.5 s > 4.0 s INP How fast the page shows a response to clicks, taps and key presses ≤ 200 ms > 500 ms CLS How much content moves without the user asking ≤ 0.1 > 0.25 INP replaced First Input Delay (FID) as a Core Web Vital in March 2024. If an old dashboard still shows FID, it is out of date. You judge each metric at the 75th percentile of page loads, for phones and desktops separately. A page passes only if all three are good at that point. Google chose the 75th percentile so that most visits get the target experience, while a few outliers do not move the number much. The key idea. Speed is three separate problems: loading, responding and staying still. Measure all three on real users, at the 75th percentile, and fix the biggest one first. Step through one page load, from the first request to the first tap. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. The critical rendering path The browser turns your files into pixels in a fixed order. It parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM. It combines them into a render tree, works out the layout, then paints. CSS is render-blocking: the browser waits for all the CSS before it paints, because later rules can change earlier ones. Some requests, such as scripts, can also stop the HTML parser until the file is handled. So stylesheets, and scripts without defer or async, in the head can delay the first paint. MDN's advice: defer what is not critical, mark scripts async, or remove them. LCP: four parts LCP has four parts. First comes the time to first byte. Then there is a delay before the LCP resource starts loading, its load time, and a delay before it is painted. The web.dev guide suggests about 40% for TTFB, about 40% for the load, and under 10% for each delay. TTFB covers redirects, DNS, the connection, TLS and the server's work. As a rough guide, most sites should aim for 0.8 seconds or less. TTFB is not a Core Web Vital , but it is the first part of LCP. The latency lesson shows why far-away servers cost so much. INP: the main thread Almost all of your JavaScript runs on one main thread, which does one task at a time. A task longer than 50 ms is a long task. While it runs, the browser cannot handle a tap. An interaction has three phases: the input delay, the time your event handlers run, and the time until the next frame is shown. A long task that is already running makes the first phase long. A slow handler makes the second phase long. CLS: things that move A layout shift counts when it is unexpected. Shifts within 500 ms of a tap, click or key press do not count. The common causes are images and videos without a size, web fonts that render larger or smaller than the fallback font, and ads or widgets that resize themselves. The biggest fixes Send less JavaScript. Large bundles cost time to parse, compile and run, and that work blocks the main thread. Split the bundle with dynamic import() and send only what the first view needs. Break up long tasks. Yield to the main thread between pieces of work, for example with scheduler.yield() or setTimeout. Make the LCP image early and small. Start loading it at the same time as the first resource on the page. If it is hidden in CSS or JavaScript, preload it with fetchpriority="high". Never lazy-load it. Use loading="lazy" only for images below the first view. Reserve space. Set width and height on every image and video, or use CSS aspect-ratio. Reserve space for ads with min-height. For fonts, use font-display: optional, or use size-adjust so the fallback font takes up about the same space. Animate with transform, not top or left. Connect early. rel="preconnect" lets the browser open a connection to an important third-party origin early. The web.dev guide reports 100–500 ms saved, but too many preconnects compete for bandwidth. Cut TTFB and cache. Serve static files and cacheable HTML from a CDN close to users. The CDN and caching lesson shows how. Fewer round trips also help, see the HTTP versions lesson. Lab data and field data Lab data comes from loading a page in a controlled setup. Field data comes from all the real users who visit it. Lighthouse is a lab tool. You can run it in Chrome DevTools, from the command line, as a Node module or in PageSpeed Insights. The two often disagree. Lab tests use one device, one network and usually a cold cache. They cannot predict when a user will tap, so they cannot measure INP directly. Total Blocking Time is a lab metric meant to help diagnose INP problems. But it is not a substitute for INP, so a good TBT does not promise a good INP. For field data, the Chrome UX Report (CrUX) shows how real Chrome users experience popular sites. But it leaves out Chrome on iOS, Android WebViews and other Chromium browsers such as Microsoft Edge. So also collect your own real user monitoring. The web-vitals library, about 3 KB compressed, reports LCP, INP and CLS from each visit to your own endpoint. redBus did this. Its real user data showed slow interactions on the search page. Loading 10 results per batch instead of 30 cut INP there from about 870–900 to 350–370. The case study gives no unit, but INP is measured in milliseconds. Overall, redBus reported 7% more sales. Option Fast first content? Good INP? Use it when Static rendering Yes HTML is ready, so TTFB stays low. Yes, if you ship little JavaScript. Pages that are the same for everyone: blogs, docs, landing pages. Server-side rendering Yes, but building HTML per request can raise TTFB. Depends. Hydration can hurt INP, because the page looks ready before it can respond. Personal or fast-changing pages that still need content in the first HTML. Client-side rendering No The browser must download and run JavaScript first. Gets worse as the bundle grows. Apps behind a login, used for a long time per visit. Lazy-load every image No A lazy LCP image starts loading later. No effect. Never. Lazy-load only below the first view. Lazy-load below the first view Yes Fewer bytes compete with the LCP image. No effect. Long pages, lists and feeds. Set image sizes too. Report LCP, INP and CLS at the 75th percentile, split by phone and desktop. Treat them like SLOs, as in the observability lesson. Ask "which metric is bad, for which pages, on which devices?" before anyone writes a fix. Add a performance budget to CI. The web.dev example is "less than 170 KB of JavaScript on mobile" for a product page. Tools like Lighthouse CI run checks on every commit to catch regressions. See the CI/CD lesson. Review every new third-party script like a dependency. Ask who owns it and what it costs on the main thread. Check that the LCP image is in the HTML, not lazy, and sized for the screen. When you show speed work to the business, use a real A/B test, like Vodafone did. "Find the LCP element on our product page. Check that it is in the initial HTML, not lazy-loaded, has width and height, and uses fetchpriority=high. List what to change." "Find event handlers in this component that do more than 50 ms of work. Propose how to split them and yield to the main thread, without changing behaviour." "Add the web-vitals library to send LCP, INP and CLS to our /analytics endpoint, with the page type and device type on each event." What to ask the agent The agent did not add loading="lazy" to every image, including the hero. Any new preload or preconnect is for a resource the page truly needs early. Too many slow other requests down. Code splitting did not move needed code behind an import() that runs on the first tap. You measured the change on real users, not only in one Lighthouse run. What to check yourself Related lessons: CDN and HTTP caching, HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, CI/CD and trunk-based development and Observability, SLOs and error budgets.

title: Webhooks and async APIs
text: Webhooks arrive late, twice, out of order, or from someone pretending to be the sender. Here is how to build both ends so none of that hurts.
body: On 15 August 2023, at 16:58 UTC, an internal GitHub job queue started to fall behind. That queue processes webhooks. The cause was a large and lasting spike in webhook deliveries. Customers waited up to 4.5 hours for some webhooks. GitHub fixed it by blocking events from the sources of the extra load. Then the backlog drained slowly. Think about what that means for a receiver. Your CI bot or deploy tool waits for a push event. The event does not come for hours. Nothing is broken on your side, so no alert fires. When the backlog drains, you could get hundreds of old events close together. Your handler must not run them all twice, run them in the wrong order, or fall over. Webhooks fail in four ways: late, twice, out of order, and fake. This lesson shows how to build both ends so each failure is boring. A webhook is the reverse of an API call. You do not ask the provider "did anything change?" again and again. The provider calls your URL when something happens. You first met them in REST API design. The provider's promise is weak. Most providers retry, so delivery is at-least-once: an event can come late, twice, or before an older event. Some, like GitHub, do not retry at all, so an event can also be lost. Anyone on the internet can also post to your URL. The key idea. Treat each webhook as a signed hint, not as the truth. Check who sent it, save it, answer fast, skip repeats, and read the current state before you act. Step through one delivery that times out and comes back. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. The receiver 1. Verify the signature. The sender signs each request with an HMAC: a hash of the body made with a secret only you and the sender know. GitHub puts it in X-Hub-Signature-256, as sha256= plus a hex digest of the payload. Shopify uses X-Shopify-Hmac-Sha256. Compute the HMAC over the raw body, byte for byte. If your framework parses and rewrites the JSON first, the check fails. Compare in constant time. GitHub says: "Never use a plain == operator." 2. Reject old timestamps. A valid signature alone does not stop a replay attack. Someone can copy a real request and send it again. So Stripe signs a timestamp too. Its header, Stripe-Signature, holds t= and v1=. The signed text is the timestamp, a dot, then the body. Stripe's libraries reject anything older than 5 minutes by default. Each retry gets a new timestamp and signature, so real retries still pass. Standard Webhooks also signs a timestamp. It uses three headers: webhook-id, webhook-timestamp and webhook-signature. It signs the id, timestamp and body together, and leaves the tolerance to you. Here is a manual Stripe-style check in Node. In real code, prefer the provider's library. import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto"; const TOLERANCE_SEC = 300; // 5 minutes export function verify(raw: Buffer, header: string, secret: string) { const parts = header.split(",").map((p) => p.split("=")); const t = parts.find(([k]) => k === "t")?.[1]; const sigs = parts.filter(([k]) => k === "v1").map(([, v]) => v); if (!t || sigs.length === 0) return false; const age = Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(t)); if (!(age <= TOLERANCE_SEC)) return false; // too old: maybe a replay const expected = createHmac("sha256", secret) .update(`${t}.`).update(raw).digest(); return sigs.some((s) => { const got = Buffer.from(s, "hex"); return got.length === expected.length && timingSafeEqual(got, expected); }); }3. Answer 2xx fast, then work. GitHub wants a 2xx within 10 seconds, or it marks the delivery failed. Shopify gives you five seconds. So verify, save the event to a queue, and answer. A worker does the real work. Stripe says a queue also protects you from spikes, like the start of the month when all subscriptions renew. 4. Skip repeats by event id. Save each processed id and skip ids you have seen. Use X-GitHub-Delivery on GitHub, X-Shopify-Webhook-Id on Shopify, and webhook-id in Standard Webhooks. Insert the id with a unique constraint, in the same transaction as the work. This is the idempotency key idea, from the other side. 5. Do not trust order. Stripe does not promise order. It also says not to use the created time to order events. Shopify says a products/update can come before products/create. So store a version or updated_at with your copy, and ignore anything older. Or fetch the current object from the API. 6. Prefer thin events. A thin event says only "object X changed". You then fetch the object. Stripe recommends thin events for new endpoints. Its SDK has a method, fetchRelatedObject(), that gets the latest version of the object. Fetching also fixes ordering: you always act on the current state. The sender 1. Never lose an event. Write the event to a transactional outbox in the same transaction as the change. A delivery worker reads the outbox and sends. 2. Retry for days, with backoff and jitter. Standard Webhooks gives an example schedule of ten tries over about three days. The first is at once. The waits after that are 5 s, 5 min, 30 min, 2 h, 5 h, 10 h, 14 h, 20 h and 24 h. Stripe retries for up to three days in live mode. Shopify retries eight times in four hours. GitHub does not redeliver failed deliveries automatically. See backoff and jitter. 3. Isolate each endpoint. Our advice: give each endpoint its own queue, or a cap on in-flight requests. Then one customer's slow server cannot hold workers that others need. Use a timeout too. Standard Webhooks suggests 15 to 30 seconds. GitHub faced a related problem in 2023. A spike from some sources slowed everyone, and it blocked events from those sources. Afterwards, it improved its ability to manage load sources. 4. Disable dead endpoints. After long, steady failure, tell the customer by email and stop sending. On 410 Gone, disable the endpoint at once. Shopify removes a subscription that keeps failing. 5. Offer replay. Customers recover from outages by asking for events again. Stripe lets you resend from the Dashboard for 15 days, and from the CLI for 30 days. A GitHub redelivery keeps the same X-GitHub-Delivery value, so dedupe still works. 6. Rotate secrets with an overlap. When Stripe rolls a secret, the old one can stay valid for up to 24 hours. Meanwhile it sends one signature per secret. Standard Webhooks puts a space-separated list of signatures in one header for the same reason. 7. Block SSRF. Customers type in URLs, and your servers call them. An attacker can use this for server-side request forgery. Check that the resolved IP is not private. Do not follow redirects. Send through a proxy that filters internal IPs, from a subnet that cannot reach internal services. Async APIs Webhooks are one way to report a slow job. Another is 202 Accepted: the job was accepted, but is not done. RFC 9110 says the body should point to a status monitor. The client polls that URL. A third way is streaming, such as Server-Sent Events, which keeps one connection open. Option Who keeps the connection Works if the client has no public URL? Main cost Use it when 202 + status URL (polling) The client asks again and again. Yes Wasted calls, and a delay between checks. Jobs of seconds or minutes, browser or mobile clients. Webhooks The sender calls you. No You need a public HTTPS endpoint. Signatures, retries, dedupe, SSRF guards. Server-to-server events between companies. Streaming (SSE, WebSocket) One long open connection. Yes Reconnects, and missed events while offline. Live screens that must update in a second. Simple rule: use webhooks for the push and a periodic reconciliation job for the truth. Shopify says your app should not rely only on webhooks. Ask of every handler: "What happens if this event comes twice, late, or before the one it depends on?" Ask: "If we miss a whole day of events, how do we catch up?" Have a backfill or reconcile job ready. On GitHub, which does not retry, you write a script that finds failed deliveries and redelivers them. You can only redeliver deliveries from the past 3 days. Log and alert on signature failures. A sudden rise means a broken deploy, a rotated secret, or an attack. Measure the age of events in your webhook queue, not only errors. Late events are silent. As a sender, add a delivery log per endpoint that customers can see and replay from. In design reviews of a sender, ask: "Can one customer's slow endpoint delay everyone else?" For payments, read the payment lifecycle. The webhook is often the only place you learn a payment settled. "Write an Express route for Stripe webhooks. Read the raw body, verify the signature with the official library, insert the event id with a unique constraint, push the event to a queue, and return 200. Do no other work in the route." "Review this webhook sender. Find every place where one slow endpoint can block deliveries to other endpoints, and every way a customer URL can reach our internal network." "Write tests for this handler: duplicate event, old timestamp, wrong signature, and an update event that arrives before its create event." What to ask the agent The signature is checked on the raw bytes, before any JSON parsing or body middleware. The compare is constant-time, such as crypto.timingSafeEqual or Python's hmac.compare_digest. The timestamp tolerance is not 0. Stripe warns that 0 turns the recency check off. The dedupe insert and the work share one transaction. A check-then-insert in two steps lets two copies through. The handler does not set a state straight from the payload. It fetches the object or compares versions. The sender's HTTP client blocks private IPs on every request and does not follow redirects. What to check yourself Idempotency, retries and timeouts: the same dedupe idea for normal API calls. Sagas, outbox and CDC: how to publish events without losing them. Queues vs logs: at-least-once delivery inside your own system. Rate limiting: how to protect your receiver when a backlog drains.

title: What "senior" really means
text: Senior is not about years or typing speed. It is about how much you own, and how well you decide.
body: This story is made up, but it is common. Rahul is a strong mid-level engineer. He writes clean code and he ships fast. His manager asks him to "build a new notification service". Users miss important messages, and the old system is slow. Rahul starts the next morning. In three weeks he has a fast service with good tests. He is proud of it, and the code review is easy. Then the problems start. The email team already planned to fix the old system next quarter. Nobody asked them. Support says users miss messages because the app turns off alerts by default. Speed was never the real problem. Now the company has two notification systems. Nobody wants to move the old messages to the new one. Six months later, Rahul's service is turned off. His code was good. The project failed anyway. He solved the problem he was given, not the problem that existed. Nobody owned the question "Are we building the right thing?" Being senior is not about writing harder code. It is about which problems people trust you to solve: how big they are and how unclear. Many company career ladders describe this with a few ideas: Scope: how big the piece of work is that you own. Ambiguity: how unclear the problem is when it reaches you. Ownership: whether you own a task or the final result. Impact: what changed for users or the business because of your work. Judgement: how well you choose, for example what to build, what to skip and what to cut. You can see this in a real, public ladder. Dropbox names its levels IC2, IC3 and so on. IC means individual contributor: an engineer who does not manage people. At Dropbox, an IC2 engineer solves "defined problems" for team-level goals. At IC3, the engineer solves "ambiguous, open-ended problems". At IC5, the staff level, the engineer delivers "multi-year, multi-team" goals. The key idea. A mid-level engineer solves the problem well. A senior engineer first makes sure it is the right problem, then owns the result until it works. Senior is also not some things people often think: Not a number of years. Some people reach senior in four years. Some never do. Years only give you chances to practise. Not being the best coder. Strong coding is the base, not the goal. Rahul was a great coder. Not knowing every tool. Seniors learn tools when they need them. They know which questions to ask about any tool. Above senior is the staff engineer. Will Larson describes four common shapes of this role: Tech Lead, Architect, Solver and Right Hand. The Right Hand helps a senior leader run a large, complex part of the company. Tanya Reilly splits staff work into three parts: big-picture thinking, executing projects, and helping other people grow. Step through how scope grows as you move up. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. Each step changes three things at once. The work gets bigger. The problem gets less clear. And you own more of the result. At mid-level, you get a defined problem and choose how to build it. At senior, you often get a vague problem, like "checkout feels slow". You turn it into a clear goal, a plan and a finished result. That middle step is new: nobody does it for you. Week to week, a senior engineer often does these things: Writes a short design doc before a big change, and asks others to find problems early. Says "no" or "not now" to work that does not matter, and explains why. Reviews code carefully and teaches through the review, not only approves. Notices risks early and tells people, even when the news is bad. Helps a newer teammate get unstuck, instead of doing their work for them. Checks that the feature really helped users after launch. Larson warns about two traps here. "Snacking" is easy work with little impact. "Preening" is work that is very visible but has little impact. There is more than one way to grow. Each one has a cost. Way to grow Helps you reach senior? Cost Watch out for Go deep on one technology Yes You become the person others ask. You may get stuck as "the database person". Depth without ownership of results is still mid-level work. Go broad across the stack Yes You see how parts connect. You may feel you know nothing deeply. Learning many tools is not the same as using judgement. Take ownership of a project Yes This is the clearest signal on most ladders. More stress, more meetings, less coding time. Do not take on so much that you finish nothing. Aim only for the title No A title alone does not change your skills. You may switch jobs for a title you cannot yet do. Titles mean different things at different companies. Simple rule: go deep enough to be trusted, then take ownership of something real. That mix grows judgement fastest. When you get a task, ask: "What problem does this solve, and how will we know it worked?" Before you build, ask: "Who else does this touch?" Talk to those teams in week one, not week six. Write down your plan in a short doc, even half a page. Writing shows the gaps in your thinking. Say what you will not do. Clear limits protect the important work. Own the result after launch. Look at the numbers, the errors and the support tickets. Ask your manager for your company's career ladder. Pick one line from the next level and practise it this month. Gergely Orosz's book is a good practical guide to these roles at real companies. AI agents can now write a lot of code quickly. So writing code is no longer the scarce skill. Deciding what to build, and judging if the code is right, matters more. The evidence is mixed, so read it carefully. In a 2025 randomized study by METR, 16 experienced developers did real tasks in large open-source projects they knew well. With early-2025 AI tools, tasks took about 19% longer. Yet the developers believed AI had made them about 20% faster. METR says the result may not apply to all kinds of work, and that these results are now out of date. Its 2026 update says developers are probably faster with newer tools, but the data is too weak to say by how much. In 2025, Google's DORA team surveyed nearly 5,000 tech workers. It found that AI acts as "an amplifier". It makes a team's existing strengths and weaknesses bigger. This is survey data, so it shows what people report, not a measured cause. The lesson for you: speed feels good but can mislead you. Your judgement is what makes the speed safe. "Before you write any code, list the questions you would ask about this task. What is unclear? What could go wrong?" "Here is my design doc. Act as a careful senior reviewer. List the three biggest risks and anything I left out." "Give me two other ways to solve this problem, with the cost of each." What to ask the agent The agent solved the real problem, not just the words in your prompt. You can explain every line it wrote. If not, you do not own it yet. It did not quietly change other files, add libraries or skip tests. You talked to the people the change affects. An agent cannot do that for you. You measured if it was faster, instead of trusting how it felt. What to check yourself How to use this curriculum: start with the lessons marked L1 (level 1, the first level). Each lesson starts with a failure, explains the idea, then shows the trade-offs and how seniors use it at work. Do the quiz at the end. Then try one "At work" habit in your real job that week. Reading builds knowledge. Practice builds judgement. A good first technical lesson: Idempotency, retries and timeouts.

title: Why distributed systems are hard
text: Once your system runs on two or more machines, parts fail on their own, messages get lost and clocks disagree. Learn what changes and where each problem is solved.
body: January 4th, 2021 was the first working day of the year for many people. Slack's traffic jumped. Client caches were cold, so apps pulled down more data than usual on their first connection. Slack's networks on AWS were linked by Transit Gateways. Under the new load, these gateways did not scale fast enough. Part of the network "had indeed become saturated and was dropping packets". The problem was in the network between the servers. Many calls between them were slow or lost. At 6:57 AM PST, about 99% of messages were sent. On a normal day the rate is above 99.999%. Then the tools for seeing the problem broke too. The dashboards and alerts ran in a different network from their databases. So they also needed the broken gateways, and they failed. The machines also read the signs wrong. Threads spent more time waiting on the network, so CPU use dropped. Autoscaling saw low CPU and removed servers. Later, as waiting threads piled up, the team tried to add 1,200 servers between 7:01 and 7:15 AM. That hit other limits. Health checks also failed at a very high rate. The load balancers have a "panic mode" for this: they spread requests across all servers anyway. That, with retries and circuit breakers, got traffic flowing again. No single machine broke. Some parts worked, some failed, and the automatic tools read the signs wrong. AWS raised the gateway capacity by hand, and the network was normal again by 10:40 AM PST. This is what distributed systems feel like. A system is distributed when it runs on more than one machine and the machines talk over a network. Your app server and its database on another host already count. So does a phone app that calls your API. On one computer, if a part fails, you usually expect the whole computer to stop. In a distributed system, one node can crash while the others keep working. Kleppmann calls this a partial failure. Faults in the network or a node can happen at any moment, with no warning. Partial failure comes with other hard problems: The network can lose, delay, duplicate or reorder messages. A caller cannot tell a slow server from a dead one. There is no shared clock that all machines agree on. The key idea. In a distributed system, "I got no answer" does not mean "it did not happen". Design every call so that the caller can live with not knowing. One call, many places to fail Gabrielson, from AWS, splits one request and reply into eight steps. The client sends the request, the network delivers it, the server checks it and updates its state. Then the same happens in reverse for the reply. Any of the eight steps can fail. The client, the server and the network fail independently of each other. Step through what the caller sees when no reply comes. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. When the client times out, the result is UNKNOWN: the work "may or may not have happened". Kleppmann gives the classic example. If a client resends a request after no reply, the server may do it twice, such as charging a credit card twice. The network is unreliable Messages can be lost, delayed, duplicated and reordered. TCP retries lost packets and removes duplicates for you. But TCP usually gives up after a timeout, typically about a minute. If a network split lasts longer, your code needs its own retries and duplicate checks. Delays can be huge. Kleppmann notes documented cases where packets inside one data center were delayed for more than a minute. You cannot tell slow from dead The usual way to spot a dead server is a timeout: send a message and wait for a reply. But silence can also mean that the message was lost or delayed. The server may also be paused. Stop-the-world garbage collection in languages such as Java can pause all threads, and on large heaps the pause can last several minutes. So a timeout is a guess. Too short, and you mark healthy servers as dead. Too long, and users wait on a server that is gone. In Slack's outage, low CPU looked like low load, but it really meant threads were waiting on the network. There is no shared clock Each machine has its own clock, usually a quartz crystal. Some run a bit fast and some a bit slow, and their speed changes with temperature. Machines sync their clocks over the network, but the network adds its own error. So two machines can disagree on "now", and timestamps from different machines may not show the true order of events. The eight fallacies These problems are old. According to Rotem-Gal-Oz, Peter Deutsch, then a Sun fellow, wrote down seven false assumptions in 1994. James Gosling added an eighth in 1997. Designers often assume: The network is reliable.
