Latency is zero. Bandwidth is infinite. The network is secure. Topology doesn't change. There is one administrator. Transport cost is zero. The network is homogeneous. Each one feels true on your laptop. Each one is false in production. For the first one, Rotem-Gal-Oz says you must plan for lost calls: retry, acknowledge important messages, and ignore duplicates or make messages idempotent. Where each problem is solved This lesson is a map. Each problem has its own lesson: Lost and duplicated messages: Idempotency, retries and timeouts, Backoff, jitter and retry budgets and Queues vs logs. Slow or dead: Failure detection and membership and Tail latency and queueing. No shared clock: Time, clocks and ordering. Copies of data that disagree: Replication and CAP, PACELC and consistency models. Agreeing on one leader or value: Consensus and Raft. One failure spreading to others: Circuit breakers and bulkheads. When a call gets no reply, you must choose what to do. Each choice has a cost. Choice Safe if the first call worked? User waits? Use it when Short timeout, then retry No, unless the call is idempotent. No Fast failover. Reads, or writes with an idempotency key. Long timeout Yes You do not resend. Yes A dead server holds users for the full time. Slow but rare work, such as a big report. Fail and show an error Yes, but the work may still have happened. No The user can safely try again later. Check the status later Yes You ask "did order 42 go through?" Some. Needs a status API. Payments and other money moves. Hand it to a queue Yes, if consumers drop duplicates. No The work is done in the background. Work that does not need an answer now. Simple rule (our advice): every remote call needs a timeout, and every retry needs a way to drop duplicates. In design reviews, point at each arrow between two boxes and ask: "What happens if this call is lost, slow or done twice?" Check that every network call has a timeout you chose on purpose. Do not trust the client library's default; look it up. Treat a timeout as "unknown", not "failed". Log it as unknown, and reconcile later if money or stock is involved. Keep monitoring away from the thing it monitors. Slack's dashboards failed because they needed the same broken network. Be careful with automatic actions based on one signal, such as CPU. A stuck system can look idle. Test failure, not just success. Gabrielson writes that engineers must assume each step of a call could fail. He also warns that distributed bugs often show up long after they are deployed. When you add a new service, list which of the eight fallacies it depends on. "List every network call in this code path. For each one, show the timeout, the retry rule, and whether the call is safe to repeat. Mark any call with no timeout." "This handler calls the payment service and then saves the order. Walk through what happens if the payment call times out but the payment really worked." "Write a test that makes the stock service reply after 5 seconds, and one where the reply is lost after the work is done. Show what our code does in each case." What to ask the agent The agent did not treat a timeout as "the call failed". Look for code that undoes work it is not sure about. Retries reuse the same request ID or idempotency key. They do not make a new one each time. Timeouts are set in the real client config, not only in comments or docs. No logic compares timestamps from two different machines to decide which event came first. Tests cover a lost reply, not just a lost request. A lost reply is the case where the work was really done. What to check yourself Start with the lessons in the map above. For the network basics underneath, see TCP/IP and the network stack. For the full Slack story, read the postmortem, and see the incident page.

title: Working with PMs and the business
text: Turn "the business wants X" into a clear goal, honest options and a plan you can keep, and say "no, but…" when you need to.
body: This story is made up, but it happens in many companies. Kavya is a backend engineer at a grocery delivery app. Her PM says: "Customers must be able to reschedule a delivery in the app. The business wants it by 1 March." Kavya does exactly that. She builds a screen to pick any day and any time slot in the next two weeks. The code is clean and well tested. In week 2 she finds a problem. The warehouse system can only change orders up to 48 hours before delivery. Fixing that needs work from another team. Kavya does not tell anyone. She hopes to find a workaround. She does not find one. The launch is three weeks late. When it finally ships, only 3% of customers use it. Most people who called support did not want a new day. They wanted to know where their order was. Nobody asked why the business wanted the feature. Nobody raised the risk while there was still time to act. Kavya's code was good. The way she worked with her PM was not. A product manager (PM) decides what the team should build and why. Marty Cagan of SVPG says the PM owns two big risks. Value: will customers want it? Viability: does it work for the business, for example sales, legal and money? The designer owns usability. The engineers own feasibility: can we build it with the time, skills and technology we have? So you and your PM are not on opposite sides. You share one goal: a result that matters to customers and the business. Cagan says a PM must ensure "a business outcome", not just that a product gets defined. Your job is to bring what only an engineer knows. What is cheap and what is costly. What could go wrong. Which simpler idea solves the same problem. The key idea. Never answer a request with only "yes" or "no". Ask what problem it solves. Then offer options, each with a cost, a risk and the value it brings. Let the PM choose with you. Cagan warns about "feature teams", where engineers only build what others decided. He says you then get only about half of the engineers' value. Product teams are measured by outcomes, not output. Step through one request, from a vague ask to a plan with check-ins. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. 1. Turn the request into a goal "The business wants X" usually names a solution. Ask questions until you find the problem behind it: Why now? What happens if we do nothing? Who asks for this, and how many of them? How will we know it worked? Which number should move? Gergely Orosz lists asking "why" again and again as a trait of product-minded engineers. Write the answers down. A goal like "30% fewer support calls about delivery times" lets you judge every option. 2. Say "no, but…" with options Rarely say a flat no. Say "not like that, but here is what we can do". Give two or three options, each with a cost, a risk and how much of the goal it reaches. Shape Up, Basecamp's book on product work, calls the time you are willing to spend the appetite. It says an appetite is "completely different from an estimate". You start from the time the problem is worth, then shape a solution that fits. So ask your PM: "How much is this worth to us? Two weeks or two months?" 3. Give estimates as ranges Early in a project, nobody knows the real size of the work. Steve McConnell's "Cone of Uncertainty" shows that estimates made at the first idea can be 4 times too high or 4 times too low. The range narrows only as you make decisions, such as writing down what you will not do. So say "4 to 8 weeks", not "6 weeks". Then add what will narrow the range: "After I test the warehouse API on Friday, I can give you 5 to 6 weeks." McConnell advises waiting to commit until the range has narrowed. 4. Cut scope, not quality Here, scope means the list of features in the project. When time is short, you can move the date, add people or cut scope. Shape Up fixes the time and lets scope change. It also says "Variable scope is not about sacrificing quality." Its test for a cut is useful: compare the result with what customers do today, not with a perfect version. Good cuts are parts that few users need, cases you can handle by hand at first, or a second phase after launch. 5. Explain technical debt in business terms "The code is messy" means little to a PM. Martin Fowler explains technical debt with money words. The messy code is the debt. The extra effort it adds to every change is the interest. Cleaning it up is paying back the principal. His example: a feature takes 4 days on clean code but 6 days on messy code. The cleanup costs 5 days. For one feature it is not worth it. For three similar features, cleaning up first is faster. Messy code that you rarely change can stay as it is. So bring numbers: "Each change here costs about 2 extra days. We plan 6 this quarter." 6. Raise risks early Share bad news early. It costs more the longer you wait. In week 2, the PM can still cut scope, move the date or warn sales. In week 8, the only choice left is to miss the date. Use a simple format: what you found, what it could cost, what you are doing next, and when you will know more. Say it the same day, even if you are not sure yet. 7. Take part in discovery Product discovery is the work of finding out what to build before you build it. Join it. Talk to users and read support tickets. Attend the meetings where ideas are judged. Feasibility is your risk. If you join early, you can raise a feasibility problem before the team commits to a plan. 8. Write for people who are not engineers When you write to the PM, sales or leaders, lead with the decision you need and the date. Then give two or three options in plain words. Put the costs in days, money or customers. Leave out class names and database terms. Orosz lists good communication with non-engineers as one of the traits. Way to respond Keeps trust? Cost Use it when Say yes to everything No Dates are missed and quality drops. Hidden: overtime, bugs, debt. Never as a habit. Flat "no" No People see you as the one who stops work. The business goal stays unsolved. Only for unsafe or illegal requests, with a reason. "No, but…" with options and costs Yes The PM can make a real choice. An hour or two of thinking. Most requests that do not fit the time. Fixed date, cut scope Yes, if cuts are agreed early. Some features wait for phase 2. Hard dates, such as a sale or a law. Fixed scope, move the date Yes, if you say so early. Others who planned around the date must adjust. Every part is a must-have, such as a compliance rule. One exact estimate early No It will likely be wrong. Lost trust when the date is missed. Avoid. Give a range and a date to narrow it. Simple rule: bring options, costs and risks early. The PM decides the trade-off with you, not after you. For every new request, ask: "What problem does this solve, and which number should move?" Answer big asks with two or three options. Give each one a cost range, the main risk and how much of the goal it reaches. Ask your PM for the appetite: "How much time is this worth?" Then design to fit it. Write the non-goals into the plan, so the scope does not grow quietly. Give estimates as ranges, and say when and how you will narrow them. Raise a risk the day you find it, with what you know and what you will check next. Keep a short list of technical debt with its "interest": extra days per change. Bring it to planning with numbers. After launch, check the number you agreed on. Share the result with your PM, even if it is bad. "Here is a feature request from my PM. List the questions I should ask before I estimate it: the problem, the users, the success metric and the hidden risks." "Give me three ways to deliver this, from smallest to fullest. For each one, list what is in, what is out, the main risk and a rough size." "Rewrite this update for a non-technical PM. Lead with the decision I need, keep it under 150 words, and remove all code terms." What to ask the agent The options are real. Check each size against your own codebase. An agent does not know your warehouse API is slow. The estimate is a range, and you can explain both ends. The business goal comes from your PM or real data. The agent may invent a plausible goal. The rewrite still says the risk clearly. Plain words must not hide bad news. You talked to the PM in person. An agent can draft the message but cannot build the trust. What to check yourself Before this: What "senior" really means. Next: estimation and planning under uncertainty, technical debt management and influence without authority.

title: Scaling from zero to millions of users
text: Most systems grow through the same few steps, from one server to many parts. Learn the usual order, what makes each step worth it, and why you should measure before you add anything.
body: This story is made up, but it is common. A small team builds a ticket booking app. It runs on one server: the web app and the database together. For a year this works fine. Then the team plans for growth. In one quarter they add Kafka, a Redis cluster, six microservices and a sharded database. They have 3,000 daily users. A popular concert goes on sale. The site slows to a crawl. The team looks at the dashboards they have, and none of them show the problem. After two days of searching, they find it. One slow SQL query with no index was reading the whole bookings table on every page load. The new parts did not help. They made the system harder to debug, and nobody had measured anything before adding them. One index fixed the problem. Scaling is not a list of tools to install. It is a series of answers to problems you can see in your numbers. A well-known chapter of ByteByteGo's System Design Interview course walks one system from a single user to millions, one step at a time. The steps are not a law. Treat them as a typical order: in our experience, each step fixes the most likely next bottleneck. The rule behind every step: find what is full, then fix only that. The chapter ends by saying that scaling a system is an iterative process. The key idea. Each part you add fixes one kind of limit and adds new ways to fail. Add a part when a measurement says you need it, not because big companies have it. Step through how the system grows. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys. 0. Measure from day one Before any step, you need numbers. The Google SRE book names four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. If you can measure only four metrics of a user-facing system, measure these. Saturation tells you what is full. Latency and errors tell you if users feel it. Use back-of-envelope estimates to guess what will fill up next. 1. One server At the start, everything runs on one server. It is cheap and easy to debug. Its weakness: if that server goes offline, users cannot reach the site. 2. A separate database Move the database to its own machine. Now the app and the database stop fighting for the same CPU and memory, and you can size each one on its own. Trigger (our advice): the app and the database compete for CPU, memory or disk on one machine. 3. Bigger machine, or more machines? Vertical scaling means a bigger machine: more CPU and RAM. Horizontal scaling means more machines. When traffic is low, vertical scaling is a good choice because it is simple. But it has a hard limit, and one machine gives you no failover. AWS's reliability advice is to replace one large resource with several small ones, so one failure hurts less. Trigger (our advice): scale up first while it is cheap. Scale out when you near the largest machine, or when one machine going down is not acceptable. 4. A load balancer and stateless app servers A load balancer spreads requests across several app servers. For this to work, the app servers must be stateless. Move session data out of server memory into a shared store, so any server can handle any request. See Load balancing for how the balancer picks a server. Trigger: one app server is near its CPU limit, or you need to survive one server dying. 5. Read replicas Many apps read far more than they write. With replication, the main database takes the writes and replicas serve the reads. Replicas can lag behind the main database, so a user may not see their own write at once. See Replication. Trigger: database CPU is high and most queries are reads. Check first that slow queries are not the real cause. 6. A cache A cache keeps often-read data in memory, so fewer reads reach the database. It adds new problems: stale data and many requests missing at once. See Caching and cache stampedes. Trigger: the same data is read again and again, and it can be a little out of date. 7. A CDN for static files A CDN is a network of servers spread around the world that serves static content, such as images, CSS and JavaScript. Users get files from a nearby server, and your servers do less work. See CDNs and HTTP caching. Trigger: static files use much of your bandwidth, or users far away see slow page loads. 8. Queues for slow work Some work does not need to finish before you reply to the user. In the chapter's example, web servers put photo processing jobs on a message queue, and workers do them in the background. The queue also lets the two sides scale and fail on their own. See Queues vs logs. Trigger: a request waits on slow work, such as sending email or resizing images, that the user does not need to see at once. 9. Sharding Replicas help with reads. They do not help when one database cannot take all the writes or hold all the data. Then you split the data across shards, each with a part of the rows. Sharding is hard to undo, and queries across shards get harder. See Sharding and consistent hashing. Figma is a real example of this order. In 2020 it ran one Postgres database on AWS's largest physical instance. By the end of 2022 it had added caching, read replicas and a dozen databases split by table. It moved to horizontal sharding only when some tables reached several terabytes and billions of rows. Their writes would also soon pass the IOPS limit of Amazon RDS. Its first sharded table shipped in September 2023. Trigger: writes or data size on one database near its limits, after indexes, query fixes, replicas and splitting tables are done. After that The chapter goes further, to several data centers. See Multi-region systems when you get there. Step What it fixes What it costs Bigger machine More CPU and memory, with no code change. A hard size limit. Still one point of failure. Separate database The app and database stop fighting for resources. One more machine and one network hop. Load balancer and stateless servers More traffic. One server can die safely. Sessions must move to a shared store. Read replicas Read load on the database. Replica lag. Users may read old data. Cache Repeated reads of hot data. Stale data, stampedes, one more system to run. CDN Static file load and distance to users. Purging old files. Cost per GB. Queue Slow work blocking requests. Duplicates, retries, a backlog to watch. Sharding Write load and data size on one database. Cross-shard queries, resharding, hot keys. Hard to undo. Simple rule (our advice): go down this table only as far as your numbers force you to. Ask "What is full?" before any scaling proposal. Ask for the graph that shows it. Fix the cheap things first: a missing index, an N+1 query, a bigger instance. Write the trigger down. For example: "We add a read replica when database CPU stays above 70% at peak." Then the decision is not a debate later. Make app servers stateless early. It is cheap when the code is small and painful later. For each new part, ask who runs it, how it fails and how you will see it fail. Use the AWS principle "stop guessing capacity": watch demand and add or remove resources to match it. Remember that cloud quotas still apply. Plan for load tests and capacity planning before big events, not after. "Here are our dashboards for latency, traffic, errors and CPU, memory and disk for each machine. Which resource is closest to full at peak? What is the cheapest change that buys us 3x headroom?" "Find any place where this app keeps user state in server memory, such as sessions, uploads on local disk or in-process caches. List what must move before we run more than one server." "List the 10 slowest database queries from this log, with how often each runs. Suggest an index or query change for each, before we talk about replicas." What to ask the agent The agent's plan starts from a measured bottleneck, not from a standard diagram. It did not suggest sharding or microservices when an index or a bigger machine would do. Any proposed cache says how data is kept fresh and what happens on a miss. Each new part comes with the metric that shows it works and an alert for when it fails. Cost is in the plan. More parts mean more servers to pay for and more on-call work. What to check yourself Every step after the first one turns your app into a distributed system. Read Why distributed systems are hard next. For reads and writes in depth, see Scaling reads and Scaling writes and hot keys.

title: A/B test
text: An experiment where some real users get version A and others get version B at the same time. You compare a metric to see which version works better.

title: attribute-based access control
text: An authorization model where a policy decides each request from attributes of the user, the resource, the action and the environment, such as department, owner or time of day.

title: access pattern
text: How an app reads and writes its data: which queries, by which keys, how often, and how fast the answer must be.

title: ACID
text: Atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability: the four promises a database transaction makes.

title: ack
text: Short for acknowledgement. A message a consumer sends to say "I am done with this one", so the broker can stop tracking it.

title: ACME
text: A protocol that lets software prove it controls a domain and get or renew a certificate with no human involved. Let's Encrypt uses it.

title: acquiring bank
text: The bank that processes card payments for a merchant. It sends each payment to the card network and collects the money for the merchant.

title: action item
text: A follow-up task from a postmortem, such as adding an alert or a safety check. A good one has an owner, a priority and a due date.

title: active-active
text: A setup where every site or region serves real users at the same time. If one fails, the others take its share of the traffic.

title: active-passive
text: A setup where one site or region serves all users while another keeps a copy and waits. On failure, you fail over to the waiting one.

title: Adapter pattern
text: A design pattern where a small class implements the interface your code expects by calling another API, often a vendor's. Vendor details stay inside it.

title: adaptive capacity
text: A DynamoDB feature that gives a busy partition more of the table's unused throughput, and can move hot items to their own partitions, so uneven traffic is throttled less.

title: adaptive throttling
text: A client watches how many of its recent requests the backend accepted. When too many are rejected, it drops some new requests itself, before sending them.

title: additive change
text: An API change that only adds something new, such as an optional field or a new endpoint, and leaves everything old working as before.

title: address space
text: The private view of memory that each process gets. Every address the program sees is virtual; the OS and hardware map it to real RAM. This is called virtual memory.

title: adjacency list
text: In graph code, a list of each node's neighbours. In DynamoDB, a pattern for many-to-many links: each entity is a partition, and each link is an item in it whose sort key is the linked entity's ID.

title: ADR
text: Short for "architecture decision record". A one- or two-page note, kept with the code, that records one decision, why it was made and what it costs.

title: advisory lock
text: A database lock on a number or name your app chooses, not on a row. The database does not enforce it. It only works if all your code asks for it.

title: AGENTS.md
text: A shared Markdown file of project instructions for coding agents, like a README for agents. Many tools read it, and the file closest to the code being changed wins.

title: aggregate root
text: The one entity at the top of a domain-driven design aggregate. Outside code may hold a reference only to the root, and the root checks the aggregate's rules.

title: alert fatigue
text: What happens when people get so many alerts, most of them useless, that they start to ignore or miss the real ones.

title: allowed lateness
text: How long a stream processor keeps a window after the watermark passes the window's end. Events for that window arriving in that time still update the result. In Flink it is 0 by default.

title: ALPN
text: A TLS extension where the client lists the protocols it speaks, such as h2 or http/1.1, and the server picks one, with no extra round trip.

title: Alt-Svc
text: An HTTP response header that tells the client the same site is also available another way, for example over HTTP/3 on UDP port 443.

title: ambient mode
text: An Istio mode with no proxy in each pod. A shared proxy per node does mTLS, and optional waypoint proxies do HTTP features like routing.

title: ambiguity
text: When the problem is not clearly defined. Nobody has decided yet what to build, why, or what "done" means.

title: anchoring effect
text: The tendency of the first number named in a negotiation to pull later offers towards it, even when that number is extreme.

title: anemic domain model
text: A design where objects only hold data, with getters and setters, and all the rules live in separate service classes. Fowler calls it an anti-pattern.

title: anti-corruption layer
text: Code at the edge of your system that translates another system's model into your own words, so that the other design does not leak into yours.

title: anti-entropy repair
text: A background job that compares replicas, finds data that differs, and copies the missing changes. Cassandra calls it repair and uses Merkle trees to compare.

title: anti-pattern
text: A common answer to a problem that looks like a solution but makes things worse. The term was coined by Andrew Koenig.

title: anycast
text: Announcing the same IP address from many places, so the network sends each user to the nearest one.

title: API gateway
text: A server in front of your services that receives every API request. It does shared jobs such as checking logins, rate limits and sending each request to the right service.

title: append-only file
text: Redis's log of every write command. On restart Redis replays it to rebuild its data. How much you can lose depends on how often it calls fsync.

title: append-only
text: Data you can only add to. Old records are never updated or deleted, so the full history stays.

title: appetite
text: How much time a problem is worth to you, decided before you design a solution. You then shape the work to fit that time.

title: asynchronous replication
text: The leader confirms a write to the client right away and sends it to followers in the background.

title: at-least-once
text: A delivery promise. No message is lost, but some may be handled more than once.

title: at-most-once
text: A delivery promise. No message is handled twice, but some may be lost.

title: atomic
text: An atomic operation happens completely or not at all. If it fails partway, every part of it is undone.

title: authentication
text: Checking who a user or service is, for example with a password, a second factor or a login at another provider. It answers "who are you?", not "what may you do?".

title: authoritative name server
text: The DNS server that holds the real records for a zone, such as example.com. Other servers only cache or point to it.

title: authoritative server
text: A game server that owns the true state of the game. Players' games only send inputs, and the server decides what really happened, which makes cheating harder.

title: authorization
text: Checking what a known user or service may do, such as reading one order or deleting a project. It must run on the server for every request.

title: auto-increment
text: A database feature that gives each new row the next number in a counter, like 1, 2, 3. One database owns the counter.

title: auto-remediation
text: Automation that fixes a known problem by itself when an alert fires, with no human in the loop. Good auto-remediation has limits: it stops and calls a person when something looks unsafe.

title: autoscaling
text: Adding or removing servers automatically as traffic goes up or down.

title: availability
text: The share of time, or of requests, in which a system works for its users. It is usually written as a percentage, such as 99.9% over a month.

title: Avro
text: A compact binary data format from the Apache project. The data has no field names or numbers, so a reader needs the schema it was written with.

title: B-tree
text: A sorted tree of fixed-size pages on disk. The database changes pages in place. Most SQL databases use it for indexes.

title: back-of-envelope estimate
text: A quick, rough calculation with round numbers and written assumptions. It tells you the size of a problem before you design for it.

title: backend for frontend
text: A small backend built for one user interface, such as the mobile app. It shapes and combines data for that client, and the UI team usually owns it.

title: backfill
text: A job that fills in or fixes data in rows that already exist, for example copying a value into a new column. On a live database, run it in small batches.

title: exponential backoff
text: Waiting longer after each failed try, for example 1, 2, then 4 seconds.

title: backpressure
text: A way for a slow part of a system to make faster parts slow down or wait, instead of being flooded.

title: backward compatibility
text: A change is backward compatible when things built for the old version keep working. New code reads old data, or a new API version still serves old clients.

title: BAI2
text: A file format many US banks use to send account balances and transactions to their customers, usually every day.

title: bake time
text: The time you wait at each rollout stage, watching metrics, before sending a change wider.

title: bandwidth
text: How much data a network link can carry per second, usually in bits per second, such as 1 Gbit/s.

title: bar raiser
text: At Amazon, a trained interviewer who joins a hiring loop as a neutral third party and helps lead the decision, so no single person decides alone.

title: base backup
text: A full copy of a database's data files, taken while it runs. Point-in-time recovery starts from it and replays the change log on top.

title: batching
text: Grouping many items into one operation, such as one network call or one disk write, so they share its fixed cost. It raises throughput but an item may wait for others to join.

title: BATNA
text: Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement: what you will do if this deal does not happen. In a job offer, it might be staying in your current job or taking another offer.

title: behavioural question
text: An interview question about what you really did in the past, such as "Tell me about a time you missed a deadline." It differs from a hypothetical question, such as "What would you do if…?"

title: billing period
text: The stretch of time one invoice covers, for example 1 to 30 November. Usage counts toward the period in which it happened.

title: bisection
text: Finding a problem by splitting the search space in half again and again, for example by time, version or region.

title: blameless postmortem
text: A postmortem that looks for the causes in systems and processes, not for a person to blame, so people share what really happened.

title: blast radius
text: How many users or systems a failure can reach. A small blast radius means a bad change hurts only a few.

title: Bloom filter
text: A small data structure that says a key is surely not in a set, or may be in it. It is never wrong about "not".

title: BM25
text: A classic ranking function for keyword search. It scores documents by how well their exact words match the words in the query.

title: broken object level authorization
text: A bug where an API takes an object ID from the client, like an order number, and uses it without checking that the caller may see that object.

title: boring technology
text: Well-known, mature tools like Postgres or cron. Not bad, just old enough that their limits and failure modes are well understood. The idea is from Dan McKinley's essay "Choose Boring Technology".

title: bounded context
text: In domain-driven design, a clear boundary, often one subsystem or one team's work, inside which one model applies and each word has one meaning. The same word can mean something else in another bounded context.

title: bounded queue
text: A queue with a fixed maximum size. When it is full, a new item must wait, be rejected or replace another item, so the queue cannot use up all memory.

title: branch prediction
text: The CPU guesses which way an if or a loop will go and starts work on that path early. A wrong guess throws that work away and costs time.

title: breaking change
text: A change to an API or data format that makes existing clients fail, such as removing or renaming a field.

title: bridge model
text: A SaaS design that mixes silo and pool, for example a shared app with a separate database for some tenants or services.

title: build artifact
text: The file a build produces and you deploy, such as a container image, a JAR or an app bundle. Build it once and deploy that same file everywhere.

title: build provenance
text: A record of how a build artifact was made, such as which source, which build platform and which inputs. When the build platform signs it, you can check it before you install.

title: bulkhead
text: A separate, limited pool of threads or call slots for one dependency. If that dependency gets slow, it can fill only its own pool, and the rest of the service keeps working.

title: burn rate
text: How fast a service spends its error budget. At burn rate 1, the budget runs out exactly at the end of the SLO window.

title: cache-aside
text: A caching pattern where the app checks the cache, and on a miss reads the database and writes the value into the cache itself.

title: cache busting
text: Putting a version or content hash in a file name, so each new version gets a new URL and caches can never serve an old copy.

title: cache hit ratio
text: The share of requests a cache answers from its own copy. A ratio of 0.9 means the cache answers 9 of 10 requests from its own copy.

title: invalidation
text: Removing or updating a cached value when the source data changes, so readers do not see old data.

title: cache key
text: The value a cache uses to decide which requests share one stored copy. In HTTP it is at least the method and the URL.

title: cache line
text: The fixed-size block that a CPU cache moves to and from memory, usually 64 bytes. When you read one byte, the CPU loads the whole line that holds it.

title: cache miss
text: A cache hit is when the data is in the cache. A cache miss is when it is not, so you must read it from the source.

title: cache purge
text: Telling a CDN to drop or mark stale its stored copies, by URL, tag or everything, so the next request fetches a fresh copy.

title: cache stampede
text: When a popular cache key expires and many requests miss at once, all loading the same data from the database.

title: cache
text: A fast copy of data that is slow or costly to get, kept close to where it is read.

title: camt.053
text: The ISO 20022 XML message for a bank account statement. It holds the opening and closing balances and every entry for the period, often one day.

title: canary
text: A small part of the fleet, such as 1% of servers, that gets a change first. You compare it with the rest before going wider.

title: CAP theorem
text: A proof that during a network partition, a replicated system cannot be both consistent (linearizable) and available. Each cut-off node must choose.

title: capacity unit
text: DynamoDB's unit of throughput. One read capacity unit is one strongly consistent read per second of up to 4 KB. One write capacity unit is one write per second of up to 1 KB.

title: card network
text: The network of a card brand, such as Visa or Mastercard, that carries payment messages and money between the merchant's bank and the card's bank.

title: career ladder
text: A company document that describes what is expected at each job level, for example scope, impact and how widely you work with others.

title: cascading failure
text: A failure that spreads. One part fails or gets slow, its callers run out of threads or connections, and then their callers fail too.

title: causal consistency
text: If one operation may have caused another, like a reply to a comment, everyone sees them in that order.

title: CDN
text: A content delivery network. Many data centers around the world that keep copies of your content close to users, so pages load faster and your servers get less traffic.

title: celebrity problem
text: One account with millions of followers overloads the system. With fan-out on write, each of its posts must be copied into millions of feeds.

title: cell
text: A full, independent copy of a workload that serves only some customers. A router sends each customer to its cell, so one failure stays inside one cell.

title: certificate authority
text: An organisation that signs certificates after it checks the requester. For most web certificates, it checks that the requester controls the domain. Clients trust a certificate if a trusted certificate authority signed it.

title: cgroup
text: A Linux feature that groups processes and limits what they may use together, such as memory and CPU. Containers use cgroups for their limits.

title: chain of trust
text: The list of certificates from a site's certificate up to a trusted root. Each one is signed by the next one up, so the client can check them all.

title: change amplification
text: When a simple change needs edits in many places in the code. It is a sign that a design decision is spread across modules.

title: change data capture
text: Reading every insert, update and delete from a database's change log, and sending them on as events to other systems.

title: chaos engineering
text: Causing failures on purpose, in a small and controlled way, to learn whether a system keeps working when real failures happen.

title: chargeback
text: When a cardholder disputes a payment with their card issuer. The money is pulled back from the merchant, often with a fee, and the issuer later decides who is right.

title: check-then-act
text: A race where code checks a condition, such as 'is the seat free?', and then acts on it in a separate step. Another thread can change the state in between.

title: checkpoint barrier
text: A marker a stream processor puts into the data stream. When the barrier has arrived from all of an operator's inputs, the operator saves its state, so all saved states match one point in the input.

title: choreography
text: A way to run a saga with no one in charge. Each service listens for events and reacts with its own step.

title: Chrome UX Report
text: A public Google dataset of how real Chrome users experience popular websites, including the Core Web Vitals.

title: chunking
text: Splitting long documents into smaller pieces (chunks) before you index them for search. The size and borders of each piece change what search can find.

title: circuit breaker
text: A guard around calls to another service. After many failures it stops sending calls for a short time, so the failing service can recover and the caller does not wait.

title: classitis
text: Splitting code into so many small classes that each one adds very little. You must learn many interfaces to get simple work done.

title: CLAUDE.md
text: A Markdown file of project instructions that Claude Code reads at the start of every session, like build commands and team rules.

title: Clean Architecture
text: Robert C. Martin's name for designs that put business rules in the centre and frameworks, databases and the UI at the edge, with all source code dependencies pointing inward.

title: clearing account
text: A ledger account that holds money only while it is on the way, for example between a payment and its payout. When every step finishes, it should go back to zero.

title: client-side prediction
text: The player's game shows the result of their own input at once, as a guess, instead of waiting for the server. The server's answer later confirms or corrects it.

title: client-side rendering
text: Building a page in the browser with JavaScript that changes the DOM. The server sends little HTML and a script bundle.

title: clock skew
text: The difference between the times shown by two clocks at the same moment, for example on two servers.

title: CNAME
text: A DNS record that makes one name an alias for another name. The resolver then looks up the other name.

title: code hotspot
text: A part of the code that changes often and is hard to work with. Tools like CodeScene suggest improving hotspots first, because you pay the extra cost on every change.

title: code splitting
text: Cutting a JavaScript bundle into smaller pieces, so the browser downloads only the code the first view needs and loads the rest later.

title: coding agent
text: An AI tool that works in a loop on your code. It reads files, edits them, runs commands and checks the results until the task looks done.

title: cognitive load
text: How much information you must hold in your head at once to understand or change a piece of code.

title: cohesion
text: How strongly the parts inside one module belong together. High cohesion means the parts serve one purpose and tend to change together.

title: commit index
text: In Raft, the position of the last log entry known to be stored on a majority of servers. Entries up to it are safe to apply.

title: commit wait
text: In Spanner, the short wait after a write picks its timestamp. Nobody can see the data until that timestamp has surely passed, given the clock uncertainty.

title: compaction
text: Background work in an LSM-tree that merges several SSTables into one and drops old versions and deleted keys.

title: compare-and-swap
text: One atomic CPU step: if a variable still holds the value you expect, set it to a new value and report success. Otherwise change nothing and report failure.

title: compensating transaction
text: A new action that undoes the effect of an earlier step, such as a refund for a charge. It does not erase the first step.

title: composite index
text: An index on several columns, sorted by the first column, then by the second inside it, like a phone book. It helps queries that filter on its leading columns.

title: conditional write
text: A write that the database applies only if a condition on the current item or row is true, such as "version is still 7". If the condition is false, nothing changes: DynamoDB returns an error, and SQL updates zero rows.

title: Cone of Uncertainty
text: A model by Steve McConnell. Early estimates can be far too high or too low. The possible error shrinks only as the team makes decisions and removes unknowns. It shows the best case.

title: confirmation bias
text: Noticing only the facts that fit what you already believe, and missing the facts that do not.

title: congestion control
text: Rules that make a sender slow down when the network looks overloaded, for example when packets get lost, so the network does not collapse.

title: connascence
text: A vocabulary for kinds of coupling. For example, two functions that must agree on the order of values in a list are connascent by position.

title: connection draining
text: Stopping new requests to a server you are removing, while letting the requests it already has finish.

title: connection leak
text: A connection borrowed from a pool that is never given back, often because an error skipped the return. Each leak makes the pool one smaller, until no connections are left.

title: connection migration
text: A QUIC feature that keeps a connection alive when the client's IP address or port changes, because the connection is found by an ID, not by its address.

title: connection pool
text: A set of open database connections that are reused, so a new connection is not opened for every request. The pool can live inside the app. Or a separate program, a connection pooler such as PgBouncer, can keep one pool that many apps share.

title: consensus algorithm
text: A way for a group of machines to agree on one value or one order of changes, even when some of them fail. Raft and Paxos are examples.

title: consistency level
text: In Cassandra and ScyllaDB, the number of replicas that must answer a read or write before it counts, such as ONE, QUORUM or ALL.

title: consistency model
text: A promise about what reads can see after writes in a system with many copies of the data, from strong to weak.

title: consistent hashing
text: A way to map keys to servers so that adding or removing one server moves only a small share of the keys.

title: consumer group
text: A set of Kafka consumers that share the work of reading a topic. Each partition is read by only one member of the group at a time.

title: consumer lag
text: How far a consumer is behind the newest message in a log, such as a Kafka partition. Lag that keeps growing means the consumer cannot keep up.

title: context engineering
text: Choosing and arranging everything a model sees for one request, such as instructions, examples, documents, tool results and history, so the useful tokens fit and the noise stays out.

title: context map
text: A picture of all the bounded contexts in a system, how they connect, and which team depends on which.

title: context propagation
text: Passing the trace ID and the current span ID along with a call or a message, so the next service can add its spans to the same trace.

title: context rot
text: The drop in a model's accuracy and recall as its context window fills with more tokens. A long prompt can hide the one fact the model needs.

title: context switch
text: The kernel stops one thread, saves its registers, and starts another. It lets many threads share one CPU, but each switch costs time.

title: context window
text: Everything a model can see at once, such as messages, files it read and command output. It has a size limit, and quality drops as it fills.

title: continuous delivery
text: Building software so that any version that passes the pipeline can be released to production at any time. A person still chooses when to deploy.

title: continuous deployment
text: Every change that passes the automated pipeline goes to production on its own, with no human step.

title: CI
text: Continuous integration. A system that builds the code and runs the tests and other checks on every change, before it is merged.

title: contract test
text: A test that checks two services agree on the requests and responses between them, without starting both services together.

title: contributing factor
text: One of several conditions that together caused an incident. Many teams list contributing factors instead of looking for one single root cause.

title: control plane
text: The part of a system that decides and configures, such as which routes and certificates proxies use. It is not on the path of each request.

title: controlled delay
text: A queue rule, first made for network routers (CoDel), that limits how long items may wait. When a queue stays full for a while, new items get a very short wait limit, so a standing queue cannot form.

title: Conway's law
text: Melvin Conway's 1968 idea that organisations which design systems produce designs that copy their own communication structure.

title: coordination service
text: A small, strongly consistent store, such as ZooKeeper, etcd or Consul, that a cluster uses for leaders, locks, membership and config.

title: Core Web Vitals
text: Three numbers from Google that describe how a page feels to real users: LCP for loading, INP for responsiveness and CLS for visual stability.

title: correlation ID
text: An ID attached to one request and passed to every service it touches, so you can find all of its logs and spans. A trace ID is one kind.

title: cost of delay
text: What you lose for each week a piece of work is not done. It combines how valuable the work is with how urgent it is, so you can rank features and cleanup work together.

title: coupling
text: How strongly one module depends on another. With strong coupling, a change in one module forces changes in the other. Stevens, Myers and Constantine described it in a 1974 paper.

title: covering index
text: An index that holds every column a query needs, so the database can answer from the index without reading the table rows.

title: CQRS
text: Using one model to change data and a different model, often a different store, to read it. Powerful for some parts of a system, but it adds complexity and lag.

title: crash loop
text: When a program crashes, restarts, hits the same problem and crashes again, over and over.

title: critical path
text: The longest chain of steps that must happen one after another. It sets the total time, so making any other step faster does not help.

title: critical rendering path
text: The steps a browser takes to turn HTML, CSS and JavaScript into pixels: build the DOM and CSSOM, make the render tree, do layout, then paint.

title: critical section
text: A piece of code that reads or changes shared data. Only one thread may run it at a time, or the data can break.

title: crypto-shredding
text: Encrypting each person's data with their own key, then deleting the key to make that data unreadable in the store and its backups.

title: CTC
text: Cost to company, the yearly total an Indian employer spends on you. It often includes variable pay, the employer's provident fund share and gratuity, so it is more than your monthly in-hand pay.

title: Cumulative Layout Shift
text: A score for how much content on a page moves without the user asking for it. Good is 0.1 or less.

title: cursor pagination
text: A way to page through a list where each answer gives an opaque token, the cursor. The client sends it back to get the items after that point.

title: CVE
text: A public ID for one known security flaw, like CVE-2021-44228. Scanners use these IDs to tell you which of your package versions are affected.

title: daily active users
text: The number of different people who use a product on a given day.

title: dark launch
text: Running new code on real traffic without letting it change results, so you can see what it would do before you turn it on.

title: data encryption key
text: The key that encrypts your data itself in envelope encryption. You store it only in encrypted (wrapped) form, next to the data.

title: data flow diagram
text: A drawing of a system that shows where data comes from, where it goes, where it is stored, and which trust boundaries it crosses. The usual starting point for a threat model.

title: data model
text: The shape you give your data, such as tables with rows, nested documents, or a graph of nodes and links.

title: data plane
text: The part of a system that carries the real traffic, request by request, such as the proxies in a service mesh. It follows rules set by the control plane.

title: data residency
text: Keeping certain data stored, and often processed, inside a given country or region, usually because a law, a contract or a customer requires it.

title: dead-letter queue
text: A separate queue for messages that failed too many times, so they stop blocking work and you can inspect them.

title: dead reckoning
text: Guessing where something is now by assuming it kept its last known speed and direction. Works for cars and ships, but not for players who turn suddenly.

title: dead tuple
text: In PostgreSQL, an old row version left behind by an UPDATE or DELETE that no transaction can see any more. VACUUM frees its space.

title: deadline
text: The time by which something must be done. For a request, passing the time left down to every call lets servers drop work nobody waits for.

title: deadlock
text: Two transactions each wait for a lock the other one holds, so neither can go on. The database usually cancels one of them with an error.

title: declarative query
text: A query that says what result you want, not the steps to get it, as in SQL or Cypher. The database chooses the indexes and order.

title: Decorator pattern
text: A design pattern that wraps a function or object to add a step, such as logging or timing, and keeps the same interface. Callers and the wrapped code do not change.

title: deep dive
text: The part of a design discussion where you take one hard piece, such as locking or scaling, and work it out in detail with its trade-offs.

title: deep module
text: A module with a small, simple interface that hides a lot of work behind it. Unix file I/O is the classic example.

title: delayed acknowledgement
text: When a TCP receiver waits a short time before confirming data, so it can send fewer confirmations. RFC 9293 limits the wait to under 0.5 seconds.

title: delayed replica
text: A replica that applies changes on purpose some time after the primary, for example 1 hour later, so you can stop it before a bad change arrives.

title: denormalization
text: Storing a copy of data where it is read, such as a comment count on the post row, so reads need fewer joins. Every write must now update the copies too.

title: dependency confusion
text: An attack where someone publishes a package on a public index with the same name as your private one, so your installer picks the public, harmful package.

title: dependency injection
text: Passing an object the things it needs, for example through its constructor, instead of letting it create them. It is about wiring, not design direction.

title: dependency inversion principle
text: The "D" in SOLID. High-level business code should not depend on low-level details. Both depend on an interface shaped by the high-level code.

title: dependency rule
text: The main rule of Clean Architecture. Source code dependencies point only inward, so business rules never import the web framework or the database code.

title: deployment pipeline
text: The automated steps every change goes through, such as build, test, package and deploy. Each stage runs only if the one before it passed.

title: deprecation
text: Marking a feature, field or API version as old and due for removal, while it still works, so users have time to move off it.

title: design doc
text: A short written plan for a piece of work, shared before you build it. It lists the goals, the options you considered, and the trade-offs.

title: design pattern
text: A named, well-known answer to a design problem that keeps coming back in a certain situation. It gives a team a shared word and a list of trade-offs, not ready-made code.

title: deterministic
text: Code is deterministic when the same starting state and the same inputs always give exactly the same result, on every machine.

title: diff
text: The list of lines added, changed and removed between two versions of code. A pull request shows its diff for review.

title: differential backup
text: A backup that holds everything that changed since the last full backup. To restore, you need that full backup plus the newest differential.

title: dirty read
text: Reading data another transaction has written but not yet committed. That data may still be rolled back.

title: disagree and commit
text: Saying openly that you disagree with a decision, then fully supporting it once it is made, so the team can move on.

title: distributed lock
text: A lock that many servers share, often kept in a store like Redis. Only one server or user can hold it at a time, usually until it expires.

title: DNS
text: The Domain Name System. A tree of names spread over many name servers, which turns names like www.example.com into IP addresses.

title: do-nothing script
text: A script that prints each step of a manual task and waits for a person to do it. Later, you replace one step at a time with real code.

title: document database
text: A database that stores records as JSON-like documents with nested fields, such as MongoDB.

title: domain event
text: A record of something that happened in the business that experts care about, such as "order placed". It does not change after it is created.

title: double-entry
text: A way to record money where every movement has at least two entries, one taking money out of an account and one putting it in, so they always sum to zero.

title: dual write
text: Writing the same change to two systems in two separate calls, such as a database and a message broker. A crash in between leaves them out of step.

title: durability
text: How likely it is that data, once saved, stays saved and is not lost. It is different from availability, which is whether you can reach the data right now.

title: dynamic secret
text: A credential made on demand for one client, with a short lease. When the lease ends, it is revoked, so there is no long-lived password to leak.

title: edge location
text: One CDN data center near users. It answers requests from its own cache and asks the origin server only when it has no fresh copy.

title: election timeout
text: How long a Raft follower waits without hearing from a leader before it starts an election. Each server picks it at random.

title: embedding
text: A list of numbers (a vector) that a model makes from a piece of text. Texts with similar meaning get vectors that are close together, so you can search by meaning.

title: end-to-end argument
text: A design rule from a 1981 paper by Saltzer, Reed and Clark (journal version 1984). Some functions, like suppressing duplicates, can only be done fully with the application's help at the ends. Lower layers can help only as a speed-up.

title: end-to-end test
text: A test that runs the whole system the way a user does, for example by clicking through a checkout in a real browser.

title: entitlement
text: What a customer is allowed to use because of their plan or contract, for example "Pro accounts can export to PDF".

title: entity interpolation
text: Drawing other players smoothly between the last two real server updates. They appear a little in the past, often about 100 ms, but based only on real positions.

title: envelope encryption
text: Encrypting data with a data key, then encrypting that data key with a second key that stays in a key service. You store the encrypted data key next to the data.

title: ephemeral node
text: A ZooKeeper entry that lives only while the session that created it is alive. If the client's session ends, ZooKeeper deletes it.

title: error budget
text: The amount of failure an SLO allows, which is 100% minus the SLO. A 99.9% SLO gives a budget of 0.1% of requests.

title: ETag
text: An HTTP response header with a short ID for one version of the content. A client sends it back to ask "has this changed?" and may get a 304 Not Modified answer.

title: eval
text: A repeatable test for an LLM feature. It is a set of test cases, a grader that scores each output, and a score you track over time.

title: evaluation context
text: The data passed to a feature flag check, such as user ID, plan or country, that the flag's rules use to decide the answer.

title: event-carried state transfer
text: Events that carry the changed data, so receivers can keep their own copy and never need to call the sender.

title: event loop
text: A loop on one thread that waits for events, such as data on a socket, a timer or a click, and runs a short handler for each, one at a time. A handler that blocks stalls everything else. Node.js, browsers and Redis work this way.

title: event notification
text: Fowler's name for the pattern where a service sends an event to say that something changed and does not expect a reply. Its events are often thin; a receiver that needs details calls the sender.

title: event sourcing
text: Storing every change to your data as an event that is never edited. The current state is rebuilt by replaying the events in order.

title: event store
text: The database that holds the events in an event-sourced system. It is the source of truth, and it can check the expected version when you append.

title: event time
text: The time an event really happened, on the device that produced it. Stream processors use it to put events in the right window, even when they arrive late.

title: eventual consistency
text: Copies or services may disagree for a while after a change. If no new changes come in, they all end up with the same, latest value.

title: eviction
text: Removing keys from a cache when it is full, for example the least recently used ones, to make room for new data.

title: exactly-once
text: A promise that each message is handled once and only once. In practice it usually means at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent handler.

title: exemplar
text: One sample measurement stored with a metric, usually together with the trace ID of the request that produced it. It lets you jump from a graph to a real trace.

title: expand and contract
text: Making a breaking change in steps. First add the new thing next to the old, then move every user over, then remove the old thing.

title: expression index
text: An index on the result of an expression, such as lower(email), instead of a plain column. A query must use the same expression to use it.

title: extensible enum
text: A list of allowed values that the API owner says may grow later, so clients must handle values they do not know yet.

title: external consistency
text: A guarantee that if transaction T1 commits before T2 starts, T1 gets the smaller timestamp. Spanner's paper treats it as the same as linearizability.

title: fail fast
text: Stopping quickly at the first sign of a problem, with a clear error, instead of waiting or carrying on in a bad state.

title: fail open
text: When a check breaks, letting traffic through instead of blocking it, so the check itself does not cause an outage.

title: failing back
text: Moving work back to the original site or region after a failover, once it is healthy and has caught up. It is best done as a planned, separate step.

title: failover
text: Making a follower the new leader when the old leader stops working, and sending writes to it.

title: failure detector
text: The part of a distributed system that decides whether another node is still alive, usually from heartbeats or pings and a timeout. It can only guess, so it sometimes calls a slow node dead.

title: fallacies of distributed computing
text: Eight false beliefs that designers of distributed systems often hold, such as "the network is reliable" and "latency is zero". First written down at Sun in the 1990s.

title: fallback
text: A second way to get an answer or do a job, used when the normal way fails or is not available. Fallback code that rarely runs is hard to test, so it can fail when you need it.

title: false sharing
text: When threads on different cores write to different variables that sit in the same cache line. The cores keep taking the line from each other, so the code slows down even though no data is shared.

title: fan-out on read
text: The system stores each new item once. When a reader asks, it fetches recent items from every source they follow and merges them, as in a feed. Writes are cheap, but every read does more work.

title: fan-out on write
text: When something new is created, the system copies it (or its ID) at once into a ready-made list for every reader, such as every follower's feed. Reads are fast, but one item for a huge audience means millions of writes.

title: fan-out
text: One request that calls many servers or services at once, then waits for their answers. In feeds and messaging, it also means copying one message to many receivers (see fan-out on write).

title: fault injection
text: Adding a failure on purpose, such as delay, errors or a stopped server, to see how the rest of the system reacts.

title: feature flag
text: A switch read at runtime that turns a piece of code on or off, for some or all users, without a new deploy.

title: fencing token
text: A number that grows each time a lock is given out. Storage rejects writes with an older number, so a client whose lock expired cannot overwrite newer data.

title: few-shot prompting
text: Putting a few worked examples of input and the output you want into the prompt, so the model copies their format and style. With no examples, it is called zero-shot.

title: field data
text: Performance numbers collected from all the real users who visit a page, on their own devices and networks.

title: field number
text: In Protocol Buffers, the number given to each field. It is written on the wire instead of the name, so it must never change or be reused.

title: FIFO
text: First in, first out. Items are handled in the order they arrived. LIFO (last in, first out) handles the newest item first.

title: file descriptor
text: A small number the kernel gives your process for each open file, socket or pipe. Each process may hold only a limited number at once.

title: fine-tuning
text: Training an existing model further on your own examples, so its weights change. It shapes how the model behaves, but facts stored in weights are hard to update or trace to a source.

title: first-class function
text: A function you can treat like any other value. You can store it in a variable, pass it to another function or return it.

title: fixed window
text: A rate limit that counts requests in fixed blocks of time, like each calendar minute, and resets the count when a block ends.

title: flag debt
text: Old feature flags that stay in the code after their job is done. Each one adds branches to test and a switch that can be flipped by mistake.

title: flaky test
text: A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails on the same code, often because of timing, order or shared state.

title: flapping
text: When a check, an alert or a node keeps switching between two states, such as healthy and failed, again and again. Each switch can move traffic or data or page someone, so flapping can do more harm than a clean failure.

title: flash sale
text: A sale of limited stock that starts at a set time, so a very large crowd arrives within minutes.

title: float
text: A number type that stores values as binary fractions. It is fast but not exact for many decimals, like 0.1, so it must not hold money.

title: flow-control window
text: The amount of data a receiver says it can accept right now. The sender may send only that much, then must wait until the receiver opens the window again.

title: flow control
text: A way for a receiver to tell the sender how much more data it can take right now, so a fast sender does not overflow a slow reader.

title: FLP result
text: A 1985 proof by Fischer, Lynch and Paterson. In an asynchronous system, no consensus protocol is sure to finish if even one process may be faulty.

title: follow-the-sun
text: An on-call rotation split between teams in far-apart time zones, so each team covers its own daytime and nobody works at night.

title: follower
text: A database copy that only takes changes from the leader. It can answer reads, but it may be a little behind.

title: foreign key
text: A column whose value must match a row in another table, such as order_items.order_id pointing to orders.id. The database rejects values with no match.

title: forward compatibility
text: Old code can still read data written by new code, usually by skipping fields it does not know.

title: fsync
text: A system call that waits until a file's changed data is stored on the disk. Without it, written data may sit only in RAM and be lost on a power cut.

title: full jitter
text: A backoff rule where each wait is a random time between zero and the capped backoff, min(cap, base × 2^n). It spreads retries evenly over that whole window.

title: functional requirement
text: Something a user can do with the system, such as "search for events" or "book a seat".

title: FX
text: Converting money from one currency to another. The rate and fees used can make the amount you receive differ from the amount you expected.

title: game day
text: A planned practice session where a team causes or acts out a failure on purpose, to test its systems and its incident response.

title: garbage collection
text: The language runtime frees memory that the program no longer uses. In many runtimes this can pause the program for a short time.

title: gc_grace_seconds
text: A Cassandra table setting: how long a tombstone must be kept before compaction may drop it. The default is 10 days. Repair must reach every replica within it.

title: glob pattern
text: A short pattern that matches file paths. For example, src/**/*.ts matches every TypeScript file under the src folder.

title: global table
text: A DynamoDB table with replicas in several AWS Regions that copy each other's writes. By default the copying is asynchronous and conflicts are settled by last writer wins.

title: god class
text: One class that knows and does too much, such as a manager with dozens of methods. Almost every change touches it, so it is hard to change safely.

title: four golden signals
text: Four things to measure for any service: latency, traffic, errors and saturation (how full it is).

title: goodput
text: The part of throughput that is handled without errors and in time to be useful.

title: gossip protocol
text: A way to spread news in a cluster. Each node passes what it knows to a few random nodes, and they pass it on, so the news reaches everyone quickly without a central server.

title: graceful degradation
text: Still serving users when part of the system fails, with less, for example a page without recommendations, instead of failing the whole request.

title: graph database
text: A database that stores nodes and the links between them, such as Neo4j. It is good at following many hops of links.

title: GraphQL
text: A query language for APIs. The client asks for exactly the fields it needs, often from many resources in one request.

title: group commit
text: When a database writes the commit records of several transactions to disk with one flush, so they share the cost of that flush.

title: gRPC
text: A framework for calls between services. A client calls a method on a remote server as if it were local, with the contract written in Protocol Buffers.

title: half-open state
text: The test state of a circuit breaker. After a wait, it lets a few trial calls through. If they work, it closes again. If they fail, it opens again.

title: hallucination
text: When a language model writes text that is false, or that does not match the context it was given, as if it were a fact.

title: happens-before
text: Lamport's rule for ordering events without clocks. Event a happens-before b if they are in one process and a comes first, if a sends a message that b receives, or through a chain of these.

title: hardware prefetching
text: The CPU notices a pattern in your memory reads, such as walking an array, and loads the next cache lines before your code asks for them.

title: hardware security module
text: A tamper-resistant device that creates and stores keys and does crypto inside itself, so the keys never leave it in plain form.

title: hash slot
text: One of the 16,384 buckets that Redis Cluster splits keys into. Each key maps to one slot, and each slot belongs to one primary node.

title: head-based sampling
text: Deciding whether to keep a trace when the request starts, before you know if it will be slow or fail. Cheap and simple.

title: head-of-line blocking
text: When one lost or slow item at the front of a line holds back everything behind it, even items that are ready.

title: health check
text: An automatic test of whether a server or service is working. Load balancers use it to stop sending traffic to failing servers. Deploys use it too. For example, a deploy watches the error rate to decide whether to continue or roll back.

title: heartbeat
text: A small message sent again and again to say "I am still alive". If heartbeats stop, others assume the sender has failed.

title: hedged request
text: Sending a backup copy of a request to another replica when the first has not answered after a short delay, then using whichever answer comes first.

title: herd effect
text: Many clients act on the same event at the same moment, such as one change notice or one restart, and all hit the same resource together. Often only one of them needed to act.

title: hexagonal architecture
text: A design by Alistair Cockburn. Business code sits in the middle and talks to the outside world only through interfaces it owns (ports). Small adapters connect each port to a real tool, such as a database.

title: high watermark
text: In Kafka, the end of the committed part of a partition's log. Consumers can read only up to it.

title: hinted handoff
text: When a replica is down, another node keeps its writes with a note (a hint) saying who they belong to. It hands them over when the replica comes back.

title: hiring committee
text: A group that reads all the written interview feedback on a candidate and decides whether to hire, instead of the interviewers deciding one by one.

title: HMAC
text: A short code made from a message and a shared secret key. Only someone with the key can make the right code, so it proves the message came from someone who has the key and that nobody changed it.

title: home region
text: The one region that owns a user's or tenant's data and takes all of its writes. Other regions may hold read-only copies.

title: home timeline
text: The main feed a user sees when they open a social app, made of posts from the accounts they follow, and sometimes recommended posts.

title: horizontal scaling
text: Handling more load by adding more machines that share the work. It avoids the size limit of one machine, and, if built for it, one machine can fail without taking the service down.

title: hosted fields
text: Card input fields served by the payment processor inside your page, so the card number goes straight to the processor and never reaches your servers.

title: hot account
text: A ledger account that appears in a large share of transactions, so many writes wait on the same row.

title: hot key
text: A single cache or database key that gets a very large share of all reads or writes.

title: hot partition
text: A partition or shard that gets far more reads or writes than the others. It hits its limit while the rest of the cluster has spare capacity.

title: hot row
text: A single database row that very many transactions update at once, such as the stock of a flash-sale product. They wait in line for its lock.

title: HOT update
text: A PostgreSQL update that changes no indexed column (BRIN aside) and fits the new row version on the same page, so no index needs a new entry.

title: HPACK
text: The header compression format of HTTP/2. Both sides keep tables of headers they have seen, so a repeated header can be sent as a small number. HTTP/3 uses a similar format, QPACK.

title: HSTS
text: A response header that tells the browser to use only HTTPS for a site for a set time, and not to let users click through certificate errors.

title: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests
text: The HTTP status code a server returns when a client has sent too many requests in a given time.

title: hybrid logical clock
text: A timestamp that follows the happens-before order like a Lamport clock, but stays close to real clock time. It fits in 64 bits.

title: hybrid search
text: Running keyword search and vector search for the same query and merging the two result lists, so you get both exact matches and matches by meaning.

title: hydration
text: Running JavaScript in the browser to make server-rendered HTML interactive. Until it finishes, the page can look ready but not respond.

title: HyperLogLog
text: A small data structure that estimates how many different items you have seen, such as unique visitors, with a small error and a small, capped amount of memory (at most 12 KB in Redis).

title: hypothesis
text: A guess about the cause of a problem that a test can prove wrong, for example "the new pool size is too small".

title: Hyrum's law
text: The observation that, with enough users, every visible behaviour of an API is relied on by someone, even behaviour the docs never promised.

title: ID token
text: A signed JWT from an OpenID Connect provider that says who logged in. The app must check its issuer, audience, expiry and, in most cases, its signature.

title: idempotency key
text: A unique id the client sends with a request, so the server can spot a repeat and return the saved result.

title: idempotent producer
text: A Kafka producer setting. The broker gives the producer an ID and drops retried copies of a message by sequence number, so a retry does not write a duplicate. It holds only within one producer session.

title: idempotent
text: An action is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once.

title: identity provider
text: The system that logs users in and vouches for who they are to other apps, such as Okta or Microsoft Entra ID. Often called the IdP.

title: immutable backup
text: A backup that cannot be changed or deleted until a set retention time ends. In its strictest mode, not even an admin can delete it.

title: in-doubt transaction
text: A prepared transaction whose participant does not know the final decision, usually because the coordinator failed. It cannot commit or abort on its own, so it keeps its locks.

title: in-sync replica
text: In Kafka, a copy of a partition that is up to date with the leader. The leader includes itself. A write is committed once every in-sync replica has it.

title: inbox
text: A table where a consumer saves the IDs of events it has already handled, so it can skip duplicates.

title: incarnation number
text: A counter that only a node itself can raise, sent with news about it. When a node hears it is suspected, it raises the number, so its "I am alive" message beats the old suspicion.

title: incident commander
text: The person who leads an incident. They hold the overall picture and give out the work, but do not fix things themselves.

title: incremental backup
text: A backup that holds only what changed since the previous backup. To restore, you need it and every earlier backup it builds on.

title: index-only scan
text: A query plan step that reads the answer from the index alone and skips the table rows. In PostgreSQL it skips the table only for pages marked all-visible.

title: information hiding
text: Giving one module sole knowledge of a design decision, such as a data format, so other modules do not depend on it. David Parnas made it famous in a 1972 paper.

title: information leakage
text: When one design decision, such as a file format, is known by several modules. If it changes, all of them must change.

title: innovation token
text: Dan McKinley's idea that a company can afford only a few new or unusual technologies, about three, because each one brings unknown problems.

title: integration test
text: A test that checks that a few parts work together, for example your code with a real database.

title: Interaction to Next Paint
text: How long a page takes to show a visible response after a click, tap or key press. It reports the slowest one on the page, ignoring a few outliers. Good is 200 ms or less.
