title: interface segregation principle
text: The "I" in SOLID. Keep interfaces small, so a caller does not depend on methods it never uses.

title: inverted index
text: A map from each term to the list of documents that contain it, like the index at the back of a book. Search engines use it to find matches without scanning every document.

title: IP address
text: The number that tells the network which machine a packet is for. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, like 10.0.4.17. IPv6 addresses are 128 bits.

title: isolation level
text: A setting that says how much transactions running at the same time can see and change each other's work.

title: issuing bank
text: The bank that gave the customer their card. It approves or declines each payment and holds the money during authorization.

title: item collection
text: In DynamoDB, all the items that share one partition key value. They are stored together and sorted by sort key, so one Query can read them.

title: JIT provisioning
text: Creating a user account at the moment of their first single sign-on login, from the attributes in the login assertion. It does not remove users who leave.

title: jitter
text: Adding a small random amount to each wait, so many clients do not retry at the same moment.

title: join
text: A query step that combines rows from two tables by matching a column, such as orders.user_id = users.id.

title: JSON Schema
text: A standard way to describe the shape of JSON data, such as which fields exist, their types and which are required. Code can check a document against it.

title: JSON Web Token
text: A compact string that carries claims, such as a user ID and an expiry time, often signed so changes are detected. A signed JWT is not secret, because anyone can read its payload.

title: keep-alive
text: Keeping an idle connection open and working. In HTTP, the connection stays open so the next request needs no new handshake. Keep-alive probes or pings check that an idle connection still works.

title: kernel
text: The core of the operating system. It runs with full access to the hardware and shares the CPU, memory and disks among all programs.

title: key encryption key
text: A key that encrypts other keys, not data. In envelope encryption it stays inside the key management service and wraps each data encryption key.

title: KMS
text: A cloud service, such as AWS KMS or Google Cloud KMS, that creates and stores encryption keys and uses them for you. You call its API; the main keys never leave it unencrypted.

title: key-value store
text: A database that stores each value under a key. You get and put by key. Examples are DynamoDB and Redis.

title: keyed state
text: Data a stream processor remembers between events, split by key, such as a running count per city. Each key's state lives with the task that handles that key.

title: keyset pagination
text: Paging that asks for the rows after the last row you saw, using its sort values, instead of skipping a number of rows. It stays fast on deep pages.

title: kill switch
text: A quick way to turn off one feature or component everywhere, without a deploy, when it is causing harm.

title: knowledge cutoff
text: The date up to which a model's knowledge is most complete and reliable. It may know little or nothing correct about later events.

title: KRaft
text: Kafka's built-in metadata quorum, based on Raft. It replaced ZooKeeper, which Kafka used to need for its cluster metadata.

title: lab data
text: Performance numbers from loading a page in a controlled setup, with one device and one network. Repeatable, but not what real users get.

title: lag compensation
text: The game server rewinds other players to where the shooter saw them, checks the hit there, then moves them back. Shots hit where you aimed despite delay.

title: Lamport clock
text: A counter on each process that goes up with every event and jumps past any counter it receives in a message. If a happens-before b, a gets the smaller number.

title: Largest Contentful Paint
text: The time from when the user starts loading a page until the largest image, text block or video in view is shown. Good is 2.5 seconds or less.

title: last write wins
text: A rule for conflicting writes: keep the one with the biggest timestamp and drop the rest. With skewed clocks, it can silently drop the newer write.

title: latency
text: How long one operation or request takes, from start to answer. Usually measured in milliseconds (ms) or smaller units.

title: layer 4
text: The transport layer of a network (TCP and UDP). A layer 4 load balancer sees connections and ports, not HTTP requests.

title: layer 7
text: The application layer of a network, such as HTTP. A layer 7 load balancer reads each request and can route by path or header.

title: lazy loading
text: Loading a resource, such as an image or a piece of code, only when it is about to be needed instead of at the start.

title: leader election
text: The way a group of nodes picks one node to do a job alone, such as taking writes or running a scheduler, and picks a new one when it fails.

title: leader
text: The one database node that accepts writes. It sends every change on to the other copies. Also called the primary.

title: Leadership Principles
text: Amazon's public list of 16 principles it says it uses every day, such as Ownership and Dive Deep. Its interviewers judge every candidate against them.

title: leaky bucket
text: A rate limit where requests wait in a queue that drains at a fixed rate. When the queue is full, new requests are rejected.

title: leap second
text: An extra second sometimes added to UTC. Code that assumes time never goes backwards can break when one is added.

title: leap smear
text: A way to add a leap second without a jump. Time servers make each second slightly longer over many hours, so the extra second is spread out.

title: lease
text: A lock or role that expires after a set time unless the holder renews it. If the holder crashes, others can take over later.

title: least connections
text: A load balancing rule that sends each request to the server with the fewest requests still in progress.

title: least privilege
text: Giving each user, service or token only the access it needs for its job, and nothing more. A leak or bug then does less harm.

title: ledger
text: A record of every movement of money (or points, credits, stock) as entries that are only ever added, never changed. Balances are calculated from it.

title: lexeme
text: A word after it has been normalized for search, for example lowercased and cut to its root. Postgres full-text search stores lexemes.

title: Lighthouse
text: Google's open-source tool that loads a page in a controlled setup and reports performance and other audits. It gives lab data, not data from real users.

title: lightweight transaction
text: A Cassandra write with an IF condition, such as IF NOT EXISTS. Replicas agree on it with Paxos inside one partition, so it costs more round trips than a plain write.

title: linearizability
text: One of the strongest consistency models for a single piece of data. The system acts as if there is one copy of the data, and each operation takes effect at one instant.

title: linter
text: A tool that reads your code without running it and flags style problems and common mistakes, the same way every time.

title: Liskov substitution principle
text: The "L" in SOLID. A subtype must behave the way its supertype promises, so code written for the supertype still works. Matching method types is not enough.

title: Little's law
text: On average, items inside a system = arrival rate × time each item spends inside. For example, 2,000 requests a second × 0.05 s = 100 requests in progress.

title: livelock
text: Threads keep reacting to each other and retrying, so they stay busy, but none of them makes progress.

title: LLM-as-judge
text: Using a language model to grade the output of another model, usually with a written rubric. It is fast and scales, but it has biases you must check.

title: LLM token
text: The unit of text a language model reads and writes. A token can be a word, part of a word, a character or a byte. Providers count cost, limits and speed in tokens.

title: LLM
text: Large language model. A model trained on a lot of text to predict the next token. It writes likely text, not checked facts.

title: load balancer
text: A service with one address that sits in front of many servers and picks which server gets each connection or request.

title: load shedding
text: Rejecting some requests on purpose when a service is overloaded, so it can keep serving the rest.

title: load test
text: A test that sends a lot of fake traffic to a system, to find how much it can handle before it slows down or fails.

title: local secondary index
text: A DynamoDB index with the same partition key as its table but a different sort key. It allows strongly consistent reads, must be created with the table, and limits each partition key value to 10 GB.

title: lockfile
text: A file, such as package-lock.json, that records the exact version of every dependency, so every build installs the same ones.

title: log segment
text: One file in the series of files that stores a Kafka partition. Kafka writes to the newest segment and deletes old data one whole segment at a time.

title: logical backup
text: A backup written as SQL statements or rows, for example by pg_dump. It is portable, but it cannot be combined with the change log for point-in-time recovery.

title: logical replication
text: Copying row changes (inserts, updates, deletes) by table and key, not by disk block. In PostgreSQL it can copy chosen tables between different major versions.

title: long-lived branch
text: A branch that stays apart from main for weeks or months. The longer it lives, the bigger and riskier the final merge.

title: long polling
text: The client sends a request, and the server holds it open until it has new data or a timeout. Then the client sends the next request at once.

title: long task
text: Any piece of work on the browser's main thread that takes longer than 50 ms. While it runs, the page cannot respond to the user.

title: lost update
text: A bug where two transactions read the same value, both change it, and the second write wipes out the first.

title: LSM-tree
text: A storage design that buffers writes in memory, writes them out as new sorted files, and merges those files later in the background.

title: main thread
text: The browser thread that runs almost all of a page's JavaScript and handles user input. It can do only one task at a time.

title: managed database
text: A database that a cloud provider runs for you. It handles setup, patching, backups and failover, so your team does less operations work.

title: many-to-many
text: A link where each record on both sides can connect to many on the other, like users and events. In SQL it needs a third table of id pairs.

title: materialized view
text: A database view whose query result is stored like a table. Reads are fast, but the data is only as fresh as the last refresh.

title: MCP
text: Model Context Protocol, an open standard that connects AI tools to outside systems such as files, databases and other tools.

title: memtable
text: The sorted table in memory where an LSM-tree collects new writes before it writes them to disk as an SSTable.

title: Merkle tree
text: A tree of hashes. Each leaf is the hash of some data, and each parent is the hash of its children. Equal roots mean equal data.

title: broker
text: A server that holds messages between the services that send them and the services that read them. SQS, RabbitMQ and Kafka are brokers.

title: message queue
text: A place where one service leaves jobs or messages and another service picks them up later. It lets slow work happen in the background. SQS and RabbitMQ are examples.

title: metric
text: A number measured again and again over time, such as requests per second or error rate. Cheap to store and good for graphs and alerts.

title: multi-factor authentication
text: Login that needs more than a password, such as a code from an app or a security key. A stolen password alone is then not enough.

title: microservices
text: A style that builds one application as many small services. Each runs on its own, talks over the network, and can be deployed and scaled on its own.

title: middleware
text: In web frameworks, a chain of functions that run in turn before a request handler, for example to log or check access. Each one either ends the request or passes control to the next.

title: minor unit
text: The smallest unit of a currency, like paise for rupees or cents for dollars. Storing ₹10.50 as the integer 1050 paise keeps money exact.

title: mitigation
text: An action that stops or reduces harm to users quickly, like a rollback, before you know the exact cause.

title: model snapshot
text: A fixed, dated version of a model with a name that does not change, such as one ending in a date. Pinning one keeps behaviour stable until you choose to upgrade.

title: modular monolith
text: One application, deployed as one unit, whose code is split into parts with strictly enforced boundaries between business areas.

title: monolith
text: An application that is built and deployed as one unit. A change to any part means deploying the whole thing.

title: monorepo
text: One repository that holds the code for many projects or services, often owned by different teams.

title: monotonic clock
text: A clock that only moves forward and cannot be set. Its value means nothing on its own, but the difference between two readings on one machine is a safe way to measure time.

title: monotonic reads
text: A promise that your reads never go back in time. Once you have seen a change, later reads will not hide it again.

title: multi-tenancy
text: One running system serving many customer organisations (tenants), which share code, servers and often databases.

title: multiplexing
text: Sending many separate conversations over one connection at the same time, by cutting them into small labelled pieces and mixing them.

title: multiwindow alert
text: A burn-rate alert that fires only when a long window (for example 1 hour) and a short window (for example 5 minutes) both pass the same threshold. Teams run several such rules with different burn rates: fast ones page, slow ones open a ticket.

title: mutation testing
text: A tool makes small changes (mutants) to your code, such as turning > into >=, and runs your tests. If no test fails, your tests missed that bug.

title: mutex
text: A lock that only one thread can hold at a time. Other threads that want it wait until the holder unlocks it.

title: mutual TLS
text: TLS where both sides show a certificate, so the server also knows which client is calling. Often used between internal services.

title: MVCC
text: The database keeps several versions of a row, so readers can see an older version while a writer makes a new one.

title: Nagle's algorithm
text: A TCP rule that holds small writes while earlier data is still unacknowledged, then sends them together. Applications can turn it off with TCP_NODELAY.

title: NAT
text: Network address translation. A router or gateway swaps private addresses and ports for its own public IP address and ports. This lets many machines share one public address.

title: near cache
text: A small cache inside each app server's own memory, in front of a shared cache. It answers the hottest keys with no network call.

title: near real-time
text: New documents become searchable after a short delay, not at once. In Elasticsearch, a refresh makes them visible, by default every second for indices that are being searched.

title: negative caching
text: Caching the answer "this does not exist". In DNS, a resolver remembers that a name has no record, so a record you create later can stay invisible for a while.

title: network partition
text: A network failure where some nodes cannot reach others, while all of them keep running.

title: nines
text: A short way to say availability: 99.9% is "three nines". Each extra nine allows 10 times less downtime.

title: noisy neighbour
text: One user or tenant that puts so much load on shared resources that others sharing them become slow.

title: non-functional requirement
text: A quality the system must have, such as speed, scale, availability or "never sell a seat twice". It shapes how you build, not what users can do.

title: non-goal
text: Something that could reasonably be a goal of a project, but that you chose to leave out. Writing non-goals down keeps the scope from growing.

title: normalization
text: Designing tables so each fact is stored in one place and other rows point to it by id. Updates touch one row, but reads need joins.

title: NTP
text: Network Time Protocol. Servers use it to keep their clocks close to a reference time. It makes clocks close, not equal.

title: NUMA
text: Non-uniform memory access. In a server with several CPU sockets, each socket has its own memory. Reading memory attached to another socket is slower than reading local memory.

title: OAuth 2.0
text: A standard that lets an app get limited access to an API on a user's behalf, through a token, without the user's password. It is about delegation, not login.

title: observability
text: How well you can understand what a system is doing from the data it sends out, such as metrics, logs and traces.

title: Observer pattern
text: A design pattern where an object tells a list of listeners when something changes, without knowing who they are. Event listeners and event emitters are common forms of it.

title: offset
text: The position number of a message in a log, such as a Kafka partition. A consumer saves its offset to remember how far it has read.

title: on-call
text: The engineer whose turn it is to answer alerts and fix problems, often outside work hours.

title: one-on-one
text: A regular private meeting between two people, often a manager or mentor and the person they support. It is for growth, problems and feedback, not status updates.

title: one-way door
text: A decision that is hard or impossible to undo, so it deserves a slow, careful process. Jeff Bezos used the term in his 2015 shareholder letter.

title: Onion Architecture
text: Jeffrey Palermo's 2008 design. The domain model is the centre, layers wrap around it, and code may depend only on layers closer to the centre. The database is an outer layer.

title: OOM killer
text: The part of the Linux kernel that ends a process when memory runs out and cannot be freed. In a container, it runs when the container reaches its memory limit and the kernel cannot free enough memory.

title: open-closed principle
text: The "O" in SOLID. A module should be open for extension and closed for modification, so new behaviour comes from new code, not edits to working code.

title: OpenAPI
text: A standard file format that describes an HTTP API, its endpoints, fields and errors. Tools use the file to make docs, client code and tests.

title: OpenFeature
text: An open specification for a vendor-neutral API for checking feature flags. A provider connects it to the flag tool you use.

title: OpenID Connect
text: A login layer on top of OAuth 2.0. It adds an ID token that tells the app who the user is, as checked by a provider such as Google or Okta.

title: optimistic locking
text: You read without a lock, then write only if the row has not changed since you read it, often by checking a version number. If it changed, you retry.

title: orchestration
text: A way to run a saga where one component tells each service what to do next and keeps the state of the whole flow.

title: order of magnitude
text: A rough size in powers of ten. 300 and 700 have the same order of magnitude (hundreds); 300 and 30,000 do not.

title: origin server
text: Your own server that holds the real content. A CDN fetches from it when its cache has no fresh copy.

title: origin shield
text: An extra cache layer between a CDN's edge locations and your origin server. Edges ask the shield, and only the shield asks the origin.

title: output encoding
text: Changing data just before you show it, so the browser displays it as text and does not run it as code. HTML, JavaScript and URLs each need their own encoder.

title: overfitting
text: Tuning a system so closely to one set of test cases that it scores well on them but does worse on new, real inputs.

title: overselling
text: Selling more units of a product than you have in stock, usually because two orders took the same last item.

title: ownership
text: Being the person responsible for a result, not just a task. The owner makes sure the work is finished, works in production and solves the real problem.

title: PACELC
text: An extension of CAP. During a partition (P), choose availability (A) or consistency (C). Else (E), choose latency (L) or consistency (C).

title: packet
text: One small chunk of data sent across a network, with a header that says where it comes from and where it goes. Big messages are split into many packets.

title: page cache
text: File data the Linux kernel keeps in RAM after a read or write. It makes repeated reads fast. Written data waits there before it goes to disk.

title: page split
text: What a B-tree does when a new key does not fit in a full page: it moves some keys to a new page and adds a pointer in the parent page.

title: parameterized query
text: A SQL query with placeholders, like "WHERE id = ?", where the values are sent separately. The database never treats those values as code.

title: partial failure
text: When some parts of a distributed system fail while other parts keep working. For example, one server or one network link breaks, and the rest of the system keeps running.

title: partial index
text: An index that holds only the rows matching a condition, such as unbilled orders. It is smaller, but only queries with a matching condition can use it.

title: partition
text: One piece of a dataset or stream that has been split up. Databases often call it a shard. In Kafka, a partition is one ordered log inside a topic.

title: pass-through method
text: A method that only calls another method with the same arguments and adds nothing. It is a sign of a shallow layer.

title: password hash
text: The result of running a password through a slow one-way function, such as Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt. The server stores only this, never the password, and cannot turn it back.

title: Paxos
text: An older consensus algorithm by Leslie Lamport. A value is chosen in two phases, and each phase needs a majority of the servers.

title: authorize and capture
text: Taking a card payment in two steps. Authorization holds the money on the card. Capture, done later, actually takes it. A hold expires if you wait too long.

title: payout
text: A transfer from your balance at a payment processor to your own bank account, usually on a schedule. One payout can contain many payments, refunds and fees.

title: PCI DSS
text: The security standard for any business that stores, processes or sends card data. The less card data touches your systems, the less of it applies to you.

title: peeker's advantage
text: In online shooters, a player who steps around a corner sees the enemy before the enemy sees them, because of network delay and buffering.

title: percentile
text: The value below which a given share of measurements fall. A p99 latency of 300 ms means 99% of requests took 300 ms or less.

title: performance budget
text: A set of limits on numbers that affect speed, such as JavaScript size or LCP. Build tools can warn when a change goes over a limit.

title: pessimistic locking
text: You lock a row before you read and change it, for example with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. Others who want to change it wait until you commit.

title: phi accrual failure detector
text: A failure detector that gives a suspicion score (phi) instead of yes or no. The score grows the longer a heartbeat is late, compared with how heartbeats usually arrive. Cassandra and Akka use it.

title: pilot light
text: A disaster recovery setup where data is copied to a second site all the time, but the app servers there stay off until you need them.

title: pipelining
text: Sending the next request on a connection before the reply to the last one arrives, so you pay the round trip once for many requests, not once each.

title: PKCE
text: An OAuth add-on where the app sends a hash of a random secret at the start and the secret itself at the end. A stolen authorization code is then useless without the secret.

title: plan mode
text: A Claude Code mode where the agent reads files and proposes a plan, but does not change your source files.

title: planning fallacy
text: The habit of underestimating the time, cost and risk of your own plans, because you think about the plan's details instead of how similar work really turned out.

title: point-in-time recovery
text: Restoring a database to its exact state at a chosen moment, by loading a base backup and then replaying the saved change log up to that moment.

title: pointer chasing
text: Walking a linked structure, such as a linked list or tree, where each step must load a node to find the address of the next one. The CPU cannot fetch ahead, so each step may wait for memory.

title: policy engine
text: A library or service that answers "is this request allowed?" by evaluating authorization rules written as code, kept apart from the application's own code.

title: polyglot persistence
text: Using several kinds of databases in one system, each for the data it fits best. It adds running cost and data to keep in sync.

title: pool model
text: A SaaS design where tenants share the same resources. Cheap and simple to run, but needs tenant ids and limits to keep tenants apart.

title: port number
text: A number that picks one program on a machine, such as 443 for a web server. An IP address finds the machine; the port finds the program.

title: postings
text: In an inverted index, the list of documents (and often positions) that contain one term.

title: postmortem
text: A written record of an incident after it ends. It covers the impact, what was done, the causes and the follow-up actions.

title: power of two choices
text: A load balancing rule that picks two servers at random and sends the request to the less busy one.

title: prepared transaction
text: A transaction that has voted yes in two-phase commit. It is saved on disk and keeps its locks until someone commits or rolls it back, even after a restart.

title: primary key
text: The column, or set of columns, that names each row of a table. No two rows may have the same value.

title: problem details
text: A standard JSON shape for API error bodies, defined in RFC 9457. It has fields such as type, title, status and detail, so clients can handle every error the same way.

title: process
text: A running program. Each process has its own private memory, its own open files and its own limits, so one process normally cannot read or damage another's memory.

title: processing time
text: The time on the clock of the machine that handles an event. It is simple and fast to use, but results change if events arrive late or a job catches up on a backlog.

title: product discovery
text: The work of finding out what to build before you build it, for example by talking to users and testing ideas cheaply.

title: product manager
text: The person who decides what a team should build and why. They own whether customers want it and whether it works for the business.

title: projection
text: A read model kept up to date by applying events or data changes one by one. The word also names the code that does this. You can throw it away and rebuild it from the source data.

title: prompt caching
text: A provider feature that saves the work done on a fixed start of a prompt and reuses it on later requests. It lowers cost and latency when the start is exactly the same.

title: prompt injection
text: An attack where text the model reads, such as a web page, file or issue, contains instructions that change what the model does.

title: proration
text: Charging or crediting only part of a fixed fee because a plan was used for only part of a billing period, for example 20 of 30 days.

title: Protocol Buffers
text: A compact binary format from Google. You describe messages in a .proto file, and each field has a number that is written on the wire instead of its name.

title: pub/sub
text: Publish/subscribe. Senders publish messages to a named topic or channel, and every subscriber of that topic gets a copy. Senders do not need to know who listens.

title: pull request
text: A proposed code change that others can read, comment on and approve before it is merged into the main branch. GitLab calls it a merge request.

title: QPS
text: Queries (or requests) per second. The usual way to say how much traffic a service gets.

title: query plan
text: The steps a database chooses to run a query, such as which index to use or whether to scan the whole table. EXPLAIN shows it.

title: QUIC
text: A newer transport protocol that runs over UDP. It has reliable streams and built-in TLS, and a lost packet only blocks the streams it carried. HTTP/3 runs on it.

title: quorum
text: The smallest number of nodes that must answer before a read or write counts. With 3 copies, a common quorum is 2.

title: quota
text: The most of something one customer may use, such as requests per second, storage or running jobs.

title: race condition
text: A bug where the result depends on the timing of threads. Two threads touch the same data at about the same time, and one change can be lost.

title: Raft term
text: A numbered period of time in Raft. Each term starts with an election and has at most one leader. A higher term always wins.

title: Raft
text: A consensus algorithm. One elected leader copies its log of changes to the other servers, and a change counts once a majority has stored it. etcd and Consul use it.

title: RAG
text: Retrieval-augmented generation. The app first searches your own documents for text that matches the question, then gives that text to the model so it can answer from it.

title: rate limit
text: A rule that caps how many requests a client may make in a period of time, and rejects the extra ones.

title: role-based access control
text: An authorization model where permissions belong to roles, such as "editor", and users get permissions by being given roles.

title: RDB snapshot
text: A compact file with a point-in-time copy of all Redis data, written by a forked child process. If it is your only persistence, a crash loses the writes made since the last snapshot.

title: re-ranking
text: A second step after search. A separate model scores the top results again, and only the best few go to the language model.

title: read amplification
text: How many places, such as pages or files, a storage engine must check to answer one read.

title: read committed
text: An isolation level where you only see data that other transactions have committed. Each statement can see newer data than the last.

title: read model
text: A copy of data shaped for one kind of read, such as a feed table or search index. It is built from the main data and updated after each change.

title: read repair
text: During a read, the node that asked several replicas sends the newest value to any replica that returned an older one.

title: read-through
text: A caching pattern where the app only talks to the cache, and the cache loads missing data from the database itself.

title: read-write lock
text: A lock that lets many readers in at the same time, or one writer alone. It helps when data is read often and changed rarely.

title: read-your-writes
text: A promise that after you save something, your own later reads will show it, even if other users see it a bit later.

title: real user monitoring
text: Measuring performance in the browsers of your real visitors and sending the numbers to your own analytics.

title: relationship-based access control
text: An authorization model where access comes from relationships between users and objects, such as "owner of this doc" or "member of a group that can view this folder".

title: rebalancing
text: Moving data or work between machines so each one has a fair share, for example after you add a machine.

title: recall@k
text: A search metric. Of the documents that should be found for a question, the share that appear in the top k results.

title: reciprocal rank fusion
text: A simple way to merge several ranked result lists. Each document gets 1 / (k + rank) points from each list, and the points are added up. It needs no tuning.

title: reconciliation break
text: A difference found during reconciliation, such as a payment that is on only one side, a wrong amount or a duplicate. Each one needs a type, an owner and a fix.

title: reconciliation
text: Regularly comparing your own records with outside records, like bank statements, and explaining every difference.

title: recovery point objective
text: The most data you accept to lose in a disaster, measured as time. An RPO of 5 minutes means you may lose up to the last 5 minutes of writes.

title: recovery time objective
text: The longest you accept a service to be down after a disaster before it works again. An RTO of 1 hour means you must be back within an hour.

title: recursive resolver
text: The DNS server your app asks. It walks the DNS tree for you, from the root down, and caches the answers it gets.

title: RED method
text: A checklist for services: rate (requests per second), errors (how many fail) and duration (how long they take).

title: Redlock
text: A distributed lock algorithm for Redis. A client takes the same lock on a majority of several independent Redis primaries, for a limited time.

title: reference class forecasting
text: Estimating from how a group of similar past projects really turned out, then adjusting for clear differences. It is a way of taking the "outside view".

title: refresh token
text: A longer-lived token that an app uses only to get new short-lived access tokens. The server can revoke it to end the login.

title: relation tuple
text: One stored fact in a Zanzibar-style system, in the form object, relation, user. For example, "doc:plan#owner@user:ravi" means Ravi owns doc:plan.

title: relying party
text: In OpenID Connect and WebAuthn, the app that relies on the provider's ID token to know who the user is. It plays the same part as the SAML service provider.

title: render-blocking
text: A file the browser must load and process before it can show the page, such as CSS or a normal script tag in the head.

title: replay attack
text: An attacker copies a real, correctly signed message and sends it again later, so the receiver acts on it twice.

title: replica
text: A full copy of a database that runs on another machine and is kept up to date with the original.

title: replicated state machine
text: Several servers that run the same commands in the same order from a shared log, so they all end up with the same state.

title: replication factor
text: How many copies of each piece of data a database keeps, on different nodes. Often written RF or N.

title: replication lag
text: How far a follower is behind the leader. A write on the leader is not yet visible on a follower during this time.

title: replication slot
text: A PostgreSQL record of how far one replica or reader has got. The primary keeps the change log until that reader has received it, so a forgotten slot can fill the disk.

title: request coalescing
text: Letting only one request load a missing key, while other requests for the same key wait and share its answer.

title: request router
text: The front door of a distributed database such as DynamoDB. It checks who sent each request, finds which partition holds the key, and forwards the request there.

title: Retry-After
text: An HTTP header that tells the client how long to wait, in seconds or until a date, before it sends the next request.

title: retry amplification
text: When retries turn one request into many calls. They multiply when several layers each retry. Three layers that each try 4 times can send 64 calls to the bottom layer.

title: retry budget
text: A limit on how many retries a client may send, such as retries under 10% of its requests. When the budget is used up, the client fails the request instead of retrying.

title: retry
text: Sending the same request again after it failed or timed out.

title: reversal
text: New ledger entries with the same amounts and opposite signs, used to cancel wrong entries without editing or deleting them.

title: RFC
text: Short for "request for comments". A written proposal shared so that others can comment before a decision is made. Many companies use it as another name for a design doc with a formal review.

title: roll forward
text: Fixing a bad release by shipping a new fix, not by going back to the old version.

title: rollback netcode
text: Each player's game guesses the other player's inputs and keeps running. When the real inputs differ, it goes back and re-runs the game from that point.

title: rollback
text: Undoing a deploy or config change by going back to the last version that worked.

title: rolling deploy
text: A deploy that replaces old servers or pods with new ones a few at a time. For a while, old and new versions run side by side.

title: root cause
text: The deeper reason a problem happened, not just its visible symptom. Big incidents often have several contributing causes.

title: root name server
text: A DNS server at the top of the name tree. It does not know final answers. It tells resolvers which servers handle .com, .org and other top-level domains.

title: round-robin
text: A load balancing rule that gives each server the next request in turn, without looking at how busy it is.

title: round-trip time
text: The time for a message to go from your computer to the server and for the answer to come back. Games often call it ping.

title: row-level security
text: A database feature that adds a filter, such as "only this tenant's rows", to every query on a table, so one missed WHERE clause cannot leak data. Superusers, and usually table owners, skip it.

title: row lock
text: A lock on one database row. Other transactions that want to change or lock that row wait until the holder commits or rolls back.

title: RSU
text: Restricted stock unit. A promise from a company to give you shares once vesting conditions, such as staying for a set time, are met. You own no shares on the day of the grant.

title: rubric
text: A written list of rules for grading an answer, such as what a strong interview answer must show, or that an AI reply "must mention the refund deadline".

title: rules file
text: A file of standing instructions that a coding tool loads into the agent's context, such as Cursor rules or Copilot instructions. It guides the agent but does not enforce anything.

title: runbook
text: A short written guide for one alert or task. It says what the problem means, how to check it and what steps fix it.

title: saga
text: A chain of small local transactions across services. If a later step fails, earlier steps are undone by compensating transactions.

title: salt
text: A random value added to each password before hashing, so two users with the same password get different hashes. Good libraries create and store it for you.

title: SAML
text: Security Assertion Markup Language. An XML standard for single sign-on. The company's identity provider sends the app a signed XML assertion that says who logged in.

title: savepoint
text: In Flink, a checkpoint you trigger by hand. You use it to stop a job, deploy new code or change parallelism, then resume from the same state.

title: SBI model
text: A way to give feedback in three parts. Name the situation, describe the behaviour you saw, and say what impact it had. It avoids judging the person.

title: software bill of materials
text: A list of every component and version inside your software, including dependencies of dependencies. It tells you fast whether a newly found flaw affects you.

title: scatter/gather
text: Sending one query to every shard and merging the answers. It is as slow as the slowest shard.

title: schema-on-read
text: The database does not force a structure on writes. The code that reads the data decides what it means, and must handle old and new shapes.

title: schema-on-write
text: The database checks every write against a fixed schema, such as a SQL table definition, and rejects data that does not fit.

title: schema registry
text: A service that stores every version of a data schema under an id, so readers can look up how a message was written. It can also reject changes that break compatibility.

title: SCIM
text: System for Cross-domain Identity Management. A REST API standard that lets a company's identity provider create, update and deactivate users and groups in a SaaS app.

title: scope
text: What a piece of work covers. In a project, it is the list of features that are in or out. In a career, it is the size of the work you own, from one task up to work across many teams.

title: scribe
text: The person in an incident who writes down what happens, with the time, such as each decision, change and status update.

title: secondary index
text: An extra index that lets you find rows by a field other than the main key, such as orders by customer ID.

title: secret scanning
text: Searching code, commits and history for things that look like passwords, API keys or private keys, so you can revoke them before someone uses them.

title: secrets manager
text: A service that stores passwords, keys and tokens, controls who may read them, and hands them to apps at run time, so they never sit in code.

title: sequential consistency
text: Everyone sees all operations in the same order, and each client's own order is kept. The order may lag behind real time.

title: serializable read
text: In etcd, a read that one member answers from its own copy without asking the others. It is faster, but it may return stale data.

title: serializable
text: The strictest isolation level. The result is the same as if the transactions had run one after another.

title: server reconciliation
text: When an old server state arrives, the client resets to it and replays the inputs the server has not processed yet, so the player does not jump back.

title: Server-Sent Events
text: A web standard where the browser opens one long HTTP response and the server keeps writing events into it. Data flows one way, from server to client.

title: server-side rendering
text: Building a page's HTML on the server for each request, so the browser gets content instead of an empty page and a large script.

title: service discovery
text: How one service finds the current network addresses of another service, while servers start, stop and move.

title: service mesh
text: A layer of proxies, often one next to each service, that handles traffic between services, such as retries, mutual TLS and metrics, without changes to app code.

title: service provider
text: In SAML, the app that receives the identity provider's signed assertion and logs the user in. Often called the SP.

title: service registry
text: A shared list of running service instances and their addresses, kept current by health checks. Consul is a common example.

title: session window
text: A window that groups the events of one key, such as one user, and closes after a gap with no events, for example 30 minutes. Its length depends on the data.

title: settlement
text: The step, often days after a payment, when banks actually move the money to the processor or merchant.

title: severity level
text: A number that says how bad an incident is, often SEV-1 for the worst. It decides who gets paged and how fast the team must act.

title: shallow module
text: A module whose interface is complex, or that does little work. Calling it is not much easier than writing its code yourself.

title: shard key
text: The field, such as a user ID, that decides which shard a record lives on.

title: shard
text: One piece of a large dataset that has been split across machines. Each shard holds a different part of the data.

title: sharded counter
text: One count split across many rows. Each write adds to a random row, so no single row gets all the writes. To read the total, you add up all the rows.

title: shuffle sharding
text: Giving each customer a random small set of workers, so two customers rarely share the exact same set and one bad customer fully hurts very few others.

title: side output
text: An extra output stream from a stream processing step. Flink can send events that arrive too late for their window there, so they are not lost silently.

title: sidecar proxy
text: A proxy that runs next to one app, in the same pod, and handles its network traffic. The app talks to it as if it were the network.

title: silo model
text: A SaaS design where a tenant gets its own resources, such as its own database or full stack. Strong isolation, higher cost.

title: single point of failure
text: One part that, if it fails, stops the whole system. You remove it by running more than one copy and making sure they do not all fail together.

title: single responsibility principle
text: The "S" in SOLID. A module should have one reason to change, meaning one group of people who ask for its changes. It does not mean "one method per class".

title: single sign-on
text: Logging in once with one account, often a company account, and then using many apps without a separate password for each.

title: single-table design
text: A DynamoDB pattern that stores several kinds of item, such as users and orders, in one table, so related items can be read with one request.

title: singleton
text: A class that allows only one instance and gives global access to it, often through getInstance(). Used as global state, it hides dependencies and can leak state between tests.

title: SLA
text: Service level agreement. A contract with customers that promises a level of service and has a penalty if it is missed.

title: SLI
text: Service level indicator. A measure of how well a service works for users, often good events divided by valid events.

title: sliding window
text: A rate limit that counts requests in the last N seconds, measured from now, so there is no reset edge to exploit.

title: SLO
text: Service level objective. A target for an SLI over a time window, such as 99.9% of requests succeed over 4 weeks.

title: sloppy quorum
text: A quorum that counts the first healthy nodes it can reach, even if they are not the key's usual replicas. It keeps writes working during failures, but reads may miss them.

title: slopsquatting
text: An informal name for a package confusion attack where someone publishes a real, harmful package under a name that AI models tend to invent, and waits for AI-written code to install it.

title: SLSA
text: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts, a framework that grades how hard it is to tamper with your builds, from Build L0 (nothing) to Build L3 (hardened builds).

title: snapshot isolation
text: An isolation level where a transaction reads from one frozen view of the database, taken at its first statement.

title: SNI
text: A TLS extension where the client sends the host name it wants in its first message, so one IP address can serve many sites with different certificates.

title: Snowflake ID
text: A 64-bit ID built from a timestamp, a machine number and a counter, first made by Twitter. IDs from one machine sort by time.

title: sort key
text: The second part of a primary key in DynamoDB or Cassandra. It sorts the items inside one partition, so you can read a range of them in order. Cassandra calls it a clustering key.

title: sorted set
text: A Redis data type that keeps unique members ordered by a number called a score. You can add, update and rank members quickly, so it suits leaderboards.

title: space amplification
text: How much disk a storage engine uses compared with the size of the live data, for example because of old versions.

title: span
text: One step inside a trace, such as one call to a database, with its start time and duration.

title: spike solution
text: A very simple program that explores one hard technical or design question and ignores everything else. It is usually thrown away. It reduces risk or makes an estimate more reliable.

title: split-brain
text: A failure where two nodes both think they are the leader and both accept writes. The two copies then disagree.

title: sponsorship
text: Using your own influence to create chances for someone else, such as naming them for a lead role or crediting their work in public. It is more than giving advice.

title: SQL injection
text: An attack where user input changes the meaning of a SQL query, because the code glued the input into the query text. Parameterized queries stop it.

title: SRV record
text: A DNS record that says where a service runs, as a host name and a port, with a priority and a weight for choosing between hosts.

title: server-side request forgery
text: An attack that tricks your server into sending requests to places the attacker picks, such as internal services or a cloud metadata address.

title: SSTable
text: A sorted file on disk that an LSM-tree writes once and never changes. New data goes into new SSTables.

title: stack trace
text: The list of function calls that were running when an error happened, printed with the error. It shows where in the code the error came from.

title: staff engineer
text: A level above senior on the technical (non-manager) path at many companies. A staff engineer often sets technical direction for problems that cross many teams.

title: staged rollout
text: Releasing a change to a growing share of servers or users in steps, checking health at each step before the next.

title: stale-while-revalidate
text: Serving an expired cached value for a short time while one request fetches a fresh copy in the background.

title: STAR method
text: A way to tell a story about past work in four parts: Situation, Task, Action and Result. Companies such as Amazon and Google suggest it for behavioural interviews.

title: starvation
text: A thread never gets the lock or resource it waits for, because other threads always get it first.

title: state backend
text: The part of a stream processor that stores its state. In Flink, the default keeps state in memory on the Java heap; the RocksDB backend keeps it on local disk.

title: state machine
text: A model where a thing is always in exactly one named state, and only listed moves (transitions) can change that state. For example, an order can go from confirmed to shipped, but not from cancelled to shipped.

title: stateless
text: A stateless server keeps no user data in its own memory between requests. Any server can handle any request, so you can add or remove servers easily.

title: statically stable
text: A system that keeps working through a failure without needing control plane changes, such as launching new servers or creating DNS records. Recovery uses only what is already running.

title: status page
text: A web page where a company tells users whether its services work, and posts updates during an incident.

title: steady state
text: In a chaos experiment, a measurable output that shows the system is working normally, such as orders per second or p99 latency. You compare it with and without the fault.

title: stemming
text: Cutting a word to a root form, so "running" and "run" or "foxes" and "fox" match the same search term.

title: sticky session
text: A load balancer setting that sends every request from one user to the same server, often using a cookie.

title: stock option
text: The right, but not the duty, to buy company shares at a fixed price (the strike price) after they vest. It has value only while the share price is above that price.

title: reservation
text: Stock held for one buyer for a short time, for example during checkout. It is released if the buyer does not pay in time.

title: stop word
text: A very common word, like "the" or "for", that a search engine often drops because it does not help find documents.

title: story bank
text: A short list of true stories from your past work, prepared before interviews. Each story is linked to the themes it can answer, such as conflict or failure.

title: strangler fig
text: A way to replace an old system bit by bit. You build new parts next to it and move behaviour across one piece at a time, instead of one big rewrite.

title: Strategy pattern
text: A design pattern that puts each variant of one decision, such as how to price an order, behind the same shape so you can swap them. In modern languages it is often just a function you pass in.

title: stretch assignment
text: Work that is a little above someone's current level, given on purpose so they can grow. It works best with clear goals and a way to undo mistakes.

title: strike price
text: The fixed price per share at which a stock option lets you buy shares. It is set when the option is granted.

title: structured interview
text: An interview where every candidate for a role gets the same planned questions, and answers are scored against the same written rubric.

title: structured output
text: A model feature that forces the reply to match a JSON schema you give. It controls the shape of the data, not whether the values are true.

title: subagent
text: A helper agent that works in its own, separate context and sends back only a short summary.

title: suspense account
text: A ledger account where you put money you cannot explain yet, so it is not lost or counted as income. Someone owns each item and moves it out once it is explained.

title: SWIM
text: A membership protocol where each node pings one random member per round, asks others to ping it when there is no reply, and spreads the result by gossip. HashiCorp memberlist is based on it.

title: synchronous replication
text: The leader waits until a follower confirms it has the change before it tells the client the write is done.

title: system call
text: A request from your program to the kernel, such as read, write or open. The CPU switches into kernel mode to do it, which costs time.

title: system prompt
text: The fixed instructions an app sends to a model with every request, such as its role, rules and output format. It is not a secret and not a security control.

title: table bloat
text: A table that takes much more disk space than its live rows need, because it is full of old, dead row versions or empty space.

title: table rewrite
text: When a schema change makes the database copy every row of a table, and often rebuild its indexes. On a big table this can take a long time and lock it.

title: tail-based sampling
text: Deciding whether to keep a trace after it has finished, so you can keep every slow or failed one. Needs servers that hold spans in memory until the trace ends.

title: tail latency
text: The latency of the slowest requests, such as the p99 or p99.9. It is what your unluckiest users feel.

title: TCP
text: The transport protocol most of the internet uses. It opens a connection and delivers bytes reliably and in order, sending lost data again.

title: technical debt
text: Weak spots in code or design that make future changes to that code slower. The extra effort is the "interest"; cleaning up is paying back the debt.

title: temperature setting
text: A request setting that controls how random a model's word choice is. Higher gives more varied text. Lower sticks to the most likely words, but output can still vary.

title: Template Method pattern
text: A design pattern where a base class fixes the order of steps and subclasses fill in the steps that differ. Passing the changing step in as a function is often simpler.

title: tenant
text: One customer organisation, such as one company, in a system that serves many customers. Its data and load must stay separate from other tenants.

title: test double
text: A fake object that stands in for a real one in a test, such as a fake payment service that always says "paid".

title: test pyramid
text: A picture of a healthy test suite. Many fast unit tests at the bottom, fewer integration tests, and a few slow end-to-end tests at the top.

title: analyzer
text: The rules a search engine uses to turn text into terms, for example split into words, lowercase them and cut them to a root form. Documents and queries must use the same rules.

title: TF-IDF
text: A way to score search matches. A term counts more if it appears often in the document and appears in few documents overall.

title: thin event
text: An event that only says what changed and which object it was, with an id. The receiver calls the API to get the object's current data.

title: thread
text: One line of execution inside a process. Threads of one process share its memory and open files, but each thread has its own stack.

title: threat model
text: A structured look at a design to find what could go wrong with its security and privacy, and to decide what to do about each risk. Best done during design and updated as the design changes.

title: 3-D Secure
text: An extra check during a card payment, where the card's bank asks the customer to prove it is them, for example with a one-time code.

title: 3-2-1 rule
text: Keep 3 copies of important data (1 primary and 2 backups), on 2 different types of storage, with 1 copy in another place.

title: three-way handshake
text: How TCP opens a connection. The client sends SYN, the server answers SYN-ACK, and the client sends ACK. It costs one round trip before any data moves.

title: tick rate
text: How many times per second a game server updates the world. Each update is one tick. A 15 ms tick means about 66 ticks per second.

title: ticket server
text: A small database server whose only job is to hand out unique numbers, for example for primary keys in a sharded system.

title: tie-breaker
text: A unique column, such as the id, added at the end of a sort order. When two rows have the same value, it decides which comes first, so the order never changes.

title: tied request
text: Sending a request to two servers at once; the first server to start work on it tells the other to cancel.

title: tiered pricing
text: A price plan where the unit price changes with volume. In the graduated form, each tier's units are charged at that tier's price.

title: time-series database
text: A database built for timestamped data points, like metrics or sensor readings. It makes writes and time-range queries cheap.

title: time to first byte
text: The time from the start of a page request until the first byte of the response arrives. It includes redirects, DNS, the connection, TLS and the server's work.

title: time to first token
text: How long a model takes to send the first token of its reply after it gets the request. It is how long a user waits before any text appears.

title: timeout
text: A time limit for waiting. If no answer comes back in time, the caller stops waiting.

title: TLS termination
text: Ending the encrypted TLS connection at a proxy or gateway. The proxy decrypts the request, can inspect it, and then forwards it, ideally over a new TLS connection.

title: TLS
text: Transport Layer Security. A protocol that encrypts data on a connection, detects changes to it, and lets the client check the server's identity with a certificate. The server can also ask the client for one. HTTPS is HTTP over TLS.

title: toil
text: Manual, repetitive work tied to running a service. A machine could do it, it leaves no lasting improvement, and it grows as the service grows.

title: token bucket
text: A rate limit where each request takes a token from a bucket that refills at a fixed rate. The bucket size sets the biggest burst.

title: tokenization
text: Splitting text into small pieces, usually words, before they are cleaned and indexed for search.

title: tombstone
text: A marker that says a key was deleted. Stores that never change old files write it instead of removing data, and clean it up later.

title: tool use
text: A model feature where the model asks your app to run a function, with arguments in a fixed format. Your code runs it and sends the result back.

title: top-level domain
text: The last part of a domain name, like .com or .org. Its name servers know which servers hold each domain under it.

title: Total Blocking Time
text: A lab metric: the total time after First Contentful Paint when long tasks block the main thread. Only the part of each task over 50 ms counts. It helps find INP problems but does not replace INP.

title: trace
text: A record of the path one request takes through many services, with the timing of each step.

title: transaction ID wraparound
text: PostgreSQL numbers transactions with a 32-bit counter that wraps around. VACUUM must freeze old rows in time, or Postgres stops new writes to keep old data from looking like it is in the future.

title: transaction pooling
text: A pooler mode, as in PgBouncer, where a client gets a database connection only for one transaction. Many clients can share a few connections, but session state such as SET or LISTEN does not carry over.

title: transaction
text: A group of database reads and writes that succeed or fail as one unit.

title: transactional outbox
text: A table where a service saves outgoing events in the same transaction as its data. A separate relay then publishes them.

title: transient error
text: An error that may go away on its own in a moment, such as a busy service or a dropped connection. These are the errors worth retrying.

title: transitive dependency
text: A package you did not add yourself, but that one of your dependencies needs. Most of the code in a typical app arrives this way.

title: transparency log
text: A public, append-only record of events such as signatures or certificates. Anyone can check it, and nobody can quietly change past entries.

title: TrueTime
text: Google's clock API used by Spanner. It returns a time interval that is sure to contain the true time, instead of a single time.

title: trunk-based development
text: A way of working where every developer merges small changes into one shared branch (trunk or main) at least daily, instead of keeping long-lived branches.

title: trust boundary
text: A point where data enters your code from a source you do not control, such as a user, a partner or another team's service. Data should be checked there.

title: trust store
text: The set of root certificates that an operating system, browser or runtime trusts. A certificate chain must end at one of them.

title: TTL
text: Time to live. How long a stored value, such as a cache entry, a lock or a seat hold, lives before it expires.

title: tumbling window
text: A time window of fixed size that does not overlap with the next one, like each minute. Every event belongs to exactly one tumbling window.

title: two generals problem
text: A thought experiment. Two sides talk over a link that can lose messages. However many acknowledgements they exchange, neither can be certain the other got the last one.

title: two-phase commit
text: A way to commit across several databases. A coordinator asks every one to prepare, then tells all of them to commit or roll back.

title: two-way door
text: A decision you can easily undo if it turns out wrong. It should be made quickly, by a small group, with a light process.

title: typosquatting
text: Publishing a harmful package with a name close to a popular one, like reqeusts for requests, and waiting for people to mistype it.

title: ubiquitous language
text: In domain-driven design, the shared words that developers and business experts use for one model. The same words appear in talk, documents and code.

title: UDP
text: A simple transport protocol that sends single messages with no connection. It does not promise that messages arrive, arrive once, or arrive in order.

title: ULID
text: A 128-bit ID with a millisecond timestamp first and random bits after it. It is written as 26 characters that sort in time order.

title: unclean leader election
text: In Kafka, making a replica that is not in sync the new leader when no in-sync replica is left. The partition comes back sooner, but committed messages can be lost. It is off by default.

title: undo log
text: In MySQL InnoDB, a record of how a row looked before a change. It is used to roll back and to show older versions to readers.

title: unit test
text: A test of one small piece of code, such as a function or a class, on its own. It runs fast, often in milliseconds.

title: upcasting
text: Converting an old version of a stored event to the current shape when it is read. The stored event itself is not changed.

title: usage-based pricing
text: Charging customers for what they actually use, such as API calls, messages or tokens, instead of only a fixed monthly fee.

title: USE method
text: A checklist for resources like CPU, memory and disks: utilization (how busy), saturation (extra work it cannot handle yet, often queued) and errors.

title: user mode
text: The restricted CPU mode your code runs in. It cannot do I/O or run privileged instructions. For that it asks the kernel, which runs in kernel mode with full access.

title: utilization
text: How busy a resource is, as a share of its capacity. A server at 90% utilization is busy 9 tenths of the time.

title: UUID
text: A 128-bit ID that any server can create on its own, with almost no chance of a clash. It is usually written as 36 letters, digits and dashes.

title: VACUUM
text: The PostgreSQL job that removes old row versions no transaction can see any more, so their space can be reused. Autovacuum runs it for you.

title: value object
text: An object defined only by its values, such as an amount of money. It has no ID and does not change. Two value objects with the same values are equal.

title: vector clock
text: A list of (node, counter) pairs kept with each version of data. Comparing two lists shows whether one version came from the other, or whether they are in conflict.

title: vector database
text: A database that finds the stored vectors nearest to a given one, for example to find similar texts. pgvector adds this to Postgres.

title: version change module
text: Stripe's name for one small piece of code that describes a single breaking change and turns a new response back into the older shape.

title: vertical scaling
text: Handling more load by moving to a bigger machine, with more CPU and memory. Simple, but there is a largest machine, and it is still one machine.

title: vertical slice architecture
text: A way to organise code by feature or request instead of by layer. Each slice holds everything one request needs, from the endpoint to the data access.

title: vesting cliff
text: A first period, often one year, in which no equity vests. At the end of it, the whole period's share vests at once. Leave before it ends and you get none.

title: vesting
text: The schedule by which granted equity, such as RSUs or stock options, becomes yours over time, for example over four years. Parts that have not vested are usually lost when you leave.

title: virtual node
text: One of many points that a single server owns on a consistent hash ring. Many small points spread keys more evenly than one big one.

title: waiting room
text: A queue page in front of a site. It lets visitors in at a rate the site can handle and shows the others their wait.

title: visibility timeout
text: In Amazon SQS, how long a received message stays hidden from other workers. If it is not deleted in that time, it comes back.

title: wall clock
text: The clock that shows the real date and time. It can jump when someone sets it, and NTP changes its speed, so it is unsafe for measuring how long something takes.

title: warm standby
text: A disaster recovery (DR) strategy where a smaller but working copy of production always runs at a second site, ready to scale up and take traffic.

title: watermark
text: In stream processing, a marker that says event time has reached a given point. It tells the engine when a window can be closed. An event whose time is already behind the watermark is late.

title: webhook
text: An HTTP request that a server sends to your endpoint when an event happens, so you do not have to keep asking for changes.

title: WebSocket
text: A protocol that starts as an HTTP request and then keeps one connection open, so the client and the server can both send messages at any time.

title: wide-column store
text: A database that splits tables into partitions by key and spreads them over many nodes, such as Cassandra. Fast queries must give the partition key.

title: working set
text: The data a system actually reads in a given time, such as one day. A cache that can hold the working set rarely has to go to the database.

title: workload identity
text: A name for a running service, proven by a certificate or token, so other services can check who is calling. In Istio it comes from the Kubernetes service account.

title: write-ahead log
text: A log where a database records every change before it applies it, so it can recover after a crash. CDC tools read it.

title: write amplification
text: How many bytes a storage engine writes to disk for each byte your app writes. Higher means more background disk work.

title: write-behind
text: A caching pattern where writes go to the cache first and reach the database later. Fast, but data can be lost if the cache fails.

title: write sharding
text: Spreading the writes for one busy key over many keys by adding a suffix, such as post42#7. To read everything for the key, you must fetch every suffix and combine the results.

title: write skew
text: A bug where two transactions read the same data, then each writes a different row. Each write is fine alone, but together they break a rule.

title: write-through
text: A caching pattern where every write goes to the cache and the database together, so the cache stays fresh.

title: XA
text: An X/Open standard for two-phase commit. A transaction manager coordinates several resource managers, such as database servers, in one global transaction.

title: XML signature wrapping
text: An attack on signed XML, such as SAML. The attacker keeps the signed part valid and adds an unsigned part that the app reads by mistake.

title: cross-site scripting
text: An attack where someone gets their JavaScript to run on your site in another user's browser. It can then read the page and act as that user.

title: zero data retention
text: An arrangement with an LLM provider where it does not store your prompts and replies after it sends the response. It is usually set up by request, not on by default.

title: 0-RTT
text: A TLS 1.3 option where a returning client sends data in its first message. It saves a round trip, but an attacker can replay that data.

title: zero trust
text: A security approach where no user, device or service is trusted because of its network location. Every request proves its identity and is checked against policy.

title: znode
text: One entry in ZooKeeper's tree of paths, such as /app/config. It holds a small piece of data and can have child znodes.

title: Atlassian: Atlassian outage: a cleanup script deleted 883 sites
text: 775 customers lost access to Jira, Confluence and other Atlassian products, and some waited up to 14 days for their sites to come back.

title: Amazon Web Services: AWS DynamoDB outage: storage servers could not get their partition lists
text: DynamoDB in US-East returned errors for about five hours, with errors settling at about 55% of requests, and SQS, EC2 Auto Scaling, CloudWatch and the AWS Console were hit too.

title: Amazon Web Services: AWS S3 outage: one wrong input removed too many servers
text: For about four hours, S3 in us-east-1 could not serve requests, and services that need S3, such as EC2 launches and Lambda, also failed.

title: Amazon Web Services: AWS us-east-1 outage: a connection storm on the internal network
text: For several hours, many AWS services in us-east-1 had errors, including EC2 APIs, the console, Route 53 APIs and STS.

title: Amazon Web Services: AWS DynamoDB outage: an empty DNS record in us-east-1
text: DynamoDB in us-east-1 refused new connections for about three hours, and EC2 launches, load balancers, Lambda and many other services failed for much of the day.

title: CircleCI: CircleCI security incident: customer secrets stolen from production
text: An attacker copied customers' environment variables, keys and tokens from CircleCI's production systems, and CircleCI told every customer to rotate all their secrets.

title: Cloudflare: Cloudflare DNS outage: a leap second made a time difference negative
text: From midnight UTC until 06:45 UTC, some DNS lookups for customers using CNAME records failed. At peak, about 0.2% of DNS queries were affected.

title: Cloudflare: Cloudflare outage: one regex used all the CPU
text: For about 27 minutes, visitors to Cloudflare sites around the world got 502 errors, and Cloudflare lost about 80% of its traffic.

title: Cloudflare: Cloudflare outage: a half-broken switch stalled etcd and set off database promotions
text: For 6 hours and 33 minutes, the Cloudflare API and dashboard were degraded. API success fell as low as 75%, and the dashboard was up to 80 times slower.

title: Cloudflare: Cloudflare wrongly throttled one customer's traffic
text: Cloudflare throttled one customer's traffic to its origin server, and the website became unusable. The throttle stayed on for almost 13 hours (12 hours 53 minutes).

title: Cloudflare: Cloudflare outage: one data centre lost power
text: For hours, the Cloudflare dashboard and APIs failed, and logs and analytics were down for almost two days, though customer traffic kept flowing.

title: Cloudflare: Cloudflare outage: a storage provider failure broke many products
text: For about two and a half hours, Workers KV failed most requests, and products built on it, such as Access logins, WARP and the dashboard, also failed.

title: Cloudflare: Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 outage: an old config mistake woke up
text: For 62 minutes, the 1.1.1.1 DNS resolver was down worldwide, so most of its users could not look up names and most websites seemed broken.

title: Cloudflare: Cloudflare outage: a feature file grew too big
text: For several hours, many sites behind Cloudflare showed 5xx error pages, and dashboard logins and Access sign-ins also failed.

title: Cloudflare: Cloudflare outage: a global config change hit an old bug
text: For about 25 minutes, about 28% of the HTTP traffic Cloudflare served got 500 errors.

title: CrowdStrike: CrowdStrike outage: a content update crashed Windows hosts
text: Windows machines running the Falcon sensor crashed to a blue screen, and many needed manual fixes to start again.

title: Datadog: Datadog outage: an automatic OS update broke networking
text: For about a day, Datadog was down in five regions, so users could not reach the site or APIs and monitors did not alert.

title: Discord: Discord voice and video outage: message queues grew faster than they drained
text: From 12:13 to 15:30 PDT, voice and video were badly degraded. Most users could not start or join calls and saw "Awaiting Endpoint".

title: Ezypay: Ezypay charged some direct debit customers two or four times
text: Some Australian customers' regular direct debit payments were processed twice, and some four times. Ezypay reversed each duplicate within 24 hours.

title: Fastly: Fastly outage: a valid customer config hit a hidden bug
text: About 85% of Fastly's network returned errors, so many large websites failed to load for most of an hour.

title: Flexcoin: Flexcoin: a race in balance transfers emptied the hot wallet
text: An attacker took 896 BTC, all the coins in Flexcoin's hot wallet, and the exchange closed the next day.

title: GitHub: GitHub outage: health checks failed a busy database over, then back
text: GitHub's main MySQL database role moved between servers twice in one day, and the site was slow until the new server's cache warmed up.

title: GitHub: GitHub outage: a 43-second network cut caused a day of trouble
text: For about 24 hours, GitHub showed stale or wrong data, and webhooks and Pages builds were delayed.

title: GitHub (npm): npm: a publish was authorized for one package and applied to another
text: A bug bounty report showed that an attacker could publish new versions of any npm package from an account without proper authorization. GitHub patched it within six hours.

title: GitHub: GitHub webhooks delayed by up to 4.5 hours
text: For about four and a half hours, webhook deliveries waited in an internal job queue. Some customers got their webhooks up to 4.5 hours late.

title: ruby-saml (open source), GitLab: ruby-saml: two XML parsers disagreed, so anyone could sign in as anyone
text: Critical bugs in ruby-saml up to 1.17.0 let an attacker with one valid signed SAML document forge an assertion for any user and log in as them. GitHub's researchers found an exploitable instance in GitLab, which shipped a critical patch.

title: GitHub: GitHub code search down, then hours out of date
text: Code search failed every query from 14:40 to 17:00 UTC. It came back with results that missed repository changes made after about 07:00 UTC, and was fully current at 23:45 UTC.

title: GitHub: GitHub requests fail when a shared database connection pool runs out
text: Some github.com requests hung for up to about 10 seconds and then failed. At the worst point, about 43% of pull request merge attempts failed, and about 3.5% of API calls.

title: GitLab: GitLab outage: the primary database was wiped by mistake
text: GitLab.com was down for about 18 hours, and about six hours of database changes, such as issues, comments and new accounts, were lost.

title: Google Cloud: Google Cloud outage: maintenance stopped network control in many sites
text: For three to four hours, several US and South American regions had heavy packet loss, and Compute Engine, Cloud Storage and YouTube were hit.

title: Google Cloud: Google Cloud outage: blank policy fields crashed API checks
text: For hours, many Google Cloud and Workspace APIs returned 503 errors across the world, touching 76 Cloud products.

title: Heroku: Heroku outage: an unplanned OS update cut network routes
text: Many Heroku customers had failed logins and broken apps, some for up to 24 hours, and the status page was slow and wrong.

title: Knight Capital: Knight Capital: a missed server lost over $460 million in 45 minutes
text: In about 45 minutes after the market opened, Knight's trading system sent millions of unwanted orders and lost more than $460 million.

title: Mailchimp (Mandrill): Mandrill outage: one Postgres shard stopped writes to avoid transaction ID wraparound
text: Mandrill, Mailchimp's transactional email service, sent only about 80% of queued email for about 40 hours, and its queues were back to normal about 43 hours after the start.

title: Meta (Facebook): Facebook outage: a maintenance command cut off every data centre
text: Facebook's services could not be reached from the internet, and even DNS lookups for its names failed.

title: Microsoft: Storm-0558: a consumer signing key opened enterprise mailboxes
text: An attacker read Exchange Online mail at 22 organizations and 503 personal accounts with forged tokens, including about 60,000 emails from the US State Department.

title: Monzo: Monzo outage: stale proxy routes, then a restart of every proxy
