text: Current account payments failed for about 80 minutes, and for the last 18 minutes the whole platform, including the app, was down.

title: Monzo: Monzo outage: new Cassandra servers answered reads with no data
text: From about 13:10, some customers could not log in, make payments or see correct balances. Most were fixed by 15:08, and all by 23:00.

title: OpenAI: ChatGPT: a Redis client bug showed some users other users' data
text: Some ChatGPT users saw chat titles from other active users, so ChatGPT was taken offline. Later checks found some Plus users' payment details (no full card numbers) may also have been visible to others.

title: PostgreSQL user (pgsql-admin mailing list): Forgotten prepared transactions stop a PostgreSQL server
text: A PostgreSQL 8.2.9 test server with 315 databases refused all commands to avoid transaction ID wraparound, and VACUUM did not fix it.

title: Reddit: Reddit Pi-Day outage: a Kubernetes upgrade renamed a label
text: For 314 minutes, Reddit showed error pages or empty home pages to people trying to use it.

title: Roblox: Roblox outage: 73 hours down after Consul broke
text: Roblox was fully down for most of 73 hours, and players came back in steps only on the fourth day.

title: Slack: Slack outage: post-holiday traffic overloaded a cloud network link
text: On the first work day of 2021, Slack was down and then slow for about three and a half hours.

title: Slack: Slack: emptied cache nodes turned each miss into a query on every database shard
text: Many users could not connect to Slack, because client boot requests failed under heavy database load.

title: xz-utils (open source): xz/liblzma: a backdoor hidden in release tarballs reached the SSH server
text: xz versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 carried a backdoor in liblzma. On some Linux distributions it was loaded into the SSH server and made logins slow, which is how a developer found it.

title: Airbnb: Avoiding double payments with an idempotency library
text: Airbnb built a shared idempotency library for payment services. It keeps database commits few, sorts errors into retryable and non-retryable, and lets failed requests heal through safe retries.

title: Amazon: How Dynamo kept the shopping cart always writable
text: Dynamo chose availability over strict consistency, using consistent hashing, sloppy quorums and vector clocks. The app merges conflicting versions, so a cart never loses an added item.

title: Amazon: What ten years of running DynamoDB taught its builders
text: The DynamoDB paper shows how the team handled fairness, uneven traffic across partitions and automated operations. They kept latency predictable without giving up availability, even at 89 million requests per second.

title: Amazon: Why queue backlogs can turn a short outage into a long one
text: A queue hides overload until the backlog takes hours to drain. Watch message age, add backpressure, move stale or noisy work aside, and plan for backlogs from day one.

title: Amazon: Shuffle sharding: shrink the blast radius of one bad customer
text: Give each customer a random mix of workers instead of one fixed shard. A bad customer then hurts only their own mix, and almost no other customer shares all the same workers.

title: Amazon: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter done right
text: Set timeouts from real latency percentiles, retry at one layer only, and cap retries. Add backoff and jitter so clients do not retry in sync and overload a service that is already struggling.

title: Anthropic: Contextual retrieval: add context to chunks before indexing
text: Before indexing, each chunk gets a short note explaining where it fits in its document. With BM25 and embeddings together, failed retrievals dropped by 49 percent, and by 67 percent with reranking.

title: Cloudflare: Pingora: replacing NGINX with a proxy written in Rust
text: NGINX tied each request to one worker and kept connection pools per worker, which hurt reuse. Pingora shares pools across threads and uses a third of the CPU and memory.

title: Discord: Fanning out messages to millions of users with Elixir
text: Sending one message to a huge server meant millions of process sends. Discord built Manifold to group sends by remote node, which spread the CPU cost and cut network traffic.

title: Discord: Why Discord rewrote a Go service in Rust
text: A Go service showed latency spikes every two minutes because Go forces a garbage collection run. The Rust version has no garbage collector, so the spikes went away.

title: Discord: Fast local SSD reads with network-disk durability
text: Discord mirrored local SSDs and network disks in a Linux RAID1 array, marking the network disk write-mostly. Reads come from the fast local disk while writes still reach durable storage.

title: Discord: Moving trillions of messages from Cassandra to ScyllaDB
text: Garbage-collection pauses and hot partitions made Cassandra painful to run. Discord moved to ScyllaDB and added Rust data services that merge identical reads, so one database query serves many users.

title: Dropbox: Rewriting the Dropbox sync engine safely
text: The old sync engine had a flawed data model that small fixes could not save. The rewrite used a clean data model, Rust, and seeded random simulation tests that replay any failure.

title: Ensemble Studios: Age of Empires: thousands of units over a slow modem
text: Instead of sending unit positions, each player sends only commands and every machine runs the same simulation in lockstep. Any difference is detected as out of sync, which also blocks many cheats.

title: Figma: How Figma's multiplayer editing works
text: Figma took ideas from CRDTs but kept a central server as the authority. That made the system simpler and faster than full CRDTs or operational transforms.

title: Figma: Horizontally sharding Postgres behind a query proxy
text: After splitting tables into separate databases, Figma sharded large tables horizontally. A proxy routes and runs sharded queries, and logical sharding came before the risky physical move.

title: Google: Spanner: a global database built on known clock error
text: Spanner exposes clock uncertainty through its TrueTime API instead of hiding it. That lets it offer externally consistent transactions across the globe, plus lock-free read-only transactions.

title: Google: The Tail at Scale: rare slowness becomes common at scale
text: When one request fans out to many servers, a rare slow server slows most requests. Google argues you should build tail-tolerant systems, reusing fault-tolerance tricks to hide slow parts.

title: Google: Zanzibar: one consistent permission system for all of Google
text: Zanzibar stores access rules as relationships and serves hundreds of services from one model. It respects the order of user actions, so a check never uses permissions older than the content.

title: Instagram: Making sortable 64-bit IDs inside sharded Postgres
text: Each ID packs a timestamp, a logical shard number and a sequence, built by a Postgres function. IDs sort by time and need no central ID service.

title: LinkedIn: How Kafka reached 2 million writes a second on cheap machines
text: Kafka gets its speed from sequential disk I/O, the OS page cache and batching small records together. Throughput stayed steady as stored data grew, with mostly default settings.

title: LinkedIn: The log: the simple idea under databases and streams
text: Jay Kreps shows that an append-only, ordered log sits under replication, data integration and stream processing. Treating the log as the source of truth makes many systems simpler to connect.

title: LMAX: LMAX: 6 million orders a second on one thread
text: LMAX runs all business logic in memory on a single thread, using event sourcing for recovery. Lock-free ring buffers called Disruptors feed it, avoiding the cost of locks and queues.

title: Meta: Scaling memcache to billions of requests a second
text: Facebook turned memcached into a large distributed cache and coordinated it with the database. The paper shows how they traded strong consistency for speed, availability and simple operations.

title: Meta: TAO: a graph cache in front of sharded MySQL
text: Facebook hid memcache and MySQL behind a small graph API of objects and links. Two cache tiers serve huge read volume, and the team chose eventual consistency over losing availability.

title: Netflix: Adaptive concurrency limits instead of hand-tuned limits
text: Fixed concurrency limits go stale as code and traffic change. Netflix measures latency and adjusts the limit automatically, like TCP congestion control, to reject extra work before queues explode.

title: Netflix: Moving the Zuul gateway to async I/O: what it really gave
text: Netflix moved its gateway from blocking threads to async, non-blocking I/O. It did not gain much CPU efficiency, but connections became cheap, which enabled push and persistent connections.

title: Notion: Tripling the database fleet with zero downtime
text: Notion grew from 32 to 96 Postgres machines while live. They copied data with logical replication, checked results, and moved traffic shard by shard through PgBouncer.

title: Notion: Sharding Postgres by workspace at Notion
text: Notion sharded every table linked to a block, using workspace ID as the key. Most queries stay inside one workspace, so cross-shard joins are rare.

title: PhonePe: Moving 100 billion events a day into Kafka
text: Services write events to local disk through a client library, and a separate process ships them to Kafka. Teams get a simple API while the platform team runs the pipeline.

title: PhonePe: TStore: one store for every payment's history
text: Every change is first written to a Kafka write-ahead log, then to HBase with indexes. Notifications go out only after both writes succeed, so readers never see unsaved changes.

title: Pinterest: Sharding MySQL with IDs that say where data lives
text: Pinterest picked mature MySQL and pre-split data into thousands of shards. Each 64-bit ID holds its shard number, and data never moves between shards.

title: Riot Games: Making VALORANT servers 20 times faster for 128 tick
text: Riot needed each server frame under 2.34 ms but started at 50 ms. They split the cost by subsystem, gave each a budget, and tuned the OS scheduler to use the CPU better.

title: Riot Games: Shrinking peeker's advantage in VALORANT's netcode
text: Peeker's advantage comes from adding up network delay, buffering, frame time and tick rate. Riot cut each piece, such as keeping the movement buffer small, to keep fights fair.

title: Shopify: Load testing the whole platform before Black Friday
text: Shopify scales its platform up to the expected peak, runs full load tests, studies the results and repeats. Doing this many times a year finds weak spots long before the real sale.

title: Shopify: Surviving flash sales with a checkout queue at the load balancer
text: Checkout writes were overloading the database during flash sales. Shopify added a leaky-bucket throttle in scriptable load balancers and sent extra buyers to a cached waiting page.

title: Shopify: Choosing a modular monolith over microservices
text: Shopify kept one codebase but split it into components with clear, checked boundaries. They judged that microservices would bring their own problems and that modularity fixed the real pain.

title: Shopify: Pods: splitting Shopify into isolated groups of shops
text: Shopify groups shops into pods, each with its own datastores, while sharing app servers. A routing layer sends each request to the right pod, so one pod's failure stays inside it.

title: Shopify: Ten habits for building payment systems that hold up
text: Shopify lists the basics: short timeouts, circuit breakers, idempotency keys, capacity planning and reconciliation. Default HTTP timeouts are often far too long for a waiting customer.

title: Slack: Flannel: an edge cache so huge teams can start fast
text: Clients of very large teams downloaded too much data at startup. Flannel caches users and channels at the edge, serves them on demand, and pushes data the client will likely need next.

title: Slack: How Slack delivers messages in real time
text: Stateful channel servers own channels through consistent hashing. Gateway servers in many regions hold user WebSocket connections and pass messages between clients and channel servers.

title: Slack: Shared channels broke the one-workspace-per-shard rule
text: Slack's backend assumed every piece of data belonged to one workspace and one shard. Letting two companies share a channel forced a rethink of how data and routing are partitioned.

title: Slack: Moving from per-workspace shards to Vitess
text: Sharding by workspace created hot shards for big customers and wasted the rest. Slack moved to Vitess, which let them shard by other keys like channel and spread the load.

title: Square: Books: an immutable double-entry accounting service
text: Square built one shared ledger service so product teams do not build their own. Entries are insert-only, and mistakes are fixed with a new correcting entry, which gives a full audit trail.

title: Stripe: Canonical log lines: one rich log line per request
text: At the end of each request, Stripe writes one line with the key facts: route, user, status, timing and query counts. Simple queries over these lines answer most questions during an incident.

title: Stripe: Idempotency keys make API retries safe
text: The client sends a unique key with each operation, and the server remembers the result for that key. A retry after a network failure then never charges a customer twice.

title: Stripe: Ledger: checking every money movement with double entry
text: Stripe records money flows as an immutable log of double-entry events. Balances that do not clear to zero point to real problems, and data-quality scores track how correct the system is.

title: Stripe: Online data migrations in four safe steps
text: Stripe dual-writes to old and new tables, moves reads, moves writes, then deletes the old data. Each step can be checked and reversed, so large migrations need no downtime.

title: Stripe: Two rate limiters and two load shedders that protect an API
text: Stripe uses two rate limiters: one for requests per second and one for requests running at the same time. They run in Redis, and rate limiting uses the token bucket algorithm. Two load shedders also drop less important traffic when the whole system is busy. The post advises that limiters fail open, so a bug in them does not take the API down.

title: Swiggy: Turning a delivery monolith into a logistics platform
text: Swiggy's delivery monolith could not scale or support new businesses. They rebuilt it as a multi-tenant platform where a job is a chain of small tasks, which allowed multi-leg deliveries.

title: Uber: Retry topics and dead-letter queues with Kafka
text: Failed messages go to a chain of retry topics, then to a dead-letter topic, so the main consumer keeps moving. Errors stay visible and can be replayed without blocking real-time traffic.

title: Uber: Moving a trillion ledger entries without downtime
text: Uber moved all its payment ledger data from DynamoDB to an immutable ledger store. Shadow validation compared old and new answers, with clear accuracy targets so the team did not chase every false alarm.

title: Uber: Schemaless: an append-only datastore built on MySQL
text: Uber built a scalable store on plain MySQL where each cell is immutable and updates write a new version. Simple, well-known parts made it easier to operate than a newer database.

title: vLLM: PagedAttention: paging GPU memory to serve LLMs faster
text: vLLM stores the attention key-value cache in small blocks, like virtual memory pages. Less wasted GPU memory means bigger batches and up to 24 times the throughput of a plain baseline.

title: Zerodha: Running billions of rows of reports on plain Postgres
text: Zerodha denormalises data, uses materialized views, and partitions tables by month. Plain Postgres handles heavy financial reporting when the schema fits the queries.

title: Zerodha: Scaling a large broker with simple, boring choices
text: Zerodha prefers simple, well-known tools over fashionable ones. The database is almost always the bottleneck, so they serve reads from Redis and use ETags to save bandwidth.
